Round 1: Online Assessment (OA) - The first round was an online assessment. There was no

resume-based shortlisting before the OA, so eligible students could directly appear for the test.

Round 2: Interview - Candidates who cleared the OA were shortlisted for the interview round.

Result - After the interview, the final selection results were announced.

1. Online Assessment (OA) - 250 Candidates

The test had a duration of 3 hours and consisted of 4 questions. The questions were designed to test
problem-solving and coding ability, and candidates had to manage their time carefully across all four
questions.
Question 1 - Maximum Number of Balanced Substrings [EASY]
One of the relatively easier questions was based on a binary string consisting only of 0 and 1.
We had to divide the entire string into a maximum number of contiguous substrings such that:

1. Every substring must be balanced, i.e., it must contain an equal number of Os and 1s.

2. The substrings must follow an alternating boundary condition. If one substring ends with 0, the next

substring must start with 1, and vice versa.

3. The complete string has to be divided into such substrings. We cannot leave any characters unused.

4. If it is not possible to divide the complete string according to these conditions, we return - 1.

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/problems/split-the-binary-string-into-substrings-with-equal-number-of-0s-an
d-1s/1
[not completely same in oa there was one more extra condition as i have mentioned]
--- PAGE 2 ---
Question 2 - Minimum Cost Path With At Most K Turns [MEDIUM]
https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-cost-path-with-at-most-k-turns/description/
Question 3 - DP: Making an Array Non-Decreasing [HARD]
Given an array, modify its elements to make it non-decreasing with minimum cost. Changing a value × to y
costs | ×-Y|. The problem requires finding the minimum total modification cost using DP.
https://leetcode.com/problems/make-array-non-decreasing-or-non-increasing/description/
[similar with the variation using only increasing version]
Question 4 - Complex DP Problem [Complex]
I don't remember the exact problem statement now. It was a complex Dynamic Programming problem and
was quite lengthy to read and understand. Considering there were already three other questions to work
through within the given time, I felt that spending too much time on this question would not be the best use
of the remaining time.
MY Personal Story of OA:
This OA was a little personal for me because I had already appeared for HackWithInfy earlier, and during
that OA I was quite nervous. There were questions where I could recognize the pattern and even knew the
possible approach, but I wasn't able to execute them completely under pressure. I ended up solving only
around 1.5 questions.
This time, when I sat for the Infosys campus OA, I decided to forget about that experience and just focus on
the test in front of me. I went in with a simple mindset: solve what I can, don't panic, and keep moving.
The first question looked fairly easy. I immediately thought of a greedy approach and started building the
logic. I spent around 20-25 minutes on it, but although my code passed some test cases, it wasn't
completely correct. Instead of getting stuck there, I decided to move on.
The second question was a DP problem, and initially it felt quite natural. I identified the states, thought
about the recursion and memoization, and implemented my approach. The sample test cases were passing,
but the hidden test cases failed. I spent around 30 minutes trying to figure out what I was missing. At this
point, around 1 hour and 15 minutes had already passed, and I started feeling a little panicked.
I took a moment, composed myself, and moved to the third question.
The third question was the hardest one, but somehow it clicked for me. I recognized that it could be solved
using recursion with a loop over possible choices, followed by memoization. I did a small dry run to
understand the states, wrote the recurrence, memoized it, and submitted.
And it passed all the test cases.
I remember feeling genuinely confident at that moment. The question that looked harder than the first two
had actually worked out for me in around 15 minutes. That gave me the confidence to continue rather than
worry about the questions I had struggled with earlier.
--- PAGE 3 ---
I then looked at the fourth question, but it was quite lengthy and complex. With the time available, I felt that
going after it from scratch would not be the best decision. Instead, I went back to the first question and tried
to identify the issue in my earlier approach. I was able to solve it in around 20 minutes.
With roughly 40 minutes remaining, I returned to the second question. I tried to fix my DP solution, but
unfortunately, I could only get some of the test cases to pass before the time ran out.
I finally submitted the OA with:

• 1 Easy question - completely solved

• 1 Hard question - completely solved

• 1 Medium question - partially solved

• 1 Complex DP question - not attempted

So overall, I managed to solve around 2.5 questions in terms of completion.
What I learned from the OA
For me, the biggest takeaway wasn't really about the number of questions I solved. It was about not letting
an earlier bad experience decide how I would perform this time.
In my previous OA, nervousness affected my ability to execute approaches that I actually knew. This time, I
still got stuck, I still had wrong submissions, and I still couldn't solve everything but I didn't let that stop
me. I moved between questions, came back to them when appropriate, and eventually cracked the question I
initially found the hardest.
Don't judge your performance in the first hour of an OA. One question clicking at the right time can
completely change your confidence.
PS: I had solved around 1,000 LeetCode problems by this point, but this OA still humbled me. I knew the
concepts, yet I made mistakes, got stuck, and had to make decisions under pressure. It reminded me that
DSA preparation is not just about the number of problems you solve. It is also about staying calm enough
to use what you already know when the clock is running.
Shortlisting for the Interview Round
After the OA, candidates were shortlisted for different interview processes based on their
performance in the assessment.
Students who solved around 1.5 questions were shortlisted for the Digital Specialist Engineer (DSE)
interview process, while students who solved 2 or more questions were shortlisted for the Specialist
Programmer (SP) interview process.
The exact level of the Specialist Programmer role (L1, L2, or L3) was not communicated to us during
the shortlisting or interview process.
--- PAGE 4 ---

2. [Offline INTERVIEWI [4 for SP/ 10 for DSE]

The interview was probably the most interesting part of the entire process for me. The interviewer had two
DSA questions ready on his laptop, and I was given around 45 minutes to solve any one of them.
I entered the room expecting a fairly serious start, but the interviewer first had a casual conversation with
me. He asked me about the best colleges in Mumbai and how I would rank colleges across Maharashtra. He
was from Bangalore and we ended up having a genuinely fun conversation. Looking back, I think this
helped me become comfortable before the actual technical discussion began.
Then, without even a formal introduction, he handed me the laptop and said to choose one of the two
questions and solve it.
DSA
Both questions were based on Dynamic Programming. I chose one which was similar in pattern to Matrix
Chain Multiplication.
I spent some time understanding the problem, writing down an example, and doing a dry run of my
approach. After around 15 minutes, the interviewer asked me about my progress. I hadn't written any code
yetI had only worked out the approach.
He then asked me to explain the problem and my approach. I explained the recurrence and my reasoning,
and he seemed satisfied with it. He then asked me:
"It will take you another 10-20 minutes to code it, right?"
I said yes and asked if I could continue coding.
He replied:
"Okay, let it be. We will continue with the technical interview."
And I remember thinking, "Ummmm... okay."
That was a good reminder that an interview isn't necessarily about completing every problem. The
interviewer had already understood that I knew how to approach the problem, so he decided to move on and
evaluate other areas.
Data Structures & Problem Solving
He then started asking me practical questions involving data structures.
For example:

• If you had to find the top K trending videos on You Tube, what would you use?

• If you wanted to add and remove songs from both the beginning and end of a Spotify playlist, what

data structure would you use?

• Questions involving priority-queue, deque, map, stack, etc.

--- PAGE 5 ---

• How would you find a particular number as quickly as possible if you were given 1 million

numbers?

• Standard time complexities of commonly used data structures and operations.

For the million-number question, I initially explained that if the numbers were sorted, I could use binary
search in O(log n), while searching an unsorted array would take O(n). He then clarified that he hadn't
asked me to store the numbers in a vector.
I then considered alternatives such as a map / binary search tree-based structure, depending on the
requirements.
The interviewer kept changing the conditions and asking follow-up questions rather than simply asking
textbook questions. This made the discussion much more conversational.
DBMS - The Deep Dive
After that, he asked me which CS fundamentals I had studied and told me to give them in my preferred
order.
I said:
DBMS → OOP → OS → CN
He started with DBMS, and this became the longest technical discussion of the interview. It went on for
almost 30 minutes, starting from basic concepts and gradually becoming much more advanced.
Some of the questions/topics he covered were:

• Normalization and denormalization

• Types of relationships in DBMS

• DELETE vs TRUNCATE

• Database indexes

• SQL joins

• ACID properties

• UNION vs UNION ALL

• Shared and exclusive locks

• Different types of database locks

• B-Tree and B+ Tree

• Hashing in databases

• Data partitioning

• Partitioning vs sharding

• CAP theorem

• Partition tolerance and real-world examples

• Database replication

• Dense vs sparse indexes

• SQL vs NoSQL

• Hashing vs encryption

--- PAGE 6 ---
The interviewer particularly deep-dived into hashing and CAP theorem, asking several follow-up
questions and real-world scenarios.
This was probably the part of the interview where I felt the most confident. I was able to answer every
question he asked, and at no point did I feel completely blank. He kept going deeper until I reached
something I genuinely didn't know.
What made the discussion interesting was that it wasn't just:
"Define this."
It was more like:
"Okay, but why?"
"Where would you use it?"
"What happens in this situation?"
"Give me a real-world example."
So understanding concepts was much more useful than simply memorizing definitions.
Electronics & Communication Background
Since my branch is Electronics and Telecommunication Engineering, he also asked me about the core
subjects I had studied.
I mentioned:

• Control Systems

• Digital Signal Processing

• Mathematics

He asked me some general questions around Laplace and Fourier transforms, including their equations
and basic applications.
This wasn't really a separate interrogation- it felt more like a conversation around the subjects I had studied,
and he expected me to remember the fundamentals despite moving towards software.
Computer Networks
We then moved to Computer Networks. Some of the topics discussed were:

• TCP vs UDP

• Authentication vs Authorization

• JWT

• Access tokens

• Refresh tokens

• DNS

• Proxy servers

• How an API request works end-to-end

--- PAGE 7 ---
Again, the questions were connected to practical implementations rather than just definitions.
Projects
Towards the end, we discussed my projects.
He asked me to explain one of my projects and draw its architecture. We then spent around 15-20
minutes discussing the project, including why I had designed it that way and questions around the
individual components.
I was able to explain the project and answer his questions, and he seemed satisfied with the discussion.
Finally, he asked if I had any questions for him.
I asked him about the kind of engineering problems and work engineers get to work on at Infosys. We had a
short discussion about that, after which I thanked him, shook his hand, and left the room.
A Few Honest Points About the Interview
I also want to mention a few things where I didn't perform perfectly, because I think these are equally
important for someone reading this experience.
In the Data Structure implementing questions, I was able to reach the correct approach, but I did need
hints and direction from the interviewer at certain points. I was able to build on those hints and explain
my reasoning, but I don't want to give the impression that I independently solved everything from scratch.
The important thing for me was that once I received a hint, I was able to understand it, incorporate it into my
approach, and move forward.
I also wasn't equally strong in Computer Networks. There were a few questions where I couldn't give
satisfactory answers or wasn't completely confident about the concepts. This was probably the area where I
felt I could have prepared better.
Apart from that, the rest of the interview went quite smoothly. The DBMS discussion in particular was long
and challenging, but I was comfortable with the concepts and was able to answer the questions and
follow-up questions. The project discussion also went well because I was able to explain the architecture and
the decisions behind it.
The Result
After the interview, there was obviously a lot of uncertainty. Even though I felt the interview had gone well
overall, I knew there were places where I had needed hints and places where I hadn't been able to answer,
especially in Computer Networks. So I didn't want to assume anything.
When the results were finally announced, I found out that I had been selected for the Specialist
Programmer L1 role.
There were two final selections from our SP/DSE interview group-I was selected for the SP L1 role,
and another student was selected for the DSE role.
Getting that result felt really special, especially considering how the process had started for me.
--- PAGE 8 ---
I had already experienced an OA through HackWithInfy where nervousness got the better of me. I had
walked into this OA with that memory in the back of my mind, but this time I consciously tried not to let it
affect me. Even during the OA, I had failed test cases on questions I thought I could solve, got stuck, and
had to change my strategy. But I kept going and eventually managed to solve the hard DP question
completely.
Then, in the interview, I couldn't finish the coding problem either. I needed hints in DSA, couldn't answer
some Computer Networks questions, and definitely wasn't perfect.
And yet, the overall process worked out.
That was probably the biggest lesson I took from the entire experience: you don't need to have a perfect
performance to get through a placement process. You need to keep yourself composed, be honest when
you don't know something, make the most of the things you do know, and keep thinking when the situation
doesn't go exactly as planned.
I feel grateful for the opportunity and, more importantly, for everything the process taught me. Looking
back, there are definitely things I would prepare differently especially Computer Networks and handling
DSA problems more independently during interviews. But I wouldn't change the fact that I went into the
process despite my previous nervous experience and simply gave it my best.
For anyone reading this who is preparing for placements: don't wait until you feel completely ready.
Prepare seriously, yes-but when the opportunity comes, go for it. Even if you make mistakes along
the way, you might surprise yourself with how far you can go.

1. Online Assessment [250-270]

About 250-270 candidates took the online test and 25 were shortlisted for interviews based on the test score
and cutoff. The test was an MCQ format 50 min covering 60 question based on cloud services and Azure
modules, SQL, aptitude, and OS basics (Linux/macOS). Had enough time for all the questions could
comfortably complete it before time. (OA time: 11.00-11.50).
Revise cloud one-liners, DBMS basics, and Linux commands, and keep your resume showing any exposure
to cloud or SQL.

2. Interview-1 [ 25 ]

25 people appeared, 10 shortlisted. It was a one-on-one interview. They asked me to expand on my intro -
from before college to now. I spoke about my committees, projects, and internships. They dug into my
Python ticket sales predictor and my web dev internship, specifically how I deployed the project, how it was
hosted. They asked about my career goals, and I said I'm interested in data analysis/debugging, not hardcore
coding, and mentioned my IBM Data Analyst course.
Tech side - they asked how I transferred a domain to Vercel and how DNS of that works, basics of DBMS
(SQL vs MongoDB). I was honest about not using cloud hands-on, just theory. I linked everything back to
projects and teamwork. My prep here was brushing up resume stories and DBMS/OS/CCN basics brush up.
Resume tip - quantify projects and show deployment/real impact.
--- PAGE 2 ---

3. Interview-2 [ 10]

From 10 people, 3 got selected (+4 waitlisted). This was a more technical + behavioural mix. They asked me
all about computer networks - OSI layers, protocols, how PCs are identified, network topologies. Any
projects that are computer network focused?
Behavioural side - family background, career goals (I said MBA in future), and they checked my
communication skills. They asked me to pick one project and explain end-to-end, so I went with the Python
ML project. They wanted detail, so I broke it step by step. What worked here was keeping answers structured
and clear.
Tip: know one project inside out and be confident when talking about goals.
They Selected 3 of us and +4 people were waitlisted.

journey.prep:
Don't measure your preparation against what everyone else around you is doing. Some people swear by
Striver's Sheet, some by pure competitive programming, some by hundreds of LeetCode questions - find what
actually helps you understand a concept rather than memorize it, and stick with that. It's completely fine to
start late, solve fewer questions, or skip a "must-do" resource, as long as you genuinely understand what you've
learned and know exactly where and how to apply it.

1. Be honest when you don't know something. If you're asked something you genuinely don't remember or

don't know, say so clearly instead of guessing or making something up. Interviewers notice and generally
respect honesty far more than a shaky, incorrect answer.

2. Know your resume and your projects inside out. Be ready to explain the "why" behind every technical

decision in your projects, not just the "what". Counter-questions are far easier to handle when you've actually
built the thing yourself and understand it end to end.

3. Don't ignore the basics - SQL, joins, and core concepts. Even in a data-focused or backend-adjacent role,

expect fairly direct questions on SQL fundamentals like joins and stored procedures, so keep these fresh.

4. Stay calm through multiple rounds and pen-and-paper style tests. If a round is unusual - like a pen and

paper test that later feeds into your interview questions - treat it seriously and think through your approach
properly, since it may well resurface later.

5. Be yourself in HR rounds. HR rounds are as much about how you communicate and handle pressure as they

are about your answers. Being honest about past rejections and what you learned from them tends to land far
better than pretending everything has gone smoothly.

In case of any further doubts, feel free to reach out, and you can also refer to the past interview experiences
shared by TPO.

1. Online Assessment (DoSelect, from home) - 22nd August

This was a standard online round conducted remotely. Around 50 candidates were shortlisted from this round
to move ahead in the process.

2. Pen and Paper Test [All 50 shortlisted candidates] - 27th August

Before the interviews began, we were made to sit for an in-person pen and paper test. This was interesting
because our answers here were later picked apart and questioned directly in the interview - so it wasn't just a
filter, it fed straight into the next round. There were 3 questions:
Problem 1: You were given a string made up of lowercase letters, uppercase letters, numbers, and special
characters. The task was to strip out all the numbers, special characters, and spaces, and then check whether
the remaining string was a palindrome or not (uppercase and lowercase versions of a letter were to be treated
as the same character).
Problem 2: You were given a string made up of vowels and consonants, and had to check it against three
constraints - the string could not contain more than 3 continuous vowels, could not contain more than 5
continuous consonants, and the total length of the string had to be less than or equal to 8. (I don't remember
the exact constraints word for word, but this was the gist.)
Example: input "abei??gh" -> output True
Problem 3: You were given an N x N matrix, and had to find how many smaller square sub-matrices could be
formed from it. For example, a 3x3 matrix can form 14 squares in total - nine 1x1 squares, four 2x2 squares, and
one 3x3 square, adding up to 14.
Some candidates were also asked to optimize the approach they had written down for these questions, so it's
worth thinking about the time and space complexity even for a pen-and-paper round.

3. Technical Interview [All 50 who cleared the pen and paper test]

My interview slot came up quite late in the day. In the interview, they went back over the pen and paper test
questions I had answered - asking me to explain my approach, pointing out what could be wrong with it, and
giving me small variations of the same questions to solve on the spot.
The interviewer then asked me to introduce myself and describe all my projects in detail. After listening to my
introduction, he picked two of my projects and asked me to explain them further - why I had used whatever
technology or approach I mentioned, and how it actually affected the problem it was solving. I answered each
project in three parts: why I made the project, how it helped me, and how I built it using everything I knew.
Make sure you know your resume thoroughly, because there were a few counter-questions along the way, and I
was able to handle all of them comfortably since I had built each project myself. We then moved to the second
project, which I explained in a similar structured way.
After the projects, he moved on to SQL. He asked me what LEAD and LAG were, followed by questions on joins -
self join, left join, inner join, and so on. Then he asked me what stored procedures in SQL were. I wasn't sure
about this one, so I was upfront and told him I knew the term but couldn't recall the exact definition, and asked
if he could give me an example that might jog my memory. He said not to worry about it and moved on to the
next question.
He then asked me what an MCP server was. I told him honestly that I didn't know the exact technical definition,
but explained it as best I understood it - that MCP servers are like functions or tools of an application that an AI
can use directly, letting it make changes within that application on the user's behalf. I gave him an example
from my own experience, where I had used Claude's Fusion 360 plugin to generate a design for me - it didn't
come out exactly as I wanted, but it was clearly doing part of the work for me.
When he asked if I had any questions, I asked him to describe what a typical day at Revvity looks like, and what
someone should do to prepare before joining.

4. HR Round

After some time, I was called back directly for the HR round. Usually the process has two technical rounds
followed by HR, but in my case I was moved straight to HR after this one technical round. The HR round was
fairly relaxed - he asked basic things like whether I'd be comfortable coming in to that location, about my family
background, and what kind of roles I preferred. He was very supportive throughout, and even when I made
small mistakes, he was patient and helped me through them - the overall atmosphere was friendly.
He then asked me to explain one of my projects again, which I did, followed by which role I would prefer and
why, and which programming language I preferred and why not another one - I got the sense he was testing
how I respond under a bit of pressure rather than looking for a "correct" answer. The conversation flowed well
after that, and we had a good discussion where he also asked about my previous rejections - what mistakes I
felt I had made, and how I worked on overcoming them. These were all fairly basic, conversational questions
overall.
Results were announced 4 days later, on 31st August, and I was selected for the Data Engineer role at Revvity.

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
Don't measure your preparation against what everyone else around you is doing. Some people swear by
Striver's Sheet, some by pure competitive programming, some by hundreds of LeetCode questions - find what
actually helps you understand a concept rather than memorize it, and stick with that. It's completely fine to
start late, solve fewer questions, or skip a "must-do" resource, as long as you genuinely understand what you've
learned and know exactly where and how to apply it.

1. Be honest when you don't know something. If you're asked something you genuinely don't remember or

don't know, say so clearly instead of guessing or making something up. Interviewers notice and generally
respect honesty far more than a shaky, incorrect answer.

2. Know your resume and your projects inside out. Be ready to explain the "why" behind every technical

decision in your projects, not just the "what". Counter-questions are far easier to handle when you've actually
built the thing yourself and understand it end to end.

3. Don't ignore the basics - SQL, joins, and core concepts. Even in a data-focused or backend-adjacent role,

expect fairly direct questions on SQL fundamentals like joins and stored procedures, so keep these fresh.

4. Stay calm through multiple rounds and pen-and-paper style tests. If a round is unusual - like a pen and

paper test that later feeds into your interview questions - treat it seriously and think through your approach
properly, since it may well resurface later.

5. Be yourself in HR rounds. HR rounds are as much about how you communicate and handle pressure as they

are about your answers. Being honest about past rejections and what you learned from them tends to land far
better than pretending everything has gone smoothly.

In case of any further doubts, feel free to reach out, and you can also refer to the past interview experiences
shared by TPO.

Hello Guys, whoever reads this, this is the honest experience of my placement process. First of
all, dont be scared, dont panic, dont be anxious, actually be a little anxious it helps to stay
focused and keep improving yourself. My journey was like most of the students who got placed,
initially the resume was not being rejected, then I couldn't clear OAs. Before this interview I had
given only one interview that too just 2 days ago for a totally different role (consultant). So
leading to this interview I had zero hopes of clearing it. I was not good at DSA, I had completed
Striver's sheet till trees only, Graphs aur DP abhi karna baaki tha, Web Dev utna accha nahi aata,
bas ML aata tha woh bhi almost sabko basic aata tha (you will learn in 6th sem). Bas SQL aur
OOPs concepts acche se kiye the. I just answered their questions confidently, spilled out
everything I knew, and boom-I got selected. So, don't be disheartened, and most importantly,
don't compare your journey with anyone else's. Everyone has their own pace and journey.
[Resume Shortlisting]
Firstly we were shortlisted on the basis of our resumes. Till now what we had experienced is that
in the name of resume shortlisting mostly only our cgpa is considered. So please try to maintain a
high cgpa as possible. For this roughly everyone above 8 were selected. Koi kitna bhi bole
CGPA is very imp aur 8.5 ke upar rakhne ka try karo. Many of my friends and I were not

OAL Around 120 students were shortlisted |

--- PAGE 2 ---
We had 45 min to 1hr to complete.

1) OA ke liye Indiabix is the best to cover all the kinds of questions. Baaki try to solve them as

My turn came fairly early within the first 5 people. Firstly the interviewer introduced himself,

He gave me details of a table and asked me a few queries, a) Find avg salary of a department b)
Find departments with avg salary > 50000 c) Find department with 2nd highest avg salary.
--- PAGE 3 ---
Firstly I asked all the necessary details about the tables, like how many columns, what was the
primary key, etc and then I wrote and explained all 3 correctly. He was impressed how I
explained the 3rd one where I used the dense_rank window function and how it works and how
other rank functions work and I kept talking about whatever I knew about it. He then asked me a
DSA question, to find duplicates in an array. I wrote the solution on the paper explaining each
and every word I was writing. This not only helps you to show your thinking but also gives you
time to review your solution on the go. Also even if you make any mistake while writing then
don't panic. Explain to them the mistake, and correct your code. They appreciate this. Like in my
case, in my DSA question's solution, by mistake I looped into the vector again while pushing
duplicate elements in the answer vector, I was supposed to loop into the unordered map in which
I had stored the frequency of each unique element. In the middle of the solution I realised this

9). We even had a little conversation about

Tech Round 2:-
In this round as well the interviewer introduced himself and told a little about his role. I started
with my introduction and project work like the first interview. He then picked a project and
asked about it in depth. It went for about 10 minutes and then he asked me a SQL question:-
SQL Question

customer_name
B
total_amount

Initially I thought I couldn't do this but then I calmed myself and decided to start small. I first

Keep speaking how you approach the problem and find a solution as it shows your problem
solving ability. I kept talking whatever I was writing and it helped me to explain my

After this he was happy with my ability to slowly build my solution rather than giving a direct

1. Resume Shortlisting

I never had an idea of how many students there were for any company or any round, so sorry, I can't provide you with the exact numbers.
Also, one of the most important things I want to tell you is: don't ever blame your resume, your skills, the TPO, or the company for not getting shortlisted. Many companies, and even the TPO, say that they shortlist on the basis of resumes, but from my experience, the process can sometimes feel random. It totally depends on your luck as well.
My roommates also had remarkable resumes, but they weren't even selected for Revvity and Infosys, and no one gives a clarification on this.
My name was also not there in the initial resume shortlist. In the evening, they sent a list in the group that had 6 names, and mine was there in it. The TPO said that we were also shortlisted and told us to join the Revvity process group.

2. Online Assessment

On 22nd August, they had the Online Assessment. The test was actually crazy. It was not hard, but the questions were from multiple domains.
Some questions were from Angular, some were from React, some Java questions were also there, and there were some aptitude questions.
Overall, the test was medium, but the questions they asked were from technologies that don't really connect with each other.
The DSA question was pretty easy. The question was something like this:
1 coding question: A string was given containing alphabets, and we were supposed to compress the string.
For example:
aaaabbbcdeee
would become:
4a3bcd3e
The test duration was 1 hour. Don't be afraid of the test. The test was conducted online.

3. Interviews

48 students were selected for interviews.
A. Physical Pen-and-Paper Test
Even though the company had told us that there would be direct interviews, they took a physical pen-and-paper test.
We had to write code on paper. They had told us it would be a 45-minute test, but it went up to 1 hour.
There were 3 questions.

1. Palindrome String

We had to check if a string was a palindrome or not, but there was a catch: we had to ignore all special characters, symbols, and whitespaces.
We also had to consider small and capital letters as equal, i.e., a and A are equal.
For example, a string like a*bA would be considered a palindrome since we had to ignore the special character * and consider a and A equal.

2. Good or Bad String

If more than three consonants or more than five vowels come serially, one after another, then it is a bad string; otherwise, it is a good string.
But the catch is that there will be question marks in the string. You can place anything in place of the question mark, either a vowel or a consonant, and then you have to calculate whether it is a good or bad string.
For example, consider:

The ? can be replaced by either a vowel or a consonant. You have to determine whether the string can be made a good string based on the possible replacements.

3. Number of Squares in an N × N Square

We were given an N × N square. We had to calculate how many maximum squares are possible in that square.
Suppose there is a 3 × 3 square. Then there will be:
9 squares of 1 × 1
4 squares of 2 × 2
1 square of 3 × 3
So, the total number of squares possible is:
9 + 4 + 1 = 14

Process Date: 9th July 2026 (OA), 10th July 2026 (Interviews)

Key Points:
There were 5 Rounds officially

1. Resume Shortlisting: Out of approximately 300 - 400 applicants, 159 students were

shortlisted.

2. OA: 159 students appeared for the OA, and 16 were shortlisted for the next round.

3. Technical Interview 1: 16 students were interviewed, and 8 advanced to the next

round.

4. Technical Interview 2: 8 students were interviewed, and 5 advanced to the HR round.

5. HR: 5 students appeared, and all 5 received offers.

1. Resume Shortlisting:

On Superset, the application was open from 3rd July to 6th July. Within this period, you
were supposed to submit your resume and apply through the Superset job profile. The JD
was shared with us as this, so tailor your resume according to the JD and try to include
relevant keywords, as they help improve ATS matching. Also, include relevant projects.
Since this was an AI Engineer role, try to highlight AI/ML-related projects.
Do not add unnecessary jargon or mention topics that you are not completely aware of. Just
knowing something superficially is not enough, because a single word on your resume can
lead to several interview questions, and you might end up digging your own gr ave. Be
authentic and do not add even a single false or misleading statement to your resume.
Use Jake's resume template from Overleaf, as it is the standard resume template that is
generally followed.
We received the shortlist first through individual emails on 8th July, along with the test
links for the CodeChef platform. Later, the same was announced on the TPO group, where
we came to know that 159 students had been shortlisted.

2. Online Assessment

The OA was conducted online on campus through the CodeChef platform. It consisted
of 28 questions, as shown above. Out of these, 3 were coding questions and the
remaining 25 were MCQs consisting of Aptitude and AI/ML -related questions. The
total duration of the test was 90 minutes.
Some of the MCQ topics that I can recollect are as follows:

• Quantization

• GGUF

• Hallucinations

• Finding the Time Complexity

• Prompting

• Inference

• Overfitting, Underfitting, Bias/Variance

• Types of ML and their identification, like Supervised Learning, Unsupervised

Learning, etc.

• GCD

• Context Window

• And many more similar questions related to AI/ML

If you have studied AI/ML well, then these MCQs are going to be quite easy. I had
chosen Artificial Intelligence as my Program Elective in the 6th semester. Because of
that, I studied NLP and Deep Learning, which were part of the AI elective subjects.
Also, since I belong to the CE department, Machine Learning was already a core
subject. I believe these subjects definitely helped me a lot. So, if you are planning to
apply for this role in the future, I would definitely recommend choosing AI as your
Program Elective.

I believe the only real concern would be the aptitude section, so practice enough
aptitude questions from IndiaBix. That would definitely help you a lot.
The aptitude section had a few calculation -based questions involving percentages,
puzzles like "what comes next" patterns, ratio questions, finding missing numbers,
comprehension-based questions, and choosing the correct logical flow.
I remember one question where if TIGER is written as QDFHS, then what would be
the code for FISH? It actually had a very simple solution, but it seemed confusing when
I first read it. The approach was to reverse the word first, so TIGER becomes REGIT,
and then write the previous alphabet for each character. Similarly, for FISH, reversing
it gives HSIF, and applying the same logic gives GRHE.
It was quite simple, wasn't it? But trust me, I spent almost 5 minutes straight trying to
crack this because I initially thought it was related to cryptography. I started thinking
about the cipher techniques we had studied, like Substitution, Transposition,
Monoalphabetic Cipher, Caesar Cipher, Rail Fence Cipher, and others. After trying
around 10-15 different approaches, I finally understood the pattern.
Honestly, it felt like I was just wasting my time on a single MCQ, but I don't know why
I took it as a challenge and wanted to crack it. When I finally did, it was a huge relief,
and I had a smile on my face because of that small feeling of satisfaction. S ometimes
we get completely involved in a question and spend more time than required.
However, I would not suggest spending 5 minutes on a single MCQ. Time management
in an OA is very important, and you need to maintain a balance between solving
difficult questions and moving ahead.

Next, as I mentioned earlier, there were three coding questions. I was able to solve one
coding question fully and another partially.  Each question carried 100 points, and the
score depended on the number of test cases your solution passed. So even if you are not
able to come up with the most optimized solution, don't just keep thinking about it on
paper. Dry-run the problem, write the brute-force solution if that's all you can think of,
and try to pass as many test cases as possible. Partial points are always better than
scoring zero by spending too much time searching for the perfect approach.
One more important point: a few students were not aware that we could switch between
coding questions. In previous placement cycles, some seniors had mentioned in their
interview experiences that there was no option to move back and forth between
questions. However, this time there was a navigation button at the top -right corner of
the interface. It was quite small, and a few students completely missed it until the very
end after wasting a significant amount of time on a single question.
So, definitely read previous interview experiences, but don't assume the process or
interface will be exactly the same. Many students went into the OA with that
preconceived notion and didn't even bother exploring the interface. Don't make that
mistake.
Moving on to the DSA questions.

1. The first question was quite easy. As far as I can remember, it was something like

this:
We were given a string S (of length N) and an integer K. The task was to find all
the unique characters that appeared in the string at least K times (frequency ≥ K).
The final output had to be a single string containing all such characters sorted in
ascending ASCII order. This meant that uppercase letters (A -Z) should appear
before lowercase letters (a-z), and each qualifying character had to be printed only
once.
Since N was up to 10^5, an O(N log N) approach using sort() would probably have
passed as well, but I solved it using the Counting Sort idea.
I simply maintained a fixed frequency array of size 256. I traversed the string once
to count the frequency of every character, and then iterated from index 0 to 255.
Since the array indices themselves represent ASCII values, the output automatically
came in sorted ASCII order without using any sorting function. This gave a clean
time complexity of O(N) with O(1) auxiliary space.
The core idea was very similar to problems like LeetCode 451 (Sort Characters By
Frequency) and LeetCode 242 (Valid Anagram), both of which I had already solved
from Striver's String module. Instead of using an unordered_map or calling sort(),
I simply used a fixed int cnt[256] = {0}; array.
Initially, I had taken the array size as 128 because we usually study standard ASCII.
Then I realized that using 256 would cover the extended ASCII character set as
well. It doesn't really hurt the complexity, so I changed it to 256 just to make sure
no valid character would be missed. Overall, it was a straightforward problem, and
all my test cases passed.

2. Chef and Shop

The second question taught me a really important lesson: always read the
constraints carefully before deciding on an approach.
The problem was something like this:
Chef loves shopping, and he specifically wants to buy oranges. However, he has
only (K) rubles to spend. There are (N) oranges available, where the (i) -th orange
has a cost (cost_i) and a weight (weight_i). Chef wants to buy a combination of
oranges that maximizes the total weight without exceeding his budget of (K) rubles.
We had to output the maximum possible weight for multiple test cases.
When you first read this problem, your immediate instinct is to classify it as a classic
0/1 Knapsack problem. That's exactly what I did during the OA. I implemented the
standard 1D Dynamic Programming solution where you maintain a DP array of size
money + 1 and iterate backwards to compute the maximum achievable weight.
The DP logic itself was completely correct for a standard knapsack problem, but I
completely overlooked the constraints. The budget, K, could be as large as 10⁸,
whereas the number of oranges was extremely small (N ≤ 10). Because of this, my
line vector<long long> dp(money + 1, -1); tried to allocate an enormous amount of
memory for the largest test cases, eventually resulting in a Memory Limit Exceeded

(MLE) on the final subtask. Even if memory had not been an issue, iterating up to

10⁸ for every test case would event ually have resulted in a Time Limit Exceeded

(TLE) as well.

Fortunately, the problem had partial scoring. My DP solution comfortably passed
all the smaller subtasks, so I still managed to secure 60 out of 100 points  for this
question.
The actual trick was hidden in the constraints. Since N ≤ 10, there was no need to
use Dynamic Programming at all. With only 10 oranges, there are just 2¹⁰ = 1024
possible subsets. So, the optimal solution was to generate every subset using
Bitmasking (Power Set), calculate the  total cost and total weight for each subset,
discard the ones that exceeded the budget, and keep track of the maximum weight
among the valid ones.
This solution runs in O(N × 2ᴺ) time, which is only about 10,000 operations per test
case, uses only O(1) extra space (excluding the input), and completely avoids any
dependence on the huge budget constraint of 10⁸.
This was honestly a great reminder that sometimes the constraints are more
important than the problem statement itself. Had I paid closer attention to the value
of N, I would have immediately recognized that the intended solution was based on
Bitmasking rather than Dynamic Programming.

3. The third question was honestly a bit of a heartbreak because I ran out of time just

when I had figured out the approach. The problem itself was actually quite
interesting.
We were given a shuffled set of travel itinerary cards. Each card contained a source
city, a destination city, and the travel cost between them. The traveller never visits
the same city twice. Our task was to reconstruct the original order of the journey,
print the itinerary in the correct sequence, and calculate the total cost.
My first thought was to solve it using graphs. Since no city was visited more than
once, the journey essentially formed a single path. The main challenge was finding
the starting city. I realized that every intermediate city would appear once as a
source and once as a destination, whereas the starting city would only appear as a
source and never as a destination. Once the starting city was identified, we could
simply follow the path until the end while printing the itinerary and adding the travel
cost.
Unfortunately, I had already spent a lot of time on the second question trying to
make my DP solution pass all the test cases. By the time I reached this question, I
was under a lot of time pressure. I had the complete logic in my head and had just
started implementing it when the timer ran out.
Looking back, this question taught me a bigger lesson than the algorithm itself.
Time management in OAs is extremely important. If a particular approach isn't
working, it's often better to secure partial marks, move on, and come back later if
time permits. I probably could have completed this question if I hadn't spent so
much time trying to optimize the previous one.
After the OA ended, we received the list of the 16 shortlisted students for the interview
round on the same night around 8 PM. We were then asked to report to college by 9:30
AM the next morning.

3. Interview Round 1:

The interviews were conducted in parallel, with three students being interviewed at a
time, as there were three interviewers from the company's side. This first technical
round was quite  resume intensive and focused deeply on my internship experience,
followed by my projects and core subjects like DBMS, AI, ML, Distributed Systems,
and DevOps.
Firstly, he asked me to give my introduction. Then the interview proceeded.
Here are some of the questions/topics that were asked to me.
DBMS:

• Design a database schema.

• Normalize it up to 3NF.

• Explain each Normal Form.

• What happens if we over -normalize a database? When should we stop

normalizing?

• Understanding of JOIN queries to retrieve data from the normalized tables.

• Foreign key references.

• Explain the ACID properties in detail with examples.

Then came a really interesting question.
Suppose you're given a table and asked to find its PK. How would you find it?  Seeing
this, I initially thought it was a pretty straightforward question. I said I would simply
use DESCRIBE table_name; to inspect the table structure. He then added a twist. He
said, "Suppose the engineer forgot to declare the Primary Key while creating the table."
For a few seconds, in my mind I was like, "Who does that, man? What kind of engineer
was that?" Anyways, I had to solve his mess.
My first instinct was to look for an AUTO_INCREMENT column because, in most
cases, that ends up being the Primary Key. Another possibility was the leftmost column
since that's also quite common. But then I immediately thought that this definitely
wasn't wh at he was expecting because I couldn't just keep looking at the columns
manually, and I even thought this  out loud. Right then, he added, "Exactly. What if
there are thousands or even millions of columns?"
So I picked up the pen and paper and started breaking the problem down.
A Primary Key is nothing but a column that is unique and cannot contain duplicate
values. So my goal was to identify the column that satisfied this property.
The approach I suggested was simple. First, count the total number of records in the
table. Then, count the number of distinct values in the candidate column. If both
numbers matched, then that column could be the Primary Key.
The SQL queries I suggested were:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_records
FROM table_name;
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT column_name) AS unique_records
FROM table_name;
If both counts were equal, then the column contained only unique values and was a
valid candidate for the Primary Key.
Initially, the interviewer looked a little doubtful, so I explained my reasoning properly.
Once I walked him through the logic, he was convinced, appreciated the approach, and
this was my final DB question.
AI/ML
Then we had a very detailed discussion about my second project. He wanted to
understand everything in depth, right from the motivation behind the project to every
stage of the implementation. He kept asking why I chose a particular approach, what
the alternatives were, what trade-offs were involved. So one piece of advice would be
to know your projects inside out. Be prepared to justify every design decision because
interviewers can dive really deep.
Some of the AI/ML topics that were discussed are as follows:

1. LangChain

2. LangGraph

3. Vector Embeddings

4. Chunking

5. Cosine Similarity

6. BM25

7. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)

8. LLM Hallucinations

9. RAG and its drawbacks

10. AI Personas

11. Context Window

12. Agentic Workflows

13. LLMs

14. Shared state vs separate state in LangGraph

15. Prompting

DevOps
The discussion then shifted towards DevOps. Some of the topics that were asked were:

1. Terraform - complete architectural explanation and why it is needed.

2. CI/CD

3. Jenkins - he asked me to explain how I would implement a CI/CD pipeline using

Jenkins from scratch.

4. Kubernetes

5. SonarQube

6. Webhooks

7. Infrastructure as Code (IaC)

8. Microservices vs Monolithic Architecture

After discussing these topics thoroughly, my first technical interview came to an end.
The interviewer said he was done from his side and asked if I had any questions for
him.
The questions I asked were:

1. While researching about AuxoAI , I found that the company primarily works

with Fortune 500 clients. I asked whether the work is limited to these companies
or if they also cater to other industries and domains, and what kind of projects
the company generally works on.

2. I also asked, "What is the one core technology or skill that you would

recommend I focus on over the next six months before joining AuxoAI so that
I can quickly catch up with the team?"
With that, my first technical interview ended. Personally, I felt it had gone really well.
I was quite confident that I would be shortlisted for the second round, and I walked out
of the interview feeling happy and satisfied.
I left the interview room and went to the conference room, thinking I would revise a
few guesstimates and quickly go through my last -minute revision cheat sheet. At that
time, many students were still waiting for or were in the middle of their first techni cal
interview, so I assumed I would have a decent amount of time before the next round.
But, to my surprise, within just 3 to 4 minutes, I was called again for Interview 2. In
fact, I was the first one to be advanced to the second round. I didn't even get enough
time to settle down, let alone open my revision PDF. Everything happened so quickly,
which, of course, made me really happy because I knew my first interview must have
gone well.

4. Interview 2:

Interview 2 also started with the standard "Tell me about yourself."
He then asked, "Why are you interested in joining AuxoAI?"
Just like Interview 1, this round also involved a deep dive into my resume and projects.
I explained my projects in detail, and from there the discussion naturally branched into
different technical topics.
Some of the topics and questions discussed during Interview 2 were as follows:
Distributed Systems

1. Lamport Logical Clock

2. Ring Election Algorithm

3. Leader Election Algorithm

4. Load Balancing - Round Robin and other algorithms

5. Proxy Gateway

Apart from these, he also asked a few other fundamental Distributed Systems questions.
After that, he switched to Machine Learning. We had a detailed discussion on concepts
like Precision, Recall, True Positives, False Positives, and other basic ML
fundamentals.
Then he referred back to something I had mentioned while explaining my project. In
my project, I had used a cosine similarity threshold of 0.85 as a final filtering criterion.
If the cosine similarity was greater than 0.85, I considered the retrieved citations to be
valid and proceeded to the next stage; otherwise, I repeated that step.
He asked me a very simple-looking question: "Why did you choose 0.85?"
Initially, I thought explaining the logic would be straightforward, but the discussion
kept going deeper. He connected it with concepts like Precision, Recall, True Positives,
False Positives, and overall model performance. He kept asking questions like, " Why
0.85? Was it just a magical number? How did you arrive at it?"
This was probably the toughest part of my entire interview. We spent around 5 to 7
minutes discussing just this one threshold. I tried explaining my reasoning in different
ways, but he still wasn't fully convinced and kept challenging my answers from
different perspectives.
Finally, I told him that I wouldn't claim 0.85 to be some standard or universally correct
threshold. It was something I had arrived at through experimentation. I had also tried
values like 0.95, 0.7, and 0.6 before settling on 0.85 because it gave me a rea sonable
balance for my use case. Since this threshold was only acting as a final gatekeeper to
decide whether to proceed with the next stage or perform another retrieval, I chose the
value that worked best for my project based on my observations.
I also admitted that I hadn't done an exhaustive study on threshold tuning and that it
was definitely an area I wanted to explore further and improve upon.
I think this was what he was looking for. Rather than insisting that my choice was
perfect, I acknowledged the trade -offs involved and admitted that there was room for
improvement. After that, he seemed satisfied with the discussion.
He then said, "Okay, let's move on to some case study and business questions. Grab a
pen and paper; you'll need them."
And with that, he started explaining the first case study.
Problem 1:
The first case study was based on Zomato launching its services in a new city.
I don't remember the exact numbers that were given, but the problem statement included
details like the daily order volume, average order value, restaurant commission,
delivery partner payout per order, and the marketing/customer acquisition cost. My task
was to calculate whether the new city was profitable or not based on these numbers.
Initially, seeing so many numbers and variables together can feel a little overwhelming,
but if you stay calm and break the problem down step by step, it becomes quite
manageable. That is exactly what I did.
The calculations themselves were quite straightforward. It was nothing more than basic
mathematics involving percentages, profit and loss, and simple arithmetic. So don't
worry too much about the calculations. The challenge was more about interpreting the
result rather than actually computing it.
I first noted down all the revenue sources and expenses on paper. Then I calculated the
total revenue generated through orders and commissions and compared it with the
delivery costs and marketing expenses. After doing the calculations, it was quite evident
that the city was running at a significant loss because the marketing spend was much
higher than the profit being generated from operations.
The interviewer then asked me, "How would you make this city profitable?"
Initially, I suggested a few straightforward business solutions. I said we could increase
the commission charged to restaurants, improve the average order value through
minimum order requirements or targeted offers, and try to increase the total number of
orders.
Then, while looking at the sheet, I casually pointed towards the delivery partner payout
and suggested that we could reduce it.
The interviewer immediately smiled and said, "Don't even think about reducing that
innocent man's salary."
We both exchanged a smile, and then he gave me another hint. He said, "You're a
Computer Science student. Think about it from that perspective."
That one hint changed my direction of thinking.
I started looking at it from a Computer Science perspective rather than just a business
perspective. He then gave me another hint saying, "You must have surely studied the
Travelling Salesman Problem."
That was the point where everything clicked. I quickly grabbed my pen and paper and
started thinking about how the routing could actually be optimized.
We then discussed how, instead of one restaurant order being handled separately every
time, the system could pick multiple orders from the same restaurant or nearby
restaurants and deliver them together to customers in the same locality. This would
reduce unnecessary travel and improve delivery efficiency without cutting down the
delivery partner's payout.
After that, we had a brief discussion about the Travelling Salesman Problem and the
Milkman's Problem.
Once we finished discussing this case, he said, "Since we are already into the food
business, let's open our own restaurant and move on to the second problem."
And with that, we proceeded to the next case study.

Problem 2:
For the second problem, he gave very minimal information initially.
He said that we were running a restaurant business and initially our target customers
were Indian families. We had a typical family -oriented menu with items like dal, rice,
and other such dishes. Later, after analysing the market, we realized that the busi ness
model that was attracting the younger generation, with items like burgers, pizzas, and
fast food, was more profitable and had higher demand. So, we decided to change our
business model and started a second model focused on this segment.
However, instead of increasing, our revenue started dropping.  The question was, what
could be the possible reason?
I asked him for a little time and took around 20-30 seconds to think about the problem.
I was trying to understand the possible reasons in my mind while also thinking out loud.
The first thought that came to me was related to the difference in customer behaviour.
I said that since our first business model was family -oriented, we were attracting
families, and generally one family would come in a group of around 4 people on
average. However, in the second model, targeting the younger generation, the number
of customers could be much lower. Apart from birthday parties or small celebrations,
young customers might come alone or with at most one other person. So, the average
number of customers could have reduced, which could directly impact the revenue.
He agreed and said, "Okay, fair enough. This could be one reason. What else?"
Then he told me that I could ask questions if I wanted. At that point, I understood that
some information was intentionally hidden, but I wanted to first try solving it based on
my intuition before asking for any hints.
I suggested another possible reason: maybe the menu pricing strategy had changed, and
that could have impacted the revenue.  To this, he immediately said, "Let's assume
everything is the same and there is no change in the pricing."  Then he added, "Okay,
there is an IPL going on."
The moment he said IPL, I was completely confused. I was like, wait, how is my
restaurant connected with IPL? Within the next few seconds, multiple thoughts started
coming into my mind. I started thinking of different possibilities:

• Is it related to sponsorships or promotions?

• Are people watching the matches at home instead of coming to restaurants?

• Are we located near a stadium?

• Have competitor restaurants installed big screens and started IPL screenings,

attracting more customers?

• Since the younger generation is our target audience, are they easily switching to

competitors because of these offers?
I started discussing these possibilities with him, and he was calmly listening to my
thought process throughout.
Finally, I decided to continue with one of my approaches and said that maybe customer
count was declining because competitors had introduced better strategies during IPL
and were attracting our customers.
He listened to my explanation and then gave me another piece of information. He said,
"There is a queue outside your restaurant."  Again, this completely changed my
perspective.
I thought, wait, if there is already a queue outside, then customers are definitely coming.
So, customer demand is not the problem. I immediately dropped my previous
assumption about losing customers and started thinking about the queue itself.
Initially, I was even trying to connect it with some DSA concepts, but after thinking for
a minute or two, I realized the actual problem.
I told him that if there is a queue outside, it means demand is clearly present. The issue
could be that the table utilization has changed. And continuing with my first approach
that I told earlier, when families came, a single table was occupied by around four
people, leading to more orders per table. But now, when younger customers come, they
might occupy the same table with fewer people and spend more time there. Since the
number of tables is limited, the waiting queue increases, and the number of customers
being served decreases.
After explaining this approach, he immediately stopped me and said, "Perfect, perfect.
You have done really well. You have cracked almost 95% of it." He told me that this
was enough for him and that he was satisfied, so there was no need to continue solving
further.
Then he explained the remaining 5% part related to IPL. The IPL connection was not
about competitors installing screens or attracting our customers away. He smiled and
revealed that the IPL setup was actually happening inside our own restaurant. That was
the moment I was like, "Wait, what a connection that was!"
The actual issue was that customers were spending more time sitting at the table while
watching the IPL match. Since they were engaged in watching the game, they were
ordering less frequently and occupying tables for a longer duration. This slowed down
the queue processing and reduced the overall restaurant throughput.
The whole discussion ended with smiles and a positive exchange.  And I realized that
this problem was somewhat similar to concepts from Operating Systems, like CPU
scheduling, processes waiting in a ready queue, and resource utilization. The restaurant
tables were basically the limited resources, and customers were the pro cesses waiting
to use those resources.
I believe the appreciation was not just for reaching the final answer but for the way I
approached the problem. I considered multiple scenarios, kept thinking out loud, and
explored different directions instead of getting stuck on one assumption. One important
thing I learned from this case study is that during such interviews, you should always
think aloud. Even if your initial direction is not completely correct, the interviewer can
guide you with additional information and help you reach the rig ht approach. The
discussion itself is what matters.
With that, this case study also ended on a positive note. The interviewer then asked if I
had any questions for him.  In such situations, you should generally avoid saying that
you don't have any questions. You can always ask something simple related to the
company, role, team, or your transition from college to a professional environment.
So, I asked him the same question that I had asked Interviewer 1:
"What is the one core technology or skill that you would recommend I focus on over
the next six months before joining AuxoAI so that I can quickly catch up with the
team?"

After this round ended I was waiting for the Final HR interview and later on around 6
PM Round 2 results were announced and we were told HR round would be online since
the HR couldn't come offline.

5. HR Round:

This was a very relaxed round. We mostly had a normal conversation where she asked
me about the overall interview process, how my experience was, and a few general
interaction-based questions.
After that, she informed me that I had been selected and that I would be receiving both
an internship plus a full -time offer. She then explained the complete CTC breakdown
and also mentioned a clause stating that if I leave the firm within 18 months, I would
have to return the joining bonus.
We continued with some casual conversation, and she told me that the official
communication would be sent to the campus the next day since it was already quite late
(around 9:30 PM). The entire discussion lasted only about 10-15 minutes.

So yeah, that was the overall process and my experience. One final piece of advice is to keep
Parkinson's Law in mind. If you aren't familiar with it, a quick search will explain how it can
help you make more efficient progress. Once you understand this law and actually apply it, you
will see a much faster improvement in your progress instead of getting stuck for a long time on
the same thing. All the best for your upcoming processes. I will also list down the resources I
followed for my overall preparation.
I always believe in one thing: whatever happens, happens for a good reason. This was the first
company interview I gave during my placements, and luckily, I got selected in the first shot.
But that does not mean everyone will have the same journey. Everyone has their own timeline,
so never get disheartened because of any missed opportunity. Sometimes that opportunity was
just not meant to happen because something better might be waiting ahead. Always try to stay
optimistic.
Even I faced a similar situation before this. The company I appeared for before this was IDFC,
where the Online Assessment was conducted from home. Unfortunately, it was raining heavily
that day, and at the exact moment when I was giving the test, the electricity went off.
I had already completed the aptitude and CS section and solved 1 out of the 2 coding questions.
I was working on the final coding question. Although I had an inverter backup, my Wi -Fi
connection was not connected to the plug point that had inverter support. Apparently, it was
connected to the other socket, and because of that, I lost my internet connection. Due to the
strict rules of the assessment, I could not rejoin and eventually got eliminated.
The funny thing was, my mom, younger brother, and dad were more disappointed than I was.
They started blaming themselves and thinking that it happened because they had changed the
plug connection. My dad even said that I should have kept an extra data pack  as a backup on
top of my daily 2GB mobile data, so that I could have used my mobile hotspot if required. This
was mainly because the assessment involved video and screen recording, so a mobile hotspot
could have been used as an alternative connection. There were multiple regrets and "what if"
situations discussed, along with many improvement plans suggested by my family. A typical
family reaction that most of us can relate to.
But honestly, I was disappointed for hardly 5 minutes. After that, I quickly moved on, became
positive again, and started focusing on the next opportunity. However, that is how families are.
They take every failure and success personally because they genuinely care about us. They will
always be there  to support you, so always try to explain things to them and make them
understand that these things are a part of the journey. Their reaction always comes from a place
of concern and wanting the best for you.
Another thing I would suggest is always do proper research. Maintain a sheet where you track
companies, job roles, eligibility criteria, and your preferences. Sort companies based on what
aligns with your career goals and target those companies accordingly.
Placements can become very hectic because openings can come anytime. Sometimes
companies open applications 3 to 4 days before the deadline, and sometimes they open 10 to
15 days earlier. Usually, you are given only 2 to 3 days to apply through platform Superset, so
making decisions quickly becomes important.
During my placements, I did not apply to every company whose openings were available
initially, such as IDfy, JPMC, Infosys, WorkIndia, IDFC, Dolat Capital, PhonePe, AuxoAI,
and others.
What usually happens is that on a particular day, multiple companies open their applications
together along with their JDs and other details. At that point, it becomes very important to make
your choices wisely. Do not just apply everywhere because the pac kage looks good. Look at
the role, your interests, and your long-term goals.
For example, JPMC had come with a non-tech role. Even though the package was good, I did
not apply because it did not align with the career path I wanted to follow. Similarly, because
of my own preferences, I skipped some companies like WorkIndia, IDfy, and Infosys. I focused
only on companies like IDFC, PhonePe, and AuxoAI because their roles matched my interests
better.
So do your own research, understand what kind of career path you want, and then make your
decisions accordingly. Placements are a long process and require a lot of time and energy. You
cannot waste your efforts sitting for every company if you are not genu inely interested in the
role.
Also note that you will receive emails for every missed opportunity, including companies
where you were eligible but did not apply. You can do this for a maximum of 10
companies for which you are eligible but choose not to apply. If you miss 10 such
opportunities, you may get debarred from further placement processes. So, keep this
point in mind as well while making your decisions during placements.
Lastly, always stay optimistic. Every setback teaches you something. Keep improving yourself,
keep learning, and keep moving forward. Everyone has their own game to play and their own
journey to win. You just need to find your game, understand your strengths, and give your best.

Resources:
These are the resources that I referred to and followed during my preparation. Apart from these,
you can always search for good YouTube playlists for any subject or topic that you want to
learn. Also, don't underestimate LLMs like ChatGPT. They are probabl y one of the biggest
tutors available today. You just need to learn how to ask the right questions.
DSA
https://neetcode.io/
https://takeuforward.org/dsa/strivers-a2z-sheet-learn-dsa-a-to-z/
SQL
https://leetcode.com/studyplan/top-sql-50/
Roadmaps for Different Topics
https://roadmap.sh/
Aptitude
https://www.indiabix.com/
https://www.youtube.com/@FeelFreetoLearn
Puzzles
https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/aptitude/top-100-puzzles-asked-in-interviews/

If you have any doubts or just want to connect, feel free to reach out to me on any social media
platform. My username is usually @theonlydevrai on LinkedIn, Instagram, X, and so on .
WhatsApp has also introduced usernames, and I have reserved the same username         there as
well. So, if that feature has been rolled out for everyone by the time you're reading this, you
can message me there too. I generally avoid sharing my personal phone number for privacy
reasons.
That said, my LinkedIn DMs are always open, and I would definitely recommend using
LinkedIn. It is one of the best professional platforms for networking, finding opportunities, and
learning from others.
Once again, all the very best for your placements. I hope this experience helps you in some
way, and I genuinely wish all of you the very best. Hope to see many of you sharing your own
success stories soon.
