journey.howSecured:
1. Resume Shortlisting

The first stage was resume-based shortlisting. Although the exact criteria are not known, having at least one
project related to AI/ML can be helpful. Try to maintain a CGPA of 8.5+, as the competition and number of
applicants are increasing, making academics an important factor in shortlisting.
Having internships of at least 3 months can also improve your chances. For Auxo Al specifically, an
internship is more useful if it is related to AI/ML, as domain-relevant experience is likely to carry more
value.
150 students were shortlisted for OA

2. OA [150 students]

The OA was of 1.5 hours and had 28 questions: 25 MCQs and 3 coding questions. The MCQS were quite
easy and were mainly based on basic ML concepts, along with some LLM-related questions and
aptitude. Questions covered topics like overfitting, tokens, embeddings, etc. The concepts covered in
ML, DL and NLP subjects were enough to solve these questions.
Coding Questions:-

1. The first coding question was based on strings and frequency. Given a string and an integer k, we had

to return only the characters whose frequency was greater than or equal to k, arranged in decreasing
order of frequency. Characters with the same frequency had to be sorted lexicographically and it also
contained both upper and lower case characters.
Example: s = "mississippi", k =2 → Output: isp.
Solved all the test cases
--- PAGE 2 ---

2. You are given a budget of k kibbles and an array of oranges. Each orange is represented by a pair

(cost, weight), where cost is the price of the orange and weight is its weight. Find the maximum
possible total weight of oranges that can be bought without the total cost exceeding k.
Example:- k=10
Oranges = I (4, 5), (5, 6), (3, 4), (6, 8) ]
Output= 13
It was a simple 0/1 knapsack problem
I was not able to clear only 1 test case of this question because i did not get time to write the
tabulation approach.

3. This question was tricky and tough. The question was based on a person who had planned a trip to

different cities and made postcards for each place, but the postcards got jumbled. We had to find the
correct order in which the cities were to be visited, given that no city was visited twice.
On reading the question, it seemed like a topological sort or BFS/DFS problem. We had to try
finding the starting city and then determine the order in which all the cities could be visited. A travel
cost was also given between two cities.
The difficult part was that the input consisted of city names, and the output required the ordered list
of cities along with the total travel cost.
Example:- Input:- [
("Lucerne", "Interlaken", 80),
("Zurich", "Lucerne", 50),
("Interlaken", "Zermatt", 120),
("Zermatt", "Geneva", 150)
Output:-
Order of cities:
Total Cost:
400
The sample test case were cleared but no hidden test case were solved for this question.
The question is easy but handling string names is tough because it requires mapping of names to
integers and vice versa.
The OA was conducted on the CodeChef platform. The errors shown for the coding questions were not very
descriptive, which made it difficult to understand and debug the code. Also, some candidates mentioned that
they were able to solve the second question using only memoization, so there is a possibility that the test
cases or questions may have varied between candidates.
15 students were shortlisted for interviews
The result came around 8 p.m.
--- PAGE 3 ---

3. Interview 1 [15 Students]

There were 15 students for the first interview round. We were given different interview slots, but due to
delays, the interviews started around 11 AM. There were 3 interview panels, and since they were running
short on time, after around 3 interviews, 2 panels started conducting the second round of interviews while
the remaining panel continued with the first round. I was then moved to another panel and ended up being
second last to give the first round interview, which was after lunch.
The interview started with "Introduce yourself, and the interviewer had my resume open on their laptop. He
then started asking questions about my projects and internships. I was asked to explain my projects and what
I had worked on during my internship. From the explanations, the interviewer picked specific topics and
started asking questions related to them. Since I had a project based on RAG, I was asked about the
complete RAG flow and some related concepts.
After covering my projects and internship, the interviewer started testing my knowledge of ML, NLP and
DL concepts. Questions were asked about Lasso and Ridge Regression, Ensemble Learning, Random Forest,
validation and testing, K-Fold Cross Validation, tokens, embeddings, RNN, LSTM, GRU, Transformers,
Attention Mechanism, and other related concepts. Most questions were focused on what these concepts are
and their general working.
I was also asked some SQL and DBMS questions, including joins, primary and foreign keys, CTES, and
normalization (INF, 2NF and 3NF). At the end, the interviewer asked if I had any questions.
Almost all questions were answered to the satisfaction of interviewer but in some questions there were some
terms that i could not recall but overall the interview was good.
This interview was around 45 minutes long.
Tip:- For interview know your resume well. Be prepared for any type of questions here. They will not leave
any topic from your resume. If you have mentioned some technology they will ask questions on it for sure.
Out of the 15 students, 8 students were selected for the next round.

4. Interview 2 [ 8 Students]

This was a technical interview, but the interviewer also included several case-study and problem-solving
questions. The interview started with an introduction, followed by a discussion about my projects. One of
my projects was skipped because my teammate had already explained it in detail during Round 1, so we
briefly discussed my other projects similar to the previous round.
I was then asked to explain TF-IDF which i was able to explain. Then i was asked about knowledge graphs
but for this i could not answer properly.
The interview then moved to case studies. We had some fun conversation about what type of questions he
should ask, and when I said he should ask something that would get me selected, he jokingly replied that he
would give me a tougher question.
--- PAGE 4 ---
The first case study was based on Zomato entering a new Tier-2 city. The expected daily orders were 10,000,
with an average order value of 7300. Restaurants gave 20% of the order value to Zomato as commission,
Zomato paid 350 per delivery to the delivery partner, and there was a fixed daily cost of <2,00,000. I had to
determine whether the business would be profitable and suggest ways to make it profitable. It involved a
simple calculation followed by an open-ended discussion about what could be changed to improve
profitability. I started with we can take like a platform fee of like Rs.10 this will make the business break
even and then i told we can pitch restaurants that we can provide them special marketing and we would
charge them 23% commission. Then I also said that we could not reduce the delivery cost but if we would
club the delivery of the same localities in that way we could reduce the cost. Since this was relatively
straightforward, I completed it quickly.
The interviewer then gave me another case study where a company's profit margin had suddenly decreased,
even though it had been gradually increasing before. I was asked to identify possible reasons for the sudden
drop. I initially suggested several possibilities such as increased competition, higher commissions, raw
material costs, import/export duties, labour costs and operational costs. However, these were not the
expected answer because none of these factors had changed.
During the discussion, he noticed my surname, Zaveri, and asked whether my family was involved in the
jewellery business. When I mentioned that I come from a business family, he jokingly said that I should be
able to solve the question and he will not help me with this question.
After I gave several more possibilities, he provided an important hint: the company's revenue had actually
increased during the period when the profit margin decreased. Based on this, we discussed the possible
reasons, and I eventually arrived at the expected answer: increased marketing expenditure. The additional
marketing cost reduced the profit margin, while the increased marketing also helped increase the company's
revenue. I was clear that the profit margin reduced suddenly so there would be a change in costing or some
extra expenditure and it was clear that cost of materials and other things are the same so i had to think of all
the expenditures that could have increased.
The interview ended with the interviewer asking if I had any questions.
This interview was around 45-50 minutes long.

5. HR Round [5 Students]

This was not an interview round, here the hr personally called and gave results.
After around 6:00 pm all the Round 2 interviews were completed, we were informed that 5 students had
been selected for the HR round. We were told that the HR round would be conducted online, so we were
asked to go home and were asked to be available around 7:30 PM.
Later, we came to know that it would actually be a phone call rather than a video interview. Based on
previous interview experiences, I expected it to be a normal conversation, but I still went through some
common HR questions while waiting.
After a long wait, I finally received the call around 9:30 PM. The HR informed me that I had been selected
for the internship and the full-time opportunity afterwards and then explained the compensation breakdown
and other details.
All 5 of them were selected for the internship and full time offer.
--- PAGE 5 ---

Process Date: 9th July (OA), 10th July 2026 (Interviews)

Preparation Tips

• During the months of June-July, I used to pick one topic each day and revise all the

problems from Striver's Sheet under that topic. (Try not to look at the solution
immediately. First, attempt to come up with the brute-force approach, then improve it
step by step until you reach the optimal solution).

• If you're starting your preparation late, don't panic. Focus on giving your best instead of

worrying about the time left. Divide your day into DSA, core subjects (DBMS, OS, CN,
OOPS, SQL, etc.), and aptitude so that you make consistent progress in all areas.

• One common mistake I see is that people spend most of their time watching DSA videos

instead of solving problems themselves. Watching solutions alone won't significantly
improve your problem-solving skills because, during interviews and OAs, you'll need
to come up with the approach on your own. Instead, use Al or YouTube to find important
problems under each topic, and then make sure you solve those problems completely by
yourself. For the remaining questions, it's fine to read the solution or watch an
explanation to cover more topics efficiently.(Read the interview experiences of
companies which visit campus and accordingly make a list of topics which should be
prioritized first)

• Internships definitely help, as interviewers often spend a significant amount of time

discussing your work experience. However, don't worry if you don't have one. In that
case, make sure your projects are strong enough to demonstrate your technical skills and
problem-solving ability.

• Prepare concise notes in advance. Before the placement season starts, make short

revision notes for every subject. They become extremely useful before OAs and
interviews when you don't have time to go through entire resources again.

• Maintain a separate aptitude formula sheet. Keep all important formulas and

commonly used concepts in one place so that you can revise them quickly before an OA.

• For SDE projects, Be prepared to explain:

• Database schema

--- PAGE 2 ---

• REST APIs and their purpose

• Why you chose your tech stack

• Why you selected a particular database

• Challenges faced during development

• Fallback mechanisms and error handling

• Possible improvements if you had to redesign the system

• For ML projects: Be prepared to explain your dataset, model architecture, training

pipeline, loss function, optimizer, evaluation metrics, hyperparameters, and why you
chose your approach over alternative methods.
Auxo Al Process:

1. Resume Shortlisting

The process started with resume shortlisting. Although I don't know the exact number of
applicants, there was a good amount of competition. My advice would be to tailor your resume
according to the job description. Since this was an AI Engineer role, I had included two AI/ML
projects and one SDE project on my resume .Based on my experience, I would recommend
prioritizing AI/ML based projects on your resume if you're applying for this role, as they
significantly increase your chances of getting shortlisted. Also make sure your ATS score is at
least 70. (Adding quantifiable metrics no of users using your platform, ML project results etc)
helps increase your ATS score).
Results: 150 students moved forward to the Online Assessment.

2. Online Assessment (150 students appeared)

This year, the OA duration was 90 minutes and consisted of:

• 25 MCQs

• 3 Coding Questions

The assessment was conducted offline on CodeChef (Java was available this year).
MCQs
I found the MCQs to be fairly easy. They were a mix of Machine Learning, LLMs, and
Aptitude.
Some of the ML/LLM topics included:

• What is a token?

--- PAGE 3 ---

• Context window/context size

• Overfitting

• Supervised vs Unsupervised Learning

• General Al concepts

The aptitude section mainly consisted of:

• Analogies

• Coding-Decoding

• Ratio & Proportion

• Basic logical reasoning

Overall, if you have a good understanding of basic ML concepts and practice aptitude
beforehand, the MCQ section is quite manageable.
Coding Questions
Q1. Frequency-Based String Filtering
You are given a string and an integer k. Return a new string containing only the characters whose
frequency is greater than or equal to k, arranged in sorted order.
This was a fairly straightforward problem and could be solved using a TreeMap (or HashMap +
sorting).
Q2. Maximum Weight within Budget
A person has k kibbles to spend, and you're given an array of (cost, weight) pairs for oranges.
The task was to find the maximum total weight of oranges that could be purchased without
exceeding the budget.
This is essentially a 0/1 Knapsack problem.
I solved it using 2D Dynamic Programming.
Q3. Reconstruct Travel Route
A person had notes for a trip in the format:
Mumbai Goa 500
Goa Bangalore 600
Bangalore Chennai 400
The notes had become shuffled, and we had to reconstruct the correct travel sequence and
--- PAGE 4 ---
calculate the total travel cost.
Unfortunately, I couldn't attempt this question due to lack of time.
I was able to solve 2 coding questions completely.
From what I observed, everyone who had solved 2 coding questions completely was shortlisted
for the next round.
Additional Points for the OA

• I would recommend attempting the assessment on Google Chrome. I initially used

Firefox, but I experienced a few minor issues with the platform. Chrome seemed to work
more smoothly.

• Unlike platforms like LeetCode, you need to write the complete code yourself, including

taking input from standard input and printing the output in the required format.

• Also check the network connectivity beforehand. Once you start the test and if there is

any network lag you won't be able to change the network so it's better to test it before the
exam.
15 students were shortlisted for the technical interviews.
We got the list of shortlisted students at around 8PM and the next day from 10 AM interviews
were going to start.

3. Technical Interview Round 1 (15 students appeared)(40-45 mins)

The interview started with a brief introduction, after which the interviewer immediately started
discussing my resume. They covered all three of my projects during the interview.
Project Discussion :
The majority of the interview was centered around my ML projects.
Federated Learning Project
The interviewer wasn't familiar with the concept of Federated Learning, so I first explained the
complete idea, why it is used, and how it differs from traditional centralized learning.
Since I had mentioned using a Reinforcement Learning (RL) Agent in my project, they went
deeper into that and asked:

• Why did you use Reinforcement Learning?

• How does the RL agent work?

--- PAGE 5 ---

• Explain the complete RL loop used in the project

• How does the agent improve over time?

SDE Project
From my backend project, they asked questions like:

• Role of Redis in my project

• Difference between Docker and Virtual Machines

• Working of Kubernetes

Small Language Model (SLM) Project
For my SLM project, they asked:

• What was the dataset format?

• Which model did you use?

• Number of model parameters

• Overall training pipeline

• What is Perplexity?

• Why did I use Mixed Precision Training?

Internship Experience
Since I had two internships on my resume, they also asked me to explain both.
For my AI Engineering Internship, they asked about the Al systems and automation solutions I
had worked on, what were the hurdles faced while development, and what security constraints
were used.
For my SDE Internship, they asked me to give a high-level overview of the projects, my
responsibilities, and the technologies I used.
SQL Questions
Towards the end, I was asked a few SQL questions, including:

• Types of JOINs

• Primary Key vs Foreign Key

• GROUP BY

• PARTITION BY

At the end of the interview, when the interviewer asked if I had any questions, I had a technical
discussion based on the work I was currently doing.
--- PAGE 6 ---
I was working on an Agentic Al project at the time, so towards the end of the interview, I asked
the interviewer how their team handles hallucinations and error propagation in multi-agent
workflows, where incorrect outputs from one agent can affect all downstream agents. This led to
a very interesting technical discussion. The interviewer first asked me to explain my project in
more detail, after which he shared some of the techniques their team follows to improve
reliability. Based on his explanation, I asked a few follow-up questions.
My Advice: Be prepared to justify every single technology, model, library, and term you
mention on your resume.
Even if you've worked with any LLM APIs, know exactly:

• Which model you used

• Why did you choose that model

• Whether it was an API-based or open-source model.

• If it's an open-source model, know its approximate number of parameters, architecture,

and why it suited your use case.
The same applies to ML projects. If you've mentioned a model or algorithm, be prepared to
explain:

• Dataset

• Model architecture

• Loss function (with intuition and formula)

• Optimizer (with intuition and formula)

• Evaluation metrics

• Learning rate scheduler

• Training pipeline

• Hyperparameters

• Why did you select that particular approach over alternatives

Also one of the panelists was from a consulting background. So he was asking a little tough
guesstimates in 1st round itself so be prepared for it.

4. Technical + Business Round (8 students appeared) (30-40 mins)

Instead of asking questions from multiple projects, the interviewer picked one of my Al
Engineering internship projects and went into great depth.
The interviewer first asked me to explain my project from start to finish.
After that, they asked several follow-up questions, including:

• The complete end-to-end workflow of the system.

--- PAGE 7 ---

• Why I designed the architecture the way I did.

• What fallback mechanisms I had implemented if one component failed.

• The major challenges I faced while building the system.

• How I identified those issues and the approach I took to solve them.

The discussion was less about definitions and more about understanding how I think while
building production AI systems.
The interviewer then moved to my ML projects.
For my projects, he asked me to justify almost every important design choice(Optimization
technique, loss function etc).
Then for my SLM project, they asked questions about the model architecture, such as:

• How positional embeddings are added.

• Where were the positional embeddings introduced in the model.

• What are positional embeddings initialized as in the pipeline

• Overall transformer flow.

• Training pipeline.

Guesstimate:
Towards the end, I was given a business case study.
The interviewer asked:
"Suppose you are the founder of Uber. You want to introduce a new pricing model
where every driver is paid ?X per kilometre. How would you determine the value of
X such that existing Uber drivers are satisfied with their earnings while also making
the platform attractive enough for drivers working with competing companies to
switch to Uber?"
This wasn't a mathematics question with a single correct answer. The interviewer wanted to
understand my approach. Also all the details won't be given to you at the start. It's important
to ask the right questions as you are moving towards the answer.
At the end of the interview, I asked him : What metrics does AuxoAl use to evaluate the quality
of responses generated by Al models and When a client approaches AuxoAl with a problem,
how do you determine whether investing in an Al solution is actually worthwhile, More
specifically, how do you measure the ROI or business impact of the AI system after it's deployed.
At the end of the day at around 6 PM when all round 2 interviews were finished, we were
informed that 5 candidates had been selected for an HR interview which is going to be online
later that evening.
--- PAGE 8 ---
Later that evening, instead of conducting a separate HR round, the company directly informed all
the shortlisted candidates that we had been selected.
Resources

• SQL: I had practiced SQL 50 on leetcode. For revising SQL concepts quickly, I found

Apna College's SQL One Shot to be helpful (Also make sure you make good notes to
revise before interviews ).

• DSA: I primarily used Striver's DSA Sheet along with NeetCode for preparation.

Although Striver's sheet itself covers almost every important DSA concept, NeetCode is a
great supplementary resource for additional practice and explanations. (For Auxo I feel
Striver's sheet is more than enough)

• Aptitude: I had practiced from IndiaBix and Code Step By Step YT channel

• Guesstimates: Be sure to prepare guesstimates thoroughly. There are plenty of good

You Tube videos that explain the approach to solving them.

• ML : https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/machine-learning/machine-learning/. And for

reading in detail about transformers and all I prefer reading blogs on Medium they
provide content in depth.
I am attaching my resume for reference: Namrata_Dalvi_Resume
For any help, reach out to me on LinkedIn.

prominently above projects.

2. Online Assessment - (153 selected for OA)

The OA was conducted on Codechef ond consisted of 28 questions covering DSA,
Machine Legrning, and Aptitude. The questions were mixed throughout the paper
rather than being divided into separate sections.
--- PAGE 2 ---
DSA (3 questions):

1) A graph based question.

Given o jumbled list of edges (city1, city2, cost). Each city can only be visited once.
We needed to find the order of travel and also the total cost.
The approach was quite simple:

1) Find the city with 0 out degree. This is the last city.

2) Trace back upto the first city.

3) Then print ans in reverse order.

2) A classic 0/1 Knapsack-style DP problem. Although constraints allowed recursion

as well.

3) Frequency relted String question. Could be done by sorting or using

min-heap/PriorityQueue.
I was oble to solve all three questions. However, one of the questions had some issue with
one testcose, it showed runtime error on thot specific test case for everyone.
Mochine Learning Section:

• The ML MCQS ranged from medium to hard and covered core ML concepts. There

was no negative marking.

• Proctising the GeeksforGeeks Mochine Leorning MCQS should provide good

preparation.
Aptitude Section:

• The optitude section was of moderate difficulty.

• IndiaBix is a good resource for practice.

3. Technical Round 1 - (15 students were selected)

15 students were shortlisted for Technical Round 1. There were three interview panels.
The interview began with a brief self-introduction, followed by a discussion on one of the
projects mentioned in my resume, specificolly my multi-agent project. As I was
explaining the overall architecture and workflow, the interviewer interrupted midway,
which I believe indicated that he was satisfied with my explanation and wanted to move
on.
Next, I was asked several conceptual questions on Generative AI and Agentic AI,
including the differences between the two. The interviewer also chollenged my responses
with follow-up questions such as,ẠIf we give a Generative AI model access to an MCP
server, does it become Agentic AI?" Other topics included whether Agentic AI is st1teful,
--- PAGE 3 ---
the concept of statelessness, authentication, What is temperture?, etc. Questions on
core subjects like OOPS, DBMS were also sked.
The discussion was highly interactive, with the interviewer frequently building upon my
answers. After exploining my reasoning and addressing the follow-up questions, he
seemed satisfied with my responses.
The next question was a case study based on Zomato's business model. I was given
details such as the average monthly revenue, commission earned, driver costs, delivery
charges, and other expenses. I had to determine whether the company was making a
profit or a loss.
It's perfectly fine to osk the interviewer to repeat or clorify the question if something isn't
clear. In my case, I initially misunderstood one component related to the delivery fee,
which led to incorrect calculutions. After the interviewer clarified the question, I
recalculated everything correctly and concluded that the business was operating at a
loss.
Finally, I was asked to suggest strategies to improve profitability. I proposed three
practical solutions, and the interviewer appeared satisfied with my approach and
reasoning.

4. Technical Round 2 - (7 students were selected)

This was primarily an in-depth technical round. We storted with brief introductions, after
which the interviewer picked one of my projects and went deep into it. The project was
inspired by a problem statement from Nomura Kakushin, and I was asked several
questions ground its architecture, workflow, scolability, and security.
I explained the complete system flow ond orchitecture, including how the different
components interacted with each other. I also discussed why the system was scalable, the
security measures I had implemented (like PII) and how I would strengthen those
measures further in a production environment. I was able to answer most of the
questions, olthough I was again interrupted midway while explaining the flow :).
The discussion then moved toward system design ond RAG. Since the project involved an
agentic workflow with RAG, the interviewer asked something along the lines of:
"Suppose you have a million documents. How would you efficiently retrieve the
relevant informationạẠạ
He also asked me to assume that computational resources were unlimited. I initially
suggested approaches such as metadata-based filtering and clustering embeddings
using techniques like agglomerative clustering. He chollenged this approach from a
--- PAGE 4 ---
real-world fedsibility perspective, which led the discussion toward keyword-based
search, information retrieval, and hybrid search approaches.
We olso discussed how systems like ChotGPT can search multiple sources on the internet
in parallel, which turned into a broader discussion around search architecture and
efficient information retrieval at scale.
After that, the interviewer storted picking rondom technologies and concepts from my
resume. Some of the questions included:

• What is CI/CD?

• What is Pydantic?

• Questions about my SPJIMR project internship experience

One interesting moment was when he osked me to rote my Python proficiency. Since
Java is my primary language and Spring Boot is my main backend framework, I
honestly roted myself around 5-6/10. He seemed slightly surprised, so I clarified thot
although I sometimes use AI assistance while coding, I am comfortable designing the
backend architecture, deciding the system flow, and understanding the implementation.
He then asked me to explain the project structure and backend organization, which I was
able to explain in detail.
Overoll, the round was heavily focused on projects, system design, RAG/LLM concepts,
backend architecture, scalability, security, and the technologies mentioned on my
resume. The interviewer also kept chollenging my initial answers with real-world
constroints, so it was less about simply knowing definitions and more about
understanding why a particular approach would or wouldn't work in production.
Then interviewer asked if I had any questions for him. I asked him what kind of agentic
workflows do they build for enterprises at Auxo. He gave an example of the work they did
recently of automating the market research step by using different personas. He also
shored o funny incident regarding cloude code.

and participate in as many contests as you can on LeetCode, CodeChef, and Codeforces. Contests really help
you get used to solving problems within a time limit.
If you're good at DSA, you'll be able to clear the OA rounds of most companies. Before Auxo Al, I had
already cleared the OAs for PhonePe and IDFC, and I learned a lot from the mistakes I made during those
interview processes.
Before your interviews, prepare your introduction and project explanations really well. Focus on your
strengths and use the breadcrumb strategy while answering questions. For example, while explaining
chunking in my RAG pipeline, I connected it to the concept of the cross-attention mechanism while
discussing how overlapping chunks can improve retrieval quality. This naturally sparked a discussion about
cross-attention, and since I was comfortable with the topic, I was able to explain it confidently.
Also, don't give generic interview answers. Research about the company and the role beforehand. Be ready
with a short story about why you're a good fit, even if your resume isn't perfectly aligned with the role.
Interviewers often care more about your analytical thinking and problem-solving approach.
One thing that's really important is keeping your CGPA above 8. It matters for shortlisting at many elite
companies.
And finally, luck is definitely a part of the placement process, but that's something you can't control. Just
keep working hard, focus on what you can improve, and enjoy the journey. Placements often come when
you least expect them.
All the very best!

journey.howSecured:
1. Resume Shortlisting

Although I didn't know the exact shortlisting criteria, around 150 students were shortlisted in this round.
From my experience, one thing that likely helped was having a resume that closely matched the job
description. So, I'd recommend including the skills, tools, and programming languages mentioned in the JD
to improve your chances of getting shortlisted.
Resume Tips:

1. Since this was an AI/ML role, I'd recommend having AI/ML-related projects on your resume. All

three projects on my resume were based on AI/ML, which aligned well with the role.

2. Try to include your model accuracy, performance metrics for your projects. It makes your projects

look more impactful and can also help improve your ATS score.

3. Internship experience is always an advantage during placements. If possible, complete an internship

before the placement season begins. Although I did not have internship experience, my projects were
closely aligned with the job description.

2. Online Assessment (150 students appeared)

The online assessment was conducted on campus and lasted 90 minutes. It consisted of 25 MCQS and 3
DSA coding questions.
The MCQs covered basic AI/ML concepts such as:

• Supervised vs. Unsupervised Learning

• Overfitting

• Tokens in LLMs

• Context Window

--- PAGE 2 ---

• Model weight storage formats

There were also a few aptitude questions on topics like Analogies, Coding-Decoding, Ratio & Proportion,
and Basic Logical Reasoning. Overall, the MCQs were fairly easy if you had a good understanding of basic
Al/ML concepts and had practiced aptitude questions beforehand.
The coding section consisted of the following problems:
Q1. Basic String Sorting
Given a string and you have to return a new string where the characters are sorted based on their frequency.
Q2. Maximum weight within Budget
You were given an array of (cost,weights) pairs representing oranges. The task was to find the maximum
total weight of oranges that could be purchased without exceeding the given budget. This was a standard 0/1
Knapsack problem.
Q3. Reconstruct Travel Route
You were given shuffled travel records in the format:
Mumbai Goa 500
Goa Bangalore 600
Bangalore Chennai 400
The task was to reconstruct the correct travel route and calculate the total travel cost.
I was able to solve 2 coding questions completely, and since the MCQS were quite straightforward, the test
went well overall. From what I observed, most students who solved 2 or more coding questions were
shortlisted for the interview rounds. In the end, 15 students were selected for interviews.

3. Technical Interview Round 1(15 students appeared)

The interview started with my introduction. After that, the interviewer picked one of my agentic Al projects
from my resume and asked me to explain it. I gave a brief overview covering all the major functionalities.
Then he started asking about the role of each agent, what tools I was using, the API endpoints in the project,
and how I had implemented one of the core functionalities. After I explained it, he asked how I could
optimize that implementation. We had a good discussion about different optimization approaches and how I
would go about implementing them.
Next, he moved on to my second project. I gave a brief introduction, and since I mentioned that it used
RAG, he started asking RAG-related questions. He asked how I was collecting data for the RAG pipeline,
how I had implemented it, how I would decide the right chunk size, and how I was retrieving context from
the vector database for the LLM.
--- PAGE 3 ---
After that, he asked how I could optimize the RAG pipeline. I mentioned things like reranking, metadata
filtering, and using different retrievers. He then asked how I would actually implement those optimizations
and how libraries like LangChain handle them internally. We also discussed common problems in RAG
systems and possible solutions.
After that, he wrapped up the interview. Before leaving, I asked him how Auxo Al handles hallucinations in
LLMs. He explained their approach and how they work on reducing hallucinations. It turned into a really
interesting discussion.
A few tips from my experience:

• Be confident while answering your questions.

• If you don't know something, it's completely fine to say you don't know. After that, you can share

how you would approach the problem or what you think the solution might be instead of making up
an answer.

• Whatever technologies you mention on your resume, make sure you know them well because most

of the questions will come from your own projects and tech stack.

• It's perfectly okay if your resume isn't packed with every possible technology. A smaller resume that

you can confidently defend is much better than a long one where you struggle to answer questions.

• I wasn't confident about deep learning, so I didn't include it on my resume. Highlight your strengths

instead, and even in your introduction, focus on the areas you're most comfortable with.

4. Technical + Business Round (8 students appeared)

The second interview round also started with a brief introduction. Since the interviewer came from a
consulting background, he wasn't focused on asking very deep technical questions.
He started with one of my projects and asked why I chose that particular tech stack, what functionalities the
project had, and what challenges I faced while building it. There was one technology he didn't understand
why I had used that particular technology in the project, so I explained the problem I was trying to solve and
how that technology helped address it. He seemed satisfied with my explanation. We had a similar
discussion about my second project as well.
After that, we moved on to the case study. He gave me a scenario where there was a restaurant outside my
college that originally served Indian food. The owner's son took over and completely changed the menu to
fast food. Students loved the new menu, there was always a long queue outside the restaurant, but
surprisingly, the restaurant's revenue had started decreasing.
I was asked to act as an analyst and analyze the situation. He gave me a few minutes to think, and then we
discussed my approach. I suggested multiple possible reasons, and he kept correcting my thought process.
Eventually, with a hint I arrived at the answer he was looking for. He then asked how I would increase the
restaurant's revenue. I answered using a real-life example that I had seen, and he seemed happy with my
response.
The interview ended with me asking him about his career journey and one of the services offered by Auxo
AI. We had a nice discussion before wrapping up.
--- PAGE 4 ---
After all the interviews were over, we were informed that five candidates had been shortlisted for an online
HR interview later that evening.
However, instead of conducting a separate HR round, the company directly informed all the shortlisted
candidates that we had been selected.

This round was based on your resume, pay attention to the ppt to understand what they want in a candidate and what the role is about, tailor your resume not only for the technical keywords but also for what the role requires, for example, the role requires us to sit close to non-technical people and observe how they work and how we can make their lives easier by simplifying their workflows.

Here is a resume I generally used:

v/s the one I applied with:

They asked to put a photo on the resume, even if they don't mention it, I think it is better to do so (might be right, might be wrong).

All in all, pay attention to what you put in your resume. I highlighted how I collaborated with different people during my internships, and how they made the product better, the role was agentic so I swapped a deep learning project for one with agentic AI and which made it easier for people to log their complaints.

Basically don't stop at keyword matching for tailoring your resume, go the extra mile to reword your experiences, because that's literally the selection criteria -- Your resume.

2. Round 2 Name:  Technical interview [Only 10 students made it to this round]

We were given a take home assessment, pay attention to ppt, that will guide you how to interpret the take home assessment, and make your solution appeal better to the interviewers. The assignment was to make interfaces for a senior leader and a risk analyst based on the given dataset, the interface should make their jobs easier by allowing them to focus on exactly where they have to make a decision and how to prioritize which case/part of the process they should look at.
My interview was around the assessment itself, all the interviews were only 30 minutes, so you need to be quick, the interviewer then asked about my work, what tools I use, how I solve a problem when given one (again, pay attention to the ppt and the job description, you will understand how to answer these questions from there).
The interviewer didn't ask me if I had any questions, but I asked the interviewer if I can ask them a question, so I asked "Was there anything about this interview that would make you think that this is not a good fit?" Of course they couldn't answer directly but they did give me feedback to be quick, specially because we only had 30 minutes in the interview.

3. HR interview: [5 Of us made it to HR]

First question was "Tell me about yourself", I began by introducing myself and how I solve problems, HR was kind enough to interrupt me and correct me "Not technical, about yourself, your hobby, interests, family background".
Be yourself in HR round thats all (of course be formal and prepare for some standard HR questions as well).

4 students were offered the job.

journey.howSecured:
Application → Resume Shortlisting → Culture Aptitude Test & Cognitive Ability Test (AON) → Technical
Interview → HR Interview → Offer
Around 200 students appeared for the initial selection process . The process began with submitting an
application through Superset, followed by registration on the UBS career portal. After completing the
application, applicants received two assessment links: the Culture Aptitude Test and the Cognitive Ability
Test. The Culture Aptitude Test consisted of around 16-18 scenario -based questions , where we had to
choose how we would respond to different workplace situations. The Cognitive Ability Test consisted of two
sections: verbal reasoning, where we had to read short passages and answer questions based on them, and a
cognitive/pattern-based section , where we had to identify and match different patterns or figures. After
completing both assessments, the candidates were further shortlisted, and 10 candidates were selected for
the Interview round. We Received results on 9/09/2026 about the shortlisting.

1. Technical Round [10 Candidates]

For the technical round, on 10 September 2026 , we were given a problem statement along with a dataset
containing around 1,000 entries. We were asked to build an AI-based solution and submit both an HTML
file containing the solution and a supporting PPT . The deadline for submission was 2:00 PM on 11
September, giving us roughly a day to understand the problem, analyze the dataset, develop the solution and
prepare the presentation. While working on the assignment, I tried to align my solution with the job
description, particularly by incorporating elements related to AI, automation and the kind of work expected
from the Agentic Automation team. Before the interview, I also researched the professional backgrounds of
the senior manager, other interviewers and the HR representative, so that I could better understand their
work and have a more meaningful conversation during the interview.
My technical interview was scheduled on 11 September at around 6:30 PM , as the panel included
interviewers working with the US team. I started with a brief introduction and then walked the interviewers
through my solution, explaining my approach, reasoning and the additional elements I had incorporated. The
senior manager particularly appreciated the way I approached and explained the solution and mentioned that

my reasoning and walkthrough were very strong. He even told me that he was "scoring me in the top," which
was a really encouraging moment for me. What I particularly enjoyed was that the interview did not feel very
formal or intimidating. The interviewers were extremely friendly, and the entire discussion was quite
casual, interactive and even had a few funny moments.  Rather than simply asking rapid -fire technical
questions, they were interested in understanding my thought process and discussing the solution with me. The
entire technical interview lasted around 30 minutes.
Towards the end, I was given an opportunity to ask questions. I asked one question about the work culture
at UBS and what it was like working within the organization. I also asked the interviewer a more casual
question: "How was your weekend?"  He had actually asked me the same question at the beginning of the
interview, so I thought of asking it back at the end. He was quite happy with the question and shared that he
had actually spent part of his weekend working on a project. That small interaction made the conversation feel
much more natural and genuine. Overall, it was a very positive and memorable interview experience , not
only because of the technical discussion and feedback on my solution, but also because of how comfortable
and approachable the interviewers were throughout the interaction.

2. HR Round [5 Candidates]

After the technical interviews on 11 September , only five candidates were shortlisted for the HR
round. We received the shortlist notification on the morning of 12 September at around 9:00 AM, and
the HR interview was scheduled for around 11:00 AM the same day. The HR interview was very Short
and lasted only around 5-6 minutes. Interestingly, the HR interviewer had also been present during my
technical interview and had been taking notes on my solution and my approach. She mentioned that the
senior manager was very happy with my solution and had rated my performance highly , so the HR
discussion was relatively short. She mainly asked me about my background, my understanding of the work
culture at UBS , and how I viewed the internship opportunity. She also explained a little about the
internship, the work environment and what I could expect from the role. Towards the end, she asked if I
had any questions. I asked her, from an HR perspective, what value and growth opportunities UBS
provides to students joining the company, and she explained how the organization supports employees
and their development. Overall, the HR round was very conversational and comfortable. The interview
was scheduled in the 11:00-11:15 AM window, but my actual discussion lasted only a few minutes. The
final results were announced at around 1:00 PM on the same day, and I was extremely happy to see my
name among the selected candidates.
4 students were offered the role and I was one of them.
Tips for the Interview:

1. Stay Calm: Interviews can be nerve-wracking, but your ability to think clearly under pressure is just

as important as your technical knowledge.

2. Know Your Projects Well: Be prepared to explain not only what you built, but also why you made

specific technical decisions and be ready to confidently justify your choices.

3. Think Out Loud: Avoid going completely silent while solving a problem. Share your thought process

with the interviewerit helps keep the conversation engaging and demonstrates how you approach
challenges.

4. Be Honest When You're Stuck:  It is completely fine to ask for a hint or admit that you are unsure

about something. What matters is how you approach the problem and respond to the situation.

5. Understand Your Resume Thoroughly: Be ready to discuss anything you have mentioned on your

resume, including your projects, technologies, internships and achievements.

6. Focus on the "Why": Don't just explain the implementation. Be prepared to discuss why you chose

a particular approach, technology or architecture and what alternatives you considered.

7. Tailor Your Resume to the Job Role: This is extremely important. Before applying, carefully read

the job description and make sure your resume highlights the skills, projects, technologies, and
experiences most relevant to the role. Avoid using the exact same resume for every position. A well
tailored resume makes it easier for the interviewer to see why your profile is a good match for the
specific role.
Resources I Followed

1. DSA: Striver's A2Z DSA Sheet

2. SQL: SQL 50

3. DBMS: Complete DBMS in 1 Video (With Notes) | For Placement Interviews

4. OOPs: GeeksforGeeks

5. Operating Systems & Computer Networks: GeeksforGeeks

6. CS Fundamentals Practice: GeeksforGeeks and InterviewBit for practicing recently asked

interview questions and strengthening core concepts.

Final thoughts:
Every interview I had before UBS, including IDFC FIRST Bank, ISS STOXX, J.P. Morgan, Quantiphi ,
and many others, taught me something new. Each experience helped me become more comfortable with
interviews and gave me a better understanding of the kind of work I wanted to pursue. At the time, not
receiving an offer was definitely disappointing, even though every interview itself was a great learning
experience. But after getting selected at UBS, I genuinely felt grateful that those earlier opportunities did
not work out. When I understood the role at UBS, I realized that this was the kind of work I ha d actually
been looking for. It made me believe even more that sometimes things do not work out for a reason. We
may not understand it at the time, but the right opportunity can eventually come along. In the end, I believe
our job is simply to keep trying,  keep learning, and keep moving forward. The rest, in many ways, is
destiny.
If you have any specific questions, please feel free to reach out on: LinkedIn
All the best for your placements!

candidates who know nothing, but JUST DSA- both of which leaves behind a great developer who
KNOWS HOW TO BUILD, IDEATE, COLLABORATE; and such candidates which are a PERFECT
VIBE MATCH FOR CULTURE.
So yes, in this part- UBS genuinely made a selection process that is 100% apt for 2026 (and coming time)
where companies want a T-shaped over an I-shaped candidate profile (just search on Internet what this
--- PAGE 2 ---
means, and it would be pretty clear). Alright, with this being said, the following were the rounds conducted
by the company-

1. Company Presentation

2. Group Coding Round (More of Group Ideating, and Presentation)

3. Pen-Paper Based MCQ Round (Best decision to use Pen-Paper)

4. Technical Interview

5. HR Round

1. Group Coding Round

So, UBS had shortlisted around 50 candidates or so for the whole process based on the resume (I presume,
as the true nature of selection was not disclosed, so am assuming it was a resume screening). In this round,
we were given a Problem Statement- "How we would optimize and better the Fraud Detection System of
UBS" (they gave a sheet, which had a small dataset, and also, the Detection System of UBS means, a
simple, rule based). So, during this time, our team split the work- now I could code, as well make a good
PPT- but everyone wanted to code (lol, cause it was NAMED as a GROUP CODING round)-so I said, I
don't mind and would rather prepare the PPT along with System Design for the same.
We were said to be given 90mins, but it was just 70mins max. We made the ppt, while my teammates
worked on the coding aspect, and in midst of that, people from UBS were asking us, WHAT OUR
APPROACH WAS, WHY, and I remember, there was this UBS Employee- not so senior- he came,
listened, and then, seemed to like our idea, and gave me a tip that, we should even look for the COLUMNS
AND THE DATA THAT IS NOT HERE- thus, I really liked the advice, and even made sure, we prep for
every scenario. It's all about, presenting, knowing your solution, and backing it with tech decisions!

2. MCQ and Small Pen-Paper Based Test

After that 70mins of grind- we were told to start with the MCQ test ASAP- so, it seemed to be a bit
overwhelming, but then, the paper was simple. It was basic DSA MCQ, then Networking, a bit of OS (ig OS
was there, am not sure atp) - then there was a pseudocode based thing, a situational approach, debugging,
and stuff.
So, it rather had more focus on HOW YOU APPROACH PROBLEM and thinking, over the normal
SYNTAX FOCUSED DSA QUESTIONS. Thus, I would say, prepare core, thinking ability, and problem
solving- as this is something that is needed. Also, one thing am gonna say- NO MATTER HOW DUMB
DSA WOULD SEEM- IF A COMPANY NEEDS TT, AND YOU NEED TO JOIN A COMPANY-
WELL DSA IS THE THING YOU NEED TO GRIND (and as I said, 1 missed two good companies- all
thanks to me forgetting the Syntax and not clicking on time!)
Once this was over, they said, we had 30mins to refine the ppt and stuff before presenting. So, we spent time
refining, I explained who would say what, and why, I made counters for each of my teammates so that they
prepare for that as well, and then- we presented. The presentation was good enough- we got some good
responses- but the end was a bit sus feeling- which made me feel a bit nervous (let's not discuss that here).
--- PAGE 3 ---

3. Technical Interview

Now, before the technical interview started, I was preparing for it, and was revising "TELL ME ABOUT
YOURSELF" and going through the things I wrote in my resume and preparing for it. After some time,
there was an announcement of the news of selects and my name was not there (No.34) and I was heavily
disheartened but after 4mins- my number came and I rushed to TPO (aka CCD). We sat in the TPO for
around 10mins, and then the interview started.
Now, before I tell what happened in the tech-interview, hear me out- the tech interview becomes highly
LUCK BASED on who is in your panel, what is their expertise, and are they in mood to hire or not. This is
very luck based and that's something that is not in your hands too!
So, I got Panel-2, it had the same sir who gave me the advice in Round-1 and was even there in the
Presentation round, along with another Ma'am who too seemed to have liked the way I presented. Now, it
started with a brief introduction- and then, asked about my resume. The things routed from My Hackathon
winning PS, to docker, k&s, Linux, to even the usage of Al and places where Al should and shouldn't be
used- ending it with a situational tech question of debugging an improper responding API endpoint- thus an
overall Cloud and Linux Heavy (my domain) interview, with some situational, and perspective based
questions to see what decisions would I be taking as a Dev.
This was a rather chill and a smooth round- I would say, DO NOT FAKE ON YOUR RESUME, and be
confident, and have a smile. Be honest, and give your best!

4. HR Round

This was a rather quick for me- my tech interview went well, and it was hardly Smins, when I was called for
the HR Round- and the things that HR asked me was- "Explain a Project as if you explaining to a layman"
and then, we talked about my current Intern at HERE Technologies, and how its in the same IT Park and
some general topics; followed by which, she explained the relocation and formality- and it ended (this was a
legit 10min of thing for me- so yes, nothing much here)

journey.howSecured:
1. Resume Shortlisting  (153 candidates appeared)

153 students applied for this role, out of which only 51 were shortlisted for the next round. One of the biggest factors behind getting shortlisted is the ATS (Applicant Tracking System) score of your resume -- mine was 87. There are several websites available to check your ATS score; I'd recommend aiming for at least 85+, though anything above that only improves your chances.
I did not have any internship experience, so I had to go through many rounds of prompting and multiple resume drafts to push my ATS score up. It took effort, but I believe optimizing your resume this way is a necessary step to clear this round -- a score of 85+ should reliably get you shortlisted.

2. MCQ Test + Group Case Study Presentation

This round was originally supposed to follow the sequence: MCQ test (pen and paper) → group coding task. However, since the recruiters arrived late, we were asked to work on our group presentations first while the test was being set up.
We were divided into groups of 7 and given a problem statement: the current fraud detection system is rule-based, and we had to propose how it could be improved using an AI/ML-based (or any other) solution that is more scalable and effective at detecting fraud in transactions than a purely rule-based system. Each group was also given a set of 4+4 guiding questions to structure the answer around. We were given 1 hour to prepare a solution and design as a group before the MCQ test.
After the hour was up, we were seated two seats apart and given the MCQ test, which had three sections:

●       Section 1: Basic Python/SQL/DSA MCQs -- 10 questions.

●       Section 2: Code-snippet based questions -- we were given a code snippet, asked to explain its intended behavior, and how we would modify it to produce the correct output. There were 4 such questions, 5 marks each.

●       Section 3: A simple DSA coding question -- write a function that takes an array as a parameter and prints the top 3 unique elements (duplicates excluded). This was easily solvable using a hash map.

After the test, the presentation round began. There were 2 panels of judges (6 judges each), and only 7-8 teams in total, split across the two panels. My team had already divided the presentation into parts, which made things easier. We had built a multi-agent AI solution for fraud detection, and since we had some spare time, we generated supporting visuals and put together a PPT (using AI tools) to present our design.
There was no strict time limit -- we were told to aim for around 15 minutes, but it wasn't enforced strictly. During the presentation, I noticed that most of my teammates got nervous in front of the large panel and didn't present as clearly as expected; ultimately only two of us -- myself included -- were able to present confidently and clearly.
The judges seemed to notice who understood the solution well and specifically directed architecture-related cross-questions toward the less confident team members instead of letting the same one or two people answer everything. Judges from the other panel also walked in during our presentation and cross-questioned us, pointing out a few flaws in our system that we had to address on the spot.
In the end, only two people from my group of 7 -- myself and one other teammate -- presented and answered well, and both of us were selected to move forward. My advice for this round: understand your proposed solution thoroughly and be ready to justify every architectural decision. Most importantly, don't let a large panel of judges intimidate or demotivate you.
The shortlist for the interview round was based on a combination of the MCQ score and the presentation, though the presentation seemed to carry more weight since the MCQs were relatively easy. Around 2-3 candidates from each team were shortlisted -- 20 candidates in total moved on to interviews, and these began very shortly after the shortlist was announced.

3. [ Technical Interview] [ 20 people ]

My interview slot came up first, right after the shortlist was announced. I was fairly calm going in, having already interviewed (and been rejected) at a few other companies like Barclays, Auxo, and Russell -- each of those experiences had taught me what to prepare better for. My approach was to imagine the panel as friends and treat it like a normal conversation rather than a high-stakes interview.
The panel had two interviewers -- one technical and one HR -- though they didn't introduce themselves, so I inferred their roles from the questions they asked. It began with the standard "tell me about yourself."

●       I was asked to elaborate on the hackathons mentioned on my resume (an offline hackathon at Meta in Bangalore that required clearing qualifying rounds, and one at Amazon). I spoke about the Meta hackathon and the projects I built there.

●       Since most of my resume projects were AI-related, I was asked whether I'd be okay if I wasn't placed in an AI-specific role. I said I would be completely fine with it, since any role would be a learning experience.

●       I was asked why I was so inclined toward AI. I had prepared for this -- I answered with how, back in 2012, a lot of what seemed like science fiction is real today, and what bridges that gap is engineers building it.

●       I was asked to name the two skills I was most confident in. I said Python and JavaScript.

●       I was then asked to write code to reverse a string in Python. I directly wrote the most optimal solution I could think of, which they seemed to appreciate.

●       When asked about SQL, I was asked to write a query to reverse a string in SQL. I honestly said I didn't know how, but mentioned I was comfortable with relational tables, joins, and general SQL concepts. They seemed fine with the honest answer.

●       The last question from the HR side was, "Give me one reason why UBS?" I hadn't paid close attention to the company's introductory presentation, so my answer was fairly generic -- but it was good enough. My advice: pay attention to the company's PPT/introduction session so you have a specific, well-informed answer ready for this.

The interview wrapped up after this, and I was called back for the next (HR) round about 30-45 minutes later.

4. HR Round [10 people  were shortlisted ]

This round was much shorter and largely non-technical:

●       I was asked to explain my role in one of my projects in very simple, non-technical language, since the interviewer didn't have a technical background.

●       I was asked to choose between learning a new skill every day versus becoming a subject matter expert in one field. I chose learning something new every day, and explained how it helps me grow and think more creatively.

●       We discussed the Pune/Hyderabad location, the compensation package, and the expectation to relocate.

●       I was asked a few questions about my family background -- mainly to understand my personal situation.

●       Finally, I was asked if I had any questions for them, and the round ended there.

Initially they selected only 9/10 people but then after 2 weeks they said they have reconsidered and that they wanted to give the ppo to all the 10 people.

4. Technical Interview [20 Students]

I very confidently walked to the cabin, knocked on the door and politely greeted my interviewers.
Surprisingly I wasn't asked for an introduction but keep one handy.

1. Walk us through your journey from school to your CET/JEE journey, what made you choose this college,

describe your past 3 years of college life and what are your future plans?
(Yes this was a single question! I think I won them with this line "I would say my journey is about a
phoenix who rose from her ashes......i:)) .

2. Out of all the achievements mentioned on the resume, which is your most significant win?

3. Since I picked my BITS finance case study as the significant win, he asked me to pitch in 1 min what I

had contributed in that? And then asked me about some non technical formulae like NPV Beta etc.

4. What's your strongest technical skill?

5. A lot of questions on my projects - what's unique, what problem is solved etc.

6. GFG Candle Puzzle .

--- PAGE 3 ---
At the end they asked me if I had any questions for them. Since my profile was AIML oriented, I really
wanted to show that I am eager to learn and grow in this domain. I asked the following questions:

1. I was looking for recent news about UBS and I learned that UBS has appointed a Chief AI Officer, it also

has its own ingrown AI, so how is UBS trying to position itself in this era of Al in comparison to other
banks ?

2. Could you explain more about the Graduate Trainee Program, how are we divided into different teams

and what would we work upon?

Tips:

I honestly felt I nailed this interview due to my confidence. I wasn't the most intellectual person amongst
the shortlisted candidates but sure I was the most confident one. So always have a learning attitude, show
them you are ready to work hard and earn your place in the company. It's okay if you aren't able to answer
all the questions, tell them your approach. Always know your resume inside out, and add stuff that you
have genuinely worked on, NEVER FAKE YOUR RESUME!

5. HR Interview [10 students]

I was immediately called for my HR Interview within 2 minutes so be prepared and don't panic. Honestly,
this felt like a breezer. But obviously you need to be calm and answer questions with utmost awareness.

1. Explain any one of your projects as if you are talking to a non technical person.

2. Tell me about your family .

3. If for the next 5 years all your expenses were paid, what would you do with this time?

4. Are you willing to relocate to Pune / Hyderabad [Alway say YES]

Finally 9 students were selected for this role and I was one of them.
Please never mention that you have any plans for higher studies. I did this mistake during my BNY Summer
Internship HR Interview and it costed me heavily.
Tips and Useful Resources :
Resume Tips -

1. Use the Jake's Resume Overleaf Template to craft your resume.

2. Deploy at least any one of your projects.

3. Understand your project in depth - its use cases, why a particular tech stack was used, alternatives for

the stack, architecture diagram of your project, schema of the database, challenges faced and if it is a
hackathon/group project mention that you worked on xyz stack.

4. Always remember that your resume is not built in one day, it takes years so start utilising your time

to learn new skills and gaining experience.

5. Participate in as many hackathons/Case Studies as you can, you will definitely end up learning more.

Interview Tips -

1. You are the one setting the direction for your interview, always answer in a way that the interviewer

is prompted to ask you questions based on what you previously answered.

2. Trust me when I say this - "Confidence has no competition". Always be confident in your answers

and practice your introduction in front of the mirror a couple of times.
--- PAGE 4 ---

3. If you don't know the answer to a question, ask the interviewer for hints.

4. Every rejection is taking you closer to your offer letter so take it gracefully. I was very fortunate

that I got my offer in the very first interview of mine but I have seen my peers face multiple
rejections, some even made it to HR and didn't receive the offer. So take a break of a day or two and
bounce back stronger .

5. I can't even emphasize enough on how important Luck is during the placement process. You could

give your 110% and yet face a panel who could ask you questions on a topic you never studied. So
just surrender your efforts to God and let Him take care of the fruits.

6. If asked about which domain you would like to work in the next couple of years: do not pick a

specific stack, rather showcase that you are flexible enough to work with multiple domains and you
want to learn and grow with the company.

7. Always research about the company values and try to include them in your answers.

customSections.content:
Present fearlessly and act like you own the stage ! You must know what you have implemented and

the overall work done by your team. Also keep in mind the business model of what you are building.

4. Technical Interview [20 Students]

I very confidently walked to the cabin, knocked on the door and politely greeted my interviewers.
Surprisingly I wasn't asked for an introduction but keep one handy.

1. Walk us through your journey from school to your CET/JEE journey, what made you choose this college,

describe your past 3 years of college life and what are your future plans?
(Yes this was a single question! I think I won them with this line "I would say my journey is about a
phoenix who rose from her ashes......i:)) .

2. Out of all the achievements mentioned on the resume, which is your most significant win?

3. Since I picked my BITS finance case study as the significant win, he asked me to pitch in 1 min what I

had contributed in that? And then asked me about some non technical formulae like NPV Beta etc.

4. What's your strongest technical skill?

5. A lot of questions on my projects - what's unique, what problem is solved etc.

6. GFG Candle Puzzle .

--- PAGE 3 ---
At the end they asked me if I had any questions for them. Since my profile was AIML oriented, I really
wanted to show that I am eager to learn and grow in this domain. I asked the following questions:

1. I was looking for recent news about UBS and I learned that UBS has appointed a Chief AI Officer, it also

has its own ingrown AI, so how is UBS trying to position itself in this era of Al in comparison to other
banks ?

2. Could you explain more about the Graduate Trainee Program, how are we divided into different teams

and what would we work upon?

Tips:

I honestly felt I nailed this interview due to my confidence. I wasn't the most intellectual person amongst
the shortlisted candidates but sure I was the most confident one. So always have a learning attitude, show
them you are ready to work hard and earn your place in the company. It's okay if you aren't able to answer
all the questions, tell them your approach. Always know your resume inside out, and add stuff that you
have genuinely worked on, NEVER FAKE YOUR RESUME!

5. HR Interview [10 students]

I was immediately called for my HR Interview within 2 minutes so be prepared and don't panic. Honestly,
this felt like a breezer. But obviously you need to be calm and answer questions with utmost awareness.

1. Explain any one of your projects as if you are talking to a non technical person.

2. Tell me about your family .

3. If for the next 5 years all your expenses were paid, what would you do with this time?

4. Are you willing to relocate to Pune / Hyderabad [Alway say YES]

Finally 9 students were selected for this role and I was one of them.
Please never mention that you have any plans for higher studies. I did this mistake during my BNY Summer
Internship HR Interview and it costed me heavily.

4. Always remember that your resume is not built in one day, it takes years so start utilising
