journey.prep:
1. Practice DSA thoroughly: Follow Striver's DSA Sheet and practice regularly on LeetCode to

build strong problem-solving skills and familiarity with common DSA patterns.

2. Practice SQL: Use LeetCode SQL 50 to practice important SQL concepts and commonly asked

query patterns.

3. Build diverse projects: Have good-quality projects in both Web/App Development and AI/ML.

This makes your profile more versatile and prepares you for both SDE and AI/ML-oriented roles.

4. Practice Aptitude and Verbal Ability: Use resources such as IndiaBix and GeeksforGeeks

(GFG) to practice quantitative aptitude, logical reasoning, and verbal ability questions commonly

asked in OAs.

5. Practice Puzzles and Guesstimates: Solve puzzles on GFG and practice guesstimation questions

through YouTube to improve your analytical and structured problem-solving skills.

6. Learn AI/ML systematically: Make use of popular AI/ML courses on Udemy and Coursera to

build strong conceptual foundations and understand practical applications.

7. Take Mock Interviews: Practice mock interviews using ChatGPT and Gemini. Ask them to

simulate technical, HR, behavioural, and role-specific interviews, and use their feedback to identify
and improve your weak areas.

8. Participate in Hackathons, Case Studies, and Research: Take part in hackathons, case study

competitions, and research projects or publish research papers to gain practical exposure to
real-world problems. These experiences help you develop problem-solving, teamwork, and
presentation skills while also strengthening your resume
My Failures
Looking back, these rejections were not just setbacks but a collection of experiences that gradually helped
me understand what different companies look for. Some rejections were because of clear skill gaps, while
others were simply situations where I felt that luck or circumstances played a role. I have tried to document
each experience honestly so that someone going through a similar placement process can learn from them.
--- PAGE 5 ---

1. JPMC - CIB

JPMC CIB was the first company to visit our campus. I cleared the OA, after which the GD was
conducted online. However, it was not a traditional GD; it was more of a group question-and-answer
discussion. Despite raising my hand multiple times, I did not get many opportunities to speak, and the
discussion also went somewhat off-topic from what I had expected. I also felt that I did not have sufficient
knowledge about some of the topics being discussed. Lesson learnt: Be proactive and speak whenever you
get an opportunity, and for JPMC CIB in particular, have a strong understanding of current affairs,
economics, finance, and business news.

2. WorkIndia

The WorkIndia OA consisted of 50 MCQS covering CS fundamentals such as Data Structures,
Operating Systems, Computer Networks, and DBMS, with the primary focus being on accuracy and
speed. I cleared it and moved to a debugging interview, where I was able to solve 1 out of 2 questions,
although I needed multiple hints. However, the interviewer was impressed by my SLM project and asked
me several questions about LLM development and system design, which I believe helped me reach the next
round. The following round consisted of DSA and schema design; I answered the schema design question
well, but the DSA problem was a difficult Graph DFS + DP question that I could not solve. Lesson learnt:
I needed to put significantly more effort into DSA, particularly advanced problem-solving patterns.

3. IDFC FIRST Bank

I cleared the IDFC FIRST OA, which consisted of CS fundamentals, aptitude, and two easy-to-medium
DSA questions. In the first technical interview, I was able to solve both DSA questions given to me.
However, I struggled with a situational question based on Object-Oriented Design, which ultimately
became the weak point in my interview. This experience made me realise that being comfortable with DSA
alone is not enough for technical interviews, especially when companies also evaluate design thinking and
problem-solving. Lesson learnt: I needed to strengthen my understanding of System Design and
Object-Oriented Design, particularly how to approach open-ended design situations.

4. UBS

The UBS process began with resume shortlisting, where 51 students were selected. I could not identify any
specific pattern based on CGPA or particular skills, so I considered myself fortunate to have been
shortlisted. The first round combined a technical case study and a pen-and-paper technical test. We were
given a problem statement, asked to develop a solution, prepare a PPT, and present it within approximately
1.5 hours. From each group, around 2-3 students progressed to the technical interview, and it appeared that
candidates who took the lead and spoke more were more likely to be selected; the pen-and-paper test did not
seem to play a major role. Lesson learnt: In group-based selection processes, take initiative and make sure
you communicate the parts of your solution that are most important from the evaluator's perspective.

5. Nomura -- GM Role

For Nomura's GM role, the initial shortlisting was based on CGPA and resume, with only 27 students
selected for the GD; most selected candidates had a CGPA above 9. I managed to clear the GD, after which
only 7 candidates were shortlisted for interviews. During the interviews, we realised that the primary focus
was on Pandas queries. Since SQL was my stronger database/querying skill, I spent the 1-2 hours before
--- PAGE 6 ---
the interview learning as much Pandas as I could. I was able to answer most of the questions but missed a
few, and ultimately only one candidate was selected. Lesson learnt: Go through the JD carefully and
identify the specific skills the company is likely to test, even if they are not currently your strongest skills.

6. ISS STOXX

ISS STOXX was one of the first processes where there was no major resume-based shortlisting, and
students from branches such as EXTC and MCA were also eligible. Around 300 candidates appeared for
the OA, which consisted of MCQs on Java, Python, Aptitude, and SQL, along with negative marking. I
cleared the OA, and around 40-45 candidates were shortlisted for interviews. The panel interviewing me
consisted of around 15-16 candidates, and I was asked approximately 8-10 Java code-output questions. I
was able to answer around 6-7 correctly, but I was still rejected at this stage. Lesson learnt: Even when
your overall preparation is good, interviews can sometimes be heavily dependent on a particular technical
area, so I needed to strengthen my depth in Java.

7. InCred

The InCred process began with resume shortlisting, followed by an OA consisting of Python coding
questions, SQL queries, and aptitude MCQS with negative marking, with a sectional cutoff for cach
section. I cleared the OA and reached the interview, where the interviewer went through my resume, asked
questions about my projects, and also gave me a guesstimate. I was not able to answer the guesstimate as
accurately as I would have liked. More importantly, after looking at my resume, the interviewer felt that my
profile was better suited to an AIML or SDE role rather than the Business Analyst role that InCred was
offering. Lesson learnt: Either tailor your resume to the role you are applying for or, if the role is
significantly different from your interests and profile, reconsider whether it is the right opportunity to
pursue.

8. BlackRock

After a relatively long gap, my next interview process was with BlackRock. The OA consisted of two
coding questions - one DSA and one debugging question - along with MCQs, and the assessment also
included an Al assistant. I believe the shortlisting may have been based on an aggregate of CGPA and test
performance, and I was selected for the SDE interview. During the interview, I was asked to explain one of
my projects, which was heavily focused on Al/ML. I explained it to the best of my ability, but I felt that one
of the interviewers, whose background was more in frontend and backend development, found some
aspects of the project difficult to relate to. I was also asked a DSA question, which I solved, although my
approach was not the most optimal. Lesson learnt: I needed to diversify my resume and have at least one
strong app-development or web-development project, since many companies visit campus primarily for
SDE roles.

9. Mastercard

I cleared the Mastercard OA, which I found to be quite difficult. I was able to solve only around 4/12 test
cases for each of the two DSA questions, yet I was still shortlisted, with 9 candidates eventually selected
for interviews held at Cummins College, Pune. The first round was a GD in which nobody was eliminated,
followed by a technical interview that lasted almost an hour and covered everything from DSA and my
cybersecurity research paper to basic AI/ML and in-depth Java concepts. I cleared this round, but in the
second technical interview I faced situational questions and detailed questions on caching, a topic I was
--- PAGE 7 ---
not sufficiently familiar with. Lesson learnt: I needed a much deeper understanding of System Design
concepts, rather than preparing only the commonly asked fundamentals.

10. JPMC - CADP Internship

The CADP Internship process at JPMC was probably the most disappointing rejection for me. Around 72
students were shortlisted for the GD based on their resumes, and after the GD, 19 candidates were
selected for interviews, including me. The interview focused primarily on situational and behavioural
questions; I was also asked to explain one of my projects, but there were no significant cross-questions on
it. I was subsequently selected for the HR round, which was again largely behavioural, and no major
technical skills were assessed throughout the process. Out of the 8 candidates who reached the HR round,
7 received offers and I was the only one who was rejected. Lesson learnt: Honestly, there was no
specific technical lesson here - it was simply a very difficult rejection to process, and at times, bad luck
and circumstances are also part of the placement process.

11. Other Attempts

Apart from these 10 major interview processes, I also appeared for companies such as Auxo AL, Wissen,
TransUnion, HSBC, and others, where I could not progress beyond the OA. Some of these assessments
had difficult DSA questions, while others tested skills or formats that I had not anticipated. For example, the
HSBC assessment included a behavioural test, which was something I had not expected; out of
approximately 58 candidates, only 9 progressed to the next round. These experiences reinforced the
importance of being prepared for a wide variety of assessment formats rather than focusing exclusively on
technical coding questions. Lesson learnt: You cannot predict every company's OA, so building a broad
preparation base and being adaptable is extremely important.
In case of any further doubts, feel free to reach out to me on Linkedin

1) Resume shortlisting - 30/9/26

2) Functional interview - 1/10/26

3) HR interview - 1/10/26

1.
[Resume Shortlisting] [ 150-200 students appeared for this round]
The first round was resume shortlisting. All B.Tech students with no active backlogs were eligible to
apply. There was no Online Assessment (OA) for this process.
The shortlisting was primarily based on the relevance of the candidate's internship experience and projects
in the AI/ML domain, as the role was more aligned with an AI/ML Engineer profile rather than a
traditional SDE role. Having two AIML projects along with relevant internship experience helped me
stand out and clear this round.
However, resume shortlisting can sometimes be quite unpredictable and may depend on several factors
beyond the candidate's control. In my experience, there is also an element of luck involved, especially when
a large number of students apply for a limited number of positions. Therefore, while having relevant projects
and experience certainly helps, getting shortlisted is not always a direct reflection of the strength of one's
resume.
Ultimately, 15 students were shortlisted for the Functional Interview round.

2. [Functional Interview] [15 candidates appeared for this round]

The functional interview began with a brief self-introduction, after which the interviewer candidly asked
me whether I was related to Kailash Kher. The interview was then entirely focused on Generative Al,
Large Language Models (LLMs), and my AI/ML projects.
The interviewer first asked me about the dot product, including what it is and why it is important in the
context of machine learning and LLMs. He then asked me to explain the Transformer architecture in brief
and discuss the key differences between BERT and GPT. This was followed by questions on orthogonal
vectors and cosine similarity.
One of the more interesting questions was about how an LLM handles repeated prompts. He gave the
example of asking an LLM to "List different designations." The model initially provides a set of
designations, but when prompted again with "Give more," it generates additional designations instead of
simply repeating the previous ones. He asked me how this works internally.
I was not completely certain about the exact mechanism, so I explained my understanding in terms of
next-token prediction and semantic similarity using concepts such as cosine similarity. The interviewer
was satisfied with my reasoning but then explained the exact mechanism to me. He then asked me about
--- PAGE 3 ---
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and their architecture. I was able to explain the different
components of a CNN and relate them to the practical work I had done during my internship, where I had
worked with CNNs as part of my project.
The interviewer then asked me to explain one of my projects, an Al-powered Legal Intelligence Tool.
While discussing the project, he asked several questions related to the technical choices I had made,
including:

• Why did you use Sentence-BERT (SBERT)?

• Why was SHAP Explainable AI required in the project?

• What are adapters in LoRA?

I explained the architecture and the reasoning behind each of these choices based on how they were
implemented in my project.
Towards the end of the interview, I asked the interviewer about the exact nature of the role at Axis, since
the job description covered a wide range of technologies, including AI/ML, cloud, frontend, and backend
development. He clarified that the role would primarily involve AIML application development, which
gave me a much clearer understanding of the position.
Overall, the interview was strongly focused on Generative AI and LLM fundamentals. My Program
Elective of Vizuara is the main cause I was aware of these concepts. 4 candidates were selected for the HR
Round.

3. [HR Interview] [4 candidates were selected for this round]

The HR interview began with questions that were more focused on getting to know me beyond my resume
and technical background. She first asked me to talk about myself, including my hobbies and interests,
and deliberately stayed away from technical questions.
She then asked me about where I stay in Mumbai and whether I would be comfortable travelling to
Lower Parel for work. My suggestion for such questions is to always answer positively and show that you
are comfortable with the practical requirements of the role, unless you genuinely have a constraint that
would prevent you from doing so.
The most important part of the HR interview was a discussion about my family background, which lasted
for almost five minutes. I mentioned that both my parents are engineers and currently work at MNCs. She
then followed up by asking a very direct question:
"If your parents are already working at MNCs, why Axis and not those companies?"
I explained that I have always wanted to build my career in the FinTech domain, and that the role at Axis
particularly interested me because it was focused on AIML application development, which strongly
aligns with my interests and the kind of work I want to pursue.
I also explained the difference between the nature of work at a typical service-based organisation and the
role I was interviewing for. I mentioned that if I joined an organisation similar to where my parents work, I
could potentially be assigned to projects across a wide range of technologies depending on the project
--- PAGE 4 ---
requirements - from frontend development and backend development to cloud and AI/ML. In contrast,
the Axis role offered me an opportunity to work specifically in an AIML-focused role within the Fin Tech
domain, which was much closer to my career interests.
This seemed to convince her that my interest in Axis was genuine and driven by the nature of the role
rather than simply the company name or the compensation. The interview ended shortly afterwards.
My biggest takeaway from the HR round: Be very clear about why you want this particular company
and this particular role. HR questions may appear simple, but follow-up questions can quickly test
whether your motivation is genuine and consistent with what you have mentioned throughout the interview.
The results were announced the next day. Out of the 4 candidates who appeared for the HR round, I was
the only candidate who received an offer.

journey.prep:
1) Try to maintain a high CGPA. A lot of people say that CGPA is not important and anything above

8 works, but from what I have seen, that is not the case. A lot of companies mention a criteria of 7.5
or 8 in their application, but then while shortlisting, they end up only shortlisting students having a
CGPA above 8.5 or even close to 9. I would say a CGPA of 8+ is a must to participate in the
processes of a lot of good companies, but try to keep it above 8.5 if possible.

2) Learn and practice Java during your placement preparation. I cannot stress the importance of

this enough, as I personally used C++ throughout my coding practice and only knew the basics of
Java and OOP. A lot of banks/finance-related companies hire on campus, and most of those
companies require Java. I would suggest C++ only if you are doing competitive programming very
--- PAGE 9 ---
seriously, but otherwise, for DSA and on-campus preparation, just go with Java as your primary
language. It will be very helpful while giving OAs for companies and also during interviews.

3) Do not focus only on DSA. This is a mistake that I, along with many others, made during our

placements. The majority of our time was spent on DSA preparation, as we thought that was the
most important thing for clearing OAs. That is not true. Be consistent with your DSA practice and,
yes, cover all the concepts, but also focus on SQL (it is equally important as DSA, as almost every
single company asks it either in the form of MCQs or by asking you to write a query in the OA),
along with development and AI/ML concepts.

4) If you are from EXTC, try and cover core CS concepts early during your preparation, as these

concepts will require revision to make sure you are comfortable with them. Comps and CSE students
have these as part of their coursework, so it is relatively easier and less time-consuming for them, but
for EXTC, study these early and then keep revising them in between to make sure you do not forget.
Focus more on DBMS and OOPS, as these are the most frequently asked topics in all companies.
Also, try and give some time to OS and CCN concepts.

5) Prepare everything on your resume early. Do not be like me and wait for the interview call to

finally prepare my resume in depth and regret it later. The resume is something that will mostly be
the same throughout the placement season (except for some tweaks according to roles and
requirements), so prepare it well in advance and be prepared for every single word that you have
mentioned in it in detail. Only mention things you are confident about, and do not fake anything.

6) Try to give some mock interviews to your friends or family members if possible, as it will boost

your confidence. I did not do this, and I had also given no interviews before BlackRock, due to
which I had O confidence going into the interview. Speaking out about points on your resume or
certain concepts helps in boosting your confidence and will be beneficial during the interview.

7) Stay calm during the interview. Even if the interviewer asks a question that you do not know the

answer to, stay calm and try to answer it in some way, and be clear in explaining your thought
process and try to bring the interviewer back to a concept that you are comfortable in. Most of the
time, instead of testing your technical skills, interviewers are testing your ability to handle pressure,
and they are more interested in your approach.
My overall experience with placements:
From my experience, placements are a very luck based process. I would say they are 80% luck and maybe
20% of your skill. If luck is not with you, no matter how skilled you are there are chances that you will
remain unplaced for a while and you will see other people all around you getting placed and celebrating.
If luck is not with you, your resume itself might not get shortlisted-which is a very random process and
nobody knows how companies actually shortlist candidates. A lot of deserving candidates get left out despite
having a high ATS score and a decent cgpa and this might happen to you as well. You will feel very
frustrated at the time the shortlist comes out but try to stay calm and focus on the next opportunity you have
as placements go on for a long time and being frustrated and angry early will not help.
If you are in EXTC, be mentally prepared for a lot of frustration. Apart from all the luck being involved in
resume shortlisting and OAs having varied difficulties of questions for everybody in some companies, being
from extc will lead to you being ineligible for a lot of top high paying companies. Sometimes, you might be
eligible for application but when the shortlist comes out, you will find out only comps and cse students have
been shortlisted for the OA. During our placement season, a lot of top companies such as JPMC(for fintech
role), IDFC, UBS, Nomura, WorkIndia, Dolat Capital and a few others did not even allow extc students to
--- PAGE 10 ---
sit for the OA. This was all highly frustrating as we did not get the opportunity just because we are not in cse
or comps but nothing could be done other than waiting for whatever opportunity comes our way next.
Overall, I would say that stay patient and wait for that one lucky day where everything goes your way!
Useful Resources:

1) DSA - I followed Striver's sheet and his youtube playlist which i believe is the best resource for

practicing DSA if you are focused only for placements. Some people also followed NeetCode's sheet but i
did not so can't comment on that. Try to solve all the major topics and their questions on striver's sheet
atleast once if possible. If you do not have enough time, focus on concepts upto trees and then do dp(almost
all companies conducting OAs this year asking DSA were asking DP questions). You can skip topics like
trees,graphs, heaps if you do not have time but try and cover atleast basics of all topics.
https://takeuforward.org/dsa/strivers-a2z-sheet-learn-dsa-a-to-z

2) For SQL, i followed SQL 50 on leetcode. I struggled a lot with SQL initially and could not solve a lot of

those questions myself and had to look up solutions. But practicing the same questions 2 or 3 times with
multiple solutions for each question helped me build a good understanding and boosted my confidence.

3) For development concepts, I followed chai aur code's playlist to learn javascript and react(these are long

playlists so only do them if you have a lot of time). I followed a gfg course to learn nextjs and for AIML
related concepts, i mainly studied them using chatgpt as i was not very interested in that so i did not need to
learn those concepts in detail. Make projects and participate in hackathons.
Javascript react playlist

4) For core CS concepts, i followed Kunal Kushwaha's playlist for OOPS(very good playlist), i used Love

Babbar's notes for DBMS and OS and watched his videos for some topic if i did not understand and for
CCN i mainly used chatgpt to revise concepts as it was a course subject in our 3rd year. After studying
concepts, i practiced MCQs on these topics using chatgpt and claude and also used gfg for some practice.
OOPS kunal kushwaha DBMS Love babbar OS Love Babbar

5) For aptitude, solve questions on IndiaBIX on different topics and also take timed tests if possible as those

can help you to solve questions under time pressure which is required in OAs. If you are not confident, ask
chatgpt to create questions on aptitude similar to that level.

6) For system design concepts, gaurav sen's playlist on youtube is the best resource i found. They are mostly

short videos which explain concepts in an intuitive way with examples.
System Design gaurav sen

7) I did not get time to practice any puzzles but some companies do ask them so if you have the time you

can solve them on gig.
https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/aptitude/top-100-puzzles-asked-in-interviews/

8) Make complete use of Al for your preparation. It is a very very helpful tool for interview and OA

preparation so make full use of it. You can also prepare concepts and projects on your resume using Al and
give tests on it.
--- PAGE 11 ---
Resume used for application : " [AarushMaheshwari_Resume_Tech.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1HxhSZCu9jlwPLXvGHNn1iKdVG3padPWN/view?usp=sharing)
Lastly, stay patient, do not lose confidence, sleep and eat well and enjoy as placements are very stressful and
go on for a long period of time so make sure you prepare well but also have fun during this time!

1) Pre Placement Talk

2) Resume Shortlisting

3) Online Assessment

4) Technical Interview

5) HR Interview

1. Pre Placement Talk and Resume Shortlisting:

The Pre-Placement Talk (PPT) was scheduled virtually on 6th August on Webex, as it was a pooled-campus
opportunity. I could not attend the PPT completely because I had an MDM lecture going on at the same
time. However, I would strongly advise attending the PPT and listening carefully to the points discussed, as
it can help you gain a better understanding of the company. It can also be helpful during the interview, as
you can refer to a point mentioned during the PPT, which might leave a good impression on the interviewer.
The eligibility criteria was simply having a CGPA above 7.5, and students from all branches were eligible to
apply. They had mentioned that there would be resume shortlisting, but in the end, I believe everyone who
applied got a chance to appear for the OA.
BlackRock did not conduct resume shortlisting, but many other companies do. Therefore, it is preferable to
maintain a resume with a high ATS score (try to keep it above 75) and tailor your resume according to the
JD and the role. However, while trying to maximize your ATS score or make yourself a better fit for the role,
do not add skills or technologies that you have absolutely no knowledge of, as they can come back to bite
you during the interview.
--- PAGE 2 ---

2. Online Assessment [285 candidates appeared ]

The test was conducted online from home on HackerRank. The total duration was 1.5 hours, and there were
7 sections, each of which was timed individually. Also the test was section locked so once a section was
submitted or if we ran out of time for a particular section, we cannot go back.
The first section was a coding question, for which we had 40 minutes. The question was different for
everyone, but in general, the difficulty level was quite high for most of us. In my case, I had to implement a
Fork/Join algorithm in Java for an airport luggage management system. The solution had to be implemented
using objects and classes. Since my primary language for problem-solving was C++, and this question could
only be solved in Java, I was unable to solve it.
An Al assistant was also available with the question, which could be used to ask queries related to the
problem, such as requesting an explanation or getting help with Java syntax.
The second section was also a coding question, and we had 15 minutes to solve it. Once again, the questions
differed for everyone. I got a codebase question based on Selenium. Honestly, 15 minutes was nowhere near
enough to solve it, as it was a very complex question that would easily take 10-12 minutes just to
understand. I was unable to solve this question either, so I moved on to the MCQ sections feeling quite
disappointed that I had not been able to solve either of the coding questions.
There were 5 MCQ-based sections after this:

1. Design Patterns (Advanced) - 15 questions, 6 minutes

2. Design Patterns (Basic) - 15 questions, 4 minutes

3. Fundamental AI Know-How, Cloud Services Exposure - 25 questions, 10 minutes

4. DB Concepts - ACID Properties, Transactions, DB Fundamentals - 25 questions, 10 minutes

5. Aptitude - 15 questions, 10 minutes

The questions in these sections ranged from easy to medium difficulty. The Design Patterns sections
involved questions based on LLD, SOLID principles, and related concepts. Most of the questions were
manageable even with a basic understanding of these topics. I had prepared these concepts for 1-2 hours the
day before the OA using ChatGPT, and I found that level of preparation sufficient to answer most of the
questions.
The AI Know-How section also involved basic questions on Al and machine learning, along with cloud
services such as AWS. Most of these questions were answerable with basic knowledge. Additionally, many
questions could be solved through option elimination, as there was often only one obvious option that could
be correct.
The DB Concepts section was also quite easy, as DBMS is asked by almost every company, and I had
prepared it well. The Aptitude section was not particularly difficult, but it was lengthy, and I found 10
minutes insufficient to answer all the questions.
After the test, I was quite disappointed because I had not been able to solve either of the coding questions. I
was very sure that I would not be shortlisted for the next round, even though my performance in the MCQ
sections had gone well.
--- PAGE 3 ---
After the OA, there was a 5-day gap before the results were announced. During this time, being very sure
that I would not be shortlisted after my OA performance, I was not focusing on interview preparation but
rather preparing in general for the OAs of other companies that were visiting the campus in the coming days.
However, the shortlist was released on 18th August at around 6 PM (interviews were to begin on 19th from
9 AM), and I was shocked to see my name on the list. My best guess after looking at the shortlist was that
BlackRock did not consider the OA results for whatever reason and rather shortlisted students based on their
CGPA. I am not sure why they did this, but I did not have time to think about all this when I saw my name
on the shortlist, as I was not at all prepared for an interview.
This was also the first interview that I would be giving during the placement season, so that was another
reason for me to stress about because I did not know how these interviews actually worked, except for
whatever I had read in previous interview experiences and what I had heard from friends.
After seeing my name on the shortlist, I started preparing everything that was on my resume in as much
detail as I could. The main focus was on preparing my projects, the tech stacks used, the architecture of the
projects, etc. Along with this, I also tried to prepare some of the design concepts that they had asked in the
OA and brushed up on some concepts of object-oriented programming.
I tried to cover whatever I could in the limited time I had and went to sleep, hoping for the best the next day.

2. Round 2 - Technical Interview [ 28 shortlisted and 10 waitlisted for SDE role ]

I received a call from the HR regarding the interview on the 18th, and I was informed that my interview
would start at 9 AM the next day. The interviews were scheduled virtually on the Webex platform, and we
were asked to report to the TPO at 8:30 AM and be ready by 8:50 AM for the interview. I was ready by
around 8:50, and at 8:55, I received a call from the HR asking me to join the link.
Introduction & Initial Questions
The interview initially started with one panelist. I greeted her, and she asked me to begin with an
introduction. I had prepared an introduction based on my resume using Claude, which covered all the
important points and ended with me mentioning my strongest project so that I could steer the interview in
that direction.
The interviewer heard my introduction and asked me some basic questions, such as:

• What languages I use for coding

• What tech stack I know

• What I am comfortable with

I answered by mentioning C++ as my primary language, so she immediately interrupted and asked me,
"What about Java and Python?" I mentioned that I had used Python in a few of my projects and had studied
object-oriented concepts in Java, so I had experience with both languages, but for problem-solving, I
primarily use C++.
For my tech stack, I mentioned most of what was written on my resume, and she seemed satisfied with it and
said, "Okay."
--- PAGE 4 ---
Next, she asked me how I make use of Al for coding, making projects, or learning purposes. I answered by
saying that for any problem I come across, I first try to come up with a solution or an approach in my mind.
I try to put it on paper, test it out with some examples myself, and then code it up. However, if I get stuck at
some point in my solution, or if I have a solution ready but am struggling with the implementation, I make
use of Al to help me and make my task easier. I also mentioned that I use Al to prepare certain concepts and
test myself on them by solving MCQ-based tests using ChatGPT or Claude.
Next, she asked me how the online assessment was and whether I found the questions challenging. I
answered honestly by stating that since the advanced coding question could only be solved in Java, and I
don't use Java for problem-solving, I could not solve it even though I could think of an approach. For the
second question, I was short on time and could not solve that one either. However, I stated that I was able to
solve most of the MCQs correctly within the allotted time.
She didn't really react to anything I was saying here, so I was not sure whether my answer was satisfactory
or not. This happened throughout the interview.
DSA Question - Valid Anagram
After this, she said something along the lines of, "Since you weren't able to solve the coding question in the
OA, let's solve one now," and asked me whether I knew what an anagram was. I said yes, and then she asked
me how I would code a solution to check whether two strings are anagrams or not.
Question on LeetCode: Valid Anagram
This was a very easy problem, and I started with a sorting-based approach and explained the approach in
detail. She did not ask me to open Notepad and write the pseudocode or anything, so I had to go through the
approach verbally.
After this approach, I stated the optimal approach of using a hashmap, but mentioned that we are
compromising on space complexity to improve the time complexity. When I said this, she asked me what the
time and space complexities were for both approaches, which I answered for every step of the code. She
said, "Okay," and seemed satisfied.
Chatbot / RAG Question
After this, she gave me a problem saying that suppose I want to build a chatbot in which we can feed a
document. The chatbot goes through the document, and later it is expected to answer any questions that we
have regarding the document or help us find any particular text in the document. She asked me how I would
build this chatbot and what the process would be.
I answered step-by-step, mentioning the use of vector embeddings and a RAG-based approach. Once again,
she just listened to whatever I said with an expressionless face, so I had no idea whether what I was saying
was what she was expecting or whether she expected something else. However, at the end of my
explanation, she said, "Okay," and moved on to the next question.
--- PAGE 5 ---
Project discussion
The discussion then moved on to one of my projects. It was an Al-powered stock analytics platform. She
asked me to explain briefly what the project was about. I had prepared a short, one-minute introduction for
this project that covered everything the project does.
She asked about the tech stack and a point on my resume that stated that the project had 10+ REST API
endpoints. She asked me what these different endpoints were and what the user could see. I answered all of
this, and then she asked me how we were getting any of the stock-related data.
Here, I mentioned that this part took us a lot of time since we were unable to get proper data regarding stock
prices, historical data, etc. I told her that we tried to perform web scraping, but that was not working because
the NSE, BSE, and SEBI websites were strict and rate-limited us. Even AI tools were not helping us with
proper libraries that could be used. After a lot of research, we found some Python libraries that could help us
with the task without having to pay.
She said, "Okay," and asked how we were fetching news feeds as well and how we were scoring any
particular stock.
While she was asking this question, a second interviewer also joined the call.
Regarding the scoring, I answered honestly and told her that we lacked in-depth knowledge of finance, so
we relied on whatever was available online and made use of AI tools to help us create a proper scoring
system for any particular stock.
She then came back to the chatbot question and asked me what if she wanted to train that chatbot, or any
chatbot, continuously based on the output it was providing.
I answered by saying that I would store whatever output I get in some kind of data structure, such as a
vector, and feed it back to the chatbot to retrain it in a kind of feedback loop. I was not sure about this
answer, but the interviewer said, "Okay."
Up to this point, the interview was mostly going smoothly, except for maybe the last chatbot question.
However, now the second interviewer started asking questions.
FastAPI Discussion
My project used FastAPI, so she started by asking what FastAPI is, what REST APIs are, and why I used
FastAPI instead of Flask. I answered this and told her about the advantages of FastAPI and why it was a
proper fit for our project since the project was backend-heavy.
She said, "Okay," but like the other interviewer, she did not give away anything, so I still didn't know
whether my answers were satisfactory or not.
The discussion continued on FastAPI, and she asked me, "What if we want to write a GET method in your
project to fetch some data? How would you write it in FastAPI?"
I knew about the GET method and routing, but I was not very sure how I would write it or what the exact
syntax was for FastAPI, as I had mostly done full-stack development using MERN. I still explained it
--- PAGE 6 ---
verbally by giving her an example of a stock having a particular ID and how we could fetch data using GET
for that particular route.
She did not expect me to write the exact syntax on Notepad but was instead looking for the logic, so I guess
she was satisfied with this answer.
She then asked me if I knew what dependency injection was in FastAPI. Throughout this discussion, I
regretted not having studied FastAPI separately, as the entire discussion revolved around concepts that I did
not know fully because I had only used FastAPI in the project and knew some basics.
I answered based on whatever I understood from the term "dependency injection," and she said that
conceptually it was fine, but asked how I would implement it and why it is used in FastAPI. I did not know
the answer, so I told her that I was unable to recall the concept exactly, even though I had heard of it before.
She said, "No worries," and then moved on to the next question.
DBMS Discussion
The discussion then moved to DBMS. I was not very confident at this point, as I believed that the FastAPI
discussion had not gone very well.
The DBMS discussion started with her asking me the difference between SQL and NoSQL, which I
answered by giving examples. I ended my answer by mentioning ACID properties since I was confident in
them and wanted her to ask me that question. So naturally, she asked me to explain what the ACID
properties are, which I explained and also gave examples for.
After this, she asked me about the CAP theorem, which I explained. Then she asked me an interesting
question. She asked that since only two out of the three properties Consistency, Availability, and Partition
Tolerance are possible, which one would I compromise on in MySQL and which one would I compromise
on in MongoDB.
I was a little surprised by this since I only knew about the theorem and what it means and had never studied
its practical applications. So, I initially answered by saying that it depends on the situation and what the
application of the database is for.
She then asked me to take an example of my choice and explain. I started with MySQL and took the
example of a banking system, stating that I would compromise on availability in this case, as consistency is
important. Even if the server is unavailable for a short period of time, it wouldn't be as much of a problem
compared to the data being inconsistent.
She said, "Okay," and asked me about MongoDB. I was not sure about this, so I answered whatever came to
mind and told her that since MongoDB stores data in the form of documents and there are no joins in
MongoDB, it would be intolerant to partitions because the entire data is together. If we partition the database
and separate the data, it would be impossible to make sense of the separated data.
This most likely was not the answer they were expecting, but I explained whatever thought process I had,
and with that, they were done with the questions.
--- PAGE 7 ---
They asked me if I had any questions for them, and I asked them about their experience at BlackRock and
what kind of work I could expect if I joined as an intern. They answered this question and that concluded the
interview.
My interview lasted around 45 minutes. Most of the interviews across panels lasted around 30-45 minutes.
After the interview, I thought there was maybe a 50% probability that I would be called for Round 2, as
there were one or two questions that I was not able to answer very well.
However, some people got a call for their Round 2 interview within 5-10 minutes of their Round 1
interview, and this made me disappointed since I did not get the call.
We were all asked to wait until all the Round 1 interviews were done. During this time, I was talking to other
people and just passing time since I thought that I would not get a Round 2 call after seeing other people get
theirs immediately.
We had lunch and were waiting outside the TPO office without any hope when, suddenly, at around 2:30
PM, I got a call asking me to join immediately for Round 2.

3. Round 3 - Techno HR [ 16 candidates for SDE ]

This round was a techno-HR round for me but varied for everybody (I am guessing it depended on the
Round 1 performance). Some people had a techno-HR mix, while some had a purely technical round as their
Round 2.
There was only one panelist for this interview, and it began with me greeting him, following which he asked
about my day and my Round 1 interview. I answered honestly, saying it went well except for maybe one or
two questions, so he asked me what the questions were that I was not able to answer, to which I replied that
they were some DBMS and FastAPI questions. Up to this point, I was not sure whether this was a purely
technical round or an HR round.
The discussion started with him asking about my internship. He said that since I had worked in a corporate
environment before, how was the experience, what was different from attending college, and also asked me
to mention three positives about the company I worked at. I stated my experience, told him about the work,
how it was my first experience in an office, and how different it was from school or college. I also stated the
positives about the company, following which he asked me to state some negatives as well.
After this, he asked me what I understood by the term "client-side requirements" while working, to which I
answered regarding one of the clients of the company I worked at and what their expectations and
requirements were from the company. While I was answering this, he interrupted and rephrased his question
by saying that what he meant was, as a software developer, what all the company is expecting from my
software/application. So I answered along the lines of website/application availability, the ability to handle
traffic, scalability, etc., and explained everything in detail.
The discussion then moved to my stock analytics project, and he asked me to explain the project and what it
does. He asked me whether it was an individual or a group project, to which I answered that we were a team
of four. So he asked that since it was a team, we would have had some conflicts while building this project,
so how did we all resolve the disagreement/conflict? I answered this by giving an example of an actual
disagreement that took place and how we resolved it, and he seemed satisfied with the answer.
--- PAGE 8 ---
He followed it up by asking that suppose I work in a corporate environment and come up with an excellent
idea that I am 100% sure will work well for the company and will be beneficial, and I have conducted
complete research on it, but none of my other team members are listening and are disregarding the idea. In
this situation, how will I react and convince others?
I answered by saying that I will talk to everybody with an open mind, as I could be wrong, and explain all
the work and research that I have done and how it will be beneficial to the company. Even if, after
everything, they are not convinced, we cannot implement the idea, but I would at least request everybody to
listen to what I have to say first.
Next, he asked me that I would know what BlackRock does and that I would have researched the company,
so how would I integrate this stock analytics platform into BlackRock's tech, and how can this be beneficial
for the company? This turned out to be in my favour since BlackRock is an asset management company, so
the stock analytics project can fit perfectly, and I was able to answer this question very well, mentioning all
the advantages and the problems the project solves.
He then asked me that if I had to learn another programming language, which one would I learn? I answered
this by saying that instead of learning a new language, I would work on improving my Java and Python
skills, as they are heavily used in the industry, and adding a new language would not mean much if I am not
comfortable with it.
He then asked me a few questions on DBMS:

• What is DBMS?

• Why do we need DBMS?

• Difference between DBMS and RDBMS and two examples of SQL and NoSQL databases.

I was able to answer all these fairly easily since they were basics, and he seemed satisfied with the answers.
He then asked me if I had any questions for him, and I asked him the same question that I asked in Round 1
regarding his experience at BlackRock and what the expectations from me would be if I joined as an intern
in January. He answered this question positively, and that concluded my Round 2 interview, which lasted
around 25 minutes.
All students who were done with Round 2 were then asked to leave, and the results were announced the next
day at around 12 PM.
8 students were selected-7 for SDE and 1 for Aladdin Data.

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
1) Try to maintain a high CGPA. A lot of people say that CGPA is not important and anything above

8 works, but from what I have seen, that is not the case. A lot of companies mention a criteria of 7.5
or 8 in their application, but then while shortlisting, they end up only shortlisting students having a
CGPA above 8.5 or even close to 9. I would say a CGPA of 8+ is a must to participate in the
processes of a lot of good companies, but try to keep it above 8.5 if possible.

2) Learn and practice Java during your placement preparation. I cannot stress the importance of

this enough, as I personally used C++ throughout my coding practice and only knew the basics of
Java and OOP. A lot of banks/finance-related companies hire on campus, and most of those
companies require Java. I would suggest C++ only if you are doing competitive programming very
--- PAGE 9 ---
seriously, but otherwise, for DSA and on-campus preparation, just go with Java as your primary
language. It will be very helpful while giving OAs for companies and also during interviews.

3) Do not focus only on DSA. This is a mistake that I, along with many others, made during our

placements. The majority of our time was spent on DSA preparation, as we thought that was the
most important thing for clearing OAs. That is not true. Be consistent with your DSA practice and,
yes, cover all the concepts, but also focus on SQL (it is equally important as DSA, as almost every
single company asks it either in the form of MCQs or by asking you to write a query in the OA),
along with development and AI/ML concepts.

4) If you are from EXTC, try and cover core CS concepts early during your preparation, as these

concepts will require revision to make sure you are comfortable with them. Comps and CSE students
have these as part of their coursework, so it is relatively easier and less time-consuming for them, but
for EXTC, study these early and then keep revising them in between to make sure you do not forget.
Focus more on DBMS and OOPS, as these are the most frequently asked topics in all companies.
Also, try and give some time to OS and CCN concepts.

5) Prepare everything on your resume early. Do not be like me and wait for the interview call to

finally prepare my resume in depth and regret it later. The resume is something that will mostly be
the same throughout the placement season (except for some tweaks according to roles and
requirements), so prepare it well in advance and be prepared for every single word that you have
mentioned in it in detail. Only mention things you are confident about, and do not fake anything.

6) Try to give some mock interviews to your friends or family members if possible, as it will boost

your confidence. I did not do this, and I had also given no interviews before BlackRock, due to
which I had O confidence going into the interview. Speaking out about points on your resume or
certain concepts helps in boosting your confidence and will be beneficial during the interview.

7) Stay calm during the interview. Even if the interviewer asks a question that you do not know the

answer to, stay calm and try to answer it in some way, and be clear in explaining your thought
process and try to bring the interviewer back to a concept that you are comfortable in. Most of the
time, instead of testing your technical skills, interviewers are testing your ability to handle pressure,
and they are more interested in your approach.

For Software Engg intern: 28 shortlisted and 10 waitlisted
For Aladdin Data intern: 8 shortlisted 6 waitlisted
Tech Interview 1[38 students for sde]
I was waitlisted and puffing hopeium lol cause last year waitlist didn't get a chance for an interview, but that
didn't matter I went with as much hope as I could muster. Interviews of shortlisted candidates started from 8
am onwards, candidates got a call from the HR and the meeting link got directly mailed to them. Please
make sure your internet connection is stable because one of my mates had a network issue ruining the
interview as the panelists have a set time allocated per candidate. (hot tip, inside tpo office itself there is
small conference room with phenomenal wifi > room 104 best room
Waitlisted candidates' interviews started around 12 pm onwards. My interview was scheduled at 3pm. I
cannot emphasize this enough that interviewers will always ask questions on what you tell em in intro and
later answers for each question. Because they don't know the person sitting across from them. Only what
you tell em.
My interview was as follows: (40ish mins)
They introduced themself and then I was asked to introduce myself and my projects. I had a set start for my
intro and later I improvised according to the interviewers. My panelists (2 interviewers) were more on the
--- PAGE 4 ---
younger side. I tried to match their energy. I shared some stuff I had been reading in blogs and tried to
connect with my projects and mentioned my strong suits and my primary language being python and
dabbled with java and javascript. I even mentioned interviews being online is a great opportunity enabling
me to demonstrate my projects as well. I picked the project I had the best grasp on and explained a tab bit in
the intro. It was a chrome extension that uses indexed db which led them to asking indexing in general. I
connected it with DBMS and BTrees. Which led them to ask questions on BTrees. Its tradeoffs and
advantages. I answered it with memory tradeoffs. How it can speed queries. I used this as a case to show
how indexing benefits or slows down when multiple columns are indexed. This led them to give a table with
3 columns and lets say the primary key is indexed. How will the operations like search and insert work here.
I answered it kinda explaining the working of BTree along with it. This led to balancing of BTree and what
if its not balanced. I compared it with skewed trees and mentioned their worst time complexity on different
operations like searching, insertion etc.
Questions shifted to them asking about my tech skills if I am good at fullstack, frontend or backend. I
personally hate frontend so mentioned about that and backend is what I am comfortable with. Then they
asked me about statically typed languages and dynamically typed languages and where does javascript lie. I
talked about python and java for this case, like in python we dont have to mention data type of variable it

Placement Process:

There were three rounds in total. The eligibility criteria were open to students from all branches with a CGPA of 7.5 or above. The entire process was conducted virtually.
There were two roles: Software Engineering and Aladdin Data, and I applied for both. The interviews were conducted through Webex, although candidates were required to attend them from the TPO office. It was a pool campus placement process, with students participating from several other colleges as well, including NIT Agartala, Manipal University Jaipur, and others.

1. Online Assessment [Around 280 people appeared for this round]

Everyone who met the eligibility criteria received the OA link via email one day before the assessment. There were seven sections in total: Basic Coding, Advanced Coding,Basic Design Patterns, Advanced Design Patterns, DBMS, Aptitude, AI and Reasoning
Each section was timed separately. Once a section was started, it could not be skipped or revisited until the allotted time was over or the section was submitted.
Since we received the OA link a day in advance and could see the section names, I prepared Design Patterns thoroughly because I had not studied them much before. The MCQs covered all 23 Gang of Four design patterns.
For Basic Coding, I received a Java and OOP-based question. The problem involved a list of baggage items with their destinations, where the bags had to be grouped by destination. If there were 10 or fewer bags, they had to be processed sequentially. If there were more than 10, the list had to be divided into two parts, processed in parallel using Fork/Join, and then the results had to be merged in right-to-left order.
Since Java is my primary language, I was able to solve it within the allotted 40 minutes.
For Advanced Coding, I received a Selenium-based debugging question. The codebase was fairly large, and it took me some time to understand the existing code and the problem. Since the section had a 15-minute limit, I was unable to solve the question.
The DBMS section was easy to moderate. It covered joins, keys, SQL queries, ACID properties, and general database concepts involving technologies such as PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Oracle.
The Aptitude section was moderate to difficult, with questions on permutation and combination, ratios and proportions, percentages, family relationships, seating arrangements, and similar topics.
The AI and Reasoning section was comparatively easier and could largely be approached using basic logical reasoning and common sense.
The coding questions varied across candidates. Some candidates received two DSA questions, while others received combinations involving OOP, debugging, or other coding concepts.

2. Technical Round 1 [ 28 students for SDE and 9 for Aladdin Data]

I received a call from HR at around 7:30 AM informing me that my interview was scheduled for 9:30 AM.
There were two panelists, and the interview started with them asking me how my day was going. I asked them the same. They then asked me to introduce myself and asked about my minor in Banking Technology from Barclays. I explained how the course developed my interest in the finance industry. I was also asked about my opinion on AI-based projects and whether I would be open to working on them.
The interview then moved to a DSA question. I was asked to share my screen and open Notepad. The interviewer gave me a string (consisting of lowercase letters and brackets) . I was supposed to reverse the string whenever I encountered a matching pair of brackets till there were no brackets left, (basically valid parenthesis but with a twist). I was asked to write the code and explain the dry run as well. I initially approached the problem recursively, and then optimized the solution using a stack.
After this, I was asked how comfortable I was with Java and Python. I mentioned that Java is my primary language and that I know the basics of Python. Since my solution involved Strings, the discussion then moved into Strings in Java. I was asked several questions, including:

● Why did you use StringBuilder?

● What do mutable and immutable mean?

● Why are Strings immutable in Java?

● What is the difference between StringBuilder and StringBuffer?

● When would you use StringBuilder and when would you use StringBuffer?

● How are Strings stored internally in Java? Can you give an example?

I was able to answer all of these questions.
The interviewer then moved on to SQL. I was asked about the difference between the WHERE and HAVING clauses. I explained what each clause does and gave an example. I also mentioned that HAVING can be used without GROUP BY, so the interviewer asked me to explain this with an example. I was then asked about the difference between a Primary Key and a UNIQUE constraint. The interviewer followed up with a conceptual question: if we can simply use UNIQUE along with NOT NULL, what would happen if there were no Primary Keys, and why do we need Primary Keys in the first place?
The discussion then moved to my projects. I was asked to give an overall explanation of my projects and was asked why I had chosen particular technologies or methodologies for them.
I was also asked about my internship experience, including what I worked on and what I learned from it.
Throughout the interview, there were also behavioral questions, including questions about my future plans, positions of responsibility, and how I respond to feedback.
At the end of the interview, I was asked whether I had any questions for them. I asked about their work experience at BlackRock and the types of projects they work on.
I initially felt that my interview had not gone particularly well because the interviewer maintained a very concise communication style and often responded briefly after my answers. The interview lasted around 35 minutes. However, shortly afterward, I received a call from HR informing me that I had been shortlisted for the next round.
The first technical round was quite different for different candidates. Some candidates were asked two three DSA questions, while others were asked questions related to React/Next.js or had a more HR-oriented discussion.

3. Techno HR [ Around 18 ]

This round was different for everyone as well. For some candidates, it was purely HR-focused, for some it was more technical, while others had a mix of both.
The interviewer started by asking how my previous round went. He then introduced himself and explained what he does at BlackRock. After that, he asked me to introduce myself.
He then asked me to explain my favorite project in depth : why it was my favorite, what the project was about, what motivated me to build it, and what problems I faced while working on it. I chose my DevOps project, which also involved system design concepts.
He then asked me to explain a particular bug I had faced and how I solved it. This discussion eventually led to me explaining my entire CI/CD pipeline in depth.
We also had a discussion around Redis, since I had used it in my project. From the way the questions were framed, I felt that he was particularly interested in understanding how I approach a problem and make technical decisions, rather than simply testing whether I knew the technology.
He then asked me: "If you could add ONE feature to this project, what would it be and why?"
The discussion then moved to my internship experience. He asked me how I handled feedback from clients, how I managed deadlines, and how I had optimized my project.
I was also asked: "What is one use of AI in your life that you are really proud of?"
Another interesting part of the interview was a discussion around core values. I was asked to name three core values I had learned during college and whether those values were already present in me before I joined college. I was also asked about a situation where I had failed badly, made a comeback, and what I learned from that experience. I discussed one of my hackathon experiences for this question.
Towards the end, the interviewer asked me if I had any questions for him. Since he had mentioned at the beginning that he had been working at BlackRock for around 14 years, I asked him: "What are three core values that you have personally learned during your time at BlackRock?" He really liked the question, and we had a good discussion around it. I then asked him what would be expected of me during the first few months if I were to join as an intern.
The round lasted around 50 minutes. One interesting thing about the process was that after the interviews of all the initially shortlisted candidates were completed, they also started calling waitlisted candidates for Round 1 for SDE role
Altogether 8 people were offered the job ( 7 SDE+1 aladdin data)
Resources:

● I started participating in LeetCode contests in my 6th semester, but I would suggest starting as early as possible. Contests helped me become comfortable solving problems under pressure and also helped me deal with OA anxiety.

● I solved NeetCode 150 first and then moved on to complete NeetCode 250.

● LeetCode SQL 50 is MUST!!!!!!

● Java: Kunal Kushwaha's YouTube channel.

● Core subjects: Academic notes, ChatGPT, and GeeksforGeeks(literally best)

● Aptitude: IndiaBix.

● DSA: Kunal Kushwaha and Nikhil Lohia's YouTube channels.

● I used to randomly read Medium articles during travel on technology and interview experiences. This helped me stay in touch with recent technical concepts.

My fav article
https://medium.com/@shivambhadani_/system-design-for-beginners-everything-you-need-in-one-art icle-c74eb702540b

● Know your resume inside out- every word. Be prepared to explain anything you have mentioned, and don't mention technologies that you cannot confidently explain.

● Know your projects thoroughly. You should understand your projects, the decisions behind them, and the different scenarios that can arise. Don't blindly build projects using AI without understanding them in depth. Even if it is a group project, try to understand the entire project and not just the part you personally implemented.

● An internship can definitely be beneficial, but if you haven't done one, don't let that discourage you. Keep working on your skills, projects, and fundamentals.

● Try to maintain a CGPA of 8+. Personally, I would consider 8.5+ to be a safer target for keeping MOST opportunities open.( i missed few companies with a cgpa of 8.39)

● Participate in hackathons. Don't get demotivated if you don't win. The experience of building, collaborating, and solving problems under time constraints is valuable in itself.

● Puzzles and CS fundamentals MCQS: GeeksforGeeks.

● If you get rejected from an interview, start working on the areas that went wrong as soon as possible- ideally the same day or the next day.

● Before the interview go through the company website especially their values/principles, tailor your answers accordingly. You can also take notes during PPT as they might ask stuff from that.

MOST IMPORTANTLY:
Don't ever feel that you are not prepared for an interview, you can never be fully prepared lol. I was asked way less than what I had prepared, I kept myself up till 5am and just got 2 hrs sleep before the interview, pls avoid this. Whatever you have studied, just answer confidently that's it. And if you dont know something dont fake it , admit it honestly. Confidence, positivity and patience are the key. Placements are a combination of hard work, preparation, and luck, but no matter how many rejections you face, don't forget to show up every single day and keep working on yourself. You never know when it will finally be your day, so don't stop believing in yourself. And always be happy and genuinely cheerful for others when they succeed. Don't compare your journey with anyone else's. Everyone has their own journey, their own timeline, and their own destiny.
END MEIN JO HOTA HAI ACHE KE LIYE HOTA HAI :))))
If you have any doubts, feel free to connect with me on LinkedIn
ALL THE BEST BE POSITIVE

journey.prep:
Placements are not purely skill-based; luck, timing and the particular interview panel can also play a role.
So, as niche as it may sound, don't let a rejection define your preparation. Keep improving and stay
consistent.
Resources:

• DSA: Striver's A2Z DSA Sheet - one of the most structured resources for placement preparation.

Focus on understanding concepts and solving the more frequently asked data structures and their
problems (Strings, Stacks, Queues, LinkedLists) at least once (Please note: Every company usually
has topics that they tend to ask more on, so do your research thoroughly and try covering the other
topics if needed).
https://takeuforward.org/dsa/strivers-a2z-sheet-learn-dsa-a-to-z/

• SQL: LeetCode SQL 50 - Repeat questions you struggle with and understand multiple approaches.

https://leetcode.com/studyplan/top-sql-50/

• Java: Kunal Kushwaha's YouTube channel for Java and OOP fundamentals.

https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL9gnSGHSqcno1G3XjUbwzXHL8_EttOuKk

• Core CS: GeeksforGeeks for OOP, DBMS, OS and Computer Networks concepts and practice.

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/interview-experiences/technical-interview-preparation/

• System Design: Gaurav Sen's content + ChatGPT/Claude for explanations and interview-style

practice.

• Aptitude: IndiaBIX, https://www.indiabix.com/aptitude/

• Puzzles: GeeksforGeeks' interview puzzles, https://www.indiabix.com/aptitude/

Interview-Day Tips:

• Know your resume thoroughly. Anything written on it can be questioned, so understand every

technology, tool and project you mention.

• Know your projects end-to-end: schema/database design, backend structure, APIs, architecture,

your contribution, limitations and possible improvements.

• Be strong in fundamentals: You don't need to know everything, but the fundamentals of every

technology on your resume should be clear.

• Prepare for follow-ups: Interviewers may keep changing the conditions of a scenario, so understand

your reasoning rather than memorizing answers.

• CGPA: 8+ is a decent position, while 8.5+ is preferable where companies have academic cutoffs.

• Prepare for HR and behavioural questions as well. Technical preparation alone is not enough. Be

ready for questions about your strengths, weaknesses, leadership experiences, failures, career goals,
and situational judgement. Answer smartly but honestly; don't try to give the answer you think the
interviewer wants to hear. Keep your responses genuine and support them with real examples from
your experiences.
--- PAGE 6 ---

• Don't lose confidence after rejection: BlackRock was the 18th company I encountered during

placements. I had previously been shortlisted by two companies but was rejected by HR in the final
rounds in both. I kept preparing and eventually got this opportunity.

• Don't convince yourself that you're underprepared: You will never feel completely prepared.

Trust your preparation and focus on the interview in front of you.

• Stay calm and patient. Take a few seconds to think before answering difficult questions and explain

your reasoning clearly.

• Sleep properly: I had only around 1.5 hours of sleep before my interview day, and it definitely

affected how calmly I handled the long day. As funny as it might sound, get adequate sleep the day
before interviews at least, and keep your setup ready beforehand.
Finally, positivity, patience and consistency are key. Placement season can be stressful and unpredictable,
so keep learning from every interview and don't compare your progress with others. Wishing everyone all
the best!!

1) Pre-placement Talk

2) Online Assessment
