4) HR Round

The pre-placement talk was conducted online on Webex platform. Since it was a pool campus placement
process, the online meeting had over 4000 students from colleges all over India. Every company shares
important pointers about the company and the roles they are hiring for that might be useful for later
interview rounds, so make sure to pay attention and note down a few important points (or any questions that
could be asked based on the preplacement talk in the interviews). BlackRock was hiring for 2 roles, namely
Software Engineering and Aladdin Data. We were asked to choose our preference and/or apply to both roles
(I applied for both roles). The eligibility criteria was open to students of all branches with a CGPA of 7.5 or
above. There was no apparent resume based shortlisting done for the Online Assessment.

1. Online Assessment [Around 285 students appeared for this round]

Everyone who had applied for either of the roles received the HackerRank test link on their email IDs a
day prior to the assessment. The duration of the test was 95 minutes, consisting of 7 timed sections, which
were as follows:
a) Coding (Advanced programming fundamentals) - 1 Question, 40 minutes
b) Coding (Basic programming) - 1 Question, 15 minutes
c) Design Pattern (Advanced) - 15 questions, 6 minutes
d) Design Pattern (Basic) - 15 questions, 4 minutes
e) Fundamental Al and Cloud concepts - 25 questions, 10 minutes
f) DB Concepts - 25 questions, 10 minutes
--- PAGE 2 ---
g) Aptitude - 15 questions, 10 minutes
The sections were timed, and once the timer ends, you are automatically moved to the next section. (Please
note, for the coding sections, the code is not auto-submitted, so please make sure you submit the code
before the timer ends).
For the Coding (Advanced) section, I received a question that involved an airport baggage-handling system
where each baggage item had a name and a destination. The objective was to group the baggage items by
destination and return the results in the required sorted order, while using Java's Fork/Join framework. I
implemented this using a RecursiveTask that returns a Map<String, List<Baggageltem. The baggage list
was recursively divided into two ranges until reaching a single-item base case, where the item was added to
a map under its destination.
For the recursive steps, I used fork to execute one half asynchronously, processed the other half directly,
and then used join to retrieve the first half's result. The two maps were then merged by combining baggage
lists belonging to the same destination using computelfAbsent. After merging, the baggage lists for each
destination were sorted by baggage name. One key detail was treating the end index as exclusive, which
ensured that the recursive ranges were handled correctly without index-out-of-bounds errors. I was able to
pass 7 out of 15 test cases with this approach.
For the Basic Coding section, I received a Selenium-based debugging question where I had to automate a
3-step verification flow that captures and persists HTML page source only when encountering a failure page.
It took me some time to thoroughly understand the existing codebase and requirements, so I was only able to
implement the input validation and Step 1 flow before running out of time.
The Design Pattern sections were based on basic LLD and related concepts, which I prepared for using
ChatGPT and Claude a day before the assessment and it fairly sufficed for the level of questions asked. The
Fundamental AI and Cloud concepts section consisted of questions based on mainly AWS and basic
questions of AI and ML. The DB concepts section consisted of questions based on ACID properties,
basic queries for transactions and fundamentals of DBMS (Please note: Oracle based questions were
also asked, which was slightly different as other OAs do not usually ask these, but they could be attempted
by option elimination and common knowledge). The Aptitude section was comparatively easier, but time
consuming, so time management was a key factor in attempting this section.
The interview shortlist and waitlist for both the roles were released on 18th August around 6 PM, 28
students shortlisted and 10 students waitlisted for the Software Engineering role, and 8 students shortlisted
and 6 students waitlisted for the Aladdin Data role. I was among the shortlisted candidates for SDE.

2. Technical Interview 1 [Around 38 students appeared for this round for SDE]

The interviews were conducted virtually through Webex on our personal laptops, but we were asked to
report to TPO at 8:30 AM for the same. Some students received the interview meeting links a night
before the interviews followed by a call from the HR confirming their slot and timing of interview. I
received my meeting link at around 9 AM, followed by a call from the HR mentioning that my interview
is scheduled for 9:30 AM, and that I will receive a call stating when to join the meeting. Make sure that
your laptop is connected to a stable internet connection as it helps you to remain calm during the
interview and avoid any technical glitches during the interview. Upon receiving the second call, I
immediately ran into some setup issues which made me delay joining the meeting, which I apologized
for upon joining the meeting.
--- PAGE 3 ---
There were two interviewers who warmly welcomed me and began by asking how I was feeling. This helped
ease some of the initial nervousness. They then asked me to briefly introduce myself. I gave a semi-formal,
resume-based introduction, while also mentioning some of my hobbies and personal interests to make the
introduction more conversational.
The interviewer then quickly moved into a technical, scenario-based question. He asked me to imagine a
situation where a client's payment gateway service had gone down in production and I was working as part
of a team of three developers. He asked what my approach would be to resolving the issue and, more
importantly, why I would choose that approach. I explained that my first priority would be to get the basic
functionality back online through a temporary patch or workaround, while simultaneously investigating
the underlying issue. I explained that in a production environment, restoring service is extremely important
for both the client and the organization. A temporary fix would not only restore essential functionality but
would also give the team additional time to investigate the root cause and develop and test a proper
permanent solution without keeping the entire service down.
The interviewer then spent a significant portion of the interview grilling me on this approach and
introducing additional constraints to the scenario. For instance, he asked how my approach would change if
the payment gateway was handling a very large number of transactions and a faulty fix could potentially
have a much greater impact. I calmly defended my reasoning while adapting it to each new condition he
introduced. I emphasized that the patch would not simply be pushed directly into production; it would first
need to go through appropriate testing, including multiple test cases and validation of edge cases, before
deployment.
The discussion then moved towards accountability. I was asked whether I would take responsibility if the
system still failed after implementing my proposed solution and customers suffered financial losses as a
result. I responded that, when working as a team, a solution should ideally be reviewed and challenged by
the other team members as well, which significantly reduces the possibility of overlooking an error.
However, if the solution ultimately failed despite these checks, I would take accountability for my decision,
particularly because I was the person who had proposed the approach. The interviewers seemed satisfied
with this response. I was also asked how I would handle the situation if the other two members of my team
did not agree with the idea of implementing a patch. I explained that I would first clearly communicate
my reasoning and the advantages of the approach, while also giving them an opportunity to explain their
concerns. Rather than forcing my approach on the team, I would compare the pros and cons of both
alternatives and try to arrive at a mutually agreed solution based on what would be safest and most
beneficial for the client and the system.
The second interviewer then shifted the discussion towards one of my projects, my regulatory compliance
platform. He asked me about the specific components I had implemented, how I had implemented them,
and some of the technical decisions I had made while developing the project. He then posed a hypothetical
question about how I would modify the system if, instead of building and maintaining my own RAG
model, I had to integrate an existing LLM.
I explained that one of the simplest approaches would be to integrate an LLM through an API using an
API key. However, I also pointed out that for a regulatory compliance platform, simply integrating an
external LLM would raise important concerns around data security, privacy, and the handling of
potentially sensitive information. This led to a few follow-up questions where I discussed how I would
approach these concerns and what factors I would consider before selecting such an integration.
--- PAGE 4 ---
Towards the end of the interview, the interviewers asked if I had any questions for them. I asked them to
briefly introduce themselves and share how their experience at BlackRock had helped them grow, both
personally and professionally. They answered the question very sincerely and shared their own
experiences and perspectives, which made the closing part of the interview quite conversational.
The interview ended on a positive note, with the interviewers asking me to stay calm and wait for
communication from HR regarding the next round, should I be selected. The interview lasted for around 50
minutes, upon which I encountered probably the toughest part of the entire process - the waiting for the call
from HR regarding the next round.

3. HR interview [Around 18 students appeared for this round]

I finished my first interview around 10:20 AM. Since some students had started receiving calls for the
second round within 10-15 minutes of their first interview, I was initially stressed when I did not receive
any communication. I tried to remain calm and waited. Finally, around 3:10 PM, I received an email with the
meeting link for the second round, followed by a call from HR asking me to join as soon as possible. I
quickly composed myself and joined the interview.
This round had only one interviewer, who started by asking how my first round had gone and how I was
feeling. He then asked for my introduction, after which he went through my resume in detail. He focused
mainly on my Al-powered regulatory compliance platform project. He asked how we came up with the
idea, the complete project pipeline, the technologies used, and my specific contribution. I explained the
technical implementation of the document ingestion pipeline and the knowledge graph component,
including how we used graph databases to represent the information.
The discussion then moved to my leadership experience as Chairperson. He asked how I had created an
impact in the role. I explained that I primarily focused on improving communication and coordination
between different teams, as miscommunication often affects the outcome of large initiatives. I also
emphasized long-term planning, which helped avoid last-minute issues. He asked a few follow-up questions
about how the experience helped me personally and professionally.
He then asked a more reflective question: if I could go back to my first year, what would I change? I asked
for a minute to think and answered that I would have said 'yes' to more opportunities, both socially, such as
making more friends and being open to new experiences, and technically, by participating in more projects
and activities that could have given me greater exposure. He also asked what I felt was currently lacking in
my resume. I mentioned that since BlackRock is a fintech company and Java is widely used for backend
development in financial services, I would like to strengthen my Java and Java-based development
framework skills further.
At the end, he asked if I had any questions. I asked for a brief introduction about himself and then asked
what a typical day for a software engineering intern at BlackRock looks like. He answered both
questions and gave me a better understanding of the internship experience. The interview lasted
approximately 20-25 minutes and was more techno-HR than pure HR, largely focused on my projects,
leadership experience, technical understanding, and self-awareness.
Finally, the results were declared the next day, and 7 students got the offer for the Software Engineering
role and 1 student for the Aladdin Data Role (total 8 students were selected).
--- PAGE 5 ---

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
Placements are not purely skill-based; luck, timing and the particular interview panel can also play a role.
So, as niche as it may sound, don't let a rejection define your preparation. Keep improving and stay
consistent.
Resources:

• DSA: Striver's A2Z DSA Sheet - one of the most structured resources for placement preparation.

Focus on understanding concepts and solving the more frequently asked data structures and their
problems (Strings, Stacks, Queues, LinkedLists) at least once (Please note: Every company usually
has topics that they tend to ask more on, so do your research thoroughly and try covering the other
topics if needed).
https://takeuforward.org/dsa/strivers-a2z-sheet-learn-dsa-a-to-z/

• SQL: LeetCode SQL 50 - Repeat questions you struggle with and understand multiple approaches.

https://leetcode.com/studyplan/top-sql-50/

• Java: Kunal Kushwaha's YouTube channel for Java and OOP fundamentals.

https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL9gnSGHSqcno1G3XjUbwzXHL8_EttOuKk

• Core CS: GeeksforGeeks for OOP, DBMS, OS and Computer Networks concepts and practice.

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/interview-experiences/technical-interview-preparation/

• System Design: Gaurav Sen's content + ChatGPT/Claude for explanations and interview-style

practice.

• Aptitude: IndiaBIX, https://www.indiabix.com/aptitude/

• Puzzles: GeeksforGeeks' interview puzzles, https://www.indiabix.com/aptitude/

Interview-Day Tips:

• Know your resume thoroughly. Anything written on it can be questioned, so understand every

technology, tool and project you mention.

• Know your projects end-to-end: schema/database design, backend structure, APIs, architecture,

your contribution, limitations and possible improvements.

• Be strong in fundamentals: You don't need to know everything, but the fundamentals of every

technology on your resume should be clear.

• Prepare for follow-ups: Interviewers may keep changing the conditions of a scenario, so understand

your reasoning rather than memorizing answers.

• CGPA: 8+ is a decent position, while 8.5+ is preferable where companies have academic cutoffs.

• Prepare for HR and behavioural questions as well. Technical preparation alone is not enough. Be

ready for questions about your strengths, weaknesses, leadership experiences, failures, career goals,
and situational judgement. Answer smartly but honestly; don't try to give the answer you think the
interviewer wants to hear. Keep your responses genuine and support them with real examples from
your experiences.
--- PAGE 6 ---

• Don't lose confidence after rejection: BlackRock was the 18th company I encountered during

placements. I had previously been shortlisted by two companies but was rejected by HR in the final
rounds in both. I kept preparing and eventually got this opportunity.

• Don't convince yourself that you're underprepared: You will never feel completely prepared.

Trust your preparation and focus on the interview in front of you.

• Stay calm and patient. Take a few seconds to think before answering difficult questions and explain

your reasoning clearly.

• Sleep properly: I had only around 1.5 hours of sleep before my interview day, and it definitely

affected how calmly I handled the long day. As funny as it might sound, get adequate sleep the day
before interviews at least, and keep your setup ready beforehand.
Finally, positivity, patience and consistency are key. Placement season can be stressful and unpredictable,
so keep learning from ev

You need to be patient. At the start of the season, I was able to clear the PhonePe OA, and got rejected
during my HM Round. I was unable to get my resume shortlisted for companies like WorkIndia, Nomura,

very little time to mentally prepare for the next one. Even though the Edra result hadn't come out yet, I was
sure I wasn't getting another round, so gave up hopes for that.
Talk to friends and family, don't bottle it up. There will be lows but keep putting in genuine efforts and the
result will show.

depends on your panel and so just prepare everything.

will definitely teach you something new and covers the most asked OA topics. YOu just need to give this 1
hour a day, that is it, be consistent and start early.

journey.howSecured:
This was a pool process, I honestly did not sit for the PPT and later came to know that 4k+ students were
attending it(including some NITs, VIT and SPIT)! BlackRock came for 2 roles: Software Engineering and
Aladdin Data, we were asked to choose our preference (you could choose both).
The process usually includes an OA, followed by 2 interviews, which are held online on the Webex Platform
and to be attended from the TPO. The GPA cutoff was set to 7.5, also while registering on Superset, they
asked for any professional qualifications, I do not have any, but also I have no idea how much weightage
they give this(probably just for the OA shortlist).

1. Online Assessment

The OA pattern had considerably changed compared to the previous year. For the advanced coding section I
got the luggage management system which could only be implemented in Java.
For the basic coding section, i received a DSA question :
https://codeforces.com/contest/1922/problem/C :
For the Design Pattern section, I had gone through a few videos from this channel and spent some time
looking for the most asked questions from any LLM. That should be enough and there was no negative
marking so you could always eliminate options or guess.
The Al section could be solved by option elimination and could be done easily. DBMS was doable with
good enough prep and Aptitude was lengthy.
Some were asked Selenium testing (15 mins!), whereas some were asked DSA for both initial sections.
We came to know the section wise details just a DAY before the OA, prev GFG and college experiences
only mentioned MCQs + Flowcharts, so this year was a huge shakeup in format.
--- PAGE 2 ---

2.
Technical Round 1[28 Shortlist + 10 Waitlist]
Interviews were held online from the TPO office, on the Webex platform. Please make sure you have your
laptop, webcam, mic, internet connection working before the process. I received a call at around 9:30 that
my interview would be scheduled at 10:30. They will tell you when to join the interview, do not barge into
the meeting.
A thing to keep in mind is that there were many panels running in parallel. Each had a different style of
questioning, some focusing more on projects, others more so on Java and DS. There is not much you can do
in such cases other than prepare / ask other people who got alloted the same panel, but this isn't in your hand
and just do your best and prepare.
I got the call to join only at around 11, so I joined the call. Be proactive here and turn on your camera
without being asked and greet them. They started off by introducing themselves and then asked me to do so
as well, however funny enough they did not want me to get into much details, and keep it very simple. I
however had a small network issue just this moment and heard that they wanted me to go into detail.
I went on for around 5 mins before they interrupted me, and told me that they did not want much detail, at
which point I realized the blunder I had made, I apologized and explained but they were very chill about it
and started their line of questioning.
They mainly focused on projects, on the problem I tried to solve and how I did it. Make sure that you can
defend each decision and explain each concept mentioned on your resume. They just wanted to know the
tech stack I used and how data got passed around the system.
My project had a bit of scraping involved, and during my explanation I said very very casually "unki API
bohot slow hai_ to which they started laughing. I still don't know why I said it in such a way, but it led to a
discussion where they asked me what I would do to make it faster. This led to a discussion on scalability and
caching.
They asked me how this slowness is measured, I was aware of terms like p99,95 latency and said so.
--- PAGE 3 ---
Other questions were still very project dependent, like explain rate limiting (I had nginx mentioned so), why
Base62 Encoding instead of hashing, high level overview of the services and how to further scale them.
The interviewers finally allowed me to ask them a few questions. Prepare 2-3 good questions, look at what
the company does and make it seem as if you are really interested in what they do and want to join the
company. I asked something very basic first to which they again laughed and said "we've been asked this
before" but gladly answered.
Next I asked something like "How much financial awareness is required to be an analyst at BlackRock?"
They were very enthusiastic to answer this, and I asked this directly as previous year interviewers directly
asked the candidates how much they know, so again a good way to show that you researched about the role.
My interview only went on for around 20-25 mins, which I felt was very short and I truly believed that I was
done for the day. Others had rounds which started before mine and ended after mine, even during the
interview I was taken aback when they ended the round in such a short amount of time, but I kept it together
and gave it my best.
However, within 30 mins of my round finishing, I got the call that my 2nd round was scheduled at 1pm.
Note: Do not compare your process to others, each panel has its own way to ask, many were even asked HR
questions along with tech in their 1st round like if they would relocate.

3. Technical Round 2 [15/16 for SDE + 3/4 for Data ]

This round was again very technical, started off in a similar fashion with their introduction and then mine.
After my introduction, they started their line of questioning, mostly based on my projects, tech stack, and
what problem I was trying to solve.
Also if you used X in your project, be prepared to explain why you used X and why you would not use X.
Be aware of the fact that Y and Z also could have been used, but why you chose not to, or if you would but
were unable to implement. It is important that they understand your line of reasoning and how you would
approach a new problem. They indirectly asked me this : "what would you have done differently if you were
to build this again".
This round was again very project dependent and so it is necessary to know what you have done and written
on your resume.
They then asked me a simple DSA question:
Given a list of N integers, where each element from 1 to N occurs exactly 1.
You need to sort this list.
Note that you need to share your screen and pseudo/code on notepad.
I explained the brute and then explained how it could be reduced to cycle sort. Keep in mind that it should
not appear as if you have learnt the solution. Be very proactive here, note down the question, literally type it
out, take sample input and simulate the operation and get to the answer.
Also when asked to code, go with good quality of code and don't use random variable names.
Next they asked me: Given a 2D array of N*3, sort the vector on the basis of the internal sum in ASC.
--- PAGE 4 ---
Example : [[1,2,4] , [1,1,1]] > [[1,1,1] , [1,2,4]]
I straightaway jumped to using a comparator for this and they seemed to be happy with the approach.
Finally, maybe just because i was writing the full code, they asked me something like : " how would you do
something like stack<I can put any data type here>"
I struggled with this, and said something like maybe custom structs, but then they straight away asked me if
I was aware of Generics and Templates in C++.
I mentioned yes, I had used it before for implementing policy based structures where I mentioned both avl
and rb tree here, i wasn't sure myself how it was internally implemented but just wanted to prove that I
wasn't bluffing and had actually used them.
They immediately caught on that I wasn't too sure about their difference and asked me, I could explain AVL
but for RB trees I just simply said that the nodes were coloured and had a set of rules.
Not too sure whether they were satisfied or not, I could barely see or hear them both. Finally I asked them
something like " what do you love about your job at BlackRock? / what is the most exciting part of your
dayi
My round went on for around 45 mins. BlackRock generally only conducts 2 rounds, so from this point
onwards it was just a waiting game, results usually arriving only on the next day.
There is no point in overthinking the results, jo hoga wo hoga, and leave it at that, focus on the next
company and learn from the mistakes you made before.
Results arrived at around 12 pm the next day.
Finally, 7 students were shortlisted for SDE and 1 for Aladdin Data.

journey.prep:
1. Start as early as you can, but if you're late, START anyway.

Don't wait for the "perfect time" to begin. I started DSA and computer fundamentals around
July-December, but I wasn't consistent initially. What mattered was that I eventually realised I needed to
take it seriously and started grinding consistently. Even if you think you're late, it's not over. Start from
wherever you are and be smart about what you cover. You don't have to learn everything; you need to learn
the right things for the roles you are targeting.

2. Be ready to change your plan.

Initially, I was almost certain that I wanted to go into non-tech roles. But after seeing the experiences of
some of my seniors, I realised I should also prepare for SDE roles. I had already been doing some DSA and
computer fundamentals from July to December, but not consistently. Then I made a major decision: I
dropped Finance preparation, even though I had been preparing for it for almost two years. I felt that with
my existing preparation, I could revise Finance in a month if needed. For the next six months, I completely
tocused on DSA and computer fundamentals. I also gave around 12-15 mock interviews to seniors and
professionals. And trust me, there was a point where I genuinely questioned whether I was even prepared.
I had set myself a target to complete DSA before March. During one mock interview around that time, I
couldn't even write basic syntax properly. LeetCode and actually sitting in front of a blank compiler are two
very different experiences, and that blank screen can be scary.
So, I started again.
From March onwards, I practised writing code from scratch, worked on my logic, and gradually became
comfortable with solving problems without relying on an online platform. I also want to clarify that I didn't
--- PAGE 10 ---
prepare every hard DSA topic. My target was to prepare DSA up to the level required for placement
interviews. Be strategic about your preparation instead of trying to master everything.

3. Don't completely depend on Finance roles.

If you're planning to rely mainly on Finance roles, first understand your college's placement scenario. Check
how many companies actually visit your campus for the specific role you're targeting. Companies like JP,
KPMG, GEP, OMP, etc. may visit, but you need to understand whether there are enough opportunities for
you. Don't build your entire placement strategy around a role without checking the actual opportunities
available on campus.

4. Sometimes taking a risk is worth it.

Taking a risk doesn't always work out, but sometimes it can completely change your outcome. I had actually
made a personal rule for myself: I would take risks during the first two months of placements, and after that,
I wouldn't. This decision was based on my understanding of my own situation and how the placement
season was progressing. The point is not to blindly take risks. Understand your situation, assess what you
have to lose, and then decide.

5. Surround yourself with the right people.

This made a huge difference in my journey. Surround yourself with people who believe in you, push you to
do better, and have a positive impact on you. Good friends can completely change how you approach
stressful situations. My friends helped me with preparation, revisions, mock interviews, notes, and
sometimes simply by reminding me that I was capable of doing it. Your preparation is yours, but the people
around you can make the journey much easier.

6. Learn from your previous mistakes.

Before BlackRock, I had already reached some of the final rounds/T2 rounds at JP and ISS. And honestly, I
made mistakes there. Looking back, those experiences taught me a lot about what I was doing wrong, what I
needed to improve, and how I should approach interviews differently,JP was the first company that came
to our campus, and I made it through the Technical Round 1. Unfortunately, I wasn't selected for the HR
round. Honestly, I still don't know exactly what went wrong. I felt that most of the technical answers I gave
were correct, so maybe the issue was my communication or the way I presented my answers. There are also
so many factors during an interview-what time you're scheduled, the interviewer's mood, how the
conversation flows, and, of course, your own performance. "I was the last person to be interviewed, and my
interviewer had joined through his phone. I still don't know what went wrong, and perhaps I simply didn't
communicate as well as I could havei Maybe that played a role, maybe it didn't. I'll never really know. But
JP definitely broke my heart a little. It was the first company, I had put in a lot of effort, and I couldn't move
on from the rejection easily. I was still thinking about it when ISS came around.
For ISS, I had to almost start from square zero. I had spent about a month preparing heavily for Finance,
and in the process, I had lost some of my grip on technical concepts. I was stressed and honestly struggling
to get back into the flow. My school friends, and college, especially Nidhi and Asmiya, supported me a lot
during this phase and helped me get back on track.
Then came my ISS interview, where I made another very simple mistake. I was asked about polymorphism,
a concept I had studied before, but I completely blanked out and couldn't explain it properly. That moment
--- PAGE 11 ---
taught me something important: knowing something and being able to communicate it under pressure
are two completely different things. After that, I started giving mock interviews continuously. I practised
explaining concepts out loud, solving problems while someone was watching, and getting comfortable with
the pressure of being questioned.
Slowly, I stopped feeling anxious during interviews and became much more comfortable communicating my
thoughts. Looking back, JP and ISS were not failures. They were probably the practice rounds I needed
before BlackRock. Every interview showed me something I needed to fix. By the time BlackRock came
around, I wasn't just technically better,I was much better at communicating what I knew under stress and
anxiety.

7. Don't Prepare for Placements - Prepare for the Role

Once you know the kind of role you want, work backwards from it. For SDE, I focused on DSA + computer
fundamentals + my resume rather than trying to study every possible CS topic. The goal isn't to know
everything. The goal is to be interview-ready for the role you are targeting.

8. Your Resume Can Decide the Direction of Your Interview

Never put something on your resume just because it sounds impressive. If you mention AWS, Oracle, AI,
Azure, React, Java, SQL, etc., assume the interviewer can ask you anything about it. Before every interview,
go through your resume line by line and ask yourself: "If I were the interviewer, what could I ask about
this?" Prepare those answers

9. Mock Interviews Are NOT Optional

LeetCode can teach you how to solve problems. Mock interviews teach you how to solve problems while
someone is watching you. Give mocks to seniors, friends, professionals-anyone who can question you
seriously. And don't just ask them, "How was my interview?"
Ask:

• Where did I hesitate?

• Was my explanation clear?

• Did I communicate my thought process?

• Did I speak too much?

• Did I speak too little?

• Where did I lose confidence?

• What would make my answer stronger?

That feedback is gold.

10. Practise on a Blank Compiler

This one genuinely matters. Solving on LeetCode and solving on a completely blank screen are very
different experiences. Before interviews, practise writing code from scratch without autocomplete or
familiar platform support. Even basic syntax can suddenly disappear when you're under pressure.
You don't want your first blank-compiler experience to be during the actual interview.
--- PAGE 12 ---

11. Don't Memorise Answers -Understand the "Why?

For every technology, project, or concept on your resume, know three things:
What is it? Why did I use it? How did I use it?
And preferably a fourth:
Why this instead of an alternative?
This helped me tremendously when interviewers started asking about my tech stack and its competitors.

12. Learn How to Say "I Don't Know"

This is an underrated interview skill. If you genuinely don't know something, don't start making things up.
You can simply say:
"I'm not completely sure about that, but based on my understanding..."
Or:
"I don't remember the exact details right now, but I have worked with this concept in..."
Honesty + whatever knowledge you actually have is much better than confidently giving a wrong answer.

13. Don't Let One Rejection Ruin the Next Interview

This was something I personally struggled with after JP. You can spend days thinking:
"What did I do wrong?"
"Why did they reject me?"
"Maybe I'm not good enough."
But eventually, you have to close that tab in your head.
Also be ready for your interview schedule in the next 10-12hrs. For some companies you literally get the
shortlist this prior.
The next company doesn't know what happened in your previous interview. Walk into every new
interview as a fresh opportunity.

14. Prepare Your "Why This Company?" Before Every Interview

Don't give a generic:
"BlackRock is a reputed company and I want to grow professionally."
Research the company, understand the role, and connect it to your own interests and experience. For
BlackRock, I was able to connect my answer with the principles they had discussed during the PPT. That
made my answer much more relevant.
--- PAGE 13 ---

15. Keep a Placement Journal

This is something I wish more students did. After every interview, immediately write down:

• Questions asked

• Questions you couldn't answer

• Topics you struggled with

• Questions that surprised you

• What you could have communicated better

• What the interviewer focused on

After 5-6 interviews, you'll start seeing patterns. Your placement preparation then becomes much more
targeted.

16. Don't Compare Your Timeline With Someone Else's

Someone might get shortlisted before you. Someone might get an offer in the first month. Someone might
get rejected from five companies and crack the sixth. Someone might get an easier interviewer. Someone
might get a tougher one. Placement season is not a race with one fixed timeline.
Focus on improving between every interview.

17. Take Care of Your Mind During Placement Season

This one is personal but important. Placement season can mess with your confidence because every few
days you're either celebrating someone else's offer or dealing with your own rejection.
Don't let your entire self-worth become:
"I got placed / I didn't get placed."
You're still the same person before and after an interview. Prepare seriously. Give it everything. But don't
destroy yourself over one result.

18. And Finally ,Don't Give Up Too Early

You genuinely never know which interview will work out. You can be rejected after reaching a final round.
You can be waitlisted and still get interviewed. You can have an interview you think went terribly and still
move ahead. And you can spend six hours thinking you've been rejected... only to get the HR call.
So stay in the game.
You don't need every company to say yes. You just need one company to say yes.
If you have any questions, please feel free to reach out on:
Whatsapp: 7558596840

The BlackRock placement process had 4 main stages:

1. Pre-Placement Talk

Tip: Pay close attention during the pre-placement talk! Companies often mention small but important details

• Important facts about the company

• Details about the role

• Skills they are looking for

• Any specific points mentioned by the recruiters

A shoutout to my friend Ronit, I had missed the PPT due to certain reasons, but i will link down the

BR_PPT_NOTES (Credits:Ronit Sonawane)
BlackRock was hiring for two roles:

• Software Engineering

• Aladdin Data

Candidates could choose their preferred role or apply for both. I applied for both roles.
Eligibility & Shortlisting
The eligibility criteria was quite straightforward:

• Students from all branches were eligible.

• Minimum CGPA: 7.5 (For safer side keep your CGPA above 8)

• There was no apparent resume-based shortlisting for the Online Assessment.

So, if you met the eligibility criteria, you had a good opportunity to directly attempt the OA and prove
yourself through the selection process.

1. Online Assesment [Around 285 students appeared for this round]

Everyone who applied for either of the two roles received the HackerRank assessment link via email one
day before the test.
The assessment was 95 minutes long and was divided into 7 timed sections. Each section tested a different
skill, so managing time was just as important as solving the questions correctly.
The sections were:
a) Coding (Advanced programming fundamentals) - 1 Question, 40 minutes
b) Coding (Basic programming) - 1 Question, 15 minutes
c) Design Pattern (Advanced) - 15 questions, 6 minutes
d) Design Pattern (Basic) - 15 questions, 4 minutes
e) Fundamental Al and Cloud concepts - 25 questions, 10 minutes
f) DB Concepts - 25 questions, 10 minutes
g) Aptitude - 15 questions, 10 minutes
BlackRock usually gives enough time to prepare between the OA and interviews so make sure you utilize it
very carefully, also put the name of company and add "gfg interview on campus experience", usually you
get to know questions or OA patterns if companies don't mention them. (we had a very different pattern than
all the previous years, and being honest and the research done it was noticed that since 2-3 years similar OA
questions were appeared in OA, except this year)
I will add few website links, from where you might get company specific OA questions:
--- PAGE 3 ---
https://oavoservice.com/en/articles/blackrock-oa-guide-question-types-real-questions-2026(credits:Nidhi
Patel)
Few more I found:
https://drive.google.com/drive/u/0/mobile/folders/1c2wIdukwLZCYtb8wIA2-T7bkqZ86xfsa
https://drive.google.com/drive/u/0/mobile/folders/16SUOj1gcmi1gqb-y8sbLig6ZdbAtBuyX
https://drive.google.com/drive/u/0/mobile/folders/1L4jLM31W-qkvqel3aSK7_ZYFCgFPmJSq/11bKpCEhP
7woxWyVQh3Rm xi1tMadSpR5?sort=13&direction=a
The sections were strictly timed, and once the timer ended, you were automatically moved to the next
section.
Important: In the coding sections, the code is not submitted automatically when the timer ends. Make
sure to submit your code before the timer runs out, otherwise your solution may not be considered.
My coding question was based on a tree height minimization problem. I was given a tree and a maximum
number of operations, where an operation could be used to move a node closer to the root. The goal was to
find the minimum possible height of the tree after performing at most the given number of operations.
I solved it using binary search on the answer. For each possible height, I used a bottom-up greedy
approach on the rooted tree to check whether that height could be achieved within the allowed number of
operations.
The Design Pattern sections focused mainly on basic LLD (Low-Level Design) and related concepts. I
prepared for these just one day before the assessment using ChatGPT and Claude, and honestly, that
preparation was enough for the level of questions asked.
The Fundamental Al & Cloud Concepts section mainly covered AWS fundamentals along with basic
AI/ML concepts.
The DB Concepts section focused on:

• ACID properties

• Basic transaction-related queries

• DBMS fundamentals

• Some Oracle-based questions

The Oracle questions were slightly unexpected since they are not commonly seen in other OAs. However,
most could still be attempted using option elimination and basic knowledge.
The Aptitude section was comparatively easier, but it was time-consuming. So, managing time efficiently
was crucial to attempting all the questions.
--- PAGE 4 ---
The shortlist and waitlist for both roles were released on 18th August at around 6 PM.
Software Engineering:

• 28 students shortlisted

• 10 students waitlisted

Aladdin Data:

• 8 students shortlisted

• 6 students waitlisted

I was shortlisted for the Software Engineering role, which meant it was time to prepare for the interview
rounds (Even though I was shortlisted for another company a very dicey thing to do, as EXTC
struggled a lot to get shortlisted, I decided to take a risk and go for BlackRock. Sometimes, taking a
risk can leave you with regret-but sometimes, you win so big that you're left with nothing to regret.
So, when you believe in yourself, take the leap.)

2. Technical Interview 1 [Around 38 students appeared for this round for SDE]

It's a rare scenario, but yes, waitlisted candidates did get a chance to appear for the interviews. In fact,
there were candidates who eventually made it to the final shortlist after initially being waitlisted. So, if
you find yourself on the waitlist, don't lose hope. It takes immense patience and calmness to get through
such a situation, but sometimes, staying in the game is all it takes for the opportunity to come your way.
My panel number was 19 (it was going all over India, later after interview i got to know my panelists
were from bangalore), and the interviews had started from 9:00 AM. Mine was scheduled for 9:30 AM.
That morning, we also received a confirmation call and were specifically instructed not to join the Webex
meeting until the HR asked us to. We were asked to bring our laptops, and the interviews were conducted
on Webex.
The 9:30 AM Moment
I reached the venue, settled myself, took a breath, and joined the meeting. I wasn't extremely nervous, but I
wasn't overconfident either. I was simply in the mindset:
"I want this. Somehow, I'm going to make it happen."
As soon as I joined, I immediately noted down the names of my interviewers. This might sound like a tiny
thing, but remember your panelists' names. If you make it to the next round, being able to address them
by name can make the interaction much more personal and confident.
They said, "Hi."
I replied with a "Good morning."
And then...
Silence.
--- PAGE 5 ---
LOL.
At that point, I realised, Okay, someone has to start this. So I took the initiative and started with my
introduction(make sure you prepare this very well.)
The first question was:
"Why Software Engineering when your branch is EXTC?
Luckily, I was very well prepared for this question, so I was able to explain my transition towards
software and why I wanted to pursue SDE. The answer seemed to satisfy them, and we moved ahead.
Internship
The interviewer then started asking questions about my internship and tech stack. They went quite deep
into what I had worked on, including questions around Azure Data Factory (ADF) and specifically:
"How did you initialise Azure Data Factory? What exactly did you do?"
Here, one important lesson came up "Drive the Interview" I deliberately explained the overview first
instead of dumping every technical detail I knew. Why? Because if you tell the interviewer absolutely
everything at once, you are essentially giving them a list of things to question you on. They can easily pick
one tiny detail and take you somewhere completely unexpected. So, don't hide things or lie, but structure
your answers intelligently. Give enough information to demonstrate your understanding, and then let the
interviewer decide where to go deeper. In my case, the interviewer had already grilled me quite a bit on
ADF, so eventually we moved to another project.
During the pre-placement presentation, BlackRock had placed considerable emphasis on Al-driven
solutions. I had already researched this beforehand and had Al-based projects on my resume, including
Oracle-based AI/GenAl solutions. I also had a minor focused on AI for Non-CS students, which helped me
here. This gave me an advantage because I could confidently discuss the concepts and projects I had actually
worked on. And this brings me to one of the biggest lessons from my interview:
Know your resume inside out.
I had maintained a separate Google Doc containing everything on my resume and prepared possible
questions for each section:

• Education: What did you actually learn/do during your degree?

• Internship: What was your contribution?

• Projects: Why did you build it? How does it work?

• Certifications: What did you learn from them?

• Tech Stack: Why this technology? Why not another?

• AI/Cloud/DB: What concepts did you actually use?

If you don't have time to revise an entire certification, at least take a screenshot of its contents/index
and ask ChatGPT to summarise the course for you. The interviewer even asked me about competitors to
the technologies in my tech stack and why I had chosen a particular technology over its alternatives.
--- PAGE 6 ---
So, once again: Your resume is not a piece of paper. It is your interview syllabus. After the project
discussion, I was asked 3 DSA questions. All three were around the easy-to-medium level.
Question 1 - Even and Odd Indices
The first problem was related to ensuring that even indices contain even numbers and odd contains odd
numbers. The interviewer explained the problem, but didn't initially provide an example.
Instead of immediately jumping into the solution, I asked:

• "Can I write down my logic on paper?"

• "Could you give me an example?"

• "Can I have a little time to think?"

• "Could you provide some edge cases?"

And here's another important lesson:
Communication is part of DSA.
I knew the solution, but normally I would approach a problem through brute force → better →
optimal. However, the interviewer specifically told me that I should directly provide the optimized
approach. So I adapted. I opened Notepad and started writing the code...
And then they stopped me:
"Please don't code. Can you explain the approach first?"
So I switched gears, took the example they provided, dry-ran my approach, and explained the logic
step-by-step. That worked. Remember: Solving DSA questions is only half the job. If you can't
communicate your approach clearly, all those questions and patterns you've practised won't help much.
You should be able to transfer your logical thinking to the interviewer clearly and confidently.
And please, start taking communication and soft skills seriously. Otherwise, you might genuinely regret
it later. I've seen people who are technically brilliant but struggle during HR rounds, GDS, or simply
communicating their thoughts. And honestly, that hurts, because you worked so hard to build the
knowledge, only to lose an opportunity because you couldn't communicate it properly. Don't let all that
hard work go to waste. Work on your communication alongside your technical skills. Trust me, you
don't want to reach the end and think, "I knew it all... I just couldn't express it." and end up in tears.
The other two questions were related to removing duplicates and anagrams. I followed a similar
approach, understand the problem, clarify the requirements, think through edge cases, and then explain the
solution.
And yes, even if you don't know a term like "anagram", simply ask. There is absolutely nothing wrong
with saying:
"Could you please explain what you mean by anagram?"
The interviewer isn't sitting there trying to defeat you. They're trying to evaluate whether you can solve
problems and communicate your thought process.
--- PAGE 7 ---
Towards the end, they started asking about my Oracle certifications and an AWS certification. Here, I
chose honesty. For AWS, I admitted that I didn't remember every detail of the certification, but I could
confidently talk about the services and concepts I had actually worked with, including SageMaker. You
don't need to pretend that you remember every single thing you've ever studied. Be honest, but
demonstrate what you actually know.
I was also asked:
"Why BlackRock?»
This was another question where the Pre-Placement Talk helped me. I referred to the five principles they
had highlighted during the PPT and connected them with why I wanted to join BlackRock. This is exactly
why I recommend paying attention during the pre-placement presentation. Sometimes the answers you
need are literally given to you beforehand.
Finally, they asked:
"Do you have any questions for us?"
Always have a question ready.
I asked "Could you tell me a little about the kind of projects the team is currently working on and the
technologies or tech stack I would get an opportunity to work with in this roleạThis not only keeps
the conversation going, but also shows that you're genuinely interested in the actual work you would be
doing. And with that, Round 1 was over. The interviewer ended with "all the best for further
interviewsạẠạ
The interviewer is not your opponent. Your job is not to know everything. Your job is to show
that you can learn, think, solve problems, and communicate.
The interview lasted around 45 minutes. And honestly, luck plays a small but real role too. Luck
does play a small role,you can't control your panelist, the questions you get, or the timing of your
interview. But preparation decides how well you handle whatever comes your way. I had friends
whose first round was HR(and very little TECH), and all of them made it to the second round. On
the other hand, I knew people who were asked some really tough DSA questions, answered them
well, and still didn't make it to the next round. So yes, you can't control everything. You can only
control your preparation, communication, and how you handle whatever comes your way. Prepare
for the worst, hope for the best, and make the most of the panel you get.
And then came the longest 6 hours of my entire life.
Honestly, I was pretty heartbroken. I felt I had given the interview a really good shot, but I still hadn't
received the HR call while everyone else had already finished their interviews.
At that point, my brain started overthinking everything.
"Okay... maybe the interviewer cooked me."
"Maybe that was their way of saying, 'All the best for your other companies.'
--- PAGE 8 ---
I had almost started convincing myself that it was over. But sometimes, the process is not as
straightforward as you think it is.
Tech Interview 2 [19 including both roles]
So finally, I got the HR call. I joined the Webex meeting and honestly, the drama had already started. The
interviewer was casually sitting there, scrolling through his phone, while I was thinking, "Okay, how do I
tell him I actually got the HR round?" I finally interrupted and said, "Hey, am I audible?" No response. My
anxiety level went up instantly. I repeated myself, and this time he noticed. He said hi and then casually
asked, "How are you? Did you have your lunch?"
After answering that, he asked, "How have you been doing while waiting for this call?" I answered
honestly, Honestly, the longest 6 hours of my life, I must say." He then asked which college I was from, and
I told him SPIT.
He then asked me, "What is one thing you liked about yourself during the interview, one thing you
didn't like, and what would you improve?i I started by mentioning my panelists from the previous round,
Riya Ma'am and Kalvi Sir, and then explained what I thought went well, what I could have done better, and
what I would improve. This was a good reminder that HR rounds are also about self-awareness. You don't
always need a perfect answer; you need to show that you understand yourself and are willing to improve.
Next, he asked me to give an informal introduction. I made sure it wasn't just the usual name, college, and
branch introduction. I included my hobbies, interests, and a little about myself beyond academics. He then
asked me to walk him through my resume, which I did. From there, we moved to my internship. He asked
what I had worked on, whether it was remote, and then started asking about my tech stack.
At this point, I noticed a very interesting pattern. Whatever I ended my answer with became his next
question. For example, I mentioned that I had worked in an Agile team, and immediately he asked, "What
do you mean by Agile?" Once I noticed this pattern, I started using it to my advantage. I consciously tried
to end my answers with topics I was confident discussing. You should never lie or deliberately mislead an
interviewer, but if you understand the direction of the conversation, you can definitely communicate your
answers strategically and help drive the interview.
He then asked me to choose one of my projects. I picked my first project and was asked to share my screen
and explain its tech stack. He then asked why I had chosen that particular tech stack, what its alternatives
were, and what competitors existed. I had prepared six tech stack beforehand, so I was able to answer those
questions confidently.
Then came a quick rapid-fire round on DBMS, SQL, and related concepts. Again, the same pattern
continued: whatever I mentioned often became the next question. So I made sure I ended my answers with
concepts I was comfortable discussing. A huge shoutout to Shahid, who helped me identify the important
topics I needed to study, and to Vikrant, who sat with me for two hours the day before the interview and
revised some of the most important DBMS topics with me.
This is something I genuinely want to highlight: have good friends. The kind of friends who show up when
you need them. My placement journey was honestly a roller coaster, and Thad Sarthak who helped me with
PPT preparation, notes, Claude-ready PDFs, last-minute revisions, and random doubts. My ex-roommate
--- PAGE 9 ---
also deserves a special mention because she would regularly check on me, especially after companies I
really wanted didn't work out. You may prepare individually, but you don't have to go through the journey
alone.
The interviewer then asked me about relocation, and I was completely comfortable with it. I said yes.
Finally, he asked, "Do you have any questions for me?" I asked him about his experience at BlackRock and
what life was like for him there. I wanted to understand the person behind the role and the actual work
environment, rather than just asking something for the sake of asking.
Throughout the interview, I also noticed that many of my answers naturally connected back to the five
principles of BlackRock that they had highlighted during the Pre-Placement Talk. This is another reason
why I keep stressing the importance of paying attention during the PPT. Those small details can come back
and help you when you least expect them.
After everything, from the OA, the first interview, the six-hour wait, and finally this conversation, I was left
with one thought: maybe the delay wasn't a rejection. Maybe it was just another part of the story.
Sometimes, you don't understand why things happen when they do. But when you finally look back, you
realise that maybe everything happened for a reason. And the next day i got to know i m Selected!!!

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
1. Start as early as you can, but if you're late, START anyway.

Don't wait for the "perfect time" to begin. I started DSA and computer fundamentals around
July-December, but I wasn't consistent initially. What mattered was that I eventually realised I needed to
take it seriously and started grinding consistently. Even if you think you're late, it's not over. Start from
wherever you are and be smart about what you cover. You don't have to learn everything; you need to learn
the right things for the roles you are targeting.

2. Be ready to change your plan.

Initially, I was almost certain that I wanted to go into non-tech roles. But after seeing the experiences of
some of my seniors, I realised I should also prepare for SDE roles. I had already been doing some DSA and
computer fundamentals from July to December, but not consistently. Then I made a major decision: I
dropped Finance preparation, even though I had been preparing for it for almost two years. I felt that with
my existing preparation, I could revise Finance in a month if needed. For the next six months, I completely
tocused on DSA and computer fundamentals. I also gave around 12-15 mock interviews to seniors and
professionals. And trust me, there was a point where I genuinely questioned whether I was even prepared.
I had set myself a target to complete DSA before March. During one mock interview around that time, I
couldn't even write basic syntax properly. LeetCode and actually sitting in front of a blank compiler are two
very different experiences, and that blank screen can be scary.
So, I started again.
From March onwards, I practised writing code from scratch, worked on my logic, and gradually became
comfortable with solving problems without relying on an online platform. I also want to clarify that I didn't
--- PAGE 10 ---
prepare every hard DSA topic. My target was to prepare DSA up to the level required for placement
interviews. Be strategic about your preparation instead of trying to master everything.

3. Don't completely depend on Finance roles.

If you're planning to rely mainly on Finance roles, first understand your college's placement scenario. Check
how many companies actually visit your campus for the specific role you're targeting. Companies like JP,
KPMG, GEP, OMP, etc. may visit, but you need to understand whether there are enough opportunities for
you. Don't build your entire placement strategy around a role without checking the actual opportunities
available on campus.

4. Sometimes taking a risk is worth it.

Taking a risk doesn't always work out, but sometimes it can completely change your outcome. I had actually
made a personal rule for myself: I would take risks during the first two months of placements, and after that,
I wouldn't. This decision was based on my understanding of my own situation and how the placement
season was progressing. The point is not to blindly take risks. Understand your situation, assess what you
have to lose, and then decide.

5. Surround yourself with the right people.

This made a huge difference in my journey. Surround yourself with people who believe in you, push you to
do better, and have a positive impact on you. Good friends can completely change how you approach
stressful situations. My friends helped me with preparation, revisions, mock interviews, notes, and
sometimes simply by reminding me that I was capable of doing it. Your preparation is yours, but the people
around you can make the journey much easier.

There were three rounds in total. The eligibility criteria were open to students from all branches with a
CGPA of 7.5 or above. The entire process was conducted virtually.
There were two roles: Software Engineering and Aladdin Data, and I applied for both. The interviews were
conducted through Webex, although candidates were required to attend them from the TPO office.
It was a pool campus placement process, with students participating from several other colleges as well,
including NIT Agartala, Manipal University Jaipur, and others.

1. Online Assessment [Around 280 people appeared for this round]

Everyone who met the eligibility criteria received the OA link via email one day before the assessment.
There were seven sections in total: Basic Coding, Advanced Coding,Basic Design Patterns, Advanced
Design Patterns, DBMS, Aptitude, Al and Reasoning
Each section was timed separately. Once a section was started, it could not be skipped or revisited until the
allotted time was over or the section was submitted.
Since we received the OA link a day in advance and could see the section names, I prepared Design
Patterns thoroughly because I had not studied them much before. The MCQs covered all 23 Gang of Four
design patterns.
For Basic Coding, I received a Java and OOP-based question. The problem involved a list of baggage items
with their destinations, where the bags had to be grouped by destination. If there were 10 or fewer bags, they
had to be processed sequentially. If there were more than 10, the list had to be divided into two parts,
processed in parallel using Fork/Join, and then the results had to be merged in right-to-left order.
Since Java is my primary language, I was able to solve it within the allotted 40 minutes.
For Advanced Coding, I received a Selenium-based debugging question. The codebase was fairly large,
and it took me some time to understand the existing code and the problem. Since the section had a 15-minute
limit, I was unable to solve the question.
The DBMS section was easy to moderate. It covered joins, keys, SQL queries, ACID properties, and general
database concepts involving technologies such as PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Oracle.
The Aptitude section was moderate to difficult, with questions on permutation and combination, ratios and
proportions, percentages, family relationships, seating arrangements, and similar topics.
--- PAGE 2 ---
The Al and Reasoning section was comparatively easier and could largely be approached using basic logical
reasoning and common sense.
The coding questions varied across candidates. Some candidates received two DSA questions, while others
received combinations involving OOP, debugging, or other coding concepts.

2. Technical Round 1[28 students for SDE and 9 for Aladdin Data]

1 received a call from HR at around 7:30 AM informing me that my interview was scheduled for 9:30 AM.
There were two panelists, and the interview started with them asking me how my day was going. I asked
them the same. They then asked me to introduce myself and asked about my minor in Banking Technology
from Barclays. I explained how the course developed my interest in the finance industry. I was also asked
about my opinion on Al-based projects and whether I would be open to working on them.
The interview then moved to a DSA question. I was asked to share my screen and open Notepad. The
interviewer gave me a string (consisting of lowercase letters and brackets) . I was supposed to reverse the
string whenever I encountered a matching pair of brackets till there were no brackets left, (basically valid
parenthesis but with a twist). I was asked to write the code and explain the dry run as well. I initially
approached the problem recursively, and then optimized the solution using a stack.
After this, I was asked how comfortable I was with Java and Python. I mentioned that Java is my primary
language and that I know the basics of Python. Since my solution involved Strings, the discussion then
moved into Strings in Java. I was asked several questions, including:

• Why did you use StringBuilder?

• What do mutable and immutable mean?

• Why are Strings immutable in Java?

• What is the difference between StringBuilder and StringBuffer?

• When would you use StringBuilder and when would you use StringBuffer?

• How are Strings stored internally in Java? Can you give an example?

I was able to answer all of these questions.
The interviewer then moved on to SQL. I was asked about the difference between the WHERE and
HAVING clauses. I explained what each clause does and gave an example. I also mentioned that HAVING
can be used without GROUP BY, so the interviewer asked me to explain this with an example. I was then
asked about the difference between a Primary Key and a UNIQUE constraint. The interviewer followed
up with a conceptual question: if we can simply use UNIQUE along with NOT NULL, what would happen
if there were no Primary Keys, and why do we need Primary Keys in the first place?
The discussion then moved to my projects. I was asked to give an overall explanation of my projects and
was asked why I had chosen particular technologies or methodologies for them.
I was also asked about my internship experience, including what I worked on and what I learned from it.
Throughout the interview, there were also behavioral questions, including questions about my future plans,
positions of responsibility, and how I respond to feedback.
At the end of the interview, I was asked whether I had any questions for them. I asked about their work
experience at BlackRock and the types of projects they work on.
--- PAGE 3 ---
I initially felt that my interview had not gone particularly well because the interviewer maintained a very
concise communication style and often responded briefly after my answers. The interview lasted around 35
minutes. However, shortly afterward, I received a call from HR informing me that I had been shortlisted for
the next round.
The first technical round was quite different for different candidates. Some candidates were asked two three
DSA questions, while others were asked questions related to React/Next.js or had a more HR-oriented
discussion.

3. Techno HR [ Around 18 ]

This round was different for everyone as well. For some candidates, it was purely HR-focused, for some it
was more technical, while others had a mix of both.
The interviewer started by asking how my previous round went. He then introduced himself and explained
what he does at BlackRock. After that, he asked me to introduce myself.
He then asked me to explain my favorite project in depth: why it was my favorite, what the project was
about, what motivated me to build it, and what problems I faced while working on it. I chose my DevOps
project, which also involved system design concepts.
He then asked me to explain a particular bug I had faced and how I solved it. This discussion eventually
led to me explaining my entire CI/CD pipeline in depth.
We also had a discussion around Redis, since I had used it in my project. From the way the questions were
framed, I felt that he was particularly interested in understanding how I approach a problem and make
technical decisions, rather than simply testing whether I knew the technology.
He then asked me: "If you could add ONE feature to this project, what would it be and why?"
The discussion then moved to my internship experience. He asked me how I handled feedback from
clients, how I managed deadlines, and how I had optimized my project.
I was also asked: "What is one use of AI in your life that you are really proud of?"
Another interesting part of the interview was a discussion around core values. I was asked to name three
core values I had learned during college and whether those values were already present in me before I
joined college. I was also asked about a situation where I had failed badly, made a comeback, and what I
learned from that experience. I discussed one of my hackathon experiences for this question.
Towards the end, the interviewer asked me if I had any questions for him. Since he had mentioned at the
beginning that he had been working at BlackRock for around 14 years, I asked him: "What are three core
values that you have personally learned during your time at BlackRock?" He really liked the question,
and we had a good discussion around it. I then asked him what would be expected of me during the first
few months if I were to join as an intern.
The round lasted around 50 minutes. One interesting thing about the process was that after the interviews of
all the initially shortlisted candidates were completed, they also started calling waitlisted candidates for
Round 1 for SDE role
--- PAGE 4 ---
Altogether 8 people were offered the job (7 SDE+1 aladdin data)
Resources:

• I started participating in LeetCode contests in my 6th semester, but I would suggest starting as carly

as possible. Contests helped me become comfortable solving problems under pressure and also
helped me deal with OA anxiety.

• I solved NeetCode 150 first and then moved on to complete NeetCode 250.

• LeetCode SQL 50 is MUST!!!!!!

• Java: Kunal Kushwaha's YouTube channel.

• Core subjects: Academic notes, ChatGPT, and GeeksforGeeks(literally best)

• Aptitude: IndiaBix.

• DSA: Kunal Kushwaha and Nikhil Lohia's YouTube channels.

• I used to randomly read Medium articles during travel on technology and interview experiences.

This helped me stay in touch with recent technical concepts.
My fav article-
https://medium.com/@shivambhadani/system-design-for-beginners-everything-you-need-in-one-art
icle-c74eb702540b

• Know your resume inside out- every word. Be prepared to explain anything you have mentioned,

and don't mention technologies that you cannot confidently explain.

• Know your projects thoroughly. You should understand your projects, the decisions behind them,

and the different scenarios that can arise. Don't blindly build projects using Al without understanding
them in depth. Even if it is a group project, try to understand the entire project and not just the part
you personally implemented.

• An internship can definitely be beneficial, but if you haven't done one, don't let that discourage

you. Keep working on your skills, projects, and fundamentals.

• Try to maintain a CGPA of 8+. Personally, I would consider 8.5+ to be a safer target for keeping

MOST opportunities open. ( i missed few companies with a cgpa of 8.39)

• Participate in hackathons. Don't get demotivated if you don't win. The experience of building,

collaborating, and solving problems under time constraints is valuable in itself.

• Puzzles and CS fundamentals MCQS: GeeksforGeeks.

• If you get rejected from an interview, start working on the areas that went wrong as soon as

possible- ideally the same day or the next day.

• Before the interview go through the company website especially their values/principles, tailor your

answers accordingly. You can also take notes during PPT as they might ask stuff from that.
MOST IMPORTANTLY:
Don't ever feel that you are not prepared for an interview, you can never be fully prepared lol. I was asked
way less than what I had prepared, I kept myself up till Sam and just got 2 hrs sleep before the interview, pis
avoid this. Whatever you have studied, just answer confidently that's it. And if you dont know something
dont fake it, admit it honestly. Confidence, positivity and patience are the key. Placements are a
combination of hard work, preparation, and luck, but no matter how many rejections you face, don't forget
to show up every single day and keep working on yourself. You never know when it will finally be your
day, so don't stop believing in yourself. And always be happy and genuinely cheerful for others when they
succeed. Don't compare your journey with anyone else's. Everyone has their own journey, their own
timeline, and their own destiny.
END MEIN JO HOTA HAI ACHE KE LIYE HOTA HAI :))))
If you have any doubts, feel free to connect with me on LinkedIn
ALL THE BEST BE POSITIVE

You must obviously be knowing all the standard resources regarding aptitude, DSA, OOPS, DBMS, SQL,
System Design, Java, OS, puzzles, CCN, development etc. Stay consistent and follow a particular resource
instead of beating around the bush in general. It won't obviously be feasible to be up to date with everything
but try as much as you can with decent depth. Just a few 'non-technical' things I wanted to share:

• Explore as much as possible, be it development, app building, ML, finance etc. Everything is fun.

• Try to maintain as high a CGPA as possible, it will obviously help in maximal shortlisting and maybe

higher studies. (at least keep it over 8 to avoid rejections during shortlisting itself).

• Having internships is nice obviously, but don't be disheartened if you don't have one. Overall

knowledge and proficiency reign supreme.

• Just enjoy college life in general. It won't come back.

• Go to hackathons and other competitions. They do help a lot in overall development.

• Try to develop confidence and clarity in interviews and presentations. Sometimes these things

triumph over intrinsic knowledge in many companies.

• Starting early helps ideally but nothing is too late. Almost everyone is serious after Sem 6 and they

all do manage so it's alright.

• Ultimately, there are way too many parameters and luck determining your placement which is

difficult to control or predict so just accept whatever comes along the way.

• Take it easy, the first job in any company or pay is not going to affect your career long term and

placement is not something worth sacrificing mental health for.

• Try to control comparisons, overthinking and anxiety as much as you realistically can. Spend quality

time with friends and family during this period.
