journey.howSecured:
Overall 5 rounds were conducted, all in a single day. All interviews were conducted online, but from
college. Their HR communicated everything and coordinated the whole process via a WhatsApp group. In
general, try to have a good grasp of basic debugging and schema design, along with core CS fundamentals.
Resume Shortlisting: Initial shortlisting was based on resume. While applying on Superset, they had also
asked specifically about your internship experience. It's not confirmed but candidates having no internship
experience were not selected so that was the distinguishing criterion. Many people must have applied, but
around 100 were shortlisted, with the list being shared a day prior.

1. Rapid Fire MCQ Round (101 students appeared for this round) - 10 minutes

It was very frantic as expected from its name. There were around 50 multiple choice questions related to
core CS fundamentals, basic programming languages and related concepts like OOPS (including loads of
Python). It contained technical questions on Java, Python and C++, like determining the time complexity,
space complexity and output of code snippets, some questions on basic OS and CCN like deadlocks and
DNS, some Github commands like listing all branches, stash and pop, some questions on prefix and postfix
increment operators and some basic data structure questions like which data structure is LIFO, FIFO etc. We
were sent a Google Forms link in our mail at around 10 am and had to submit it in around 10-12 minutes.
The only constraint was time since many questions weren't necessarily straightforward and needed some
time to think. I believe it was expected to properly solve around 20-25 questions and if possible, mark all
other questions as let's say B since there was no negative marking. We had been asked to attempt as much as
possible since it was designed to be fast paced and clumsy.

2. APT Debugging Round (52 students appeared for this round) - 30 minutes

We were split in 4 slots each having 13 students. It's unclear whether shortlisting order was based on the
previous round's results but it's obviously more beneficial to be placed in the earlier slots or panels. We were
sent the shortlists and G-Meet links for each candidate which we had to join from any room in the TPO.
There were 2 interviewers in it. They asked to choose any language of choice from Django, Golang, FastAPI
or Node. I chose Django. This is because I had read the previous year's interview experience and both the
selected candidates had chosen Django so I had more clue in general about what to expect. (obviously any
language works and it's not compulsory to choose Django only). I had read all basic frameworks, file
structures, common errors etc in this language a day before. Then the interviewer sent a link to a small
existing Django codebase containing an Attendance Tracker project, with a README file containing
instructions on what was to be performed. To my surprise, the same scenario and the project had been asked
to me which was also asked in the previous year. So obviously I was very fortunate since I knew beforehand
about the bugs and their solutions. Initially, while starting the server, there were 2 bugs that were required to
--- PAGE 2 ---
be fixed. One bug was in the models.py, a syntax error in the choices parameter passed to a
models. CharField.
Expected syntax: status = models. CharField(max_length=20, choices-[('active', 'Status active'), ('inactive',
'Status inactive')])
Given syntax: status = models. CharField(max_length=20, choices=['active', 'inactive])
The second bug was in the views.py, another syntax error in which the key of a python dictionary was being
accessed incorrectly.
Expected syntax: [s['name"] for s in students]
Given syntax: [s.name for s in students]
Both interviewers were very helpful and it's advisable to constantly communicate your thought process with
them. They will guide you for sure instead of an awkward silence. I remember there was some issue related
with permission viewing in settings.py file but they explicitly told me to allow * in hosts.
After fixing the errors, I started the server. Then, I was asked to implement an API endpoint to mark a
student's attendance. Time was running out so I explained my basic thoughts (like unique together
constraint, ORM, why to create a foreign key in a separate table etc). Note that they will also ask lots of
conceptual questions about the language so just debugging won't do. For example, they asked me many
basic questions in general (for example, why do we do makemigrations before migrate). Not many people
could start the server itself so I knew that I was progressing to the next round. Obviously, it's not expected to
know the syntax or actual code of the language, we were allowed to use Google (including that Al mode
which automatically opens on searching anything). They cared about overall approach and thought process
more than actual debugging or coding. Also it had been noticed that people in the subsequent slots were
asked much deeper conceptual questions since it was assumed that they already knew the bugs of their
respective language from the previous rounds' candidates so it was a bit of a disadvantage for them. Most
people had chosen Node or FastAPI. I think that debugging was sufficient to proceed to further rounds, API
writing was additional but no one could completely finish that due to time constraints. Overall the whole
process started around 10.30 and we were given further shortlists at around 3 pm. (I think 2-3 students were
given a choice of app development in this round as well due to their resumes but they chose debugging only)

3. DSA and Schema Design (16 students appeared for this round) - 75 minutes

Last year, they were separate rounds but this time, they were merged in 1. We were sent the shortlist at
around 3 and split into 2 slots of 8 panels. (I don't think it's a coincidence that all the final selected students
were from slot 1 in this round). Again, each panel had 2 interviewers. They were very friendly, made me
comfortable, asked for basic introduction and started with the DSA question. I was asked to open a Google
Docs and try to communicate my thought process from there. My question was a bit ambiguous and open
-ended. It was to design a class for shuffling n songs when each song can be repeated after at least k other
songs. I asked lots of clarifying questions about the problem. The intended solution was to use a queue (to
keep track of order) and a set (for checking duplicates in k songs). I couldn't exactly reach it but explained
my thought process as clearly as I could. They asked lots of other basic related questions like time
complexity, pros and cons of the provided solution etc. The discussion lasted around 30 minutes and they
were generally very helpful and responsive. The schema design followed next. It was a pretty basic problem
around a ticket booking system. They dwelled deep into types of attributes, entities, relationships etc (basic
ER diagram intricacies). They also expected some low level code connecting classes and their objects,
which I couldn't implement properly. All in all, again they were more interested in the thought process,
approach and communication clarity rather than actual coding. Other DSA problems asked were standard
like Trapping Rainwater, multi source BFS etc. The schema design is relatively easier for everyone. The
--- PAGE 3 ---
round ended with me asking some questions regarding scamming by employers in the app and how do they
monitor it and about legal compliances being a startup.

4. HR and Culture Fit Round (6 students appeared for this round) - 30 minutes each

Immediately after my interview, I got a call from their HR about scheduling the further interviews and was
sent the Meet link along with the time. Both interviews were very chill honestly. They asked me to be
myself and not fake anything for the sake of 'cracking' the interview. Standard questions were asked like the
highest moments in life, the lowest ones, best projects, hackathon experiences, college experiences, daily
routine, explaining 1 project to a 5 year-old etc. Questions like comfort regarding relocating to Bangalore
and working in a high pace environment with less 'work-life balance' were also asked. Overall, it was just a
friendly and honest talk regarding compatibility of the company and the candidate. Basic questions from
resumes like minor degree, motivation to do engineering and the trends of AI were also discussed. Both
rounds felt more personal and absolutely non-technical. So all in all, just be yourself here, maintain some
basic confidence and stay as honest as you can.
Overall the whole process ended around 8 pm (special mention to TPCs as well who were also very helpful
and patient throughout the day). We got the result the next day around 6 pm. 5 students were given the offer
finally.

journey.howSecured:
There were a total of 6 rounds of shortlisting(resume shortlist, rapid fire MCQs and 4 rounds of interview).
All rounds of interviews were conducted online as the company staff was in Bangalore.

1. Round 1: Resume shortlisting (more than 200 candidates appeared for this round)

A resume with work experience is preferred during shortlisting. Try to include an unpaid internship, it will
help basically everywhere. Along with this, it is highly recommended to be honest with your projects. DO
NOT lie about them. Though I wasn't asked much about them, many candidates struggle to explain the
details of their projects in general, leading to a bad impression. Maintain a CGPA of more than 8.5 or at least
8 as in many cases, it is the first criteria during shortlisting.
Nearly half of the students were selected for the process.

2. Round 2: Rapid fire MCQ (101 candidates appeared for this round)

The rounds were held in the college from here on. In this particular round, we were expected to complete 50
MCQs in under 10 minutes. The questions were on basic C, Java and Python along with core CS subjects
like Computer Networks, OS, DBMS, etc. No one completes it all. Just keep marking answers without
thinking much(even if you don't know the answer). Make sure you submit it on time.

3. Round 3: API Debugging Round (52 candidates appeared in this round)

The interview officially begins here. We were given a google meet link. We joined it from the TPO cabins.
The interviewer asked me to introduce myself. He then got straight to the point and gave me a list of options
for the round. I selected Nodejs as nearly all my development projects use this. After that he pasted a link in
the chat section. It was like VS Code inside the browser. It has a bunch of folders consisting of code for a
web application in nodejs(backend only obviously) and a jupyter notebook for testing API. In this round,
you are expected to:
--- PAGE 2 ---

1. Debug what is wrong with the currently written APIs(syntax and other errors)

2. Create a new API for a different purpose.

The application was for student attendance as far as I remember. I was asked to check why the API made for
creating a new student was not working as intended. You will have to search through the files for finding the
syntax error. It was a normal JS syntax error where an object was passed as a parameter where boolean was
expected. I corrected the code. He then asked what was actually wrong, which I explained.
It is highly advisable to KEEP TALKING. Do not go blank if you can't see the error right away. Ask the
interviewer for hints. Ask questions on what this particular section of code does. Ask for clarifications. I
took some time but was able to identify the syntax errors in both APIs.
After that, he asked me to write a code for an API. I would rate that question moderately difficult as it
involved some logic. I was not able to code but I told my approach and he was like "Okay, time's up!".
It lasted for about 1 hour. Before leaving, he asked me if I had any questions about the company. I came
prepared for this moment. I asked, "Did you encounter a situation during your time at WorkIndia where you
learned a completely new technology from scratchạ
ẠạiHe answered firmly, giving some examples.
It took some time to get results. We were waiting while discussing what we were asked. 16 students were
selected for the next round.

4. Round 4: DSA & Database Round (16 candidates appeared in this round)

This round started almost in the evening. The interviewer again asked me to introduce myself. He then asked
me to open a google doc page. He started dictating the DSA question which was as follows:
You are given a n * n matrix with values 0, 1 and 2.
0 -> Empty cell
1 -> Wall
2 -> Power cell
In 1 second, a power cell(2) can transform the empty cells around it to power cells. Calculate the time to
convert all empty cells to power cells, return -1 if not possible.
It was a classic, Striver style graph traversal question. I explained both the BFS and DFS approach. He
asked me to write a pseudocode in the doc, which I did.
As I was explaining my code, he was satisfied with my answer. He asked me, "Do you like DSA? Personally
I don't like it that much'. I still don't know whether it was a trick question or not but I said, "I like DSA
decent enough, I like System Design more than this!" He then started with the database design question.
It was a classic question of schema design for an ola/uber like app. This was more of an open ended
discussion after I suggested what the basic tables will look like.
Now the question part, I again asked the same question as the previous round. Along with that, I also asked a
question about CI/CD pipelines(I suggest preparing for more than one question).
It was a chill conversation which also lasted for about an hour.

5. Round 5: HR Round (6 candidates appeared in this round)

--- PAGE 3 ---
As I went downstairs after completing the DSA round, I almost immediately got a call from HR for this
round, which was scheduled 30 minutes later. It was full of classic HR questions, talking about family,
hackathons, projects, priorities, deadlines, etc. It lasted for about 20 minutes.

6. Round 6; Culture Fit Round (6 candidates appeared in this round)

Honestly, this was the most challenging round which I wasn't expecting at all! He started with a completely
random hypothesis, "What will you do if I give you 100 crores, right now?" I tried to answer from this
perspective of finance, since I have some finance background. He said he isn't expecting that, he wants to
know what value will I generate from than 100 crores for the community. Since I was watching some reels
about the data center water issues in the past few days, I immediately suggested researching data centers to
solve this issue. We had a 5-minute quick conversation and he said we're good.
The results didn't come until the next day, 5 students were selected for the role, I was one of them.

journey.prep:
An interview is not just about how much you know, but also about how well you can communicate and
display what you know. You can have strong technical knowledge, but if you are nervous, unable to explain
your thought process, or try to give answers you think the interviewer wants to hear, it may not come across
properly. That is why I would suggest focusing on the non-technical aspects of interviews as well. These are
just as important as technical preparation and can make a big difference in how your interview goes.
I have listed the non-technical tips first because I genuinely think they are important, followed by the
technical preparation that helped me.
Non Technical Tips :

• Be confident during the interview. It is completely okay to not know everything, and it is okay to

make mistakes. Accept them, learn from them, and move on. Don't let one mistake affect the rest of
the interview.

• Remember that the interviewers are not your enemies. They are generally very helpful, so don't

hesitate to ask for hints or clarify your doubts. Knowledge is important, but that is not the only thing
--- PAGE 6 ---
they are looking for. Your willingness to learn, passion for what you do, and readiness to explore
new things matter a lot as well.

• If you feel that the interviewer is taking the conversation in a direction where you don't have much

knowledge, be honest about it. You can also ask if you can discuss another topic or project that you
are more confident about. One of my friends did exactly this. After feeling that her interview had not
gone well, she asked the interviewers if she could talk about one of her projects instead. They
allowed her to do so, and she ended up getting selected.

• Don't claim to know things that you don't. Be confident about what you actually know. Sometimes

interviewers may intentionally question your answer or make you feel like you are wrong to see how
you react, so don't immediately doubt yourself if you are confident in your answer.

• Be honest and real with the interviewer. Don't try to suck up to them or give what you think is the

"perfect" answer just because you think that is what they want to hear. Let them understand who you
actually are.

• Don't be nervous and overthink the interview. Just prepare well, give it your best, and move on. You

will get what's meant for you.

• Don't get too attached to one particular company. The placement process can be very unpredictable,

and constantly worrying about one company can become an unnecessary mental distraction. Focus
on each opportunity as it comes and keep moving forward.
Technical Tips :
You probably already know the basic resources for DSA and interview preparation, but I am attaching my
notes and some resources as well, just in case they are useful. My biggest suggestion is to stick to one good
source and complete it properly. Don't try to cover every resource available online because you will mostly
end up wasting time switching between them.

• For DSA, unless you are specifically aiming for companies like PhonePe, Striver's A2Z DSA Sheet

is more than enough for most companies. Try to finish it at least 2 months before the placement
process starts. After that, focus on solving random questions, revising concepts, and getting
comfortable with problems you haven't seen before.

• Know your resume inside out. Don't fake anything or add things just because they look good. Be

realistic about what you know. You should be able to explain even the smallest details of every
project, internship, or experience mentioned on your resume.

• Don't put every technology you have ever touched under your skills. Mention things you have

actually worked with and have at least some confidence in. Interviewers can easily pick something
from your skills and start asking questions about it.

• Be ready to explain why you chose the technologies and frameworks used in your projects. Don't just

know how to use something - understand why you chose it over other options and what problem it
solved.

• Make sure your CS fundamentals are strong. At the very least, revise DBMS, Computer Networks,

OOPs, and Operating Systems. These basics come up frequently in technical interviews.

• Practical experience is much more useful than only having bookish knowledge. Get your hands dirty

and actually build things. If you don't have good projects, build something. It really doesn't take that
much time these days to make a decent project, and the experience you get from building and
debugging something yourself is much more valuable.

• Be prepared for basic system design as well. You don't necessarily need to know advanced system

design for every company, but you should understand how to break down a system into components
and explain the decisions you make.
--- PAGE 7 ---

• Practice SQL properly. I would recommend doing LeetCode's SQL 50. Make sure you actually

understand the queries instead of just memorising solutions.

• Keep C++ or Java as your primary programming language for DSA and interviews. Pick one and

become comfortable enough that you can focus on the problem rather than struggling with the
language syntax during the interview.
The overall goal should be to finish your main preparation well before placements start. Once the basics are
covered, use the remaining time to practise, revise, and improve your problem-solving rather than constantly
starting new resources.
I have not failed. I've just found 10,000 ways that won't work." - Thomas Edison
Yes, you've seen this quote in college, and so have I. It was written on one of the doors in college, and for
some reason, it really stuck with me. A lot of what I have learned throughout college has come from failing,
making mistakes, trying again, and figuring out what works. I genuinely believe that failing is one of the
best ways to learn.
So don't be afraid of getting things wrong. Try things, make mistakes, learn from them, and keep going.

journey.howSecured:
Resume shortlisting was the first stage of the process, with around 100 students selected for the interviews.
Having good project experience and a strong resume seems to be preferred, so it is important to highlight
relevant projects, internships, technical skills, and any practical experience clearly.

• Round 1 - Rapid-fire MCQ round covering programming, CS fundamentals, and basic coding

concepts under a strict time limit.

• Round 2 - API debugging round focused on debugging, backend concepts, and implementing a new

API module.

• Round 3 - DSA and schema design round covering problem-solving, optimisation, database design,

and system concepts.

• Round 4 - HR round focused on background, projects, work culture, and work-life balance.

• Round 5 - Culture fit round focused on situational questions, decision-making, motivation, career

goals, and workplace expectations.

1. Rapid Fire MCQ Round - (around 100 students appeared) - 10 minutes - 10:00 AM

Round 1 was a rapid-fire MCQ round conducted through Google Forms. There were around 60 questions to
be attempted in just 10 minutes. The questions were mainly code-based and covered C++, Java, and Python,
with basic loops, conditions, and output-based questions. There were also questions on CS fundamentals like
OS, OOPS, Computer Networks, and basic data structures and their working. Overall, the questions were
quite easy and focused mostly on basic concepts.
The main challenge was the time limit. There were a lot of questions, so the key was to move quickly and
not spend too much time on any single question. When the timer was close to ending, I had not even reached
one-third of the questions. So, don't overthink the questions. There will be many easy ones that you can
answer immediately without spending much time. I think I was able to attempt around 20 questions.

2. APL Debugging Round - (52 students) - 30 minutes - 11:30 AM

Round 2 was an API debugging round. There were multiple options for the tech stack, including Django,
FastAPI, Node.js, and I think Go. There were 4 slots with multiple panels, and I was in the 1st slot. The
interview was conducted on Google Meet, and I joined from the conference room opposite the TPO. There
were 2 interviewers, both SDE 2s.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Most of my latest projects are built using FastAPI, but I chose Node.js for this round because I feel it is
easier to work with and has fewer complications. It was also the technology I started my backend journey
with, so I was more comfortable with it.
They shared a link that gave access to a VS Code environment. The project was something like a student
records management system, and there was a README file with all the instructions. They first asked me to
run the server. It did not start properly, so I had to debug it. I immediately found the first bug: the config was
not declared correctly. It needed to be declared using const and then exported. I was not completely sure
about the exact syntax, so they allowed me to Google it.
The next bug was in the get students route. The route was supposed to return all students, but it was
returning only one student by ID. I checked the type of data being returned from the route and noticed that it
was an object instead of an array. I fixed it so that the route returned an array containing all the students.
After that, they asked me to create a new module for marking student attendance date-wise. I first explained
my approach and then copied the existing student module files and started making the required changes.
They seemed satisfied with my approach and understanding of the code. They then asked how I would check
whether a student had already been marked for a particular day and prevent duplicate attendance. I
suggested keeping the student ID and date together as a primary key, so duplicate entries for the same
student and date would not be allowed. They were satisfied with the answer.
I was almost done writing the code when the time was about to end. They asked me where I would register
the new route after completing the module. I was able to point out the exact file and explain how I would
register it. They said okay and then asked if I had any questions.
I asked them what the company was doing to compete with platforms like Naukri and Indeed. They
explained that WorkIndia targets a different audience, mainly focusing on blue-collar jobs. After that, the
interview ended.
After the round, I got to know that this was the exact same question that had been asked the previous year as
well. I had no idea about this during the interview, so I just solved it normally based on my understanding.
So, if you can, it is better to prepare for questions from previous years as well.
One important thing I would suggest is to just keep talking and don't get tensed. The interviewers are very
helpful, so don't hesitate to ask for hints if you get stuck. It is completely fine to ask. The round is more
about your concepts and approach than remembering the exact syntax.

3. DSA and Schema Design - (16 students) - 40 minutes - 4:20 PM

Round 3 was a DSA and schema design round. There were 16 students split into 2 slots. I think the students
in the 1st slot were the preferred candidates because they were fast-tracked, while students from the other
slot were eliminated. I was in the 1st slot. We were told to go for lunch and come back by around 3:30. The
results were announced by around 4. Google Meet links were sent and we joined from the interview rooms
in the TPO. Some people started around 4:10, while my interview started around 4:20 because they were
still figuring out the rooms.
There was a single interviewer. I think he was an SDE 3. He first introduced himself and then asked me to
introduce myself. After that, he asked me to share my screen and shared a Google Doc with me. The
document had 2 questions, and he asked me to attempt the first one.
--- PAGE 3 ---
The first
question
was
based
on
the Trapping Rain Water problem:
https://leetcode.com/problems/trapping-rain-water/description/. The way it was initially explained was a
little unclear to me, so I asked a few questions and used examples to clear my doubts. I first explained the
brute force approach, where I would find the previous greater element (PGE) and next greater element

(NGE) for every element using loops. This would take ON?) time. He asked how I understood that I needed

to find the PGE and NGE for every element, and I explained that these values determine the level of water
that can be stored above each position.
I then moved to a better approach where I would pre-calculate the PGE and NGE information and then use it
to calculate the water height. This takes O(2N) time and ON) space. He asked me to write the pseudocode
on the Google Doc.
Then he asked if I could optimise it further. I explained how I could combine the PGE and NGE process into
a single iteration and calculate the heights while popping elements from the stack. This gives ON) time and
ON) space. He asked me to make the necessary changes to my code.
He then asked if there was any further optimization possible. I initially couldn't remember it, but then the
two-pointer approach struck me. I explained that I could keep left and right pointers and move them towards
the centre while calculating the trapped water. This gives ON) time and O(1) extra space. For anyone
preparing, the two-pointer approach is worth understanding properly. There is a good explanation of it by
Striver here: https://youtu.be/1_5VuquLbXg.
I fumbled a little while writing the final code, but I started working through examples while coding, and the
interviewer understood that I had the approach right. He said okay and moved on. There were 2 questions in
the document, but he did not ask me the second one. By around 4:40, the DSA part was done.
After that, we moved on to schema design. He shared another document with a scenario for a food delivery
platform similar to Swiggy. The requirements were to store restaurant information, their menus, customer
details, and orders. I also had to account for cases where multiple restaurants operate from the same physical
location, like cloud kitchens.
I started by listing out the different entities and then defined the relationships between them. I also added the
appropriate primary and foreign keys, including composite keys wherever required. He seemed pretty
satisfied with the design.
He then made the problem slightly more complicated by saying that an order could contain items from more
than one restaurant and involve multiple drivers. I made the necessary changes to keep the design as
decoupled as possible and avoid storing repeated or redundant information. The idea was to structure the
relationships properly rather than duplicating the same information across multiple tables.
He then asked how I would implement a driver tracking system. This felt more like a system design question
than a schema design question. I explained that instead of continuously polling the server, I would use
WebSockets to maintain a connection and push location updates to the customer regularly. He was satisfied
with the answer.
He then asked if I had any questions. I asked him about his experience working at the company, and after
that the interview ended. I was out by around 5.
--- PAGE 4 ---
Overall, this round was quite fast for me. It took around 40 minutes, while some of my friends' interviews
lasted around 70-90 minutes.
The key for this round was to keep speaking and explain whatever I was thinking. In DSA, always start with
the brute force solution and then work your way towards the optimised solution. In schema design, don't be
afraid to make changes if you realise something needs to be changed. Try to keep the design decoupled and
avoid redundant information. If you make a mistake carly in the schema, you can get trapped when the
interviewer starts adding more complications to the problem.
Most importantly, be very open with the interviewer and don't hesitate to ask questions or clarify your
doubts.

4. HR Round - (6 students) - 40 minutes - 5:15 PM

Around 5 minutes after my DSA and schema design round, I got a call from HR saying that I was moving to
the HR round. I was asked to join at 5:15.
The interview started around 5:20 and was mostly like a casual conversation. He first introduced himself and
then asked me to introduce myself. He also asked me about my favourite project. I talked about the project
that had helped me win the SE Hack. I explained the full story of how it started as a challenge that my team
decided to take up, even though we had zero knowledge about the topic, and how we managed to figure
everything out and crack it that night.
The questions were mostly basic and nothing out of the box. By around 5:40, the main interview was done
and he asked me if I had any questions. I asked about the work-life balance and work culture. He was honest
and said that the work can be a little fast-paced. He also explained why some deployments are done at night,
which can sometimes cause work to extend late.
We ended up talking about this for around 20 minutes, and the interview finally ended at around 6.

5. Culture Fit Round - (6 students) - 50 minutes - 6:15 PM

In the previous year, the HR round was the last round, so I thought my interview process was over. However,
around 5 minutes after my HR round, I got another call from HR saying that I was selected for the Culture
Fit round and had to join by 6:15.
The interview was with a single interviewer. I introduced myself and then he introduced himself. He had
been working for around 7 years. He started the conversation by explaining that WorkIndia is a fast-paced
environment and that things can sometimes get hectic. He asked if I would be comfortable handling that
kind of environment. I was honest and said that I don't mind putting in extra hours when required, as long as
I could expect some relief or flexibility in the following days.
He then asked me a few situation-based questions. For example, he gave different projects with different
conditions, where one could bring in a lot of money but was still under development, while another was
ready to ship but had lower returns. There were around 3-4 such conditions, and I had to choose which one I
would prioritise and explain why. In these kinds of questions, I don't think there is always a single right
answer. They are more about understanding how you think, how you prioritise things, and how you handle
different situations while also respecting decisions made by your seniors. He also asked what I would do if I
disagreed with my manager.
--- PAGE 5 ---
He also asked me about some of my highs and lows during college and the experiences that shaped me. I
answered honestly and explained the things that I felt had been the most important experiences for me
throughout college.
I then asked him about the learning curve at WorkIndia and what kind of projects I could expect to work on.
I was particularly interested in ML since I enjoy working on it and already had some experience in the area
He explained some of the different types of projects happening at the company and said there was scope to
work across different domains.
He was curious about why I specifically asked about the projects and what motivates me. I was honest and
said that both technical growth and financial growth motivate me. Since I had mentioned freelance projects
on my resume, he asked whether I had earned from them and whether financial growth was an important
factor for me. I explained that I had worked on those projects alongside college, mostly during my free time,
and that they gave me an opportunity to learn a lot while also earning some money on the side.
The conversation then became more personal, and he asked whether I had specific things in mind that
motivated me to earn. I said that I obviously had things I wanted to do, like travelling, buying vehicles and
getting some of the things I wanted, while also becoming financially independent and not having to rely on
my parents for everything. He then asked where I saw myself in 5 years.
Overall, this round did not really feel like a formal interview. It was more like a chill conversation where
both of us were asking questions and getting to know each other.
My main advice would be to not try too hard to say what you think the interviewer wants to hear. Be
prepared for the usual HR questions, but be honest and be yourself. Apart from helping you get through the
interview, it also helps you understand whether the company and its work environment are actually a good
fit for you.
I was the first person to have all my rounds completed, at around 7 PM. There were still people in their HR
and DSA rounds when I finished. The results were announced the next day at around 6 PM, and 5 students
were selected.

journey.howSecured:
This year's drive was very PhonePe level. The OA was definitely more difficult than last year's OA. But I'll
say that in my opinion, the DSA asked in the technical rounds did become slightly easier than the ones
asked last year. (Still, the technical rounds were difficult, as, at the end of the day, its PhonePe :p)

1. Online Assessment [ Around 310 candidates appeared for this round]

Everyone with >6.5 CGPA was sent the link. I never checked the ATS score for my resume, although it's advisable
to do so.
Problem 1: Task Assignment (50 Points) We were given two arrays, tasks (difficulty) and workers (capability),
plus an integer K denoting the maximum number of tasks a worker is allowed to perform. A worker can only do a
task if their capability is greater than or equal to the task's difficulty. The goal was to find the minimum value of k
(1 <= k<= K) such that all tasks are assigned and no worker does more than k tasks.
I used two pointers to efficiently allocate the tasks first and maintained a counter. I knew the optimal solution
required binary search on the answer, but I was confident my two-pointer approach would pass most test cases.
I coded it quickly to save time and planned to come back to it later. My approach passed 9/14 test cases. The
optimal approach is indeed doing a binary search on the value of k. This question was fairly easy and a lot of
people solved it.
Problem 2: Network Routers and Regions (70 Points) You are given a tree of N nodes and N-1 edges. The
network has exactly one central server, several routers, and multiple regions. The server connects only to
routers, routers connect to the server and one or more regions, and regions connect to exactly one router. We
had to determine the number of routers and regions.
This was again a fairly simple problem. The standard method most people used was creating an adjacency list:
the number of regions equals the nodes with degree 1, and the routers equal N - regions - 1.
I actually solved it using an entirely different method. I ran a BFS from each node to check if it was the central
hub, based on the observation that the maximum depth from the hub can only be 3. Once I tound the central hub,
the number of routers became adj[hub].size() and regions became adj[adj[hub][0]]. size(). Ikind of
overcomplicated this, but if it works, it works. Passed all test cases.
Problem 3: Codeforces 1665C (110 Points) The ideal approach can be found in the Codeforces editorial. I was
pretty much out of time from trying the 4th problem (which was a trap), so I just printed N. This passed 4/22 test
cases. We had to take the number of test cases as input first and run the solve function T times, making it very
--- PAGE 2 ---
Codeforces-like. I think they did this to avoid people brute-forcing or just returning standard values like -1 for
easy points.
Problem 4: Codeforces 8C (120 Points) This was a 2000-rated Codeforces bitmask DP problem. I don't even
know how to talk about this problem. I tried DP with bitmasking, which was the right approach, but coding it
would have taken 1.5 hours alone. I wasted a lot of time on this and eventually gave up.
In total, I solved 1 completely, got 9/14 on the first, and 4/22 on the third. Thanks to those 4/22 test cases on Q3, I
received an extra 15 points since that question had a high weightage. No one was able to solve 3 completely; the
maximum was around 2.5.
Keep in mind, your aim in these OAsis not to solve the questions completely, but to extract as many points
as you can. Build a habit of leaving questions if they feel like they are taking too much time, and always
solve the ones you feel confident in first. In my case, I solved the 50-point question first because it was the
easiest.
The shortlisting criteria ended up being around 1.5 questions. We received the shortlist around 10:00 PM, and
roughly 26 people were selected for the technical rounds.

2. Technical Round 1[26 people appeared]

We were asked to come at around 9:00 AM the next day. They called us in the order of how we finished in the
OA. I was in the second batch of students.
(For context, Batch 1 was osked "Most Stones Removed with Same Row or Column" and something similar to
"LeetCode 992: Subarrays with K Different Integers". Batch 3 had "LeetCode 632: Smallest Range Covering Elements
from K Lists" and another question of graphs.)
Here is what I was asked in Batch 2:
Problem 1: LeetCode 827 - Making A Large Island (Pretty standard)
I started with a brute-force approach: doing a DFS for every 1 encountered. I then suggested optimizing it using
DSU pre-computation. He asked me not to use a DSU, so I proposed storing the parent for each component in a
separate auxiliary matrix.
He agreed both solutions would work, but he wanted me to try another method: assigning an ID for each
component directly inside the given matrix. I agreed it would work, but I pointed out that I generally avoid
modifying the given data in a problem as a standard engineering practice. He was satisfied with that reasoning,
had me write the pseudo-code, and we moved on.
Problem 2: LeetCode 3203 - Find Minimum Diameter After Merging Two Trees
I wasn't explicitly told this was a tree. I was only told it was a "cluster of N nodes and N-1 edges, and M nodes and
M-1 edgesi I asked him if it contained any cycles, and he told me to prove it myself. I proved it by observation,
since the clusters cannot be disconnected based on the problem constraints. I then asked, "Can I assume it's a
tree?" He asked me to prove that too, which I did using a tree's formal definition.
Note: Even though I knew it was a tree immediately, directly jumping to tree algorithms can get skeptical looks from
an interviewer. It's best to lead them to agree with you first.
I started with the brute force of trying every possible vertex pair from the two trees to find the maximum
distance. When asked to optimize, I said I would use the diameter of a tree to find the radius by doing d/2. He
asked how I would find the diameter, which led me to proving why the 2-DFS solution works. I proved my
--- PAGE 3 ---
algorithm by contradiction, constantly saying things like, "I claim that XYZ." We had a lot of to and fro, which is
very common.
He said, "It looks fair to me, you can assume this is right and continue." I handled the edge cases (like taking the
ceiling of d/2 if the diameter is odd, taking max (d1, d2, r1+r2+1)) and quickly fixed my logic when prompted. In the
meantime, he actually checked online about the 2-DFS solution and told me, "It's correct, don't worry. I checked it
online." I wrote the pseudo-code quickly. (Shoutout to Competitive Programming Handbook ")
Wrap Up & Takeaways
The round ended on a fun note, and I asked him about how PhonePe uses distributed services. He indirectly told
me to get ready for the next rounds.

• Communication is everything: My interviewer didn't know the standard 2-DFS diameter algorithm, so I

had to prove it to him. I kept asking if we were on the same page or if he wanted me to go more in-depth
just to show I was communicating properly.

• CP helps a lot: About 6-7 people in my batch of 10 solved both problems because 5 of us did CP

regularly, making this round relatively easy for us.

• Don't panic about HM routing: A few people were called directly for the HM round after this. Don't worry

if this happens or doesn't happen to you-they often call people for HM out of order just to run interviews
in parallel and save time.
Technical Round 2[16 people appeared] [Duration: ~1 hr]
This round was a rollercoaster. It started with my introduction and an unexpected question about why I built an
Al agent during my Russell Investments internship. I answered it well, but it definitely took me by surprise to get
a resume question in a technical round.
Problem 1: M - Candies (AtCoder DP contest - just look it up and go to the M problem)
I immediately recognized it as a DP problem. I explained the overlapping subproblems and defined my state as
dp[I][k] = dp[i+1][k-j] (where | can be a[i] at max).
I wrote the code, but then he asked me to dry run my O(nk^2) DP. I never dry run DP in Codeforces; I just trust my
transitions. I struggled to do it manually, and when I took too much time, he assumed my approach was incorrect
and wanted to move on. I almost lost hope, but I realized he had the wrong idea of my DP state. I calmly walked
him through my transition, and he agreed it worked. He wanted a prefix-sum optimization (which almost no one
got), but since time was running out, we moved to the next question. (So, make sure your interviewer is extremely
clear with your approach). Honestly, this was the question where I felt that I might be cooked, so I made it clear
to give my best shot. Even though I wasn't able to fill my DP table, I made sure to not stop thinking out loud while
Tilling my DP table up.
Problem 2: Maximum Strong Pair XOR II (LeetCode)
The question asked for the maximum XOR between two numbers with the condition abs(x-y) <= min(x,y).
Assuming x is less than y, I simplified this to y <= 2x. I talked through my thoughts out loud and suggested
running a binary search on the largest y such that y <= 2x, combined with a Trie. The tricky part was checking if
an active bit existed within that specific subarray. I'll be really honest here, I went completely blank after the 2nd
condition was put forth. I made sure to speak my mind out, saying things like "I've solved a similar problem with
BIT trie, "We should take the MSB complement first greedily, so I need a way to check if there exists complement
BIT", so yeah, I was struggling a lot, even then I received no help, so I figured I'm pretty much going to have to
derive from scratch. Seeing I have to do something with complement and I also need to have the valid indexes, I
--- PAGE 4 ---
got the intuition to store the indices directly in the Trie nodes. When checking for a complement bit, I'd just verify
if a valid index existed down that path. He was highly skeptical and did a lot of dry runs with me, but my logic held
up against every single test case. He finally let me treat the Trie as a black box and write the pseudocode. He was
impressed because he hadn't thought of that approach, and I was the only candidate across panels to use it.
Wrap Up
We had 5 minutes left, so we briefly revisited the DP question, and he reassured me my logic was fine. Yet, I could
only fill up half my DP table. At the end of the interview, I asked him how PhonePe handles deadlock
management in transactions.
The interview was way more difficult than round 1, where I had to talk a lot, although it was mostly me talking to
myselt.
Throughout the interview, I got zero hints and felt intimidated a few times, but I managed to convince him on both
approaches. When I asked for feedback, he smiled and told me, "In the HM round, make sure the projects on
your resume are actually built by you and not git cloned. HM Round bacha hai na?"
I knew right then I was moving forward. A lot of candidates got eliminated here because they couldn't solve the
Trie question.

3. HM Round [Around 9 people appeared for this round] [Around 2 hr ]

The HM round started late in the evening with an Engineering Manager at PhonePe. He opened by asking how the
OA was, and I told him I thought it was well-balanced but definitely more difficult than last year's. When he asked
how my day was, I went with, "Tiring but equally exciting" (copied from a senior's past PhonePe interview
experience
This was by far the most exhausting round for me, lasting a solid two hours. I was asked about every single thing
on my resume. He went all the way back to my position in the TPO and my experience at SPTBI from a year ago,
even though I had my recent internship at Russell Investments there. I honestly didn't think a recruiter would go
that far back, so be ready for anything.
To my surprise, he specifically targeted a project that was not my flagship project. I think he did this to check if I
actually knew the details of all my work, or if I had only prepared for the most impressive one. He spent about an
hour just scraping every little detail off my resume, to the point that I can probably recall it word-for-word now.
Guys, please prepare your resume extensively and most importantly, do not bluff.
He also threw in some generic behavioral questions:

• "How did you handle conflicts between teammates in the TPO/committee?"

• "Why did you choose statistics in TPO?"

• "How did you handle a conflict between you and your professor?"

• "What were your key takeaways from Russell Investments?"

Then, he asked if I had any startup ideas. I honestly pitched him an idea I had thought of, and he asked me to
explain the data flow of the startup. (So I guess keep a well-thought-out startup idea handy as a backup plan).
From there, he very smartly turned that conversation into a system design round for an Autopay system. We
discussed my designs, where they would fail, and what the improvements could be. He was discussing
everything in depth, going into things I didn't even know. But again, very smartly, he guided the conversation so
that he made me derive the solution that I thought I built on my own.
--- PAGE 5 ---
The interview ended on a positive note. When he asked if I had any questions, I asked him how PhonePe handles
the tradeoff between consistency and availability, since network partitions are a given. He very calmly and
intelligently explained the answer to me.
Final Results
The day ended with only 9 HM rounds being conducted (3 people had been rejected after Round 1 itself). After
10-15 minutes of internal discussion, they came out and announced the results.
A total of 6 offers were given out:

• 2 Internship + Placement (I+P)

• 4 Internship only (Performance-based PPO)

A small tip that genuinely helped me:
I fed ChatGPT previous PhonePe interview experiences, gave it a detailed prompt to act as an interviewer, and
used Voice Mode to simulate real interviews.
I honestly didn't have much time to prepare before the placement process because I was simultaneously
interning at Russell. Being at a disadvantage compared to many candidates who had more preparation time, I had
to make every hour count. Most of my time went into revising core subjects. I skipped DSA practice during the
final few days and relied almost entirely on GPT mock interviews because they gave me the highest return on my
limited time.
The biggest lesson I learned is that when placements are around the corner, optimizing your time matters more
than trying to do everything.
If you're someone who believes in God, trust His plan, especially during moments of fear, anxiety, or imposter
syndrome. Things have a way of working out if you keep putting in the effort.
Some tips that helped me:

• Do a lot of CP, especially CSES and AtCoder. With online assessments and interviews becoming

increasingly difficult, competitive programming gives you a huge advantage. Participate in contests
regularly. Striver's A2Z Sheet is almost a must. I had completed around 99% of it and marked selected
problems for revision, which made revising much easier.

• Always ask for the constraints first. They often reveal the expected time complexity and help you

converge on the optimal approach much faster.

• Don't stop at DSA. Have a solid understanding of distributed systems, system design, and software

engineering concepts. Show interviewers that you're more than just another CRUD developer. Having at
least one well-built distributed systems project on your resume goes a long way. My engineering
manager was impressed with one of my projects.

• Build projects with a purpose. Whether they solve a real problem or exist purely for learning, there

should be a clear motivation behind why you built them.

• There will be moments when you feel like you've already lost the interview. That's completely normal.

What matters is how you recover and continue thinking clearly instead of giving up mentally.

• Treat the interview as a conversation, not an exam. Keep checking whether you and your interviewer

are on the same page. Ask if they'd like you to go deeper into a particular idea or move on. The best
interviews feel like collaborative problem-solving sessions.
--- PAGE 6 ---

• Give as many mock interviews as you can. ChatGPT works surprisingly well, but if you have access to a

senior or mentor whose level you aspire to reach, that's even better. I was almost certainly not the best
DSA candidate in the process, but I was confident in one thing, that very few people could articulate their
thought process as clearly as I could. That's a skill I'd unknowingly been practicing for months by
discussing problems with friends, letting them solve them first, and then walking them through my
approach. Once everyone reaches a similar level of problem solving, communication is often what
decides who gets the offer.

• Articulation matters just as much as problem-solving, if not more. It doesn't matter how elegant your

solution is if your interviewer can't follow your thought process. Once you reach a certain level, many
candidates have similar DSA ability. What differentiates them is how effectively they communicate their
reasoning.

• For PhonePe specifically, don't over-prioritize core subjects. In my experience, they focused almost

entirely on problem-solving and projects rather than DBMS, OS, CN, or OOP.

• Know every inch of your resume. I was grilled extensively to verify whether I genuinely understood

everything I'd listed. Fortunately, I'd built every project from scratch rather than relying on vibe coding, so
I could confidently answer every question.

• Get enough sleep. It sounds simple, but being mentally fresh has a huge impact on how clearly you think

and communicate during interviews.

• Stop comparing yourself to everyone else. There will always be people who know more than you. At

the end of the day, your preparation, your mindset, and your performance are the only things you can
control. Give it your best, trust the process, and leave the rest to God.
Lastly, please please have trust in god. On my first day at Russell, I was already indirectly given a hint that I
won't be getting a PPO. Even though I was sad initially, I believed god had a plan for me, so yeah it worked
out for me.

journey.prep:
• Don't get discouraged in the post-GPT era. It's easy to compare yourself with others, but

consistent practice of your craft will always compound over time.

• Believe in yourself and trust the process. Confidence doesn't come from motivation-it comes

from struggling, making mistakes, and gradually understanding your own strengths and weaknesses.

• Your resume is your biggest selling point. Build high-quality projects, gain internship experience if

possible, and know your work inside out. Be prepared to justify every design choice, the alternatives
you considered, and why you made those decisions.

• Develop a problem-solving mindset, not just a problem-solving library. Understand why a

solution works instead of memorizing it. Over time, you'll naturally recognize patterns and apply
ideas across different problems. Solve at least one problem regularly and challenge yourself with
contests or harder questions to keep growing.

• Communication is as important as technical ability. Learn to explain your thought process clearly,

ask good questions, and guide the discussion naturally. Public speaking, hackathons, presentations,
and interviews all help build this skill.

• Everything you do contributes to your growth. Whether it's writing clean code, using Git

properly, resolving merge conflicts, documenting your work, or making
small
optimizations nothing goes to waste.

• Previous interview experiences are a goldmine. Read them multiple times. Don't just memorize

the questions - understand what the company is trying to evaluate, why those questions were asked,
and what their ideal candidate looks like.

• Start early and stay consistent. Don't wait for placement season to begin preparing. Build habits

that you can sustain over months and years, stay curious, and aim to become a better engineer than
you were yesterday.

System Design
System Design for Beginners (Article) :
System Design For Beginners: Everything You Need in One Article | by Shivam Bhadani | Medium
Hello Interviews- System Design Playlist : Hello Interview • Playlist
Looking back, I don't think I was the smartest candidate that day. There were definitely people stronger than
me in Competitive Programming, DSA, and System Design. What helped me was believing in myself,
communicating my thought process clearly, staying curious, and trusting the process even when I got stuck.
One thing that genuinely helped me throughout the process was visualization. Long before the interviews
actually happened, I would often imagine myself sitting across from the interviewer, explaining my
solutions, discussing my projects, getting stuck, recovering, and answering confidently. It wasn't about
pretending the interview would be easy - it was about making the situation feel familiar before I ever
walked into the room.
Throughout the day, I kept reminding myself of one simple thing: focus on the goalpost, not the noise
around it. There were six openings, but I only needed one. I couldn't control how everyone else performed,
but I could control how well I prepared, how clearly I communicated, and how I carried myself in every
round. My only job was to give it my absolute best, and I did.
The funny thing is, just a few days before these interviews, I wasn't even supposed to sit for PhonePe
because I had already accepted my internship at Russell Investments. I certainly never expected to get
shortlisted, let alone receive an offer. Even then, I never stopped solving problems, learning System Design,
participating in hackathons, or simply trying to become a better engineer every single day. Looking back, all
of those small, consistent efforts quietly compounded into this opportunity.
I was fortunate to have incredible seniors and peers whose interview experiences, advice, and guidance
shaped the way I prepared.
Wishing you all the very best. I hope to read your interview experience here next!!
