My strategy going into the OA was simple: I estimated that solving around 2-2.5 questions would most
likely be enough to get shortlisted. Instead of chasing every question, I focused on maximizing my score.
Knowing your limits during OA is just as important as knowing DSA.
Problem 1: Task Assignment (50 Points)
We were given two arrays, tasks (difficulty) and workers (capability), plus an integer K denoting the
maximum number of tasks a worker is allowed to perform. A worker can only do a task if their capability is
greater than or equal to the task's difficulty. The goal was to find the minimum value of k (1 <= k <= K)
such that all tasks are assigned and no worker does more than k tasks.
Even though this was Question 1, I solved it last because this is the one with the least points. I initially
started off with sorting both the arrays and using two pointers to just greedily assign the task to the current
worker if possible either till it becomes invalid or we exceed k. This passed 9 out of 14 cases.
While implementing it, I noticed: if a particular value of k works, then every value greater than k also
works. That immediately confirmed the answer was monotonic, making it a perfect candidate for Binary
Search on the answer.
Luckily, I had solved a Binary Search problem just before, so recognizing the pattern was almost instant. I
replaced my greedy solution with a Binary Search + feasibility check and ended up passing all the test cases.
Question 2 : Network Routers and Regions (70 Points)
You are given an undirected tree with N nodes representing a network. The network consists of exactly one
central server, multiple routers, and multiple regions. The server is connected only to routers, each router is
connected to the server and one or more regions, and every region is connected to exactly one router. The
task is to determine the number of routers and regions present in the network using the given tree.
Note: Whenever you get an extremely wordy graph or tree problem, DON'T rush into coding. Spend a
minute drawing the structure on paper.
--- PAGE 2 ---
When I actually drew the tree, I understood that the "regions" they kept talking about were literally just the
leaf nodes. And since the problem clearly mentioned there is exactly one "central server" (which is basically
the root of the tree). From there, the solution became almost trivial.
Regions = Count all nodes with degree 1
Routers = N - Regions - 1
All I needed to do was calculate the degree of every node, count the leaves, and apply the formula. It passed
all the test cases.
Problem 3: Problem - 1665C - Codeforces - Tree Infection (110 Points)
You are given a rooted tree with n vertices where vertex 1 is the root. Initially, all vertices are healthy. Every
second, two operations occur in the following order:

1. Manual Infection (Spreading): You can choose exactly one healthy vertex and infect it.

2. Natural Infection (Spreading): For every infected vertex, the disease naturally spreads to exactly

one of its healthy siblings (vertices sharing the same parent).
Your goal is to find the minimum number of seconds required to infect all the vertices in the tree.
I attempted this first because this problem carried a lot of points, so I really wanted to give it the time it
deserved. Right in the start, I noticed that the time needed to infect the entire tree is monotonic, which
immediately told me I could use Binary Search on the answer.
Note: Whenever a question asks for the minimum or maximum value of something like time, days, capacity,
or cost, always stop for a second and check whether the answer space is monotonic. If it is, Binary Search
should be one of the first ideas that comes to mind.
Knowing I needed Binary Search was the easy part; the hard part was figuring out how to actually model the
tree for my check(mid) function. Initially, I kept thinking in terms of the entire tree structure, but after
dry-running a few examples, I realized I was overcomplicating things. Instead of treating it like a tree
problem, I grouped nodes based on the number of children they had and sorted those groups in descending
order.
In my check(mid) function, the greedy logic was simple: we should manually infect the largest groups first.
Because of how the time flows in the problem, group i will naturally infect mid - i nodes on its own. If a
group has more nodes than that, it means we have to step in and use extra manual injections to finish it off.
I coded it up but only passed about half of the test cases due to some annoying implementation bugs. It was
tempting to sit there and debug,but I forced myself to move on to grab points from the other questions.
Luckily, I managed to come back to it at the very end, tweaked a few things, and passed a few more cases.
Problem 4: Problem - 8C - Codeforces (120 Points)
This was the heaviest question on the OA. By the time I got here, I hardly had any time left to fully
understand the intricate details, let alone write out the code for it. I immediately recognized that the optimal
solution would require a Bitmask DP approach, but I knew I didn't have the time to implement it. Instead of
--- PAGE 3 ---
giving up, I tried writing a smart brute-force solution to target specific edge cases (like the sample test cases
provided) just to grab some partial points. Unfortunately, it didn't pass any hidden test cases, but the attempt
was worth the shot.
Takeaway: Knowing how much time to invest in each problem and to stay calm under time pressure will be
the key to your performance...

2. Technical Round 1 [26 People ]

I was in Panel 1
First we had a quick introduction and moved towards the problem
Problem 1: Maximum Points Activated with One Addition - LeetCode
To be completely honest, I started off on the wrong foot.
I proposed a simple two-hashmap approach to keep the frequencies of x and y separately, thinking I could
just pick the max frequency x and y to form a new point. As soon as I tested it out on a sample test case, I
quickly realized on my own that this new point could overlap with an existing point, giving us a wrong
answer.
Then I confirmed with the interviewer how the answer was for the question. I kept thinking out loud and
asked my interviewers for feedback. They hinted that I should try keeping x and y together. Looking at my
hashmaps and talking to them, I started drawing lines between activated points and asked, "Wait, is this
actually a graph problem?" The interviewer didn't reject it, so I dug in.
I realized it was a Connected Components problem. If we connect points that share an x or y, we just need to
find the size of the two largest components. By greedy logic, we pick a new point that connects them,
returning largest_component + second_largest
_component + 1.
I decided to use a Disjoint Set Union (DSU) approach. But then the interviewer asked me how do you
model the graph without hitting an O(N^2) worst-case complexity by checking every point against every
other point?
I had to think on my feet and looked at the two hashmaps I had dry runned earlier and it hit me. I came up
with a way to append 'y' to 'x' and 'x' to 'y' to track collisions. The interviewer liked it, and later asked how I
would reduce the edges further. I realized I could just use indices instead of storing the actual values, which
fully satisfied them.
Then I was asked to write code, they initially mentioned to consider DSU as blackbox but I still explained
to them how my find and union function would look like, and I would be using size and parent lists in the
DSU for memory. I wrote the other things quickly and considered the case of finding two max properly
which my interviewer wanted to see if I got it correct or not and then he asked me to write union function of
DSU and I wrote it quickly all the time explaining what i was doing to them to show how I normally code
just to keep conversation flowing and showcasing How I generally work.
--- PAGE 4 ---
Problem 2 : Subarrays with K Different Integers - LeetCode
I quickly explained the O(N^2) brute force and moved to the optimal sliding window approach. But during
the dry run, I messed up. Because I recognized the problem, I blindly used a standard sliding window
template, forgetting that the problem asked for exactly K, not at most K. I talked about using two loops to
calculate atMost(K) - atMost(K-1), but then tried to over-engineer it into a single loop, I even wrote the
sliding window template code properly but my interviewer asked me to dry run what I was doing and I kept
getting stuck on it.
My interviewer came in clutch again and asked me back to the two-loop approach and I quickly discussed
what I would do. This is where thinking out loud helped me because I had proposed the ways before it
helped me and I was able to complete both the questions within time.
After the interview ended my friend showed me a single loop with a three pointer approach that worked
beautifully.
Because I had put out wrong approaches out there I was able to get to the correct one in both problems and
more importantly was able to communicate better to the interviewers. Some people were able to solve
problems and had better op skills but did not get shortlisted further because of lack of communication and
the ability to pitch your solution to the interviewer clearly, what they want to see is the entire process and
not just the final solution.
They asked me for any questions and I asked them what makes you excited and thinking on your feet at
work like we have hackathons and competitions at college. The interviewer gave a detailed answer, noting
that in an organization, the focus often shifts from pure algorithm optimization like ON) vs O(2N) to
scalability, cost reduction, and impact and smiled at me. I left the interview feeling confident.
Takeaway: Keep the conversation alive and be transparent with your thought process so the interviewers
can see how you think, even if you start with the wrong approach. This gives them a chance to guide you in
the right direction. Also, try to gather as much information from them as possible, both verbally by
asking questions and non-verbally through their eye contact and facial cues

3. HM Round [9 People ]

I was immediately called for the Hiring Manager (HM) round, and we moved to a different room. He started
off by asking about the project I was most proud of. I actually hadn't included it on my resume because I was
trying to tailor it strictly to the Job Description (JD), but I went ahead and explained it anyway.
A quick tip: you don't always need to blindly follow the JD, especially when there is no ATS shortlisting
involved. I even opened the project's GitHub repository right there on the HM's laptop and showed him a
YouTube video demo I had made.
He then asked me to explain the system design of that project in detail. We had a great discussion about what
I did right, what I should have done differently, and potential improvements. At one point, he asked me,
"Why did you choose Kafka instead of RabbitMQ?" I answered honestly, saying, "Because I simply
wanted to learn Kafka." He smiled and said, "Fair enough." Then, he tested my knowledge on the history of
asynchronous programming. I recalled async/await and Promises, and he kindly walked me through how
callback functions fit into the picture.
--- PAGE 5 ---
Next, the conversation shifted when he asked, "Have you used the PhonePe app?"
I was prepared for this. I told him that while I hadn't used the app personally, I had actually integrated the
PhonePe SDK during my previous internship. This opened up a deep discussion about that integration. He
threw a lot of edge cases at me, asking how I would handle them. For example, he asked me to imagine a
scenario where a payment succeeded, but the callback URL failed and the webhook was down. I suggested
polling the server once it comes back online.
He smiled and said,
"Exactly. That's what we call Recon at PhonePe."
That was probably one of my favorite moments in the interview because it felt like my reasoning aligned
with how they handled the problem in production.
After that, he asked me what my favorite app was, which is again commonly asked in interviews. I replied
with "LeetCode," which smoothly transitioned us into a system design discussion. We designed the
architecture for taking code input from the website, running it, and returning the result. He grilled me on the
specifics: How would I send the code? How would it execute safely? I suggested using Docker containers,
and he pushed further on exactly how the container would access the code where I replied through a signed
URL from AWS S3 Blob or if we are storing code locally then we can just make the docker container access
the shared files from root OS.
Once we wrapped up the system design discussion, we moved on to a few behavioral and
teamwork-oriented questions. He first asked me how I handle conflicts within a team.
Instead of giving a generic answer, I shared an incident from one of my hackathons where our team became
frustrated after losing. Rather than letting the disappointment affect us, we sat together, analyzed what had
gone wrong, identified the areas we could improve, and converted that setback into a learning experience for
our next competition.
The discussion naturally transitioned into how we collaborate during hackathons. He asked how we manage
a shared codebase with multiple people working simultaneously.
I explained that we usually divide the project into independent modules - frontend, backend, Al, etc,so that
everyone can work in parallel with minimal dependencies. Once the individual components are ready, we
integrate everything together while resolving any integration issues as a team.
He then asked how we plan and track progress when working under tight deadlines.
I discussed how we loosely follow an Agile workflow by breaking the project into small milestones,
conducting regular check-ins, discussing blockers, and continuously evaluating whether we're on track to
finish within the available time. Finally, he pushed the discussion one level deeper.
He asked, "Even if everyone is working on separate modules, what kinds of merge conflicts do you still
expectạẠại
I talked about common integration problems such as shared schema changes, modifications to common data
structures, configuration conflicts, and API contract mismatches between different modules.
--- PAGE 6 ---
Then came something I genuinely wasn't expecting. He asked for my GitHub ID.
I assumed he simply wanted to note down my username, but instead he opened it right there. He spent a few
minutes exploring my repositories, opened my portfolio, browsed through my blog, and even looked at some
of my recent work. I was genuinely surprised but smiled because this was my strong point. He was
impressed by no. of followers,stars and the projects.
Seriously, Put your best work out there and keep it publicly visible! I also talked to him about what I am
currently working on, mentioning my deep dives into Large Language Models (LLMs) and Reinforcement
Learning (RL), and how I am actively blogging about those topics too.
When it was my turn to ask questions, I asked him about the journey from being a fresher to becoming an
Engineering Manager. He gave a very thoughtful reply, explaining that it is a gradual process. He talked
about how your understanding of code quality, design patterns, and architectural decisions (like choosing
between Kafka and RabbitMQ) evolves over time. He mentioned that his main job now is setting up the
right platform and environment for everyone on his team to fulfill their goals. While answering, he kept
using examples like, "If you were on my team, then..." which gave me a huge hint that I had done something
right. I really loved his answer.
Towards the end, he also asked about my internship at Russell Investments and whether interviewing
elsewhere was allowed. I explained that we had been given an NOC, which made us eligible to sit for
placements. Honestly, I still feel incredibly grateful that we even got this opportunity. A huge credit goes to
Aaryan and Harshav, who coordinated with both Russell HR and our TPO to make it happen.
Finally, I asked him for feedback on my interview. He told me, "You have curiosity, you have strong
technical fundamentals, and you have the drive. I think there is one more round for you as a standard
procedureạỊại
Walking out of that room, I felt something I hadn't felt after the previous round.
It wasn't a relief. It was validation.
For the first time that day, I genuinely felt that all the hackathons, side projects, blogs, GitHub repositories,
and countless hours spent exploring technologies beyond the syllabus had actually mattered.
Takeaway: Looking back, this round isn't something you can prepare for in the last month before
placements. It is the compounding of everything you do throughout your degree - participating in
hackathons, building side projects, learning computer science fundamentals, understanding why systems are
designed a certain way instead of just what they do, writing blogs, maintaining your GitHub.
Start building early. Stay curious. Understand why, not just what. Build things, share your work
publicly, and let your passion for technology show naturally during the interview.

4. Technical Round 2 [16 People ]

There was quite a long gap before Technical Round 2 started, and I used that time to think strategically
rather than just revising randomly. I noticed that the first technical round had already covered Graphs and
Greedy, but they hadn't touched Dynamic Programming or Tries two topics that PhonePe has historically
loved asking. So instead of trying to revise everything, I spent the break mentally preparing for those
specific areas.
--- PAGE 7 ---
As luck would have it, I got the same interviewer from my first technical round. He even asked another
panelist if it was okay for him to take my second round as well, and they agreed. That immediately made me
feel more comfortable because we had already built a good rapport during T1.
Problem 1 : M - Candies
Sure enough, the first question was Dynamic Programming. I started by explaining the brute-force recursive
solution that tries every possible candy distribution. From there, I pointed out the overlapping subproblems
and naturally transitioned into a memoized solution.
Note: Whenever you're discussing a DP solution in an interview, always explain these five things before
writing any code:

• State - What does dp[i][i] actually represent?

• Transition - How do we compute the current state from previously solved states?

• Base Case - What are the initial conditions that start the DP?

• Order of Evaluation -In what order should the states be computed so dependencies are already available?

• Return Value - Which DP state contains the final answer?

Interviewers care much more about your DP formulation than your syntax. I wrote all of these down on paper
and even mentioned that in Python, I could simply use the @cache decorator to memoize the recursive
function.. He liked the approach but asked me to write the iterative (bottom-up) code instead. I walked him
through how to convert my memoized function into a tabulated DP. My logic was correct, but the time
complexity was O(N.K^2). He asked me to optimize it to ON K).
This was the first time in the interview where I genuinely got stuck. I kept staring at the transition, trying to
figure out how to eliminate the inner loop. The interviewer then gave me a small but brilliant hint.
He asked me to simply expand the recurrence relation on paper.
The moment I wrote out a few consecutive DP states, the pattern immediately became obvious.
The second I wrote the expanded equation out, the pattern clicked - it was a Prefix Sum optimization! I
pointed it out, and he smiled and said, "Yes, that's exactly what we were looking for."
Problem 2: Maximum Strong Pair XOR II - LeetCode
Right on cue, here was the Trie problem. I knew immediately that we needed a Binary Trie to maximize the
XOR. But the trick was handling the strong pair condition: x - y <min(x, y).
Initially, I suggested storing the original indices inside the Trie and verifying if the condition held true while
traversing for the max XOR. The interviewer wasn't satisfied. He asked me to optimize that. I thought out
loud and suggested sorting the array first. He told me I was on the right track and asked me to open up the
mathematical condition on paper. Assuming x< y, I simplified |x - y| < x down to y< 2x.
Once we had that, I explained that we could use Binary Search to find the upper bound, but we also needed
an efficient way to remove the "stale" elements from the Trie (elements strictly less than x) as we moved
forward. He gave me a hint to think about a new function inside the Trie. I spent a lot of time here. I was
honestly struggling and eventually suggested maybe keeping a count variable at the end of the Trie nodes.
By this point, time was up. I asked him for the intended solution, and he explained that I was extremely
close: the trick is to keep a frequency count on every single node in the Trie. You increment the count while
--- PAGE 8 ---
adding a number, and subtract from the count while removing a number. That way, you know if a bit path is
still valid simply by checking if its count is greater than zero. Even though I missed that final piece of the
puzzle and couldn't code the optimal solution completely, Even though I couldn't fully implement the
optimal solution, I didn't let the interview end there.
Instead, we spent the remaining time discussing the overall algorithm, along with its Time and Space
Complexity.
Takeaway: By the time we were wrapping up, I had lost almost all my stamina, and my brain felt
completely foggy. It is absolutely crucial to stay in the zone and fight through that fatigue, especially when
T2 is your final technical round and you need to bring your A-game. I had almost lost my thinking abilities
at the very end, but my years of consistent practice and muscle memory are what ultimately carried me
across the finish line.

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
• Don't get discouraged in the post-GPT era. It's easy to compare yourself with others, but

consistent practice of your craft will always compound over time.

• Believe in yourself and trust the process. Confidence doesn't come from motivation-it comes

from struggling, making mistakes, and gradually understanding your own strengths and weaknesses.

• Your resume is your biggest selling point. Build high-quality projects, gain internship experience if

possible, and know your work inside out. Be prepared to justify every design choice, the alternatives
you considered, and why you made those decisions.

• Develop a problem-solving mindset, not just a problem-solving library. Understand why a

solution works instead of memorizing it. Over time, you'll naturally recognize patterns and apply
ideas across different problems. Solve at least one problem regularly and challenge yourself with
contests or harder questions to keep growing.

• Communication is as important as technical ability. Learn to explain your thought process clearly,

ask good questions, and guide the discussion naturally. Public speaking, hackathons, presentations,
and interviews all help build this skill.

• Everything you do contributes to your growth. Whether it's writing clean code, using Git

properly, resolving merge conflicts, documenting your work, or making
small
optimizations nothing goes to waste.

• Previous interview experiences are a goldmine. Read them multiple times. Don't just memorize

the questions - understand what the company is trying to evaluate, why those questions were asked,
and what their ideal candidate looks like.

• Start early and stay consistent. Don't wait for placement season to begin preparing. Build habits

that you can sustain over months and years, stay curious, and aim to become a better engineer than
you were yesterday.
Resources:
DSA
TakeU Forward (Striver) : take U forward - YouTube
CSES Problem Set : CSES Problem Set - Tasks
Aryan Mittal (Graphs / DP / Greedy Interview Problems) Aryan Mittal - YouTube
Colin Galen (Advanced Competitive Programming) : Colin Galen - YouTube
--- PAGE 9 ---
System Design
System Design for Beginners (Article) :
System Design For Beginners: Everything You Need in One Article | by Shivam Bhadani | Medium
Hello Interviews- System Design Playlist : Hello Interview • Playlist
Looking back, I don't think I was the smartest candidate that day. There were definitely people stronger than
me in Competitive Programming, DSA, and System Design. What helped me was believing in myself,
communicating my thought process clearly, staying curious, and trusting the process even when I got stuck.
One thing that genuinely helped me throughout the process was visualization. Long before the interviews
actually happened, I would often imagine myself sitting across from the interviewer, explaining my
solutions, discussing my projects, getting stuck, recovering, and answering confidently. It wasn't about
pretending the interview would be easy - it was about making the situation feel familiar before I ever
walked into the room.
Throughout the day, I kept reminding myself of one simple thing: focus on the goalpost, not the noise
around it. There were six openings, but I only needed one. I couldn't control how everyone else performed,
but I could control how well I prepared, how clearly I communicated, and how I carried myself in every
round. My only job was to give it my absolute best, and I did.

journey.prep:
• CP isn't mandatory, but it definitely helps. It teaches you to stay calm under pressure and

develop solutions for unseen problems during OAs and interviews. I'd recommend starting
with Codeforces, CSES (especially Graphs and Trees), and AtCoder DP Contest. Once you're
comfortable with algorithms, move on to LeetCode. Learning topics like Tries, DP variants,
Bridges, SCC, etc., can give you an edge. Try solving leetcode hards don't get scared by
seeing the length and meaning of it. A hard problem is just a combination of multiple
medium problems. Just take the problem step by step. Just stay consistent and just enjoy the
process

• Have 2-3 strong projects on your resume. Quality matters much more than quantity. Build

projects that are unique and solve real problems. Know everything about them the
motivation, architecture, design choices, challenges, and your exact contribution.

• Know your resume inside out. Every single word on your resume is a potential interview

question. Never mention a skill or technology unless you're comfortable discussing it.
--- PAGE 7 ---

• Communicate your thought process. Make sure you and the interviewer are on the same

page. Ask clarifying questions, explain your approach, and treat the interview like a technical
discussion rather than an exam THINK OUT LOUD.

• For PhonePe, don't spend time preparing Core CS subjects. In my experience, the

interviews focused mainly on DSA, problem solving, projects, and resume discussions.

• Rejections are part of the process. One bad OA or interview doesn't define your

capabilities. Learn from your mistakes, improve, and move on to the next opportunity.

• Never memorize solutions. Focus on understanding the intuition behind algorithms so that

you can adapt them to new variations in interviews.

• Most importantly, trust the process and keep believing in yourself. Every interview is a

learning experience, whether you get selected or not. If one opportunity doesn't work out,
don't get discouraged,there are always more opportunities waiting for you. Stay consistent,
keep improving, and trust God's timing. The right opportunity will come. Just a few days
before these interviews, I had already secured an internship at Russell Investments, but there
was no certainty of receiving aPPO. Looking back, I'm glad things unfolded the way they
did. It was another reminder that you never really know which opportunity will turn into
something life-changing
All the best for your placements!!!

1. Online Assessment [ 320+ students appeared for this round]

Based on my experience, this year's PhonePe OA was much tougher and felt like a true PhonePe-level
assessment than the previous years, so don't assume the difficulty level will be the same just because earlier
OAs were considered easy. The questions required strong problem-solving skills and good implementation
under time pressure. According to me, the technical interview questions were actually much easier than the
OA. So, make sure you prepare well for the online assessment, as clearing it is probably the hardest step in
the entire interview process.
The OA was of total 350 points
Question 1: Task Assignment (50 Points)
We were given two arrays, tasks (difficulty) and workers (capability),plus an integer K denoting the
maximum number of tasks a worker is allowed to perform. A worker can only do a task if their capability is
greater than or equal to the task's difficulty. The goal was to minimize the maximum number of tasks that
each worker could do and we have to complete each and every task after assigning a max fixed number of
tasks to any worker. We can to output max tasks completed and max number of tasks assigned to any worker
Initially, I misunderstood the problem and completely missed the condition to minimize the maximum
number of tasks assigned to any worker. So, I used a greedy approach by sorting both arrays and assigning
tasks using two pointers, which passed 9/14 test cases. After spending around 10 minutes on it, I moved on
to the other question instead of getting stuck. This is something I'd recommend if you're stuck, solve the next
questions first and come back later. In the last few minutes, I reread the problem carefully and realized the
intended approach was Binary Search on the Answer combined with a feasibility check using two pointers.
Unfortunately, there wasn't enough time left to implement it completely. The biggest takeaway is to read the
problem statement carefully before jumping into a solution.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Question 2 : Network Routers and Regions (70 Points)
You are given an undirected tree with N nodes representing a network. The network consists of exactly one
central server, multiple routers, and multiple regions. The server is connected only to routers, each router
is connected to the server and one or more regions, and every region is connected to exactly one router. The
task is to determine the number of routers and regions present in the network using the given tree.
This was a tricky problem because understanding the statement was the hardest part. Once I understood the
network structure, the solution became quite straightforward. The key observation was that every region is a
leaf node, so it has a degree of 1. The server is the only node connected directly to all the routers and never
to any region, while each router is connected to the server and one or more regions. So, I first calculated the
degree of every node. Then, for each node, I counted how many of its adjacent nodes had degree 1. The
node whose neighbors represented all the leaf nodes while the remaining neighbors acted as routers was
identified as the server. Once the server was found, the number of routers was simply the number of its
neighbors, and the number of regions was obtained by counting all the degree-1 nodes connected through
those routers.
I was able to solve this problem completely
Question 3 : Codeforces 1665C (110 Points)
This was a Codeforces problem with the statement slightly reframed. If you've seen the original problem
before, you'll recognize it immediately. Unfortunately, I wasn't able to recall the exact approach during the
OA. I spent around 15 minutes trying different ideas and deriving a pattern from the sample test cases. I
came up with a heuristic based on counting the number of children of each node and performing a simple
calculation, but I knew it wasn't the correct solution. As expected, it passed only 4/22 test cases.
Some people printed -1 or the total number of nodes itself and got a few test cases passed but it was an
actual difficult question to solve within 90 minutes. So don't get discouraged if you aren't able to solve
some questions.
Question 4 : Codeforces 8C (120 Points)
This was a Codeforces problem with the statement slightly reframed(Again C). This was 2000 rated on
codeforces the most difficult part of this questions wasn't finding minimum time but it was printing the
sequence so for finding minimum time i used dp with bitmasking including submask decomposition so it's a
pattern for dp generally only used in Competitive programming. So first calculate time for all masks and
then dp on it. So that wasn't the difficult part. Sadly I spent almost 30 min on this problem '
then I again
switched to question 1.
Takeaways:
After the OA there were people who had solved more questions so I was disappointed with myself. Yet i
knew there was still a chance of getting shortlisted
So it doesn't matter how many people appear for the OA.Your competition is always with top 50
people only. You don't have to solve all the problems just have to be better than the rest 90%.
Everything ultimately depends on how many points you score rather than how many problems you
solved. Try to get maximum number of points as much as possible. Brute force it do anything. Always
--- PAGE 3 ---
keep switching between the questions you never know you get an approach for a difficult question faster
than the approach for easier question. Here my competitive programming helped me lot i gave it just like a
normal CF Contest
So the OA ended around 6 pm and we got shortlisting around 10pm. All the people who solved 1.5
questions or above means whose score is 100+ were shortlisted.
26 people were shortlisted for interviews.

2. Technical Round 1 [ 26 students appeared for this round]

We were asked to come at around 9:00 AM the next day. They called us in the order of how we finished in
the OA. I was in the second batch of students. For the first batch students these were the questions
https://leetcode.com/problems/maximum-points-activated-with-one-addition DSU related
https://leetcode.com/problems/subarrays-with-k-different-integers Sliding window related
For the third batch students these were the questions

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
• CP isn't mandatory, but it definitely helps. It teaches you to stay calm under pressure and

develop solutions for unseen problems during OAs and interviews. I'd recommend starting
with Codeforces, CSES (especially Graphs and Trees), and AtCoder DP Contest. Once you're
comfortable with algorithms, move on to LeetCode. Learning topics like Tries, DP variants,
Bridges, SCC, etc., can give you an edge. Try solving leetcode hards don't get scared by
seeing the length and meaning of it. A hard problem is just a combination of multiple
medium problems. Just take the problem step by step. Just stay consistent and just enjoy the
process

• Have 2-3 strong projects on your resume. Quality matters much more than quantity. Build

projects that are unique and solve real problems. Know everything about them the
motivation, architecture, design choices, challenges, and your exact contribution.

• Know your resume inside out. Every single word on your resume is a potential interview

question. Never mention a skill or technology unless you're comfortable discussing it.
--- PAGE 7 ---

• Communicate your thought process. Make sure you and the interviewer are on the same

page. Ask clarifying questions, explain your approach, and treat the interview like a technical
discussion rather than an exam THINK OUT LOUD.

• For PhonePe, don't spend time preparing Core CS subjects. In my experience, the

interviews focused mainly on DSA, problem solving, projects, and resume discussions.

• Rejections are part of the process. One bad OA or interview doesn't define your

capabilities. Learn from your mistakes, improve, and move on to the next opportunity.

• Never memorize solutions. Focus on understanding the intuition behind algorithms so that

you can adapt them to new variations in interviews.

• Most importantly, trust the process and keep believing in yourself. Every interview is a

learning experience, whether you get selected or not. If one opportunity doesn't work out,
don't get discouraged,there are always more opportunities waiting for you. Stay consistent,
keep improving, and trust God's timing. The right opportunity will come. Just a few days
before these interviews, I had already secured an internship at Russell Investments, but there
was no certainty of receiving aPPO. Looking back, I'm glad things unfolded the way they
did. It was another reminder that you never really know which opportunity will turn into
something life-changing
All the best for your placements!!!
In case of any queries / help, feel free to reach out to me.
Email : harshav.shah23@spit.ac.in

journey.prep:
Have faith in God and trust the process. Even if things don't go as planned-like not getting a
summer internship-I know how discouraging it can feel. I was selected for the JPMC Code
--- PAGE 9 ---
for Good Hackathon but didn't receive the internship afterward, and it was definitely
disappointing.
Instead of dwelling on the past, keep moving forward. Stay consistent in your efforts, maintain
a positive mindset, and believe in your abilities. Every experience, whether it feels like a
success or a setback, teaches you something valuable and brings you one step closer to your
goal. Keep learning, keep improving, and trust that the right opportunity will come.

1. Be consistent with DSA practice.

I didn't do competitive programming at all, but I was very consistent with solving DSA problems on
platforms like LeetCode, GeeksforGeeks, and Coding Ninjas. Try to solve DSA problems every day because
it's a skill that takes time to develop. Don't get discouraged if you're unable to solve a problem immediately.
Spend enough time thinking about it first, and only look at the solution if you're genuinely stuck. After
understanding the solution, solve more problems on the same concept to strengthen your understanding. I
would also recommend exploring competitive programming, as it significantly improves your ability to
solve complex problems under time constraints.

2. Don't avoid hard problems.

Practice LeetCode Hard problems even if they seem intimidating at first. With consistent effort, you'll
gradually become comfortable solving them. During your practice, get into the habit of thinking out
loud consider multiple approaches, explain why one is better than another, and work towards the most
optimal solution. Always analyze the time complexity and space complexity of your final approach, as
interviewers often expect this.

effectively under pressure, collaborate with teammates, and quickly learn and apply new technologies.
Hackathons also provide an opportunity to build unique projects that solve real-world problems, which can
significantly strengthen your resume. Beyond the technical skills, they demonstrate to interviewers that you

journey.howSecured:
So the whole process was conducted in 2 days span with OA being on 5th July while on 6th July all the
interviews were conducted.
Online Assessment | Around 310 candidates appeared for this round] - 5th July
So basically there are 4 DSA questions asked in this round with a time limit of 1 hr 30 mins. All questions
had different marks weightage and the testcases also had different marks allocated to them based on how
tricky that testcase was.
Problem 1: Task Assignment (50 Points) We were given two arrays, tasks (difficulty) and workers
(capability),plus an integer K denoting the maximum number of tasks a worker is allowed to perform. A
worker can only do a task if their capability is greater than or equal to the task's difficulty. The goal was to
find the minimum value of k(1 <= k <= K) such that all tasks are assigned and no worker does more than k
tasks.
The question was similar to this but framed a bit differently. Each project had a skill level, and each
employee also had a skill level. An employee with a skill greater than or equal to a project's skill level could
perform that project and could take at most k projects. We had to return two integers: the maximum number
of projects allocated to any employee and the total number of projects assigned at the end.
I started by implementing the brute force approach. I sorted both arrays and assigned projects to employees
until an employee had reached either their skill limit or the maximum number of projects they could be
assigned. With this approach, I was able to pass around 9 out of 13 test cases, scoring around 30/50. Seeing
this, I moved on to the next question.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Problem 2: (110 marks) The question was as follows: we were given a 1-rooted tree, and at every second,
we could do one of the following two operations:

1. Manually turn on a node.

2. If a parent node had one of its child nodes turned on, then it could automatically turn on its other

child node.
We had to return the minimum time required to turn on all the nodes. The nodes were numbered from 1 to N,
and a parent array was given that represented the connection between each node and its parent.
I approached this question by using a map to store the count of children for each node. Later, I realized that
the problem essentially became one of handling groups of children, where if one child in a group was turned
on manually, the remaining children in that group could be turned on automatically in the following seconds.
So, I used a variable totDistinct to represent the number of nodes that had to be turned on manually. I
also maintained an array containing the sizes of the children groups in descending order, along with a free
variable. Whenever a node was turned on manually, I increased the free variable by the size of the next
element in the children group array, representing the additional children that could now be turned on
automatically.
Then, I ran a loop with ind from 0 to n. If there were free available children, I increased ind by 2;
otherwise, I manually turned on a node, so ind increased by only 1. The answer was the number of times
this loop was executed.
So by this approach i was able to pass around 12/22 testcases and got a score of 60/110 in this question and i
moved onto next question.
Problem 3: Network Routers and Regions (70 Points) You are given a tree of N nodes and N-1 edges.
The network has exactly one central server, several routers, and multiple regions. The server connects only
to routers, routers connect to the server and one or more regions, and regions connect to exactly one router.
We had to determine the number of routers and regions.
I approached this question by calculating the indegrees of all the nodes. A leaf node would always have an
indegree of 1, while a router node would have an indegree greater than 1. (The edge case I may have missed
was that the root node's indegree could also be equal to indegree of router.).
I maintained a map of each node to its indegree. The number of routers would be the largest distinct count of
nodes having the same indegree greater than 1, which became my first answer. The second answer would be
the number of leaf nodes divided by the number of routers.
With this approach, I was able to pass around 8 out of 13 test cases, scoring 40/70.
Problem 4: (120 points) I didn't attempt this question because I was almost out of time, and it was quite
difficult. From my understanding, the question was as follows:
We were given a set of 2D coordinates representing items. A person was standing at a fixed coordinate
where a treasure chest was located. In a single trip, the person could pick up at most two items from the
--- PAGE 3 ---
given coordinates, return to the treasure chest, and place the items back. The time taken to travel between
coordinates was the Euclidean distance.
We had to return the minimum possible time required to collect all the items and also print the path taken.
This was my understanding of the question.

Tips: The OA is largely about how well you can perform under limited time and immense pressure. You

should be prepared to solve questions as quickly as possible. Even if you are only able to solve a question
partially, it is still worth attempting. I solved three questions partially, and later found out that many other
students weren't even able to solve that much.
My suggestion would be to first go through all the questions and then attempt the ones you find easier than
the others. Try to implement any approach that comes to mind, even if it is a simple brute-force solution, as
it may still pass a few test cases and earn you partial marks.
Most importantly, stay calm and confident-don't panic under pressure, as that can affect both your
thinking and your speed.

2. Technical Round 1 [26 people appeared][1 hr]

The format of the technical round was usually as follows: you were given two DSA questions, one at a time,
with a difficulty level comparable to LeetCode Hard problems. You first had to explain your approach to the
interviewer. If your approach was close to the optimal solution, the interviewer would then ask you to write
the code on paper and explain it in detail, along with its time and space complexity.
The interview calls were most likely scheduled based on the OA rankings. I was the first student in the
second batch, and each batch consisted of around 10 students.
Problem 1-https://leetcode.com/problems/making-a-large-island/
As soon as the interviewer started explaining the question, I knew that the optimal solution was to use a
Disjoint Set (DSU). So, without wasting any time, I directly explained the optimal approach. He told me that
it was correct and asked me to write the code on paper. While writing the code, I made sure to speak out
loud and explain whatever I was writing.
The optimal solution was to first traverse the entire grid. For every land cell, if there was another land cell in
any of the four directions (up, down, left, or right), I performed a union by size operation between them.
After completing this traversal, I traversed the grid again. Whenever I encountered a water cell, I checked all
four directions for adjacent land cells. If those land cells belonged to different islands, I added their sizes to a
temporary variable tmp. I then updated the answer as max (ans, tmp + 1).
Later, the interviewer asked me to write the code for the Disjoint Set class as well, which I did. He then
asked me to think of any edge cases that I might have missed. One edge case was when all the cells were
water, which I had already handled by initializing ans to 1. Another edge case was when there was no water
--- PAGE 4 ---
cell in the grid. I had missed this test case initially, but after he pointed it out, I explained how I would
handle it.
He seemed satisfied with my approach, and then we moved on to the next question.
Problem 2 - https://leetcode.com/problems/find-minimum-diameter-after-merging-two-trees/description/
I initially approached this question by explaining the brute-force solution. I said that I would use
Floyd-Warshall's algorithm to compute a matrix containing the shortest distances between every pair of
vertices. Then, I would choose the vertex with the minimum maximum distance from all other vertices in
each tree, connect those two vertices, and finally compute the diameter of the resulting tree.
The interviewer then asked me to optimize the solution. I struggled for a while to come up with a better
approach, but I kept explaining my thought process out loud. After giving me a few hints, I was able to
derive the optimal solution. I explained that I would first find the diameters of the first and second trees. The
resulting diameter would then be:
max (d1, d2, r1 + r2 + 1)
where r1 and r2 are the radii of the two trees, computed as the ceiling of d1 / 2 and d2/2, respectively. I
then wrote the pseudocode for this approach and explained it to the interviewer.
Later, the interviewer asked if I had any questions. Make sure to ask a few thoughtful questions, as this
shows your curiosity and genuine interest in joining the company. Try to ask questions related to the
interviewer's domain of work.

Tips:

Think out loud throughout the interview. Clearly explain what you are currently thinking, even if you are
unsure of the answer. The interviewer wants to understand your problem-solving process and see that you
are making a genuine effort to reach the solution. If they see that you are approaching the problem in the
right direction, they may even give you hints to help you arrive at the optimal solution.

3. Technical Round 2 [13 people appeared]

Six people were directly selected for the Hiring Manager (HM) round (out of which only three were allowed
to proceed to Technical Round 2), while the remaining 10 candidates, including me, first had to go through
Technical Round 2.
Problem 1:
The question involved an array children, where each element represented the maximum number of
candies a child could receive. There were a total of m candies, and we had to return the number of ways to
distribute all the candies among the children such that every candy was distributed and no candies remained.
--- PAGE 5 ---
I told the interviewers that it was a Dynamic Programming (DP) problem. They then asked me to explain the
solution by directly deriving the tabulation approach with a dry run. However, I wasn't able to construct the
DP table directly. Instead, I explained my thought process in sequence, starting from the backtracking
approach, then memoization, and finally tabulation.
For some reason, they still didn't fully understand my approach, so I drew the entire recursion tree and
demonstrated the overlapping subproblems. Even then, they weren't completely convinced. They were
actually looking for a more optimized solution using prefix sums (although, from what I heard later, most
students were unable to solve it using that approach).
I then wrote the code for my DP approach. By this time, a significant amount of the interview had already
been spent on this question, so the interviewer asked whether I wanted to continue trying to find the optimal
solution or move on to the next question. Without wasting more time, I chose to proceed to the next
question.
Problem 2: maximum-strong-pair-xor-ii
I first explained the brute-force solution for the problem by checking all possible pairs that satisfied the
given condition and returning the maximum XOR among those pairs. The time complexity of this approach
was O(n').
The interviewers then asked me to optimize it. I explained that I would first sort the given array and then use
a two-pointer approach along with a Trie. I would keep increasing the right pointer until the given condition
was violated. While moving the right pointer, I would insert each number into the Trie (from the most
significant bit to the least significant bit, i.e., 32 bits).
Whenever the condition was violated for the first time, I would find the maximum XOR of the element at
the left pointer with the numbers currently present in the Trie. Then, I would keep moving the left pointer
until the condition was satisfied again, removing the corresponding numbers from the Trie as I moved it.
This was the optimal approach. The interviewers then asked me to write the complete code in detail, which I
did, while explaining each part of the implementation as I wrote it.
So the time complexity became Onlogn)
Then, they suggested that we revisit the first question. After a lengthy discussion, we agreed on a solution
with a time complexity of O(n × k × k).
Once we finished discussing the coding questions, I asked them a few questions about their line of work and
the kind of projects their team works on.
After the interview was over, I realized that it had lasted for almost 1 hour and 45 minutes.

Tips:

The duration of interviews can vary, so don't worry if your interview lasts much longer than others. A longer
interview does not necessarily indicate anything negative.
--- PAGE 6 ---
Also, even if you get stuck at some point or the interviewer says that a part of your code is incorrect, don't
immediately assume that you are wrong. If you genuinely believe your logic is correct, be confident and
explain your reasoning by dry-running your code on a few different test cases. This happened to me during
this interview, and it helped clarify my approach.
Finally, never stop trying to reach the optimal solution. Even if you don't arrive at it immediately, keep
explaining your thought process and refining your approach. Interviewers often value your problem-solving
process just as much as the final answer.
4 Hiring Manager Round [Around 9 people appeared for this round] [Around 1 hr 15 mins ]
This round was taken by a Senior Engineer. It started with him giving a brief introduction about himself,
after which he asked me to introduce myself as well. He interrupted my introduction midway and directly
opened my GitHub account, which was quite a surprise for me because, based on previous years' interview
experiences, this had never happened.
He then asked me which project on my GitHub was my favorite. I pointed to one of my hackathon projects.
He opened that repository and asked me about my role and my teammates' roles in the project. I clearly
explained that I had worked on the backend and Al/ML along with one other teammate, while the other two
teammates handled the frontend.
He then opened the backend folder of my project and asked me to explain the purpose of each folder. I
explained that I had written the backend in a modular way:

• controllers - contained the main business logic.

• db - handled the database connection.

• middlewares - contained all middleware functions.

• models - defined all the database models.

• routes - contained all the API routes.

• services - included reusable or recurring service logic.

• utils - contained utility functions.

• app-js - configured the main application, middleware, and API routes before passing them to the

route modules.

• index.js - served as the entry point of the application, where the server was started and the port was

configured
I explained all of this to demonstrate how I had structured the backend.
He then opened index. js and asked me what CORS was and why it was used, which I answered. After
that, he noticed that I had hardcoded the allowedOrigins inside the CORS configuration and asked me
why I had done that. I honestly told him that since it was a hackathon project, my teammates and I had
hardcoded the list of allowed URLs. However, in a professional environment, I would usually keep such
values in environment variables so they could be configured through env files. The interviewer
appreciated this answer and was very friendly and understanding, considering it was a hackathon project.
Later, he opened the controllers folder, randomly selected one of the files, and asked me to explain the
complete flow of how that function was invoked in the backend. I started by showing him how the request
first reached app. js, then how it was forwarded to the appropriate route file inside the routes folder,
--- PAGE 7 ---
and finally how that route invoked the corresponding controller function. From this discussion, he got a
good idea that I had a strong understanding of the code I had written.
He then asked me about Git branching strategies. I told him that it completely depends on the application
and its scale. Branches can be created based on different modules, individual features, or even assigned to
different developers working on the project.
Finally, he asked me how I would resolve merge conflicts. I explained that one approach is to use git rebase,
and another is to resolve the conflicts manually using a merge editor by selecting the required portions of
code before completing the merge.
He then shifted the conversation to my internship and asked me what exactly I had worked on there. After
that, he asked me to explain JWT in detail and even provided me with a paper and pen to illustrate it.
I explained that a JWT consists of three parts: the header, the payload, and the signature. The header
contains the token type and the signing algorithm, the payload contains basic user information and claims,
and the signature stores the hashed value of the header and payload generated using a secret key.
While I was explaining, he asked me a few follow-up questions in between to test my understanding, all of
which I was able to answer.
I then explained the complete authentication flow. When a client logs in, the server first verifies the user's
credentials. If the user is authenticated, the server creates a JWT using a secret key and sends it to the client,
where it is typically stored as an HTTP-only cookie to help prevent XSS attacks.
Whenever the client sends a request to a protected endpoint, the JWT is sent along with the request as a
Bearer token. The server then verifies the token by again hashing the header and payload using the same
secret key and comparing the result with the signature present in the JWT. If the signature matches, the
token is considered valid, and the server authorizes the user and serves the requested resource.
I explained this entire flow in detail using the paper, and the interviewer seemed satisfied with my
explanation.
He then asked me to draw the high-level system design of the project I had worked on during my internship.
I drew the complete architecture in detail and explained every component, along with why I had chosen a
particular technology or design decision over other alternatives. While I was explaining the architecture, he
asked me several follow-up questions related to SQL vs. NoSQL databases and many other system design
concepts, all of which we discussed in detail.
Later, he asked me about async and await in JavaScript. I explained that JavaScript is a single-threaded
language, so if a long-running synchronous function blocks the main thread, it can affect the responsiveness
and overall performance of the application. async and await are used to handle asynchronous operations
in a cleaner and more readable way, allowing the event loop to continue processing other tasks while waiting
for an operation to complete.
He then asked what was used before async/await in JavaScript. What was used before that which was
Promises and before that which was callbacks.
--- PAGE 8 ---
At the end of the interview, he asked if I had any questions for him. I made sure to ask a few thoughtful
questions about his experience working at PhonePe, the team's culture, and the kind of work they do.
Some of the questions I asked included:

• How has your growth journey been at PhonePe, and what does the typical growth curve look like for

a new joiner!

• Given that PhonePe processes tens of millions of transactions every day, how do you approach

testing and staging for payment-critical services? Do you rely more on shadow traffic, canary
deployments, feature flags, or other strategies?

• I also asked a few other questions related to the team's day-to-day work, engineering practices, and

the technologies they use.
The interviewer appreciated my curiosity, and we had a good discussion around these topics before
concluding the interview.
Lips:
Always be thoroughly prepared for everything mentioned on your resume, as interviewers can ask questions
on any detail you include.
Be honest in your responses. If you haven't explored a particular technology deeply, it's better to admit it
rather than attempting to give incorrect or fabricated answers.
Stay prepared for unexpected situations. For instance, interviewers may review your project code directly
from GitHub. Even if you're not fully prepared for that, maintaining calmness and confidence can help you
navigate such questions effectively.
Focus on building meaningful projects where you have a strong understanding of the implementation. Be
ready to answer in-depth questions about every aspect of those projects, including the technologies used,
design decisions, and challenges faced.

2 of us got internship + fte
And 4 including me got internship + performance based full time

customSections.content:
Have faith in God and trust the process. Even if things don't go as planned-like not getting a
summer internship-I know how discouraging it can feel. I was selected for the JPMC Code
--- PAGE 9 ---
for Good Hackathon but didn't receive the internship afterward, and it was definitely
disappointing.
Instead of dwelling on the past, keep moving forward. Stay consistent in your efforts, maintain
a positive mindset, and believe in your abilities. Every experience, whether it feels like a
success or a setback, teaches you something valuable and brings you one step closer to your
goal. Keep learning, keep improving, and trust that the right opportunity will come.

1. Be consistent with DSA practice.

I didn't do competitive programming at all, but I was very consistent with solving DSA problems on
platforms like LeetCode, GeeksforGeeks, and Coding Ninjas. Try to solve DSA problems every day because
it's a skill that takes time to develop. Don't get discouraged if you're unable to solve a problem immediately.
Spend enough time thinking about it first, and only look at the solution if you're genuinely stuck. After
understanding the solution, solve more problems on the same concept to strengthen your understanding. I
would also recommend exploring competitive programming, as it significantly improves your ability to
solve complex problems under time constraints.

2. Don't avoid hard problems.

Practice LeetCode Hard problems even if they seem intimidating at first. With consistent effort, you'll
gradually become comfortable solving them. During your practice, get into the habit of thinking out
loud consider multiple approaches, explain why one is better than another, and work towards the most
optimal solution. Always analyze the time complexity and space complexity of your final approach, as
interviewers often expect this.

3. For dsa-Striver's sheet, cses - cses atleast you should have a strong hold on this dsa sheets, they cover

most of the important dsa topics. Also do all advance level topics too - Disjoint set,tries,binary
lifting,segment trees, etc.

4. For DP and graph follow stiver's playlist.

5. For javascript backend - backend

6. Oops - kunal kushwaha [not much important for phonepe]

7. System Design - HLD [for phonepe HLD is enough], LLD , yt hld example [HLD is a must for phonepe]

8. Actively participate in hackathons.

From my experience, participating in hackathons is incredibly valuable. They teach you how to work
effectively under pressure, collaborate with teammates, and quickly learn and apply new technologies.
Hackathons also provide an opportunity to build unique projects that solve real-world problems, which can
significantly strengthen your resume. Beyond the technical skills, they demonstrate to interviewers that you
can work well in a team, adapt to challenging situations, and deliver results within tight deadlines.

9. For other core concepts not asked much in phonepe] - chatgpt is the best, can watch any one shot video on

youtube too.

10. AIML - Krish Naik

--- PAGE 10 ---

11. SQL is also very important [not asked in phonepe] - practice from leetode sql 50.

Feel free to connect with me and ask me any doubts you have - Linkedin
Resume - resume
Lastly,
Keep compiling your dreams until they run successfully.
In case of any further doubts, you can refer to the past interview experiences shared by TPO.

journey.prep:
Learn the Patterns through High-Volume Practice: Consistency is everything. Make it a daily habit to
solve the CSES Problem Set, participate in Codeforces and CodeChef contests, and grind LeetCode. Lock
down the standard variations of foundational problems then study the variations.
Compete Offline: Participate in as many offline competitive programming contests as possible. Competing
in person drastically boosts your confidence, sharpens your focus, and perfectly simulates the
nerve-wracking environment of an actual physical interview.
Build High-Effort, Unique Projects: Avoid generic, copy-pasted CRUD applications. Spend 3 to 4 months
deeply engineering unique projects. You must know every single aspect of the architecture, from the
database schema to the actual production deployment.
Prioritize System Design: Development isn't just about writing code; it is about scaling it. Focus heavily on
system design concepts. Understand load balancing, caching, and the tradeoffs between consistency and
availability in distributed systems. You will be tested on how your projects handle scale.
Collaborate and Mentor: Do competitive programming and software development in groups. Discussing
complex game dev algorithms with a peer or breaking down CP mindsets for junior engineering students
forces you to articulate your technical logic clearly. If you can explain it to a peer, you can explain it to an
interviewer.
If you have any doubts, feel free to connect with me:-

journey.howSecured:
On Sth July, 2026 we were asked to report around 2:40 for the PPT(Pre Placement Talk) followed by OA at
4:30 . Be attentive in the PPT.

1. Online Assessment [ Around 300+ candidate appeared for this round] (conducted on 5th July, 4:30

PM)
There were 4 questions for this round having 50-70-110-120 points respectively and a total of 90 Minutes
(1Hr 30 Min).
The questions of the OA are a bit more difficult than the previous years. I was idle for 15 minutes before
starting and understanding the question and coding the questions like before the starting attempting the
question.
Problem 1: Task Assignment (50 Points)
Problem Statement:
You are given an array tasks of size M representing the difficulty levels of various tasks, and an array
workers of size N representing the capabilities of available workers. You are also given an integer K, which
denotes the absolute maximum number of tasks any single worker is allowed to perform.
A worker can only be assigned to a task if their capability is greater than or equal to the task's difficulty
(workers [1] >= tasks [j]).
N<=2e5 , M<=2e5 , k<=1e3
Your goal is to perform a two-step optimization:
--- PAGE 2 ---

1. Find the maximum possible number of tasks that can be completed using the given workers,

assuming each worker can do up to K tasks.

2. Find the minimum value of k (0<=k<=K) such that the exact same maximum number of tasks can

still be completed without any single worker exceeding k assigned tasks.
After drawing the diagram I just realized that it is just a sorting and greedy approach and then binary search
on the answer, so I coded it and forgot the edge case of k=0 after adding that got AC in that question
completely.
Problem 2: Network Routers and Regions (70 Points)
Problem Statement: You are given a network topology represented as an unweighted tree data structure
consisting of N nodes and N-1 edges.
The network contains three distinct types of components:

1. Exactly one central server.

2. Multiple routers.

3. Multiple regions.

The connections within the network adhere strictly to the following rules:

• The central server connects only to routers.

• A router connects to the central server and to one or more regions.

• A region connects to exactly one router.

Minimum of both is 2.
Given the edges of this tree, your task is to write a program that determines the total number of routers and
the total number of regions in the network.
Initially, I misread the question (assuming node 1 was always the root, which wasn't mentioned). Once I
cleared that confusion, I realized it was a straightforward brute-force problem. If you know how to calculate
the size of a subtree, it becomes super easy. I just brute-forced all nodes as a potential root and checked if its
size was >= 2 and if each subtree size minus 1 was >=2. It passed all test cases.
Problem 3: Codeforces 1665C - Tree Infection (110 Points)
Problem Statement:
You are given a rooted tree with n vertices where vertex 1 is the root. Initially, all vertices are healthy. Every
second, two operations occur in the following order:

1. Manual Infection (Spreading): You can choose exactly one healthy vertex and infect it.

Natural Infection (Spreading): For every infected vertex, the disease naturally spreads to exactly
one of its healthy siblings (vertices sharing the same parent).
Your goal is to find the minimum number of seconds required to infect all the vertices in the tree.
--- PAGE 3 ---
When I first read this, my mind immediately jumped to Tree DP. I spent about 10 minutes trying to figure
out the states and transitions before deciding to move on to the 4th question. Not attempted for the partial
scores forgot about that you should try for that.
Problem 4: Codeforces 8C - Looking for Order (120 Points)
Problem Statement:
You start at a fixed base coordinate (the chest) and need to collect N objects (relics) scattered at various 2D
coordinates. You have a carrying capacity constraint: you can carry a maximum of 2 relics at a time before
you must return to the base to drop them off.
Your goal is twofold:

1. Find the minimum total distance traveled to collect all N relics and return to the base.

2. Explicitly print the sequence of steps (the optimal path) taken to achieve this minimum distance.

Input Format:

• The first line contains the base coordinates X_0, Y_O.

• The second line contains an integer N (1 <N<= 24), the number of relics.

• The next N lines contain the X, Y coordinates of each relic.

Output Format:

• The first line should print the minimum total distance.

• The second line should print the sequence of indices visited (with $O$ representing the base).

As soon as I read the problem, the N<=24 constraint and the traversal nature immediately gave it away as
Bitmask DP. Having grinded through similar city traversal and graph DP problems on CSES, the state
definition was clear to me: let dp[mask] be the minimum distance to collect the subset of relics represented
by the active bits in the mask.
I got the core logic half-right, but I completely messed up on two fronts: handling the 2-relic collection limit
optimally and printing the actual path.
Looking back, if I had approached it more calmly instead of panicking over the complexity, I definitely
could have written a less optimal solution just to extract some partial points.
Online Assessment Results & Shortlist:
Overall, I scored 120 out of 350 points in the OA. We received the shortlist results around 10:00 PM that
same night. Roughly 26 people were selected for the technical rounds, which were scheduled to begin at
9:00 AM the following morning.
--- PAGE 4 ---
Key Takeaways & Tips for the OA:

• Stay Calm & Read Thoroughly: Read every question calmly. The key is to map the OA question to

patterns or similar questions you have solved in the past.

• Volume of Practice Matters: To successfully relate OA questions to known patterns, you need a

strong foundation. You have to solve a large volume of problems first.

• Consistency Pays Off: Honestly, if you have consistently practiced CP or done rigorous DSA for

about a year, clearing the OA and securing an interview is very doable. Focus on extracting partial
points whenever you are stuck!

1. Technical Round 1(6th ,july) [26 people appeared ][Duration: 50-60 mins]

We were asked to come at around 9:00 AM the next day. They called us in the order of how we finished in
the OA. I was in the second batch of students.
There were 10 panels so there were 3 batches for this round. I was in batch 2. I was asked for the following
problems.
Problem 1: LeetCode 827 - Making A Large Island
https://leetcode.com/problems/making-a-large-island/description/

• I took about a minute to structure my thoughts and then spent 3-4 minutes conveying my approach

and covering all the edge cases. (Honestly, my rigorous practice with CSES graph problems really
paid off here; I didn't even realize this was classified as a "Hard" problem until later).

• I first proposed a Disjoint Set Union (DSU) method: track the size of every connected component of

1s. Then, iterate through every 0, temporarily treat it as a 1, use a set to fetch the unique parent IDs
of its neighboring components, and sum their sizes plus one.

• The interviewer then asked if I could achieve this using DFS instead of DSU. I explained that the

core logic remains exactly the same-we can just use standard DFS or BFS to traverse the matrix,
explicitly marking each component with a unique Parent ID and storing its size in an array or map.

• He was visibly impressed with my speed and clarity. He then asked me to write the complete code,

which took me about 15-20 minutes.
Problem 2 :- LeetCode 3203 - Find Minimum Diameter After Merging Two Trees
https://leetcode.com/problems/find-minimum-diameter-after-merging-two-trees/description/

• I started by doing some manual casework. I mathematically proved to the interviewer that picking

any node other than a node on the diameter to connect the two trees will always yield a sub-optimal
maximum distance.

• He was convinced by this initial proof. After receiving one minor hint from him, I further proved that

the optimal connection point on the diameter is exactly its middle node (the center).

• Once the logic was locked in, I explained the standard 2-BFS method for calculating the diameter of

a tree and proceeded to write the code.
This round lasted for me around 50mins - 60 mins.
--- PAGE 5 ---
From every slot of panels 3 students were asked to give HM round first. From the 10 people in my panel, 3
students including me were asked to give HM round first.

2. Hiring Manager (HM) Round _[6(after T1) + 3 (after T2) ][Duration: ~1 hr 45 mins]

• The round started in the afternoon, just 15 min after my T1, and was, without a doubt, the toughest

of all three rounds. It kicked off with a standard introduction, followed by a deep dive into my past
work experience and internships.

• I have three highly unique and strong projects on my resume. The interviewer started by asking

about the first two smaller projects. I explained the core problems they solved and my initial
motivations for building them.

• The "Vegha" Deep Dive: Once we moved to my third project, Vegha, the intensity skyrocketed. We

spent a solid 40 minutes discussing this single project. The interviewer grilled me on the actual
production deployment, the architecture, and exactly how I solved specific technical bottlenecks.
This wasn't just a surface-level summary; he wanted to know the engineering reality behind the code.

• Throughout this entire project discussion, behavioral and technical questions were seamlessly mixed

together. I had to defend my technical choices while demonstrating how I handle challenges, making
it an exhausting but engaging conversation.
The System Design Pitch (E-Commerce Startup):

• Next, he asked me to imagine I was launching an E-Commerce startup and to design the

system for it, including browsing, ordering, and third-party delivery integration(3r party).

• Phase 1 (Initial Launch): I had to design the architecture to support 10,000 visitors and 100

actual buyers, assuming all sales were restricted exclusively to my own website.

• Phase 2 (Scaling Up): He then introduced new constraints. What happens when the customer

base rapidly increases? How do we scale the system when we integrate third-party platforms
like Amazon and Flipkart into our sales pipeline?

• Phase 3 (Architecture Evolution): We discussed the necessary architectural changes to

handle this distributed scale. I had to build out the evolving system design on the spot,
incorporating caching layers, load balancing, and data consistency across multiple platforms.

Tips:

• Deployment Matters: It is not enough to just build a project locally. You must know the ins

and outs of how your project is actually deployed and how it behaves in a production
environment.

• System Design is Dynamic: Don't just memorize standard system design templates (like

"Design Twitter"). Be ready to apply scalable architecture concepts (like caching and
third-party API integration) to your own ideas on the fly.

• Know Your Story: Because behavioral questions are mixed directly into technical

explanations, practice explaining why you built something, not just how.

• Be 100% Genuine in the HM Round: The Hiring Manager will strip away the fluff and test

the engineering reality behind your resume. Be completely truthful about what you built,
what failed, and what your specific role was. If you bluff about a technical bottleneck, a
seasoned Engineering Manager will catch it immediately.
--- PAGE 6 ---

3. Technical Round 2 | 13(after T1) + 3 (after HM) ][Duration: 60-70 mins]

I was one of 3 student who cleared the T1 and HM
Problem 1 : -
Similar to the solution of this problem - https://codeforces.com/contest/2236/problem/F2
In that problem distributing the prime
The Problem: We were given an array of N children, each with a different maximum candy limit, and K
candies to distribute. We needed to find the number of ways to distribute all K candies without exceeding
any child's maximum limit.
The Process: I read the problem and instantly related it to a similar distribution problem I had solved
recently in a Codeforces Div3 (Problem F2). Within the first two minutes, I laid out my initial observation:
if all children had infinite capacities, this would be a simple "Stars and Bars" (or Beggar's Method)
combinatorics problem.
However, because the limits varied, the combinatorics approach (Inclusion-Exclusion) would get too
complex, so I pivoted to Dynamic Programming. I started by writing out the pure recursive relation, then
converted it into a tabulation state.
Once the O(NK^2) transition was clear, I applied a prefix-sum optimization to bring the complexity down.
To push the envelope, I briefly discussed how this could theoretically be optimized even further using
Generating Functions.
I coded the full recursive approach and then wrote out the optimized tabulation loops. The interviewer was
highly satisfied with how I evolved the solution step-by-step.
Problem 2:- Maximum Strong Pair XOR II (LeetCode 2935)
https://eetcode.com/problems/maximum-strong-pair-xor-ii/description/
The Process: This one took me a bit more time. I started by mathematically deriving the valid range for the
pairs. Assuming x <= y, I simplified the strong pair condition down to y <=2x (meaning for a fixed y, x must
be in the range [ceil[y/2],y]). I proved this derivation to the interviewer to ensure we were on the same page.
Once the math was locked in, I figured out it required a Bit Trie. The standard optimal solution here involves
a sliding window over sorted elements, but that didn't click for me in the moment.
Instead, I came up with an alternative: I treated it almost like a Digit DP problem. I wrote a custom walk on
the Trie where I maintained the lower bound of ceil (y/2). When searching for the maximum opposite bit for
y, my search function explicitly verified if a valid index existed strictly within the [y/2, y] range down that
specific Trie path.
I partially coded my custom Bit Trie structure and the specialized search function. Like I was running out of
time so the coding part was a bit messy.
I was the last one to finish this round.
--- PAGE 7 ---
Results were announced
2 of us got internship +fte
And 4 including me got internship + performance based full time
