[ List down the rounds that were conducted and any specific information related to it ]

1.    Online Assessment:  [149 Candidates appeared]

The Online Assessment was conducted on HackerEarth platform. It consisted of 20 MCQs and 5 SQL
questions. Surprisingly, there were no DSA based coding questions. 20 MCQs were easy to test the
understanding of basics of Java, C++ and SQL, along with a few easy logical questions in the form of code
behaviour/output. Next, 5 SQL questions were also ea sy, they tested your basic SQL syntax knowledge and
there was minimal usage of joins to solve the questions.
The round was of 45 minutes overall. The questions were relatively easy, especially the MCQs, it was
basically a race against time, how quickly you can solve all the questions. A total of 38 students were selected
for the interview round.
For the MCQs, I had prepared using GeeksForGeeks and solved Leetcode and Codeforces problems to
build my logic and problem-solving ability. I had practiced the SQL 50 problems from Leetcode for the SQL
questions, as well as websites like SQLZoo and W3Schools.

2. Interview Round 1:    [38 candidates appeared]

After the shortlisted candidates list came, we were told that the interviews would be held 2 days later.
As we didn't have much time, so being prepared early on is the key. All shortlisted candidates were called
at 8 in the morning for pre placement talk, which eventually began at 9 , where the directors explained
many important and key things about the company, internship and about the interview process. I would
recommend to listen to the presentation attentively and note down the relevant points as well as the names
of the Directors, as it might help you later on.

There were 6 panelists and the interview was one-to-one. I was the third candidate in my panelist.

When I entered the interview room, the interviewer asked to introduce myself and took a moment to read
my resume. He asked some basic questions about my projects, its feasibility, how many of them were
individual or done in groups, etc. He also asked few basic HR type questions also. Next, he dived into my
projects and asked me to explain anyone whichever I liked in complete detail. He cross -questioned me
based on certain features which I answered. He told me to write down the code whatever I remember. I
had done my project in Python, so I tried to recall the syntax and wrote down the basic ones which I know
of the back of my mind. He kept on asking me particular questions about me code, projects because of
which I was distracted from writing the code and made some mistakes while answering. But I pulled
myself and covered it up to my ability.

After this, he asked few questions about my skills, on Java, C++, and asked me what my preferred
language was. My go to language was C++, so he asked me difference between NULL, 0, undefined and
pointers and pointers exception. He wrote pieces of  code (of strings) in C++ and asked me to state the
output in each case. I was told to explain time and space complexity and give the same of a piece of code
he showed in his laptop. He questioned me about DBMS Joins and I explained them verbally and using
Venn diagrams as well. At last, he gave me two tables on paper and asked me to perform full outer join
and give the correct output.

3. Interview Round 2    [19 candidates selected]

This interview was taken by the senior person who gave the talk at the start of the day , he took few
moments to look at my resume and asked me to explain any project or any problem which I would like to
share. I explained my AIML project on the resume as well as the purpose and intention behind the resume.
He asked me things about the dataset features, how I cleaned it, which features were important and how I
decided them, which model gave the better result and how I deduced that and similar questions. I answered
as per the question and he cross -questioned me based on my answer. He told me to explain one specific
project on my resume, I explained it and the same process went on where he cross-questioned some aspect
or the other. The interviewer migh t or might not agree or validate your answer, so do not wait for any
positive response and just answer to the best of your knowledge.

[Finally 16 Students were selected for the Internship]

There we 3 parts of the process:-

1. Online Assessment (OA)

2. Technical Interview Round 1

3. Interview Round 2

1.
Online Assessment (OA) (No. of candidates:

149) (Date: 27/07/25) (Time: 45 mins)

The initial stage of the process was an online assessment hosted on the HackerEarth platform, which was a
sprint against the clock. The test was composed of 20 Multiple Choice Questions and 5 SQL queries.
The MCQS were designed to evaluate our grasp of fundamental concepts in Java, C++, and C#. A few of
these were logical questions where we had to predict the output of a given code snippet. The 5 SQL queries,
on the other hand, seemed straightforward but required the use of less mainstream functions like type casting
and the || operator. While I had braced myself for complex Data Structures and Algorithms questions, partly
through some last-minute trick-sharing sessions with friends (a method I wouldn't necessarily recommend),
the assessment surprisingly did not include any.
For me, the single biggest challenge was time management; I genuinely struggled to pace myself effectively.
Based on my experience, I would strongly recommend that future candidates attempt the SQL questions first
before moving on to the MCQs.
In terms of preparation, my main advice is to practice as many MCQS as possible. In a test with such a tight
time limit, your final score is heavily dependent on them. For SQL, a good cheatsheet was invaluable for a
quick revision. Lastly, I'd suggest connecting with individuals who have recently taken the company's OA;
there's a high chance the core concepts and pattern will be similar. Speed and accuracy were the deciding
factors, and 38 candidates, including myself, advanced to the interview rounds.

2. Technical Interview Round 1 (No. of candidates:

38) (Date: 29/07/25) (Time: 1 hour 10 mins)

--- PAGE 2 ---
After we assembled in the auditorium, the Barclays team gave a presentation about their work and
culture. I paid close attention, as this proved invaluable. They mentioned that they were beginning to
explore Generative Al, a key detail that was also confirmed by a few seniors I had spoken with.
My interview began with a discussion of my resume. Armed with the knowledge of Barclays' new focus,
I strategically highlighted the Generative Al components within my existing projects, discussing their
underlying architectures. After about 20 minutes of this targeted discussion, the interviewer seemed
convinced of my understanding and posed a significant challenge based on our conversation: "If we
wanted to deploy a project with these capabilities at Barclays, how would you do it?"
This is where the interview took an unexpected turn into cloud architecture design. Drawing from the
morning presentation, I noted that we would host it on AWS. Despite my resume having no mention of
cloud deployment, I was asked to design a complete, resilient architecture from scratch, specifying
regions and availability zones to ensure high availability.
The challenge peaked when I was asked to code a 'fail-safe' architecture that could self-heal from server
issues. The interviewer requested the code in Java, but I explained that Python was my core language
and asked if I could use it instead, which he allowed. The entire exercise was done with pen and paper,
so definitely be prepared for that. My core strategy was to answer every question unless I was
completely unaware of the topic. I was transparent about not having direct deployment experience but
then immediately attempted to reason through a logical solution for every problem posed. This included
troubleshooting specific issues like the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) and "CUDA out of memory"
errors.
Following the intense architecture discussion, he asked two specific Java questions: one on calling a
function without public static void main, and another describing the JRE, JDK, and JVM. I answered,
again noting that Python was my area of expertise. The interview then shifted to DBMS. Although my
resume only lists MySQL, I was prepared for broader questions on topics like horizontal vs. vertical
scaling, the CAP theorem, SQL vs. NoSQL databases, and ACID properties, all of which I answered
confidently.
When I asked for feedback, the interviewer was candid. He praised my problem-solving but wryly
suggested I remove Java from my resume!
Key Takeaways from my experience:

• Pay close attention to pre-interview presentations and talk to seniors; they contain valuable clues

about a company's focus.

• Make an attempt to answer every question. However, this doesn't mean providing incorrect answers.

If you're unsure about something, acknowledge it honestly and explain that, based on your
knowledge, the issue might be approached or solved in a particular logical way. Unless you are
completely blank on a topic, always try to reason through a solution. This showcases your thought
process. [Do not answer wrong things]

• Be prepared to go far beyond what's on your resume. Interviewers test your ability to reason, not just

recite.

• It's okay to request coding in your preferred language, but be ready for pen-and-paper rounds.

--- PAGE 3 ---

• Honesty is the best policy. It's better to admit a lack of experience and then attempt a logical solution

than to feign expertise.

3. Interview Round 2 (No. of candidates:

19) (Date: 29/07/25) (Time: 45 mins)

The second and final interview was with one of the company's directors, and it felt like a conversation
designed to see how I think, rather than just what I know.
As the interview began, I noticed the director had already thoroughly read the description of my 7-month
ISRO internship on my resume. Instead of repeating what he already knew, I made a strategic choice to
discuss my Smart India Hackathon (SIH) winning project when he asked me to talk about a project I was
passionate about. My reasoning was that the SIH project was architecturally diverse, offering more
avenues for a broad, high-level discussion.
This turned out to be the right move. The director was more interested in the 'why' than the 'how'. We
discussed the high-level architecture, the project's features, and its potential impact, rather than granular
implementation details. It felt like a hybrid HR-technical round where he was gauging my product sense
and communication skills.
Pleased with the discussion, he then asked me to choose one more project to talk about. The
conversation followed a similar high-level pattern, but a crucial moment arose when we had a friendly
disagreement about one of my project's features. This is a delicate situation, and my approach was to
never directly state that a director is wrong. I handled it by saying: "Yes sir, you have pointed out a very
valid concern. It's something our team also thought about. However, we intentionally designed it this
way because we wanted users to have a specific kind of experience, which we feel is still very helpful."
When he suggested an alternative use for my Al agent, I acknowledged its potential by agreeing that his
idea was partially applicable. This approach keeps the conversation collaborative and shows that you are
confident in your decisions but also respectful of other viewpoints.
The interview concluded with him asking about the team size for my projects and if I had any questions.
Overall, it was a mature conversation where both parties were learning about each other. Ultimately, 16
of us were selected for the internship.
Key Takeaways from my experience:

• Be Strategic in Project Selection: Don't just pick your longest or most complex project. Choose one

that allows for a broad discussion and, if you can, one the interviewer hasn't already deeply read
about. Read the room.

• Know Your Audience: A conversation with a director will likely be about high-level impact and

architecture. Focus on the "what" and "why" more than the minute details of the "ho% &

• Navigate Disagreements Gracefully: Never say "you're wrong." Acknowledge their perspective,

validate their point, and then calmly explain your team's rationale. It shows maturity and confidence.
Finally 16 candidates were offered the internship.

1. Round 1 - Online Assessment [ 149 candidates appeared for this round]

This was a 45-minute online assessment carrying 100 marks. It consisted of 20 MCQS (worth 50 marks) and
5 SQL queries (worth 10 marks cach). The MCQs focused heavily on object-oriented programming concepts
and included language-specific programming logic questions in C, C++, and Java. It is important to revise
OOP concepts thoroughly and be familiar with the syntax and logic of all three languages. I primarily use
C++, so I was already comfortable with that section. For Java and OOPS, I referred to the PSOOP notes and
PPTs to brush up. The SQL section had one basic query using the WHERE clause, while the others were of
moderate to high difficulty. Knowledge of SQL date functions (like MONTHNAME) and string functions
(like CONCAT) was essential to solve these. Understanding core SQL concepts such as GROUP BY,
HAVING, LIKE, and JOINS is also important. Personally, I found the MCQS manageable and aimed to
solve them quickly and accurately to save time for the SQL queries. Since I hadn't revised string functions
well, I was able to solve only 3 out of the 5 SQL queries. For SQL preparation, I would highly recommend
using
resources
W3Schools
and
Apna
College's
SQL video
YouTube:
https://www.w3schools.com/sql/ and https://youtu.be/hlGoQC332VM?si=tfQubtGhr0SQMkSQ. Overall,
accuracy, speed, and solid revision of both programming concepts and SOL fundamentals are key to
performing well in this round

2. Round 2 -Technical Interview [38 candidates appeared for this round]

Based on the online assessment, 38 students were shortlisted for the interview round. Before the interviews
began, the Barclays team gave us a brief session introducing their culture, core values, and the overall
selection process. Coming to my interview, it started with a basic self-introduction. The interviewer then
asked me about my comfort level with SQL, following which he gave me a schema and asked a few queries
which I solved using SELF JOIN and GROUP BY with the HAVING clause. He then inquired about my
preferred programming language, which was C++. Based on that, I was asked to write a snippet involving
querying data from two nested maps (a map within a map). After this, he asked me conceptual and coding
questions related to Binary Search Trees (BSTs), including writing basic code snippets. The discussion then
moved to the projects section of my resume, where I was asked to briefly explain one of my projects.
Follow-up questions included how I handled security in the project, what the most challenging part was, and
how I approached solving it. The interviewer also gave a few scenario-based questions such as: how I would
ensure effective communication and equal contribution within a team, what I would do if asked to work with
a tech stack I was unfamiliar with, and how I would handle situations where my point of view differed from
--- PAGE 2 ---
my team members'-including whom I would listen to. There were also some questions related to Git,
especially about handling merge conflicts. Finally, the interviewer asked if I had any questions for him. My
interview lasted for about an hour, while some of my peers had interviews that concluded in 30 minutes-

- SO

don't panic whether your interview feels longer or shorter; each panel takes its own time to evaluate. In
summary, this round tested my SQL skills, coding/DSA fundamentals, understanding of my projects, and my
communication and problem-solving approach in team-based scenarios. I would suggest being well-prepared
with a strong self-introduction and at least a couple of meaningful questions to ask the interviewer. Also, it's
crucial to think out loud during problem-solving, even if your answer isn't perfect the interviewer is more
interested in your thought process than just the final solution. One very important thing to keep in mind is
that if you do not know the answer to a particular question, it is absolutely okay to politely say that you
don't know, rather than trying to make up something. Honesty is something Barclays values a lot, and being
transparent reflects positively on you. Confidence, clarity in communication, and showcasing your reasoning
are key to doing well in this round.

3. Round 3 -Technical Interview [19 candidates appeared for this round]

Based on the previous interview round, 19 of us were shortlisted for the second technical interview. This
round was quite similar in nature to the first technical round, again focusing on projects, backend skills,
database knowledge, and DSA. The interview began with the usual "Introduce yourself" question, after
which the interviewer moved straight to the projects section. He asked me which parts of the project I had
implemented personally and requested that I write a function related to the portion I had worked on. Since I
was comfortable with backend development, I wrote a function accordingly. Next, we discussed
databases he asked whether I was comfortable with SQL and NoSQL databases, to which I responded that
I had knowledge of both. He presented three schema diagrams and asked fundamental questions such as
identifying the primary and foreign keys, and which columns could potentially serve as keys. He also asked
a question related to data anomalies, specifically what would happen if an entry with a null foreign key were
inserted into a table. Following this, he gave me a few SQL queries involving JOINS and GROUP BY. The
interview then moved to object-oriented programming he asked how two objects could be compared, and
later inquired about my preferred programming language (which was C++). Based on that, he asked me to
explain the concept of a Doubly Linked List and write a couple of code snippets related to it. Finally, the
interview ended with him asking if I had any questions for him. Overall, this round tested similar skill areas
as the previous technical interview-SQL, programming fundamentals, object-oriented concepts, and depth
of involvement in projects. It was important to demonstrate clarity in thought, accurate understanding of
concepts, and hands-on experience in coding and database handling.
After all the interview rounds, 16 of us were finally selected and got the opportunity to intern at Barclays.

You probably won't be the best in everything, which they expect, but try to balance everything (including

company's interest, you have a better chance.

• Be honest, always. Mention your weaknesses beforehand. If you don't know any concept or tool,

admit it before you are caught.

• Always show a learner attitude. They aren't looking for someone who knows more stuff, they're

looking for someone who is willing to learn and work with them.

• Try to ask questions. Questions on how you could work on your weaknesses and suggestions based

on their experience could show your learner attitude and make you stand out a bit.

• Think of the interview as a discussion rather than a Q&A session. Your interactiveness is important,

questioning the interviewer and discussing certain scenarios gets them a bit more inclined to work
with you rather than the rest.

• Avoid having expectations. As your expectations rise, so does your anxiousness thinking about

what's at stake and the pain if you aren't selected. This could weaken your confidence.
So, just be thorough with your resume, know that it's okay to not know stuff, be interactive and confident,
and most importantly, be calm, composed and think of this as just one of the many opportunities coming
your way. :)

journey.prep:
--- PAGE 3 ---

1. Only Add What You Know to Your Resume

Your resume is the foundation of your interview - don't treat it like a wishlist. Only include technologies,
languages, and tools you're actually comfortable with. Interviewers often pick up on one small keyword and
dive deep into it. If you're not confident in what you've written, it can create a negative impression. It's
better to showcase fewer things and answer strongly than to list a lot and struggle during questioning.

2. Be Thorough with Your Projects

Expect to be grilled on your projects -- not just what they do, but how they do it. Be prepared to explain
your project's architecture, tools used, problem-solving approach, and even alternatives you considered.
Interviewers love to see ownership and clarity. A shallow understanding of your own work is a red flag, so
revise your code, flow, and logic before the interview.

3. Understand the Tools, Not Just Use Them

It's not enough to implement tools like JWT, MongoDB, or OAuth - you need to understand how they
work under the hood. Interviewers may ask why you chose a certain tool, how it functions internally, and
what its limitations are. This shows depth and maturity in your technical decisions. Learn the why and how,
not just the what.

My solutions to questions in Technical Interview 1:

(1) To calculate the maximum attendance frequency for a student, first determine the college's total

weekly "student-day" capacity by multiplying its simultaneous class capacity (number of classes *
capacity per class) by the number of operational days per week. Next, sum the total number of
unique students across all years. Finally, divide the total weekly "student-day" capacity by the total
number of unique students. This quotient represents the average maximum attendance frequency per
student if the college fully utilizes its available capacity to maximize student presence throughout the
week.
Given the college has 4 classes with a capacity of 200 each, its total simultaneous capacity is 800
students. Over a 5-day week, the college can therefore accommodate a total of 800 students/day×5
days/week=4000 "student-days" per week. With year strengths of 600, 400, 300, and 200, the total
number of unique students is 1500. To find the maximum attendance frequency per student if all
available capacity is utilized, we divide the total weekly student-day capacity by the total number of
students: 4000 student-days/week/1500 students~2.67 attendances per student per week. This
implies, on average, students can attend classes approximately 2 to 3 days per week to fully utilize
the college's capacity.

(2) Primarily, order of numbers doesn't matter in addition or multiplication of two numbers. Next, if we

have to retrieve a value associated with some other value, hashmap or simply map is the fastest way
(O(1)) to do so. So we can build a top level hashmap consisting of operators as keys. Below them we
will have a hashmap, having a pair of numbers as the key and their operation as the value. For
addition and multiplication, we have to store both the pairs (a,b) and (ba)) for optimization.

understanding of concepts, but who did it faster made it to the next round. 38 candidates were shortlisted for
the next round through this round.

2. Technical Interview - 1

(No. of candidates:

38) (Date: 29/07/25) (Time: 30 mins)

Candidates assembled in the auditorium at 8 am for the presentation from the Barclays team. It was
important in terms of understanding culture and expectations of panelists.
My interview began with an introduction, where I described my technical skills and interests in
Competitive programming and Deep Learning. After reviewing my resume, the first question was about my
work at ISRO as an AI ML research intern. After describing my role and responsibilities, there weren't any
technical questions based on my work at internship. Next, the interviewer started asking about OOPS
concepts, which I felt were more relevant to Java OOPS. The questions included concepts like inheritance,
overloading, overriding, static, etc. Next on I was held with pen and paper, and had to come up with pseudo
code for 4 DSA like questions. The first two were easy, the next 2 were interesting based on real world
situations. Let me describe the 3rd and 4th questions. (1) We have to give the frequency (max attendance
possible) of a student in a college which has 4 classes with a capacity of 200 each, each year has the strength
--- PAGE 2 ---
of 600, 400, 300, 200 respectively. The college is operational for 5 days a week. (Try to think on your own,
else refer to my solution in the end). (2) The last question was about server optimization, where we had
simple function taking 2 integers and an operator (+, -, *, /) as input, if we had already calculated the
answer once, we should directly retrieve it from the database, else calculate and store it in the database. How
will you achieve it and which data structure will you use? (Try to think on your own, else refer to my
solution in the end).
Next, he moved towards SQL. Initial questions were easy, then he asked me to get the names of
employees with the second highest salary from the employees table, which I did using subqueries. But then
he asked me to achieve this without using sub queries, which i failed to do (Actual solution was to use
LIMIT and OFFSET). Next, he asked me if I knew React, I answered I know the basics but haven't built any
major project using it, so he skipped it. He asked me about git merge and git rebase. I have used and hence
answered about git merge being simply merging branches, but I wasn't sure about git rebase which I failed to
answer properly. Next, he ended the interview asking some HR questions, specifically about mistakes I
made during my recent ISRO internship, any help I requested from colleagues and about solving idea
clashes in a team.
Overall, it was a test of basic and core concepts across domains. 19 candidates were selected for the
next round, eliminating the remaining 19.

3. Technical Interview - 2

(No. of candidates:

19) (Date: 29/07/25) (Time: 15 mins)

The second round focused more on my roles in projects on my resume and my personal favourite
ones. The interview was conducted by one of the directors. He skimmed through the resume and asked me to
describe the project that I was closest to. I have worked on Precipitation Nowcasting using a modified Latent
Diffusion model for 7 months at ISRO and hence I was able to explain it with enough technical details.
Next, he asked if there is any other project I would like to describe. I briefed about the SIH winning project
which was about Deepfake Detection, and described the secondary SIH project in great detail, which was
about optimizing city traffic flow using Deep Reinforcement Learning and minimal hardware costs.
Next, he concluded by asking the number of people on the team in the described projects and asked
me if I had any questions. I had one concern about Barclays storing their data on AWS servers, which he
cleared explaining the security layers applied on them and the cost benefits of using AWS specifically.
Overall, it felt like both the technical and HR round, where both the parties had to know each other
better. 16 candidates were finally selected for the summer internship.

customSections.content:
For Java and OOPS, I watched the playlist of Kunal Kushwaha (on 1.5x) covering all the major and
important concepts. Attempting contests on Codeforces and AtCoder helped me in logic building. Also, as
mentioned before, w3schools SOL content helped in solving SQL questions. About the tips, being prepared,
calm and confident is the way, no other fancy advice would guarantee selection.
--- PAGE 3 ---
Talking about improvements, I should have used and understood git better. Also, I should build at
least one full-stack project using any tech-stack, in order to understand the working of web components
better.
My solutions to questions in Technical Interview 1:

(1) To calculate the maximum attendance frequency for a student, first determine the college's total

weekly "student-day" capacity by multiplying its simultaneous class capacity (number of classes *
capacity per class) by the number of operational days per week. Next, sum the total number of
unique students across all years. Finally, divide the total weekly "student-day" capacity by the total
number of unique students. This quotient represents the average maximum attendance frequency per
student if the college fully utilizes its available capacity to maximize student presence throughout the
week.
Given the college has 4 classes with a capacity of 200 each, its total simultaneous capacity is 800
students. Over a 5-day week, the college can therefore accommodate a total of 800 students/day×5
days/week=4000 "student-days" per week. With year strengths of 600, 400, 300, and 200, the total
number of unique students is 1500. To find the maximum attendance frequency per student if all
available capacity is utilized, we divide the total weekly student-day capacity by the total number of
students: 4000 student-days/week/1500 students~2.67 attendances per student per week. This
implies, on average, students can attend classes approximately 2 to 3 days per week to fully utilize
the college's capacity.

(2) Primarily, order of numbers doesn't matter in addition or multiplication of two numbers. Next, if we

have to retrieve a value associated with some other value, hashmap or simply map is the fastest way
(O(1)) to do so. So we can build a top level hashmap consisting of operators as keys. Below them we
will have a hashmap, having a pair of numbers as the key and their operation as the value. For
addition and multiplication, we have to store both the pairs (a,b) and (ba)) for optimization.

First, there was an OA round. Then the second round was a technical interview round lasting around 35-40 minutes.
The third round was also a technical round. There was no HR round this time.

1. Round 1(OA): 128 Candidates appeared for these round

This round was 45 minutes long and consisted of 20 MCQ questions and 5 SQL queries that you had to execute and
submit. For this round, the first 18 questions were on JAVA, C, and C++ concepts. Study OOPS concepts as they are
essential for this round as well as the second round. Also practice OOPS questions in both JAVA and C++ languages.
Then practice questions where you have to predict the output. You can practice these types of questions on GFG. I
strongly suggest studying JAVA, OOPS, and C++ from the InterviewBit website as it helped me a lot. The next 2
questions were on MySQL and DBMS concepts, so for these I also suggest studying from InterviewBit. For the 5 SQL
queries, practice the TOP 50 SQL questions from Leetcode-they will be more than enough. I solved about 45-46 of
the Top 50 questions the night before the OA, as we learned about the OA pattern only one day before the test. The 5
SQL queries carried the highest weightage in the OA, so give them high priority. I was able to solve all 5 queries and
scored the 2nd highest in the entire OA test. The OA results came the next day in the afternoon, and 38 students were
selected for interviews scheduled for 29/07/2025-giving us only 1.5 days to prepare for the second round.

2. Round 2 38 students were selected

All 38 selected students were asked to arrive at 8 o'clock in the morning with their resumes and laptops, dressed in
formals. First, a PPT presentation was held at 9 o'clock by the Barclays Director. Take a notebook with you and try to
note all the Barclays representatives' names as it will be helpful, and also note the points presented in the PPT that you
think are important. Then the first technical interview started at 10:30 AM. We were called in batches of 6 students as
there were 6 panelists, and my interview started at 11:10 AM. When I entered the panelist's room, he didn't introduce
himself nor ask for my introduction-he just took my resume and read it for 2-3 minutes, then asked me directly to
describe one of my projects, so I started describing my project. After I described my project, he asked about some
legal aspects of one of the features. This was just a tricky question designed to lower your confidence. Don't fall for
these types of questions-answer honestly and confidently with what you know, and if you don't know something, just
say no. They won't deduct marks for these types of questions as they only test your confidence. Then he asked 2
normal HR-based questions like what I had done when I encountered a bug in projects, and asked me to describe a
time when I collaborated with a team and how I managed effective communication among team members. After
hearing my answer, he asked me what I would do if I were a team project leader managing 53 people when they all
start working on the project. Then he asked me to describe what GitHub is. Next, he gave me the first coding question,
which I had to solve: swap two numbers without using a third variable. After that, he gave me 2 pattern printing
--- PAGE 2 ---
questions using stars (*) with the constraint that I could only use two for loops and not more than that. I initially
struggled with the second question, but after thinking for about 5 minutes, I was able to solve it. While writing the
solution, explain to the interviewer how you are solving it and what your approach is, as they want to see your thought
process rather than just the correct solution. After this, he said my interview was done and asked me to leave. (He
didn't ask if I had any questions, so I left.)
3.
Round 3 Name 19 were selected
For the second round, things were a bit chaotic for me. My first round finished around 11:40 AM, after which we were
told to sit in room 205 and not interact with each other. About 10-15 minutes after I finished, someone came into the
room and told me I was being called to the TPO office with my resume. I rushed to the office and was surprised to
learn that my second interview was starting immediately-especially since more than half of the people still hadn't
finished their first round, and no one else had been called for their second interview yet. They asked me to wait for 5
minutes because my interviewer wasn't there yet, so I began preparing. I thought it might be an HR round, so I asked
the TPC staff who would interview me, and they said it would be the Director himself. I was a bit panicked, but soon
the Director arrived and my second interview started at 12:00.
Just like the previous round, he didn't ask me to introduce myself. He reviewed my resume for about 2 minutes and
then asked me to describe one of my projects. It turned out to be the same project I'd discussed in the first round. Since
it was mostly a MySQL project, he asked me to name all the tables, then the column names for each table, and then
about the features I implemented and how I implemented both the backend and frontend. He also asked me to write an
SQL query related to my project and whether I had implemented a specific feature; I honestly told him no. Always be
truthful-interviewers are very experienced and can tell if you're not being honest. Check out the RISES principles on
the Barclays page: one of the principles is Integrity-be honest with them and with others as well.
He spent almost 30 minutes asking about that one project. Then, he asked if I had any favorite project I'd like to talk
about. I described my latest project, and he asked one basic question about it. After that, the interview wrapped up and
he asked if I had any questions for him-I asked a question I had prepared beforehand. Always prepare thoughtful
questions to ask the interviewer and avoid anything trivial.
My interview ended around 12:50, and I was told to return to room 205. Up to that point, I was the only person who
had completed the second interview, which made me happy but also anxious because I hadn't had any preparation
time. The official second interviews for the other candidates didn't begin until after 2 PM, and results for round 1 were
announced around 4 PM. I know it all seemed quite chaotic, but try to stay calm-this kind of thing happens a lot. At
7 PM, round two officially finished. I had to wait for around 7 hours just to hear the result, and by 6 PM, I was getting
impatient and panicky because there were no updates for hours. Take my advice: remain calm and don't panic, even
though I know it's hard. Staying calm and confident really helps in these situations because unexpected things can
happen to anyone.
At 7:30, they started calling the names of candidates (from the 19 students left) and told us to sit in a room. Then, they
played a bit of a prank on us before telling us that we were all selected. It was one of the best moments of my life and
made all the waiting worth it.
A total of 16 students were selected for the Summer Internship

1. Online Assessment: [128 candidates appeared]

The round lasted 45 minutes and consisted of MCQs and SQL queries.
The MCQS focused on Java, OOPs, and C. I had asked my seniors about the topics covered previously and,
since these subjects were part of my coursework, I prepared for them accordingly.
Out of the 5 SQL questions, I was only able to submit 3 due to a server issue, but my MCQ section went
well overall.
Interestingly, there was no DSA round this time, which was surprising since DSA is usually a part of online
assessments and was included in the previous year. It's possible that next year's OA might include DSA
again.

2. Technical round [ 38 candidates appeared ]

The interview process took place on the same day as the placement round.
There were two separate interview panels, one for full-time roles and another for internship candidates. My
turn came after the lunch break, around 2 PM.
The interview began with a general introduction. The interviewer asked me to introduce myself, and then
reviewed my resume, noting down my listed skills. He proceeded to ask questions related to my projects and
the technologies I had mentioned.
The technical discussion started with Python. I was asked how Python differs from other programming
languages, along with the advantages and disadvantages of this difference. He followed up with:

• Why has Python gained popularity so quickly?

• What are its primary use cases?

Since I had mentioned Pandas as a skill, the interviewer asked basic questions such as:
--- PAGE 2 ---

• What is Pandas used for?

• What advantages does it offer over SQL or other systems?

He then gave me a scenario: If we have three databases in different formats - SOL, CSV, and another - is
it possible to merge and analyze them using Pandas?
Next, we moved on to REST APIs whether I had used them in any of my projects and how.
The discussion then shifted to DBMS and SQL.
He asked me to explain normalization. He then created three tables and asked me to write queries involving
JOINs, aggregation, and time-based functions. I managed to solve them partially.
Finally, we talked about Scikit-learn. He asked which models I had used in my ML projects and what the
differences were between them.
At the end of the interview, he asked if I had any questions. I asked about the career path an intern or a new
recruit could expect at Barclays.
The round lasted for about 50 minutes.

3. HR Round [19 candidates appeared]

My second-round interview was scheduled around 4 PM. Before going in, I'd heard from a few people who
had already been interviewed that this round was pretty technical and heavily focused on your projects --
like deep dives into how your ML models work and even writing Javascript code. So I spent most of my
prep time reviewing my own project code and making sure I had a solid grasp of every decision I'd made.
When I finally got called in, I found out that my interview was being taken by someone from the full-time
engineering panel. He started by scanning through my resume and then moved straight to project-related
questions.
He asked whether the projects were solo or team efforts, what kind of challenges I faced, how I resolved
them, and whether I'd taken help from professors or peers. Later I realized these were soft skill checks in
disguise, basically trying to see how well I collaborate and whether I'm someone who can work in a team.
There was also a question about whether I had to make any tough decisions during development. I brought
up a time when I had to pick between improving an existing feature or building a new one. But the
interviewer felt that this was more of a common trade-off rather than a genuinely difficult call, though he did
mention that perspectives can differ, to which I replied that in the context of the project it was a pretty big
decision.
He then shifted to another one of my projects. He asked what made me build it, what I expected out of it,
and whether I had made any major mistakes along the way. I explained that I usually work in small iterations
and fix bugs as they come up, which is like Agile methodology, but I forgot to use the term during the
interview.
--- PAGE 3 ---
I also shared the motivation behind the project, it came from a real problem I faced at a conference. That
part led to a mini discussion on whether I had shared the app with others, how I would go about doing that,
and why I hadn't already.
There was quite a bit of back-and-forth, and looking back, I think some of the questions were a bit repetitive
on purpose, probably to test my patience and see if I mess up or contradict myself.
The interview ended up lasting more than an hour.
[16 people got selected for the internship ]

journey.howSecured:
The recruitment process consisted of the following stages:

• Pre-Placement Talk (24 June 2026)

• Resume Shortlisting (Out of 300, only 122 students were shortlisted)

• Online Assessment (27 June 2026)

• Technical Interview Round 1(03 July 2026)

• Technical Interview Round 2 (03 July 2026)

• HR Interview (03 July 2026)

• Result Declaration (03 July 2026)

1. Pre-Placement Talk & Resume Shortlisting

The Pre-Placement Talk (PPT) was held on 24th June at 2:00 PM. We were informed about it only a day
before, around 9:00 PM
J.P. Morgan Chase was hiring for three different roles:

• Banking (Investment Banking)

• FinTech

• Corporate Risk

The session began with an introduction to the company, followed by an overview of the three roles, their
--- PAGE 2 ---
responsibilities, and the kind of work involved. While attending the PPT, pay close attention to the skills and
qualities they emphasize, as these often reflect what they look for in candidates.
After the presentation, there was a Q&A session. This is a good opportunity to clear your doubts, but make
sure your questions are genuine and related to the presentation or the role. They do notice the students
being interactive in the session so ask good questions and interact well. Our PPT was online so it
didn't make a lot of difference but in case of offline presence it would matter more.
After the PPT, we had to register on the J.P. Morgan Chase careers website and fill out the Google Form
shared by the Training and Placement Office (TPO). We also had to submit our final resumes, so it is
important to have your resume completely ready before this stage.
I had my Resume already ready for all 3 roles, I just made minor changes to tailor better to the Job
Description. The resume shortlist was announced on 26th June at around 5:30 PM, just one day before the
online assessment.
The company does not officially disclose the criteria used for resume shortlisting, but it is generally believed
that the ATS score plays an important role. You can check your ATS score on ResumeWorded Website. My
ATS score was 80. Anything above 72 is safe.

2. Online Assessment [ 122 candidates appeared for this round]

Test Pattern: CCB Risk Test
MCQ Assessment - 30 Qtns - 45 Mins - 60 Marks
Section 1: 27 Qtns
Section 2: 3 Qtns
Test Pattern: CRG Junior Analyst Banking
MCQ Assessment - 45 Qtns - 45 Mins - 45 Marks
Section 1: Corporate Finance and Financial Accounts - 10 Qtns
Section 2: Market Awareness - 10 Qtns
Section 3: Quantitative Aptitude - 15 Qtns
Section 4: English Usage - 10 Qtns
Test Pattern: CRG Junior Analyst Fintech
Paper 1: MCQ Assessment - 40 Qtns - 60 Mins - 40 Marks
Section 1: Puzzles and Probabilty - 18 Qtns
Section 2: Logical Reasoning - 10 Qtns
Section 3: Coding MCQ - 12 Qtns
Paper 2: English Usage - 10 Qtns - 10 Mins - 10 Marks
The Online Assessment (OA) consisted of Aptitude, Logical Reasoning, and Quantitative Aptitude
questions. The quantitative section mainly covered topics like Time and Work, Trains, Permutations and
Combinations, Pipes and Cisterns, Calendars, and similar concepts. I paid more attention to Probability
as that is given a lot of weightage in aptitude tests.
The questions were of moderate to difficult difficulty and were quite time-consuming, so regular practice is
important. You can practice from websites like IndiaBix and also solve easy CAT-level aptitude questions,
as they are at a similar level. You can also refer to CareerRide (They have on youtube as well)
Depending on the TPO, this round can be conducted either online or offline. In our case, it was an online
assessment taken from home using Aon's proctoring software. We had to solve 30 questions in 45
--- PAGE 3 ---
minutes under strict online monitoring with +2/-1 negative marking.
Only 32 students were shortlisted out of 122 who appeared for the test.

3. Technical Round 1 [ 32 students were shortlisted]

• Interview Duration and Panel

My technical interview lasted for around 25 minutes and was conducted by two panelists, one of whom
was a Vice President (VP) at J.P. Morgan Chase. I was the first person to be interviewed among all
students so I wanted to put up a good start.

• The panel started with asking me to give a brief introduction about myself followed by a question

from my resume - I had mentioned Tedx in my resume so I was asked about the speaker who came
at Tedx and why did I organise this event. I was also asked about my experience at E-CELL as I
had been a part of this committee for 3+ years and what I learned here.

• Then they asked me about my projects- out of 3 projects they asked me to explain 2. Note that you

need to be thorough with each and every word in your resume. They can ask you anything
from the resume so be crystal clear. I had used ML techniques in one of the projects so I was
counter questioned on why using this method and not any other. In such cases you need to know
everything about your project- Why, What, How you did wrt technologies used/ data/ results
everything.

• They were pretty happy with my projects and the way I explained everything and then moved on to

a guesstimate puzzle. I was asked about the number of Indian marriages taking place in India
every year. Note here- they want to see your approach and how good you are at problem solving
and breaking a complex problem into smaller parts. Its fine if your final answer is not fully correct.
I explained by dividing the 12 months into 3 parts (Jan- March, April-July, Aug-Dec) and
classified the parts wrt high/low/medium no of marriages and then solved wrt to states/region wise
population to get the overall number.

• They also asked a follow up question like which industries benefit in Indian marriages to which i

firstly mentioned gold/silver as in Indian Tradition its a symbolic to give gold/silver and the
apparel/fashion industry along with event management and hospitality companies.

• Then they asked me why I want to join JPMC and why am I fit for this role to which I

mentioned about JP morgan being one of the largest financial institutions overall and the
experience and learning opportunities which I could get. They hadn't asked me anything about Risk
yet so I myself mentioned that Risk is something which every financial institution/ company needs
to mitigate whether its a bank or a company that needs to make decisions. I mentioned that I want
to help the company make important decisions through risk assessment and mentioned some of my
skills like dealing with large datasets, proficiency in SQL and Python etc. Don't talk a lot about this
unless they ask. Since they asked me at the end so i could speak but sometimes they will follow up
and grill if you mention some skills which you don't know.

• Questions I Asked the Interviewers

At the end of the interview, they asked if I had any questions. I asked, "How does an average day
look like for a person working in the Risk Management Team?" They spoke about both the roles-
The Risk Monitoring and Project Management and how they make reports, analyse data use
different tools etc.

• Overall Interview Experience

--- PAGE 4 ---
The panel wanted to see whether I genuinely understood every project mentioned on my resume
and whether I could explain it confidently. They want to see how good you are at communicating.
The most important tip here is to be completely thorough with your resume. Don't mention
anything that you don't know/ can't talk about.

4. Technical Round 2 [ 16 students were shortlisted]

• In this round the focus was more on technical skills and knowledge rather than only resume. It

started with a brief introduction about myself followed by my internship experience. I had done
an Investment Banking Internship at Avendus so I was asked to explain what I did there and what I
learnt.

• The interviewer then asked me to rank myself wrt proficiency in Python and SQL. I gave 8.5 in

both. I was then asked an SQL query related to 2 tables which I solved by using INNER JOIN.

• I was also asked some specific questions like if i have a very large dataset how will i import it if its

not happening on excel using Get Data and about a Tableau Dashboard - if the content is not
showing correctly what could be the reason for that.

• I honestly didn't know the exact answer but I answered by saying I am unable to recall the exact

library but I have used something similar in my project and then I just explained my Project. She
seemed satisfied with my way of answering. This was the catch I learnt from my IB interview on
the previous day which is to not fake anything (I will talk about it at the end of the interview
experience)

• She also asked me about which role I would prefer- Risk Monitoring or Project Management and if

I'm aware of the roles and responsibilities in the JD.

• Overall Interview Experience

This interview was much more detailed than the first one. They also looked at how I approached
problems, explained technical concepts, and communicated my thought process when faced with
unfamiliar questions.

5. HR Round [10 students were shortlisted]

• Interview Experience

The HR round was the most relaxed out of all the interviews. It started with a casual conversation where
the interviewer asked how my day had been and how I felt about the overall interview process. The
atmosphere was friendly, and it felt more like a conversation than a formal interview.

• General Discussion

• The interviewer asked me about my roles and responsibilities of this role which I explained

thoroughly.

• She then asked me about my strengths and also a question about my leadership experience to

which I gave the example of my Committee involvement as the VCP of E-CELL where I
had to manage multiple tasks and take responsibility for all events, manage sponsors,
stakeholder management and ensuring Teamwork and coordination across the entire team.

• Try to give real life examples to make your answer better like I gave the example of

E-Summit with multiple events.

• Role Expectations

The recruitment process consisted of the following stages:

• Pre-Placement Talk (24 June 2026)

• Resume Shortlisting (Out of 300, only 122 students were shortlisted)

• Online Assessment (27 June 2026)

• Technical Interview Round 1(03 July 2026)

• Technical Interview Round 2 (03 July 2026)

• HR Interview (03 July 2026)

• Result Declaration (03 July 2026)

1. Pre-Placement Talk & Resume Shortlisting

The Pre-Placement Talk (PPT) was held on 24th June at 2:00 PM. We were informed about it only a day
before, around 9:00 PM
J.P. Morgan Chase was hiring for three different roles:

• Banking (Investment Banking)

• FinTech

• Corporate Risk

--- PAGE 2 ---
The session began with an introduction to the company, followed by an overview of the three roles, their
responsibilities, and the kind of work involved. While attending the PPT, pay close attention to the skills and
qualities they emphasize, as these often reflect what they look for in candidates.
After the presentation, there was a Q&A session. This is a good opportunity to clear your doubts, but make
sure your questions are genuine and related to the presentation or the role. Avoid asking questions just to
get noticed or because everyone else is asking.
After the PPT, we had to register on the J.P. Morgan Chase careers website and fill out the Google Form
shared by the Training and Placement Office (TPO). We also had to submit our final resumes, so it is
important to have your resume completely ready before this stage. The resume shortlist was announced on
26th June at around 5:30 PM, just one day before the online assessment.
The company does not officially disclose the criteria used for resume shortlisting, but it is generally believed
that the ATS score plays an important role. Make sure your resume aligns with the job description of each
role. Before submitting your resume, check it on multiple ATS evaluation websites such as Enhancv and
Resume Worded. Since different platforms calculate ATS scores differently, comparing results from two or
three websites gives a better idea of how your resume might perform. A score of around 72 or higher is
generally considered a good ATS score, although there is no official cutoff.

2. Online Assessment [ 122 candidates appeared for this round]

Test Pattern: CCB Risk Test
MCQ Assessment - 30 Qtns - 45 Mins - 60 Marks
Section 1: 27 Qtns
Section 2: 3 Qtns
Test Pattern: CRG Junior Analyst Banking
MCQ Assessment - 45 Qtns - 45 Mins - 45 Marks
Section 1: Corporate Finance and Financial Accounts - 10 Qtns
Section 2: Market Awareness - 10 Qtns
Section 3: Quantitative Aptitude - 15 Qtns
Section 4: English Usage - 10 Qtns
Test Pattern: CRG Junior Analyst Fintech
Paper 1: MCQ Assessment - 40 Qtns - 60 Mins - 40 Marks
Section 1: Puzzles and Probabilty - 18 Qtns
Section 2: Logical Reasoning - 10 Qtns
Section 3: Coding MCQ - 12 Qtns
Paper 2: English Usage - 10 Qtns - 10 Mins - 10 Marks
The Online Assessment (OA) consisted of Aptitude, Logical Reasoning, and Quantitative Aptitude
questions. The quantitative section mainly covered topics like Time and Work, Trains, Permutations and
Combinations, Pipes and Cisterns, Calendars, and similar concepts.
The questions were of moderate to difficult difficulty and were quite time-consuming, so regular practice is
important. You can practice from websites like IndiaBix and also solve easy CAT-level aptitude questions,
as they are at a similar level.
--- PAGE 3 ---
Depending on the TPO, this round can be conducted either online or offline. In our case, it was an online
assessment taken from home using Aon's proctoring software. We had to solve 30 questions in 45
minutes under strict online monitoring with +2/-1 negative marking.
Do not underestimate this round. It had the highest elimination, with only 32 students shortlisted out of
122 who appeared for the test.

3. Technical Round 1[32 students were shortlisted]

• Interview Duration and Panel

My technical interview lasted for around 20 minutes and was conducted by two panelists, one of
whom was a Vice President (VP) at J.P. Morgan Chase. The interview was very conversational, and
almost all the questions were based on my resume and the projects I had mentioned.

• DCF Valuation Project

The discussion started with my Discounted Cash Flow DCF) valuation project on Apple (AAPL).
They asked me to explain the complete valuation process, the assumptions I had used, and how I
arrived at the final valuation. Since I had also included a Monte Carlo Risk Model in the project, they
spent some time asking how I built it, why I used it, and what insights it provided. They also tested
my fundamentals by asking basic finance concepts such as the difference between Enterprise Value
and Equity Value.

• Case Study on Financial Crises

My next project was a case study covering Lehman Brothers, Silicon Valley Bank, and Credit Suisse.
The panel asked me to explain the Lehman Brothers crisis in detail, identify the type of risk
involved, and describe the Subprime Mortgage Crisis. They were interested in understanding
whether I knew not just what happened, but also why it happened and how it eventually led to
Lehman Brothers' collapse.

• Python Prediction Model

They then moved to my Python-based prediction model. I was first asked to give an overview of the
project, after which the discussion focused on the technical aspects. They asked me about the data
cleaning process, the Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) I performed, and the different Python
libraries I used. I explained each library, why I chose it, and how it contributed to building the final
model.

• HR and Behavioral Questions

Since one of the interviewers was a VP, the interview also included a few HR questions. They asked
me about my strengths and weaknesses, and why I believed I was the best fit for the role. These
questions were aimed at understanding my personality, confidence, and how well I understood my
own profile. I had also added about E-Cell and the different speakers we had hosted, so one of the
questions was which speaker I liked the most and why.

• Questions I Asked the Interviewers

At the end of the interview, they asked if I had any questions. I askedạẠIf you select me today, what
should I work on during the next six months and throughout my internship so that I am better
prepared and you feel selecting me was the right decision?" They appreciated the question and
advised me to focus on AI and automation tools, as these are becoming increasingly important in the
industry.

• Overall Interview Experience

Looking back, the interview was less about solving difficult technical questions and more about
--- PAGE 4 ---
understanding what I had actually worked on. The panel wanted to see whether I genuinely
understood every project mentioned on my resume and whether I could explain it confidently. They
also evaluated if my skills, experience, and personality were a good fit for roles within Corporate
Risk, such as Middle Office & Reporting, Risk Controller, Project Management, and Data Analysis.

4. Technical Round 2 [ 16 students were shortlisted ]

• Interview Duration and Focus

This interview also lasted for around 20 minutes and was completely based on my resume.
Compared to the first technical interview, this round was more detailed, with the interviewers
focusing on specific parts of my projects and asking deeper follow-up questions to test my
understanding.

• DCF Valuation Project

The interview started with my DCF valuation project. They asked me about the different risk
metrics I had used and how I monitored them. I explained that I had tracked various financial ratios
and margins and used a RAG (Red-Amber-Green) system with predefined thresholds to identify
potential risks. I also gave a practical example to make my explanation clearer. They again asked
about the Monte Carlo Simulation, specifically how I had built it in Excel and which functions I
had used to generate the simulation.

• Case Study on Financial Crises

They once again discussed my case study on Lehman Brothers, Silicon Valley Bank, and Credit
Suisse. This time, the focus was on why the Lehman Brothers collapse triggered a global
financial crisis. They wanted to understand whether I could explain the chain of events and the
broader impact on the financial system.

• Python Prediction Model

The discussion then moved to my Python prediction model. They asked how I had performed
feature engineering, why I created those features, and how they improved the model. They also
revisited the data cleaning and Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) steps. Based on my answers,
they gave me a scenario-based problem and asked how I would solve it using Python, including the
code and the syntax I would use.

• SQL Questions

After Python, they asked me a basic SQL question on the difference between WHERE and HAVING. I
answered it confidently and correctly, and since they were satisfied with my explanation, they did not
ask any further SQL questions.

• Tableau Discussion

They then asked about my experience with Tableau. I explained that I had practiced using a few
datasets and created dashboards to learn the tool. They followed this up by asking the difference
between Measures and Dimensions in Tableau. Initially, I wasn't sure of the answer, so I politely
asked for some clarification. They explained it using an example, which helped me understand the
question, and I was then able to answer it correctly.

• Puzzle Round

I was also given a logical puzzle involving water jars. The question was how to measure 4 litres
using a 5-litre and a 3-litre jar. They were more interested in my thought process and approach
than just the final answer.

• Questions I Asked the Interviewers

At the end, I was again given an opportunity to ask a question. I asked, "Which department do you
work in, and how has your journey there shaped your personal and professional experience?" The
--- PAGE 5 ---
interviewers genuinely appreciated the question and spent nearly 2-3 minutes talking about their
own experiences and career journey. It turned into a very natural conversation and ended the
interview on a positive note.

• Overall Interview Experience

This interview was much more detailed than the first one. The interviewers carefully tested whether I
genuinely understood every project listed on my resume rather than simply memorizing the content.
They also looked at how I approached problems, explained technical concepts, and communicated
my thought process when faced with unfamiliar questions.

5. HR Round [10 students were shortlisted ]

• Interview Experience

The HR round was the most relaxed out of all the interviews. It started with a casual conversation
where the interviewer asked how my day had been and how I felt about the overall interview process.
The atmosphere was friendly, and it felt more like a conversation than a formal interview.

• General Discussion

The interviewer asked me about my hobbies and interests to get to know me better. They also asked
whether I had spoken to any seniors who had interned or worked at J.P. Morgan Chase and what I
knew about the internship experience. I told them that I had interacted with a few seniors and shared
the insights they had given me about the internship and the kind of work involved. This showed that
I am eager to join and prepared for what the internship will demand.

• Why I Was a Good Fit

One of the main questions was why I believed I was the best suited for the role. I answered that I
genuinely enjoy finance and risk management because of my Corporate Finance and Investment
Banking minor. At the same time, I also enjoy coding and working with real-world data. Since this
role combined both finance and technology, I felt it matched my interests and skills well. The
interviewer seemed to really like this answer.

• Role Expectations

The HR interviewer clearly explained that the Corporate Risk role would be based entirely in
Bengaluru and asked whether I was comfortable relocating. They also mentioned that the work
could involve irregular shift timings and wanted to know if I was comfortable with that as well.
These questions were mainly to ensure that I understood the nature of the role and was willing to
adapt to its requirements.

• Overall Interview Experience

This round was mainly to understand my personality and check whether I would be a good fit for J.P.
Morgan Chase's work culture. The focus was not on technical knowledge but on my attitude,
communication, and willingness to take up the role. My advice for this round is simple-be
yourself, answer honestly, and speak with confidence.
ALL THE 10 STUDENTS APPEARING FOR THE HR ROUND WERE SELECTED.
ALSO NOTE THAT JPMC CAN AND DOES REMOVE STUDENTS FROM THE HR ROUND AS
WELL. SO BE PREPARED AND DO NOT TAKE IT LIGHTLY.
--- PAGE 6 ---

1.
[Pre Placement Talk]
This session was conducted online. The speakers introduced themselves, explained the different roles
offered by JPMorgan Chase, and discussed the work culture, expectations, and hiring process. One
suggestion I'd give is to note down the names and roles of the presenters, because there is a possibility that
one of them may appear in your interview panel. It also helps in making the interview feel more familiar.
Pay close attention during the presentation because interviewers sometimes ask questions related to the
company, business areas, or the role, and many of these are explained during the PPT itself.
Regarding asking questions, I personally don't think it has a major impact on your selection. However, if you
do ask something, ensure that it is relevant and thoughtful rather than asking just for the sake of asking.

2. Resume Shortisting.

In my opinion, this was the most important stage of the entire process.
Everything that happened during the interviews revolved around my resume. Almost every technical
question was asked based on the skills, projects, and experiences that I had mentioned.
My biggest advice is:
--- PAGE 2 ---
Tailor your resume according to the Job Description instead of trying to showcase every
project you've ever built.
For this role, there were multiple business areas such as:

• Risk Reporting

• Risk Controllers

• Middle Office

• Data Analytics / Intelligent Solutions

Among these, I felt the Data Analytics track aligned best with my background.
To strengthen my profile, I created a Business Analytics Dashboard project before the interviews because it
directly matched the responsibilities mentioned in the JD. I intentionally kept its description general enough
to discuss comfortably during interviews while still making it relevant.
I also added a few skills such as Excel and Power BI even though I wasn't highly proficient in them at that
time. Since they were explicitly mentioned in the JD, I made sure to learn the basics thoroughly before the
interview through YouTube tutorials and practice.
Important Advice

• Do not add skills just to fill space.

• If you mention something on your resume, be prepared to explain it confidently.

• Interviewers can ask questions from any single word on your resume.

3. [Online Assessment] [ 122 Candidates Appeared ]

The Online Assessment was conducted from home through the AON Assessment Platform.
The company specifically instructed us to sit in a quiet environment with minimal background disturbance.
The assessment mainly consisted of Verbal Ability, Quantitative Aptitude, Logical Reasoning, Number
series, Overall difficulty: Easy to Medium
Initially, we were informed that pen and paper would not be allowed, but later permission was granted.
Since time was limited,

• I first completed Verbal and Logical Reasoning.

• I kept Quantitative Aptitude for the end because calculations generally take more time.

• No calculator was allowed.

One small tip: During online proctored assessments, try to keep your focus on the screen. Even before using
my rough sheet, I showed both the pen and paper to the webcam to avoid unnecessary suspicion.

4. [Technical Interview Round 1] [ 32 Candidates Shortlisted]

Duration: Approximately 20-25 minutes, Panel: 2 Interviewers
--- PAGE 3 ---
The interview started with brief introductions from the panel, followed by,"Tell us about yourself." I kept my
introduction concise by mentioning Diploma, Current degree, Areas of interest, Internship experience. Since
this round felt technical, I skipped hobbies and focused only on my academic and professional background.
The questions I remember are:

1. Tell me about yourself.

2. Walk me through your projects.

3. You mentioned using an LLM in your project. How did you prevent hallucinations?

• I explained the use of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to provide context-aware

responses.

4. Explain SQL Joins.

5. What do you know about Excel? Where have you used it?

6. Since Power BI and Tableau were mentioned on my resume, they asked about my experience with

them.

• I honestly told them I did not have hands-on experience but had worked extensively with

Zoho Analytics, which serves a similar purpose. I then explained my Business Analytics
Dashboard project.

7. Explain Data Cleaning and Data Preprocessing.

8. How do you remove duplicates in Python?

9. Explain Encapsulation and Abstraction along with their differences.

This question is memorable because I panicked a little
*. Initially, I mistakenly explained dropna () for
removing null values. The interviewer clarified that she was asking about duplicates. Then, due to
nervousness, I switched to explaining duplicate removal in Excel! After taking a deep breath, I finally
answered correctly using drop_duplicatesO
Towards the end, the interviewers explained the role in detail and asked if I had any questions. I asked, "I
recently read that J.P. Morgan has been investing heavily in AI. How is Al currently being used within this
roleại
This led to a good discussion and left a positive ending to the interview.

5. [Technical Interview Round 2 ] [ 16 Candidates Shortlisted]

Duration: Around 20 minutes, Panel: 2 Interviewers
This interview was much more conversational. It had been raining heavily that day, and the panel started
with a casual discussion about the weather before moving into technical questions, they asked me to "Walk
us through your resume." Initially, I only introduced myself. One interviewer smiled and said, "Walk us
through your projects as well." After explaining each project briefly, they asked:
Questions

1. Write a Python program to find the maximum element in a list. I honestly didn't expect live coding,

since screen sharing would consume time, I verbally explained:

• Using max ()

• Sorting the list

--- PAGE 4 ---

• Iterating through the list while maintaining the current maximum

2. Explain the different types of Risk.

3. What does JPMorgan Chase do?

4. How does a bank earn profit?

5. Multiple follow-up questions related to Risk Management and JPMorgan.

6. Surprisingly, they also asked an HR question: Tell us your three strengths and three weaknesses.

My suggestion for this round, learn the basics of Risks, its types and management, along with famous
examples such as Lehman Brothers, Silicon Valley Bank, Harshad Mehta Scam. Explaining concepts using
real-life events makes your answers much stronger.

5. ¡HR Interview] [ 10 Candidates Shortlisted]

This was the most relaxed round. The interview began with casual questions like "How has your day been?".
Then she moved towards role-specific HR questions. Some questions I remember:

• You've lived in Mumbai all your life. Are you comfortable relocating to Bengaluru?

• Are you comfortable working in rotational or night shifts?

• Why this role?

• Why JPMorgan Chase?

Unlike traditional HR interviews, there were very few generic HR questions. Most questions focused on
your motivation, company values, role expectations, adaptability

1. Pre-Placement Talk & Resume Shortlisting

The PPT, held on 24th June, covered the three open roles - Banking, FinTech, and Corporate
Risk along with the responsibilities and skill sets expected for each. This session is worth taking
seriously: several interview questions later circled back to points discussed here, and referencing
it shows genuine interest in the role. I took detailed notes, which helped me a lot in later rounds.

2. Online Assessment [122 Candidates Appeared ]

questions to be completed in 45 minutes with negative marking (+2/-1).

The quantitative section covered topics such as Time & Work, Trains, Pipes & Cisterns,
Permutations & Combinations, Calendars, Percentages, and Profit & Loss. While the
concepts were manageable, the biggest challenge was completing the paper within the time limit.

2. Technical Interview Round 1[32 Students appeared for this round]

Around 32 candidates were shortlisted for the first technical interview. The interviews were
conducted across 7 panels, each consisting of two interviewers. My interview lasted
approximately 25 minutes and was almost entirely resume-driven.
The interview began with "Tell me about yourself." I would strongly recommend preparing this
answer well, as it sets the direction of the interview. My introduction focused on my interests in
finance, analytics, technology, and leadership, which naturally guided the discussion towards
my strengths.
--- PAGE 3 ---
The panel then asked me to walk them through my resume, beginning with my internships.
Research Internship - SPJIMR
We discussed my research on greenwashing, where I explained the concept, my role in
conducting literature reviews and stakeholder outreach, and the risks associated with misleading
sustainability claims. This led to a discussion on different types of risks, including Credit,
Market, Operational, Liquidity, Compliance, Reputational, and Regulatory Risk, along
with real-world examples.
Web Development Internship
Next, the interviewers discussed my internship at the SWIS Foundation, focusing on the
challenges I faced while redesigning the website, the REST APIS I integrated, backend
automation, and my overall problem-solving approach.
Projects
The interviewers spent the majority of the interview discussing my projects.
Financial Modeling & Valuation (DCF)
They first asked about my DCF Valuation project.
Some of the questions included:

• Why would you use EV/EBITDA instead of a P/E multiple?

• Why are EV-based multiples generally preferred while comparing peer FMCG

companies?

• What conclusions did you derive from your valuation?

The discussion revolved around valuation methodologies, peer comparison, and understanding
the assumptions behind financial models rather than simply memorizing formulas.
InvoSmart - GST Billing & Accounting Platform
They then moved to my InvoSmart project and asked me to explain the complete workflow.
The discussion included:

• OCR-based bill extraction.

• GST and non-GST invoicing.

• Why PostgreSQL was chosen.

• Tally-compatible journal exports.

--- PAGE 4 ---

• Backend architecture.

• APIs used for automation.

The interviewers wanted to understand how each component fit together to solve a practical
business problem rather than testing framework-specific knowledge.
Banking Stock Market Analysis Dashboard
This project generated the most discussion.
I explained how I analyzed 25,000+ trading records across five NSE-listed banks using Power
BI and DAX.
The interviewers asked:

• On what basis did you calculate the performance of each bank?

• Which financial metrics did you compare?

• How did you evaluate risk and return?

• What conclusions did you draw from your analysis?

I explained that the dashboard primarily analyzed stock performance using opening price,
closing price, daily price movement, trading volume, returns, volatility, and consistency of
stock performance over time. I also described how interactive visualizations helped compare
different banks on multiple parameters, making it easier to identify trends, relative stability, and
risk-return characteristics.
Case Competitions & Risk Management
The discussion then shifted to my national case competition experiences, including CRED's IPO
strategy, Greenko's sustainability initiatives, and an inclusivity-focused business strategy,
where the interviewers were interested in my approach to solving business problems.
Since I had mentioned risk mitigation, they further asked about different risk mitigation
strategies, Basel Accords, and how regulations evolved after the 2008 Global Financial Crisis.
I supported my answers using real-world banking examples.
Why JPMorgan Chase?
Towards the end, they asked:

• Why JPMorgan Chase?

• Apart from being one of the world's largest investment banks, what do you know about

the company?
--- PAGE 5 ---
Questions for the Interviewers
At the end of the interview, I was asked if I had any questions.
I asked: "If I were selected for this internship, what skills or areas should I focus on before
joining so that I can contribute effectively from Day One? Also, are there any areas where
you think candidates typically need improvement for this roleại
