Technical Interview Round 2 [ 16 Students appeared for this round]
Duration: Approximately 25-30 minutes
Panel: 2 Interviewers
The second technical interview was significantly more in-depth than the first. While Round 1
focused on understanding my experiences, this round tested my technical knowledge and the
reasoning behind every project on my resume. Almost every answer was followed by multiple
follow-up questions, making it a highly interactive discussion.
The interview began with "Tell us about yourself" and "Walk us through your resume," after
which the discussion moved into technical concepts.
Technical Fundamentals
Since several of my projects involved data analytics and machine learning, the interviewers
asked me about my technical stack and programming experience.
They first asked me about my primary programming language, followed by questions on my
proficiency in Python and SQL. Instead of simply asking me to rate my skills, they wanted me
to justify my ratings with examples of projects where I had applied them.
The discussion then covered SQL queries and joins, their use cases, and practical applications.
They also asked me to explain the complete machine learning pipeline, from data preprocessing
and EDA to feature engineering, model selection, evaluation, visualization, and the Python
libraries used throughout the workflow.
Financial Modeling
The panel then revisited my DCF Valuation project, but this time the discussion was
significantly more detailed.
Some of the topics covered included:
--- PAGE 6 ---

• Assumptions used while building the model

• Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC)

• Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM)

• Beta

• Peer company selection

• Valuation multiples

• Final investment conclusion

Rather than checking whether I remembered formulas, the interviewers wanted to understand
why I had made certain assumptions and whether I could defend my conclusions logically.
Al & Agent-Based Systems
One of the interviewers asked whether I had worked on any Al/agent-based systems. Although
this project was not mentioned on my resume, it turned into one of the most engaging
discussions of the interview.
I explained that the system consisted of:

• A three-tier Al architecture

• Seven specialized Al agents

• A Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) layer

• An LLM layer using Grok, with the output of each layer acting as the input for the next

Next, instead of discussing only the architecture, the interviewer wanted to understand why we
built the project. I explained that:

• The idea originated from challenges I encountered during my web development

internship.

• We identified repetitive workflows that could be automated intelligently.

• This led us to design an Al-powered solution capable of handling complex tasks in a

structured manner.
Further in the interview, I was asked: "Tell us about a situation where you tried everything to
solve a problem, but nothing worked. What did you doạ
I answered that when every possible solution has been explored, it's important to escalate the
problem to someone with greater expertise rather than wasting time. I illustrated this with
my Al project, where our faculty mentor suggested adding an additional LLM layer, which
significantly improved the system's performance.
Banking Dashboard & Analytics
--- PAGE 7 ---
The discussion then shifted to my Banking Stock Market Analysis Dashboard, where the
interviewers asked about my experience with Power BI, Tableau, and Alteryx.

• I explained that I had worked extensively with Power BI and gained hands-on experience

with Tableau through my Business Data Analytics coursework.

• Since I hadn't worked with Alteryx, I answered honestly and mentioned that I had

already started exploring it and was eager to learn it before joining.
Later in the interview, I was asked, "Can you tell us about something that isn't on your
resume?" I spoke about PYQ Space, an HMI project my teammate and I built.

• Web scraped the college's DSpace repository and built a user-friendly platform for

accessing PYQs.

• The project was supported by our HOD, who helped facilitate its rollout across the

college.

• It received 5,000+ views, 200+ registered users, was widely used during exams, and our

team received certificates for the initiative.
Leadership Experience
The interviewers also discussed my leadership experience, focusing less on my responsibilities
and more on how I handled real-world challenges, including:

• Managing teams with different opinions

• Resolving conflicts and meeting tight deadlines

• Taking ownership under pressure

The discussion was aimed at understanding my decision-making, communication, and leadership
style.
Understanding the Role
Towards the latter half of the interview, one of the interviewers asked: "If selected, which
Corporate Risk function or team would you prefer to work in, and whyại
This was one question I had specifically prepared for after carefully attending the
Pre-Placement Talk (PPT). During the session, different leaders from JPMorgan Chase spoke
about the various functions within Corporate Risk, explaining their responsibilities, the type of
work involved, and the skills required for each team. Paying close attention during the PPT
proved extremely valuable, as it gave me a much clearer understanding of the role beyond the
job description. The interviewers appreciated that my answer reflected a genuine understanding
of the role and how it aligned with my background and long-term career goals.
--- PAGE 8 ---
Closing Discussion
Towards the end of the interview, the conversation then became more HR-focused.
Some of the questions included:

• Tell us about your hobbies.

• How do you manage stress during challenging situations?

• How do you feel about relocating to Bengaluru?

• Why JPMorgan Chase?

• Do you have any questions for us?

I once again asked: "If I'm selected for this internship, what skills or areas would you
recommend I focus on before joining so that I can contribute effectively from Day One?ạ

3. HR Interview [10 Students appeared for this round]

Around 10 candidates were shortlisted for the HR round. This was the most relaxed interview of
the day and lasted approximately 15-17 minutes. Unlike the technical rounds, the discussion
focused on my personality, communication skills, values, and overall fit for JPMorgan Chase.
The interview began with a casual conversation about how my day had been before moving on to
questions about my interests, career goals, and understanding of the Corporate Risk role.
Some of the questions I was asked included:

• Tell me about yourself.

• Why JPMorgan Chase?

• Why do you think you're a good fit for Corporate Risk?

• Have you interacted with any seniors working at JPMorgan Chase?

• Tell me about a time when you witnessed something unethical or wrong. How did you

handle it?

• Are you comfortable relocating to Bengaluru?

• Are you comfortable working flexible or extended hours if required?

The HR interviews concluded at around 4:45 PM. We then waited anxiously on campus until
around 6:00 PM, when we were informed that the results would be announced online. After
what felt like the longest wait of the day, the final results were declared at 7:49 PM.

customSections.content:
• Know your resume thoroughly. Every internship, project, skill, certification, leadership

role, and competition mentioned on your resume is a potential discussion point. Be
prepared for detailed follow-up questions.

• Prepare a strong self-introduction. It sets the tone for the interview and often

determines the direction of the discussion.

• Understand the role, not just the company. Read about JPMorgan Chase, Corporate

Risk, and the different teams discussed during the Pre-Placement Talk. Paying attention
during the PPT can be surprisingly helpful during interviews.

• Build a solid foundation in finance. Revise the basics of Risk Management, Credit

Risk, Market Risk, Operational Risk, Liquidity Risk, Basel Norms, and financial
statements.

• Stay updated with current affairs in banking and finance. Read about major events

such as the 2008 Financial Crisis, Silicon Valley Bank collapse, Credit Suisse crisis, and
recent RBI announcements. Interviewers appreciate candidates who connect concepts
with real-world examples.

• Practice aptitude regularly. The Online Assessment is highly competitive, so solve

questions under timed conditions to improve both speed and accuracy.

• Focus on your thought process. Interviewers are more interested in how you approach a

problem than in memorized answers.

• Be honest. If you don't know an answer, admit it confidently instead of guessing.

Interviewers appreciate honesty and a willingness to learn.

• Ask meaningful questions. Prepare one or two thoughtful questions for the interviewers.

It demonstrates genuine curiosity about the role and the organization.

• Stay calm. Confidence comes from preparation, and interviews become much easier

when you treat them as discussions rather than interrogations.

through the formulas and terms I'd mentioned in my resume. As my project also involved some ML work,
they followed up by asking how I had integrated the ML pipeline. From there, the conversation shifted to a
more conceptual question on how risk affects banks and financial firms, which I answered by explaining the
different types of risk and their impact. The panel then lightened up a bit, asking about my hobbies, followed

question. Towards the end, they asked if I had any questions, so I asked about the Al tools they've recently
started using and the workflow followed within the Corporate Risk team.
Overall, this round was essentially about convincing the panel why I was the right fit for the role.

grounding and critical thinking. The questions asked were:

• A detailed walkthrough of my DCF model explaining the entire workflow, how each calculation was

done, the formulas used, and what they meant

• A brief overview of my ML project

• A short explanation of another project that combined tech and finance elements

• Whether I knew any financial ratios, along with a detailed explanation of one of my choice

question on how I'd use a website to encourage more people to take up painting
--- PAGE 3 ---

• A guesstimate question assuming Mumbai has a population of 2 crore, how would I estimate the

number of cars running daily in the city

• A general awareness question on what I knew about JPMC

Overall, this round was more about testing how I think and how I apply that thinking to real situations.

5. HR Interview (10 shortlisted candidates)

Around 10 candidates were shortlisted for this final round, which was much more conversational and
relaxed compared to the earlier rounds. The questions asked were:

• A quick self-introduction

• Location preference, along with details about shift timings and cab facilities provided by the

company

• A situational question whether I had ever faced a moment in life where I was asked to do something

wrong, and how I responded to it
This round was largely focused on understanding my location preference and getting a sense of my
personality and values rather than testing technical knowledge.

The Online Assessment was conducted on 27 June 2026 from home on a proctored platform.
The platform monitored eye movement, hand movements and general activity through the webcam.
Therefore, avoid attempting to deceive the proctoring software. You may use rough sheets for calculations,
but ensure that your face remains visible to the camera throughout the assessment.
The test consisted of 30 questions with a +2/-1 marking scheme.

• 27 Questions: Quantitative Aptitude

• 3 Questions: Probability and Permutation & Combination

The quantitative section mainly covered: Profit & Loss, Time, Speed & Distance, Work & Time, Ratios
Train Problems, Basic Quantitative Aptitude. The questions were of MBA aptitude level but were
manageable with proper practice. Time management was the biggest challenge.

3. Technical Interview Round 1(32 shortlisted candidates)

The interview shortlist was released on 2 July 2026 at around 8.30 pm.32 candidates were shortlisted for the
first interview. Due to the weather conditions, interviews were conducted online from the college campus.
There were multiple interview panels conducting interviews simultaneously.
This round mainly focused on my resume and getting to know me as a candidate.
Some of the questions asked were:

• Tell me about yourself.

• Walk me through your resume.

• Explain your projects.

• Why did you choose Electronics & Telecommunication instead of Computer Science?

• Questions based on my skills and certifications.

• Discussion around my interests and experiences.

The biggest takeaway from this round was that confidence matters only when it is backed by knowledge.
They can easily identify whether you genuinely know your work or are simply trying to impress them.

4. Technical Interview Round 2 (15 shortlisted candidates)

The second round was comparatively more technical and involved deeper discussions. Unlike the first round,
where the interviewers tried to understand my profile, this round focused on verifying my knowledge. Most
questions revolved around my projects. Since I had personally worked on them, explaining the
implementation, challenges and learnings was comfortable.
The interviewers also asked follow-up questions based on my answers to assess whether I genuinely
understood the concepts. This round reinforced an important lesson: if you have genuinely built your
projects yourself, there is nothing to fear. Simply explain your work honestly and confidently. You can ask
them any sensible question if you wish to do so.

day. The discussion focused more on personality, professionalism and flexibility rather than technical

• Willingness to relocate.

• Comfort with working hours.

Resume Suggestions

• Keep your resume to one page.

• Mention only what you can confidently explain.

• Be thorough with every project, skill and certification.

• Focus on gaining knowledge rather than collecting certificates.

• Revise aptitude concepts and manage time well during the test.

• Avoid guessing due to the +2/-1 marking scheme.

Interview Tips

• Know your resume thoroughly. Be honest if you don't know an answer.

• Maintain eye contact, smile naturally and communicate confidently.

• Speak slowly, think before answering and be prepared for cross-questions.

• Sleep well before the interview and report to the college on time.

• Stay calm, be yourself and show genuine interest in the role.

• Confidence backed by preparation makes the biggest difference.

• Know your resume inside out. You should be able to justify every number, assumption, and

achievement mentioned on your resume. Interviewers can pick any small detail and ask you to

are working in the same team, pay attention during the PPT, ask relevant questions, and go through
previous year interview experiences

• If you have the time, you can do introductory courses like CFI's (right now its paid so you can access

the same content on coursera) Introduction to Risk and Fundamentals of Credit. They provide a good
foundation and make it easier to understand the discussions during the interview

• Read about a few important banking case studies such as Lehman Brothers, Silicon Valley Bank,

and Credit Suisse. Also keep yourself updated with recent events in the banking industry. During
my interview, I connected the issues that hdfc bank was facing with different types of risk, and the
discussion went well from there

• Having a basic understanding of finance is definitely helpful, especially if you're applying for

risk-related roles

• From the beginning of my sixth semester, I was primarily preparing for the CIB role. Unfortunately, I

wasn't selected for it, but I ended up getting the Corporate Risk role instead. One thing I would
strongly recommend is maintaining a balance between tech and non tech preparation. For me, non
tech was more of a fallback option because I had already invested enough time in technical
preparation through DSA, CP, and projects. That gave me the confidence to apply for both types of
roles instead of depending entirely on one. Keep practicing DSA, build a few good projects, and have
a solid understanding of your technical fundamentals by the end of your sixth semester. Many
students who prepared only for non tech roles couldn't clear the OAs for non tech or were not
shortlisted.

2. Technical Round 1 [ Close to 33]

The names of the shortlisted candidates for the CR role were released almost two days before the interview.
However, for the CIB and FinTech roles, the shortlist was announced only a day before the interview. My
advice is to start your preparation early because you may not get enough time between the shortlist
announcement and the interview.
Because of heavy rains, the interview was conducted online from the college campus.
Some key points from my interview experience:

• The interview was entirely based on my resume.

• My panel consisted of two interviewers from the risk team. If the interviewers don't introduce

themselves, politely ask for their names and remember them. It leaves a good impression.

• The interview began with my introduction. I spoke about my finance minor, case competitions,

Python, and data analytics experience. Your introduction is very important because it often sets the
direction for the rest of the interview.

• I had mentioned an M& A focused case competition presentation in my projects and had also

completed the CFI Accounting Fundamentals course. Based on this, I was asked finance related
questions such as:

• Why did you use the Precedent Transactions model instead of the DCF model?

• How do changes in depreciation and tax rates affect the balance sheet?

• One of my hackathon projects involved using an LLM with RAG. The discussion revolved around:

• What problem was the project solving?

• Why did you choose to build it?

o How did the overall solution work?

• I was also asked about the tools and technologies relevant to the role. Since I had studied the job

description carefully and spoken to a few seniors beforehand, I discussed tools such as Power BI,
Tableau, Alteryx, Python, and the libraries I had used.

• Towards the end, they asked how Al is impacting the banking industry and the job market. To which

I told them everything is an abstraction. Earlier we used to have assembly now we have Al and stuff.

• They also asked which track from the job description I would like to join as an intern. Pay close

attention to the PPT and the JD because this is a common discussion point. Asking thoughtful
questions related to them also creates a positive impression.

• The round ended with me asking them a question about the tracks, how do they use ai and stuff in

their workflows.
Overall the interview lasted around 25 minutes and was quite conversational. Personally I found it to be a
relaxed experience. In fact, the day before the interview I was busy solving Codeforces and LeetCode
problems for the PhonePe OA that was scheduled the following day.
One important piece of advice is to know your resume inside out. Every project, course, skill, and
achievement you mention is fair game. While my interview focused mainly on data analytics, finance and
projects, some of my friends were asked core technical subjects such as Object Oriented Programming &
SQL.
If you're mentioning numbers on your resume then you should be ble to justify them.
--- PAGE 3 ---

3. Technical Round 1 [ Close to 10-12]

Just like the previous round, this interview was heavily focused on my resume, so make sure you know
every single point you've mentioned.
Some of the topics discussed during my interview were:

• Be prepared to explain every number, assumption, and result in your projects. For example, I had

built a DCF model for CDSL, so I was asked about the assumptions I had made, the numbers I had
used, and concepts such as WACC and CAPM.

• I was asked about my Python and data analytics experience and whether I was comfortable using

Python. I answered honestly by saying that C++ is my primary programming language because of
competitive programming. I am comfortable solving DSA problems in Python as well, but for my
projects I have also relied on Al assistants and official documentation whenever required.

• The interviewer then asked about my understanding of the role and my knowledge of risk and credit

since I had completed the Coursera course Introduction to Risk and Credit. I explained that the role is
a combination of data analysis, reporting, and stakeholder communication. I had a good
understanding of the role because I had spoken with seniors who were already working in the same
department.

• To explain my understanding of risk, I discussed real world examples such as the recent issues faced

by HDFC Bank, the collapse of Lehman Brothers, and the Credit Suisse crisis. I also spoke about
how JPMorgan Chase acquired Bear Stearns and Washington Mutual during the 2008 financial crisis
to help stabilize the financial system.

• We further discussed Basel norms and a few important banking ratios such as the Capital Adequacy

Ratio (CAR) and the Leverage Ratio (LR), including how these metrics are used to assess the
financial health of banks.

• Towards the end, I was asked to rate my proficiency in Python and Tableau on a scale of 1 to 10. I

honestly rated myself around 7.5 to 8 because I had used both tools in multiple case studies and as
part of my Business Analytics with Python coursework.
The interview concluded with me asking the interviewer a question.
Overall, this round lasted for about 25 minutes. It was technical but conversational, and once again the
discussion revolved almost entirely around my resume. My biggest advice would be to thoroughly
understand every project, course, certification, and skill you've mentioned because the interviewers can dive
deep into any of them.

3. HR Round [ close to 10 people]

This was the shortest and the most relaxed round of the entire process. The interview lasted for only about
10 minutes.
The interview started with a brief introduction where I spoke about myself, where I am from, and how
pursuing a Finance minor sparked my interest in the finance domain.
The questions asked were mostly HR and role related, including:
--- PAGE 4 ---

• Tell me about yourself.

• How do you think a typical day at jpmc would look for you in this role?

• Are you comfortable working afternoon or night shifts if required?

• Are you willing to relocate to Bangalore?

Overall, the conversation was very casual and focused on understanding my interest in the role, my
expectations, and whether I was a good cultural fit for the team. There were no technical questions in this
round, and it concluded within 10 minutes.
Results were announced almost 3 hours after the HR round around 8:30PM.
Everyone who appeared for this round was selected for the role.

1. Pre-Placement Talk and Resume shortlisting

The recruitment process started with an online Pre-Placement Talk conducted on 24 June 2026. During the
session, the company provided an overview of its organization, various teams, the Corporate Risk team, the
internship opportunity, and the qualities and skills they generally seek in candidates.
My Tip: Pay close attention during the pre-placement session, as the information shared can be useful
throughout the selection process. It is a good idea to note down important points and, if there is a Q&A
session, make use of the opportunity to ask relevant and thoughtful questions.
Following the session, interested students were required to submit their applications through the JPMorgan
Chase Careers Portal using the link shared by the TPO. The submitted applications were then reviewed by
the company as part of the initial shortlisting process.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Candidates who were selected for the Online Assessment were informed about their shortlisting on 26 June
2026 at approximately 5:30 PM.

2. Online Assessment (122 shortlisted candidates)

Test Pattern: CCB Risk Test
MCQ Assessment - 30 Qtns - 45 Mins - 60 Marks
Section 1: 27 Qtns
Section 2: 3 Qtns
(The photo provided by ced before test)
The Online Assessment was conducted from home on 27 June 2026 using a company-designated proctored
platform. The assessment was remotely monitored through continuous video recording, while the screen was
locked to ensure that candidates could focus solely on the test. Tab switching and access to other
applications or browser windows were restricted throughout the assessment.
The test consisted of 30 questions with a +2/-1 marking scheme.

• 27 Questions: Quantitative Aptitude

• 3 Questions: Probability and Permutation & Combination

The aptitude section consisted of questions ranging from easy to moderate difficulty, with some questions
requiring a level of understanding comparable to basic CFA concepts. The questions were not extremely
difficult, but having a strong grasp of fundamental concepts was important for maintaining both speed and
accuracy.
For preparation, I referred to resources such as IndiaBix and BodhiPrep. I also followed the CareerRide
YouTube channel, which helped me strengthen my fundamentals and improve my approach to solving
aptitude questions efficiently.

3. Technical Interview Round 1 | 32 Students appeared for this round]

The interviews were conducted across 7 panels, each consisting of two interviewers. My interview lasted
approximately 20-25 minutes.
The interview started with "Tell me about yourself." I had prepared a 2-3 minute introduction covering my
background, skills, projects, achievements, and key points from my resume.
The first technical question was unexpectedly about Al-whether I knew about it, had used it, and had
worked on any Al-related projects. Since I had mentioned an Al project on my resume, I was able to explain
--- PAGE 3 ---
it confidently. I was then given a practical scenario: how AI could help employees or HR teams manage a
large number of emails and ensure that important emails are not missed. I could answer this well
because I had recently worked on a similar project. Even without prior experience, I would recommend
thinking through such real-world problems logically and explaining the system design clearly.
The next panelist asked system design questions, including how I would design a matrimonial website and
the architecture of an ATM system. Since I had listed Java in my technical skills, I was also asked questions
on Java fundamentals. I was asked some basic questions on python on the libraries that I used in my projects
and questions like why this specific library and not the other one.

4. Technical Interview Round 2 [15 shortlisted candidates]

My interview for this round lasted around 22 minutes. It started with a brief introduction, after which I was
asked detailed questions about my internship, including:

• What exactly did you work on during your internship?

• Explain the complete architecture of the project.

• Why did you choose a particular technology/system for the backend?

• How did you implement the frontend?

Since I had completed a Software Development internship, the interviewer focused on understanding both
my technical contribution and the reasoning behind the technologies I used.
I was then asked to write a SQL query, which was LeetCode Medium SQL problem. After that, I was
given a Python-based problem involving how to open and process a large Excel file of more than 10 GB,I
was aksed to write a code for it on pen and paper.
The interview then moved to my projects. I was asked to explain each project in detail. One of my Data
Analytics projects, Job Market Analysis, particularly caught the interviewer's attention. I was asked what
technologies and libraries I had used, why I had selected them, and to walk through the entire project step by
step. I was also asked about the errors or challenges I encountered during development and how I identified
and solved them.
Another important question was why, as an Electronics and Telecommunication Engineering student, I
had chosen to apply for this role. (EXTC students should be prepared for questions like this).
Towards the end, I was asked if I had any questions for the interviewers. I believe it is always a good
practice to ask relevant and thoughtful questions, as it shows genuine interest in the role and the
organization, so I made sure to ask a question as well.

5. HR Interview (10 shortlisted candidates)

The final HR round had around 10 shortlisted candidates and was easily the most relaxed and informal
interaction of the entire selection process. It began with a short introduction, followed by a conversation
focused mainly on my willingness to relocate and my overall personality and suitability for the role.
The HR also discussed practical aspects of the job, including shift timings, working hours, and whether I
would be comfortable working longer shifts. Unlike the earlier rounds, there was little emphasis on
--- PAGE 4 ---
technical questions, with the conversation primarily aimed at understanding the candidate on a personal and
professional level.
The HR interviews concluded at around 5:00 PM, and the final results were announced between 7:50 and
8:00 PM.
All 10 candidates who appeared for the HR round were selected and received internship offers.

journey.prep:
Resources and tips:

• Do relevant CFI courses on Finance and Risk from Coursera.

• Practice aptitude from Career Ride (Youtube) and IndiaBix regularly - please don't let this be the

cause of elimination from any company.

• Regularly read news from newspapers or from apps like TOI, The Economic Times or The Hindu - I

made a habit to read news daily from the start of my 6th semester while travelling.

• Read about relevant case studies related to risk mishaps like Global Financial Crisis of 2008,

Lehman Brothers, SVB, Credit Suisse, HDFC bank etc - you can include them in your answers if
you're confident enough. Sometimes, these topics can be asked by the interviewer too (I was asked
about Lehman Brothers in my JPMC CR round 2).

• Read and learn deeply about types of risks, their metrics, how the bank manages that kind of risk,

relevance to the role - I used ChatGPT and YouTube to study about these topics in great depth.

• Prepare about financial ratios and ratios important for a bank.

• Learn about derivatives and greeks.

• Revise Python and SQL.

• Try to make unique and tailored projects according to the role - it was one of the things that

impressed the interviewers most in my case.

• Also, go through the 100 puzzles from GFG and guesstimates as they can be asked (well they

weren't asked in CTC interview, but are asked frequently for CIB and CR interviews, and also in
other companies).

• In interviews, you can always write on the sheet provided to clearly communicate your thoughts.

My personal experience :)
Even though I had a tech background where I used to do DSA regularly, did an internship as an SDE intern,
and participated in hacks, I've always had this inclination towards finance and wanted to work in JPMC, I
was always so fascinated by it. I liked participating in case studies from my 1st year itself. Even though it
felt like an unreachable dream at the moment, I started doing CFI courses in my 6th semester alongside my
--- PAGE 6 ---
tech routine, and my minor in Financial and Strategic Management helped me as well - needless to say - it
was hectic as hell. But I kept on studying.
In July, JPMC came for the CIB and CR roles. Initially, I had just prepared for the CIB role, but
unfortunately, I could only reach till the 1st round. Then, I had my CR interview the next day, but I got
eliminated after the 2nd round. I was really heartbroken since I got rejected by JPMC for 2 consecutive days
and gave up on it.
Heartbroken, I resumed preparing for tech roles. I got rejected by companies for a whole month - sometimes
I knew the reason why I didn't get ahead, and sometimes I didn't even realise why. At first, I used to get
really anxious, sad and tense daily, but then over time, I just surrendered my fate to God and kept on
working hard and studying regularly.
Obviously, I took a break from finance since I was prepping for tech roles. But then, out of nowhere, JPMC
announced it is coming back for a completely new role. It felt like a second chance at redeeming myself.
From that day onwards, I started preparing for it, deep dived into the JD, prepared tailored projects for the
role, learned about different types of risks and their metrics, historic case studies, revised finance concepts
and also did mock interviews with Claude and GPT - do it with your friends too.
Finally, I would just like to say that you might feel depressed and overwhelmed when you see your friends
and peers get placed, but I would stress on this - LUCK plays a very important factor. But, Luck can only
help you in things like getting a good panel, getting easier questions in OAs etc., other than that, you always
need to be prepared to jump and take the opportunity that comes your way - so don't ponder much on things
like why isn't luck on my side etc and just keep on grinding and studying hard - because the day Luck is on
your side, it's your job to shine the brightest!!
All the best guys, keep faith in yourselves and stay resilient, you can do it!!

Since the role was open to all branches, there might be 250 or 300+ resume applicants. One consistent thing
I noticed across both JPMC CIB and JPMC CTC roles were, people who had 12th marks below 80%, got
out in this round itself. Apart from this, make sure to at least have your CGPA above 7.5, but preferably try
to keep it above 8 for other companies as well.
Tailor your resume according to the role- try to align your projects as closely to the role as possible, try to
make some projects related to risk and finance, include relevant courses and certifications, put keywords
according to the JD and ofc don't mention anything you won't be able to justify as ANY of the keywords or
anything you put in the resume can be asked in the interview.
Lastly, make sure to have a good ATS score above 70 of your resume on Resume Worded.
We had to apply both on superset and JPMC website, so try to fill out the application as soon as possible.
There were some people who filled the application late and didn't get shortlisted for the test, as JPMC
reviews applications on a rolling basis.

2. Online Test [ 120 students shortlisted for the online test ]

--- PAGE 2 ---
The online test was from home. The pattern was the same as the CIB test. There were 4 sections, no negative
marking and total 45 questions in 45 mins of total 45 marks.
Section 1 - Corporate Finance and Financial Account (10 gs) - Basic finance questions based on ratios,
gross profit, profit and loss.
Section 2 - Market Awareness (10 gs) - Included questions on current affairs, budget, recent laws on taxes
and finances, and some basic macroeconomics logical questions. Make sure to regularly read the news.
Section 3 - Quantitative Aptitude (15 gs) - The most time consuming section. The questions were of
medium level based on topics like probability, cards, PNC, speed, profit loss, percentage etc.
Section 4 - English Usage (10 gs) - Easiest section. Basic grammar based fill in the blanks, comprehension
type questions, order the sentences type qs, and two bar graph based questions.

3. Group Discussion Round [ 29 students appeared for the GD]

The shortlisted candidates list came one night before the interviews around 9 pm.
A GD round was declared the night before. No topic was given for the GD, unlike the CIB role where a
topic is mostly given beforehand.
The rounds began at around 10.30 am the next day. There were 4 groups made with 7 - 8 people in each
group and 2 panels in total - so each panel conducted 2 GDs.
Each group was given a different topic. In my group, there were 7 people. The topic given to us was - "Is AI
making college degrees less relevant and valuable?"
Try to speak as soon as possible, as in that way, you can put the unique points forward first. I spoke second
in the GD. Make sure to speak confidently, try to use real life examples and numbers or stats if possible to
back your points. Don't try to interrupt or overpower others, and even if you disagree with someone, do it
politely. (4 people got selected for the next round from my group)

4. Interview Round 1[14 people appeared for this round]

Since there were 2 panels, each panel interviewed 7 students.
Through other students, I came to know that my panel was grilling hard based on the resume, so I kept on
revising my projects until my chance came.
(I'll try to keep my experience as detailed as possible to help you guys - my round lasted for about 40-45
mins so it's gonna be pretty longg !!)
My chance came just after the lunch break, and I entered confidently with a smile on my face and greeted
the interviewers (a sir and a ma'am) and shook their hands - this always sets a good impression from the
start!
They introduced themselves and asked how I was feeling, how was the GD and then asked me for my
introduction. Make sure to have an interesting and a story like introduction which could justify why being an
engineering student, you wanna go into finance and risk dept.
I was then asked about my first project on credit risk analysis, how did I make it, from where did I get the
idea (sir seemed very interested in the project), since he knew obviously things like these aren't taught to us
--- PAGE 3 ---
in college, so he wanted to know from WHERE did I think about this project- to which I replied that I went
for a case study in another college and made some friends there and asked them about the topics being
taught to them in finance and took an interest in risk related topics, so I asked them for materials and made
this project with the help of Al after learning the concepts. Things like these also help them understand that
you have good communication and interpersonal skills. I was then asked for a deep dive into the project. The
interviewers seemed impressed and mentioned that my project was very identical to the work people
actually do in credit risk.
Similarly, sir asked me about my 2nd project - which was based on portfolio risk analysis using Modern
Portfolio Theory. I was asked about the aim and overview of the project - I supported my answers by making
the Risk vs Return graph of my project on a sheet and explained the figure in great detail. The interviewers
seemed satisfied with my explanations.
Then ma'am went through my skills section and asked whether I knew about financial statements and asked
"Which statement should a bank see of a company before giving out a loan to them" - I then talked about
the 3 financial statements, how they connect, how the answer should be cash flow statement and not the PnL
statement as CF statement shows the actual liquidity, then threw in some concepts about how a company can
be solvent but illiquid etc. It's important to throw in some extra things you know related to the questions
asked as they always help you out!
I was then asked if I followed the markets, I said at a macroeconomic level, yes. Then I was asked how the
war is affecting the economy, repo rates, inflation, role of RBI etc. I then asked them if I could also explain
how change in interest rates affect banks, to which they happily replied "Sure!', so I talked about Asset
Liability Management and the scenarios when assets reprice faster than liabilities and vice versa and what
effect they have on the NII in the short term, then I was asked some follow up questions as well.
Then I was asked to explain any one kind of risk. I took up market risk, coz my project already included
credit risk, and explained what market risk is, how it can affect banks, metrics of market risk like VaR and
ES.
Then, I was asked if I knew about derivatives- to which I said yes, and then I was asked about options. So I
explained what options are, call and put options with examples. This led on to a conversation on Greeks.
Then sir asked me, what experience I have in tech, to which I replied that I have experience in development,
my primary language is Java in which I do DSA and I talked about my internship as an SDE intern where I
had to work with a completely new tech stack in NEXT/NEST Js. So then I talked about how the tech stacks
don't matter if we know the underlying concepts clearly. Then I said that I know Python at a medium level
since I don't code in it regularly, as my primary language is Java, then talked about how most of the
concepts are pretty similar with some differences such as in OOPS, to which ma'am quickly asked me to
explain the difference in Java and Python OOPS so I talked about multiple inheritance, diamond problem,
MRO in python etc. I was also asked about the difference between linear and logistic regression.
Then sir asked me, how did I take an interest in finance, on which I talked about my background that I've
always had this balance between tech and finance since my cousins are all in tech and my father is an MBA
graduate, how I started doing case study competitions from my 1st year and gradually learned more and
more about finance by taking up my minor in Financial and Strategic Management and through some CFI
Courses. I also talked about how hectic my 6th semester had become due to daily DSA, dev, my internship,
--- PAGE 4 ---
college and finance courses all at once, but I learned how to manage my time. I talked about how my parents
trade in stock markets and lightened the convo by bringing in how my parents get sad if they don't get
allotted any IPO and talked about some recent IPOs and the interviewers smiled and shook their heads as
well.
At the end I was asked where I lived. Then I asked them questions about the AI tools being used in JPMC
and how they make work easier for the employees and how the risk team helps the main IB and front office
teams.

5. Interview Round 2 [6 people appeared for this round]

This round was stricter and harder than the previous round, as in this round, most of the questions were
scenario based and not resume based, as they wanted to know if we understood concepts clearly. There were
2 interviewers, a sir and a ma'am. I was first asked why I wanted this role.
Then ma'am grilled me on liquidity risk, so I talked about liquidity risk, how it's important to a bank, ratios
like LCR and NSFR, on which I was further grilled on the ratios and topics like High Quality Liquid Assets,
where they are present in a bank's balance sheet etc.
Then I was asked which type of risk is the most relevant in today's time, I related it to the geopolitical
scenario and said Market Risk and Interest Rate Risk and explained the reasons why.
The next question was - "If I were to take a bond from the Mumbai Airport, what factors would I assess
before taking itạ so I talked about secured bonds, interest rate factors, yield etc.
Then sir asked me to do a deep dive into my DCF Project. Be sure to explain it deeply from start to finish in
this manner:

• what the company is about

• how their balance sheets are, is it a cash heavy, loan heavy company

• how you made the assumptions for projections for the components of FCFF, explain the components

too and what they tell you about the company, for example what a negative WC would tell you about
the company etc, then arrive at the FCFF

• then talk about the whole derivation process of Cost Of Debt, Cost of Equity - talk about how you

got the beta, what you infer from it, CAPM model - then arrive on WACC

• then arrive at Enterprise Value, Equity Value, Intrinsic Price of share derived in your model vs the

actual share price and your recommendation for the share and why.
You should be able to talk about the whole flow of DCF while explaining and justifying your steps and
talking about the formulae used, in a very clear and orderly manner.
I was then asked if I knew about Comparables method of valuation, so I explained about that method, then I
talked about ratios like P/E, EV/EBITDA etc. and how different types of companies would use different
kinds of ratios based on their profitability. I was then asked about EBITDA, debt related ratios like
Debt/EBITDA, D/E etc.
I was then asked about a case study of mine where we won first place and what we did in it.
--- PAGE 5 ---
The interview ended with me asking them questions like "What skills should I learn so that I become the
best version of myself while joining JPMC if I get selectediằ

6. HR Round [ 3 people appeared for this round]

This round was pretty chill and relaxing, the HR ma'am was very sweet and asked me how my previous
rounds were, why this role, why JPMC, as being a CSE student, I could've gotten some other tech company
as well, and how my interest in finance grew. Then I was asked a scenario based question, "Tell me about a
time where you made a mistake and you had to apologize for itẠạThen I was asked questions like where I
lived, if my schooling and everything was done in Mumbai itself etc. The interview ended with HR ma'am
saying "All the best, results would be declared at the EOD."
About an hour after the HR Rounds, the result was announced and 2 people got selected for the role.

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
Resources and tips:

• Do relevant CFI courses on Finance and Risk from Coursera.

• Practice aptitude from Career Ride (Youtube) and IndiaBix regularly - please don't let this be the

cause of elimination from any company.

• Regularly read news from newspapers or from apps like TOI, The Economic Times or The Hindu - I

made a habit to read news daily from the start of my 6th semester while travelling.

• Read about relevant case studies related to risk mishaps like Global Financial Crisis of 2008,

Lehman Brothers, SVB, Credit Suisse, HDFC bank etc - you can include them in your answers if
you're confident enough. Sometimes, these topics can be asked by the interviewer too (I was asked
about Lehman Brothers in my JPMC CR round 2).

• Read and learn deeply about types of risks, their metrics, how the bank manages that kind of risk,

relevance to the role - I used ChatGPT and YouTube to study about these topics in great depth.

• Prepare about financial ratios and ratios important for a bank.

• Learn about derivatives and greeks.

• Revise Python and SQL.

• Try to make unique and tailored projects according to the role - it was one of the things that

impressed the interviewers most in my case.

• Also, go through the 100 puzzles from GFG and guesstimates as they can be asked (well they

weren't asked in CTC interview, but are asked frequently for CIB and CR interviews, and also in
other companies).

• In interviews, you can always write on the sheet provided to clearly communicate your thoughts.

My personal experience :)
Even though I had a tech background where I used to do DSA regularly, did an internship as an SDE intern,
and participated in hacks, I've always had this inclination towards finance and wanted to work in JPMC, I
was always so fascinated by it. I liked participating in case studies from my 1st year itself. Even though it
felt like an unreachable dream at the moment, I started doing CFI courses in my 6th semester alongside my
--- PAGE 6 ---
tech routine, and my minor in Financial and Strategic Management helped me as well - needless to say - it
was hectic as hell. But I kept on studying.
In July, JPMC came for the CIB and CR roles. Initially, I had just prepared for the CIB role, but
unfortunately, I could only reach till the 1st round. Then, I had my CR interview the next day, but I got
eliminated after the 2nd round. I was really heartbroken since I got rejected by JPMC for 2 consecutive days
and gave up on it.
Heartbroken, I resumed preparing for tech roles. I got rejected by companies for a whole month - sometimes
I knew the reason why I didn't get ahead, and sometimes I didn't even realise why. At first, I used to get
really anxious, sad and tense daily, but then over time, I just surrendered my fate to God and kept on
working hard and studying regularly.
Obviously, I took a break from finance since I was prepping for tech roles. But then, out of nowhere, JPMC
announced it is coming back for a completely new role. It felt like a second chance at redeeming myself.
From that day onwards, I started preparing for it, deep dived into the JD, prepared tailored projects for the
role, learned about different types of risks and their metrics, historic case studies, revised finance concepts
and also did mock interviews with Claude and GPT - do it with your friends too.
Finally, I would just like to say that you might feel depressed and overwhelmed when you see your friends
and peers get placed, but I would stress on this -

journey.prep:
The biggest thing that helped me get selected was understanding concepts rather than simply
memorising definitions. I made sure I knew my resume thoroughly and could explain every project and
skill mentioned on it. For the technical rounds, having strong fundamentals in risk management, corporate
finance, accounting, derivatives, fixed income, and macroeconomics was extremely useful. I also tried to
connect concepts to real-world banking examples and explain the logic behind my answers instead of giving
textbook definitions. For the GD, presence of mind and current affairs were extremely important. I
would recommend having a strong understanding of basic macroeconomics and keeping up with financial
news. You do not need to speak 10 times-3-4 meaningful entries are enough if each contribution adds
something new to the discussion. Listen carefully to what the panel is actually asking and focus on building
the discussion rather than simply naming schemes or facts. In my case, I focused on concepts such as the
trade deficit, dollar demand, FIl outflows, safe-haven assets, interest rates and geopolitical events. I
was also fortunate to have watched a video on the Indian Rupee just two days before the GD, which helped
me significantly. During the interviews, I tried to stay confident, maintain a positive attitude, ask clarifying
questions when necessary, and reason through questions instead of panicking if I did not immediately know
the answer. One mistake I made was not preparing questions to ask the interviewers beforehand; I would
strongly recommend preparing 2-3 thoughtful questions because it takes very little time and can leave a
strong final impression. Overall, know your resume, understand the fundamentals, stay updated with
markets, communicate clearly, and focus on quality rather than quantity of answers.
The following are the resources I used during my preparation. I will also attach my detailed list of the risk
topics I studied for this role separately.

Silicon Valley Bank Case

• Market Awareness / Current Affairs: Regular financial and market news

• Quantitative Aptitude: IndiaBix + 1-2 CAT previous-year papers

• Resume / ATS: Resume Worded

• Concept clarification: ChatGPT / Claude

• Indian Rupee / GD

• Resume (my resume is very basic, refer other resumes too)

Feel free to contact me anytime if you have any doubts regarding the preparation or interview
process.

PPT - 31/7/2026

Round 1: Resume Shortlisting - 4/8/2026

Round 2: Online Assessment (Online) - 5/8/2026

Round 3: Group Discussion- 11/8/2026

Round 4: Technical Interview 1 - 11/8/2026

Round 5 : Technical Interview 2 - 11/8/2026

Round 6: HR Interview - 11/8/2026

1. Resume Shortlisting [250+ students applied]

More than 250 students applied, out of which 118 students were shortlisted for the next round. The basic
eligibility criterion was a CGPA of 7.0+. I would recommend maintaining a CGPA of 8.0+, as this makes
you eligible for almost every company during placements, while 8.5+ is a very strong position. For the
resume, I would recommend maintaining an ATS score of 70+ as a safe target and ensuring that the resume
is relevant to the job description. I used Resume Worded to check and improve my ATS score rather than
relying on random ATS-checking websites, and I would recommend using it as well. My resume was
average overall, but I had specifically tried to make it ATS-friendly and included relevant projects and skills
aligned with the role, which I believe helped me get shortlisted. There was no interview or test in this round;
the main focus was on meeting the eligibility criteria and getting through the resume screening. My main
advice is to maintain a good CGPA, keep the resume to one page, use relevant keywords from the job
description, and highlight projects that demonstrate skills related to the role.

2. Online Assessment (Online) |118 students shortlisted]

The Online Assessment was attempted by 118 shortlisted students and consisted of 45 questions in 45
minutes for a total of 45 marks, with four sections: Corporate Finance & Financial Accounting (10
questions), Market Awareness (10 questions), Quantitative Aptitude (15 questions), and English Usage
(10 questions). There was no negative marking, with 1 mark awarded for every correct answer. The
Corporate Finance and Accounting section was easy to moderate and required a good understanding of
--- PAGE 2 ---
fundamentals such as financial statements, cash flows, and basic corporate finance concepts. Market
Awareness was the most difficult section, ranging from medium to difficult, and required both general
market awareness and some niche financial knowledge; I would strongly recommend staying updated with
the latest finance and market news through regular current-affairs reading. Quantitative Aptitude was easy
to moderate, and preparation from IndiaBix is more than sufficient for the level of most questions; I also
solved 1-2 CAT previous-year papers, and a few questions in the test were directly similar to questions
from those sources. The English Usage section was very easy and did not require separate preparation.
Overall, the test was quite time-consuming, and I had only around 3-4 minutes remaining when I
submitted it, so time management is extremely important. For preparation, I would recommend
strengthening basic Corporate Finance and Accounting concepts, regularly following financial and market
news, practising Quant from IndiaBix along with a few CAT-level questions, and focusing on speed rather
than spending too much time on any individual question.

3. Group Discussion [ 29 students were shortlisted after OA ]

After the Online Assessment, 29 students were shortlisted for the Group Discussion, and the shortlist
was released just one day before the GD. Unlike investment banking roles where the topic may
sometimes be provided beforehand, the topic for this GD was given on the spot, so I had prepared
mainly with the interview rounds in mind. There were 8 candidates in my panel and 2 panelists
conducting the discussion. At the beginning, the panelists asked whether we were more comfortable
discussing the Indian economy or the US economy. I took the initiative and said that I was comfortable
with the Indian economy and asked the other candidates about their preference. Since no one objected,
we decided to go with the Indian economy, which worked in my favour because I had a strong
understanding of macroeconomics. The topic given was "How is the Indian Rupee performing currently,
what affects it, and discuss its impact." The panel was primarily testing whether candidates understood
the fundamental factors affecting the rupee, such as trade deficit, foreign investment, interest rates, dollar
demand, and global events, rather than simply naming government schemes. I made around 3-4 entries,
but focused on making each one meaningful and building on the discussion. My first entry focused on
the trade deficit and India's dependence on the US dollar. In my second entry, I discussed how during
periods of geopolitical uncertainty, investors tend to move towards safe-haven assets such as US
Treasury bonds, which can lead to foreign investors withdrawing investments from emerging markets
such as India, increasing demand for dollars. I then connected this to the rupee, explaining that when
dollar demand increases while dollar supply is relatively insufficient, the dollar strengthens against the
rupee; combined with India's trade deficit, this puts additional pressure on the rupee. A major lesson for
me was that understanding the underlying economic concepts is more important than simply memorising
schemes or current-affairs facts. Several candidates discussed government schemes, but that was not
really what the panel was testing. I also made one small mistake during my first entry by looking directly
at the panelist instead of addressing the group, but I noticed her reaction and immediately corrected
myself; interestingly, she later mentioned that she had noticed this and appreciated my presence of mind.
I was also told during my second technical interview that my GD contributions had helped build the
framework for the discussion. My biggest recommendation for a GD is do not speak just for the sake of
speaking around 3-4 strong entries are enough if each one adds a new perspective or builds on an
existing point. Be clear about what the panel is actually asking, understand basic macroeconomics, stay
updated with current events, listen to the other candidates, and most importantly, maintain your presence
of mind throughout the discussion.
--- PAGE 3 ---

4. Technical Interview 1 [14 students were shortlisted]

After the Group Discussion, 14 students were shortlisted for Technical Interview 1. There were two
interviewers, one from Liquidity Risk and the other from Credit Risk. I entered the room confidently,
greeted both interviewers with a smile, and tried to maintain a positive and conversational atmosphere from
the beginning. One of the interviewers asked me about my favourite risk domain. Since my resume included
a Credit Risk project, I answered that I found both Credit Risk and Liquidity Risk interesting, which
allowed me to connect with the areas of expertise of both interviewers. The Liquidity Risk interviewer then
asked what I found interesting about liquidity risk, so I explained the concept with a banking example and
connected it to the Lehman Brothers collapse. I also tried to use realistic figures and examples involving
large banks wherever possible rather than keeping my answers purely theoretical. She then realised that we
had not started with my resume and asked me to walk through it. I had a DCF valuation model of Apple on
my resume, and the Credit Risk interviewer asked me to explain it in detail. I explained the complete
valuation process, including Cost of Equity, Cost of Debt, WACC, and the significance of each
component. They were satisfied with my explanation and then asked whether I knew other valuation
techniques. I mentioned that I had heard about LBO valuation, after which they asked me about peer
comparison/comparable companies analysis. I clarified whether they meant peer comparison and then
explained it using examples, including Apple and companies from different industries. I explained that
companies should be compared with businesses having similar operating models and customer segments
rather than simply comparing companies because they sell similar products; for example, Apple would be
better compared with companies such as Samsung than with a company whose business model and
consumer segment are fundamentally different. They liked the answer and then asked me to explain the
basic balance sheet of a bank, including where loans and customer deposits appear. I was then asked a
macroeconomics question: what does the RBI do with interest rates during inflation, and why? I
explained that inflation essentially means rising prices or "mehngai", and walked through the mechanism in
simple terms: when inflation is high, the RBI can increase the repo rate, which makes borrowing more
expensive, reduces loan demand and overall spending, and eventually helps bring demand closer to the
available supply, thereby controlling inflation. I made sure to explain the entire chain rather than simply
saying "RBI increases rates during inflation." The interview then moved towards technology, where I was
asked whether I knew about LLMs. I mentioned that I had two LLM-related projects in my technical
portfolio and briefly explained my financial-literacy project using Agentic Al, although it was not
included on my resume. Another question was "When does the seller of a call option make money?" My
approach was to reason it out rather than immediately quote a formula. I explained that I had mostly
approached options from the buyer's perspective: a call-option buyer benefits when the underlying price
rises; therefore, the seller benefits when the buyer's position loses value, meaning the option expires out of
the money or its value falls sufficiently relative to the premium received. The interviewer was impressed by
the reasoning-based approach. At the end, I was asked whether I had any questions. One mistake I made
was not preparing questions beforehand. I eventually came up with a question on the spot about how a
global bank such as J.P. Morgan manages regulatory compliance across different countries, particularly
when regulations from authorities such as the RBI and the US Federal Reserve differ. However, I would
strongly recommend preparing at least 2-3 thoughtful questions beforehand, as it takes only a few
minutes and can leave a strong final impression. Overall, the biggest lesson from this interview was to
understand the fundamentals deeply rather than memorising definitions. If you can explain concepts
logically, connect them to real-world examples, and remain confident when you do not immediately know
an answer, the interview becomes much more conversational
--- PAGE 4 ---

5. Technical Interview 2 [6 students shortlisted]

After Technical Interview 1, 6 students were shortlisted for Technical Interview 2. There were two
interviewers, and interestingly, they were the same panelists who had conducted my Group Discussion.
This helped because they already had some context about my performance in the GD, and the interview
gradually became quite conversational as I became more comfortable with them. The interview started with
the usual "Tell me about yourself', after which they cross-questioned me on my resume, particularly my
Credit Risk project, and asked me to explain what credit risk means. They then noticed that I had
mentioned Financial Derivatives in my skills and began questioning me on derivatives. I started with the
basic definition that derivatives are financial instruments whose value is derived from an underlying asset,
and then explained the four major types: forwards, futures, options, and swaps. I explained that forwards
are generally OTC contracts, then moved to futures and discussed their exchange-traded nature and
concepts such as margin calls. I then explained options, highlighting the key difference that the buyer has
the right but not the obligation to exercise the contract, and finally explained swaps using an interest-rate
swap as an example. They were satisfied with the explanation and then asked whether I knew about option
Greeks. I explained the major Greeks and, in particular, connected Delta and Gamma to the concepts of
speed and distance/time from physics. This was one of the answers that seemed to impress them the most
because I was not simply giving textbook definitions but connecting financial concepts with concepts I
already understood from another domain. They then asked me about the banking balance sheet, specifically
where loans appear. I first asked a clarifying question about whether they meant loans taken by the bank or
loans given by the bank, and after they clarified that they meant loans given by the bank, I explained their
treatment on the balance sheet. The interview then moved to the fixed-income market, where they asked
how bonds and interest rates are related. I explained the inverse relationship between bond prices and
interest rates with examples and discussed why changes in interest rates affect existing fixed-income
securities. Towards the end, the interview became much more casual, and the interviewers asked me to
loosen up and tell them how I would introduce myself if they met me in a social setting. I spoke about my
interests outside academics, including football, and this helped make the conversation more natural. Finally,
they asked me why I had chosen this role, which brought the interview to an end. My biggest takeaway
from this round was that interviewers can move from very technical questions to casual questions very
quickly, so candidates should be comfortable with both. More importantly, do not just memorise
definitions-try to connect concepts to real-world examples or ideas from other subjects, because
demonstrating how you think can make a much stronger impression than simply reproducing textbook
answers.
HR interview [3 students appeared]
After Technical Interview 2, 3 students appeared for the HR Interview. It was a short and relaxed round.
The interviewer went through my resume and asked why I wanted the role, to which I explained my interest
in both finance and technology and how this role lies at the intersection of both. She also asked where I
stay and one behavioural question: "Tell me about a decision you made that people did not like." I gave a
brief example from my experience as Head of Operations at E-Cell, where I sometimes had to ask
teammates to stay until work was completed, highlighting my sense of ownership and responsibility. The
interview then ended, and the results were announced around 45 minutes later, with 2 out of the 3 students
selected.
--- PAGE 5 ---

1) Pre Placement Talk - 24 June.

2) Resume Screening - 26 June.

3) OA - 27 June.

4) Interviews - 2 July.

1. Pre Placement Talk] [300 + students attended]

The pre placement talk for JPMC was conducted online via a zoom meeting on 24th June in the afternoon.
The hiring team consisted of HR, people from Corporate Risk, and also from the CIB department. All of
them briefed us in depth on the work JPMC does. It was a very informative session.
I would recommend paying utmost attention to what each and every person is saying in the PPT, and make
notes if possible. At the end of the PPT, we were allowed to ask questions if any. Please refrain from asking
questions related to the hiring process. Ask questions related to the job role, and only if you genuinely have
questions. Do not ask random and obvious questions. As many students were raising their hands in the zoom
meeting, only a few students were allowed to ask questions due to time constraints.

2. Resume Screening] [ Approx 150 - 200 students applied for Banking Role. ]

On 24th June itself, we had to apply on the JPMC website with our details and fill a google form. The
process of resume screening is a huge bottleneck so make sure your resume is tailored as per the role and
relevant. Allot enough time to prepare your resume. Do not blindly apply with your Tech resume. As seniors
have told, check your resume score on the Resume Worded website, and try to take it above 60. Mine was
somewhere between 65 and 70.
Note - I will recommend really giving enough time to prepare the resume for this role, make sure there are
no special characters in your resume, no mistakes and errors. I will suggest if you are keen on applying for
--- PAGE 2 ---
JPMC, prepare a non tech profile resume well beforehand, because the application process might take long
and has to be completed within 1 day.

3. [OA] [66-67 students were shortlisted to give the OA. ]

The shortlist for OA was given at 5:30 pm on the day before the OA was scheduled. The pattern for the
OA was given to us.
Section 1: Corporate Finance and Financial Accounting. 10 Qns
Section 2: Market Awareness 10 Qns
Section 3 : Quantitative Aptitude 15 Qns
Section 4 : English Usage.
Our OA was scheduled at 10:30 am, in the morning. It was online from home, on a third party platform
fully proctored. Section 1 was medium difficulty overall, u need to prepare Financial Statements, basic
accounting and ratios well. Section 2 was tough, you need to prepare current affairs, currently ongoing
financial events well. Section 3 was easy to medium, simple aptitude questions. You need to prepare from
IndiaBix website. Section 4 was simple English, so it was a scoring and easy one.

4. [Group Discussion] [55 students were shortlisted for this round.]

The shortlist for GD was shared with us at around 8:30 pm on 1st July. Hence, it is important to keep
preparing for interviews even if you have no guarantee that you will be shortlisted. Due to heavy rains,
the JPMC hiring team decided to conduct an online selection process this year. However, all students
were supposed to be present on campus. 55 students were divided into 6 groups of approx 9 people in
each group. The GD was conducted on a zoom meeting. The topic for GD was given to us along with the
shortlist. The topic for GD was - suppose you are the CEO of a company and due to certain situations,
the lead time and cost of your shipping has gone up, how will you approach this problem. It wasn't word
to word like this, I am just giving you a basic idea of what it was about.
My group had 9 people and our GD started at 9:45 am on 2nd July. Since it was an online GD, everything
was structured, we had to raise our hands in order to speak and put forth our points. The panel consisted
of 2 people sitting in the JPMC office and was mainly moderated by the VP. The following 3 questions
were introduced to facilitate the GD:

1) How to approach the on paper losses that the company will bear

in this situation 2) Suppose a supplier needs your help in this situation, will you help them.

3) Once the

situation is eased, how will you approach to get back on track.
In my panel, most of us spoke a lot on each and every question being introduced by the panelists, the
moderator praised all of us at the end of the GD. I will suggest that you take 3-4 good entries in the GD
to get noticed. I took around 4-5 entries in the GD. Due to anxiety, I fumbled a lot while speaking,
however I was able to put forth my points strongly. Your points should not just repeat what has already
been said by someone else, instead it should add on to it or give a different angle to the situation being
discussed.
--- PAGE 3 ---

5. Interview Round, [29 students were shortlisted for interviews.]

My interview was scheduled at 12 p.m, however I got a call at around 11:30 from the interviewer, asking if I
could join the zoom meeting immediately. I immediately said yes and asked the TPO coordinators who
arranged a cabin for me.
The interviewer asked me to introduce myself. As soon as I was done introducing, he asked me apart from
M&A advisory what else Investment Banks do. I answered - Trading and Brokerage, Asset Management and
Capital Market stuff (ECM and DCM). He immediately asked to explain what Asset Management does. I
explained to him in simple terms about Asset Management. At this point he suddenly asked me the
difference between Asset Management and Private Equity. Now this was the point where I had to be super
careful, I wasn't aware much about Private Equity, and he really found it out fast enough. He suddenly
started asking me "Are you sure ?", "Is that really True?" to confuse me. Finally he explained to me briefly
about the exact difference.
The next question was "If you are a manager in asset management, what metrics will you use to determine
performanceằ
ẠạI replied with IRR and elaborated on two types of IRRS. He gave me a scenario related to that
and asked me to solve for both the types of IRRs. I was able to correctly calculate around 50-60% of the
sum, to which he seemed to be satisfied
Later he asked me to explain the happenings in the stock market in the last 6 months. This was a general
question so if you keep track of markets and basic news, you should be able to answer it correctly.
Lastly he gave me a simple sum: a person goes from A to B at 5 km/hr and returns from B to A at 10km/hr,
calculate the Avg speed. It took me 2 - 3 attempts to finally solve this question, however in each attempt my
thought process was correct, so he guided me through the question when necessary. I was able to solve the
question correctly in the end.
The interview ended with him asking me to drop off from the call without asking any questions.
Note - This interview was completely different from typical round 1 interviews being conducted for JPMC
banking roles, as you may read in other students' documents. The key to cracking interviews in such
scenarios is to talk out your thought process because that tells the interviewer if you are at least thinking in
the right direction, even though you are not able to reach the final answer.
Do not lose hope even if your interview goes tough. For many students, 2-3 technical rounds were taken
before advancing to the HR round. In my case, I was directly shortlisted for the HR round without any more
technical rounds. Do not lose hope or leave for home without having full confirmation that you are out of the
process. Always be ready and keep a positive mindset.
One more thing I will suggest during interviews - if the interviewer is correcting you and explaining
something to you, always listen to them positively and acknowledge them for the knowledge that they have
given to you.
--- PAGE 4 ---

6. HR Round] [10 students appeared for this round.]

It was around 3:45 pm and I finally decided to sit and apply for other tech companies that were coming to
the campus. Suddenly a list of students was declared and my name was in it. The HR round was again
conducted online via zoom meeting.
The round started with greetings. The HR Madam introduced herself and then asked me to introduce
myself. Later she asked me to explain any one of my projects. No further questions were asked regarding
my project. Then she asked me "If you are hiring for analysts / interns, what 3 qualities will you look for
in themại This is a standard HR question and there is no right / wrong answer. I answered the questions
and she seemed happy with it, because she extended more on the qualities that I mentioned. Later I was
given the chance to ask questions if any, so I asked 2 questions: one about the culture at JPMC, and
another about the attitude of interns which gets them hired for a full time role.
Note - In HR rounds, always be expressive and positive when you speak. Try not to talk about any
negative stuff, as it could give a bad impression about you. HR Rounds are generally very chill, you just
need to be yourself and be polite. Always greet the other person at the start and end of the interview.
The results were declared after about 45 minutes and all 10 students were selected.

Out of all the applications received, 67 students were shortlisted for the next round, the Online
Assessment (OA). This stage is often underestimated, so it is highly recommended to prepare your
resume well in advance.
A good ATS score alone does not guarantee a resume shortlist. Although the minimum CGPA criterion

Do include one or two finance-related projects, relevant internship experience, participation in case
competitions (especially finalist or winning positions), and any relevant certification courses you have
completed.
Once the company shares the registration link after the PPT, make sure to submit your application as
early as possible.

2. Online Test

Our OA was held online from home. It consisted of 45 MCQS, with 1 mark for each question. The total
duration was 45 minutes, so speed and accuracy are very important.
Corporate Finance & Accounting (10 Questions):
This section had basic finance and accounting questions. Topics included inflation, repo rate, financial
statements, financial ratios, bonds (callable and put bonds), GDP, and other fundamental concepts. If
your basics are clear, this section is quite manageable.
Market Awareness (10 Questions):
This section was very random and mostly based on current affairs related to finance and business.
Reading financial news regularly and staying updated with recent developments can help, but many
questions are from the if you know it, you know it category.
Quantitative Aptitude (15 Questions):
The questions were similar to those on IndiaBix. AP & GP, Permutations & Combinations, Probability,
Ratios, Profit & Loss, Time & Work, Speed, Time & Distance, Mixtures, SI-CI.
English (10 Questions):
This section included 2 reading comprehension questions, several sentence correction and
--- PAGE 2 ---
grammar-based questions, along with vocabulary and basic English usage. There were around 2
questions based on bar graphs or pie charts. It was pretty straightforward.
For me, English and Quant were the easiest sections. Finance can also be a good scoring section if your
basics are clear. However, Market Awareness was the toughest, as it is largely based on current affairs

questions, where you have more control over your performance. Also, make sure to practice Quant

approximately 2x longer for around two months, and shipping costs have increased, affecting financial
metrics. As the CEO, how would you tackle this situation?"
We were divided into 6 panels, with each pane; consisting of around 9 students. Around 20 minutes
were allocated, but this wasn't a typical GD. We were asked specific questions and were expected to
express our views only on those questions. Hence, it is important to understand the GD topic in depth,
research it thoroughly, and also think about the possible subtopics or follow-up questions that could be
asked based on the main topic.
Try to speak at least 2 to 3 times during the discussion, and make sure your points stay relevant to the
topic. Be clear and confident, and support your arguments with statistics or insights from reputed firms
such as BCG or Mckinsey wherever possible. Be civil throughout the discussion, listen to others, and
avoid trying to dominate the conversation.
Out of 55, 29 students were selected for the next round (Interview).

1. Interviews

There are 2 interviews, mainly focussing on your finance knowledge. Know your resume
inside out, and be thorough with your basics in accounting.
Round 1 (Around 45-50 minutes):

1. Tell me about yourself

2. Do you know about the 3 financial statements?

3. What is depreciation? Impact on income statement. He then gave several scenarios and asked about

4. Any recent activities going on in the market? (IPO: its share price, market cap, ratios)

--- PAGE 3 ---
Here I also told him about Anthropic filing for an IPO draft recently, and discussed this in length. He
