research and awareness of the market.

5. What is repo rate? How is it related to inflation? What is the current repo and reverse repo rate?

6. What does an Investment Banker do?

7. What is India's GDP? (Answer in crores)

8. What is Sensex and Nifty? How to calculate them.

9. What is PE ratio? Should it be high or low? Explain

10. What is Enterprise value? Formula. Why do we add debt and subtract cash to find EV.

11. Mental Math Qns: (do without pen paper)

• Square root of 0.1

• 78*83

• Average speed question (formula is 2xy/x+y)

12. Any questions? (Prepare 3-4 questions beforehand, and frame it in an interesting

way, shouldn't be a forced question)
My Round 2 was a cultural fit interview with the Vice President for the CRG role (25
minutes)

1. Introduce, why investment banking?

2. Walk through your DCF project. Explain WACC, beta

3. For which sector do we find beta values greater than 1?

4. When to not use DCF?

5. Other ways to perform valuation of a company? (Precedent transaction, Comparable Multiples, LBO)

The recruitment process consisted of the following stages:

• Pre-Placement Talk (24 June 2026)

• Resume Shortlisting

• Online Assessment (27 June 2026)

• Group Discussion (3 July 2026)

• Technical Interview (3 July 2026)

• HR Interview (3 July 2026)

• Final Result Declaration (3 July 2026)

The entire interview process was conducted online from the college campus due to the heavy rainfall and
red alert in Mumbai. Candidates were required to report to college, from where all interviews were
conducted virtually.
The process was highly dynamic. Different interview panels followed slightly different formats, with
interview duration, number of technical rounds, and order of shortlisting varying across candidates. Some
candidates had multiple technical interviews, while others were directly shortlisted for HR after a single
technical interview. Therefore, it is important not to compare your process with others during the day or
assume the outcome based on interview duration or the order in which candidates are called.
For the Banking role, the overall selection process was:

• 67 candidates were shortlisted after resume screening.

• 55 candidates were shortlisted after the Online Assessment.

• 29 candidates were shortlisted after the Group Discussion.

• 10 candidates shortlisted for the HR round.

• 10 internship offers rolled out for the Banking role

1. Pre-Placement Talk and Resume Shortlisting

The process began with the Pre-Placement Talk (PPT), followed by registration through the official
JPMorgan Chase Careers portal. While many students treat the PPT as a formality, I would strongly
recommend attending it attentively. The session gives you a clear understanding of the different business
divisions, the responsibilities associated with each role, the internship structure, and the qualities the firm
looks for in candidates. Take notes throughout the session, as several discussion points from the PPT can
later be incorporated into your interviews and the questions you ask the interviewers. If given an
opportunity, ask thoughtful and role-specific questions instead of speaking just for the sake of visibility.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Resume shortlisting is one of the most important elimination stages of the process. For the Banking role,
your resume should demonstrate a genuine interest in finance rather than just listing certifications. I would
recommend having at least one strong finance project that you can confidently discuss in depth. Interviewers
thoroughly evaluate your understanding of every project and internship mentioned on your resume, so only
include experiences that you have personally worked on and can defend confidently. Along with finance
projects, relevant internships, case competitions, leadership positions, and certifications help create a
well-rounded profile.
Remember that interviewers often try to understand the story behind your resume rather than
simply verify its contents. If your profile spans multiple domains, be prepared to explain how
your experiences connect to your interest in finance and why you chose this role.

2. Online Assessment (67 Candidates appeared for this round)

The Online Assessment was conducted online from home on the AON platform and consisted of 45 MCQs
to be completed in 45 minutes. There was no sectional timing, allowing candidates to manage their own
time.
The paper consisted of four sections:

• Corporate Finance & Accounting (10 Questions)

• Market Awareness (10 Questions)

• Quantitative Aptitude (15 Questions)

• English (10 Questions)

• Corporate Finance & Accounting (Moderate): Tested fundamental concepts such as financial

statements, financial ratios, inflation, bonds, GDP, and basic accounting. Focus on understanding
concepts rather than memorizing definitions.

• Market Awareness (Difficult): This was the toughest section for me. Questions were based on

recent business and financial developments, making it difficult to predict. Regularly reading financial
news is far more effective than last-minute preparation.

• Quantitative Aptitude (Easy-Moderate): Similar to IndiaBix-level questions covering Profit &

Loss, Time & Work, Ratios, Probability, Permutations & Combinations, SI-CI, Mixtures, and Speed,
Time & Distance.

• English (Easy): Includes Reading Comprehension, Grammar, Vocabulary, and Sentence Correction.

Overall, it was straightforward.
Preparation
The resources that helped me the most were:

• IndiaBix for Quantitative Aptitude.

• CFI courses (Coursera) for Accounting and Corporate Finance fundamentals.

My strategy was to maximize my score in Quant, English, and Finance, as these sections are relatively
more predictable, while avoiding spending excessive time on difficult Market Awareness questions.
Out of 67 candidates, 55 were shortlisted for the Group Discussion round.
--- PAGE 3 ---
Tips

• Strengthen your accounting and finance fundamentals rather than focusing on advanced valuation

concepts.

• Practice Quant under timed conditions.

• Read financial news consistently instead of relying on last-minute preparation.

• Manage your time well; speed is just as important as accuracy.

3. Group Discussion Round (55 Candidates appeared for this round)

The shortlist for the Group Discussion was announced the night before the interviews, along with the
topic. This leaves very little preparation time, so start researching as soon as the shortlist is released.
GD Topic: "Your company sells through both online and offline channels and sources a meaningful share of
its inventory from overseas. Due to a disruption in global shipping, inbound lead times are approximately
2× longer for around two months, and shipping costs have increased, affecting financial metrics. As the
CEO, how would you tackle this situation?"
The discussion lasted around 20-25 minutes with 8-10 candidates per panel. Unlike a traditional GD, this
was moderator-driven. The moderators asked specific questions, guided the discussion, and ensured that
everyone had an opportunity to contribute.
I spoke four times, but each contribution either introduced a new perspective or built upon an existing point
rather than speaking just to increase my count.
Tips

• Focus on adding value rather than speaking the most.

• Research the topic from multiple perspectives, as moderators may ask follow-up questions.

• Don't disagree just to stand out. If you agree with someone, acknowledge their point and build

upon it. I often built on another candidate's ideas instead of contradicting them, and I believe this
demonstrated teamwork rather than competition.

• Listen actively. The moderators ensured everyone had a fair opportunity to speak, so there was no

need to interrupt or dominate the discussion.

4. Technical/Finance Interview (29 Candidates appeared for this round)

Out of 55 candidates, 29 were shortlisted for the interview round. One thing worth mentioning is that there
was no fixed interview structure. Different panels followed different formats, some candidates had one
technical interview, others had two, and a few had three. Similarly, some candidates who had only one
interview were shortlisted further, while others were eliminated after a single round. Do not compare your
process with others or assume your chances based on the number or duration of interviews.
Personally, I had one 15-minute technical interview with a Vice President. The interview was fast-paced
and focused almost entirely on finance fundamentals rather than my resume. The questions asked were:

• Tell me about yourself.

• "You look like a marketing girl. Why finance?"

• Buy Side vs Sell Side.

--- PAGE 4 ---

• Private Equity vs Venture Capital.

• Investment Banking vs Commercial Banking vs Corporate Banking.

• IPO vs FPO.

• Tata Capital IPO.

• Is the current market favourable for IPOs? How is it different from last year?

• Difference between a Merger and an Acquisition.

• Mention a recent M&A deal and explain it (I discussed L'Oréal's acquisition of Innovist).

Looking back, I realised that the interviewer wasn't looking for textbook definitions. Most questions were
followed by "why?" or "explain further," so having conceptual clarity was far more important than
memorising one-line answers. I knew many of the concepts but struggled to articulate a few of them under
pressure, which reinforced the importance of practising finance discussions aloud rather than only reading
notes.
Preparation & Tips

• Be extremely comfortable with finance fundamentals, especially:

• Buy Side vs Sell Side

PE vs VC

• Types of Banking

• IPO vs FPO

• M&A

• Financial Statements

• Financial Ratios

• Prepare your introduction well-it often determines the direction of the interview.

• Don't panic if you cannot answer a question immediately. Explain your thought process and reason

through the problem.

• Most importantly, don't judge your performance based on interview duration or compare

yourself with other candidates. I walked out convinced I had performed poorly, but eventually
received the offer.

5. HR Interview (10 Candidates appeared for this round)

Around 10 candidates were shortlisted for the HR round, and everyone who reached this stage was
eventually offered the internship. My HR interview lasted approximately 15-17 minutes and was the most
relaxed conversation of the day.
Unlike the technical interview, the HR round was not a question-answer session. After asking me to
introduce myself, the interviewer made an interesting observation: "You look like a marketing girl. Why
finance?ạ
I spoke about my internships, particularly my experience working with Mastercard during my internship at
McCann Worldgroup, and how it made me realise that finance is at the core of every business decision,
ultimately leading me to pursue Corporate Finance and Investment Banking through my minor and finance
projects.
The rest of the interview was largely conversational, giving me an opportunity to ask questions and
understand the firm better.
--- PAGE 5 ---
Tips

• Treat the HR round as a conversation, not an interrogation.

• Have a clear and authentic reason for why finance and why JPMorgan.

• Prepare thoughtful questions for the interviewer. It shows genuine curiosity and leaves a strong final

impression.

• If you reach this stage, stay calm and let your personality come through. The interview is largely

about assessing cultural fit rather than testing technical knowledge.
All 10 students who gave this round were selected.

journey.prep:
Looking back, I do not believe I was selected because I answered every question perfectly--I certainly did
not. There were questions where I had to think before responding, and there were moments where I felt I
could have articulated my answers better. What I believe made the difference was my strong conceptual
foundation, genuine interest in finance, structured thought process, and the ability to reason through
unfamiliar questions instead of panicking.
More importantly, I had spent the last two years deliberately building my profile around finance. Through
internships, valuation projects, case competitions, leadership experiences, and continuous self-learning, I
had gradually developed both technical knowledge and confidence. The interview simply became an
opportunity to demonstrate that journey.

1. Your Resume is Your Biggest Asset

Know every line of your resume thoroughly. Every internship, project, certification, competition, leadership
position, and even a single word or name mentioned on your resume can become the subject of detailed
questioning.
Only include experiences that you have genuinely worked on and can confidently defend.

2. Build Concepts, Don't Memorise Answers

Instead of memorising interview questions, understand the concepts deeply.
Practice explaining topics such as:
 Three Financial Statements
 Valuation
 DCF
 Comparable Company Analysis
 M&A
 Working Capital
 Corporate Finance
out loud, exactly as if you were explaining them to an interviewer.
The interviewers are evaluating your thought process, not your ability to reproduce textbook definitions.

3. Treat the Group Discussion as a Business Discussion

The objective is not to speak the most.
The objective is to contribute meaningful ideas.

Come prepared with 3-4 structured perspectives, listen carefully to others, and whenever appropriate,
acknowledge someone's point before building upon it.
This demonstrates maturity, collaboration, and professional communication.

4. Never Compare Your Journey with Others

This is probably the biggest lesson from our process.
Different candidates had:
 Different interview panels.
 Different technical questions.
 Different interview durations.
 Different numbers of technical rounds.
Some candidates had one interview.
Some had two.
Some had three.
Some finished within 15 minutes.
Others continued for much longer.
None of these factors indicated whether they would eventually be selected.
Focus only on your own preparation and performance.

5. Continue Preparing While Waiting

There can be long waiting periods between rounds.
My Technical Interview concluded at around 11:50 AM, and my HR Interview was completed by
approximately 12:20 PM. However, several other candidates continued with their technical interviews until
3:00-4:00 PM, and the final results were declared only around 5:00 PM.
Don't get distracted , just focus.

6. Never Underestimate the Online Assessment

Personally, I found the Online Assessment to be one of the most stressful stages because it is a major
elimination round and many highly capable candidates are filtered out at this stage.
Looking back, I feel I could have performed even better with more timed practice and additional preparation
for Market Awareness.

Do not assume that a strong resume alone is sufficient--the Online Assessment deserves dedicated
preparation.

7. If I Had More Time...

Looking back, there are a few things I wish I had done even better.
 I would have attempted CFA Level I before placements if my academic schedule had permitted.
 I would have tried to gain additional finance work experience, particularly through boutique
investment banks, research firms, or valuation-focused internships.
 I would have started following global financial markets even earlier and in greater depth.
Although none of these were mandatory for selection, they would have further strengthened my profile.

8. Learn AI Alongside Finance

One area that I found increasingly valuable throughout my preparation was the application of Artificial
Intelligence to finance.
During my interviews, I discussed how I had used AI tools responsibly to improve my understanding of
valuation, financial modelling, research, and market analysis. We also had discussions around Large
Language Models (LLMs), their applications, and how they can improve productivity while still requiring
strong financial judgement.

9. Stay Curious

Throughout my preparation, I realised that interviewers appreciate candidates who are genuinely curious.
Read annual reports.
Read investor presentations.
Follow major transactions.
Understand why companies merge.
Learn how businesses create value.
Do not prepare only for interviews.
Prepare to become a better finance professional.
.

journey.howSecured:
The recruitment process consisted of the following stages:

● Pre-Placement Talk (24 June 2026)

● Resume Shortlisting

● Online Assessment (27 June 2026)

● Group Discussion (2 July 2026)

● Technical Interview (2 July 2026)

● HR Interview (2 July 2026)

● Final Result Declaration (2 July 2026)

The entire interview process was conducted virtually from the college campus  due to heavy rainfall and a
red alert declared in Mumbai. Although the interviews were online, all shortlisted candidates were required
to report to the college, from where the complete selection process was coordinated.
One important observation is that the interview process was highly dynamic . Different interview panels
followed slightly different formats, and there was no fixed sequence of rounds for every candidate. The
duration of interviews, number of technical rounds, and the order in which candidates were shortlisted
varied significantly across panels. While some candidates had two technical interviews before the HR round,
others were directly shortlisted for HR after a single technical interview. Therefore, do not compare your
process with that of other candidates during the day or draw conclusions based on interview duration,
the order in which candidates are called, or the number of rounds they undergo.  Each panel evaluates
candidates independently.
For our batch, approximately 54 candidates were shortlisted after the Online Assessment and were divided
into 6 Group Discussion panels, with around 9 candidates in each panel. Each GD panel was evaluated by

two interviewers. Following the GD, approximately 3-4 candidates from each panel were shortlisted for the
interview stage.
The interview stage was also divided into 6 interview panels, each comprising senior professionals from J.P.
Morgan. In my case, I was interviewed directly by a Vice President (VP) My selection process consisted of
one Technical Interview followed by one HR Interview . However, this should not be considered the
standard format, as several candidates underwent multiple technical interviews before moving to HR.
Throughout the day, the process remained flexible, and interview schedules were continuously adjusted based
on panel availability. My advice is to stay calm, avoid speculating about your chances based on others'
experiences, and remain mentally prepared for any interview format. Focus only on your own
performance, as the evaluation process differs across panels.

Selection Statistics (Banking Role)
The recruitment process for the Corporate & Investment Banking (Banking) Internship  was highly
competitive.
 275+ students applied across the Banking and Risk roles during the campus recruitment process.
 After resume screening, 67 candidates were shortlisted for the Banking role.
 55 candidates progressed to the Online Assessment stage.
 29 candidates were shortlisted for the Group Discussion round.
 10 candidates advanced to the HR Interview.
 Finally, 10 internship offers  were rolled out for the Banking role, with the internship carrying the
opportunity for a Performance-Based Pre-Placement Offer (PPO).
Overall, the selection process was highly competitive, with multiple elimination stages evaluating not only
technical knowledge and aptitude, but also communication skills, commercial awareness, structured thinking,
and overall cultural fit with the firm

Pre-Placement Talk  (300+ Candidates appeared )
The recruitment process began with the Pre-Placement Talk (PPT), followed by the application through
the official J.P. Morgan Chase Careers Portal. While many students consider the PPT to be a routine
introductory session, I strongly recommend treating it as the first round of your preparation rather than a
formality.
The PPT provides valuable insights into the firm's businesses, culture, internship structure, expectations
from interns, and the specific responsibilities associated with each role. Pay close attention to the discussion,
as many of the points shared during the session can later be incorporated into your interview answers,
particularly for questions such as "Why J.P. Morgan?", "Why this role?", and "What do you expect from this
internship?"
 Take detailed notes throughout the session. Instead of relying solely on the presentation slides,
write down important points regarding J.P. Morgan's businesses, the Corporate & Investment
Banking division, the Banking role, and the qualities the firm values in its employees. I also
recommend taking screenshots of important slides for future reference.
 Understand the role in depth. Note the responsibilities, day-to-day work, required skills, and how
the Banking division fits within J.P. Morgan's overall business. This understanding will help you
tailor both your resume and your interview responses.
 Do not ask questions merely to gain visibility. During our PPT, the presenters repeatedly
encouraged students to keep their questions relevant to the role. If you genuinely have a thoughtful
question related to the internship, business, or role, ask it confidently. However, avoid asking generic
or unnecessary questions simply to be noticed.
 Pay attention to the speakers. Make a note of the names and designations of the HR
representatives and business professionals conducting the session. While the same individuals
may not necessarily interview you, referring to insights shared during the PPT demonstrates genuine
interest in the firm.
 Read the Job Description (JD) thoroughly--word by word. This is one of the most overlooked
aspects of preparation. Every requirement mentioned in the JD indicates what the firm is looking for
in a candidate. Understanding these requirements will help you refine your resume, highlight
relevant experiences, and significantly improve your chances of getting shortlisted.

 Start following financial markets well in advance. Ideally, begin reading business and financial
news at least a year before placements. Develop the habit of tracking:

o Major Mergers & Acquisitions
o IPOs
o Equity and Debt Capital Market transactions
o Global macroeconomic developments
o Interest rate decisions by major central banks
o Geopolitical events affecting financial markets
o Significant transactions advised by leading investment banks such as J.P. Morgan, Goldman
Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, Citi, HSBC, Barclays, and others.
This long-term preparation will not only strengthen your market awareness but also help you perform
better during Group Discussions and interviews, where commercial awareness is evaluated
extensively.
The PPT is your first opportunity to understand exactly what the firm is looking for. If you use it
effectively, it becomes much easier to align your preparation, resume, and interview answers with the
expectations of the role. Looking back, I found that several points discussed during the PPT directly helped
me answer interview questions and demonstrate a clearer understanding of both J.P. Morgan and the
Banking role. Below I have shared the ss of my ppt talk.

Have attached the JD  of the CIB role here :
https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Qn2iY49f_UGcuhViQE5krD2IlGejWU74/view?usp=sharing

2.     Resume Shortlisting (67 candidates shortlisted)

In my opinion, resume shortlisting is the most important elimination stage of the entire recruitment
process. Before you get an opportunity to demonstrate your technical knowledge, communication skills,
or market awareness, your resume must first convince the recruiters that you are a suitable fit for the role.
For our process, 67 candidates were shortlisted from the resume screening stage, making it one of the
most competitive elimination rounds.
One important observation from our recruitment process was that several candidates with exceptionally
strong profiles were not shortlisted . The exact shortlisting criteria were never disclosed  to us, and
therefore it is difficult to conclude that selection depends on any single factor such as CGPA, internships,
or certifications alone. My advice would be to focus on building the strongest and most balanced profile
possible rather than trying to optimize for one particular metric.
For the Banking role, your resume should demonstrate a consistent and genuine interest in finance rather
than simply listing finance-related certifications or buzzwords. The strongest resumes usually tell a
coherent story, where internships, projects, competitions, leadership positions, and certifications
collectively reinforce your interest in Corporate & Investment Banking.
During my preparation, I spent over two months working exclusively on my resume. It went through 8-
9 major iterations , incorporating continuous feedback from seniors, mentors, professionals working in
Investment Banking, and placement coordinators. Every revision focused on improving clarity,
quantifying impact, strengthening Investment Banking-specific terminology, and ensuring that every
bullet point reflected work I had genuinely performed. Include all the things in a numerically ,
quantifying all the things u have mentioned with IB related words
Before submitting my final resume, I also evaluated it using multiple ATS (Applicant Tracking System)
platforms, including Resume Worded, where it achieved a score of 91. While ATS scores should not be
treated as the sole indicator of resume quality, I would recommend maintaining a score of 80+ to ensure
that your resume is ATS-friendly and appropriately optimized. Equally important is ensuring that your
resume is free from grammatical, formatting, spelling, and alignment errors, as even minor mistakes
can create a poor impression or affect automated screening systems.
Although the minimum eligibility criterion for our process was a CGPA above 7 , I would strongly
recommend maintaining the highest CGPA possible throughout your academic journey. In addition to your
undergraduate performance, Class X and Class XII academic records may also be considered by
recruiters, even though the exact evaluation methodology is not disclosed. Therefore, maintaining
consistency across your academic record is always beneficial.
Your resume should ideally contain  two strong finance projects that you understand thoroughly, rather
than multiple superficial projects. Every project listed on your resume is a potential discussion topic during
the interview. Interviewers frequently ask detailed follow-up questions to assess the depth of your
understanding, so never include a project that you have not personally completed or cannot
confidently defend . It is always better to present fewer, high-quality projects than a long list of
experiences that lack substance.(I had represented 3)
Apart from projects, I strongly encourage participating in finance case competitions organised by IIMs,
IITs, and other reputed institutions. These competitions provide practical exposure to valuation, financial

modelling, M&A, corporate finance, and strategic decision-making while significantly strengthening your
resume.
Leadership is another aspect that recruiters value. Try to hold one or two meaningful Positions of
Responsibility (PORs)  where you can demonstrate measurable impact. Focus on contributing
meaningfully rather than simply collecting titles, and wherever possible, quantify your achievements.
If possible, secure at least one relevant internship or work experience before placements. While this is
not a mandatory requirement , it significantly strengthens your profile and provides valuable practical
exposure. Obtaining a finance internship can be difficult, especially initially. Personally, I faced numerous
rejections while applying through LinkedIn and cold emailing professionals, HRs, boutique investment
firms, and research firms before eventually securing an opportunity. My advice is to remain persistent
network actively, reach out to professionals, and do not be discouraged by early rejections.
Professional certifications such as the CFA Program can further strengthen your profile and demonstrate
a genuine commitment to finance. Although I was unable to attempt the examination before the recruitment
process due to time constraints, I believe that clearing CFA Level I  can positively differentiate your
profile. However, it is important to emphasize that it is not a prerequisite for selection . In our batch, 9
out of the 10 selected candidates had not completed CFA Level I , clearly indicating that recruiters
evaluate the overall quality of your profile rather than any single certification.
Finally, remember that your resume is not merely a document--it becomes the blueprint for your
interview. Every line can become the subject of detailed questioning. Build a profile that reflects genuine
interest, tailor your resume specifically for the role, eliminate every possible error, and include only
experiences that you can discuss confidently and honestly.
Remember that interviewers often try to understand the story behind your resume rather than simply verify
its contents. If your profile spans multiple domains, be prepared to explain how your experiences connect
to your interest in finance and why you chose this role.

Online Assessment  [55 students were shortlisted from this round ]
The Online Assessment was conducted on the AON Assessment Platform  and consisted of 45 Multiple
Choice Questions (MCQs)  to be completed within 45 minutes. There was no sectional timing , allowing
candidates complete flexibility in deciding how to allocate their time across the different sections. Since the
assessment was heavily time-bound, both speed and accuracy played an equally important role.
For our recruitment process, 67 candidates  appeared after the resume shortlisting stage, out of which 55
candidates progressed to the Group Discussion round.
Assessment Pattern
The paper consisted of four sections:
 Corporate Finance & Accounting - 10 Questions
 Market Awareness - 10 Questions

 Quantitative Aptitude - 15 Questions
 English Language - 10 Questions
Although the difficulty level of the overall assessment was moderate, the Market Awareness section was
relatively the most unpredictable, whereas the remaining sections rewarded candidates with strong
fundamentals and consistent practice.
Section-wise Analysis

1. Corporate Finance & Accounting (Easy)

This section primarily tested fundamental financial concepts  rather than advanced Investment Banking
knowledge. Candidates preparing specifically for valuation or M&A should not neglect these basics, as almost
every question originated from core finance concepts.
The questions were based on topics such as:
 Financial Statements
o Income Statement
o Balance Sheet
o Cash Flow Statement
 Relationships between the three financial statements
 Revenue, Expenses and Profitability
 EBITDA, EBIT, Net Income
 Depreciation & Amortisation
 Working Capital
 Capital Expenditure (CapEx)
 Operating, Investing and Financing Cash Flows
 Financial Ratios
o Liquidity Ratios
o Profitability Ratios
o Leverage Ratios
o Efficiency Ratios
 Bonds

o Coupon Rate
o Yield
o Bond Prices
o Interest Rate Relationship
 Inflation
 GDP
 Time Value of Money
 Basic Corporate Finance Concepts
The assessment did not require advanced financial modelling or valuation . However, candidates with a
strong understanding of accounting fundamentals found this section relatively straightforward.
Preparation Resources
For this section, I would strongly recommend:
 CFI (Corporate Finance Institute) courses on:
o Accounting Fundamentals
o Corporate Finance
o Reading Financial Statements
These resources are more than sufficient for the Online Assessment.

2. Market Awareness (Moderate)

This was undoubtedly the most unpredictable section of the assessment.
Unlike the other sections, there is no predefined syllabus. Questions were based on recent developments in:
 Indian Economy
 Global Economy
 RBI Policies
 Federal Reserve Decisions
 Inflation
 Interest Rates
 IPOs

 Mergers & Acquisitions
 Equity Markets
 Fixed Income Markets
 Commodity Markets
 Currency Markets
 Major Corporate Developments
 Banking Sector News
 Geopolitical Events affecting Financial Markets
Questions were largely application-based rather than factual recall.
Preparation Strategy
Do not prepare for this section one week before the assessment.
Instead, develop a habit of reading financial news consistently.
Recommended sources include:
 Financial Times
 The Economic Times
 Mint
 Business Standard
 Bloomberg
 Reuters
 Wall Street Journal
Rather than memorising headlines, try to understand:
 Why did this transaction happen?
 How was it financed?
 Which Investment Banks advised the deal?
 What impact will this have on financial markets?
This approach helped me much more than simply reading current affairs.

3. Quantitative Aptitude (Easy-Moderate)

The Quantitative Aptitude section was largely comparable to questions available on IndiaBix and similar
aptitude preparation platforms.
Major topics included:
 Profit & Loss
 Time & Work
 Ratios & Proportions
 Probability
 Permutations & Combinations
 Simple & Compound Interest
 Mixtures & Alligations
 Speed, Time & Distance
 Percentages
 Averages
 Time & Distance
 Number System
 Basic Logical Reasoning
The questions were conceptually straightforward but required quick calculations under time pressure.
Preparation
I primarily used IndiaBix, which was more than sufficient for this section.
The key is timed practice, not simply solving questions.

4. English Language (Easy)

The English section was relatively straightforward and consisted of:
 Reading Comprehension
 Grammar

 Vocabulary
 Sentence Correction
 Para Jumbles
 Error Detection
Candidates with regular reading habits should find this section manageable.
My objective was to maximise my score in the Quantitative Aptitude, English, and Corporate Finance
sections, as these are comparatively more predictable and controllable.
For the Market Awareness section, I focused on developing a consistent habit of reading business newspapers
and understanding financial markets rather than trying to memorise current affairs shortly before the
examination. This strategy allowed me to maximise marks in the predictable sections while attempting as many
Market Awareness questions as possible.

GROUP DISCUSSION (29 STUDENTS WERE SHORTLISTED)
The shortlist for the Group Discussion (GD) was announced on the evening before the interviews, along
with the discussion topic. This left candidates with very little preparation time. My advice would be to begin
your research immediately after the shortlist is announced instead of waiting until the next morning.
Personally, I spent approximately four hours researching the topic the previous night and another one
hour revising and organising my thoughts on the morning of the interview. This preparation proved
extremely valuable, as the discussion required structured thinking rather than spontaneous opinions.
"Your company sells through both online and offline channels and sources a meaningful share of its
inventory from overseas. Due to a disruption in global shipping, inbound lead times are
approximately twice as long for around two months, and shipping costs have increased, adversely
affecting financial metrics. As the CEO, how would you tackle this situation?"
Unlike a conventional Group Discussion based on current affairs, this was a business case discussion where
candidates were expected to think like senior management and propose practical, well-reasoned business
solutions.
The discussion lasted approximately 20-25 minutes, with 8-10 candidates in each panel. It was a
moderator-driven discussion, meaning the moderators actively guided the conversation, asked follow-up
questions, and ensured that every participant had a fair opportunity to contribute. Rather than allowing

candidates to debate freely, the moderators frequently directed questions toward specific individuals and
encouraged discussion from multiple perspectives.
In my panel, I contributed four times during the discussion. Instead of speaking frequently simply to
increase my participation count, I ensured that each contribution either introduced a new perspective,
expanded upon an existing point, or proposed a practical solution. I believe this approach demonstrated
structured thinking and collaborative problem-solving rather than merely trying to dominate the discussion.
One important point to note is that candidates were not permitted to refer to written notes during the
GD. Therefore, while researching, avoid preparing lengthy scripts. Instead, focus on understanding the case
thoroughly and memorising the key ideas, frameworks, and important facts so that your responses appear
natural and conversational.
Preparation Strategy
Since the preparation window is extremely limited, I would recommend using multiple sources to
understand the problem from different perspectives. I primarily used Google and Gemini to gather
information on supply chain disruptions, global shipping, inventory management, logistics, freight costs,
inflationary pressures, and the financial implications of delayed imports. Rather than simply collecting facts,
my objective was to understand the complete business context and think like a CEO responsible for making
strategic decisions.
While researching, try to analyse the case from multiple perspectives, such as:
 Supply Chain & Logistics
 Operations & Inventory Management
 Finance & Cost Management
 Customer Experience
 Risk Management
 Procurement & Vendor Diversification
 Pricing Strategy
 International Trade & Geopolitical Risks
This broader understanding allows you to answer follow-up questions confidently and contribute meaningful
insights during the discussion.
 Treat the GD as a business discussion, not a debate. The objective is to solve the problem
collectively rather than prove that your opinion is superior.
 Focus on adding value instead of speaking the most. A few meaningful contributions are
significantly more impactful than speaking repeatedly without introducing new ideas.
 Research the topic from multiple perspectives. Moderators frequently ask follow-up questions to
evaluate the depth of your understanding.
 Build upon others' ideas whenever appropriate. You do not have to disagree simply to stand out.
If another candidate makes a good point, acknowledge it and extend the discussion further.
Demonstrating collaboration often creates a better impression than unnecessary confrontation.

 Listen actively. Since the moderators ensured that everyone had an opportunity to speak, there was
no need to interrupt or compete for speaking time.
 Maintain a structured approach. Present your thoughts logically, explaining not only what you
would do but also why you would do it and how it would affect the business.
 Remain calm and confident. The moderators are evaluating your thought process, communication
skills, business acumen, and ability to work as part of a team--not whether you arrive at the perfect
solution.
Looking back, I believe that thorough preparation, structured thinking, and collaborative participation
were the biggest factors that contributed to my performance in the Group Discussion. Rather than trying to
impress the panel by speaking the most, I focused on making every contribution meaningful, practical, and
relevant to the case. I believe this approach aligned well with what J.P. Morgan was looking for in
prospective interns. One observation from our recruitment process was that many candidates who had
performed confidently during the Group Discussion were called for their interviews relatively early in
the day. While I cannot confirm whether this was an official evaluation criterion or simply a scheduling
decision, it was a noticeable pattern during our process.
For instance, interviews across the different panels began at approximately 11:30 AM, and I received my
call for the Technical Interview at around 11:35 AM, immediately after the Group Discussion. However, I
would advise future candidates not to draw conclusions based solely on the order in which interviews
are conducted, as scheduling may vary depending on panel availability and logistics.
Irrespective of the interview order, treat the Group Discussion as one of the most important stages of the
recruitment process. Enter the discussion with 3-4 well-structured points prepared around different
aspects of the case rather than memorising complete answers. Since written notes are not allowed during the
discussion, focus on understanding the business problem thoroughly so that you can speak naturally and
confidently.
Finally, do not let anxiety affect your performance. It is natural to feel nervous before speaking, but
excessive stress often causes candidates to forget points they have already prepared. Trust your preparation,
listen carefully to the discussion, and contribute thoughtfully whenever you have something meaningful to
add. Remember that the panel is evaluating your ability to think logically, communicate effectively, and
collaborate with others, not the number of times you speak. In my experience, remaining calm and
composed helped me articulate my thoughts much more effectively than trying to force additional
contributions.

Technical/Finance Interview  ( 10 students where shortlisted for HR)
Out of the 55 candidates who cleared the Online Assessment, 29 candidates were shortlisted for the
interview stage.
One important observation from the recruitment process was that there was no fixed interview structure.
Different interview panels followed different formats. Some candidates had one technical interview, others
had two, while a few underwent three technical interviews before the HR round. Similarly, some

candidates were shortlisted after a single interview, whereas others were eliminated despite having multiple
rounds. Therefore, do not compare your interview journey with others or judge your chances based on
the number, duration, or order of interviews. Every panel evaluates candidates independently, and the
process is highly dynamic.
THE GD WAS TAKEN AT 9.00 IN THE MORNING AND GOT OVER BY 9.40 (CONSIDERING A
TIMING DELAY )
INTERVIEW GOT STARTED BY 11.35 ( APPROX 1 HR GAP SO I REVISE ALL I COULD)

I was one of the first ones to be called for the interview. The interview started about at 11.30 and I was
called in at 11.35 .Be ready and keep atleast 3 copies of resume with you.
In my case, I had one Technical Interview followed by one HR Interview. My Technical Interview lasted
approximately 15-20 minutes and was conducted by Mr. Farhad Collabawala (Vice President, J.P.
Morgan Chase & Co.)
The interview was conducted in a very friendly yet fast-paced manner. Unlike many other candidates whose
interviews focused extensively on their resumes, my interview primarily evaluated finance fundamentals,
valuation concepts, accounting knowledge, and corporate finance, with only a brief discussion on my
resume.

Questions Asked

1. Walk me through your resume.

The interviewer began by asking me to briefly introduce myself through my resume.
I kept my answer concise by covering:
 Educational background
 Finance internships
 Major valuation projects
 National-level finance case competition achievements
 Leadership positions

Advice: Keep this answer under 2-3 minutes. Do not explain every bullet point. Instead, provide a

structured overview that naturally highlights your strongest achievements and creates interest for follow-up
questions.

2. Why did you pursue the SPJIMR Minor in Management?

The interviewer asked about my decision to pursue the Minor in Management offered in collaboration with
SPJIMR.

The discussion revolved around:
 Subjects taught
 Key learnings
 Relevance to finance
 How it complemented my engineering curriculum

3. Explain the linkage between the three financial statements.

This was one of the most detailed discussions during the interview.
The interviewer gave a practical example involving a company with inventory and asked me to explain how
selling inventory would affect the:
 Income Statement
 Balance Sheet
 Cash Flow Statement
I explained the complete flow covering:
 Revenue recognition
 Cost of Goods Sold
 Gross Profit
 Net Income
 Inventory reduction
 Cash generation
 Retained Earnings
 Working Capital movement
 Cash Conversion Cycle
The discussion further extended to:
 Working Capital Management
 Cash Conversion Cycle
 Inventory Accounting
The interviewer also asked follow-up questions on:
 FIFO
 LIFO
 Their impact on profitability
 Their relevance in industries such as FMCG
This was a conceptual discussion where the interviewer continuously built upon previous answers rather
than asking isolated questions.

4. Tell me about a valuation methodology other than DCF.

Since DCF is the most commonly discussed valuation technique, the interviewer specifically wanted to
evaluate my exposure to other valuation methods.
I discussed my project on the Sun Pharmaceutical - Organon acquisition, where I had built an
Accretion/Dilution Merger Model for the USD 11.75 billion transaction.
The discussion covered:
 Merger Modelling
 Purchase Consideration
 Accretion & Dilution Analysis
 Strategic rationale behind the transaction

5. Apart from DCF, what other valuation techniques can be used?

This discussion focused on relative valuation.
I explained:
 Comparable Company Analysis (Trading Comparables)
 Precedent Transaction Analysis
We further discussed various valuation multiples, including:
 EV / EBITDA
 EV / EBIT
 Price / Earnings (P/E)
 Price / Book (P/B)
 Enterprise Value based multiples
 Equity Value based multiples
The interviewer then asked which valuation multiples are appropriate for different industries.
I explained that multiple selection depends on:
 Industry characteristics
 Capital structure
 Profitability
 Business model
For example, I discussed why:
 Banks are commonly valued using Price-to-Book (P/B) and Return on Equity because Enterprise
Value is not meaningful due to the nature of debt in banking institutions.
 Manufacturing companies frequently use EV/EBITDA because it allows comparison independent of
capital structure.

6. Why do we use EV/EBITDA instead of Market Capitalisation / Net Income?

This question tested conceptual understanding rather than memorisation.
The interviewer asked:
 Why EV is paired with EBITDA.
 Why P/E uses Net Income.
 Why Enterprise Value cannot be compared with Net Income.
I explained that valuation multiples should always compare like with like.
Enterprise Value represents the value attributable to both debt and equity holders, whereas EBITDA is a
pre-interest operating metric that is independent of financing decisions.
Similarly,
Market Capitalisation represents only the value attributable to equity shareholders.
Therefore,
 Enterprise Value is compared with EBITDA or EBIT.
 Market Capitalisation is compared with Net Income using the P/E multiple.
I also explained how EBITDA removes the impact of:
 Capital Structure
 Interest Expense
 Taxation
thereby enabling better comparison across companies with different financing structures.

7. Questions on Mergers & Acquisitions

The interviewer further asked several conceptual questions on M&A.
The discussion covered:
 Types of Synergies
 Revenue Synergies
 Cost Synergies
 Financial Synergies
 Strategic rationale behind mergers
 Why companies pursue acquisitions
 Value creation through M&A
The emphasis was on understanding the business rationale rather than memorising definitions.

8. Why not MBA?

Towards the end of the interview, the interviewer asked:
"Why are you choosing Investment Banking now instead of pursuing an MBA?"
I explained that I wanted to build a strong foundation in finance through practical deal exposure before
considering higher studies. I also mentioned that working in Investment Banking would provide
significantly greater learning opportunities, exposure to transactions, mentorship from experienced
professionals, and a valuable professional network, all of which would contribute more meaningfully to my
long-term career than pursuing an MBA immediately after graduation.

Overall Experience
My interview was highly conceptual. Very little emphasis was placed on memorised definitions or
theoretical answers. Instead, the interviewer continuously asked follow-up questions to evaluate the depth of
my understanding and whether I could logically connect different finance concepts.
One important takeaway is that every answer can lead to multiple follow-up questions. Therefore, avoid
preparing finance topics in isolation. Build a strong conceptual understanding of accounting, corporate
finance, valuation, financial modelling, and M&A, as interviewers often connect multiple concepts within
the same discussion.
Looking back, I believe that my preparation in financial statements, valuation methodologies, corporate
finance fundamentals, and merger modelling played the biggest role in helping me perform confidently
during the technical interview.
One important point I would like to emphasize is that my interview was heavily finance-oriented, which
was primarily a reflection of my resume. Since my resume was built around Corporate Finance,
Valuation, Financial Modelling, M&A, Equity Research, and finance case competitions, the interviewer
chose to assess me almost entirely on these areas. The discussion remained technical throughout, with very
limited focus on behavioural or general aptitude questions.
However, this does not imply that every candidate will have the same experience. During interactions
with other shortlisted candidates after the process, I found that several interview panels asked quantitative
aptitude questions, logical reasoning, estimation problems, and puzzles, while others focused
extensively on resumes, internships, or behavioural questions. Therefore, do not prepare only based on
someone else's interview experience. Every panel has its own interviewing style and areas of focus.
Over the last two years, I had deliberately invested significant time in learning Corporate Finance,
Financial Statement Analysis, Valuation, Financial Modelling, and M&A through internships, case
competitions, self-study, and practical projects. Since these topics were prominently reflected throughout my
resume, the interviewer naturally chose to explore them in depth. This reinforced an important lesson for
me:

Your resume largely determines the direction of your interview.
Every skill, project, internship, certification, or keyword that you mention becomes a potential area for
detailed questioning. Therefore, never include topics that you have only a superficial understanding of.
Instead, build a resume around experiences that you genuinely understand and can discuss confidently.
Another interesting aspect of my interview was that I had mentioned Professor Aswath Damodaran in my
resume as one of the resources I regularly followed for valuation and corporate finance. The interviewer
noticed this and immediately asked follow-up questions related to valuation concepts and Professor
Damodaran's approach to valuation. This further highlighted that even a single name or reference on your
resume can become the starting point of an in-depth technical discussion.
My advice is simple: treat every line of your resume as interview material. If you mention a company, a
project, a framework, a software tool, a certification, or even a finance author or educator, be prepared to
answer detailed questions about it. Interviewers often use your resume to identify areas where they can
assess the depth of your knowledge rather than simply asking standard technical questions.

HR Interview (10 Candidates Appeared)
Following the Technical Interview, candidates who were shortlisted proceeded to the HR Interview. In our
process, 10 candidates advanced to this stage, and all 10 eventually received internship offers.
One interesting observation was the timeline of the interviews. My Technical Interview concluded at
approximately 11:50 AM, and by around 12:00 PM, only two candidates (including myself) had been
called for the HR Interview while the remaining technical interviews across different panels were still in
progress. The rest of the shortlisted candidates completed their technical rounds throughout the afternoon
and subsequently appeared for HR. The final results were announced at approximately 5:00 PM.
Although the HR interview was significantly more conversational than the Technical Interview, I would
strongly advise candidates not to treat this round lightly. At this stage, the interviewers are not
evaluating your technical knowledge; instead, they are assessing your personality, communication skills,
motivation, professionalism, cultural fit, and whether you genuinely align with J.P. Morgan's values.
My HR interview lasted approximately 15-20 minutes and was conducted in a relaxed and interactive
manner. Rather than asking rapid-fire questions, the interviewer encouraged a natural conversation while
exploring my motivations, thought process, and career aspirations.

Questions Asked

1. Tell me about yourself.

I gave a concise overview of my journey, covering my engineering background, interest in finance,
internships, finance projects, case competition achievements, leadership experiences, and my long-term
interest in Corporate & Investment Banking.
The objective was not to narrate my resume but to provide a structured story connecting my experiences.

2. Why Investment Banking?

This formed the core of the discussion.
I explained that what attracts me most to Investment Banking is the opportunity to solve complex strategic
problems, advise clients on high-impact transactions, work on mergers and acquisitions, capital raising, and
corporate finance decisions while learning continuously in a highly challenging environment.
I also mentioned that my internships, valuation projects, finance competitions, and research work gradually
confirmed that this was the field in which I wanted to build my career.

3. Why J.P. Morgan?

This was one of the most important questions.
One question that stood out during my HR interview was when the interviewer asked me to recall two key
takeaways from the Pre-Placement Talk. Since I had taken detailed notes during the session, I was able to
answer confidently by referring to specific discussions and insights shared by the speakers.
Rather than giving generic answers, I mentioned several key points discussed during the PPT, including the
firm's client-centric culture, the collaborative nature of the Corporate & Investment Banking division, and
the expectations from interns. I also referred to some of the professionals who had addressed us during the
session, demonstrating that I had genuinely paid attention rather than treating the PPT as a routine
introductory event.

To further demonstrate my interest in the firm, I mentioned that I had been following J.P. Morgan's
Investment Banking activities beyond the campus recruitment process. I referred to a recent LinkedIn
post by Anu Aiyengar, Global Co-Head of Mergers & Acquisitions at J.P. Morgan, where she discussed
one of the firm's landmark transactions. I also spoke briefly about J.P. Morgan's involvement in advising on
SpaceX's recent USD 2.5 billion debt financing, explaining how I had been following major transactions
advised by the firm as part of my preparation.
I believe this made a positive impression because it demonstrated that my interest in J.P. Morgan extended
beyond simply securing an internship. It reflected genuine curiosity about the firm's work, recent
transactions, leadership, and position within the global Investment Banking industry.
If possible, spend some time before the interview researching J.P. Morgan itself, not just general finance
concepts. Read about:
 Recent landmark transactions advised by J.P. Morgan.
 Major IPOs, M&A deals, and debt/equity capital market transactions.
 Senior leadership within the Corporate & Investment Banking division.
 Recent thought leadership articles, interviews, or LinkedIn posts by senior bankers.
 The firm's recent achievements, awards, and strategic priorities.
You do not need to memorise facts or force these points into every answer. However, if an opportunity
naturally arises during the interview, referring to a recent transaction, a leadership insight, or something
discussed during the Pre-Placement Talk demonstrates genuine enthusiasm and differentiates you from
candidates who have only prepared standard interview questions.
One final piece of advice: The interviewers can easily distinguish between candidates who have memorised
information and those who have developed a genuine interest in the firm. If you reference a recent deal or a
leadership post, make sure you understand it well enough to discuss it if the interviewer asks follow-up
questions. Authentic curiosity always leaves a stronger impression than rehearsed facts

5. What qualities do you think make a successful Investment Banking analyst and what would u look

if u were a part of the recruitment team ?
This was one of the questions that stood out during my interview. The first thing I told is TRUST TRUST
TRUST . THAT IS THE THING JPMC  stands for  .

Instead of answering from my personal perspective, I framed my response around J.P. Morgan's
expectations.
I emphasised qualities such as:
 Client-first mindset.
 Integrity.
 Ownership.
 Attention to detail.
 Strong analytical thinking.
 Teamwork.
 Ability to perform under pressure.
 Continuous learning.
 Clear communication.
 Professionalism.
Throughout my answer, I repeatedly connected these qualities back to client service, explaining that every
analysis, model, presentation, or recommendation ultimately exists to create value for the client. I believe
this alignment with J.P. Morgan's client-centric culture resonated well with the interviewer.

6. Questions for the Interviewer

Towards the end of the discussion, I was given an opportunity to ask questions.
I asked thoughtful questions related to:
 Learning opportunities during the internship.
 Team structure.
 Exposure to different transactions.
 Expectations from interns.
 Qualities that distinguish interns who receive PPOs.
This led to a very engaging conversation and helped me understand the role better.
Overall Experience
Unlike the Technical Interview, the HR Interview was not intended to test finance knowledge. Instead, it
focused on understanding who I was as a person, how I think, what motivates me, and whether I would be
a good cultural fit for the organisation.

However, do not assume that a conversational interview is an easy interview. Every response is being
evaluated carefully. The interviewer is assessing not only what you say but also how you communicate,
structure your thoughts, and whether your motivations appear genuine.
Throughout the discussion, I ensured that my answers consistently reflected the themes that J.P. Morgan had
emphasised during the Pre-Placement Talk--particularly client service, teamwork, ownership, integrity,
professionalism, and continuous learning. Rather than providing generic HR responses, I connected each
answer to the firm's values and to my own experiences, making my responses more authentic and relevant.
Tips for Future Aspirants
 Do not take the HR round lightly simply because it is conversational. This is the final stage of
evaluation, and every answer contributes to the overall assessment.
 Prepare convincing answers for "Tell me about yourself," "Why Finance?", "Why Investment
Banking?", "Why J.P. Morgan?", and "Why not MBA?"
 Understand J.P. Morgan's culture and values, particularly its emphasis on client service,
teamwork, integrity, and excellence.
 Structure every answer with examples from your own experiences rather than giving generic
responses.
 Prepare 2-3 thoughtful questions for the interviewer. This demonstrates curiosity and genuine
interest in both the role and the organisation.
 Most importantly, be authentic. The interviewer is not looking for rehearsed answers but for
candidates who communicate clearly, think logically, and genuinely align with the firm's culture.
Looking back, I believe the HR Interview was less about finding perfect answers and more about
demonstrating maturity, professionalism, and a genuine motivation to build a long-term career in Investment
Banking at J.P. Morgan
All 10 students who gave this round were selected

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
Looking back, I do not believe I was selected because I answered every question perfectly--I certainly did
not. There were questions where I had to think before responding, and there were moments where I felt I
could have articulated my answers better. What I believe made the difference was my strong conceptual
foundation, genuine interest in finance, structured thought process, and the ability to reason through
unfamiliar questions instead of panicking.
More importantly, I had spent the last two years deliberately building my profile around finance. Through
internships, valuation projects, case competitions, leadership experiences, and continuous self-learning, I
had gradually developed both technical knowledge and confidence. The interview simply became an
opportunity to demonstrate that journey.

1. Your Resume is Your Biggest Asset

Know every line of your resume thoroughly. Every internship, project, certification, competition, leadership
position, and even a single word or name mentioned on your resume can become the subject of detailed
questioning.
Only include experiences that you have genuinely worked on and can confidently defend.

2. Build Concepts, Don't Memorise Answers

Instead of memorising interview questions, understand the concepts deeply.
Practice explaining topics such as:
 Three Financial Statements
 Valuation
 DCF
 Comparable Company Analysis
 M&A
 Working Capital
 Corporate Finance
out loud, exactly as if you were explaining them to an interviewer.
The interviewers are evaluating your thought process, not your ability to reproduce textbook definitions.

3. Treat the Group Discussion as a Business Discussion

The objective is not to speak the most.
The objective is to contribute meaningful ideas.

Come prepared with 3-4 structured perspectives, listen carefully to others, and whenever appropriate,
acknowledge someone's point before building upon it.
This demonstrates maturity, collaboration, and professional communication.

4. Never Compare Your Journey with Others

This is probably the biggest lesson from our process.
Different candidates had:
 Different interview panels.
 Different technical questions.
 Different interview durations.
 Different numbers of technical rounds.
Some candidates had one interview.
Some had two.
Some had three.
Some finished within 15 minutes.
Others continued for much longer.
None of these factors indicated whether they would eventually be selected.
Focus only on your own preparation and performance.

5. Continue Preparing While Waiting

There can be long waiting periods between rounds.
My Technical Interview concluded at around 11:50 AM, and my HR Interview was completed by
approximately 12:20 PM. However, several other candidates continued with their technical interviews until
3:00-4:00 PM, and the final results were declared only around 5:00 PM.
Don't get distracted , just focus.

6. Never Underestimate the Online Assessment

Personally, I found the Online Assessment to be one of the most stressful stages because it is a major
elimination round and many highly capable candidates are filtered out at this stage.
Looking back, I feel I could have performed even better with more timed practice and additional preparation
for Market Awareness.

Do not assume that a strong resume alone is sufficient--the Online Assessment deserves dedicated
preparation.

7. If I Had More Time...

Looking back, there are a few things I wish I had done even better.
 I would have attempted CFA Leve

positive and confident.

5. Interview Round 1 [29 students were shortlisted for this round]

Before the interview rounds, one thing to keep in mind is that there is no fixed interview
structure. Some candidates had only one interview, while others went through two or even three
rounds. The process varies from person to person, so don't compare your process with others.
Stay patient, trust the process, and focus on giving your best in each round.
There were 6 interview panels, and my interview was scheduled last in my panel.
My first interview lasted around 45-50 minutes. During the interview, I faced network issues on
many occasions-once while the interviewer was asking a question and another time while I was
answering. I remained calm, politely informed the interviewer whenever the connection was
interrupted, and resumed the conversation once it was resolved. If you face a similar situation,
make sure to immediately inform both the interviewer and the TPO. Handling such situations
professionally leaves a much better impression than panicking.
Questions asked:

• Find the total number of squares on a chess board(8x8)

• 67*73 (wanted the final answer)

Any questions? At the end of the interview, I was asked if I had any questions. I
asked about:

• The career progression and growth opportunities for a fresher joining the CIB Banking

role.

• How is Al being used in the day-to-day workflow at JPMorgan Chase, and do analysts in

this role get to use tools such as SQL and Power BI?

• What are the primary sources of data that analysts work with in this role?

(Prepare 3-4 questions beforehand, and frame it in an interesting way, shouldn't be a
forced question)

6. Interview Round 2

I was called for this round immediately after Round 1, so I would recommend staying near the
TPO throughout the recruitment process. Although I was informed that it would be an HR round,
it turned out to be another interview round instead. So, be prepared for any type of interview,
regardless of what the round is called. This round lasted around 15-20 minutes and was
conducted by a single panelist. At the beginning, the interviewer mentioned that the interview
would be fast-paced and that he might interrupt me while I was answering to save time, so I
shouldn't take it personally. He also made it clear that he would be tough, and the interview
reflected that.
--- PAGE 6 ---
Most of the questions were based on my responses, with each answer leading to several
follow-up questions. The interviewer asked a few trick questions, repeatedly asked "Are you sure
about that?" "Do you want to try again?", and even explored topics I had admitted I wasn't
familiar with. The aim was to assess both my understanding of investment banking concepts and
how I handled pressure. My advice would be to stay honest and maintain a learning
attitude don't pretend to know something you don't, as interviewers love to grill on it.
Questions asked:

1. Introduce yourself

2. What do you think investment bankers do apart from investment banking?

3. What is the difference between buy side and sell side?

4. What are PE firms and VC? What's the difference between them? Give 2

examples

5. Do you invest in stock markets? (to which I stated no, but I follow it regularly)

6. What sector do you think will grow in the near future? Why?

7. Tell me 2 stocks of that Sector(I had said Pharma) and their PE ratios?

8. What is PE ratio? Should it be high or low? (trick question... are you sure)

9. Gave a hypothetical situation of 2 companies one having PE 5 and other 10,

which would you choose to invest in? How to check if stock is undervalued /
overvalued

10. Can you explain what an IPO is? Why does a company opt to go public?

11. Could you walk me through the key steps involved in the IPO process?

12. Tell me about one recent IPO you have followed closely. What was your analysis

or takeaway from it? (I told him about the upcoming Jio IPO in depth)

13. During the IPO book-building process, if investors bid at $10, $15, and $20,

which price would the company ideally choose as the issue price, and why? Does
the stock usually list at the same price?

14. Have you heard of the Greenshoe option? (I had read about this, but didn't know

it in depth, so I told him whatever I knew and an example when it is used)
That was the end of the interview. I wasn't able to answer some of the questions, and whenever I
didn't know something (for example, whether a higher or lower P/E ratio is preferred), I was
honest about it and said I would read more about it instead of guessing. The interviewer
remained very serious throughout the interview and simply asked me to leave once it ended.
Since the interview lasted only about 15 minutes, I walked out feeling that I had fumbled a few
questions and wasn't very confident about my chances of getting through.

7. HR Round

--- PAGE 7 ---
This round took place almost 2 hours after Round 2. By then, I was completely exhausted and
had almost convinced myself that I should start focusing on other companies, as I felt Round 2
hadn't gone well. The TPO then called out the names of 8 shortlisted students and asked us to
come inside. We weren't told whether it was another interview round or the HR round, so there
was a bit of uncertainty until we entered.
There were two interview panels, and I was the second candidate in my panel. The interview
lasted around 10 minutes and felt more like a conversation than a formal interview.
The interviewer was very friendly and immediately recognized me from the Pre-Placement Talk.
He asked, "You're the one who was asking and answering questions during the PPT, right? You
seem quite excited about this opportunity. " That instantly boosted my confidence.
He started by asking how my day had been and how I felt about the recruitment process so far.
We then moved on to a few standard questions, including Tell me about yourself," "Why
Finance?", "Why JPMC?", along with questions about my family and where I live.
He was also curious about the volunteering work I had done as part of my second-year
community project. We discussed the impact of the initiative and what I had learned from the
experience. Towards the end, he asked about the Minors in Finance and Strategic
Management mentioned on my resume and how they had sparked my interest in the field of
finance. He also asked about my future plans. In the end again I was asked if I had any questions
so keep 1-2 hr related questions also ready.
Although many people consider the HR round to be the easiest, don't take it lightly. Try to frame
your answers around the following points:

• Show a genuine interest in finance and a willingness to learn and explore the field.

• You know about the Company and have well-researched about it and the roles being

offered. So, be attentive during the pre-placement talk and also read about JPMC's
mission, vision, goals, and values from their website.

• Highlight your extracurricular activities and leadership experiences to demonstrate that

you can work well in teams and handle responsibilities. Use examples from your
committee or other leadership roles wherever possible.

• If asked about higher studies say NO. Instead, mention that you would first like to gain

practical experience in finance, build a strong foundation, and pursue professional
certifications such as CFA.
10 students were offered the role.

Useful Tips:

--- PAGE 8 ---

• Start preparing for finance at least by the beginning of 6th semester. The earlier, the

better. At the same time, keep doing tech side-by-side.

• Build your basics well. Knowing fewer topics in depth is much better than knowing many

things superficially. Remember that the interviewers know you're from an engineering
background, so they don't expect you to know everything.

• Your introduction guides the entire interview. Make it unique and interesting so the

interviewer wants to know more about you.

• Don't take the PPT or resume shortlisting lightly. They are a very important part of the

process.

• Start building your finance base carly by taking up finance minors, certifications, or

case study competitions. Winning doesn't matter-the exposure and learning do.

• Have something apart from academics on your resume, whether it's committee work,

leadership roles, sports, or any hobby you genuinely enjoy. It always adds value.

• Maintain a decent CGPA. From what I observed, 8+ generally works well, and JPMC

also seemed to consider 10th and 12th scores during shortlisting.

• Be very thorough with your resume. Know every small detail mentioned in it, as many

interview questions come directly from there.

• Always keep a smile on your face, no matter how the interview is going. Stay positive,

trust your preparation, and give your best.
For me, what carried me through the entire process was confidence and a positive attitude. I had
decided from the very beginning that I would give it my best. I was actively involved during the
PPT by answering and asking questions, and I feel that confidence stayed with me throughout the
interviews. I also believe my committee experience and leadership roles played a big part.
Interacting with juniors, faculty, sponsors, and other stakeholders taught me how to communicate
with people and stay confident in conversations.
Finally, the placement process is mentally exhausting and full of ups and downs. In the end, it
comes down to hard work and a bit of luck. You can't control luck, but you can control your
preparation. Your efforts are never in vain-they always teach you something and
eventually pay off. Keep working hard, stay patient, and your opportunity will come.
Resources:

• Check your resume score using https://resumeworded.com/score.php (keep it above 75)

My resume: Shlok_JPMC (ATS score was 81)

• Aptitude: https://www.indiabix.com/

CareerRide

• Guesstimates: (There's a ton of videos available on their channel so make sure to explore)

ALL THE VERY BEST!!!
(feel free to reach out to me on whatsapp or LinkedIn if you have any more doubts)

1. Pre-Placement Talk [open to all]

The recruitment process begins with the Pre-Placement Talk (PPT), where senior leaders from
CIB, Risk, and HR introduce the company, explain the roles being offered, and provide an
overview of the recruitment process and expectations.
Although many candidates treat it as a formality, it is a valuable opportunity to learn about the
company and make a positive first impression. Stay attentive throughout, participate whenever
appropriate, and ask thoughtful, role-related questions during the Q&A instead of generic ones
like CTC or the number of candidates being hired.
In my case, the HR representative who conducted the PPT was also one of my interviewers. He
remembered my participation during the session, and it helped establish a positive rapport at the
--- PAGE 2 ---
start of the interview. So, don't underestimate the PPT-it can give you an advantage even before
the actual interview rounds begin.

2. Resume Screening

Candidates need to submit their applications on both the JPMC Careers Portal and the Google
Form shared by the TPO. It is advisable to apply as early as possible. While applying on the
JPMC portal, you'll be asked to upload your resume and have the option to attach a cover letter.
Although optional, I would recommend including one.
As communicated by the TPO, While the stated eligibility was a 7+ CGPA, I would recommend
maintaining a CGPA of 8.0-8.5 or above to be on the safer side, as shortlisting can be
competitive. Based on previous years' trends, having a strong academic record (especially in 10th
and 12th - 80%+) and meaningful achievements outside academics can further strengthen your
profile. Publications, research work, leadership roles, and certifications such as CFA Level I
are also viewed positively, though don't guarantee a shortlist.
Resume Tips:

• Follow a latex template - Resume. Keep it single-column and try to minimise

white-spaces as much as you can (remove the lines having just 1-2 words...optimise
whitespace)

• Target a 80+ ATS Score. (Link - https://resumeworded.com/)

• Include your 10th and 12th marks in the Education section, especially if they are strong.

• Keep the sections in a logical order: Education → Work Experience → Positions of

Responsibility → Projects/Publications → Achievements/Extra-curriculars → Skills.

• Tailor your resume to the job description by incorporating relevant keywords and

highlighting impactful achievements.
67 candidates were shortlisted for the next round.

3. Online Aptitude Test

The test window was 10:30-11:00 am and the duration was 45 mins. It had 4 sections, with no
negative marking and navigation was allowed.

• Basics of Finance and Accounting : 10 questions

3 financial statements, ratios, Depreciation, effect of changes in line items on all 3 statements,
dividend yield, and basic corporate finance

• Market awareness: 10 questions. Questions were not necessarily finance based but general

current affairs.

• Quantitative Aptitude: 15 questions.

--- PAGE 3 ---
Questions based on Profit and Loss, Workers and Time, AP GP HP, Probability, etc. (Normal
Aptitude questions).

• Verbal Skills: 10 questions.

Passage based, rearranging, standard questions.
The test was lengthy so try to attempt things you know and equal parts from all sections rather
than acing one section. Check for negative marking, generally the Risk role carries -1 marking
for wrong answer.
55 students were shortlisted. The result was announced only a day before the interview, so even
if test was bad, don't stop preparing there's always a chance.

Tips:

• Practice aptitude questions from IndiaBIX. Cover all major topics first, then switch to

timed mock tests, as speed and accuracy are equally important.

• For aptitude concepts, I found this playlist very helpful: CareerRide. It covers most of

the commonly tested topics.

• Build the habit of following business and financial news. I used Finshots Daily and

Zerodha AfterMarket Report podcasts. This helps not only in the current affairs section
but also during interviews.

• Keep your accounting fundamentals & corporate finance basics clear, especially the

three financial statements and financial ratios.

4. Group Discussion

[55 students were shortlisted for this round]
The results were announced on 1st July, one day prior at approx 8pm, which was just one
day prior to the process. The topic for the GD was also given late at night at approx 9pm.
GD Topic -
"Your company sells through both online and offline channels and sources a meaningful
share of its inventory from overseas. Due to a disruption in global shipping, inbound lead
times are approximately 2x longer for around two months, and shipping costs have

Due to heavy rains, we were informed that rest of the process will be held online [online

We were called at 8:15 am for the GD, and 55 students were divided into 6 groups of
9-10 candidates. In my panel there were a total of 3 panelists, one was the moderator, and
introduced new sub-topics and questions, the rest panelists were seen to make notes and
judge body language, and points you make.
