--- PAGE 4 ---

• Try to have at least 1 entry for each new sub-topic, and make sure your body language is

positive and confident.

• It's okay if you haven't got a chance to speak, the moderators will ask you about your

opinion, and give you a chance to speak.

• Everyone can and will have similar points and example, try to have a unique and different

angle to the same topic (ex. Some political viewpoint, or view from a manager/CEO
which mattered in our topic... for this try discussing the same with relatives, friends in
finance). This had given me an edge.

• Try using good examples, or numbers to back the points you make, please make it

relevant to the sub-topic in discussion.

5. Interview Round 1 [29 students were shortlisted for this round]

Before the interview rounds, one thing to keep in mind is that there is no fixed interview
structure. Some candidates had only one interview, while others went through two or even three
rounds. The process varies from person to person, so don't compare your process with others.
Stay patient, trust the process, and focus on giving your best in each round.
There were 6 interview panels, and my interview was scheduled last in my panel.
My first interview lasted around 45-50 minutes. During the interview, I faced network issues on
many occasions-once while the interviewer was asking a question and another time while I was
answering. I remained calm, politely informed the interviewer whenever the connection was
interrupted, and resumed the conversation once it was resolved. If you face a similar situation,
make sure to immediately inform both the interviewer and the TPO. Handling such situations
professionally leaves a much better impression than panicking.
Questions asked:

1. Tell me about yourself.

2. What do you expect your responsibilities to be if you're selected for the CIB

R&A Banking role?

3. Explain the three financial statements, how they are linked, and the impact of a

$10 decrease in depreciation across all three statements.

4. What is working capital? Explain its components and how changes in each

component affect cash flow.

5. Do you actively follow or invest in the financial markets? What sectors do you

track and why?

6. What are the Nifty 50 and Sensex? How are they calculated, what are their

current values, and what has been the recent trend in these indices?

7. What is the Repo Rate and Reverse Repo Rate? What are their current values?

8. Why does the RBI increase or decrease the repo rate?

--- PAGE 5 ---

9. How does the government/RBI use the repo rate to control inflation and support

economic growth?

10. How has the RBI used the repo rate in response to recent geopolitical and

economic events?

11. What is valuation? Explain the different valuation methods.

12. Explain what is meant by Enterprise Value and Equity Value. Formula. Why do

we add debt and subtract cash to find EV.

13. Among the three commonly used valuation methods, which one do you think

provides the most realistic valuation, and why?

14. What is FCFF, how is it calculated? Why Net Profit isn't used to calculate the

Enterprise Value.

15. How is the discount rate calculated? Have you heard of WACC. Can it be used to

1. Pre-Placement Talk [X]

• Participate actively, but avoid repeating points others have already made.

• Ask meaningful, role-specific questions don't ask questions just for the sake of speaking (e.g.,

"How many people are you hiring?").

• Focus on understanding the role, responsibilities, career growth, team structure, training, and

relocation requirements (if applicable).

• HR may also ask questions based on the PPT, such as: "What are two things you liked about the

pre-placement talk?" (I was asked this question in HR round)

• Maintain professional etiquette throughout the session.

Key Takeaway: Use the PPT to learn about the role and company and location of job.

2. Resume Shortlisting [X → 67]

Your resume is one of the most important parts of the selection process. Start early and tailor it to the role
you are applying for.

• Keep it to one page and use a single-column LaTeX format.

• Optimize for ATS; check your resume on ResumeWorded (aim for a good ATS score).

• Include relevant projects, internships, coursework, achievements, and case competitions.

• For finance roles, add 1-2 strong finance projects and relevant finance certifications.

• You can make small role-specific changes to your resume before interviews.

• Use format Resume

"Walk me through your resume", " What was your job role and overall internship experience" (I was
asked these questions in Technical round)
Key Takeaway: You will be asked questions based on your resume so make it so that it steers the interview
towards your strengths and away from your weaknesses.
--- PAGE 3 ---

3. Online Aptitude Test [67→55]

• Format: 45 MCQs, 45 minutes (1 mark each). Speed and accuracy are crucial.

Sections:

• Corporate Finance & Accounting (10): Inflation, repo rate, financial statements, financial ratios,

bonds, GDP, and basic accounting concepts.

• Market Awareness (10): Current affairs in finance and business. Stay updated with financial news,

but expect some unpredictable questions.

• Quantitative Aptitude (15): AP/GP, Probability, Permutations & Combinations, Ratios, Profit &

Loss, Time & Work, Speed-Time-Distance, Mixtures, SI/CI (IndiaBix-level).

• English (10): Reading comprehension, grammar, sentence correction, vocabulary, and a few data

interpretation (bar/pie chart) questions.
Preparation Tips:

• Maximize your score in Quant, English, and Finance, as they are more predictable.

• Focus on finance and accounting fundamentals rather than advanced valuation topics.

• Practice Quant under strict time limits to improve speed and accuracy.

Key Takeaway: Completely Finish Indiabix.com, get basics of financial ratios, interest rates, bonds strong
and read key happenings ie. which manufacturing plants are inaugurated recently etc.

4. Group Discussion [ 55 → 29]

The topic for the group discussion was revealed on 2nd July around 8pm and the next day we had to report
around 8:30 am so make sure to do your research prior to the d-day.
G.D. Topic: "Your company sells through both online and offline channels and sources a meaningful
share of its inventory from overseas. Due to a disruption in global shipping, inbound lead times are
approximately 2x longer for around two months, and shipping costs have increased, affecting financial
metrics. As the CEO, how would you tackle this situationại

• Format: Around 9 students per panel. This is not a traditional GD the moderator asks specific

questions, and the discussion evolves around those questions with follow-up prompts.

• Research the main topic and its possible subtopics, as follow-up questions are common.

• You will typically get to speak only 2-3 times, so make each opportunity count. Aim for 30-45

second responses with 2-3 relevant points each.

• Avoid memorized or rigid viewpoints. Be open to changing your stance as the discussion progresses.

• Don't interrupt or dominate the conversation. Agree when appropriate, disagree respectfully when

you have a valid reason, and build on others' points.

• Support your arguments with facts, examples, or insights from reputed sources (e.g., BCG,

McKinsey, World Bank, RBI) when relevant.

• Stay calm, humble, and articulate. Quality of contribution matters far more than speaking the most.

Key Takeaways: 2-3 Short 30s bursts of quality information in a calm and humble way should do the trick.
Think of unique points and not the plain simple stuff.
--- PAGE 4 ---

5. Interviews [29 → 10]

A) Technical Interview [10 minutes]
Please refer to other experiences for non resume-oriented interview styles,
My technical interview was almost entirely resume-driven, with most of the discussion centered around my
internship in Portfolio Management. The interviewer was less interested in definitions and more interested
in whether I could think like someone actually working in the role.

• Be prepared to explain every line of your resume in detail. Expect follow-up questions on what you

did, why you did it, how you did it, and why you chose a particular approach.

• Use proper financial terminology and clearly communicate the objective, methodology, and outcome

of your work.
My Interview Experience
After asking me to explain my Portfolio Management internship, the interviewer said:
"Suppose you are my portfolio manager. What would you do?"
From there, the interview became a live portfolio construction exercise.

• I first assessed the client's risk profile, investment horizon, and objectives before recommending an

investment strategy.

• Based on the assumed risk appetite, I proposed an equity allocation across major Indian sectors

(Banking & Financial Services, IT, Pharma, FMCG, Capital Goods, Auto, Energy, Defence etc.).

• For every sector allocation, he asked:

• Why this sector?

• Why not allocate more or less?

• What macroeconomic or industry factors support your decision?

• Once he was satisfied with the sector allocation, he went one level deeper.

• He then asked me to recommend 3 specific stocks (My ans included one pre-ipo stock) and justify

every choice using company fundamentals, growth prospects, competitive positioning, valuations,
and overall investment thesis.

• Throughout the discussion, he continuously challenged my assumptions and asked me to defend my

reasoning rather than simply state an answer.
A fortunate aspect of my interview was that 2 of the stocks I recommended had gained around 4% during
the trading session (the interview was around 2:30 PM, with about an hour left before market close). While
this was because i'd looked at them one night prior, a large coincident, it strengthened the credibility of my
recommendations and led to further discussion on why I had selected those companies.
Preparation Tips

• Know every project and internship on your resume in depth.

• If you mention portfolio management or equity research, be ready to discuss:

• Asset allocation

• Sector allocation

• Stock selection

• Risk profiling

• Portfolio construction

Current market outlook

• Investment rationale using financial terminology

--- PAGE 5 ---

• Expect interviewers to keep asking "Why?" until they understand your complete thought process.

Key Takeaway: Technical interviews are often practical rather than theoretical. Your ability to justify
decisions with structured reasoning is far more important than simply knowing finance concepts.
A small observation from my experience: almost everyone around me had 2-4 technical interviews, each
lasting 20-30 minutes, whereas I had only one technical interview that lasted about 10 minutes, and I
was among the last candidates to be interviewed. At the time, it was easy to overthink this, but it turned out
fine. Don't judge your chances based on interview length or compare yourself with others. My only
objective throughout the interview was to have a genuine finance conversation, explain my thought
process honestly, and learn wherever possible and that mindset helped me stay calm and perform
naturally.
B) HR Interview [15 minutes]
The HR interview was conversational and relaxed. Stay calm, be genuine, and avoid saying anything
inaccurate or contradictory.

• Expect questions based on your resume, including activities beyond academics. For example, I was

asked about my marketing gigs and other extracurricular experiences.

• Most candidates who reach this stage are typically being evaluated for fit rather than technical

ability, so enjoy the conversation and let your personality come through.
10 students were shortlisted for the Banking role.
Not getting selected immediately doesn't mean it's over-another 10 students were shortlisted for the CR
role the next day from the separate candidate list for CR role.
--- PAGE 6 ---

Technical & HR Interviews

Current Affairs

• https://affairscloud.com/

• CNBC news especially at 3:30

Financial Accounting Fundamentals:

• If you're taking FSM (Financial Services Management), pay attention in class. The subject

provides an excellent foundation for finance interviews, and a significant proportion of the
selected candidates in our batch had taken FSM.
Resources given by my seniors (not completely used by me but very useful): Non TechPrepList
--- PAGE 7 ---
Final Tips

• A CGPA above 8 is always helpful, but don't get discouraged if yours is lower.

• Take the GD seriously-it's often one of the biggest differentiators.

• Start building your profile early through internships, projects, certifications, and case

competitions.

• If you don't have an internship, compensate with a strong finance project that demonstrates practical

skills.

• Be confident with finance fundamentals; interviewers value clear basics over advanced knowledge.

• Read financial news consistently, not just a few days before the interview.

• Be polite, professional, and dress formally (light shirt, dark trousers; a suit/tie is perfectly

appropriate).

• Network with other aspirants(always grateful for my friend Nitya's inputs) -- you'll learn a lot by

preparing together.

• Stay humble throughout the process and don't judge your chances until the results are out.

Have fun with finance!!!
As someone who came from a tech-first background, I went into the interview simply hoping to have a
great finance conversation and learn from the interviewer. That genuine curiosity helped me stay
relaxed, think clearly, and, I believe, made a stronger impression than trying to sound perfect.
This is your journey, and your experience will be different from everyone else's. Keep learning, keep
improving, and give your best every single day.
Focus on the effort, not the outcome. Control what you can, trust the process, and let the results take
care of themselves.
I'm always excited to have a good conversation about finance, markets, investing, or careers- whether it's to
exchange ideas, learn something new, or help however I can.
Feel free to reach out to me anytime in uni or on Whatsapp if you have any questions or just want to talk
finance.
Wishing you all the very best!

• The most important thing to remember is that there is always a luck factor involved in these

processes - you might have done everything right but sometimes it just is not your day. You can

• Even if you don't know the answer, try explaining your thought process. They help you reach the

will feel the most tensed while going to give the GD, if that goes well then you will be confident

prepare without worrying about the results.

• Practice generic HR questions - What are your short term and long term plans, plans for further

• Talk to your seniors in your target company, talk to people already working in your target industry,

The pre-placement talk was scheduled online on 24th June. Try to ask questions and give answers if you
can. They ask questions like any specific major IPO or M&A deal that occurred within the last 2 years.

1. Resume Screening: Deadline 26th June

2. Online Aptitude Test: 27th June

3. Group Discussion (Online)

4. Interview round 1 (Online)

5. Interview round 2 (Online)

6. Interview round 3 (Online)

7. HR round (Online)

Rounds 3-6 were scheduled on 2nd July.
Just a general heads-up: the number of interview rounds is completely random. I had to go through three
finance interview rounds, while some candidates had only one. So don't be surprised if your interview
process differs from someone else's.

1. Resume Screening

We had to submit all details and resume via the JPMC portal. You are also allowed to attach a cover letter,
although not mandatory, do submit one.

• Use the latex template and add only things you are confident about. Keep it single column, one page.

• You will need around 5 to 6 copies of your resume as your panel may have more than one

interviewer.
67 students were shortlisted for the next round.

2. Online Aptitude Test

The test window was 10:30-11:00 am and the duration was 45 mins. It had 4 sections, with no negative
marking and navigation was allowed.

• Basics of Finance and Accounting : 10 questions

• Market awareness: 10 questions. Questions were not necessarily finance based but general current

affairs.
--- PAGE 2 ---

• Quantitative Aptitude : 15 questions.

Questions based on Profit and Loss, Workers and Time, AP GP, Probability, etc. (Normal Aptitude
questions), CAT level.

• Verbal Skills : 10 questions.

Passage based, rearranging, standard questions.
The test was lengthy so try to attempt things you know and equal parts from all sections.
56 students were shortlisted. The result was announced less than a day before the interview so be prepared.

3. Group Discussion | 56 selected students were divided into 6 panels of 9/10 each. We had Around 30

mins]
The GD topic was revealed on 1st July, just one day before the process:
"Your company sells through both online and offline channels and sources a significant portion
of its inventory from overseas. Due to a disruption in global shipping, inbound lead times have
doubled tor approximately two months, and shipping costs have increased, negatively impacting
financial metrics. As the CEO of the company, how would you tackle this situation?"
A few important things about the GD:

• No notes or reference material were allowed during the discussion.

• There were 2 panelists observing the GD.

• Instead of a free-flowing discussion throughout, the panelists introduced different situations one after

another, and the group discussed each before moving to the next.
The situations included questions such as:

1. Should the company increase the prices of its best-selling products to offset the higher shipping

costs?

2. If the entire disruption were resolved overnight, what would be the first thing you would do as the

CEO?

3. How to approach while keeping in mind the on paper losses?

Tips for the GD

• Aim to speak in at least 2-3 of the situations.

• Quality matters far more than quantity. You do not need to speak for a long time if your points ar

well-structured and relevant.

• Wherever possible, support your arguments with numbers, percentages, or business metrics. This

makes your points more credible.

• Try to make unique, insightful points that others can build upon. A good indicator of a strong

contribution is when other participants reference your point before adding their own perspective.
Finally, GD performance influences your interview order. Candidates who performed better were generally
scheduled for interviews earlier. I was the first person called for Round 1 after the GD. The overall process
is quite lengthy, so don't lose patience while waiting for your turn.
28 students were shortlisted for round 1
--- PAGE 3 ---

4. Interview Round 1 [ My round lasted for about 40 mins]

There were 6 interview panels, and my interview was scheduled first in my panel.
The interview began with the interviewer asking me to introduce myself. Make sure you have answers to the
standard HR questions prepared, as I was asked to introduce myself in every interview round.
The discussion then progressed as follows:

• She asked me what I thought my role would involve.

• She moved on to the stock market, asking about Sensex and Nifty. Make sure you know the previous

day's closing values for both indices.

• She asked whether I invest personally and which sectors I would invest in, along with the reasoning

behind my choices.

• Next, she asked about the RBI, its monetary policies, inflation, and the current RBI Governor.

Tip: If you don't know the answer, don't guess. It's better to admit that you haven't read about
it than to give incorrect information.

• She then shifted to financial statements:

o Explain the link between the Income Statement, Balance Sheet, and Cash Flow Statement.

• She gave a scenario: "If depreciation expense is overstated by 710, how would it impact all

three financial statementsạẠạ

• She also asked about recent trends in the financial markets, so stay updated with current business and

economic news.

• She asked me why IB?

The interview concluded with a few analytical and puzzle-based questions, including:

• An average speed problem

• The classic water jug puzzle

• Finding the angle between the hour and minute hands of a clock at a given time.

Always end the interview by asking a thoughtful question. Don't waste the opportunity by asking generic or
easily searchable questions. Instead, ask something that demonstrates genuine curiosity about the role or the
team. A strong closing question can leave a positive final impression.

5. Interview Round 2 [ This round was for 15-20 mins]

I was called for Round 2 approximately 45 minutes after completing Round 1.
This round had one panelist. The interview began with the usual "Introduce yourself" question, followed by
a few questions based on my resume.
The interviewer then shifted to core finance concepts, focusing primarily on valuation:
Explain Enterprise Value (EV) and Equity Value.
What is the difference between Enterprise Value and Equity Value?
How do you calculate each of them?

• When is Enterprise Value preferred over Equity Value, and vice versa?

He also asked me about several valuation ratios, including:

• P/E (Price-to-Earnings) Ratio

• EV/EBITDA

For each ratio, he expected me to explain:
--- PAGE 4 ---

• What the ratio represents.

• Why is it used?

• What insights it provides about a company.

• In which situations it is most useful.

He then gave me a valuation case study. He provided the market capitalization and P/E ratio of two
companies and asked me to calculate the combined P/E ratio after the two companies merged.
I wasn't able to solve it immediately, but I explained my thought process and approach at every step.
Whenever I got stuck, the interviewer provided small hints, and using those inputs I was able to work
through the problem and arrive at the correct answer.

6. Interview Round 3 [ This round was for 20-25 mins]

I was called for Round 3 approximately 45 minutes after completing Round 2. There was one panelist for
this interview. The interviewer started by asking me how the overall interview process had been. Keep your
response positive and professional. Throughout the interview, maintain good eye contact, smile naturally
when appropriate, and stay confident.
The discussion then moved into valuation concepts:

• Enterprise Value (EV) and how it is affected by debt and cash.

• Why debt is added and cash is subtracted while calculating Enterprise Value.

• FCFF (Free Cash Flow to the Firm):

• What it is.

• The formula used to calculate it.

• Why FCFF is used for Enterprise Value valuation.

• Difference between FCFF AND FCFE.

• Why do we need both Enterprise Value and Equity Value instead of just one valuation metric?

• EV/EBITDA:

• Why is EBITDA used in the denominator?

• Why Net Income is not used instead.

The interviewer was particularly interested in how I arrived at my answers, not just the final response. Even
if you're unsure, explain your reasoning and thought process clearly. Interviewers often provide hints if they
see you're approaching the problem logically.
My Round 2 and Round 3 interviews did not go as well as I had hoped, but I was still shortlisted. One
interview rarely determines the final outcome, so don't lose confidence if you feel you've made a few
mistakes. Stay calm, composed, and positive throughout the process.
At the end of the interview, I asked a few questions about:

• The company's growth opportunities.

• Career progression within the organization.

• The kind of work and learning opportunities available for new hires.

10 people were selected for the HR round.
--- PAGE 5 ---

7. HR Round [ Around 10 mins ]

This was the easiest round of the process. There was one interviewer, and the discussion was largely
HR-focused. The interview started with the standard "Introduce yourself" question, followed by:

• Why Investment Banking despite having a Software Engineering background?

• Do you plan to pursue higher studies or any professional certifications in the future?

• What would your plan be if you were not selected for this role?

For questions about your future plans, it's important to demonstrate a strong commitment to a career in
finance. Even if you have long-term plans for higher studies, avoid giving the impression that this role is
only a temporary stop. Instead, communicate that you genuinely want to build your career in finance and are
excited about the opportunity the company offers.
Throughout the conversation, make it clear that:

• You have a genuine interest in finance.

• You are eager to learn and grow within the organization.

• You see yourself building a long-term career with the firm.

At the end of the interview, I was asked if I had any questions. I asked about:

• Growth opportunities within the organization and what differentiates employees who progress

quickly.

• The role of HR in the recruitment and employee development process, and how HR collaborates with

different business teams throughout an employee's journey.
These questions led to a good discussion and helped end the interview on a positive note.
The process on the 2nd started around 9 and we got the results by 5 pm. 10 students were selected for the
Banking role.

1. Resume Shortlisting

Out of all the applications received, 67 students were shortlisted for the next round, the Online Assessment
(OA). This stage is often underestimated, and your resume plays a crucial role in securing a shortlist.
Take your time to build your resume and follow a clean, professional, and consistent format. Carefully check
for formatting issues, grammatical errors, and spelling mistakes before submitting. A good ATS score alone
does not guarantee a shortlist; the overall quality and relevance of your profile matter significantly.
Although the minimum CGPA criterion specified by the company was 7.0, it is advisable to maintain a
CGPA of at least 8.0 to remain competitive.
For your resume, try to include:

• One or two finance-related projects, preferably including a Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) valuation

project.

• At least one FinTech or data analytics project that demonstrates technical and analytical skills.

• Relevant internship experience and positions of responsibility.

• Participation in case competitions, especially if you were a finalist or winner.

• Certifications relevant to finance, analytics, or technology.

Wherever possible, quantify your achievements by including meaningful numbers and measurable impact.
Tailor the skills section of your resume according to the job description provided by the company and
highlight the skills most relevant to the role.
Once the company shares the registration link after the PPT, make sure to submit your application as early as
possible.
--- PAGE 2 ---

2. Online Assesment [67 students were selected]

The Online Assessment (OA) consists of 45 multiple-choice questions (MCQS), with 1 mark awarded for
each correct answer. The section-wise breakdown is as follows:

• 10 Questions: Corporate Finance and Accounting

These are primarily basic finance and accounting concepts. If you have prepared well for finance
fundamentals, this section should be manageable.

• 10 Questions: Market Awareness

Stay updated with current affairs, business news, recent mergers and acquisitions (M&As), and
major developments in the financial markets, as questions can be asked from a wide range of topics.

• 15 Questions: Quantitative Aptitude

The questions are generally easy and doable, but the section is time-constrained. Practising under
timed conditions is highly recommended. I used IndiaBIX for preparation, which I found quite
helpful.

• 10 Questions: English

This section is relatively straightforward. If your fundamentals in grammar, vocabulary, and reading
comprehension are clear, you should not face any major difficulties.
The OA is an important stage of the selection process, so start your preparation well in advance. Also, there
is no negative marking for CIB (Banking), so make sure to attempt all the questions, even if you are
unsure of some answers.
Out of 67 students 56 went for Group Discussion

3. Group Discussion [56 students were selected]

The GD topic and shortlist were shared just one day prior, at around 9:00 PM, so don't lose hope if you
haven't received an update yet-keep preparing and stay patient.
GD Topic:
"Your company sells through both online and offline channels and sources a meaningful share of its
inventory from overseas. Due to a disruption in global shipping, inbound lead times are approximately 2x
longer for around two months, and shipping costs have increased, affecting financial metrics. As the
CEO, how would you tackle this situationạ
We were divided into 6 panels, with each panel consisting of around 9 students. Approximately 20 minutes
were allocated for the GD. However, this was not a traditional group discussion. The discussion was
conducted more like a Q&A session, where we were asked specific questions and were expected to share our
views only on those questions.
Therefore, it is important to:

• Understand the GD topic in depth and research it thoroughly.

• Think about possible subtopics and follow-up questions that may arise from the main topic.

• Stay updated on current affairs and business trends related to the topic.

A few tips for the GD:
--- PAGE 3 ---

• Try to speak at least 2-3 times during the discussion.

• Ensure that all your points remain relevant to the topic being discussed.

• Be clear, structured, and confident while presenting your views.

• Avoid using heavy jargon unless you fully understand its meaning and can use it appropriately.

• Listen carefully to others, be respectful, and maintain a civil discussion.

• Do not try to dominate the conversation; evaluators value quality of inputs and collaborative

behaviour more than the quantity of speaking time.
Remember, the evaluators are looking not only at your knowledge but also at your clarity of thought,
confidence, communication skills, and ability to think under pressure.
28 students were selected for the interview

4. Technical Round [28 students were selected]

The shortlist for the interview was released quite quickly after the GD round.
The interview was primarily focused on the resume, so make sure you know every point on your resume
thoroughly. Be prepared to answer questions on your projects, internships, positions of responsibility,
certifications, and any achievements that you have mentioned.
Apart from your resume, the interviews also tested general financial knowledge. Some commonly asked
topics included:

• How to value a company

• Valuation methodologies and valuation multiples

• Macroeconomic concepts such as the repo rate and its impact

• Puzzles and guesstimates

• Basic accounting and finance concepts

The questions varied significantly across panels, and every panel seemed to have a different approach.
Therefore, it is difficult to predict the exact questions that will be asked. The best strategy is to have a strong
grasp of your resume and a solid understanding of finance fundamentals.
The interview process was also quite uncertain and dynamic. Some candidates had to go through three
technical rounds, while others had only one interview round before receiving a decision. Hence, be patient
throughout the process and do not lose hope if your process differs from that of others. Focus on your
preparation and trust the process.

4. HR Round students students were selected]

The HR round was very relaxed and felt more like a casual conversation than a formal interview. The key is
to stay confident, communicate clearly, and showcase your personality while aligning your answers with
JPMC's core values.
Some of the questions that were asked included:

1. Tell me about yourself and why you want to pursue a career in finance.

2. A detailed discussion on one of the projects mentioned on my resume.

3. What is one thing you liked about JPMC from the Pre-Placement Presentation (PPT)?

--- PAGE 4 ---

4. Do you have any questions for me?

The questions can vary from panel to panel, but overall, the HR round is primarily aimed at understanding
your motivations, communication skills, and cultural fit for the firm.
A few tips for the HR round:

• Be genuine and conversational rather than sounding overly rehearsed.

• Have a clear answer for "Why Finance?" and "Why JPMC?"

• Know your resume and projects well, as they may ask you to elaborate on any point you have

mentioned.

• Read about JPMC's values, culture, and ethics beforehand and try to reflect them naturally in your

answers.

• Go through the job description (JD) carefully and understand the qualities the firm is looking for.

For example, the JD for this role placed significant emphasis on team collaboration, so I
consciously highlighted instances where I worked effectively in teams and incorporated this point
into my answers.

• Prepare a few thoughtful questions to ask the interviewer at the end.

• Stay calm, smile, and treat the interaction as a normal conversation.

Overall, the HR round was very chill and was more about getting to know you as a person than testing your
technical knowledge.
10 students were selected for CIB banking role

--- PAGE 1 ---
Vedant Agarwal
Computer Engineering

Company: J.P. Morgan Chase & Co. (JPMC)

Job Profile: Corporate & Investment Banking (CIB)

1. Resume Shortlisting

The first round was resume shortlisting. Although JPMC never disclosed the exact criteria, from what we
observed, factors like your Class 10 and 12 marks (there seemed to be an unofficial 80% cutoff), CGPA,
relevant projects, internships, certifications (I had completed CFA Level I), and the overall quality of your
resume all seemed to matter.
Preparation

• Tailor your resume according to the role you're applying for.

• Make sure you're comfortable explaining every single point on your resume.

Tips

• Keep your resume clean, concise, and free of grammatical or formatting mistakes.

• Check your ATS score using Resume Worded. Don't stress too much about the score though-I

know people with scores around 60-70 who still got shortlisted.

• Don't add skills or projects just to fill space. If it's on your resume, be prepared to talk about it in

detail.

2. Online Assessment (From Home)

Duration: 45 minutes
The test consisted of:

• Basics of Finance & Accounting (10 questions): Financial ratios and basic corporate finance.

• Market Awareness (10 questions): These weren't necessarily finance-based. Many were simply

current affairs and business news. (Few questions were very random so do not worry about them. For
eg, i had a question "What is the duration of long crops according to Kisan Credit Scheme")

• Quantitative Aptitude (15 questions): I practiced from IndiaBix → General Aptitude → Arithmetic

Aptitude, which was more than enough.

• Verbal Skills (10 questions): Sentence arrangement, grammar, graphs, averages, and similar

questions.
Preparation

• Revise your finance fundamentals.

• Stay updated with current affairs and business news. I personally read The Economic Times daily for

about a month before the test.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Tips

• Time management is really important, especially in the Quant section since some questions can be

lengthy.

• If you're stuck on a question, move on and come back later instead of wasting too much time.

3. Group Discussion (Online - Zoom)

The GD topic was shared a day before, so everyone had enough time to prepare. On the day of the interview,
we were divided into panels of around 6-7 students each.
My Experience
Our panel wasn't a traditional GD where everyone keeps jumping in. The panelists asked questions, we had
to raise our hands on Zoom, and they picked people to answer. They also made sure everyone got a chance
to speak at least once.
I spoke twice, for around 30 seconds each time. Since everyone gets the topic beforehand, most people end
up preparing using the same resources (and ofc ChatGPT), so naturally a lot of the content overlaps. I'd
suggest trying to speak within the first two or three people so your points haven't already been covered.
From what I telt, they weren't really checking whether your content was unique-they were looking at how
well you listened to others, whether you could build on someone else's point, and how confidently and
clearly you presented your ideas. If you know the answer to a question, raise your hand confidently. At the
same time, don't interrupt others or try to dominate the discussion-it leaves a bad impression.
Tips

• Focus on making meaningful points instead of speaking the most.

• Listen carefully to what others are saying and build on their ideas whenever possible.

• Stay calm and communicate clearly.

4. Technical Interview

My technical interview was actually much shorter than many other candidates. (around 10 minutes)
Questions Asked

• Walk me through your resume.

• What's the difference between Investment Banking and Commercial Banking?

• How do Investment Banks earn fees?

• Guesstimate: Assume India has a population of 1,000 people and you're the only supplier of TVs.

Nobody currently owns a TV. Estimate how many TVs you would sell.
Preparation
--- PAGE 3 ---

• Revise everything you've mentioned on your resume.

• Be ready to explain your projects in detail.

Tips

• If you don't know an answer, don't panic. Just explain your thought process they're often more

interested in how you think than whether you reach the perfect answer.

• Ask at least one question at the end. Since I had completed CFA Level I, I asked about the CFA

culture at JPMC and whether employees are encouraged to pursue the higher levels while working.
S. HR Interview
The HR interview was much more conversational than the technical one.
Questions Asked

• Tell me about yourself.

• Tell me about your family background.

• If you were the interviewer, what three qualities would you look for in a candidate?

• How do you handle a conflict?

• Explain the case study competition that you won.

Preparation

• Prepare the common HR questions beforehand.

• Read about the company, its values, and any recent news.

Tips

• Be genuine. Don't try to give textbook answers.

• Wherever possible, support your answers with examples from your own experiences.

• Prepare a couple of questions for the interviewer. I built on the question I'd asked during the

technical interview and asked why JPMC reimburses CFA exam fees for employees who clear the
exams while working there. It turned into a nice conversation.
Useful Tips

• The waiting time between rounds can honestly be more stressful than the interviews themselves. Try

to keep yourself busy by watching something or keep revising. In my case, the waiting time
throughout the day was longer than all my interviews combined, so I ended up watching Suits to take
my mind off the anxiety.

• Personally, I prepared for the following questions as well:

o any recent IPO, MnA, stock you would recommend

• JPMC share price, JPMC full form, JPMC values

o Current NIFTY, SENSEX, gold, silver, brent oil prices
--- PAGE 4 ---

• All current RBI and US-Fed rates (repo, reverse repo, CRR, SLR, MCLR, inflation targets -

just check them on the RBI official website)

• Foreign exchange rates (US-INR, EUR-INR)

• Know your resume inside out.

• Don't lose confidence if one round doesn't go exactly how you expected.

• Lastly, just be polite, humble, and communicate your thoughts clearly. That goes a long way.

it. You can't change your mind in the middle.

• If you feel you don't have any knowledge on the topic then it's okay to let a few people speak as it

will allow you to gather some info and you can then think of a point or you could agree/disagree with
someone's opinion. DO NOT DOMINATE THE DISCUSSION.

• Ensure that you speak 2-3 times during the discussion. If you have spoken more than that, then you

could allow someone else to speak who hasn't spoken at all. That shows the moderator that you
include everyone into the conversation and consider everyone's opinion.

4. Business Round

19 people were shortlisted for this round and I was the first to interview. The interview was online on zoom
with two people from JPMC. The interview lasted for 40-45 minutes. First I wished both the interviewers
Good Morning and asked them how they were doing. Following are the questions asked during the
interview:-

1. Tell me about yourself.

2. Tell me about a project from your resume.

3. In this project what were the challenges you faced and how did you resolve them?

4. Since the project I explained was an agentic Al project they asked me to explain the graph structure

and what LLM i used for the agents and why. Also they asked the latency and cost factors.

5. If you are given a dataset how would you analyze it and what tools would you use? Tell the entire

process

6. Tell me about a time you were on a project and you had no experience with that field or the tools

used for it? What did you do?

7. Have you used Al tools like Github Copilot, Claude Code, etc.

8. How do you write a good prompt for Claude?

9. Do you have any experience with python, alteryx, etc.

--- PAGE 3 ---

10. Do you know how to make Al agents?

11. Why should we hire you?

5. HR Round

8 people were shortlisted for the HR interview. This was the most chill round which lasted for 15-20 minutes
and I was asked easy and casual questions like:-

1. Tell me about yourself besides what's on your resume.

2. Where do you live and where are you originally from?

3. Tell me about a time when a team member was sidelined/overshadowed by others and their opinions

were not considered in the decision making process? What did you do and how did you solve this?

4. Tell me about a time when an argument broke out between team members. How did you approach

this situation and solve it?

5. Tell me about a weakness that you think you have.

6. Where do you see yourself in five years?

Out of the 8 people, 7 were finally selected and I was among them !!!.

Useful Tips:

• Know your resume thoroughly. [MOST IMPORTANT] Every project, technology, and skill

mentioned on your resume can lead to follow-up questions. Be prepared to explain your project's
architecture, the challenges you faced, the decisions you made, and the reasoning behind them. Your
resume is your selling point. You have to pitch them your skills and experiences!!!

• Based on what I've seen in this year's placement cycle, DSA isn't as important as it used to be. More

emphasis is on Al concepts and Al tools and how you have used them in your projects. I suggest
solving only easy and medium questions in DSA (unless you want to give FAANG interviews!) .
Agentic AI, GenAl, Claude Code,etc. are what companies are interested in these days!

• Internships are something that will favour you in an interview as it gives you something to talk about

and show that yes, this person does have some corporate experience. So I suggest doing at least 1
internship before placements.

• Based on the rapidly changing job market, I suggest not preparing for just ONE role. Rather its good

to have both tech and non-tech experience since you never know what you will end up doing.
Hence, don't limit yourself to one role. Explore everything !!!!! (preferably in 3rd year itself since it
gives you time and options to decide.....)
--- PAGE 4 ---

• Practice aptitude regularly. The Online Assessments are highly competitive and often the most

difficult round, so solve questions under timed conditions to improve both speed and accuracy. For
Aptitude, IndiaBix website (https://www.indiabix.com/aptitude/) is the best and CareerRide youtube
channel.

• For Interviews:-

a. Prepare a strong self-introduction: It sets the tone for the interview and often determines
the direction of the discussion.
b. Understand the role, not just the company: Read about JPMorgan Chase, the role offered,
and the different teams discussed during the Pre-Placement Talk. Paying attention during the
PPT can be helpful during interviews. Bringing a few points up from the PPT into the GD or
interview surprises interviewers !!!!
c. Focus on your thought process: Interviewers are more interested in how you approach a
problem than in memorized answers.
d. Be brutally honest, no lies: If you don't know an answer, admit it confidently instead of
guessing. Interviewers appreciate honesty and will move on to the next question.
e. Ask meaningful questions: Prepare one or two questions for the interviewers. It
demonstrates genuine curiosity about the role and the organization.
f. Stay calm: Confidence comes from preparation and interviews become much easier when
you treat them as discussions rather than interrogations. Imagine you know them beforehand
and they are your friend (but don't get too casual and friendly, formality also has to be
maintained!)

• Topics Worth Revising before interviews

a. Python fundamentals, pandas, and data cleaning
b. SQL queries, joins, aggregations, and subqueries
c. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) and data visualisation
d. Basic statistics and analytical reasoning
e. Machine learning fundamentals, if mentioned on your resume
f. Al agents, LLMS, RAG, and prompt engineering,
g. Project architecture, technology choices, limitations, latency, and cost
h. Group discussion topics related to Al, automation, remote work, and digital payments
i. Behavioural questions on teamwork, conflict resolution, leadership, and adaptability

• The placement process is grueling and competitive. It eats you up and starts affecting your attitude

and behaviour. I interviewed for 7 companies before JPMC and i had given up also but everyday you
have to keep moving forward despite the past. I never expected to get placed at JPMC and I had no
hopes going into the process as well. But I was determined to give my best despite the results and
voila!! I cracked it. So bottom line NEVER GIVE UP NO MATTER WHAT. Believe in yourself
and keep moving forward. Preparation and determination will always open doors for you and make
opportunities run towards you !!!!!
--- PAGE 5 ---
I hope this interview experience helps you prepare for the Corporate Analyst Development Program at
JP Morgan Chase. The questions and recruitment process may vary, but I hope my experience gives you a
useful starting point.
Phone No: 9324268237
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/dwayne-fernandes-8398a0345/
Resume: https://drive.google.com/file/d/163PMX9-u3huiP91LJHI6erRC-SccJ8Gp/view?usp=sharing
In case of any further doubts, you can refer to the past interview experiences shared by TPO.
ALL THE BEST !!!!!

The first stage was resume shortlisting, followed by three rounds: Group Discussion, Business Round
(Interview 1), and HR Round (Interview 2). All the 3 rounds were held in an online zoom meeting.
For this particular role, your resume can include both technical and non-technical projects or internships, but
make sure you are thoroughly familiar with everything you mention. Try highlighting relevant skills such as
Advanced Excel, Power BI, or similar tools that align with the role requirements. The 3 core domains were:
project management, process improvisation and intelligent analytics - read about them from the job
description and gain basic knowledge about them. Lastly, ensure your academic scores, particularly 10th,
12th and CGPA, meet the 75%+ or 7.5+ CGPA safety benchmark.
You can check your ATS score using Resume Worded (60-70 is a good range).

1. [Group Discussion] [77 students were selected after the resume shortlisting]

Each group had 12 participants and was given around 15-20 minutes to discuss the topic and arrive at a
conclusion. My group was given the topic "Mobile Wallets - Advantages and Disadvantages." The topic
was relevant to recent developments around MDR charges on UPI for vendors and other initiatives
promoting digital transactions. Another group was given "Work From Home vs Offline Work." Hence, it is
advisable to stay updated with current and trending topics such as Al replacing manual work, digital
payments, changing workplace trends, etc., since the topic is given on the spot with no preparation time.
If you are strong with content but face communication issues, make good use of the mock GD sessions
conducted by the college. Focus on speaking fewer but valuable points, while also being an active listener
and building on others' arguments rather than trying to dominate the discussion.

2. [Business Round] [ 19 students were selected for this interview and divided into 2 panels]

Most interviews begin with the standard question "Introduce yourself", so prepare this well and highlight
your key skills, experiences and achievements. Follow-up questions are often based on your introduction, so
know your resume thoroughly-anything mentioned can be questioned. I was asked about the case
competitions I had won and even about leverage and D/E ratio since it was mentioned in my resume.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Apart from resume-based questions, I was asked about current topics such as "What is your view on MDR
charges? Are they necessary?" and "What is the impact of the Make in India initiative on you as a youth?" I
was also asked situational questions, such as whether, as a JPMC manager, I would reduce a team from 20 to
2 after implementing an Al system with 98% accuracy, and if not, how I would justify the investment.
Hence, prepare for situational and decision-making questions as well.
Finally, if you mention Excel, Python or Power BI on your resume, be prepared for basic questions such as
syntax and implementation of VLOOKUP, handling null values in Python, etc. In case you prepared only for
non tech roles and do not know the python syntax tell them that you do not code or do dsa but focus on
finance, case studies, power bi and related stuff and give evidence for the same projects/internships (they
will divert the question in that direction and its better than saying i dont know or a wrong answer)

3. HR Round] [8 candidates were selected for this round]

In this round, your presence of mind, interpersonal skills and confidence are tested, so it is important to
remain attentive, composed and confident throughout. You may be asked to introduce yourself again or
share something about yourself that is not mentioned on your resume. Questions like "Why this role?" and
"Why do you want to work at this company?" are common, along with situational questions based on your
resume. For example, since I was the Vice President of a Rotaract Club, I was asked about a situation where
I had a disagreement with another club member and how I handled it. Towards the end of the interview you
will be asked if you have any questions for them - you can ask any valuable question or something you are
genuinely interested to know like the work culture there, whether they encourage interns and employees to
pursue CFA levels or an equivalent course, what qualities should a good intern possess to progress, etc.
Overall, show genuine interest in the company and role, communicate clearly, and maintain a professional
attitude throughout the interview.

Before starting with everything I first want to say that you will hear alot of people saying that LUCK
matters alot during placement season. I personally feel it's not always about luck but also about timing.
When your luck and timing aligns, that is the day you achieve everything that you have ever wished for.
So till then keep your head down, do your work and become that best version of yourself! :)
If you are from EXTC - I have listed the names of the company that didnt allow extc to sit for
placements. Some companies might allow EXTC students to participate during your placement
season, but it's good to be prepared.
Pre-placement talk - 25th September
For this all I can say is just listen to what the speakers are saying and personally I never once raised
my hand to ask a question during any of the PPT sessions because I never felt the need to. But for
some people it works. So always ask genuine questions if you have any and don't ask just for the sake
of asking . The interviewers might hardly remember your name as they interact with so many people
on a daily basis.
If you feel you have good questions then keep them for the interviews as interviewers might like your
questions and they might remember you.
Always take screenshots so during the interviews you can refer and ask questions.
Also keep in mind that this role is a 2-year rotational program after your internship. During those 2
years you will have 3 rotations each of 8 months and then you will be promoted to ASSOCIATE role at
JP Morgan ( got this from one of our alumni, they don't mention this during the talk). The 6 months
internship stipend will be 60k . The ctc for the two years was not disclosed . But it will be the same as
other roles offered by jpmc (found this also from the seniors:)).
--- PAGE 2 ---
Resume Shortlisting [around 200 students who were unplaced]
My resume for JPMC - por [Navya_Sinha_JPMC.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1c6driT6Zb7uVfMQrye36hA2Bqe_eH3U8/view?usp=sharing)
My SDE resume -
Por [Navya_Sinha_SDE (2).pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1hh49TH_qGiwizLupMSB-3TTN62m7_cCb/view?usp=sharing)
Since the role had analytics in it, I added 2 data analytics projects and one DCF valuation and one ml
project. The shortlisting was mainly on the basis of 12th std marks and your CGPA. If you have 1-2
semesters left try to keep your pointer above 8 because most of the companies have this criteria. Try
to keep your ATS score above 75. Keep altering your resume according to the requirements of the
company and ATS score increases if you add numbers, So try to add a few metrics around your
resume.
We received the list of shortlisted candidates around 7pm, before the day of interviews.

2. Group Discussion- 29th September [approx 75 students ]

6 groups were made each of around 12-13 students.
Our topic was - Mobile Wallet (Pros and cons)
Some more topics that I got from my friends - Work From home (beneficial or not), UPI payments.
The GD was conducted in online mode and we weren't given any time for the prep. So as soon as the
topic is given make sure you unmute yourself and start speaking. Also there wasn't a thing like raising
your hands and then the speaker lets you speak, so everyone will try to speak together, make sure you
stop whenever someone else is speaking and if you have a valid point then continue so that the person
in front stops (it's kinda messy but it works).
Always give some examples relating the topic to your own personal experience.
Speaking 2-3 times is more than enough and always keep nodding your head when someone else is
speaking (this shows you are paying attention).
Always try to be among the first 3 people who start the discussion. This creates a good impression.

3. Technical Interview [19 students ]

My interview started after the lunch break around 2 pm. There were 2 panels and in every panel
there were 2 panelists. The panelists made me comfortable by asking "did i have my lunch" and
greeted me. One important thing to remember for any interview is to keep smiling. Have a small
smile on your face ALWAYS. I cannot stress on how much it tells about your confidence to the
interviewer.
The round started by them introducing themselves and asking me for my introduction.
Now I wanted my introduction to be unique so that they actually listen to me rather than just
looking at my resume. I gave my introduction like -ạI am Navya Sinha, currently an extc student at
spit minor in blah blah", then i said "from the first year of my college everyone around me started
doing courses in tech and due to peer pressure even i started focusing on my technical skills and
that's how I landed up an internship at XYZ company" then talking about my internship and what I
did there. (Both the interviewers smiled when I said it like this).
--- PAGE 3 ---
Make everything in your resume like a story. Example for extracurricular activities - "Apart from
academics major part of my college life has been about teamwork and leadership and hence i
served as VCS in student's Council...." This creates a better impression than just saying "I interned
at this company" and "I was also VCS in the student's council".
After my introduction, one of them directly asked me to explain a particular project and what i did
, why i did, was it even necessary. Make sure to know each and every word in your resume and
justify how your project was actually needed.
My webscrapping project was the one that caught their attention and it was basically about
automation (Since automation is the work that we might do during our internship)
So he asked me every question possible.
I was also asked for counting the number of null values which python function I used
(df.isnull.sum()
Then they asked me

• What is non-controlling interest?

• What is the credit conversion cycle?

• What is meant by assets and liabilities in terms of credit conversion cycle? (Amounts receivable

and payable, and which comes under what)

• What is meant by deferred revenue? Does it come under current or non current liabilities?

• Explain me the steps involved in a company going public (basically non disclosure agreement,

due diligence, how sebi works, roadshows etc)
They were quite impressed that I knew the answers since it was analytics role, then they asked me
situational questions

• If your senior manager takes the credit for all the work that is done by you and your team how

would you react?

• What are your strengths and weaknesses? (Always try to answer these questions honestly and

in weaknesses mention how you are overcoming it)

• If one of your team members is overshadowed and is an introvert how would you help him

open up and share his ideas?
(In situational based questions try your best to relate it to the real world as if it has happened with you
and how you tackled the problem).
For JPMC REMEMBER TO ANSWER IN SUCH A WAY THAT YOU PUT CLIENTS FIRST AND AT TOP
PRIORITY.
Then the worst nightmare of my life.
My interviewer said "Since you are from EXTC, tell me something about the semiconductor industry"
OMG my jaw dropped when he asked me this question. (Lets be serious nobody expects this) I still
smiled and started saying anything that came to my mind, I can't even remember it clearly, but I said
something about taiwan, Gpt astra came and now pobs can also be designed blah blah ...
Then as I was saying something he stopped and asked "So are you saying that there won't be jobs
when the semiconductor industry booms? " At this point I knew I had to say something crazy so that
he would stop asking me about this topic. I gathered all the confidence I had and explained "I am not
saying it won't create jobs, All I am saying is it won't create entry level jobs and freshers would be
--- PAGE 4 ---
expected to know more than usual as Al can now do all the basic tasks for which interns were
requiredỊẠi
He was quite impressed, So then again he asked "So tell me how a chip is manufactured and goes to
production. Give me all the steps includedỊạ
At this point I was like "Isko reject hi karna hai toh muh pe karde na bhai. Analytics ke role mei chip
production kon puchta hai". Being an EXTC student, because of the pressure I couldn't even
remember eaglecad where we design the layout. So now I thought, 'I'm going to get rejected anyway
so "gracefully reject hote hai" Hence I said something gibberish whatever came to my mind.
Now, when I look back, I feel the reason I got selected was because I kept smiling and answering with
confidence even when such out of the box questions were asked. So always always be confident.
Lastly I was asked if I had any questions. I asked them 2 questions -

1. How has your journey been in JPMC and what values have you learnt from the organisation

(they love talking about themselves)

2. As a working professional what advice would you give to a young student who is going to join

the company (again they love giving advices)
The answer to the last question was so traumatizing that after that I was so sure I was getting
rejected.
The answer was - "Your generation don't listen to understand, they listen to respond"
I felt it was targeted towards me so I just smiled and said I will remember this point and left.

4. HR Round [8 students ]

After round 1, I had lost all hopes and went down. My main concern was the semiconductor question
and then the answer that the interviewer gave. I was sitting outside tpo with my friends almost
with tears in my eyes and till then 2 people had already called for HR from the other panel. Then
suddenly tpc comes and calls my name and tells me I have my HR round scheduled. It was just 10
mins after my first round 1. Along with me, all my friends were shocked as I had told them "aaj toh
nahi ho raha"
I got up and went inside, I knew HR as she was the one presenting during the pre placement
talk and I really liked her energy. She asked for my introduction and then asked me 3 questions

• Why JPMC and Why CADP? (classic question, One response I had memorized was -

"JPMC is a place for me where I'll join to learn but I'll stay to lead" one of my friend told
me this)

• What is the most complex problem you have ever solved and how did you approach it?

• Have you ever faced disagreements during your internship, and how did you handle

them?
Then she asked me if I was okay with relocation and working night shifts as we have to work
according to the US timings. She asked me if I had any questions and I asked her the same question
about advising.
--- PAGE 5 ---
Overall this round was chill.
My HR was over by 3:30 pm and we had to wait till 8pm for the results. Now everyone keeps telling
me "ho jayega" But I have had bad experiences with HR . I had given 7 interviews before JPMC and in
every interview I went to HR and got rejected. Hence for me clearing HR was the biggest challenge.
Around 8pm the results were announced and 7 students were selected, and thankfully I was among
them!
A backstory of my placement season (read only if you have time)
I was primarily interested in SDE role from 2nd year. I won hackathons and had good tech projects. So
I never really focused on non tech roles. Infact when JPMC came for the first time in July, I only
filled the form for fintech role. It is August when I started preparing for Non tech when JPMC came
for the second time for CTC role but i couldnt clear the assessment.

Pre-Placement Talk (25th September) (online):
Be attentive during the meeting and listen carefully to role-specific discussions and the information shared
by the team. This will help you understand the role better and prepare relevant questions for the interview. It
is also recommended to note down the names of the speakers and HR representatives, as you might be asked
about them during the interview( not mandatory but recommended).
Take screenshots of important slides whenever required so you can refer to them later. If you get an
opportunity to ask questions, ask something genuine that you are actually curious about. Avoid asking
questions just for the sake of it or using GPT-generated questions without understanding them. A thoughtful,
relevant question is always better than a forced one.
--- PAGE 2 ---
1.
Resume Shortlisting [~200 students had applied]
Por Soham Jadhav Resume_JPMC.pdf
Since this was an analytical role, I included two data analytics projects, a DCF valuation project, and a
Power BI project. I also added a technical AI/ML project, as I was comfortable with that domain. Keep your
resume to a single page, aim for an ATS score of 75+(ResumeWorded can be used to check ats score), and
tailor it according to the company's job description (JD).
Your 12th-grade percentage and CGPA can play a significant role in shortlisting, as many companies have
eligibility criteria such as 80%+ in 12th and an 8+ CGPA. If you meet these requirements, that can be an
advantage. However, at the end of the day, shortlisting also depends on several factors, and luck plays a
major role in whether your resume gets selected and at times it is a bit random too, but keep going.

2. Group Discussion [ 76 students ]

Six groups of around 12-13 candidates were formed, each with a different GD topic. My panel discussed
"Should organisations opt for work from home for selected roles?" (topic given on spot) Another panel
discussed digital payments and India's transition towards a cashless economy. The GD was conducted on
Zoom (from college campus) for around 20 minutes, with one minute to think and note down points.
However, candidates in my panel started speaking almost immediately.
Starting or concluding the GD is a plus. I spoke third and got three opportunities to put forward my points,
either continuing the discussion or presenting a positive counter-argument. Since there was no raise-hand
option, we had to find our own opportunities to speak. Be mindful of when to interrupt and when to let
others finish, ensuring your points are relevant and constructive.

3. Business Round (Technical Round) | 19 students]

My interview was scheduled for around 12:30 PM. There were two panels, each consisting of two
interviewers, on the Zoom call.
The interview started with me greeting the interviewers, followed by a short and crisp self-introduction.
They then moved on to the projects mentioned in my resume.
Since DCF valuation was the first project on my resume, the first question was: "What is DCF?"
They asked a few basic questions about DCF, and I explained what I had done, how I approached the
valuation, and what my analysis concluded.
The obvious follow-up questions were:

• Why did you choose DCF instead of other valuation methods?

• What made you interested in studying finance when you had initially been inclined towards

technology?

• When did you start preparing for finance?

--- PAGE 3 ---
They then asked about my technical project, including what I had built, how I implemented it, and which
technologies I had used. I explained the complete project workflow, its implementation, and the target
audience it was designed for.
The interviewer seemed satisfied with my explanation, after which the other interviewer moved on to
situational and general questions to understand my thought process and point of view.

1. If you are working in a team and the other members are not contributing, what would you do? How

would you handle their responsibilities? The interviewer followed up by asking what I would do if
they still failed to coordinate even after I had helped them.

2. What would you do if your manager disclosed sensitive information publicly or used it for personal

benefit? I had recently read about a similar case, so I supported my answer with that example.

3. What is the difference between chip design and chip development? I wasn't fully aware of the

technical details, and the interviewer also seemed to be exploring the topic. I tried to support my
answer with another example, which helped keep the discussion going.

4. Given the current situation, should the Indian government invest more in technology, considering

that many Indian companies primarily provide services to multinational corporations?
At the end, I was given the opportunity to ask questions. I asked three:

1. A question about the role and its responsibilities.

2. How the growth and learning curve at JPMorgan Chase would look for someone joining this role.

3. If I received an offer, what standout qualities would they expect from an intern to help them perform

well and become a stronger prospect for the company? I was advised to ask this question during the
HR round if I progressed further.

4. HR Round [ 8 students ]

I was called for the HR round at around 4 PM, after a long wait. The interview was relatively short, lasting
approximately 15 minutes.
The HR introduced herself and asked me to introduce myself. After greeting her, I gave my introduction.
She then asked me to "Tell me something outside your resume." I spoke about my hobbies and shared a
little more about myself.
The HR asked a few questions to understand my personality, teamwork, and approach to challenges.

1. Tell me about a time you faced obstacles while working on something and how you tackled them. I

framed my answer in a way that also showcased my interest in finance.

2. If a teammate wants to contribute but feels left out, how would you handle the situation? I used an

example from one of my hackathons to explain my approach.

3. How have you handled a situation where you disagreed with a teammate? I shared another relevant

example to explain how I approached the disagreement.

4. What attracted you to this role?

5. Do you currently have any offers?

6. Would you be comfortable relocating for the job, and would you be comfortable with the job

requirements?
--- PAGE 4 ---
I tried to keep the conversation playful, friendly, and positive throughout the interview.
Towards the end, I asked two questions:

1. JPMorgan Chase has a strong legacy and established policies, ethics, and values. How does the

organisation ensure these principles are upheld in everyday work?

2. If selected, would I get opportunities to explore domains beyond the three verticals mentioned

earlier?
At around 8pm the final results were out and 7 students were selected out of 8.

journey.prep:
From the start of the placement season my target was non-tech companies, this didn't mean that I did not
apply for tech companies. You never know, an opportunity can appear out of thin air and you must be ready
to grab it. So keep applying and not losing hope. The entire process can be stressful and unpredictable, but
rest assured that you will have multiple but limited opportunities. You just have to be brave enough to apply
and give it your best shot each and every time. I got dropped in the very last round of two companies which
were also very good opportunities but there was something better planned for me. So staying at it is a must!
Here are a few tips to prepare for non tech companies:
Note: I am considering data analyst roles as non-tech too
Keep your Aptitude strong and this is by far non-negotiable. Practice a variety of problems, time yourself
and keep working on speed. You can use IndiaBIX and can practice CAT pyqs for a greater difficulty. Give
timed tests if possible, you can find these too on IndiaBIX.
Practice Business Case Studies thoroughly and visualize how you will answer such problems in an
interview.
--- PAGE 4 ---
These books might help:
por [IIMI 2023-24.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1wz_Kg1WBYoDivEf4bnByCSNhq2sMS-rp/view?usp=drive_link)

Por [6.-Wharton-Casebook-2017.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1b8E2xfixgawxUEdVq3sbSFA5Lz0TptcJ/view?usp=drive_link)
Por [ISB_Consulting_Casebook_CO2020.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1vzt-6AHUnhJS9Nwxn3amfuB52kK6jXVu/view?usp=drive_link)
Practice Guesstimates: have a few guesstimates already prepared based on your resume (e.g my resume had
a project based on data analysis of amazon so prepare a guesstimate on how many deliveries amazon makes
in a day in mumbai) apart from that practice guestimates in general. You must know a few numbers like the
population of India/Maharashtra/Mumbai, age wise percentage breakdown, land area in sq km of mumbai,
etc. This book might help
PoF [Guesstimates-Book-Volume-1.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1sdgPLrCbGrqlC-_opkyhvnIdvUuj1g6b/view?usp=drive_link)
Practice Puzzles from geeks for geeks, they are genuinely interesting so you can go through them during
your commute/free time and discuss them with your friends.
Learn Python and its libraries, I learnt it while working on my projects but knowing a couple of libraries in
and out comes in handy (numpy, pandas etc)
Practice SQL problems, learn the basics and solve the Leetcode SQL50. Don't go for very complex queries;
anything above 10-12 line queries is not necessary.

1. Pre placement talk

2. Resume Shortlisting

3. Group Discussion

4. Technical Interview

5. Hr Interview

Pre-Placement Talk (Online) - 25th September 2026
The Pre-Placement Talk is the best place to get to know about the role you are applying for apart from the
Job Description. There were multiple presenters that day and explained everything thoroughly which
included what the job role is, what they expect from a candidate, the pay and finally the entire hiring
process. I feel when it comes to JPMC or any other company for that matter, it is important to religiously
attend the pre placement talk as sometimes they do ask in interviews (they didn't in this case) about what
was discussed in the pre placement talk or who were the presenters of the talk etc. Be active especially in an
online setting keep your camera on, ask doubts only if you genuinely have any.

1. Resume Shortlisting [Approx. 200 students]

It is very difficult to exactly point out the Dos and Don'ts for the resume shortlisting as it seems to be a bit
random. However some good practices are having a single page resume and having an ATS score of 70 or
above. Your CGPA and 12th scores matter a lot for specific companies so ensure they are mentioned
correctly. My goal in maintaining my CGPA was to be 8.00+ but I feel with increasing resume shortlisting
for many companies being 8.5+ is safer. Most Importantly you must have projects that align with the role
also your skills section should be role based. For the CADP role I had put up 3 projects, 2 data analysis
projects and 1 Business Analysis project (DCF modelling). I have attached the resume I had applied with
below:
Port [JPMC_HHG_CADP.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1NmAAfSizhpDVGASXFnT8-0VV0aFQl3hH/view?usp=sharing)
--- PAGE 2 ---
Note:- They mentioned in the pre-placement talk that this is not a finance heavy role and it is okay if you do
not have a lot of finance knowledge, but again it always comes in handy to know the basics if you are
applying for a bank.

2. Group Discussion (online) [76 Students ]

Groups of 12 people were made and there were 2 panels. Topics were not given beforehand, instead the
topics were given on the spot and we were given 2 minutes to think and start the discussion. The topic for
my group was "Are digital payments secure in India and are they helping us grow towards a healthy
cashless economằ We were allotted 15 minutes for the discussion. Some key points to remember are, do
not talk too less or even too much. 3 entries are more than enough excluding the intro and/or conclusion.
The major issue in this round since it was online was to get a turn to speak, as when one person finished
their point many would unmute and start speaking which lead to a lot of cross talk and unprofessionalism, be
patient but not passive. When you speak, ensure your points are unique and assertively conveyed. Do not
argue with anyone and try to constructively build from a point someone else has mentioned which has
similar meaning to your point. This doesn't mean that you always have to speak following others line of
thought, feel free to give your own unique ideas just ensure you do not sway off topic.

3. ¡Business Round (Interview round 1) | 19 Students ]

The interview started with a classic "walk us through your profile." My biggest takeaway here is to have a
compelling introduction prepared beforehand don't just wing it. Keep it engaging and ensure it provides a
strong gist of your resume. When asked about my approach to understanding clients as a new intern, I
emphasized the importance of internal communication. I mentioned that I would first talk to colleagues and
teammates to understand who the client is and gauge their expectations, ensuring I follow the proper chain
of command before initiating any direct contact.
We then moved to technical discussions, where I was asked to explain a project I was most comfortable
with. I detailed my data pipeline project since I was very thorough with its architecture. When they asked
who the project benefited, I was initially a bit unsure but honestly stated it was primarily a skill-building
exercise for me. However, I made sure to acknowledge how crucial it is to understand the real-world
business application of any project. Following this, they presented a scenario about using Al to summarize a
peer meeting and gauge audience expectations. I asked them to elaborate on the question first for clarity.
Once clear, I suggested deploying a live meeting recorder that notes discussion points, assigns weights based
on predefined criteria and time spent on topics, and generates a real-time summary by the end.
The behavioral questions tested practical decision-making and time management. When asked about a time I
considered a shortcut, I shared an instance from a case study competition. With less than an hour to the
deadline, we had five slides done and three pending. We considered using Al to instantly generate the
remaining three, but the output lacked consistency and quality. Instead of forcing eight mediocre slides, we
adapted and strongly concluded our presentation on the sixth slide itself. Finally, for a scenario involving
clashing deadlines between a manager's project and a client's last-minute modification, my approach focused
on transparency and delegation. I explained that I would politely inform the client that late changes are
challenging, assess the magnitude of their request, and either implement it fully (if small) or partially (if
large) to keep them satisfied. To manage the clashing internal deadline, I would temporarily delegate parts of
the manager's task to teammates to ensure both deliverables stay on track.
--- PAGE 3 ---
Most importantly: Ask very good and unique questions to your interviewers. I asked two questions at
the end of my interview. I say it is important because good questions can take an interview from
mediocre to a great right at the very end.

4. HR Round (Interview round 2) [ 8 Students ]

The HR round focused on cultural fit, personal values, and basic logistics. When asked to share something
not on my resume, I steered the conversation toward my sports background. I explained how my experience
in sports has shaped me into a collaborative team player and honed my ability to make difficult, real-time
decisions- qualities that directly translate to a fast-paced work environment. Later, they asked a behavioral
question on what "doing the right thing" means to me. I answered that it means upholding my own morals
and the ethics of the institution I represent, ensuring that I don't hurt anyone in the process of achieving
goals.
They also tested my communication approach by asking how I would explain a technical concept to a
non-technical audience. I pitched the idea of gamified learning, explaining that turning a complex concept
into a game makes the learning process much easier, relatable, and fun. For the standard logistical questions
regarding my willingness to relocate and my comfort with working across different time shifts, I kept it
straightforward and answered yes to both.
The googly of the round was when they asked what one thing would persuade me to quit this job for another
offer. I took a moment to genuinely think about it before answering. Ultimately, I chose to be honest and told
them that, at this point, I couldn't think of anything that would make me want to leave.
Again, I asked a couple of questions to conclude the interview.
7 students were offered the job
