Out of the three sections in Paper 1, the Probability section was the toughest of all. Going through JEE-level
probability and the probability topics studied in engineering might prepare you for this section, but it is still
very calculation-heavy, and time management became a crucial factor.
The next section was Logical Reasoning, which contained medium-level aptitude questions. One can expect
relatively straightforward questions on topics such as probability, mathematics, speed, distance, time &
work, profit & loss, etc.
The Coding MCQ section consisted of code snippets where you had to select the correct output. The
questions were of medium difficulty, similar to those covered in the PSIPL course, and all the questions
were based on the C programming language.
The last paper was English Usage, and the questions were of an easy level. They were based on vocabulary,
reading comprehension, grammar, etc.
Out of this round, only 9 candidates were shortlisted for the next round.

The candidates shortlisted for Technical Round 1 were divided into two panels consisting of 4 and 5
candidates, respectively. I was the second candidate in the first panel. My panel consisted of two
interviewers.

Technical:
This section started with the interviewer asking me about the four pillars of Object-Oriented
Programming (OOP) and explaining what each of them meant.
Next, he asked me what a palindrome is and how I would determine whether a given string/number is a
palindrome.
He then wanted to know my approach to printing an inverted triangle using stars/dots.
The discussion then shifted to Python and data structures in Python. I was asked about the differences

journey.prep:
1. Keep your options open. I initially intended to sit only for pure technical roles and had been

extensively preparing for them. At the same time, I was always open to exploring other
opportunities. I hadn't specifically prepared for non-tech roles, but unless it's a complete no-no for
you, I'd definitely recommend sitting for JPMC. It's one of the best opportunities we get on campus.

2. Understand the role and its progression. Do note that this Fintech role eventually transitions into a

Junior Analyst role after receiving a PPO. Keep the long-term progression of the role in mind and
decide accordingly before applying.

3. Use the few minutes before the interview wisely. Since our interviews were online, we got a

minute or two before joining the Zoom meeting. I used that time to calm myself down and gather my
thoughts. It often gets quite chaotic outside the TPO, so taking a moment to settle yourself before the
interview really helps.

4. Be yourself during the interview. Speak naturally instead of trying to fit in technical jargon

wherever possible. Using buzzwords without fully understanding them can land you in trouble if the
interviewer decides to explore them in depth.

5. Learn to breadcrumb the interviewer. At the same time, you can subtly guide the direction of the

interview. For example, DCF valuation is something that would normally be expected on the resume
of a Banking candidate rather than a Fintech one. I intentionally built a project around automating
that workflow and prepared every concept related to it thoroughly. This allowed me to steer parts of
the interview towards topics I was comfortable with. Breadcrumbing simply means introducing a
concept or technical term in your answers that is likely to catch the interviewer's attention and
naturally lead the next question in that direction.

6. Never judge your interview yourself. After my first technical interview, I genuinely wasn't

confident about my chances. Although I answered most of the questions, I found the interviewer
quite intimidating and he hardly gave away any reactions. He smiled only towards the very end when
I asked him about his journey at JPMC. At one point, he even thought I was using a calculator during
a mental math question, whereas I was just making calculations on paper. I had to show him my desk
to reassure him, and that was probably the second time he smiled. The rest of the interview was
completely poker-faced, so I walked out thinking I hadn't done well.

7. Make use of the time between rounds. While waiting, I had already started looking at other

opportunities on Superset, assuming I wouldn't make it through. Then, out of nowhere, I received a
call asking me to be ready for the next round. That experience taught me never to assume the
outcome of an interview. The time between rounds is extremely valuable. Use it to revise your
concepts instead of overthinking what went wrong.

8. Prepare good questions for the interviewer. Have at least 2-3 thoughtful questions ready. Avoid

asking the usual generic questions that interviewers hear all the time. Listen carefully to their
responses and ask meaningful follow-up questions based on what they say. It turns the interview into
a genuine conversation and leaves a much better impression.

9. Smile and tell stories during the HR interview. For the HR round, keep the widest smile possible

on your face. Try to answer questions using small anecdotes or experiences rather than giving
one-line responses. Stories make your answers more memorable, authentic, and convincing.

10. Get enough sleep before the interview day. We received the interview shortlist quite late the

previous evening, and I ended up pulling an all-nighter preparing for the interviews. Looking
back, I wouldn't recommend doing the same. The interview process is long, mentally
demanding, and can be quite exhausting, so getting a good night's sleep beforehand will help
you stay focused, think more clearly, and perform consistently throughout the day.
--- PAGE 8 ---
Final Thoughts
As we all know, a significant amount of luck is involved in the placement process. There are only so many
things that are within our control. What we can control is the effort we put into every opportunity that comes
our way. There will be times when shortlists feel unfair. There will be moments when you genuinely believe
you did everything right but still don't get the outcome you hoped for. That's a part of placements, and
almost everyone experiences it at some point.
The important thing is to never let one result define the rest of your placement season. Pick yourself up,
learn whatever you can from the experience, and move on to the next opportunity with the same enthusiasm.
Every interview teaches you something, and often the preparation you do for one company ends up helping
you crack another.
During this phase, surround yourself with the right people. The placement season can be mentally
exhausting, and having roommates, friends, seniors, and family who genuinely support you makes a huge
difference. Celebrate each other's successes, help one another prepare, and remember that everyone is
fighting their own battle.
Finally, enjoy the process.
Give every opportunity your best, stay curious, and trust that the Jigsaw will fall into place.
"Reach for the stars, so if you fall, you land on a cloud."
~ Kanye West - Homecoming (02:071
All the very best!

1. Resume Shortlisting [ 400+ appeared for this round]

The resume shortlisting for this role is quite rigorous, as comparatively fewer candidates are selected than
for other roles offered by the company. It is important to tailor your resume according to the job description,
focusing on relevant keywords, technologies, and projects that demonstrate automation and problem-solving
skills. For this role in particular, a strong academic profile is beneficial. While there is no official cutoff,
having a good CGPA along with consistently strong academic performance in 10th and 12th grade
(generally 80%+) appears to strengthen your chances of getting shortlisted.
Your resume should highlight relevant coursework, internships or work experience, certifications,
achievements, and positions of responsibility, which includes leadership roles in college committees or
organizations.
Since this is a Fintech role, including at least one finance-related project is highly recommended as it reflects
genuine interest in the domain. Personally, I took an extreme approach by keeping all my projects centered
around Fintech, machine learning, and automation, but a combination of finance-focused and technically
strong system design projects works equally well. Most importantly, include only those projects that you can
confidently explain end-to-end. For this role, interviewers place significant emphasis on concepts such as
data sourcing, data quality, data handling, analytics, visualization, and automation, so having a clear
understanding of these fundamentals is essential.
We got the final shortlist for OA a day before the test.
--- PAGE 2 ---

2. Online Assessment [ 34 candidates appeared for this round]

Test Pattern: CRG Junior Analyst Fintech
Paper 1: MCQ Assessment - 40 Qtns - 60 Mins - 40 Marks
Section 1: Puzzles and Probabilty - 18 Qtns
Section 2: Logical Reasoning - 10 Qtns
Section 3: Coding MCQ - 12 Qtns
Paper 2: English Usage - 10 Qtns - 10 Mins - 10 Marks
The Online Assessment was another crucial elimination stage, with only around one-third of the candidates
progressing to the interview rounds. The test was conducted online from home and consisted of two separate
MCQ-based assessments.
Paper 1: MCQ Assessment (40 Questions | 60 Minutes)

• Section 1 & 2 - Quantitative Aptitude, Probability and Logical Reasoning (28 Questions):

These sections required proper problem-solving rather than direct formula application. The questions
covered topics such as Probability, Permutations & Combinations, Speed, Time & Distance, Time &
Work, Pipes & Cisterns, Percentages, Profit & Loss, Ratios, Averages, Number Systems, Logical
Reasoning, Blood Relations, Seating Arrangements, Syllogisms, Coding-Decoding, Pattern
Recognition, and Analytical Reasoning. A strong aptitude foundation and familiarity with common
solving techniques significantly helped in managing time.

• Section 3 - Coding MCQs (12 Questions): This section did not involve writing code but instead

tested programming fundamentals through code snippets. Questions included predicting the output of
programs, completing missing parts of code, recursion-based output questions, basic data structures,
arrays, strings, functions, loops, and language fundamentals. Some recursion questions were fairly
tricky and required careful dry runs before selecting an answer.
Paper 2: English Usage (10 Questions | 10 Minutes)
The second assessment was entirely English-based and comparatively easier. It included a short reading
comprehension passage followed by questions based on it, along with MCQs covering vocabulary, grammar,
subject-verb agreement, sentence correction, sentence arrangement, and ordering sentences to form a
coherent paragraph or story.
Overall, the first assessment was not as straightforward as it may initially appear and required strong
aptitude and logical reasoning skills. It is important to prepare Quantitative Aptitude and Reasoning
seriously, as knowing standard solving patterns and shortcuts can make a significant difference. The coding
section also demanded patience, especially for recursion and output-based questions. For preparation,
platforms such as IndiaBIX and PrepInsta are more than sufficient, while the CareerRide Quantitative
Aptitude YouTube channel is widely used for conceptual understanding and practice. The English
assessment, on the other hand, was relatively easy and should not pose much difficulty with basic
preparation.
--- PAGE 3 ---

3. Technical Interview 1[9 candidates appeared for this round]

The interviews were scheduled for the very next morning, and all shortlisted candidates were asked to report
to the campus by 8:30 AM. Due to heavy rainfall, the interviews were conducted in online mode. There
were two interview panels, and my panel consisted of five candidates. The interview lasted for
approximately 30 minutes.
My interviewer was extremely interactive but equally intimidating. Interestingly, there was no formal
introduction; he immediately began by asking whether I had spoken to any seniors about the role and the
company. I would recommend doing so beforehand, as it demonstrates genuine interest and initiative in
understanding the role. I mentioned a senior I had interacted with, after which the interviewer questioned me
in detail about my understanding of the role based on those conversations. The discussion eventually became
two-sided when I asked him about the role and his day-to-day responsibilities, leading to an engaging
conversation.
The interviewer then shifted his focus to one of my projects that involved DCF valuation and the automation
of an equity research analyst's workflow. Since I anticipated questions on this topic, I had prepared
thoroughly. We discussed intrinsic valuation, discounted cash flows, WACC, its calculation, and the
reasoning behind each component. He then moved beyond finance concepts and explored the technical
implementation of the project, asking about the end-to-end workflow, data sourcing, the financial APIs used,
how the data was stored in a structured format, how financial ratios were computed, and how the final
valuation and peer benchmarking were performed.
One interesting discussion revolved around handling live market data. The interviewer pointed out that stock
prices are constantly changing and wanted to know how my system handled this challenge. I explained that
instead of continuously querying APIS, the application monitored rolling Z-score anomalies and refreshed
market data only when a significant deviation was detected, thereby optimizing API usage while ensuring
fresh data for valuation. He seemed satisfied with this approach.
Towards the end, he presented a practical scenario: given an Excel sheet containing financial data for peer
companies in the same sector, how would I build a complete analytics pipeline and an interactive dashboard
to generate meaningful insights? He expected a detailed end-to-end technology stack and implementation
workflow, and he cross-questioned the choice of every technology I suggested, making it important to justify
each design decision rather than simply naming tools.
The interview concluded with a few mental aptitude and reasoning questions, including calculations such as
102 × 98 mentally and finding the angle between the hour and minute hands of a clock. For such questions,
it is important to think out loud and keep the interviewer involved throughout your reasoning process.
Explaining your approach often matters just as much as arriving at the correct answer, as it gives the
interviewer confidence in your analytical thinking. I concluded the interview by asking the interviewer about
his journey at the company and his experience working in the role, which led to a pleasant closing
conversation.
Out of the five candidates in my panel, two were shortlisted for the next round, while one candidate
progressed from the second panel, making a total of three candidates selected for Technical Interview
2.
--- PAGE 4 ---

4. Technical Interview 2 [ 3 candidates appeared for this round ]

The second technical interview was conducted next and I was the last candidate to be interviewed. The
interviewer was at a senior position and began by introducing himself in detail before asking me to introduce
myself and walk him through my resume. It is advisable to have a well-structured introduction prepared, as I
covered my coursework, internship, ongoing rescarch publication plans, and finally my projects. Rather than
simply listing them, I explained the motivation behind each project, the problem it aimed to solve, and the
journey that led me to build it.
The interviewer then focused on my multi-agent financial intelligence platform. He questioned why I had
chosen a multi-agent architecture instead of using a single large language model for the entire workflow. I
explained that the system was designed with specialized agents, each responsible for a specific task, closely
resembling how an actual equity research team operates. By performing stage-wise inference with dedicated
agents, human-in-the-loop validation, and specialized responsibilities, the system produces more reliable and
explainable results than relying on a single prompt handled by one large model. This discussion revolved
more around architectural decision-making than the implementation itself.
He then shifted to understanding my motivation for applying to the role. Since I come from a Computer
Science background and had completed a technical internship, he asked why I wanted to pursue a Fintech
role instead of a traditional software engineering position. This is a question worth preparing for, as the
interviewer expects a genuine and convincing answer. I explained my long-standing interest in the
intersection of finance and technology, highlighting how most of my projects revolved around financial
analytics, automation, and decision support. As a follow-up, he asked why I had not opted for a pure finance
or investment banking role if finance interested me so much. It is equally important to have a clear answer
for this question, explaining why the blend of technology and finance aligns better with your interests than a
purely finance-oriented role.
The interview also included a guesstimate question. I was asked to assume that the population of India was
1,000 people and estimate how many of them would have worn a tie at least once in their lifetime. For such
questions, the interviewer is not interested in the final number but rather in the structure of your thinking. I
was given time to think and explained the assumptions, segmentation, ratios, and factors I would consider
before arriving at an estimate. Throughout the process, I kept communicating my reasoning to the
interviewer, who even challenged one of my assumptions by asking whether gender should influence the
estimate. Once I had laid out a logical approach, he was satisfied and did not ask me to compute the final
value.
Towards the end of the interview, we discussed my internship in detail, including the work I had carried out,
the research aspects involved, and the publication that was currently in progress. This was followed by an
insightful discussion about the team's work culture. The interviewer mentioned that the role was not a
conventional 9-to-5 job and could be demanding at times, but he also emphasized that the team maintained a
healthy, collaborative environment with ample opportunities for learning and professional growth.
I concluded the interview by asking a few questions of my own regarding the technologies used within the
team, the nature of the work, and his personal journey at the company. This made for a positive and
engaging end to the discussion.
2 candidates were selected for the next round.
--- PAGE 5 ---

5. HR Interview [ 2 candidates appeared for this round]

The HR interview was the most relaxed round of the process and was primarily focused on assessing
whether you would be a good cultural fit for the team. My panel consisted of two interviewers from the HR
and Early Talent teams. They began by introducing themselves, after which I introduced myself. It is
advisable to slightly modify your introduction for this round by placing greater emphasis on your previous
work experience, leadership positions, extracurricular responsibilities, and personal interests rather than
diving deep into technical details.
The interview began on a light-hearted note when they asked how my day had been. I replied, "Exciting, to
say the least," and followed it up with a brief anecdote, which made both interviewers laugh and instantly
broke the ice.
One of the first questions was about my key takeaway from the pre-placement presentation (PPT). It is a
good idea to pay close attention during the session and make brief notes, as questions related to it can be
asked. I also referred to one of the speakers by name while answering, which reflected that I had been
attentive throughout the presentation.
The interviewers then walked through my resume and noticed that I had a Computer Science degree, a minor
in UI/UX, a machine learning internship, and was now interviewing for a Fintech role. They wanted to
understand the reasoning behind this journey. I explained that I enjoy exploring interdisciplinary domains
and have always been interested in applying technology to solve problems in different fields. I supported
this by discussing how my projects consistently revolved around the intersection of finance, automation, and
software engineering, which naturally led me to pursue this role. The conversation then shifted to my
positions of responsibility, where we discussed the leadership experiences I had gained through college
committees. They also took an interest in my hobbies, particularly music and the instruments I play, making
the discussion much more conversational than evaluative.
Towards the end, I asked a few questions about the internship onboarding process, the learning curve for
new joiners, and the opportunities available for growth within the organization. I also asked both
interviewers about their individual journeys at the company, following which they shared their experiences
and spoke about the collaborative work culture within the team. The conversation ended on a very positive
and engaging note, making it a comfortable conclusion to the interview process.
After the HR interview, we had to wait for the Banking role interviews to conclude before the results could
be announced. Our interviews were wrapped up by the afternoon, so it was a long wait until the evening.
Finally, the entire CCD team gathered to announce the results. It was a tense yet unforgettable moment, with
everyone anxiously waiting to hear their names.
2 candidates were offered the role.
Resources:

1. Resume

Make sure to align it with the JD.
Follow the standard: Jake's Resume Template.
Check ATS scores using: ResumeWorded.
--- PAGE 6 ---

2. Online Assessment

Complete aptitude, quant and reasoning practice can be done on websites like: India Bix, PrepInsta.
You can also follow Career Ride's YT playlist, if you prefer videos.

3. Technical Interviews

Know your projects inside out. This is probably the biggest takeaway for this role. Be ready to
explain everything from the overall workflow to why you chose a particular technology. The team
also uses tools like Selenium, VBA, and Alteryx extensively for automation-related tasks. If you
mention any of these on your resume, expect questions on them, so only include them if you're
comfortable discussing them in detail. OOPS concepts and python were also asked to other
candidates.
Prepare computer fundamentals well using GFG and InterviewBit, just in case.
For System Design:

1. HLD: Follow Gaurav Sen's playlist.

2. LLD: code WithAryan.

Note: For this role specifically, in depth system design knowledge is not a necessity. You should just
make sure that you can justify the design of your projects well with all its strengths and trade-offs.

4. Finance

For this role, you are not expected to know corporate finance inside out. What matters is that you
have a solid understanding of the financial concepts you have explicitly mentioned in your resume or
used in your projects. Be prepared to explain every financial metric, model, and term you have
included, along with the reasoning behind using them.
My biggest piece of advice is to make ChatGPT your friend throughout your preparation. If you're
relatively new to finance, don't hesitate to ask it to break down concepts to the simplest possible
level. Keep asking follow-up questions until you truly understand the "why" behind each concept. I
followed the same approach for my entire financial preparation, using it to build my understanding
from first principles, and it proved to be immensely helpful during the interviews.
Additionally, do prepare the basics of the financial markets, as a few candidates were asked simple
conceptual questions on terms such as NIFTY 50, BSE Sensex, NSE, NASDAQ, and other
fundamental market definitions. A basic understanding of these topics is more than sufficient.

5. Puzzles and Guesstimates

Puzzles can be practiced on GFG: Top 100 puzzles asked in interviews.
For guesstimates, this cheat sheet is an excellent resource for making realistic assumptions and
structuring your estimates during interviews: https://180dcsrcc.in/guesstimate-cheat-sheet-2025/.

of a Banking candidate rather than a Fintech one. I intentionally built a project around automating
that workflow and prepared every concept related to it thoroughly. This allowed me to steer parts of
the interview towards topics I was comfortable with. Breadcrumbing simply means introducing a
concept or technical term in your answers that is likely to catch the interviewer's attention and
naturally lead the next question in that direction.

6. Never judge your interview yourself. After my first technical interview, I genuinely wasn't

confident about my chances. Although I answered most of the questions, I found the interviewer
quite intimidating and he hardly gave away any reactions. He smiled only towards the very end when
I asked him about his journey at JPMC. At one point, he even thought I was using a calculator during
a mental math question, whereas I was just making calculations on paper. I had to show him my desk
to reassure him, and that was probably the second time he smiled. The rest of the interview was
completely poker-faced, so I walked out thinking I hadn't done well.

7. Make use of the time between rounds. While waiting, I had already started looking at other

opportunities on Superset, assuming I wouldn't make it through. Then, out of nowhere, I received a
call asking me to be ready for the next round. That experience taught me never to assume the
outcome of an interview. The time between rounds is extremely valuable. Use it to revise your
concepts instead of overthinking what went wrong.

8. Prepare good questions for the interviewer. Have at least 2-3 thoughtful questions ready. Avoid

asking the usual generic questions that interviewers hear all the time. Listen carefully to their
responses and ask meaningful follow-up questions based on what they say. It turns the interview into
a genuine conversation and leaves a much better impression.

9. Smile and tell stories during the HR interview. For the HR round, keep the widest smile possible

on your face. Try to answer questions using small anecdotes or experiences rather than giving
one-line resp

journey.howSecured:
1. Online Assessment [230 students]

The TPO informed us only a night before that Quantiphi was coming to campus, so everyone had
to apply overnight. Because of the shortage of time, I believe there was no resume shortlisting in
this drive. Keep in mind, though, that resume shortlisting is usually a major stage, since it alone
decides whether you even get to appear in the process. Try to keep your ATS score above 80
given the current level of competition, and include projects that are relevant to the kind of firm
you are applying to, whether tech or non-tech.
Coming to the Online Assessment, I went in feeling fairly hopeless. I had not cleared a single OA
in the previous one to two months, and I had even skipped the pre-placement talk. Do attend the
PPTs, because you never know which company's final HR round you might reach, and the HR
may ask you something taken straight out of the presentation. The OA was conducted on campus,
on Unstop, in a heavily proctored mode; the Unstop SmartHire + On-campus setup ensures
fairness.
The OA was divided into three sections: Aptitude and English (45 questions), CS Fundamentals
(30 questions), and 3 DSA questions, with a total time of 1 hour 30 minutes. The special feature
of this OA was that you were shortlisted for a role based on the section you excelled in. I did the
Aptitude and English sections quite well, while CS Fundamentals and DSA went average. I
managed to pass only a few test cases of one DSA question because there was no time left at all.
So plan your sections accordingly: if you think you can do well in Aptitude and English, focus on
that, and attempt DSA and CS Fundamentals seriously only if you are confident in them and
genuinely want to pursue the FE or MLE role. Many fairly smart students juggled between the
aptitude and DSA sections and could not get through the OA. Honestly, I had zero expectations of
clearing it until I learned that section-wise selection was in place.
The cutoff for the BA role was, I believe, quite achievable if you approached the paper wisely.
Around 60 students were shortlisted for the BA role and moved on to the Group Discussion
round. For English, read the questions carefully and pick the appropriate option; in many

questions the correct option was fairly obvious. For Aptitude, practise IndiaBIX thoroughly.

2. Group Discussion [around 60 students]

We were called in at 9 a.m. for our GDs. I was fairly confident about clearing the Group
Discussion, as this has always been my strong suit. There may be situations where your group
decides in advance who will start and who will conclude; try to make sure that does not happen,
and ask the group to let the discussion flow naturally. That said, everyone must remain respectful
of each other at all times.
Our topic was "Should 75% attendance be mandatory?". In our group we had already assigned
one person to start, although I made sure no further sequence was fixed. The person we assigned
began the introduction, then fumbled and stopped midway. That is exactly the moment you have
to seize, and carry the discussion forward.
In a GD you have to be loud enough to be heard by everyone, and especially by the panellist. At
the same time, if someone else is speaking, wait for them to finish before putting forward your
point. If you are unable to generate points of your own, take someone else's point, agree with it,
and rephrase it in a better way. If someone fumbles or cannot recall a point, help them out; that
shows you are actually taking part in a group discussion rather than delivering a one-way speech.
Ultimately it comes down to individual ability, but practice definitely helps.

3. Technical Round 1 [19-20 students]

This was the most dramatic turn of the entire day. Despite performing exceptionally well in the
GD, I was told that I had not been shortlisted for the next round. I went back home flabbergasted,
and just as I was about to open my front door, more than an hour later, I received a call from the
TPC saying there had been a mistake: another student's name had been shortlisted instead of
mine, and I had to attend the interview within 40 minutes. I rushed back downstairs in despair,
took a rickshaw from Kandivali, and was literally preparing for the interview in traffic. I had no
hopes left and simply wanted to get the experience and be done with it.
Then the technical interview began. The interviewer was quite friendly, and it was a one-to-one,
in-person interaction. She first asked me how the process had been so far. I replied that this was
the most unique process I had seen any company conduct, as it recognised candidates according
to their skill set instead of applying a blanket cutoff, and she agreed. Then came the usual "tell me
about yourself", followed by an explanation of my projects from scratch. After that she asked a
few questions: the difference between Gen AI and Agentic AI, the difference between AI and
ML, and what Big Data is. She then asked me to write a simple SQL query using LIMIT and
ORDER BY, followed by a few case study questions, such as how I would acquire new customers
for a retail store that operates both online and offline using data analytics.
One thing I would recommend is that, along with knowledge, you should be able to communicate
it well. Most of the time, interviewers for roles like this one are not looking for a completely
accurate answer; they focus on how clearly you can explain your thinking, how well you

communicate, and how confident you are. There was also a situational question: if you do not
know a technical term and are asked about it in a meeting, what would you do? The ideal answer
is that you would not try to deceive the client by making something up, but would instead take it
as a follow-up and get back to them later. When I answered this, the interviewer seemed quite
convinced and said that was more or less what she was looking for. The interview went on for 40
to 50 minutes and felt more like a conversation than a grilling, but the next interview was tougher.
10-12 students were shortlisted for Round 2.

4. Technical Round 2 [10-12 students]

After waiting for two to two and a half hours, I was called in for the second round of interviews.
The interviewer seemed friendly and initially asked me about my hobbies and similar things, then
moved on to a general introduction. After that, he asked me to explain two of my projects from
scratch in layman's terms. I was able to explain the entire pipeline clearly. You need end-to-end
clarity on your own projects, and you need to be able to explain them to someone who has no idea
what they are about. For this role, explaining technical projects in simple language to a
non-technical person was the main requirement, and that is why I kept getting questioned on my
projects.
After the projects, he moved on to some maths questions. One of them was: if 5 people build 5
houses in 10 days, how many days would 10 people take to build 10 houses? I answered
incorrectly at first, but he asked me to recheck, and then I stuck confidently to my final answer.
From previous Round 2 experiences, I knew that fumbling over your answer, whether it is right or
wrong, leads to immediate rejection.
After that, he asked which role I would be interested in. Make sure you study the JD properly and
answer accordingly. The interview went well, but I had low hopes, as most of my peers were
eliminated at this stage.

5. HR Round [7 students]

The HR round took place late at night, at 9:15 p.m., and everyone was clearly exhausted. The HR
came in, started with a general introduction and a few other questions, and mentioned that there
would be no technical questions at all in this round. He then asked me to tell him something
interesting about myself, and honestly, I could not recall a single interesting thing. I tried hard but
could not come up with anything, so he moved on to the next question.
He asked why, having had such a tech-oriented education and so many technical projects, I would
want to switch to the Business Analyst path. I answered clearly, without letting the previous
question affect me: even though I have worked on highly technical projects, I have also held
various positions of responsibility throughout my studies that required both technical and
communication skills.
He then asked me to name one skill I could count on for a lifetime. I thought of saying SQL, but
that would have been too narrow, so I answered public speaking, which is something I can truly

rely on.
After that came some basic questions, such as naming five specific things about Quantiphi and
describing my background. He then mentioned that I might have to work overtime and that the
work culture could be debatable, to which I replied that we had worked overtime throughout
engineering, so it is nothing new for me. There was a lot more that I had to respond to, but
including all of it would make this account far too long. The HR interview ended with me asking
two or three questions and listening carefully throughout. By the end it had become quite
conversational, and we both finished on a positive note.
THE KEY TAKEAWAY IS THIS: EVEN IF ONE QUESTION GOES WRONG OR
YOU ARE UNABLE TO ANSWER IT, DO NOT LET IT AFFECT YOUR OTHER
ANSWERS. THAT ONE GLITCH DOES NOT DEFINE THE OVERALL
INTERVIEW.
6 students were offered the BA role, 2 the FE role, and 1 the MLE role.

trying, don't stress and most importantly don't be jealous of others because placements is a lot about luck so

Resume shortlisting: Approximately 220 people shortlisted for OA

Round 1: Online assessment

Round 2: Technical Interview 1

Round 3: Vibe coding Round

Round 4: Technical Round 2

Round 5: HR Round

1. [Online Assesment] [ 220-230 approx]

The OA was conducted on Unstop platform and had many sections
2-3 sections of MCQS across sections like english, coding fundamentals, aptitude, this time a little bit of ai
based questions were also asked. The mcqs were quite easy and doable just time management was needed as
90mins for around 95 questions(including 3 DSA) so the OA needed to be completed at very fast speed
I was confident in DSA so I very quickly did the mcqs and gave myself 50mins for DSA in which i managed
to solve 2 questions entirely
Then next section had 3 DSA questions(each person had different set of questions)
1)house robber variation- given array of values (1 indexed array)
You can select an element at index i and then you can select element at index j only if j%i=-0
So if index 1 then any index allowed if index 2 then only 4,6,8 and so on..
This question i was able to solve and the recursive solution was enough to pass all the test cases no need of
memoization
--- PAGE 2 ---

2) Some extremely difficult question. Like given n vertices of a polygon as coordinates, sort in anticlockwise

order and then find area of the polygon( no formula or anything given)
This i skipped entirely
3)given an array of elements choose a subarray such that the OR of elements of the subarray is equal to the
OR of elements of the remaining array
For this question i provided a brute force solution (iterate over all subarrays compute OR and another loop
for OR of the array excluding current subaary and then just match both results)
TIP: solve questions with brute force at least to pass most of the test cases and then if time permits go for
optimal approach
Practice DP in advance because such questions can be solved in pressure only with lots of practice in
advance(Focus on arrays all variations(2 pointer,sliding window,prefix sum+hashmap,binaryh search all
types) and DP ‚trees and graphs only if time permits)
Do well in OA ‚you will get shortlisted for your preferred role(role based shortlisting was done by the
company but students were allowed to switch to another role in the interview round. Most students solved
one/two DSA were shortlisted for FE and MLE role ,for BA some people solved 1 or partial question)

2. Technical Round 1: 6 people for MLE 16 for FE

This round was purely focused on the project. The interviewer asked me to introduce myself and then moved
on to view my Resume and ask me about the projects. He was only focused on projects where ML was
used. In this round basically only I had to speak a lot explaining my project and on the basis of whatever
I say the interviewer will cross question. The interviewer went into the extreme details of each project
like I had an anomaly detection model so he asked about why this model,alternatives,exact input
features, why embeddings made? which transformer used?
Next he asked about my Movie recommendation system project in which i explained to him content based
and collaborative filtering. He tried to ask 1-2 random questions like the full form of TFIDF which i had
used in the project(generally 1-2 specific questions are asked so that they can judge if you actually did
the project or not). So make sure you know your project perfectly along with all the tech stack and
justification of why that tech stack.
At the end of the round I asked the interviewer a few questions like
What qualities/skills do you expect from a fresher candidate, In an MLE role will we get to deploy
models or only build them. Also the career progression as MLE in two-five years.

3. Vibe coding round: approximately 15-18 people in total (4MLE 9 FE)

This was a non elimination round so all people had to give the next round by default.
We had to share our screen on unstop,the interviewers could view whatever we were doing on screen.
Any ai tools were allowed and we were given a simple problem statement and 90 minutes to complete
I used antigravity to make the project it took only 20mins even with errors)
--- PAGE 3 ---
The remaining time I took to understand the project,see all the api routes, DB schema and details about react
hooks used(because mainly frontend was only required). We had to upload the project on github and
paste the link in unstop.

4. Technical round 2: approximately 4MLE 9FE

In this round general Machine learning related questions were asked, nothing related to projects.
I was asked about confusion matrix ,all the metrics like precision,recall,f1 score, when to use which
metric and why(imbalanced dataset).
He also saw the vibe coding round project but didn't ask me much about the details.
Also some questions related to LLMs were asked like how to evaluate RAG models(faithfullness,
correctness and other metrics).
What is the algorithm for retrieving top K chunks? (I said top k is decided based on most semanticly similar
chunks based on the cosine similarity, which I don't know was the answer he was expecting or not)
He asked me about temperature variable in LLMs(used to control randomness of output. Keep low value for
less hallucinations).
Then he asked me if I had any questions. I asked him what is one thing that changed since you joined
Quantiphi and I asked him how often would we interact directly with the clients. He said on a day to day
basis we are expected to take full ownership of code and interact with clients even as a junior level role.

5. HR round: 1 MLE(only me)

I was asked to introduce myself, say something about me. Then I was asked for 5 points as to why I wanted
to join Quantiphi. Then I was asked some other basic HR questions.
This round was at 1:00a.m. at night so the interviewer was also in a hurry. This process was too long from
9a.m. in the morning to 1:00a.m. at night. A lot of patience was needed throughout the process.
Finally only I was selected for MLE role
2 for FE role, 6 for BA role
--- PAGE 4 ---

journey.prep:
• Practice and study aptitude, general knowledge, and HR questions, and work on your speaking and

communication skills. These are important for both tech and non-tech roles, but they matter even
more for non-tech roles, so don't neglect them.

• Don't lose confidence because of early rejections. I wasn't shortlisted for JPMC, InCred, and a few

other non-tech roles before this, which was upsetting since I felt I was genuinely skilled for non-tech
profiles, and at one point I felt like giving up. This opportunity came about a month into the
placement cycle - it was the first company that shortlisted me, and I got selected directly. So trust
your skills, stay patient, and don't give up after a few setbacks.

• Keep your CGPA in mind -- aim for a minimum of 7, and preferably 7.5 or above, so you don't miss

out on eligibility for any companies. Mine was 7.26 after the 6th semester.

• In GDs, take the initiative to speak early, organize your points logically, and stay updated on general

knowledge and current affairs.

• Always communicate politely and respectfully, regardless of the round -- panels notice how you

interact, not just what you say.

• Expect interviewers to apply pressure or push back on correct answers to test your composure

stay calm, stick to your reasoning, and don't second-guess yourself unnecessarily.

• If interviewers try to discourage you from the role or the company, treat it as a test of your

conviction, and use it as a chance to reaffirm why you're a strong fit.
--- PAGE 3 ---

• Above all, confidence is the common thread across every round - carry it through the GD, the

aptitude and technical rounds, and the HR round alike.
Feel free to reach out to me on LinkedIn for any doubts. All the best!
In case of any further doubts, you can also refer to the past interview experiences shared by TPO.
journey.howSecured:
The process began with an online test that all 233 candidates appeared for, out of which 44 were shortlisted
for the Business Analyst role. The test was 90 minutes long and included aptitude questions, technical
MCQS, and 3 coding questions. During the pre-placement talk, the company had specifically advised
candidates to focus on aptitude for the Business Analyst profile. Keeping that in mind, I concentrated on the
aptitude and technical MCQ sections and completed them in about 30 minutes, and chose not to attempt the
coding questions at all.

Tips: Pay close attention to the pre-placement talk, as companies often hint at what they prioritize in the test.

For a Business Analyst role, that was clearly aptitude. Being efficient with your time matters more than
attempting every section; I finished the aptitude and MCQ portions quickly and didn't waste time on the
coding questions, since they weren't a priority for this profile. Focus your prep and your test-time effort on
what's actually relevant to the role you're targeting.

1. Group Discussion (GD) [233 candidates appeared]

The process began with a Group Discussion round for the Business Analyst role. Out of the 233 students
who appeared, 44 were shortlisted after the GD, and of those, 19 candidates were selected to move on to the
next round.

Tips: Try to initiate the discussion, as it creates a strong first impression. Structure your points clearly and

cover the key aspects of the topic rather than speaking at length without substance. Keep basic general
knowledge updated, since GD topics can draw on current affairs. Most importantly, stay polite and
respectful while communicating - interrupting others or being aggressive can count against you even if
your points are good.

2. Interview Round 1[19 candidates appeared, roughly 10-12 selected]

Of the 19 candidates who cleared the GD, around 10-12 advanced from this round. Since my interview slot
was scheduled quite late in the day, I was interviewed virtually instead of in person. The round focused on
general aptitude and guesstimate questions, and the panel also went through my resume in detail, asking
questions about the projects and experiences listed on it.
--- PAGE 2 ---

Tips: Brush up on quantitative aptitude and practice a structured approach to guesstimates (state assumptions

clearly, break the problem down, and sanity-check your final number). Be ready to explain every line on
your resume, since interviewers often probe deeper into whatever you mention.

3. Interview Round 2[10-12 candidates appeared, 7 selected]

Out of the 10-12 candidates who appeared, 7 advanced from this round. This interview involved an in-depth
discussion of my resume, including detailed questions on all my projects and internships, along with some
math-based questions. The biggest challenge in this round was handling the pressure the interviewer
deliberately applied - even when I gave the correct answer, the interviewer kept asking me to recheck it,
seemingly to test how I would react.

Tips: Stay confident and stick to your answer once you're sure it's correct, even if the interviewer pushes

back repeatedly - this is often a deliberate pressure test rather than a sign that you're wrong. Interviewers
may also try to talk you out of joining the company or downplay the role; treat this as another test and use it
as an opportunity to convince them why you're a strong fit, rather than getting discouraged.

4. HR Round [7 candidates appeared, 6 selected]

Of the 7 candidates who reached this stage, 6 were finally selected. The HR round varied from candidate to
candidate; in my case, the discussion was centered around my family background.

Tips: Be genuine and comfortable discussing personal background questions. As with the earlier rounds,

staying confident and consistently conveying that you are a good fit for the company goes a long way in this
round as well.
6 out of 233 students were finally offered the job.

The first round consisted of 50 MCQS covering English Aptitude, GK and Current Affairs, Stock Market,
Basic Python, Pandas, NumPy, Scikit-learn, basic Machine Learning and Data Cleaning.

1. English Aptitude (Comprehension)

The English aptitude section consisted of paragraphs with multiple questions based on matching and
logical reasoning. For example, A likes B, B doesn't like C, and you had to determine who would sit next to
whom. There were also questions involving matching colours with people and similar arrangements.
This section was quite tricky because some questions were not very clearly worded. One paragraph could
have multiple questions based on the same information. There was a decent amount of this section.
Tip: Try solving these questions at the start, but as soon as you realise a question is not solvable or
is taking too much time, make a random smart guess and move ahead.

2. GK, Current Affairs & Stock Market and other basic Finance Questions

There were questions related to GK, Current Affairs and the Stock Market. For example: Which giant
payments company had their IPO listed in 2021? - Answer: Paytm.
If you trade in stock markets or have basic knowledge of the markets, some questions can be answered
through option elimination, but they do require prior knowledge.
Finance questions were related to terms in banking like withdrawals, formula of SI and CI.

3. Python & Machine Learning

The Python part was basic and mainly covered Pandas functions and related concepts. There were also
theory questions on Machine Learning, including Supervised, Unsupervised and Reinforcement Learning,
along with basic data cleaning concepts.

Round 2: Coding Test - Python L1 & Python Coding Assessment

No DSA was asked in this round. The assessment consisted of Python, Pandas, Matplotlib, Scikit-learn
and Seaborn basics, along with differentiation between these libraries, Data Cleaning concepts and very
basic Machine Learning questions based on supervised and unsupervised learning.
MCQs: 15 questions in total.
Coding: 2-3 simple Python coding questions.
The coding questions were very simple. They provided a function and we needed to complete it. One
question was as simple as sorting an array and one was like finding max value from an array.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Important: The function codes provided were syntactically incorrect and, in some cases, logically
incorrect as well. Therefore, even if your function logic was right, the platform would not accept the
answer. I had to rewrite the function body itself.
The shortlist for this test was based on marks, time taken to complete the test and the number of
submission attempts required to complete the function codes.

Round 3: Tech Interview (Offline)

Around 25-30 people were shortlisted for the technical interview. There were two panelists.
My panelist grilled on the Machine Learning projects mentioned on my resume and asked deeper
questions about the concepts behind the projects. He also asked basic concepts related to Machine
Learning and Data Analytics, especially Data Cleaning and related topics.

Round 4: HR Interview (Same Day, Offline)

A total of 10 people were shortlisted from the technical rounds for HR, out of which 9 received the offer.
The HR interview was relatively light. Questions were mainly about family background, resume
achievements, hobbies and general personal questions.
Tip: If you reach the HR round, stay calm and don't become too ecstatic. They paid attention to body
language and overall confidence as well.
Final Outcome
Out of the Summer Interns, all 9 of them received PPO offers after completing the internship.
Tips

1. Revise Data Science and Basic ML Concepts

Revise Python, Pandas, NumPy, Scikit-learn, Data Cleaning, Data Preprocessing and the fundamentals of
Supervised, Unsupervised and Reinforcement Learning before the tests and interviews.

2. Study Your Projects in Depth

Do not prepare only what you actually implemented. Be ready for questions about the problems you faced,
their resolutions, why you selected a particular approach, what could have been done differently, limitations
and future scope.

3. Manage Time in the Tests

Some aptitude questions can consume a lot of time. If a question is becoming too difficult or
time-consuming, make a smart guess and move on.

4. Stay Calm in HR

The HR round is comparatively light. If you reach this stage, remain calm, confident and natural, while
maintaining good body language.
Contact
For any genuine questions or doubts, reach out to me on LinkedIn.
LinkedIn: https://in.linkedin.com/in/darsh-bajaj.

O.
Pre Placement Talk
You should be here with all ears. Note down all the important points, names of people who
came and presented, and everything that you think that you can ask during the interview
when the interviewer is going to ask you if you have any questions for them. Use this advice
for all the processes. Don't do this just for the sake of doing it. It's a good practice to be
attentive in general and have information about all companies. You can also ask questions at
the end of PPT if they let you. Don't ask silly and illogical questions (e.g. how many students
they are going to hire, anything about their internal policies, anything controversial). You can
stand out here but try to stand out in a good way

1. Online Assessment: 3 Sections (Around 165 People)

1. Aptitude - 20 mins

2. Core CS fundamentals - 30 mins

3. Coding Section - 40 mins

* The Aptitude section was among the most challenging parts of the assessment. It

consisted of 15 questions to be completed in 20 minutes, and the use of calculators was
not permitted. The section included a mix of quantitative aptitude and logical
reasoning problems. Topics covered included Time and Work, Cubes (opposite faces
and cube orientation), Mixtures and Alligations, Mean and Variance, Probability, and
a CAT-style DILR arrangement set. There were also sequence- and ordering-based
--- PAGE 2 ---
puzzles similar to those found in banking aptitude exams, where a single puzzle was
followed by multiple sub-questions. Overall, the difficulty level of this section was
moderate to difficult, with the strict time limit making it particularly demanding. A good
resource for preparation is IndiaBIX for quantitative aptitude practice, along with
banking-style puzzle sets such as sequence and arrangement questions.

* The Core CS Fundamentals section primarily consisted of MCQS covering code

snippets, flowcharts, DBMS, Operating Systems, SQL, OOPS, and basic software
engineering concepts. The overall difficulty level ranged from easy to moderate for
candidates with a strong grasp of core subjects, though several questions had closely
related options that could be confusing. A significant number of questions required
analyzing code snippets and flowcharts to determine the output or behavior of the
program. Some of these involved recursive functions, requiring careful tracing of
execution. Questions related to code snippets of confusing pre and post increments
were also there. The section also included conceptual OOPs questions, such as method
overriding, whether static methods can be overridden, object interactions, and message
passing. Additionally, there were questions comparing SOAP and REST APIs, where
candidates had to identify incorrect statements or distinguish between their
characteristics. Overall, the section tested conceptual understanding rather than
memorization, with an emphasis on reasoning through code and applying core computer
science principles. GFG for preparation of CS fundamentals. Sanfoundary and Indiabix
for output-based questions.

* The DSA section consisted of two coding questions of medium difficulty.

Question 1:
The first problem involved two integers, X and Y.
Starting with the number X, you had to form new
numbers by appending digits to its end and
determine the smallest such number that
is
divisible by Y. The challenge was to efficiently
search for the minimum valid number while
preserving the original prefix.
FUNCTION smallestNumber(x, y)
// If x itself is divisible by y
IF x MOD Y = 0 THEN
RETURN x
END IF
base + x
WHILE TRUE DO
// Append one zero to x
base + base × 10
remainder + base MOD y
Pseudo-code:
IF remainder = 0 THEN
minAdded + 0
ELSE
minAdded + y - remainder
END IF
// Check if the required addition fits within
// the current number of appended digits
IF minAdded < (base / x) THEN
RETURN base + minAdded
END IF
END WHILE
END FUNCTION
--- PAGE 3 ---
Question 2:
The second problem was a classic 2D Dynamic Programming question on matrices. Given a
grid of integers, the objective was to find the maximum path sum from the top-left cell to the
bottom-right cell while moving only in the allowed directions (typically right and down). It was
essentially a variation of the standard matrix path DP problem, with the optimization criterion
changed from minimizing the path sum to maximizing it. Similar Problem of leetcode
Pseudo-code:
FUNCTION getMaxValue (values, m, n)
CREATE 2D array dp[m][n]
// Initialize first cell
// Fill first row
FOR j + 1 TO n - 1 DO
END FOR
// Fill first column
FOR i + 1 TO m - 1 DO
dp[i][0] + dp[i - 1][0] + values[i][0]
END FOR
// Fill remaining cells
FOR i + 1 TO m - 1 DO
FOR j + 1 TO n - 1 DO
dp[i][i] + MAX(dp[i - 1][i], d[i][j - 1]) + values [i][i]
END FOR
END FOR
RETURN dp[m - 1][n - 1]
END FUNCTION
MAIN
INPUT m, n
CREATE matrix values[m][n]
FOR i + 0 TO m - 1 DO
FOR j + 0 TO n - 1 DO
INPUT values [i][]]
END FOR
END FOR
answer + getMaxValue(values, m, n)
OUTPUT answer
END MAIN
Overall, the coding section focused on problem-solving ability and familiarity with common
DSA patterns, particularly number manipulation and dynamic programming.
Sources for DSA preparation are mentioned in the end.

2. Technical Interview 1 (L1) (48 candidates )

I entered the room, greeted both interviewers, and after intro of both sides was immediately
given a DSA problem.
The coding question was to count the number of palindromic substrings in a given string. The
problem itself was fairly straightforward, but due to the pressure of the interview, I could only
come up with the brute-force approach. I wasn't able to derive the optimal solution during the
--- PAGE 4 ---
interview, even though it uses a standard optimization technique. Looking back, it was a
reminder that interview pressure can affect even familiar problems.
After the coding question, the discussion shifted almost entirely to core computer science
fundamentals, with a strong focus on Object-Oriented Programming in both C++ and Java.
Some of the topics discussed included:

• Different types of inheritance and their use cases

• Hierarchical vs. multilevel inheritance

• Virtual functions

• Interfaces

• Multiple inheritance in C++ and how Java handles it differently

• Destructors- what they are, why they are needed, and when they are invoked

One interesting question was whether a virtual constructor can be overridden. I wasn't
completely sure of the answer, so instead of guessing confidently, I explained my reasoning and
thought through the problem aloud.
One thing I learned from this interview is that it's perfectly acceptable to admit when you don't
know something, provided you genuinely try to reason about it. Interviewers often appreciate
seeing your thought process rather than hearing a memorized answer.
Meanwhile, the second interviewer started going through my resume.
Since I had listed React, Node.js, and Express in my projects, he asked several questions related
to them:

• Is Node.js single-threaded?

• How does the Event Loop work?

I remembered the basics of the Event Loop and explained them to the best of my ability.
The first interviewer then switched to Operating Systems and asked questions on:

• Concurrency

• Deadlocks

• Banker's Algorithm

--- PAGE 5 ---
After that, the second interviewer noticed Git and GitHub on my resume and asked about the
difference between Git Merge and Git Rebase, along with when each should be used. I
answered based on my understanding and practical usage, although I'm still not entirely sure
whether my explanation matched what they expected.
The entire interview lasted only about 40-45 minutes. Shortly after it ended, I received a message
asking me to be ready for the Level 2 interview which happened 2-3 hrs later.
Key Takeaways
The biggest lesson from this interview was that not solving the coding question optimally did not
immediately eliminate me. While DSA was important, the interview quickly shifted toward
evaluating my understanding of core CS concepts. It felt like the interviewers were testing not
only my technical knowledge but also how I handled pressure and responded when I encountered
unfamiliar questions.
For preparation, I would strongly recommend thoroughly revising:

• Object-Oriented Programming (OOP)

• Operating Systems (OS)

• Database Management Systems (DBMS)

• SQL

• Computer Networks (CN)

A quick and effective revision strategy is to search for "<subject> interview questions GFG"
(for example, OOP interview questions GFG or DBMS interview questions GFG) and work
through those lists.
Don't limit your preparation to only core CS subjects. Review every language, framework, and
technology mentioned on your resume, because interviewers often ask questions directly from
your listed skills. For example, if your resume includes Java, C++, Python, JavaScript,
TypeScript, React, Node js, Express, MongoDB, SQL, DBMS, OS, OOP, or Computer
Networks, be prepared to answer conceptual questions about each of them.
In my case, I had revised OOP particularly well, and fortunately, a significant portion of the
interview revolved around those concepts.

3. Technical Interview 2 (L2) (20 candidates )

Unlike the first round, there were no introductions from the interviewers, and they didn't ask me
to introduce myself either. I simply greeted them, asked how they were doing, and we got
straight into the interview.
--- PAGE 6 ---
This round was heavily focused on my projects and SQL.
The interviewer started with my Job Portal project, particularly the Role-Based Access Control

(RBAC) implementation. He asked me to explain how I had implemented different user roles and

permissions. From there, the discussion became very detailed. He asked about almost every API
I had built, what each endpoint did, and how access was controlled for different users. He also
questioned how I was using access tokens and authorization throughout the application.
The discussion on RBAC alone lasted around 15 minutes. While I was explaining my
implementation, the interviewer kept counter-questioning almost every statement I made. At
times, it felt as if he wasn't convinced or didn't fully understand what I was trying to explain. I
had to explain the same concept in different ways nearly five or six times.
One important lesson I learned from this experience is not to panic when interviewers keep
challenging your answers. They may simply be testing how well you understand your own
project and whether you can defend your implementation under pressure. Throughout the
discussion, I stayed calm and remained consistent with my explanation instead of changing my
answer every time I was questioned. Eventually, I was able to communicate my implementation
clearly. Although I couldn't really tell whether the interviewer was completely satisfied, I was
confident that I had explained exactly how my project worked.
The discussion then shifted to my second project. Since it was relatively simple, the interviewer
asked me to explain all of its major functionalities and how each feature worked internally. I
walked them through the complete flow in detail.
The second interviewer then focused on the technologies mentioned in my resume. She asked
questions about several project-related technologies, including:

• JWT

• Cloudinary

• Multer

Most of the discussion revolved around JWT. She asked me about the structure of a JWT token,
its three components, how authentication works using JWT, and the complete request-response
flow.
Towards the end of the interview, I was asked to write an SQL query.
The question was based on two tables: Employee and Department. I had to write a query to
display the employee name along with the corresponding department name for the employee(s)
--- PAGE 7 ---
who received the maximum salary in the previous year. The interviewer specifically mentioned
using SQL date functions to determine the previous year.
SELECT e.employee_name, d.department_ name
FROM Employee e
JOIN Department d
ON e.department id = d.department_id
WHERE YEAR(e.salary_date) = YEAR(CURDATEO) - 1
AND e.salary = (
SELECT MAX(salary)
FROM Employee
WHERE YEAR(salary_date) = YEAR(CURDATEO) - 1
The interview concluded after the SQL question. Before leaving, I asked both interviewers for
their names and thanked them for their time.
Key Takeaways
This round reinforced the importance of knowing your projects inside out. If a technology or
feature is mentioned on your resume, be prepared to explain not just what it does, but also why
you chose it, how you implemented it, possible alternatives, and how the complete flow works.
Another important observation was that interviewers may intentionally challenge your
explanations repeatedly. Staying calm, reasoning through your answers, and confidently
defending your implementation leaves a much better impression than changing your explanation
under pressure.
Finally, revise SQL thoroughly. Be comfortable with:

• Joins

• Aggregate functions

• Subqueries

• GROUP BY and HAVING

• Date functions

• Basic optimization concepts

A single SQL query can become an in-depth discussion if the interviewer asks follow-up
questions about your approach. This round lasted for 40-50 minutes.
--- PAGE 8 ---

4. HR Round (10 students appeared for this round)

I was called for the HR round about 15-20 minutes after my previous interview.
The interviewer began by introducing herself and then asked me to introduce myself. I hadn't
planned anything special for this question, but instead of giving a standard introduction, I spoke
honestly about my journey. I talked about moving from my hometown to Mumbai, how the city
had changed me as a person, and the experiences that shaped me over the last three years of
college. I also spoke about the responsibilities I had taken up through various committees,
events, and extracurricular activities.
To my surprise, she seemed genuinely interested in my story and kept listening attentively
instead of interrupting with follow-up questions.
She then asked whether I planned to return to my hometown in the near future. I understood that
she was trying to assess my willingness to relocate, so I answered that I was open to working
wherever the company required me.
The conversation then moved to behavioral questions.
She asked me to describe a situation where I had resolved a conflict within a team. I shared one
of my experiences from my committee work, explaining the situation, how I handled it, and the
outcome. She even asked whether the incident had actually happened, to which I replied that it
was a real experience.
Another interesting question she asked was:
"Suppose your manager is extremely busy and doesn't assign you any work for 20-25 days. What
would you doẠạ
There wasn't a single correct answer to this question. It felt more like they wanted to understand
my attitude in such a situation. Rather than saying I would sit idle or become frustrated, I
explained that I would first try to understand the team's priorities, explore the existing codebase
or documentation, learn independently, and proactively reach out to my manager or teammates to
ask if I could contribute anywhere. The idea was to show initiative instead of waiting passively
for work to be assigned.
Soon after that, she informed me that the round had to end because I had been shortlisted for the
next round.
Before concluding, she asked if I had any questions for her. I asked about the most common
challenges she had observed while working with freshers and interns. Interestingly, she said that
--- PAGE 9 ---
the very scenarios she had asked me about-such as relocation flexibility and how someone reacts
when they are temporarily not assigned work-were among the common issues they encountered.
After the discussion, she personally escorted me to another room, where my Level 3 interview
was scheduled virtually with a senior employee from the company. I waited for around 10
minutes before the interviewer joined the Google Meet.
Key Takeaways
This round was much more about personality, communication, and attitude than technical
knowledge. The interviewer seemed interested in understanding how I think, whether I can adapt
to new situations, and how I would behave in a professional environment.
My advice would be:

• Be genuine during your introduction instead of trying to recite a memorized script.

• Use real experiences while answering behavioral questions.

• Show ownership and initiative in hypothetical workplace scenarios.

• Demonstrate flexibility regarding relocation and work assignments if you're comfortable

with them.

• Always ask at least one thoughtful question at the end of the interview-it leaves a positive

impression and often provides useful insights about the role and the company.

5. Technical Interview 3 (L3) (10 candidates )

The final interview was conducted virtually over Microsoft Teams with a senior engineer from
the company.
The discussion once again revolved around my projects. The interviewer started with my Job
Portal project and asked me to explain the Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) implementation.
While discussing it, he pointed out a limitation in my design. I had implemented RBAC using
different APIs for different user roles. He explained that this approach would not scale well in a
real-world application with a large number of roles, as creating and maintaining separate APIs
for every role would become difficult.
At that moment, I didn't have the ideal solution. Instead of staying silent, I tried to reason
through the problem and suggested an approach that was closer to how it could be solved in
practice. Although my answer wasn't perfect, it was enough for us to move on to the next topic.
--- PAGE 10 ---
The interviewer then switched to my second project, which used SQLite. He asked me about the
database schema, the tables I had created, the relationships between them, and how the data
flowed throughout the application. Most of the discussion focused on understanding whether I
genuinely knew the internals of my own project.
Towards the end of the interview, he asked me to write a simple SQL query.
The problem consisted of two tables-Student and Department. I had to return the student names
along with their department names, but only for students belonging to the IT and CS
departments.
SELECT s.student_name, d.department_name
FROM Student s
JOIN Department d
ON s.department_id = d.department_id
WHERE d.department_ name IN ('IT", 'CS');
The interview ended shortly after the SQL question.
Key Takeaways
This round reinforced an important lesson: know the design decisions behind your projects, not
just the implementation. The interviewer wasn't trying to find mistakes in my project-he
wanted to understand whether I had thought about scalability and how I would improve my
design when faced with real-world constraints.
If you don't know the perfect answer, don't panic. Explain your reasoning, discuss possible
alternatives, and show that you can think through the problem logically. Interviewers often value
your approach to problem-solving as much as the final answer itself.
Finally, make sure you are comfortable with writing basic SQL queries involving JOINs,
filtering, and multiple tables, as these are frequently asked even in project-based interviews.
This round lasted for 40-45 minutes.

--- PAGE 11 ---
Must read
Placement season was one of the most challenging phases for me.
When it started, I got rejected from the JPMorgan Chase FinTech role, then PhonePe, and I
couldn't even make it into the WorkIndia process. Every day I was coming to college either for
an online assessment or an interview. In most companies I reached the last round, only to face
another rejection. It was discouraging, and after every rejection it became harder to get up the
next morning and prepare with the same energy.
But I kept trying.
Looking back, I don't regret anything I did for my preparation. Yes, I was constantly stressed and
anxious, sometimes overthinking every small thing. That pressure made me more attentive and
pushed me to prepare better. At the same time, I learned that you shouldn't let stress take over
your preparation. Use it as motivation, not as something that controls you.
Every rejection taught me something valuable that eventually helped me crack IDFC First Bank
JPMorgan made me realize that I needed a much stronger understanding of my projects and CS
fundamentals. PhonePe exposed the gaps in my DSA preparation. Instead of treating those
interviews as failures, I treated them as feedback.
One mistake I made was stopping DSA practice almost two months before placements. I was
going through a difficult phase personally and wasn't in the right state of mind to prepare. I only
started studying seriously once companies had already started visiting campus. It was extremely
difficult to catch up, and I would never recommend doing what I did.
No matter what is happening in your life, placement season is an opportunity you cannot afford
to ignore. Even if you feel overwhelmed, even if you feel like giving up, you still have to show
up for yourself. No one else can prepare on your behalf. It's just a matter of a few months, but
those months can shape the beginning of your career.
Work hard. Study consistently. Put in the effort every single day.
If you're consistent, the workload never becomes overwhelming. DSA is not something you can
master or revise in a day. I had already studied it before, yet I still couldn't revise everything
during placements. The same applies to CS fundamentals, projects, SQL, operating systems,
DBMS, computer networks, and everything else on your resume.
Know your resume inside out. If someone points to any line on it, you should be able to explain
it confidently, discuss the design decisions you made, the alternatives you considered, and the
--- PAGE 12 ---
challenges you faced. There should never be a point on your resume that surprises you in an
interview.
Start preparing early so that when placement season begins, you are improving-not rushing.
And finally, don't lose hope because of rejections.
I know how painful they feel. I questioned myself after every rejection. But every interview
made me better than I was before. If I had been selected in one of the earlier companies, I might
never have learned the lessons that helped me succeed later.
Your job is not to predict when you'll get your offer or which company it will be. Your job is
simply to prepare, learn from every experience, and give your best every single time.
The right opportunity will come. When it does, all the preparation, all the rejections, and all the
difficult days will finally make sense.
# Backstory (read only if you have time. Has nothing to do with interview prep. Fun tho)
Even after all my interview rounds were over before almost everyone else's, my result still wasn't
announced.
The first list of selected candidates came out, and my name wasn't on it.
I can't even explain how stressed I was. I was already emotionally drained after multiple
rejections, and at that moment I genuinely felt like I couldn't handle another one. Later I found
out that there were two L3 interview panels, and the results from my panel were still pending.
But at that time, I had no idea. All I knew was that everyone else seemed to be getting their
results while I was still waiting.
Then came one of the most embarrassing moments of the placement season.
Our TPC, Apurv Jaiswal, started announcing a few names. He was actually reading out the
names of students whose results were still pending, but he didn't mention that before starting. We
had already been waiting for hours, so my brain immediately assumed he was announcing the
final selected candidates.
The moment I heard my name, I completely believed I had been selected.
I started crying right there.
For a few seconds, I thought the dream had finally come true... only to realize those weren't the
final results. Safe to say, I'll never forget that moment.
Eventually, we were told to go home and that the final results would be declared the next day. I
was convinced there was no way I was going to sleep that night.
Then another legend stepped in.
Samudra Banerjee called me. The first thing he said was, "Bad news..."
My heart absolutely sank.
--- PAGE 13 ---
He paused for a second and then said,i...you can't sit for tomorrow's process because you're
selected in IDFCại
I don't even remember what happened after that. I was literally jumping around the house.
After everything-the preparation, the anxiety, the interviews, the waiting, and the rejections-that
phone call made every bit of it worth it.
A huge shoutout to Apurv Jaiswal, Samudra Banerjee, and the entire TPC team. We often only
see the announcements, but there's a tremendous amount of work happening behind the scenes to
coordinate companies, schedules, interviews, and communication. They put in a lot of effort to
make the placement process as smooth as possible for everyone, and they truly deserve the
appreciation.
