The  only  difference  was,  instead  of  min,  we  had  to  take  the  max  path  sum.  Standard  2D  DP.
Solution  to this problem.
Was able to pass 12/12 test cases.
The  shortlist  (40  students)  was  released  2  days  before  the  interviews.  An  additional  shortlist
(+10  students)  was  released  a  day  before  the  interview.  We  were  asked  to  report  at  8:30  AM  on
8th  July.  1  candidate  was  selected  in  PhonePe.  1  candidate  was  absent  for  the  further  interview
rounds.

1. [Technical Round 1]  [48 people appeared for this round ]

This  round  was  taken  by  2  interviewers  and  lasted  about  50-55  minutes.  The  crux  of  this  round
was  to  test  your  core  CS  Fundamentals  -  Basic  programming,  OOP,  CCN,  DBMS  and  OS.  The
interviewer  began  by  asking  "What  are  SOLID  principles?"  I  said,  idk  I  haven't  studied  it,  but  they
are  some  kind  of  design  rules  used  in  OOP.  He  then  asked  why  to  use  switch()  when  you  have
if()?  He  then  proceeded  to  ask  me  a  few  basic  questions  on  Data  Structures  -  Arrays  vs  Linked
Lists?  What  to  use  if  I  want  to  insert  an  element  in  constant  time?  Which  is  faster  for  searching
an  element?  He  then  gave  me  a  pattern  printing  question  (basically,  print  a  diamond,  using  the  *
character).
He  asked  me  to  write  a  function  to  find  the  Nth  Fibonacci  Number,  along  with  TC  and  SC,  and
further  optimize  it.  He  then  asked,  what  happens  when  you  type  a  URL  on  the  browser  and  hit
enter? What is TCP? What is UDP? Give an example when you could use UDP.
Objects,  Garbage  collection,  ThreadSafe,  method  overloading  and  overriding,  constructor
overloading,  pass  by  value,  pass  by  reference  in  Java.  Exception  Handling,  what  is  it?  Difference
between  'throw'  and  'throws'?  Do  you  have  multiple  inheritance  in  Java?  What  happens  when  2
interfaces have the same method definition? (wasn't able to answer the last one)
Then,  the  interviewer  gave  me  a  case  to  design  a  basic  library  DBMS.  Highlight  the  entities,
attributes,  why,  with  constraints  (PK  /  FK  /  NOT  NULL  etc).  I  explained  the  purpose  of  each  table
and entity, why they were needed, and how they would be used in the overall system.
He  then  asked  a  few  SQL  queries  to  be  performed  on  the  same  tables  that  I  had  designed.
These  were  quite  simple,  just  2  queries  -  one  using  GROUP  BY  +  HAVING  and  second  using
UNION.  He  asked  about  SQL  vs  NoSQL.  What  are  the  different  kinds  of  databases  I  am  aware
of? Any examples for graph databases? (Facebook friends network)
Make  sure  you  explain  your  approach  from  scratch,  think  out  loud  ,  don't  just  jump  and  say  "this  is
the  answer"  Approach  >  Answer  .  Ask  questions  if  you  are  not  sure,  I  blanked  out  in  between
once,  while  he  was  asking  a  question.  So,  I  politely  requested  if  he  could  repeat  it.  Although  this
shouldn't happen but yeah make it sound like you are trying to clarify the question.
He  then  asked  questions  about  OS  -  Processes  vs  Threads,  do  processes  share  memory?  Do
threads  share  memory?  What  is  a  deadlock?  What  is  virtual  memory?  Why  do  you  need  it?  How
to resolve deadlocks?
I  was  able  to  answer  all  but  2  or  3  questions  where  I  mentioned  "I  am  not  sure  about  this,  but  I'll
look into it"  .
The round ended on a positive note with me asking them 2 questions :

-  How does banking work via calls? (Something related to IVR as they mentioned)

-  What do you expect from freshers?

Other  students  were  asked  easy-medium  DSA  questions(eg:  Longest  palindromic  substring,
Valid parentheses, find the repeating number, basic tree traversals - these are what I can recall)
Port numbers of various web services (MySQL, PostgreSQL, Mongo, Docker, http etc),
In  depth  Java  questions(really  deep).  Honestly,  this  depends  quite  a  lot  on  your  panel  but  overall
DBMS schema+DSA+Computer Fundamentals to a basic understanding level was consistent.
For  this  round,  just  have  clarity  with  the  concepts  and  your  answers.  Be  calm  and  don't  show
evident  confusion  on  your  face  at  any  point.  Be  loud  and  clear.  Don't  murmur.  Also  I'd  highly
suggest,  do  not  give  direct  answers  or  one  liners.  For  instance,  'throw'  vs  'throws'  can  be
answered  in  one  line.  But  try  to  first  give  a  gist  about  exceptions,  then  use  scenarios/examples
to  support  your  answer.  This  does  2  things  -  shows  clear  understanding  of  the  topic,  and  eats  up
more  time  in  the  interview.  Try  to  'control'  the  interview,  although  I'm  using  a  strong  word  here  but
basically learn to speak a bit more.

2. [Technical Round 2]  [20 people appeared for this round ]

This  round  was  again  conducted  by  two  interviewers  and  lasted  about  40-45  minutes.  It  began
with  my  introduction,  followed  by  a  deep  dive  into  RAG,  what  it  is,  how  it  works  under  the  hood,
and  an  explanation  using  an  example.  I  was  also  asked  about  the  vector  database  I  had  used.
Next,  I  was  asked  about  my  favorite  subject.  I  answered  DBMS  and  explained  why,  using
examples  from  my  projects  to  show  how  databases  helped  me  build  a  stronger  practical
understanding  than  subjects  like  OS  or  Computer  Networks.  I  also  emphasized  that  I  believe
every core subject is equally important in engineering and software development.
He  then  looked  at  'ETL  Pipeline'  that  I  mentioned  in  my  internship  points,  and  asked  me  to
explain  it  clearly,  "what  is  ETL?  Explain  it  to  your  Mom."  I  explained  my  internship  project  and  the
project  lifecycle.  He  later  got  confused  why  Barclays  is  mentioned  as  an  education  field,  I
explained  everything  about  MDMs  and  what  this  minor  was  about.  He  then  told  me  to  print  a
christmas tree(using *), something like this:
I  divided  the  problem  into  two  independent  parts:  the  triangular  canopy  and  the  rectangular  trunk.
For  the  canopy,  each  row  has  N  -  i  leading  spaces  and  2*i  -  1  stars,  producing  a  centered
isosceles  triangle.  After  printing  all  N  rows,  I  printed  a  centered  trunk  by  calculating  its  width  and
left padding. He followed up by asking the TC and SC.
Another  question,  which  was  pretty  random,  but  worked  well  in  my  favour  (maybe  because  I  was
able  to  answer  this  in  3-4  seconds)  was,  he  asked  me  to  "Find  12%  of  730".  Just  multiplied
12*73,  which  was  876  and  divided  that  by  10.  He  asked  me  to  iterate  my  approach  loudly  later.
Nothing  major,  I  guess.  Maybe  they  were  just  testing  whether  I'd  get  stressed  on  getting  a
sudden mental math question.
The  next  question  was  "Explain  different  problems  that  can  arise  after  you  push  a  project",  so  I
took  example  of  my  Flash  sale  order  manager  project,  and  explained  how  I  first  used  MySQL  for
the  entire  thing  but  it  resulted  in  dropping  orders  due  to  heavy  traffic  on  server  (multiple  POST
requests  hitting  at  the  same  instant).  To  solve  this  problem,  I  used  a  Redis  queue  and  a  worker
service  which  helps  maintain  the  order  and  consistency  in  the  order  count.  Although  this  was
slightly  off  wrt  the  question,  I  intended  to  leave  an  impression  that  I  have  studied  design  concepts
and implemented them in my project.
The round concluded, again on a positive note, with me asking 2 questions to the interviewers:

-  "This  might  sound  a  bit  crazy,  but  since  IDFC  is  trying  to  expand  its  reach  in  tier  2,3  cities

in India, is there any solution where you can have offline payments? Just curious"

-  What  do  you  suggest  one  should  focus  on  in  the  next  6  months  before  joining  the

company?
Within  five  minutes,  I  was  shortlisted  for  the  next  round.  The  HR  then  requested  my  email  ID
from the TPC to send the meet link for the virtual L3 interview.

3. [HR Round]  [ 10 students appeared for this round ]

This  was  more  of  a  casual  conversation  that  lasted  for  around  10  minutes.  The  point  of  this
round  is  to  judge  you  as  a  person  and  the  character  that  you  bring  to  the  table.  I  was  asked  the
typical  "Why  do  you  want  to  join  IDFC?".  Further  questions  -  Why  not  a  tech  company  and  a
bank  instead?  What  is  your  favourite  app  you  have  on  your  mobile  phone  and  why?  Do  you  use
any  banking  apps?  What  is  that  one  feature/characteristic  that  you  would  want  the  mobile
banking  app  to  have?  What  if  you  are  assigned  a  project  where  you  do  not  like  the  technologies
being  used,  or  the  project  itself?  Where  are  you  from?  Where  are  your  parents  from?  Are  you
comfortable with relocating to any other location?
The  round  concluded  by  me  asking  a  question  to  the  HR  representative,  "What  do  you  expect
from interns?"
Some  candidates  had  their  HR  round  before  the  L3  interview,  while  others  had  the  L3  interview
first.  The  L3  interview  was  scheduled  within  a  fixed  time  window  for  each  candidate,  and  the
invitation  email  included  a  Microsoft  Teams  meeting  link  along  with  our  resume  for  the  senior
manager to review.

4. [Technical Round 3]  [10 students appeared for this round ]

This  round  was  conducted  virtually  by  a  senior  manager  on  Microsoft  Teams  and  focused
primarily  on  my  resume  and  projects.  After  a  brief  introduction,  the  interviewer  noticed  my  Minor
in  Banking  Technology  and  asked  about  it.  I  highlighted  topics  such  as  BFSI,  Agile/Scrum,  and
Enterprise  Risk  Management,  and  mentioned  that  we'd  be  working  on  a  related  project  in  the
upcoming semester.
He  then  directly  picked  my  first  project.  He  asked  me  specific  concepts  and  their
implementation,  one  by  one,  for  each  project.  He  asked  questions  like  "Why  did  you  use  Redis",
"What  is  NGINX  and  how  is  it  balancing  the  load",  "Explain  the  CI/CD  Pipeline  you've  created  in
your project".
My  second  project  was  based  on  NLP  and  RAG.  He  asked  me  how  RAG  works,  do  you  need  an
LLM  layer  or  not  for  the  RAG  Pipeline?  What  would  happen  without  it?  With  it?  What  is  the  vector
DB  you  have  used?  Why  have  you  used  MongoDB?  (to  store  the  files),  but  why?  U  just  need  to
chunk  and  store  the  embeddings  right?  I  answered,  for  file  history  that  can  be  accessed  on  the
user  profile.  For  the  third  project,  he  just  asked  me  to  explain  the  authentication  flow  in  the
project.
He  then  gave  me  2  tables-  orders1  and  orders2,  and  then  asked  me  to  write  a  SQL  query  to  find
the maximum amount from both the order tables, which can be solved using UNION.
SELECT MAX(amount) AS max_amount
FROM (
SELECT amount FROM orders1
UNION ALL
SELECT amount FROM orders2
) AS all_orders;
The  round  concluded  with  me  asking  him  how  his  journey  at  IDFC  was,  and  how  he  has  grown
professionally.  Also  one  advice  that  would  help  me  become  a  better  fit  and  better  engineer
overall.  He  gave  some  good  insights.  I  was  the  last  person  to  give  this  round  and  come  out  of  the
TPO. It ended at 9:40pm lasting about half an hour.
The  final  results  were  announced  at  10:40  PM,  when  I  was  on  my  way  home.  My  phone  started
ringing,  notifications  started  flooding  in.  Everything  changed  in  an  instant,  leaving  a  moment  and
feeling that was difficult to process and explain.
At  one  point,  the  previous  day,  I  didn't  feel  confident  I  would  make  it  past  even  R1,  as  I  was  quite
exhausted  after  PhonePe  and  WorkIndia  and  had  not  revised  anything.  But,  things  started  turning
out  well  at  every  stage,  and  I'd  just  say  this  ki  "jis  din  tumhara  placement  hona  hai,  uss  din
pakka  ho  ke  rahega."  It's  a  fact  that  you  cannot  change,  you'll  have  to  personally  withdraw  from
the process to prove this otherwise.
[ 8 students received the offer at the end, including me.]
---------------------------------------------------------------------
A little background about my placement journey that I would like to share,
I  wasn't  able  to  clear  the  OAs  for  JPMC  CFG,  Barclays'  and  UBS'  and  Mahindra  Finance
Summer  internships.  I  reached  the  Interview  R1  for  Russell  Investments  but  did  not  make  it
further.  It  did  hurt  a  bit  after  every  rejection,  but  every  experience  was  a  stepping  stone.  It  is
important  to  acknowledge  things  are  not  in  our  hands  all  the  time.  Now  that  I  look  back,  had  I
cracked  Barclays  SI  last  year,  I  would  not  have  got  this  opportunity.  There's  always  a  better
opportunity  ahead.  Keep  your  head  high  and  just  keep  working  towards  your  goal,  is  what  I  have
learnt over these 1.5 years.
Over  time  you'll  realise,  luck  plays  a  huge  role  in  placements.  You  might  be  the  best  candidate  in
terms  of  preparation,  but  you  might  not  get  an  OA  shortlist  (it  happens,  IDFC  shortlists  before  the
OA  round  were  kinda  random).  You  might  miss  the  interview  shortlist,  for  whatever  reasons
(again,  it  happens  more  often  than  you  would  imagine).  Your  selection  depends  on  the  interview
you  give  which  depends  on  the  kind  of  panel  you  get,  at  every  stage.  There's  at  least  a  50-60%
luck  factor  involved  in  placements,  which  is  not  in  our  control.  What  is  in  our  hands  is  our
preparation  and  our  temperament.  Focus  on  what  you  can  control.  Don't  leave  any  room  for
regrets.

journey.howSecured:
1. OA

2. Level 1 Technical Interview

3. Level 2 Technical Interview

4. Level 3 Technical Interview

5. HR/Cultural Fit Round

Eligibility Criteria:
CGPA > 6.75, 10th & 12th > 60%, EXTC not allowed
My Resume.
--- PAGE 2 ---

1. OA [165 Candidates were shortlisted based on the company's internal criteria]

Consisted of 3 Sections:-

1. Aptitude (15 questions, 20 mins)

There were all sorts of questions on stats, probability, reading paragraph and answering questions. There
were also visual imagination questions, like suppose if I break a cube open on each of its edges, how will
that look. Each side of the cube had a unique design.
I didn't practice aptitude at all as I didn't have time. You should definitely practice, because the
questions might be easy, but doing them in the time limit is challenging. Maine khudne 4 questions thoke
the. I have read from the interview experience of my seniors that IndiaBix is a pretty good platform for
aptitude, I never opened it though.

2. Core + Other general CS questions (25 questions, 30 mins)

DBMS, OS, OOPs questions were there. Also there were questions on types of APIs, flowchart was
given and you had to tell the output, some mutex/locking code was given and you had to predict the
output.

3. DSA (2 questions, 40 minutes)

Q.1 Literally the same question, just in a story form
https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/maximize-path-sum-from-top-left-cell-to-all-other-cells-of-a-given-
matrix/
Other similar questions to practice
https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-path-sum/description/
https://leetcode.com/problems/unique-paths/
https://leetcode.com/problems/unique-paths-ii/
https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/problems/gold-mine-problem2608/1
Q. 2
A positive integer N is said to begin with X if the decimal representation of N starts with the decimal
representation of X. Given two positive integers X and Y, find the smallest positive integer that begins
with X and is divisible by Y. If X is already divisible by Y, then X itself is the answer.
Example:
Input:
50 3
Output:
501 3
Explanation:
Numbers beginning with 50 are:
50, 500, 501, 502, ....
The first one divisible by 3 is 501.
Similar pattern practice questions
https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/260/A
https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/490/C
--- PAGE 3 ---
Now comes the interview section. I wouldn't recommend doing what I did. I raw-dogged the entire
interview process. I never gave a mock interview, didn't even prepare a self-introduction, and simply
walked in and spoke whatever came to my mind. I was completely frank from start to finish in every
round. Even for the HR round, I didn't prepare answers for the common questions, I just answered
honestly based on what I genuinely felt and thought.
I hadn't touched DBMS and OOPs since third semester. So whenever I got the chance to overkill my
answers during the interview, I did it to compensate for the fact that I wasn't very confident in these
subjects. Thankfully, I was asked DBMS and OOPs questions only in the first round, so again, luck
played its role. For eg. One of the questions I was asked in one of the tech rounds was, how do you
automate infrastructure provisioning. Explained the entire architecture of Terraform, the files (main.tf,
variables.tf,
outputs.tf, providers.tf, terraform.tfstate, .terraform.lock.hcl ...etc),
commands,
Idempotency, etc.
I also noticed that the interviewers in L1 were expecting a simpler, high-level understanding of the
technologies mentioned on my resume, particularly Cloud and DevOps. The reason I went into so much
depth was that I had a strong understanding of these technologies, especially at the operating systems
and networking level. However, this approach can easily backfire if you don't know significantly more
than what you've already explained. It was a high-risk, high-reward strategy.

2. L1 Tech Round [40 students were initially shortlisted, 10 more were added after a day of the initial

shortlisting, so 50]
First, I was asked to introduce myself.
OS:- What is Thrashing? What is Paging? What is the difference between Thread and Process
(overkilled, explained the types of threads, task_struct,... etc).
CCN:- What is the difference between TCP and UDP (overkilled, explained QUIC in detail too), What
are the use cases? What are the OSI layers?
DBMS:- Design a student management system, they kept adding the requirements as I was designing.
After the final design, they asked me to write a query to fetch all the students who have never failed and
have CGPA > 8.
OOPS:- As I didn't have Java in my resume, they asked very basic questions. What are the 4 OOPs
principles? What is multilevel Inheritance(I was not able to answer this)?
Cloud & Devops:- Architecture of K8S, How do you ensure that a minimum number of pods are always
up? HPA, what is Ingress in K8S(I was not able to answer this)? How do you automate infrastructure
provisioning(overkilled)?
GoLang: - What is the difference between slice and string(overkilled, explained the underlying structure
of a slice and array, then string)? What are goroutines(overkilled, explained the entire GMP model)?
DSA:- https://leetcode.com/problems/longest-substring-without-repeating-characters/description/
Gave 2 approaches, first using map and then a slice of 128 size, map lookup time is O(1) but still
hashing and resolving the collisions takes time.
--- PAGE 4 ---

3. L2 Tech Round [22 students were shortlisted for this round ]

This round was mainly focused on my projects, so I'll only mention the parts that weren't
project-specific. While answering questions about my projects, I was cut off 2-3 times because I was
going a little too deep into the explanations. During the interview, I was asked about my hobbies and my
favourite sport. I said Table Tennis, and we ended up having a brief conversation about it. I was also
asked about the motivation behind one of my projects, so I explained the entire story behind it.
To start, I was asked which question from the previous round I had been unable to answer. I said I
couldn't recall what Kubernetes Ingress was. He then asked me to explain it, and I answered. This was
followed by a question on reverse proxy and forward proxy (overkilled it). Based on my answer, he
asked where TLS operates in the OSI model (overkilled it again by explaining the entire packet lifecycle
along with the OSI layers). After that, I was asked to introduce myself.
The remaining questions were: What is Blockchain? Explain it as if you were explaining it to someone
with no technical background. Explain RSA (I wasn't able to recall it properly, but I said whatever I
could). What is the difference between hashing and encryption? (overkilled it). What is Event-Driven
Architecture? (overkilled it). The last question was to write an API template for one of my project's
functions/features. I didn't really understand what he meant. I asked him 3-4 times whether he wanted
me to write code or draw a diagram, but I still couldn't understand what he was expecting. In the end, he
simply asked me to write a cURL request and then asked where the API key would be passed in the
request.
After that, he asked if I had any questions for him. I asked three questions, all of which were based on
points covered in the company's presentation and their projects.

4. L3 Tech Round [10 Students were shortlisted for this round]

This round was conducted online by a very senior engineer. I felt that this round went quite bad, I was
traumatized. So I don't remember much of what happened in this round. It lasted 20 mins, I'll just write
what little I do.
I was first asked to introduce myself. Then I was asked how Go differs from Java, followed by several
follow-up traumatizing questions on Java (probably because I hadn't prepared Java at all). After that, I
was asked about my favourite engineering subjects, and I answered Cloud Computing and Physics. This
led to follow-up questions on cloud and on-premise infrastructure, the cost of running each, which one
would be a better choice in different scenarios, and related topics. I was then asked why a company
needs a DevOps engineer, followed by several cross-questions based on my response.
At the end of the interview, I was asked if I had any questions. I asked the same 2/3 questions that I had
asked in L2, along with one new additional question.
--- PAGE 5 ---

5. HR/Cultural Fit Round [The same 10 students gave this round]

This round was conducted about 5 minutes after my L3 interview. The first question I was asked was
how my previous interview rounds had gone. I answered honestly, and after that, we had a casual
conversation on a variety of topics. This round lasted for around 20-25 minutes. The HR-related
questions that I remember are listed below:-

1. If your manager constantly micromanages you, for example, asking for updates every 10 minutes and

not trusting you, what would you do? I first asked whether the manager had always been like that or had
become that way after I made a mistake. The interviewer replied that the manager had always been like
that. She also mentioned that the manager belonged to the Boomer generation, she (the interviewer) was
a Millennial, and I was Gen Z, so there could be differences in ideologies and work styles.

2. Suppose you have a strict deadline to deliver an application to a client, but a few days before the

deadline, you realize that the product cannot be delivered on time. What would you do?

3. What are your future plans and long-term goals?

4. You probably have an account with another bank. If you could change one feature of that bank, what

would it be?

5. Have you ever been in a situation where one of your teammates simply wouldn't listen while working

on a team? If yes, how did you handle it?

6. Why do you want to join us? What do you like about us? What motivates you?

After all the interviews were over, I called home and told them that it was over for me because of how
badly I felt my L3 had gone. About 20 minutes later, I found out that the first four shortlisted candidates
had been selected. Another 10 minutes later, those four candidates were called to Room 105 by the Head
HR, and I was one of them. She informed us that we had been selected. Later, I came to know that I was
the first shortlisted candidate, which was completely unbelievable given how I thought my L3 had gone.
The interviews concluded around 21:40, and everyone had left by 21:50 PM. The next four selected
candidates were announced online at around 22:30 PM.

journey.howSecured:
In total, 3 rounds were conducted - 1 Online Assessment round, 1 Technical Interview round and
1 HR round (however Managing Director was also present in the HR round and he also asked
Technical questions). The CGPA criteria was kept at 8.

1. Resume/CGPA Shortlisting [ Around 220 candidates]

The first round was fairly simple, resume shortlisting was done and in all fairness resume
shortlisting is very unpredictable. The best thing to do is list as many technical skills as possible
(but also learn them) because the number of technical skills is a big factor. Also check ur ats
score keep it above 70+

2. Pre-Placement Talk

The Managing Director of the Mumbai branch gave the talk, and a detailed salary breakdown
was given as well. Try to listen to it carefully so that you can ask better questions in the HR
round as it matters alot. Other than that it's ur call to ask questions or not in ppt as for my case it
did not matter however try to avoid asking stupid ai related questions only ask genuine questions
--- PAGE 2 ---

3. Online Assessment Round [ Approx 210 candidates]

This was by far the trickiest round. So this was the structure of the test
15 Java mcqs
15 Python mcqs
3 sql mcqs
10 Al output scenario based questions (this also was indirectly 5 java and 5 python based
questions)
25 Aptitude Questions
Let's discuss one by one :

1) Since Java was my primary language I focused on this section alot and solved around

12/15. Because of negative marking I was very cautious to attempt these questions.
Topics to prepare : Classes, Objects, generics, Collections framework, error handling,
Interfaces and abstract classes, enums, steams, Lamda functions.

2) I don't use python and I had only a basic understanding of python so my strategy was to

study 7-8 standard patterns which were asked from claude using all the interview
experiences. I only remember the single question of Method Resolution Order in python
. However, OOPS of python was asked well in depth. Some people mentioned that this
section was very hard so dont solely rely on it. I attempted 10/15 questions

3) This section was very standard. If you are aware of various types of aggregate functions,

window functions and CTE in sql then this section will be a breeze for you. I attempted
all the 3 questions.

4) This again as I mentioned was indirectly test java and python knowledge in a different

format. The main goal was to read the prompt properly and identify what the code is
intended to do, then you can easily find the correct option which is the correct snippet of
code . I attempted 9/10 questions .

5) This was fairly simple. Some 11th std Physics and common sense will do the trick,

however try to complete the 100 gfg puzzles I incorrectly attempted 1 question.
It was the question known as 8 identical balls where 7 have the same weight and 1 is
slightly heavier. 1 attempted 24/25 questions
So in total before the test I was aiming for 50+ questions and I answered 60/70. The
main thing was to not waste time on lengthy questions, utilising every minute and
maintaining a fairly consistent pace, not slow and not fast.

2. Technical Interview Round | 44 candidates appeared ]

Now after the mcq round the candidates were called for second round in batches of 5. This made
everyone very tense as results were announced after a while (after 1 hour). Panels were allotted
based on the OA performance (I confirmed with my senior) so panel 1,2,3 were allotted to
people who performed fairly consistently in all the sections.
--- PAGE 3 ---
Lets Jump into the interview directly :
I was very nervous and it was visible in my body language and answers, however luckily the
interviewer was an Alumni of Spit this single fact made me 10x relax and after that Introduction
was given by him and he asked for mine as well. I had prepared it in advance and It was
structured in this format Name -> Year, Branch and Cgpa -> Languages and frameworks I use
for development and Dsa > A brief overview of all my 3 projects > followed by thanking him
for patiently listening.
He first asked me for my favourite project and told me to explain it in depth. And I explained
everything related to the project from why it was made to what features it had, end to end API
life cycles of every user request and User flows for every use case. It had docker in it as well so
asked about my proficiency in docker and I answered honestly that I had working understanding
of docker however I have never used it in production and he was satisfied with it. Other then
that he was very impressed with my project explanations. Try to answer every tech stack
decision, libraries used and system design choices properly so that U wont get cross questions
related to the project.
Then He started with Core Subjects →
He directly asked me to explain the concept of OOPs so I had to started with the core problem
before OOPs and then followed by explaining Classes and Objects. Then he asked for 4 pillars
of OOPs. Again I first mentioned all 4 pillars then started explaining them one by one and I
went in a little more depth in Abstract and difference between abstract classes and interfaces
(dont forget to mention interfaces are contracts which are enforced when implemented). He was
satisfied with the OOPs then he moved to DBMS.
He first asked Full Form of ACID properties and Idk what Happened but I got froze and I got
stucked and forgot what I and D. Luckily he was chill and asked me how much Sql I know and I
answered that I have strong foundational knowledge and I can solve complex questions.
And I was then asked to write a Query to find Top 3 salaries of Employees For Each department
. This was a standard window function question. I was first using RANKO function however
then he cautioned me by asking how RANK works for ranks skips the next ranks if There are
two person with same salary so there may be a case where 3 highest earners will all have rank 1
and directly then next employee will be assigned to 4th rank. Since I answered the working
correctly he asked me, "What if he does not want to skip ranks and the next person should be
given 2nd rank. So I then explained to him how dense rank is correct for this scenario then I
completed the query.
Then He gave me a scenario of How to show a table of 1 million rows in Db i.e He was
indirectly asking me what Pagenation is . I explained to him the approach correctly but could not
--- PAGE 4 ---
answer what this concept is called as (th i just answered logically without thinking of
pagination).
Then he asked me the difference between Encryption and Hashing. Which I explained correctly
by mentioning that Hashing is irreversible and Encryption is reversible (i.e there can be 2 stages
Encryption and Decryption) . Now I also mentioned / gave examples of Private and Public key
cryptography. So he asked me for an algo which uses both public and private key and SomeHow
remembered the Diffie Hellman Key Exchange Numerical in CNS so I explained to him that algo
itself and he was impressed.
Then he asked me what RESTful apis are so again in Classic dhruv fashion I didn't remember
the fullform however I explained to Him what it meant and what it introduced. He then asked
me HTTP methods and the difference between GET and POST methods. I answered them
correctly and also said that the POST method can also be used to read data from the server,
however it is generally a bad practice. (BTW he directly asked next 3 candidates how POST
method is used to fetch data from server)
He then asked me what I know about about Queues and RabbitMQ, I honestly answered him
that I am aware about the concept however I have not used any of them for my projects. So he
skipped this section for me.
Then Came the DSA section, he first asked my current progress in DSA and I answered him
about my familiarity in Linear and Non Linear Data Structures. Now he then straightaway asked
me Least Frequently Used cache and I had no clue what it was so I told him about it and to
explain me the Problem and I then explained him what I interpreted from the question and started
thinking of what data structure can be used before anything else. I first told him hashmap will be
necessary and then Maybe a priority queue to acces the term which is least frequently used in
o(1) time. this was wrong however he told me that he needed something simple and also
mentioned that he loves simple solutions not fancy and complicated answers. Then after trying
for 2 minutes he moved on to the next question.
He then asked me how to print all elements in a linkedList in reverse without tampering the
original list and answered Stack in an instance and explained my approach within 10 seconds
then he accused me knowing this question beforehand which i laughed and defended me by
mentioning that i had learned it from striver sheet and it one of the foundational questions of
stack .
With this he concluded my interview and asked me if I had any questions:
I asked these questions -

1) How the first 3 months for an intern in ISS will look like.

--- PAGE 5 ---

2) I explained him my 3rd project then told him this project has inspired me create a new project

related to cricket and asked him to approach the data creation part for the new problem statement

Selected for HR

This was according to me the easiest round of them all since The panelists were fairly tired I

Smile on your face and have a respectful tone while speaking and this helps a lot just trust me on

journey.prep:
• Know your resume inside out. Every project, internship, and technical skill mentioned on your

resume should be something you can confidently explain in depth, as interviewers can pick any point
and ask detailed follow-up questions.

• Be honest and confident. It's perfectly acceptable to use Al tools while building projects, but make

sure you understand the implementation and can explain your design decisions and debug the code
independently.

• Stay calm under pressure. Interviewers may intentionally challenge your answers or create a stressful

environment to evaluate your confidence and thought process. Don't let this affect your performance.

• Treat the interview as a conversation. Think aloud while solving problems, communicate your

approach clearly, and if you don't know something, admit it honestly instead of guessing.

• Every interview is a learning experience. Whether you get selected or not, take note of the questions

asked, work on your weak areas, and keep improving. Consistency and self-belief matter far more
than one successful or unsuccessful interview.
Placements are a journey filled with both highs and lows. Trust your preparation, keep learning from every
experience, and don't compare your journey with anyone else's. The right opportunity will come with
consistent effort and perseverance.
All the very best for your placement journey! Hope this experience helps you in securing your dream
offer.

journey.howSecured:
The recruitment process consisted of the following rounds:

1. Online Assessment (MCQ Test)

2. Technical Interview

3. Techno-HR Interview (Technical + HR)

Resume Shortlisting | 214 students were shortlisted]
The first stage of the recruitment process was resume shortlisting. While the exact shortlisting criteria were
not disclosed, I believe my academic performance, relevant projects, and an ATS-optimized resume played
an important role in getting shortlisted.
I maintained a CGPA above 8.7 throughout engineering, which met the company's eligibility criteria of 8+
CGPA. I would strongly recommend maintaining a CGPA above 8 (preferably above 9), as it keeps you
eligible for a larger number of placement opportunities. Before the placement season, I optimized my
resume using Resume Worded, where it achieved an ATS score of approximately 83. (A score above 70
would help you get shortlisted for most of the companies) I also ensured that the resume was concise, one
page long, included quantified achievements, and highlighted projects relevant to software engineering.
My advice would be to regularly improve your resume, keep it ATS-friendly, tailor it wherever possible to
the job profile, and be prepared to justify every point mentioned during the interview. (Do not mention any
technical skill on your resume unless you are confident discussing it in depth during the interview.)

1. Online Assessment 214 students appeared for the test ]

The first round was an offline on-campus Online Assessment conducted through Google Forms. The
assessment was held from 8:30 AM to 10:00 AM (90 minutes) and consisted of approximately 70
multiple-choice questions.
Marking Scheme

• +1 for every correct answer

• -0.25 for every incorrect answer

--- PAGE 2 ---
Since negative marking was involved, accuracy was much more important than attempting every question.
My strategy was to attempt only those questions where I was reasonably confident instead of making
random guesses.
The assessment consisted of five sections:

• Java

• Python

• SQL

• Al-based Code Review / AI Output Evaluation

• Aptitude

Java (Approximately 15 Questions)
Java was my primary programming language, so I spent a significant amount of time preparing for this
section. The questions were primarily output-based and conceptual rather than definition-based. Instead of
asking direct theoretical questions, the assessment tested whether the candidate truly understood the internal
working of Java.
The important topics included:

• Object-Oriented Programming concepts

• Method Overloading and Method Overriding

• Collections Framework

Generics and Wildcards
Optional Class

• String vs StringBuilder

• Exception Handling

• Lambda Expressions and Streams

• Access Modifiers

• Interfaces and Abstract Classes

• Code Output Prediction

Several questions contained subtle edge cases where a small conceptual misunderstanding could easily lead
to an incorrect answer. My recommendation would be to understand why a particular output is produced
rather than memorizing definitions, as most questions tested conceptual understanding instead of factual
knowledge.
Python (Approximately 15 Questions)
Although Python was not my primary programming language, the questions mainly focused on conceptual
understanding and output prediction.
The important topics included:

• Object-Oriented Programming

• Method Resolution Order (MRO)

• Mutable vs Immutable Objects

• Object References

--- PAGE 3 ---

• Shallow Copy vs Deep Copy

• Function Behaviour

• Lists, Dictionaries and Sets

• Basic Python Internals

Many questions revolved around Python-specific behaviors that are commonly overlooked during interview
preparation. Since I was comparatively less comfortable with Python, I focused on attempting only those
questions where I was confident, which helped avoid unnecessary negative marking.
SQL (3 Questions)
This was the shortest and comparatively easiest section of the assessment. The questions were
scenario-based, where a problem statement was provided and candidates had to identify the most appropriate
SQL query among multiple options.
The topics primarily included:

• SELECT Statements

• JOINs

• Aggregate Functions

• GROUP BY

• HAVING Clause

• Filtering Conditions

I had completed the LeetCode SQL 50 before the assessment, which covered almost every concept required
for this round. As a result, I was confident in this section and attempted all the SQL questions. For future
candidates, I would strongly recommend completing the LeetCode SQL 50 questions, as they provide
sufficient practice for assessments of this level.
Al-Based Code Review / AI Output Evaluation (Approximately 10 Questions)
This was one of the most interesting and unique sections of the assessment. Instead of testing theoretical
Artificial Intelligence concepts, the section evaluated whether candidates could critically analyse
Al-generated responses. Each question presented a prompt along with one or more Al-generated solutions.
Candidates had to determine whether the generated response was correct or identify logical flaws and
choose the most appropriate alternative.
The questions mainly tested:

• Identifying logical mistakes in Al-generated code

• Selecting the most accurate Al-generated solution

• Recognising incorrect programming approaches

• Reviewing Al-generated SQL and programming snippets

• Understanding whether the generated output actually satisfied the given prompt

Aptitude (25 Questions)
The aptitude section was comparatively straightforward and highly scoring. The questions covered standard
quantitative aptitude topics such as:
--- PAGE 4 ---

• Time, Speed and Distance

• Work and Time

• Profit and Loss

• Simple Interest

• Probability

• Geometry

• Ratios and Proportions

• Logical Reasoning

• Scalar and Vector Concepts

• Minimum Weighing Problems (Ball Puzzle)

• Basic Quantitative Aptitude

Most of these questions were very similar to those available on IndiaBIX, and regular practice from the
platform was sufficient.
Out of 25 aptitude questions, I attempted 21, choosing accuracy over quantity because of the negative
marking. Since I was confident about the questions I attempted, I preferred leaving uncertain questions
unanswered rather than risking unnecessary deductions. I would strongly recommend solving IndiaBIX
topic-wise before the placement season begins, as aptitude plays a significant role in many company
assessments and is often underestimated by students.
Overall, I attempted 55-60 questions during the Online Assessment while ensuring that I attempted only
those questions where I was reasonably confident. Rather than trying to maximise the number of attempts,
my focus was on maintaining accuracy throughout the assessment because of the negative marking.

2. Technical Interview [ 44 students were shortlisted]

The technical interview lasted around 30-35 minutes and was primarily based on my resume, Java
fundamentals, React, and project discussions.
The interview began with a self-introduction. During my introduction, I mentioned one of my React projects

(ToyStation) and that it was deployed. The interviewers immediately opened the website on their own

laptop and started exploring it themselves. They clicked through different pages, asked how various features
were implemented and questioned my technology choices. This taught me that if you mention a deployed
project, be prepared for the interviewer to open it live and ask questions from any part of the
application.
One of the first questions was whether the project was Al-generated. I honestly explained that Al had
assisted in development but that I clearly understood the implementation and could explain every technical
decision. The interviewers emphasized that using Al is completely acceptable, provided you understand the
code and can debug or extend it independently.
The discussion then moved towards React and frontend development. Some of the questions asked were:

• How would you persist a field (such as age) across multiple pages in React?

• Why did you choose TypeScript instead of JavaScript?

• Why did you use Tailwind CSS?

• Which parts of the project were implemented by you and which were Al-assisted?

--- PAGE 5 ---
The next part of the interview focused on Java. The interviewers displayed multiple code snippets on their
laptop and asked me to predict the output. They also modified the snippets during the interview to test my
understanding of different scenarios.
The major topics covered were:

• Exception Handling (try-catch-finally)

• Collections Framework

• Java Streams

• Output Prediction

• Edge cases involving Stream terminal operations

Towards the end of the interview, I noticed that my project, which was highly relevant to ISS STOXX's ESG
domain, had not been discussed. Before leaving, I politely requested a few additional minutes to explain the
project. The interviewers asked questions related to ESG, RAG, hallucination reduction, and the overall
architecture of the solution. They challenged several of my answers to understand my thought process, but I
remained calm and justified my design decisions confidently.
Preparation & Suggestions

• Be prepared to explain every project on your resume in depth.

• If a project is deployed, expect the interviewer to open it live and ask questions from any page or

feature.

• Be honest about using Al tools. Interviewers care more about your understanding than whether Al

was used.

• Revise Java thoroughly, especially Exception Handling, Collections, Streams, and output-based

questions.

• Stay calm if interviewers challenge your answers they are often evaluating your reasoning rather than

expecting perfect answers.

• If an important project is not discussed, politely ask if you can explain it. It demonstrates confidence,

communication skills, and genuine interest.

3. HR Interview [ 20 students were shortlisted]

After the technical interviews, the shortlisted candidates for the final round were announced. Since many
candidates were being rejected in my technical interview panel, I was initially unsure about my
pertormance. However, when my name was announced for the final round, it was a huge confidence boost.
The final round lasted around 25-30 minutes and was conducted by the Managing Director and the HR
Head. It was a combination of technical discussion and HR questions.
The interview began with basic HR questions about my family background, hometown, and whether I would
be comfortable working from the Mumbai office five days a week.
The discussion then shifted to my internship experience. I was asked to explain my role during my NET
internship, the projects I worked on, how I handled deadlines, and a situation where I received constructive
feedback on my work. I answered these questions using the STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result)
approach, explaining how I improved after receiving feedback and the importance of writing maintainable
production-quality code.
--- PAGE 6 ---
The HR also asked about my hobbies and interests. The Managing Director then took over the discussion and
asked me to explain my project in detail. The discussion focused on:

• Overall project architecture

• Why I chose RAG

• How hallucinations were reduced

• How the chatbot retrieved relevant ESG information

Compared to the technical interview, I was much more confident while explaining the project and was able
to answer the follow-up questions calmly. Towards the end of the interview, I was asked whether I would be
comfortable working with technologies outside my current skill set, such as NET. I explained that I enjoy
learning new technologies and would be happy to contribute to any team where I could learn and grow.
Finally, I was given the opportunity to ask questions. I asked "What does a typical day in the life of an
intern at ISS STOXX look like?" The interviewers explained the work culture, mentorship, and
collaborative environment, which gave me a positive impression of the company.
Preparation & Suggestions

• Prepare your internship experience thoroughly, including your contributions, challenges, and

learnings.

• Keep at least 2-3 STAR-based stories ready for common HR questions on teamwork, deadlines,

conflict, and feedback.

• Be honest about your strengths, weaknesses, and learning experiences.

• Show enthusiasm towards learning new technologies instead of limiting yourself to a specific tech

stack.

• Always ask at least one thoughtful question at the end of the interview, as it reflects genuine interest

in the role and the organization.
Later that evening, the final list of 12 selected candidates was released. Seeing my name on it was a
moment of immense happiness and relief, and it felt rewarding to see all the hard work finally pay
off. Approximately a week later, the company released another list, selecting 3 additional
candidates, taking the total number of offers to 15.

In total, 3 rounds were conducted - 1 Online Assessment round, 1 Technical Interview round and 1 HR
round(I felt it more to be techno-HR). The CGPA criteria was kept at 8 and they followed it throughout in
my knowledge, so preferable to keep it above 8 and 8.5 if possible (Mine was 8.56).

1. Resume/CGPA Shortlisting [ Approx 210 candidates]

ISS-STOXX requires a photo on their resume so I made it accordingly. Tailor your resume to the JD it really
helps, keep only those projects and tech stack that you can talk about for hours, don't fill it unnecessarily it
only creates holes that they can poke in the interview rounds. Use resumeworded or enhancv for ATS score
checking, keep it above 60 preferably 70, mine was 65 but I think that was a factor of rejection in some
shortlistings.
--- PAGE 2 ---
2.
Pre-Placement Talk
They took the PPT online at around 3:00 PM. I always made it a point to note down the names of the
speakers, important points, their values, anything that could help me talk or indicate that I was paying
attention during it, it shows interest as well so I'd suggest you'd do the same. Previous interview
experiences noted they were asked the names of the speakers in the HR round so it is important.

3. Online Assessment Round [ Approx 210 candidates]

The OA round was conducted offline on-campus, the test ran from 8:30 AM to 10:00 AM. The format of the
test was changed slightly this year; 70 questions were to be solved in 90 minutes on google forms. 15 Java
output, 15 python output, 3 SQL, 12 Al proficiency, 25 Aptitude. Correct answers awarded +1 and wrong
gave -0.25.
Java section included a lot of Streams fundamentals like Collectors.groupingBy)) output type (and basic
stream filter and mapping problems like from a list = [1, 5, 7, 9, 3, 8], take only those numbers greater than
3 and square them and print the output), wildcards and generics knowledge (List<? extends Number> and
List<? super Integer> type questions), static methods and variables, polymorphism, String concepts (one
where s = "Hello"; s.concat(" World"); print(s);), Inheritance and Exception handling. Overall it was doable
if prep was targeted on this.
Python section was overall doable (even though I primarily use Java, the concepts transfer here as well).
Some questions on MRO, Multiple inheritance handling, use of namedtuples and @dataclass, difference
between _init
_ and exec, exceptions, etc. It was very similar to java outputs but some python quirks were
tested.
SQL section was easy to moderate, with question on UPDATE, DELETE and one SELECT query, all were
well defined on what to do with 4 query options for each with minimal differences but easy to spot if enough
practice done beforehand (Even tho I had dbms trauma at one time I did it)
Al Proficiency was something new this time, but the questions were easy to moderate with questions like the
Al generated this data schema or this Java snippet, these issues are popping up, choose one of the alternate
code or maintain that original code is correct. And some general questions I couldn't recollect like vector
DB and also a vector addition one where a triangle where AB + BC = AC property applied and we had to
choose the wrong equation out of 4. Overall nothing Al heavy instead it was to check if we can review and
identify issues in the code it generated so more like good knowledge of SQL and Java code.
Aptitude was easy to moderate with questions on permutations and combinations (balls w/o replacement),
bayes theorem, river problems, train and pole, etc. Standard problems on IndiaBIX nothing too out of scope.
I attempted around 55 / 70 questions and I assume I got 48-50 correct answers at minimum.
--- PAGE 3 ---

2. Technical Interview Round [ 44 candidates appeared ]

We were shortly given the shortlist and funnily enough it was the same number as last year. I was 3rd on my
panel which helped me for sure compared to being near the end of the list. I still maintain that luck plays a
pretty big role for which panel you get. Some of my friends got a panel where they asked 3-4 Java output
questions and asked them to explain it and ended the interview in 10-15 minutes, and a lot of candidates
were rejected in that time as well.
I went for my interview at 12 noon and greeted the interviewer after I went in. He had already asked for my
resume beforehand and went through it before I went in so it wasn't spontaneous. I wasn't asked for my
proper introduction but he asked how my OA round went, how would I assess how I performed, to which I
replied that it was definitely the best one I had given yet, all the questions were challenging but doable
because of my prep which felt satisfying. I was asked to take one project, go super deep into it, explain what
I did, it's architecture, basically whatever I want to talk about it.
I chose my GSoC project and started with the problem statement with how OpenMRS (my org) consisted of
about 800+ different API endpoints and how it was tough to document all the changes (Additions /
Deletions) that occurred so a new developer may understand what is the correct way to process it. He
interrupted me here and asked me what is an API, what are REST APIS in particular and what do their
different types mean. When I answered each method had a specific purpose he put me in a scenario where I
am designing an API where I have to take in a very very large input from the user, say for example a RAG
pipeline where the input is a 1000 lines so how would I exactly send it to the backend? I answered that GET
is the ideal method since it is the endpoint that returns a response, but I was fuzzy on the specifics on how
exactly big responses are passed. I said chunking might be an option which he didn't really like, I answered
back saying yes since the requests are not guaranteed to be ordered, it might fail so a chunk would disappear
etc. He asked me whether we can use a POST method for this purpose, to which I answered that it's a
workaround and not the ideal use of it. He told me to answer CAN we before moving onto SHOULD we? I
said yes it should be possible as we can fill in the fields with whatever input we get and send it to the
backend. But I was still kind of stuck on what he was asking but I came around. He asked me how exactly
but I wasn't able to pinpoint what he expected so we moved ahead.
He started with a DSA question asking me whether I knew about the fizzbuzz problem which I had heard the
name of but did not know the specifics which made him happy. I was given a list of numbers from 0 to 100,
if the number was divisible by 3, print 'fizz', if it was divisible by 5, print 'buzz', if it was divisible by both
then print 'fizzbuzz'. He wanted me to write it in any language but it should be clean and simple, not
complicated at all. He hated it. So I made a class and main function in Java and wrote a basic for loop from
O to 100 and suggested 3 if else conditions starting with the both divisible case and moving onto others. This
was the tricky part that he did not want me to use the both divisible if condition. I sat there and thought
about alternatives but I just couldn't. I kept trying and suggested an approach where I use a 2nd for loop to
go through the multiples first then go to the other ones which he rejected. Eventually he gave me a micro
hint to write the output for 3, 5 and 15 and observe it carefully. Then it clicked for me to use a StringBuilder
where if i % 3 then append fizz, if i % 5 then append buzz and print the string if it's not empty. He was
satisfied and moved onto the next problem.
I was given a singly linked list with a 100 nodes and I had to print the values of the nodes in reverse without
changing the input linked list in any way. He again iterated he liked simple not complicated and I should
keep it in mind. I suggested a way where we take a list, iterate through the linked list and adding values and
--- PAGE 4 ---
reversing the list in the end or backwards for loop whatever he wants. He asked me to think of more
approaches so I asked him if I should explore making a dummy linked list which he rejected. I suggested
using a stack, and with his reaction I understood that's what he wanted from me and he asked me how
exactly I would use it. Then he asked me to think more and I suggested using a deque which was the same
so I kept on thinking but couldn't think more. I came home and looked at it, and understood he wanted a
recursion approach which did not click for me but it's alright.
I was asked how good I was with DBMS for which I said I'm decent. He asked me the difference between
PRIMARY and UNIQUE keywords which I answered. I was then asked a query on an Employee table with
attributes of name, dept, age and salary to get the 2nd highest salary where the age is between 15 and 25 and
asked me to write the query. I wrote SELECT name FROM Employee WHERE age BETWEEN 15 AND 25
ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1; He read it, accepted it and we moved ahead.
He was also interested in knowing why java and go and why not some other language where I told him
language did not matter for me, I look at the requirements and decide accordingly, like I would use python
for ai projects because of vast library support, go for concurrency like my HTTP server project since I
wanted to understand how it worked which he appreciated and initially I only used what I knew but I don't
do that anymore.
We moved onto my projects and he asked me about kafka and how I used it in my project, I made a small
diagram showing my flow and showed him that kafka was ingestion intended and not user facing so I don't
have to wait for http requests to end and could do it async and made it for future features of notifs and email
services as well. I justified why I did not use rabbitmq and he asked me if we really need kafka then? We
could have a column or table in postgres where we handle it somehow but I told him the ease of doing it in
kafka made me choose this approach.
He asked me about redis and what is redis based distributed deduplication. I explained to him how redis puts
a lock on a request so multiple requests for the same thing do not go out. He asked me what if the request
failed then it would fail for everyone right? In the moment I told him yes it's a weakness but it's something I
could do like retry it afterwards.
One thing I'll mention was he was particularly happy that I used Golang and not python just for the sake of
everyone using it, because he worked entirely on go and it really made an impact on him. So in the end I
asked what was his role in the company and to elaborate on it for which he told me he worked on the
platforms team so managing the k8s which he told me were 300ish pods active. And he managed everything
cloud wise which was on prem but they partnered with google recently for ai purposes and cloud as well so
that's going on. I asked him about the open source summit and his thoughts on it so I could share some
interests that way. It really felt so natural talking to him and he was very knowledgeable for sure. GSoC
played a really big part in this round as he was aware of open source and it gave me a very big edge.

3. HR Round [19 candidates appeared]

My HR round started at around 3:30 PM, where it was taken by the MD and the HR head of ISS STOXX
The madam introduced herself and then proceeded to ask me about my hobbies, whether I'm planning to
watch odyssey, and asked me my favorite Nolan movies and I named a couple like the prestige and
--- PAGE 5 ---
oppenheimer etc. She asked me what else are you interested in, I said I follow everything so she asked me
my thoughts about the england vs argentina world cup semis.
She then asked me why I chose Computer Engineering, my biggest achievement yet where I referred to my
GSoC experience again and went very deep on how I prepped for it, submitted a proposal and worked on
such a great real world experience. She was very interested and asked me how it worked and I told her the
whole process about open source orgs and what they needed and how google provides stipend to new
contributors. Then the sir chimed in and asked me about how I chose this particular project, I told him I went
through each org and how they worked, and then I came to proposals where I researched on each one and
saw which one I could do naturally where ideas came so that's how. He asked me why I used a maven plugin
for example and if the org had asked me to use it. I was asked what was a mistake or difficulty that I had
faced during the project phase for which I described a real incident where I was not notifying my mentors
about my daily progress due to breakthroughs happening every 3-4 days not daily, but I worked on that habit
and learnt to show my work in a better way.
Throughout the round I focused on showcasing how much I value the non-coding parts. I highlighted that
the most important part of the project was not the coding phase but the architecture design and planning
phase where I spent a month since I needed a strong foundation. Also that documentation was really
essential as just creating a project was not useful but deep description really helps other developers to
continue maintaining it which is much more important.
They noticed that python was missing from my resume and asked why Al projects were omitted for which I
told him I explored Al as well where my mini and major projects are both Al domains showing I'm not just
one dimensional. It was just preference and I could adapt to anything that was given to me. He asked me
what if I was put in the backend domain or frontend would I have a preference? I answered that I have learnt
how to adapt to anything in the past 3 years so I could work with anything, language did not matter if the
fundamentals are clear which they liked.
They asked me what my family members did, where I lived and how would I travel to their office where I
told them I'm used to coming to college and it's the same route so completely doable. She also asked me why
I didn't go into the navy like my dad for which I said I don't like complacency and a government job felt like
that so didn't go there.
In the end they asked me if I had any questions for which I told them I really liked what my previous
interviewer did and can I put a preference to work under them for which they told me I'll go through
training, assessment after which if requirements exist then sure but they can't guarantee anything. I also
asked them about their products of esg and corporate governance and do they see a meaningful difference
between them for which the guy answered they're different domains and they do answer different questions
even though they're both governance.
Out of the 19 candidates, 12 were offered the role. Honestly it came to fine margins here because everyone's
HR went well so it's a shame.

customSections.content:
Throughout my preparation phase, I tried my best to balance both development and DSA, but I made sure I
had one standout achievement that really showed my strengths. I was not very successful at hackathons, but
I did not let that deter me. I made open source a big part of my toolkit, I was really passionate about it and
the fact it helped me was just an added bonus on top.
--- PAGE 6 ---
A really good tip I'll give is never make one company your ultimate goal. It's good to have a ranking or a
collective of potential companies but having just one of them (PhonePe or JPMC most of the times) and if
unfortunately it doesn't go your way would hurt in ways you'd never imagine. Take every experience as a
lesson and don't make the same mistake twice.
I thought I had a good rounded out profile but I was rejected from Barclays summer internship interviews in
round 1, couldn't clear aptitudes of Mahindra Finance internship, PhonePe, IDFC and then for AuxoAl,
UBS didn't even get my resume shortlisted which I couldn't handle on that day, but I cooled off, talked to
my friends and resetted and gave it my all in this process and God handled everything else. It does get better.
Hang in there because there is something promised for you and life is a long race that does not determine
anything other than a start. If there's anything you can always reach out to me. (+91 9967577570) LinkedIN

journey.howSecured:
1. Resume Shortlisting

2. OA

3. Technical round

4. HIR

1. Resume Shortlisting (200+ candidates)

Maintain a GPA above 8 (I will personally recommend to keep it above 9, as it opens many doors).
Check the ATS score from Resume Worded. Mine was 65.

2. OA (200+ students)

Marking Scheme: +1 for correct, -0.25 for wrong
The Online Assessment consisted of around 70 questions with 90 minutes divided into the following
sections:

• Java: 17 Questions

--- PAGE 3 ---

• Python: 18 Questions

• SQL: 3-4 Questions

• LLM / AI Basics: 5-10 Questions

• Aptitude: 30 Questions

Java (17 Questions)
The Java section required a strong understanding of core Java concepts, especially Object-Oriented
Programming. Most of the questions were guess-the-output type questions, where understanding the
internal behavior of Java was far more important than simply remembering definitions.
The questions revolved around topics such as:
OOP concepts, Generics, Lambda Expressions, Method References, Pass-by-value vs Pass-by-reference,
Overriding hashCode () and equals () , Collections Framework, Access Modifiers
I would highly recommend practicing Java MCQs from Exam Veda and Sanfoundry.
Apart from these resources, one preparation strategy that helped me a lot was using ChatGPT to generate
tricky edge-case MCQS. Instead of asking generic questions, ask it to create questions that intentionally
include common traps and edge cases. These are the kinds of scenarios that are often tested in MCQs.
Python (18 Questions)
Similar to Java, the Python section also consisted primarily of guess-the-output questions.
The important topics included:
Dictionaries, Sets, Lists, Shallow Copy vs Deep Copy, Copying in 1D and 2D Lists, Object Referencing,
Various edge cases involving mutable and immutable objects
A lot of questions tested whether you truly understood how Python handles references and object copying
rather than just knowing the syntax. I would again recommend practicing edge cases separately, as they can
be quite tricky. Use GPT, prompt well.
SQL (3-4 Questions)
The SQL section wasn't based on writing lengthy queries. Instead, they described a particular operation that
needed to be performed and asked which SQL query would be the most appropriate.
Some of the important topics included:
Subqueries, GROUP BY, HAVING, Aggregate Functions
For preparation, I would recommend first completing the 70 SQL questions from SQL Practice, followed
by the Top 50 SQL Questions on LeetCode. Together, these should cover almost everything required for
this level of assessment.
--- PAGE 4 ---
LLM / AI Basics (5-10 Questions)
The LLM/Al section mainly focused on basic concepts and current trends.
Preparing this section doesn't require an in-depth understanding of Machine Learning. Simply use ChatGPT
to understand the currently trending AI topics and revise the basic concepts around Large Language Models,
Generative Al, and related terminology. That should be more than sufficient.
Aptitude (30 Questions)
Believe me, this is the most scoring section of the entire assessment.
For Java and Python, you either know the concept or you don't. If you're unsure about a question, don't
spend too much time thinking about it. Solve it if you're confident; otherwise, skip it and preserve your time
for the aptitude section.
I genuinely believe that attempting 25+ aptitude questions is achievable if you have practiced IndiaBix
thoroughly.
The questions were from topics such as:
Upstream & Downstream, Time, Speed & Distance, Permutations & Combinations (for example, committee
formation involving x men and y women), Basic One-Dimensional Kinematics, Probability (make sure you
understand Bayes' Theorem), Work & Time, Fractions, Averages.
I also have some actual aptitude questions that appeared in the assessment. I've attached the link below for
reference:

• Aptitude questions (link)

(ADVICE): To master aptitude, I would strongly recommend solving IndiaBix thoroughly. If you already
have a natural aptitude for solving these problems, that should be sufficient. Otherwise, you can refer to R.S.
Aggarwal's Quantitative Aptitude book or CareerRide(YT) to learn faster solving techniques and
shortcuts.
One thing I strongly feel is that aptitude is highly underrated. Everyone talks about DSA/ CP, but very
few people emphasize aptitude. While DSA is undoubtedly important, aptitude is equally important because
the majority of companies include it in their OAs.
My advice would be to start preparing for aptitude as early as possible. Once you become comfortable with
it, you'll be able to focus entirely on projects, DSA, core CS subjects, and interview preparation during the
later stages of the placement season instead of worrying about aptitude at the last moment.
--- PAGE 5 ---

3. Technical round (44 candidates)

The Technical Interview began with a very common question:
"Tell me about yourself."
Don't worry-I have shared the framework that I used to answer this question later in this document.
The interviewer then asked me to explain one project of my choice. The discussion wasn't limited to just
the project's objective. They went into considerable depth and asked about:

• The aim and objective of the project.

• The complete tech stack used.

• The justification behind choosing every technology.

• Alternative technologies that could have been used and why I didn't choose them.

I would strongly recommend preparing your projects thoroughly. Apart from knowing the implementation,
make sure you're able to justify your technology choices. Be prepared to discuss topics such as scalability,
future enhancements, possible optimizations, and why your chosen architecture is suitable for the given
problem statement. These are very common follow-up questions.
The interview then shifted towards Java fundamentals.
I was asked about the different access modifiers in Java, followed by another question on which access
modifiers can be applied to constructors.
I was confident that public, private, and default constructors are allowed. However, I wasn't completely
sure about protected. Instead of guessing, I honestly conveyed that I wasn't entirely sure about that
particular modifier.
Always admit when you're unsure rather than confidently giving an incorrect answer. Interviewers generally
appreciate honesty over bluffing.
Then he asked me to input 2 complex numbers and show the addition of them.
My response:

• Complex Number addition (link)

Then he asked me to write a solution where I need to print from 1 to 10 in any language of my choice, but
without using any loop.
I couldn't think of any other solution. I froze. I asked for a hint, when he answered, RECURSION!!
Again, it was a very simple answer but I couldn't think in that direction, anyways, now that I knew, I wrote
the solution and explained the flow of execution with a dry run.
E [Recursion](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Q6fofcUy70U8y8tKWBlFeag42RDwHCo-UeaWNBHBtKc/edit?usp=drive_link)
The interviewer then asked me a puzzle, given 3 jugs, 12, 8 and 5 litres, with the 12 one completely filled,
and rest empty, how do I measure 6 L exactly, which unfortunately I couldn't solve completely.
Never say "I don't know" or "I can't solve it' immediately. Keep thinking, communicate your thought
process, and if you get stuck, politely ask for a hint. Once the interviewer provides a hint, continue building
--- PAGE 6 ---
upon it and try solving the problem yourself. Showing your problem-solving approach is often just as
important as arriving at the correct answer.
At this point, I genuinely felt that my interview had gone terribly. I was convinced that I wouldn't get
shortlisted. I had almost lost all hope and even thought of going home. Thankfully, my friends encouraged
me to stay back and not lose hope.
A little while later, completely out of nowhere, I saw my name in the shortlist for the next round!!!
Learning: Never judge your own interview performance. Many times, the interviewers evaluate far more
than just whether you solved every question correctly. Your communication, honesty, approach towards
problems, and willingness to learn also play a significant role in the overall evaluation.

4. HR Round (19 candidates)

Compared to the technical round, the HR interview was much more conversational and comfortable.
The interviewers started by asking me about my background, where I stay, my daily commute, and some
general questions about myself.
The discussion then moved towards my project experiences.
One interesting question they asked was:
"Can you tell us about a situation where you made a decision during a project and later realized it
wasn't the right decisionại
Whenever you're answering such behavioral questions, make sure you always end your answer on a
positive note. The interviewer is less interested in the mistake itself and more interested in what you learned
from it. Also, try to relate your answer back to software engineering whenever possible.
The example I shared was from one of my hackathon projects.
Initially, we implemented session-based authentication because it was quick to set up. However, as the
project progressed, we realized that it had scalability limitations. After evaluating the trade-offs, we
migrated the entire authentication system to JWT-based authentication.
I concluded my answer by saying that not every decision we take will be correct. What's important is
accepting the mistake, learning from it, and being willing to rework the solution from scratch if necessary.
After all, quality is always more important than simply finishing quickly.
--- PAGE 7 ---
(ADVICE):

• Never answer in just one or two words. Always respond in complete, professional sentences.

• Whenever you're discussing failures, disagreements, or mistakes, always conclude by explaining

what you learned from the experience.

• Try to remember the names of your panelists.

• Finally, don't leave the interview without asking meaningful questions. Some good questions you can

ask are:

• How is Al being adopted within ISS?

• What does a typical day look like for an intern at ISS?

• What kind of learning opportunities can freshers expect during the internship?

These questions show genuine curiosity about the role and the company, and help leave a positive final
impression on the interviewers.
Finally 12 were offered the role, I was one of them.
