journey.howSecured:
First of all, let me say ki placement is purely based on Hardwork + Luck , the luck part is not in ur hand, however u can max out the hardwork part!!
Keep on trying for all companies without being choosy, u never know what u might end up with !!
In terms of the placement process for ISS Stoxx ,It had a total of 3 rounds
(OA , Technical Round , HM round)
OA (All MCQ) -> 15 java + 15 python + 3 sql + 12 ai + 25 aptitude based
Note -> mcqs had -ve marking of 0.25 !!
Than were Technical Round & than HM round

1. Online Assessment -> [ Around 215 students had appeared for this round ]

There were 2 Categories in this test i.e Technical and Aptitude questions (45 questions each),and note that there was -ve marking as well of 0.25 marks and a total of 90 minutes for OA
For Technical Questions -> Most questions for java were based on OOPS, deep/shallow copy based,exception handling , collections,threads,java streams,pass by reference or value, interfaces and abstract classes, for python they were mainly based on OOP ,Inheritance, MRO ,List comprehensions, Slicing, Dictionaries ,Sets ,Copy vs deepcopy , now for the sql part ,it was comparatively easier, based on group by having , get nth highest salary , and the ai part was based on some code in java or py ,where most questions asked to detect the mistake or code smells
For Aptitude Questions -> It was pretty simple but lengthy (this was unexpectedly more difficult than i thought)
It contained ->Stocks & Shares ,Probability,Speed, Time & Distance, Boats & Streams , Profit & Loss , Simple & Compound Interest, Trains, Percentage, Ratio & Proportion,Clock,Height & Distance (Trigonometry)
Here remember to practice Stocks and Shares, since its the only extra topic asked here compared to other company OAs
The best daddy resource is Sanfoundry, Sandfoundary_java & Sandfoundary_py
it consists of 1k python and 1k java MCQs, however i recommend to try only 300-400 questions based on relevancy to this OA and on top of that u can practice extra on Indiabix
For sql, since here sql is comparatively simpler,refer geeksforgeeks playlist 20 vids or SQL50 if u want more practice
And finally for Aptitude , Indiabix_apti shd be more than enough
If u complete all these mentioned resources, u shd be good to go!!
Personally for me , i found aptitude very time consuming and difficult and the rest was easy to medium And learn to manage ur time properly since each question weighs the same leave any Q which u are not sure about or might consume too much time, i learned it the hard way!
I was able to solve 13-14 questions from Java and Py section , and all 3 for sql , for ai i solved roughly 8, For aptitude i was only able to solve 15-16 questions
At the end of this round, 45 candidates were selected

2. Technical Interview [45 students appeared for the interview]

This round had a total of 6 panels, all interviewing in parallel
The interview started with Me introducing myself, and immediately, interviewer asked me about my dsa and dev language , i said in terms of DSA i prefer java and for dev i work with JS,
So he started asking me questions inDepth Java, it started with him telling me to make a object arraylist which will be first made than at index i , that particular object must be removed, pretty simple
Than he started by asking, lets say if i have a string s = "abc" and i have a line like s.replace("xyz") than if i print s, will it print the Original string, i said yes and than explained about String pool and pass by reference V/S by value and explained that string is an immutable class, based on that he asked me a follow up question to write down a class ,where everything is immutable (use private+final) ,
and then he asked me about the classic integer pool cache question of Integer class , like Integer a=128 wala question ,search it up on google/gpt , these type of questions are based on java pools
After that he moved on and asked about .equals() v/s == in java ,i explained it in depth regarding recursive content checking in .equals() and reference checking in ==
Then we moved on to Exception handling , where he asked me about the main two classes in error handling mechanism, which are Error class and Exception class, and asked about when to use which class, and what are the different subclasses within the Exception and error class, after that he gave a faulty try catch final block and asked me to fix ,it was just that the different catch blocks were arranged randomly and not to their hierarchy in exception class, where according to the Exception class, the most abstractive (uppermost) class shd be at the last catch and the subclasses within that uppermost class must come before it when writing catch (so bottom-up) , and asked me about a real life use case where i needed to write finally, like in production why do we even need finally , if code is faulty ,catch handles it ,if not, try works , he asked why use finally??
He asked when making dev projects in JS, what do u use for async and await, i said i am used to handling such async reqs using the library async-handler so i didnt have much exp with try catch finally in JS
Than he asked me about JVM,JRE and JDK ,after that he asked me about creation of two objects with different content in it , say name is an variable within that class, so two classes with 2 different names, than how do i return true for a statement like obj1.equals(obj2) , this was the only question where i found myself, questioning myself ,i thought for a minute and i told him that i know that this is something related or something to do with reference ,but i cannot get the keyword which i can add to return true instead of false , since he said u cannot change the obj or the reference of it, u have to add something in this "obj1.equals(obj2)" same statement to make it return true, later i admitted i am unable to solve this !
Than he started checking my resume (skills section),first he asked me a lil bit about my projects and internship and what tech stack i used, i think he found none relevant to his Professional Experience ,so than he asked a few sdlc based questions so i mentioned during my internship we worked on JEERA and how we operated thro it , and asked me a few questions regarding state space in langGraph and orchestration and how it works on crew ai
Later he moved on to sql , he asked me 1 group by having question and a simple subquery of returning 2nd smallest salary , than he asked a sql question where i have 2 existing tables in my db , namely employee and Employee , and if i run select * from EMPLOYEE, will it run ? i said no , and explained how sql is case sensitive , than he asked a follow up question,that what shd u add in this select query to not get an error , at that moment i thought to myself saying add a comment in front of select will be stupid to answer for such a highly framed question, i tried everything i knew, but the question said to not update or remove anything, only add !! i admitted idk the answer for it. Later, now that i have check all resources, the answer was indeed add a comment :) lols, i would recommend whatever u think of , just say it out loud , dont think for a complex path how much soever u have practiced, try the most simple and logical approach first
Than he asked me if i know and have used JAVA Collections, i replied affirmatively,than he told me to draw the collection interfaces and classes and asked a few question about it and asked what is a better coding practice to write ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>() OR List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(), here explain that on the referrer side (LHS) rather than referring to the class itself refer to the uppermost interface in Collections,so in future u can change a ArrayList to a LinkedList or to any other DS,based on requirement!
He than asked me to write a thread using Runnable in java and than asked follow up regarding thread vs process and asked deadlocks and their prevention algo along with the 4 conditions which must be true for a deadlock to occur, I wasn't asked much on core subjects!
There are probably a few questions which i dont remember , but i have covered the major ones,which i found interesting and still remember , probably there were a few simple questions on oops , interface and abstract default methods, super and new keyword and diamond problem in java
Some tips i think will help -> Stay confident throughout the interview, back urself with whatever u have studied, JAVA is something u absolutely need to master for this process in general for this process i.e OA+technical round, learn OOPS in depth from geeksforgeeks it has 3 sheets on OOPS , for everything else again refer sanfoundary , Sandfoundary_java -> Great source to brush up and learn new concepts ,but for oops refer the geeksforgeeks
Keep a smile always, and dont overcomplicate stuff when explaining, only speak what u know, be honest and in times where u for sure dont know the answer -> reflect it to the interviewer, and in cases where it is a lil bit fuzzy , say i will look into it and try it for some time until correct and also dont hesitate to ask for hints ,
Always when solving a question follow the "Think out Loud" method , i found it very very useful!!
My interview finished after 1 hr ,compared to others who had theirs finished within 30mins, however irrespective of time i was confident that i will pass to the next round as the interviewer seemed happy !
Also at the end he asked me if i had any questions , and i asked about worklife balance for interns vs senior engg and how was his initial weeks in this company , and how will be the interns integrated into the current projects.

3. HM Round [ 21 candidates appeared for this round ]

This was a very simple and easy round, it was like talking to a friend (keep it formal tho), where i started with my introduction and was asked about my internships , my best project, and what are the weaknesses that u encountered during building stage and what are ur strengths, how do ur friends describe u, describe urself in 3 words, then asked me about my hobbies, i replied with football and then we talked about my career as a football player and i got asked why didnt i apply for nationals ,and i replied honestly with i was simply not good enough :) hahahahaa. Than she asked why do u think is indian football federation failing as a system and than i talked about unavailable infrastructure and money cycle for football,there is a huge market for football viewers yet no revenue generation and so on , later she asked about my family bg, and than Managerial Director (MD) asked me about my projects (give a high level view), tip->dont go on rambling about ur project
and then asked me about why i didnt join my fathers field which was IT as well, than she asked me about the worst day in my internship exp

Tips : Dont prepare too much for this round, the more u prepare the more it seems for HR that u r robotic and lying ,keep it natural and honest ,and in between talks and gaps maintain a smile,and keep the environment formal throughout the interview,and if possible crack a joke or two (usually not advisable but i did so) so that the build up decreases and also maintain a personality that u r always ready to learn adapt and excited to join a MNC as big as this, do prepare the already known stuff like best projects , the intro for it , the weaknesses and what u learned from

In the end i was told to ask any questions,and i asked how does a successful intern look like at iss stoxx, and what do my next line manager expect from me :)
Also another thing i learned is never say anything negative, keep the tone +ve, like for example say all -ve stuff than add "but in the long run , i learned from it things like blah blah blah " Also i ended the interview by making a joke about them SACRIFICING their dinner for us students, and hr joyfully corrected me, saying POSTPONED never sacrificed :) hahahaha
Also i was the 4th last for the interview ,so it was around 9pm when my interview started and the Company staff had very less time so they decided to give all next candidates only 15 mins each (compared to 1 hr for each student before me ), so i thought to myself that i was already at a disadvantage .
The duration of my interview was just 20 mins , whereas compared to all other students (1 hr),even tho my round went well, i had already fixated my mind that i had been rejected that day because of past rejections from UBS & WorkIndia, and while going home, i was counting and noting down all of the
mistakes that i made during HR and technical ,all of this to later find out at around 10:30 night that i was selected :), much love ;)
A total of 12 students were selected for i+p in the end !

journey.prep:
• Aim to keep your CGPA above 8.5. A 9+ CGPA is generally the safest zone for meeting eligibility

criteria across most companies.

• Before applying to any company, share your resume and the Job Description with ChatGPT and ask

for a resume match analysis. Alternatively, you can use Resume Worded and aim for a score of 70+.

• Stay active on your TPO WhatsApp group and Superset. Check them once a week and don't miss any

placement opportunity.

• Practice OA using IndiaBix, Sanfoundry, Career Ride and make use of Chatgpt and Claude to

generate tougher questions. Focus on understanding concepts instead of memorizing formulas.
Strong OA performance often helps you get an earlier interview slot.
(Lang - specific question, SQL, (OS+CCN rarely) , aptitude, DSA)

• For DSA, prepare thoroughly. Being comfortable with Trees and Graphs is usually sufficient for

many companies, but it's best to complete the entire DSA and DAA syllabus to maximize your
chances.

• Know your resume inside out. Be prepared to explain every project, skill, technology, and term

you've mentioned. Interviewers may also ask questions beyond your resume. In my experience, until
the ISS interview, my resume was rarely discussed, the questions were mostly from core subjects and
concepts I had studied during college end-semester exam preparation.

• DSA : https://takeuforward.org/dsa/strivers-a2z-sheet-learn-dsa-a-to-z, Daily Leetcode

• GFG puzzles: Top 100 Puzzles Asked In Interviews - GeeksforGeeks

• DP : Aditya Verma playlist

OOPs: Kunal Kushwala

• OS + CCN + DBMS : Gate Smashers (Watched during ESE)

journey.howSecured:
Total 3 rounds were conducted: Online Assessment, a Technical Interview, and an HR Interview, although
the HR round was more of a techno-HR interview. The min CGPA req was 8.0. The application process
was open around 9th July I guess, and remained open until approx 11:00 AM the following day. Candidates
were also instructed to attach their latest photo to their resume.

1. Resume Shortlisting [All Eligible Candidates applied]

We were informed around 7th July to keep our resumes with a photo attached at the left corner. At that
time, my primary focus was on preparing for the AuxoAl interview, so I postponed the task of updating my
resume with the photo. A day before my AuxoAl interview, the ISS STOXX application opened on
Superset, with the resume submission deadline set for 11:00 AM the next day. That day was particularly
hectic. After completing the AuxoAl assessment, I returned home and had to prepare for the AuxoAl
technical interview. At the same time, I also had the UBS 2 online test to be completed by EOD, which itself
took about an hour. Because of these commitments, I couldn't get around to adding the photo to my resume.
--- PAGE 2 ---
The next morning, with only about an hour left before the submission deadline of ISS, I submitted my
resume without the photograph. Later, after facing rejections from AuxoAI, UBS, and Nomura, I was feeling
a little dejected and was concerned that the missing photograph might affect my chances of getting
shortlisted for the OA. Fortunately, I was shortlisted for the OA, which was released just a day before the
PPT. My resume had an ATS score of around 70. For the on-ground rounds, I used the same resume after
with a photo attached.

2. Pre-Placement Talk [Approx 200 students]

The PPT was conducted online at around 3:30 PM and lasted until approximately 5:00 PM. I note down the
names of the speakers, important points discussed, and examples shared during the session. I would suggest
doing the same, as in previous interview experiences, candidates were asked about the names of the
speakers and key points from the PPT during the HR round. It is also advisable to join at least 10
minutes before the scheduled time, which helps avoid any last-minute issues or not being admitted by the
host. Also I did not ask any questions during the PPT, it is always better to ask at least one relevant
question related to the PPT discussion, as it shows curiosity and active participation.

2. Online Assessment Round [Approx 200 students]

The first round was an Online Assessment (OA) consisting of MCQS. The marking scheme was +1 for
every correct answer and -0.25 for every incorrect answer, so avoid random guessing. If you are
completely unsure about a question, it is often better to leave it unanswered rather than lose marks.
The assessment was scheduled to begin at 8:30 AM, so make sure to reach at least 30 minutes early. We
were instructed to use the college PCs, but I highly recommend carrying your own laptop as a backup
in case of any technical issues. In my allotted room, there was one TPC coordinator and one HR
representative from ISS STOXX. Both were extremely helpful throughout the process. If you face any issue
while accessing the Google Form, politely inform them instead of panicking.
The OA had three sections:
Technical (45 Questions) - Java, Python, and SQL
Aptitude (25 Questions)
AI Section (newly introduced this year)
I started with the Java and Python questions since they were mostly conceptual and theory-based. After that,
I solved the Aptitude section. I intentionally kept the AI section for the end because the questions contained
long prompts and code snippets, making them more time-consuming to read.
JAVA
It was of easy to medium difficulty if your concepts were clear. The questions mainly covered:
OOP concepts, Streams API (filter, forEach), Lambda expressions , String concatenation
Generics, Collections Framework, Records, Optional class, Access Modifiers, Overriding equals) and
hashCodeO, Code output prediction
My Prep : I used ChatGPT to generate medium-to-hard conceptual MCQS from these topics. Practicing
those questions made this section feel quite manageable during the actual OA.
Python
Most questions were based on conceptual understanding and output prediction. Important topics included:
--- PAGE 3 ---
Dictionaries, Sets, Lists, Mutable vs Immutable objects, Shallow Copy vs Deep Copy, Copying in 1D
and 2D Lists, Object Referencing,
new_O vs_init_0 (2 questions), await and asynchronous
programming, Method Resolution Order (MRO), Output-based coding questions
My Prep : Practiced by asking ChatGPT to generate medium-to-hard conceptual questions from these topics.
SQL
The SQL section was relatively straightforward. Questions were based on:
Joins, Subqueries , Aggregate Functions, GROUP BY and HAVING, TOP / LIMIT, output prediction
Preparation Resources: LeetCode Top 50 SQL Problems and ChatGPT-generated SQL practice questions
AI Section
This was a newly introduced section and was probably the most time-consuming due to the lengthy prompts.
Most questions focused on Prompt Engineering. A technical prompt along with multiple Al-generated
responses was provided, and you had to choose the response that best satisfied the prompt.
Identifying incorrect Al-generated responses
Programming-related prompts involving SQL, debugging, and code generation
Evaluating different Al outputs
Basic AI concepts such as Sparse vs Dense Vectors
Although I did not prepare specifically for this section beforehand, I found it completely doable. The biggest
challenge was the amount of reading required because many prompts and code snippets were quite long.
Recommendation: Attempt this section towards the end so that lengthy reading does not consume valuable
time meant for easier sections.
Aptitude
I had been practicing aptitude regularly for about a month before every company OA. I solved questions
from the first 1-2 pgs on IndiaBIX and also used ChatGPT to generate higher-difficulty quantitative aptitude
questions. Topics asked in this OA included:
Boats and Streams, Permutations & Combinations, Probability, Stocks and Shares, LCM, Sets,
Arrangements, Linear Programming (objective function maximization), Statistics (Normal Distribution)
There were also several well-known logical puzzles, including:
100 Lockers Problem, 8 balls puzzle (same which was asked in russel they gave me vague statement)
101 Coins Nim Game where you could choose 1 or 2 or 3 coins. 2 player game, last to pick loses.
50 Prisoners and 50 Boxes Problem.
Overall, I would rate the OA as medium in difficulty. The time provided was sufficient if you managed it
well. I was able to complete all the sections with around 15 minutes remaining, which gave me enough time
to revisit unmarked questions. Keep an eye on the timer to avoid submitting at the very last moment.

3. Technical Interview Round [ 44 students appeared]

The OA ended around 10:15 AM. Around 11:30 AM, the TPO started sharing the shortlisted students' names
on the TPO group, but my name was not announced initially. Later, around 12:30 PM, an Excel sheet was
shared, and I saw that my name was second last in my panel. The first thing I felt was relief and gratitude
that my name appeared after the OA round. I believe the shortlist was probably based on a combination of
CGPA and OA performance (not confirmed though).
--- PAGE 4 ---
While waiting for my turn, I started revising Java concepts. Along with that, I was also listening to the
questions being asked in other panels to understand the interview pattern. I noticed that my Panel 6 was
conducting interviews quite quickly, with many interviews lasting around 10-20 minutes. I also observed
that some candidates were getting rejected shortly after their interviews, which made me slightly
nervous. However, I continued revising topics like Java Streams, equalsO, previous year interview
questions, and the questions being asked to current candidates.
Around 3:00 PM, my interview was scheduled. I entered the room, greeted the interviewers, and handed
over my resume to both panel members. My panel consisted of two interviewers. They started with a brief
introduction. Since I knew the panel was conducting interviews quickly, I kept my introduction concise. I
covered:

• My educational background (SPIT + SPJMR Minor with CGPA)

• My interests backend and ML

• Project names with brief descriptions

• extracurricular activities

Then one interviewer asked an HR-related question: "Where do you see yourself in 2 years?"
After that, he noticed that I had mentioned a Teaching Assistant role for DBMS and asked whether I was
comfortable with SQL and database concepts. I confidently said yes. He then asked: Difference between
INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN. I was able to answer that properly with examples. Next, one of the
interviewers drew this table and asked me to predict the expected output. I solved it correctly.
Table 1
Table 2
C1
C2
1
1
2
2
2
1
Then he noticed Redis mentioned in my tools section and asked whether Redis is single-threaded or
multi-threaded. I answered that it is single-threaded and explained the reasoning behind it. Till this point, I
felt the interview was going well and that I had handled most questions confidently.
After that, he moved towards language-based questions. He asked whether I knew Java. Since my primary
language is C++, I honestly mentioned that I understand Java code but am more comfortable with C++. He
then asked a Java Stream-related question reuse operation from GFG, a theoretical MCQ-based
concept. I didn't know, so instead of guessing, I suggested that I know high-level understanding of Java
Streams.
Then he moved directly to the next Java question which was based on OOP concepts. Due to the previous
question, I was slightly underconfident, but I still worked through it and gave the output. After that, the
--- PAGE 5 ---
interviewer said that my interview was complete. I was a little surprised because the interview had ended
earlier than expected. I thanked both interviewers and left.
Later, I realized that I had forgotten to ask them a follow-up question at the end. Since I had not answered =
Java-specific questions, while many Java-focused candidates were having 30-minute interviews and
answering several questions, I felt uncertain. I packed my bag and waited near the TPO area for the final
selection update. Unexpectedly, my name appeared in the selected candidates list. I was genuinely surprised
and grateful. What surprised me even more was that some candidates who answered 8-9 questions and had
longer interviews than me were not selected by the same panel.
This experience taught me that interviews are not only about the number of questions answered but also
about the quality of answers, confidence, honesty, and overall interaction with the panel. Also, try to add
some hints or share whatever you know about the topic instead of directly saying "I don't know."
Even if you are not completely sure about the answer, explaining your understanding or approach shows
your thought process and willingness to engage with the question.

4. HR Round [ 19 students appeared]

I was called for the HR round around 4:00 PM. Until then, I was revising some HR questions that I had
already prepared for myself and also going through company-specific questions. When I was entering the
cabin, I noticed that the interviewers were quite exhausted and were about to inform the TPO that they
needed a break. However, after seeing me, they decided to complete my HR round first and then take their
break. I was grateful for that and thanked them before handing over my resume. As expected, they were the
same people who had interacted with us during the PPT session.
The round started with a brief introduction, followed by a question about my overall day and placement
process experience. I replied that it was a great experience but equally exhaustive due to the rounds and
waiting time. They then asked about the difficulty level of the OA. I mentioned that it was moderate to
hard, but the time was sufficient enough to complete the paper comfortably. After that, they asked some
background-related questions, including: My family background and what my family members do and
my location. I told them that I am from Vashi and had already travelled to college regularly for the past three
years, so commuting would not be an issue. I also mentioned that I have alternative routes apart from trains,
which made the travel manageable. Then they asked about whether I have been given feedback from
professor or friend and how I improved that. They then asked about my interests. The discussion
moved towards my SPJIMR course experience. They asked what I had learned through the program
and how it differs from students who had taken other company-specific courses like Barclays and
Finance. I explained the broader learning experience and how SPJIMR helped me develop a more holistic
perspective. After that, they moved to my resume and asked about topics I had learned beyond the
academic curriculum. I tried to show genuine curiosity towards exploring concepts outside the syllabus.
They then asked me to explain one of my projects in layman terms. I explained the project in a way that
was understandable from a non-technical perspective. Till now all these questions were asked by HR and she
was noting it down in her laptop.
After this, the other interviewer took over and asked technical questions related to my project. Since
my project was based on a Small Language Model, he asked about terms mentioned in my resume, such as
attention mechanisms and decoder-only transformers. These concepts were relatively new to him, so I
explained them using real-world examples while ensuring that the technical essence was maintained. The
discussion then shifted towards SPJIMR and whether I would consider pursuing an MBA in the
--- PAGE 6 ---
future. I explained that the management exposure I received helped me understand how to make
informed decisions, and that having business insights alongside technical knowledge is valuable in
today's era. I felt that this answer aligned well with their expectations.
Finally, they asked if I had any questions for them. I asked follow-up questions to both interviewers, which
helped end the conversation on a positive note.
[ 12 were offered the role, though everyone's HR round went well O]
[3 more students were selected after a week, so a total of 15 students were offered the role.]
My Placement Journey:
During the internship season, I couldn't clear the OAs for Trilogy, Barclays, UBS GOTO Internship,
and Mahindra Finance.
JPMC CFG Summer intern: only way that jpmc hire for tech roles
The OA difficulty was easy to medium: Rotating array/problem and String-based problem.
I solved almost both questions and received the Al interview link the following week.
One thing I noticed was that I attempted both tests on the last day. I followed the same strategy this year
for the CFG Software Engineer role and again received a comparatively easier version. Although our team
performed well during the CFG Hackathon, I wasn't selected for the internship. Looking back, one possible
reason could be that my strongest backend skills were in Python (FastAPI), while my team primarily
preferred JavaScript, which limited my ability to contribute at my full potential and this yr CFG didnt
happen
Russell Investments: first company where I cleared the OA. The entire process happened in a single day:
OA + Technical + HR
The shortlisted candidates were announced in batches throughout the day. Since nothing was announced for
several hours, I assumed I had been rejected and stopped revising. Around 4 PM, I was unexpectedly called
for Technical Round 1 and I couldn't clear. One important lesson I learned: Never stop preparing until you
receive an official rejection from that company.
Now placement season,
JPMC FinTech Role: I applied because the role matched my profile well: it required Python, SQL, and
problem-solving skills. Unfortunately, I couldn't clear the OA. The questions felt extremely difficult (almost
CAT-level aptitude), and the proctoring was very strict. Even looking down while writing on paper triggered
"Face not detected" warnings, making it difficult to solve longer questions comfortably.
PhonePe: The OA was heavily focused on DSA problems(Binary Search + Graph + DP). I couldn't clear it.
AuxoAl: The shortlist was largely based on CGPA, Class 10 and 12 marks, and OA performance.
The MCQs were straightforward for almost everyone. The coding section had three questions, and I solved
around 1.5. During the interview, I experienced anxiety because it had been a long time since my previous
interview. I also couldn't revise properly that day, and my interview was scheduled in the last slot (around 4
PM) putting me in waitlist. The interview was with a consulting guy so focused on guesstimates and
business reasoning.
Some questions included: Travelling salesperson scenario, Profit and loss calculations Restaurant revenue
estimation, Pizza sales on a Saturday night, Car pricing, What is attention? SLM vs LLM. Unfortunately, I
wasn't selected.
UBS :
--- PAGE 7 ---
It consisted of multiple stages. Complete the UBS 2 test on that day itself increases the early shortlist.
OA (Pen and Paper): Easy SQL questions, Predict/correct output, Basic system design and performance
failure scenarios
Group Assessment: The key takeaway was that they were more interested in thought process and
communication than implementation. Speaking up, contributing ideas, and collaborating effectively
mattered much more than arriving at the perfect technical solution. Btw they didnt need technical
implementation.
Interview: It started with an intro and brief about a project. Then moved to technical questions which
covered:
SQL Outer Joins, CAP Theorem, Git Pull vs Git Fetch, Caching layer in a Legal Al system, Handling
production failures, Monolithic vs Microservices, Redis vs Redis Cluster, Docker, Kubernetes And in
technical also asked some HR questions like:
What are your master's plans?
What would you do if you're assigned work that doesn't excite you?

• Practice consistently rather than cramming at the last minute. Consistency in DSA, CS

fundamentals, and aptitude pays off.

The recruitment process consisted of the following stages:
14 July 2026 :

• Pre-Placement Talk

• Resume Shortlisting

17th July 2026 :

• Online Assessment

• Technical Interview

• HR Interview

• Result Declaration

1.
Resume Shortlisting [ 214 students were shortlisted]
The first stage for almost every company is resume shortlisting, and this is often the most unpredictable
round. My resume wasn't shortlisted for companies like UBS and AuxoAI. There can be several reasons for
this-it could be the ATS parser, your resume not aligning well with the job description, or sometimes
simply luck.
After facing a few resume rejections, I spent time improving my resume. I tailored it specifically to the job
description, quantified my achievements wherever possible, and optimized it for ATS. This increased my
ATS score to around 77. You can check your resume's ATS score on ResumeWorded-a score above 60 is
generally considered good.
One thing worth noting is that this company had an eligibility criterion of &+ CGPA, whereas many
companies usually have a cutoff of 6 or 7. My advice would be to maintain a CGPA of 8 or above if
possible, as it keeps you eligible for a larger number of opportunities.
The shortlist was released three days before the interview process, giving us enough time to prepare for
the subsequent rounds.

2. Online Assessment [ 214 students appeared ]

--- PAGE 2 ---

Round 1: Online Assessment (OA) (90 mins 8.30 am - 10am)

The first round was an Online Assessment (OA) consisting entirely of MCQS. This year, the test had three
sections: Technical (45 questions) covering Java, Python, and SQL, Aptitude (25 questions), and a newly
introduced Al section.
The Java and Python sections were primarily output-based, testing conceptual understanding rather than
direct theory. In Java, questions revolved around OOP, the Collections Framework, Records, the Optional
class, and code output prediction. Python focused on concepts like slicing, OOP, Method Resolution Order
(MRO), and output prediction. The SQL section had around 3-4 query-based questions involving joins,
subqueries, aggregate functions, and TOP/LIMIT clauses.
The newly introduced Al section consisted of basic Al-related MCQS which were slightly lengthy but
completely doable. Most questions were prompt-engineering based, where a technical prompt and multiple
Al-generated responses were provided, and you had to identify the output that best satisfied the prompt.
There were also questions where you had to spot inaccuracies or suggest corrections to Al-generated
responses. Overall, the section tested your ability to effectively interact with Al tools while also evaluating
your technical judgment. Many questions required you to identify the best Al-generated response for
programming-related prompts involving SQL, code snippets, debugging, and other technical concepts, rather
than testing theoretical knowledge of machine learning or AI.
The aptitude section was comparatively easy, with questions from topics such as Boats and Streams,
Permutations & Combinations, Probability, Stocks and Shares, and other standard quantitative aptitude
concepts. I had been practicing aptitude consistently for the last 1-2 months using IndiaBix, and I feel that
solving one timed test for each topic on the website is more than enough for placement preparation.
The marking scheme was +1 for every correct answer and -0.25 for every incorrect answer. Because the
negative marking wasn't too high, it made sense to take educated guesses when you could eliminate one or
two options. However, if you were completely unsure about a question, it was better to leave it unanswered
rather than lose marks unnecessarily.
Since Java is my primary language for DSA, the Java section wasn't much of a challenge. I revised Java
theory from TPoint Tech, which covers placement-relevant concepts very well, and used the same website to
brush up on Python topics. During the final stage of my preparation, I also used ChatGPT and Claude to
generate mock online assessments and attempted them under timed conditions. This helped me improve both
my speed and accuracy before the actual OA.

3. Technical Round [ 44 students appeared ]

Round 2: Technical Interview (45 - 60 mins)

After an anxious wait, the placement team started calling students in batches of 4-5 to the TPO cabins. The
complete shortlist had not been announced yet, but after seeing three or four batches go in, I had almost lost
hope. I even stopped revising and stepped out of the auditorium for some fresh air. Suddenly, my friends
started spam-calling me saying, "Arushi, you've been shortlisted!" I literally ran back to the TPO office,
excited and relieved.
--- PAGE 3 ---
When my turn came, I entered the room, smiled, asked, "May I come in?", and took my seat. There were two
interviewers on the panel. Having already appeared for interviews at Barclays, JPMC CR, and
WorkIndia, I was familiar with the process and had my introduction ready. However, after greeting me, one
interviewer said, "Tell us about yourself but we already know you're Arushi, a final-year student from SPIT
blah blah so, directly talk about your technical knowledge and projects" That immediately set the tone for a
purely technical interview.
I started by briefly discussing the two internships I had completed, explaining my role and the key features
I worked on. I then mentioned that I had also built several personal projects. They asked me to explain one
of them, so I chose my latest project and walked them through the problem statement, key features,
architecture, and the tech stack. They seemed satisfied with the explanation.
The interviewer then handed me a sheet containing two API endpoints:
GET /api/products/mobile/iphone
GET /api/products/laptop/dell
He explained what these endpoints did and asked me to describe the complete request flow in an
e-commerce application- from routes to controllers, services, models, database, and finally the response
returned to the client.
He then followed up with, "If tomorrow you need an endpoint for Samsung phones, will you create a new
API?" I explained that this wasn't scalable and introduced the concept of path parameters and query
parameters for building dynamic endpoints. Although I couldn't recall the exact syntax on paper, I clearly
explained the logic behind parameterized routes that can handle thousands of products through a single
endpoint. He smiled and said, "I was looking for the logic, not the syntax, " before moving on.
Next, he asked whether I knew Java. I replied that Java is my primary language for DSA. Although I
didn't have hands-on experience with Spring Boot, I confidently mentioned that I was comfortable with Java
fundamentals and could quickly adapt to Java backend development. Never say never I knew the companies
techstack had springboot so I beforehand mentioned my capability of adapting to it.
The next problem was Java-based:
Given a List<Student>, return the students with the highest marks from each department.
Before jumping into the solution, I asked a few clarifying questions about the requirements. Since the
company primarily worked with Java, I proposed using a HashMap with the department as the key and a
List<Student> as the value. I explained that while iterating through the list, if the department wasn't present,
I would create a new entry. Otherwise, I would compare the current student's marks with the highest marks
stored for that department-replacing the list if the marks were higher, adding the student if the marks were
equal, and ignoring the student otherwise.
He then asked me to write the map declaration, which I wrote as:
HashMap<String, List<Student map = new HashMap 0;
He followed up with another question: "What if I want this to be a TreeMap instead?" This gave me the
opportunity to discuss programming to interfaces and the concepts of loose coupling vs. tight coupling. I
--- PAGE 4 ---
explained that both HashMap and TreeMap implement the Map interface, so declaring the reference using
the interface makes the implementation easily replaceable. I then wrote:
Map<String, List<Student>> map = new TreeMap<>0;
Finally, he asked a DSA question on finding the length of the longest substring with unique characters. I
first explained the brute-force approach along with its time complexity and then optimized it using the
sliding window technique with a HashSet and two pointers, discussing the improved time complexity.
Towards the end, they asked if I had any questions for them. I asked about the biggest challenges fresh
graduates face during their initial months in the company. Both interviewers answered enthusiastically,
sharing their experiences and expectations from new hires. We had a brief but insightful conversation before
I thanked them for their time and walked out hoping for the best.

3. HR Round [21 students appeared]

Round 2: HR Interview (approx 25 mins)

The final round was an HR interview conducted by the HR Head (Asia Pacific) and the Managing
Director. The interview began on a very light and friendly note. They asked how my day had been, how the
OA went, whether it was lengthy, and made me feel comfortable before moving on to the actual questions.
They then asked me to introduce myself, followed by questions about my family, where I lived, and how I
planned to commute to the office at Goregaon. I mentioned that although I live in Navi Mumbai, I currently
stay in a PG. They asked what I would do if my parents wanted me to shift back home. I answered
positively, saying that my family has always supported my career decisions and that I believe ISS STOXX
would provide me with excellent opportunities for growth, so we would manage accordingly. One thing I
would recommend is to always answer such questions positively-the interviewer is often trying to
understand your commitment rather than looking for a perfect answer.
The conversation then shifted towards my hobbies and whether I still actively pursued them. They also
asked about my internship experience, the technologies I had worked on, my responsibilities, and the size of
my team. This gave me a chance to naturally mention that I had worked in an Agile environment using Jira
for project management.
I was also asked how I learn technologies outside my college curriculum. While answering, I mentioned that
I regularly take online courses and referred to a few Coursera certifications I had completed. I also used
this opportunity to talk about my hackathon victory, even though it wasn't directly asked. Remember, you
don't always have to wait for the interviewer to ask about your achievements-if there's a natural opening,
confidently bring them into the conversation. Lastly, they asked me about a project that had created a
meaningful impact. I spoke about my Women's Safety Application mentioned on resume, explaining the
motivation behind it and answering a few follow-up questions.
Towards the end, they asked if I had any questions for them. I asked them about their first six months at
ISS STOXX and what their onboarding experience had been like. The Managing Director laughed and said
that he had been with the company for so many years that he barely remembered his first six months
--- PAGE 5 ---
anymore. I smiled and mentioned that I recognized him from the Pre-Placement Talk (PPT), which made
the conversation even more engaging.
The other interviewer then shared her journey at ISS STOXX, talking about how she had grown within the
organization and the experiences that shaped her career. Towards the end of her answer, she spoke about the
core values of ISS STOXX. I took that opportunity to connect my own aspirations with the company's
culture and mentioned that those values genuinely resonated with me. I also added that ISS STOXX, being
at the intersection of finance and technology, perfectly aligns with my interests and career goals,
making me feel that I truly belong here and was excited about the opportunity to contribute and learn.
I thanked both the interviewers for their time, wished them a great day, and walked out of the room with a
smile, hoping for the best.
Overall, the HR round felt more like a conversation than an interview. My biggest advice would be to be
genuine, answer confidently, and keep the conversation natural. Don't hesitate to highlight your
achievements whenever you get the opportunity, whether it's internships, certifications, hackathons, or
projects. Most importantly, keep a smile on your face throughout the interview. No matter how nervous you
feel on the inside, projecting confidence and enthusiasm leaves a lasting impression.
Later that night, the final list of 12 selected candidates was released. Seeing my name on it was a moment
of pure happiness and relief. All the hard work had finally paid off.

The recruitment process consisted of an initial resume shortlisting stage, followed by three
evaluation rounds: an Online Assessment (OA), a Technical Interview, and a combined
Techno-HR Interview. Throughout the interview process, the company placed a strong emphasis
on Java, and candidates were expected to demonstrate a solid understanding of Java
fundamentals, object-oriented programming, collections, multithreading, and related concepts.
So u need a strong hold over Java to clear this company
1.
[Online Assessment] [214 students were shortlisted]
The Online Assessment was the first elimination round after resume shortlisting. The company
was fairly lenient during the resume screening stage, and almost everyone who applied through
the campus recruitment process was shortlisted for the OA.
The assessment consisted of five sections and had negative marking:

• Java: 15 multiple-choice questions

• Python: 15 multiple-choice questions

• SQL: 3 multiple-choice questions

• AI: 10 multiple-choice questions

• Quantitative Aptitude & Logical Reasoning: 25 questions

There was sufficient time to complete the assessment, and time management was generally not
an issue.
Java Section (15 Questions)
--- PAGE 2 ---
Most questions were output-based and some of them were conceptually related to Java heap
memory. Some of the major topics covered included:

• String immutability

• Heap memory and object creation

• Object-Oriented Programming (inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction, encapsulation)

• Java Collections Framework

• Java Streams API

• Exception handling

There were also conceptual questions on the Collections Framework, such as: What does
Collectors.groupingByO return? Map<K, List<T>
Python Section (15 Questions)
The questions primarily covered: Classes and Object-Oriented Programming, Method
Resolution Order (MRO), Multiple inheritance, Tuples, Sets, Dictionaries, List operations, Basic
Python built-in functions Many questions tested conceptual understanding rather than requiring
code writing. To prepare, I generated a large HTML-based quiz using Claude covering all these
Python concepts and repeatedly practiced those questions. If you're short on time, creating or
using such topic-wise quizzes is a very efficient revision strategy.
SQL Section (3 Questions)
The SQL section was straightforward. Questions covered: Aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM,
AVG, MAX, MIN), Basic SELECT queries, GROUP BY and Simple filtering conditions Since
all questions were multiple-choice, option elimination made this section quite manageable.
AI Section (10 Questions)
This was a relatively new section introduced in the assessment. The questions were not about AI
algorithms or machine learning theory. Instead, they presented Al-generated responses involving
Java, Python, or SQL and asked candidates to determine whether the generated answer was
correct or identify the correct alternative. The primary challenge in this section was not the
difficulty but the length of the questions. Reading each scenario carefully took a significant
amount of time.
Aptitude (25 Questions)
I personally found this to be the easiest section. Every standard questions were asked in this
section and few gfg puzzles were asked.... The only puzzles that I found particularly challenging
were: The 100 Prisoners Puzzle and The Nim Game Puzzle Apart from those, I was able to
solve nearly all the questions. I attempted 23 out of the 25 questions in this section.
--- PAGE 3 ---
Candidates with a decent aptitude background should be able to score well here.
[Technical Round] [ 44 candidates appeared]
Candidates who cleared the Online Assessment were shortlisted for the first interview round,
which was a dedicated Technical Interview. By the time my turn came, I was the last candidate
waiting outside the interview room. Nearly four to five candidates had already completed not
only their Technical Interview but had also finished their subsequent Techno-HR round.
One thing I would like to emphasize is that the order in which you are interviewed does not
affect your chances of selection. Even if you are among the last candidates, stay calm and
remain confident. My interview panel was progressing slowly, and despite being the last
candidate, I had a very positive interview experience. The interviewer maintained a completely
expressionless face throughout the interview, which initially felt intimidating. However, I later
realized that this was simply his interviewing style. Do not try to judge your performance based
on the interviewer's facial expressions they often deliberately avoid giving any hints about
whether your answers are correct.
The interview immediately began with Java and remained heavily focused on it. Although Java
is not my primary programming language (I am more comfortable with C++), I had revised the
fundamentals beforehand. From my discussions with other candidates, I found that if someone
was uncomfortable with Java, the interviewer was sometimes willing to switch to Python.
However, if you mention Java on your resume or claim familiarity with it, be prepared for
detailed questioning.
It started with What is an immutable class? Is String an immutable class? Why? The interviewer
System. out.println(s); I explained that the output would still be: Hello because String objects are
immutable and replace returns a new String rather than modifying the original object. He then
asked how I would make it print "World". I answered that the returned string should be
reassigned: s = s.replace("Hello", "World");
The discussion then moved to object comparison. The interviewer asked me to explain the
difference between: = and equals He provided a scenario involving a Student class containing
fields such as id and name and asked how I would override the equals method so that two
student objects could be compared logically rather than by reference. As a follow-up, he also
asked me to list some commonly used methods present in Java's Object class, such as equals,
hashCode, toStringO, getClass and what each method does..
Then we discussed about exception handling. What is difference between error and exception He
wrote a snippet of code where IO exception was caught after normal exception and asked to find
mistake in the snippet. Then we asked abt why general exceptions are caught later than specific
--- PAGE 4 ---
ones. He asked about the purpose of the finally block and when it executes. Additionally also
asked me to write a custom error class
I was asked to explain ArrayList and then solve a problem involving removing elements while
iterating through the list. I initially mentioned removing elements directly, but then discussed
why doing so causes a ConcurrentModificationException. I wrote the solution using an Iterator,
which safely removes elements during iteration. Although I occasionally made syntax mistakes
because Java is not my strongest language, I clearly explained the underlying concepts, which
the interviewer appreciated.
Then we moved onto SQL vs Nosql discussion CAP theorem and ACID properties..The
interviewer next asked me to write a Java thread using the Runnable interface. This naturally led
to several operating system questions, including Thread vs Process, Deadlocks and conditions
I was then given a simple coding problem: Find the frequency of every word in a given sentence.
I solved it by using a HashMap<String, Integer> to count the occurrences of each word. The
interviewer was more interested in my approach than in the exact syntax Surprisingly I wasn't
asked much on my resume..Some of my friends were asked about Rest APIs and basic Spring
questions as well..
[Techno -HR Round! [22 candidates appeared]
The final round was a Techno-HR interview, but don't mistake it for a purely HR round. Along
with behavioral questions, the interviewer also discussed my resume and one of my projects in
detail. The interview started with a brief self-introduction, followed by questions about where I
stay and whether I would be comfortable travelling from Mulund to the Goregaon office five
days a week. I was prepared for this and explained that I had been travelling a similar distance to
college almost every day for the past three years, so commuting would not be an issue.
I was then asked why I wanted to join ISS. I connected my answer to my interest in the fintech
domain and mentioned that, along with my engineering degree, I was also pursuing a Minor in
Management from SPJIMR, making the role a good fit for my long-term career goals. The
interviewer also asked which other companies I had applied to and why I wasn't selected. I
mentioned companies like UBS, Nomura, IDFC FIRST Bank, and J.P. Morgan, and explained
that every rejection helped me identify areas for improvement and motivated me to upskill
further. Another question was whether I would still join the company if I did not initially get my
preferred role, to which I replied that learning and growth within a good organization were more
important than the initial role.
The interviewer also asked about my hobbies. Since I mentioned football, there were a few
follow-up questions about recent matches and tournament results. I was then asked to describe an
--- PAGE 5 ---
incident that demonstrated accountability, where I shared an example of taking ownership of a
project task and ensuring it was completed successfully.
Towards the end, the interviewer randomly picked one of my projects from my resume instead of
letting me choose. The discussion focused much more on the design decisions than on technical
implementation. I was asked why I chose a particular architecture, why I selected certain
technologies, and what alternatives I had considered. One thing that worked well for me was
highlighting the initiative I had taken during the project rather than simply explaining what I had
built. Overall, my advice would be to prepare a good introduction, have a convincing answer for
"Why ISS?", revise every project on your resume thoroughly, and be ready with examples that
demonstrate accountability, ownership, and initiative.

since only the top student per department needs to be stored.
(Initially, I said Map<Department, List<Student>>,after understanding the
requirement was only the highest scorer but tie could be possible, so list of Student per
department is sufficient.)
They then asked:
'How would you insert students into this data structure?
I explained the algorithm:

• Iterate through each student.

• Check whether the department already exists in the map.

• If it does not exist, insert the student.

• If it exists, compare marks with the current top scorer.

• Replace the stored student if the current student has higher marks.

Time Complexity:

• O(n), since each student is processed exactly once.

The interviewers seemed satisfied with the explanation, and we discussed the approach
for around 20 minutes.
Overall Experience
The interview was more focused on:

• API design

• Object-oriented thinking

• Backend architecture

• Choosing appropriate data structures

• Explaining your reasoning clearly

There was very little emphasis on writing code. They were more interested in how you
think through a backend design problem.
--- PAGE 7 ---
The duration varies by panel. Mine lasted around 20 minutes, while some candidates had
interviews close to an hour.
I received my Technical Round 2 interview slot at around 2:00 PM.

3. Round 3: Technical + HR Interview

Around 19 candidates were shortlisted for the final round.
My interview was conducted by Dipesh Sir and Jyoti Ma'am. I remembered both of
them from the pre-placement talk (PPT), which made the interaction feel a little familiar.
The interview started on a very friendly note.
They first asked:
"How has your day been?"
Instead of giving a generic answer like "good' or "nice," I replied that it had been
rocking.
They smiled and asked,
"Why rocking?"
I explained that I had cleared every stage so far and had now reached the final interview,
so the day was definitely going in my favour. They appreciated the positive response, and
it helped create a relaxed atmosphere.
Introduction
I gave my introduction, after which they asked:

• Why ISS STOXX?

• Tell us about your internship.

• You have been interning for almost two years. What kind of work have you done?

• You are also pursuing the IIT Madras BS degree. How do you manage both

college and your internship?

• Did you find today's MCQ round easy or difficult?

The discussion then shifted towards my projects.
Mini Project Discussion
--- PAGE 8 ---
Dipesh Sir directly asked me to explain one of my projects.
I talked about our online proctoring system, where we used:

• Webcam monitoring

• TensorFlow.js

• Browser-based Al inference

• COCO-SSD object detection

They asked several follow-up questions.
Why Tensor Flow.js?
They wanted to know why we chose browser-based inference instead of running
everything on a centralized server.
I explained that if 200+ students were taking an exam simultaneously, sending every
webcam frame to the server would:

• Create significant infrastructure costs.

• Increase server load.

• Introduce latency.

• Make scaling difficult.

Running inference directly in the browser distributes the computation to each candidate's
device, reducing backend infrastructure requirements while providing real-time detection.
They seemed satisfied with this reasoning.
Product Design Questions
They continued with practical design questions such as:

• How would you decide the confidence threshold for object detection?

• At what confidence percentage should a student be flagged?

• Should every detection trigger a warning?

• How would you implement fullscreen detection?

• What other anti-cheating mechanisms would you include?

The discussion was less about coding and more about product thinking and design
decisions.
Internship Discussion
--- PAGE 9 ---
Next, they asked about my internship project (xresume.ai).
Topics discussed included:

• Overall architecture

• Resume parsing workflow

• Technologies used

• LangChain integration

• End-to-end workflow

• Problems I faced during development

• Improvements 1 suggested to the product

• Challenges while deploying and maintaining the system

They also asked how I generally approach solving difficult engineering problems and
whether I had encountered situations where I was initially stuck but eventually found a
solution.
Questions I Asked
At the end of both Technical Round 1 and the final interview, I asked a question that led
to some of the most interesting conversations of the day.
Instead of asking about work-life balance or company culture, I asked:
"Can you share an incident or a project at ISS STOXX where you felt you
had done something extraordinary for the company-something that made
you feel proud of your contribution?"
(In Hindi, it: "ISS STOXX mein aisa kya kiya jiske liye aapko laga ki 'haan, maine
company ke liye kuch khaas kiya haiạ)
The interviewers genuinely appreciated the question.
One of them even smiled and said:
"My Boss should have asked this question, and was very difficult"
They then shared memorable experiences from their time at ISS STOXX.
One interviewer spoke about a critical project where senior leadership was considering
shutting it down because of various challenges. Instead of giving up, he and his team
prepared a detailed proposal, presented their vision to the leadership, convinced them to
continue investing in the project, and successfully turned it around. He explained how
--- PAGE 10 ---
leading the team through that period and seeing the project succeed was one of the
proudest moments of his career at ISS STOXX.
Hearing stories like these gave me a much better understanding of the ownership,
leadership, and impact engineers can have within the company than any standard answer
about company culture could.
Overall, the interview felt more like a technical discussion than an interrogation. The
interviewers were approachable, encouraged conversation, and genuinely wanted to
understand my thought process rather than just test technical knowledge.
My Advice

• Be honest and conversational rather than giving rehearsed answers.

• Be prepared to explain every project on your resume in depth.

• Justify your design decisions with logical reasoning and trade-offs.

• Think from a product and scalability perspective, not only from an

implementation perspective.

• Ask thoughtful questions at the end. A good conversation with the interviewers

leaves a lasting impression.
Overall, it was one of the most enjoyable interview experiences I've had.
[In total 12 were given]
Can be ignored (for knowledge purpose)
Reflections, Preparation Strategy, and Advice for Future Candidates
Looking back at my placement journey, I believe getting selected was the result of consistent
preparation over a long period rather than preparation for a single interview. Before receiving
this offer, I had gone through multiple placement processes where I reached the later stages but
did not convert the opportunity. Those experiences helped me identify my weak areas and
improve them before the ISS STOXX process.
What Worked Well

1. Strong understanding instead of memorization

--- PAGE 11 ---
For technical preparation, I focused on understanding concepts rather than memorizing interview
answers. During the online assessment, many Java and Python questions tested language
internals and edge cases instead of syntax. Similarly, the interviews emphasized reasoning, API
design, scalability, and trade-offs rather than writing large amounts of code.

2. Knowing every project in depth

I made sure I could explain every project on my resume end-to-end:

• The problem it solved

• Why specific technologies were chosen

• Alternative approaches considered

• Design decisions and trade-offs

• Challenges faced

• Improvements I would make today

Whenever interviewers asked follow-up questions, I tried to justify every technical decision with
reasoning instead of simply stating what I had implemented.

3. Drawing from real internship experience

My internship gave me practical examples to discuss instead of only theoretical knowledge. I
could explain how APIs were designed, how production issues were handled, how features
evolved over time, and how engineering decisions were made while balancing scalability,
maintainability, and business requirements.

4. Treating interviews as discussions

I tried to keep the interviews conversational rather than reciting prepared answers. When asked
how my day was going, I responded naturally instead of giving a generic reply, which helped
establish a comfortable interaction from the beginning.
Throughout the interviews, I explained my thought process while solving problems instead of
rushing to an answer.

5. Asking thoughtful questions

At the end of each interview, I asked questions that went beyond standard topics like work-life
balance or salary.
For example, I asked the interviewers to share a moment at ISS STOXX where they felt they had
made a significant impact on the company. This led to meaningful conversations about
--- PAGE 12 ---
ownership, leadership, and engineering culture and helped build a genuine connection with the
interviewers.
Areas Where I Could Have Performed Better
Although the overall process went well, there were areas where I could have improved.

• During the online assessment, I found a few Java and Python language-internals

questions challenging. I realized that revising only common interview topics is not
always enough; understanding how the language works internally is equally important.

• There were a few logic and puzzle-based aptitude questions where I was not completely

confident. Because of negative marking, I chose not to guess. Practicing more standard
puzzle patterns beforehand would have helped.

• In one of the design discussions, I initially suggested a broader data structure before

refining it after understanding the exact requirement. This reminded me of the importance
of clarifying requirements before proposing a solution.

• There were moments where I could have communicated my ideas more concisely. While

thinking aloud is useful, structuring the explanation before speaking makes answers
easier for interviewers to follow.
Lessons from Previous Rejections
This was not my first interview process.
In earlier placement opportunities, including companies where I reached the later stages but was
not selected, I realized that reaching the final rounds does not guarantee an offer. Instead of
treating those outcomes as failures, I used them to identify gaps in my preparation.
Those experiences helped me:

• improve the depth of my project explanations,

• become more confident during technical discussions,

• learn to justify engineering decisions with clear reasoning,

• and approach interviews with a calmer mindset.

Every interview-whether successful or not-became valuable preparation for the next one.
General Tips for Candidates

• Read every line of your resume carefully. Anything you mention is fair game for

discussion.

• Focus on understanding concepts instead of memorizing answers.

--- PAGE 13 ---

• Be able to explain the reasoning behind every design decision.

• If you do not know something, admit it honestly rather than trying to bluff.

• Clarify requirements before jumping into a solution.

• While solving problems, explain your thought process clearly.

• During system or API design questions, discuss validation, error handling, scalability,

and maintainability instead of only the happy path.

• Keep a positive attitude throughout the interview. Interviewers often evaluate

communication and collaboration skills alongside technical ability.

• Ask thoughtful questions at the end. It demonstrates curiosity and genuine interest in the

company.
Final Thoughts
The biggest takeaway from this journey is that placement preparation is cumulative. The
concepts learned, projects built, internship experience gained, and even previous interview
rejections all contributed to this opportunity.
Treat every interview as a learning experience. Even if an interview does not result in an offer,
the lessons you gain often become the reason you succeed in the next one.
Wishing everyone the very best for their placements!

The company shortlisted around 116 students. I didn't make any changes to my resume for this role. My
resume was AI/ML- data science based. Use ResumeWorded, and keep ATS > 65.

2. Pen-Paper Test] [116 students appeared for this round]

1. Aptitude: 8 questions, +3 for every right answer and -1 for every wrong answer. Age problems,

speed-distance problem, basic math, profit-loss, time-work, geometry, permutation-combination.

2. Python Coding: 2 questions, total 4 marks. (no -ve marking). Find the number pattern and code it

out.
Sequence 1: 3, 6, 15, 24 .. N. so this is N^2 + 2N
Sequence 2: 2, 9, 28, 65,.. N and this is N^3 + 1

3. SQL: 4 questions, 2 marks each (no -ve marking)

3 tables were given - one for Sales, one for Region and one for Quarter.

1. Find best, worst and average sales for each salesman

2. Find second best sales

3. Rank average sales by region

--- PAGE 2 ---

4. Find count of salesmen who did no sales in a quarter

3. [Technical Round] [ 29 students were selected]

I was among the last 4-5 candidates to be called. They collected our resumes and called people randomly
instead of following the written test rankings.
Tip: Stay calm even if you're called last. You may be asked to wait, go back, or sit outside while the process
continues. Don't get frustrated - just follow the instructions. In my case, despite being among the last few
candidates, the interviewers were still fresh because there were several breaks between interviews.
The interviewer first asked me to introduce myself. I kept it short, covering my name, year, department, and
internship experience.
Tip: Tailor your introduction to the role. For SDE roles, talk about your tech stack and development
experience. For Business Analyst roles, focus on analytics, business understanding, and problem-solving.
He then asked about my internship. I explained that I worked at an early-stage startup where I collected and
analyzed data and built dashboards to answer business questions for the CFO. He also asked what the startup
did. I explained that it helped users manage household finances, bills, and budgeting using AI. When he
asked how the AI worked, I honestly told him I wasn't involved in that part but guessed it likely used
historical spending patterns, bill history, and user behavior. He didn't seem to mind.
Next, he asked what subjects we had in the previous semester (ML, Generative Al Fundamentals, Build
ChatGPT from Scratch, SPCC, and DevOps). He then asked if I had built any projects. I explained my Build
ChatGPT from Scratch project in detail, including the architecture, preprocessing pipeline, and why each
preprocessing step was necessary.
Tip: Know your projects inside out. Explain the architecture, workflow, and design decisions before the
interviewer even asks follow-up questions.
He then asked where I lived. After I answered [my location], he gave me a case study:
> Would you give a loan to a toy retailer from [my location]?
I first clarified a few details - the exact shop location, loan history, and whether there was a guarantor. I then
explained that I would evaluate the retailer's CIBIL score, income stability, repayment history, existing
loans, EMI record, and the guarantor's financial stability.
The interviewer then asked me to assume there was no guarantor and that the shop was in a well-known
market, "X." I estimated the retailer's income based on daily sales. My initial estimates were too high, and
the interviewer challenged me to consider transportation costs, procurement costs, and profit margins. Atter
revising my assumptions, I concluded that the retailer's actual income would be too low to comfortably
sustain the business and repay the loan, so I wouldn't approve the loan. The interviewer seemed happy with
my approach and reasoning.
He then asked whether I had done any traditional ML projects. I explained one from my third semester,
although it wasn't on my resume anymore. Since it had been over two years, I couldn't recall every detail, so
I admitted that honestly. He didn't seem to mind.
--- PAGE 3 ---
Towards the end, he asked whether I planned to pursue a Master's. I said no because I wanted to gain
industry experience first and understand the kind of work I enjoyed before making that decision. He also
asked why I wanted this role, and I explained that I wanted to explore the business side after working in
analytics during my internship and because I found business problem-solving more interesting.
Finally, he asked whether I had attended the PPT. This was probably to check whether I had paid attention. I
said yes, and he asked what I liked about it and whether I had any questions. I asked about the company's
three-year growth plan and responsibilities at each stage, and also about how they were using Al internally.
He answered both questions, and once I had no further doubts, he ended the interview by saying, "That's it.
Thank you for comingại
4.
[HR Round] [ 11 students were selected ]
I was the Sth/6th person to be interviewed. My panel consisted of the HR and two other interviewers. I
noticed that they had my pen-and-paper test answer sheet and scores with them. There was also an additional
score from my first-round interview written at the top.
They asked me to introduce myself again. This round was much more relaxed - the interviewers were
smiling and joking throughout the conversation.
The main question was a case study:
> How would you increase Zomato's profits? (Assume Blinkit is not included.)
I regained my composure and came up with several innovative as well as standard ideas covering customers,
delivery partners, and the business.
They then asked me to group my ideas into categories such as customer retention, improving existing
operations, and new business strategies, which I did successfully.
The HR then asked, "What's the first thing you would do if you were given a large dataset?"
I first clarified the objective - whether I was trying to increase profits, acquire new customers, or detect
anomalies. She asked me to continue with the profit objective. I said I would group orders by pincode,
identify peak-hour demand, and allocate more delivery partners to high-demand areas.
She then challenged my approach by asking, "Those areas are already profitable. What would you do for the
ones at the bottom of the list?" I replied that I would focus on those underperforming areas and apply the
strategies I had proposed earlier to improve demand and operational efficiency. She smiled, which made me
feel I was on the right track.
Towards the end, they asked where I lived and how many members were there in my family. Finally, they
asked if I had any questions.
I had already asked most of my questions in the first round, so I made the mistake of asking how I had
performed.
Tip: Avoid asking this. It can give the impression that you're looking for feedback to use in future
interviews. Thankfully, they were very friendly and simply said that I had done well since I had reached the
second round, and that the final decision would be communicated through the TPO.
--- PAGE 4 ---
Result: Out of all the candidates interviewed, 5 students were offered the job.
Motivation:
I enjoy AI/ML - Data related work but most companies that come in the beginning of the placement season
do not offer such roles. So, if you're doing AI/ML - data related projects, then be ready for a bunch of
rejections initially. In general, SDE people get placed before and with higher packages. So, choose wisely.
Also, with the rapid progression of AI, I am not sure which roles will last so just check the job market
requirements before choosing a particular side. Be ready to adapt.
I did minors in finance and strategic management which helped me a lot! I was able to land a somewhat
non-technical role because of this and quick thinking, problem solving attitude.
Resume shortlisting is sometimes random but mostly if your CGPA is above 9 and you have good projects,
you stand a good chance of getting shortlisted. Also, don't just say "IDK", say - "I can't seem to get to the
answer, can you give me a hint?"
Keep smiling, don't look nervous/serious/angry/frustrated. It's a long process.
"Comparison is the thief of joy" - Idk who
So, don't compare yourself with others. Everything happens for a reason and you can build from there.
Kabhi na kbahi kuch toh accha hoga, law of averages hai.
