journey.howSecured:
1. Resume Shortlisting [313 Students Appeared]

This year, many companies began their recruitment process with resume shortlisting, probably because our
batch size was larger. From what I observed, CGPA played a significant role in the initial screening. A
CGPA of 8.5+ is generally a safe benchmark for getting shortlisted in the early phase of placements,
although this can vary across companies.
One of the biggest mistakes students make is submitting the same resume everywhere. Tailoring your
resume according to the job description is essential. I personally maintained different versions of my resume
and tweaked them based on the role I was applying for. I mainly used Claude to rephrase bullet points and
present my existing work in a way that aligned better with the JD.
If you're targeting different roles (SDE, Data Analyst, AI/ML, etc.), try to build projects relevant to each
domain and include the 2-3 projects that align most closely with the specific role in the resume you submit.
Also, don't overlook your minors, positions of responsibility (PORS), leadership experiences, certifications,
and achievements if they're relevant. In my case, pursuing a Management Minor proved to be very
beneficial. It not only strengthened my resume for a Business Analyst role but also gave the interviewers an
interesting topic to discuss, helping steer the conversation toward an area where I was comfortable.
One piece of advice I'd definitely give is don't list skills or technologies just for the sake of filling up your
resume. If you've mentioned something in your skills section, be prepared for the interviewer to dive deep
into it. It's completely fine to have a shorter skills section, but make sure everything you mention is
something you're genuinely comfortable explaining. A resume should create confidence, not unnecessary
pressure during the interview.
--- PAGE 2 ---

2. Pen & Paper Test [116 Students Appeared]

The pen-and-paper test lasted 75 minutes and was divided into two sections. One important thing to note is
that both sections had individual cutoffs.
Section 1: Aptitude (24 Marks)
The first section consisted of 8 aptitude MCQS, with a marking scheme of +3 for every correct answer and
-1 for every incorrect answer. The questions were fairly straightforward and covered topics such as:

• Time and Work

• Speed, Time and Distance

• Profit and Loss

• Basic Mathematics

• Age-based problems

• Permutation & Combinations

I found this section to be relatively easy. Even if you weren't able to directly solve a question, most of them
could be answered using option substitution or the elimination method, so don't spend too much time stuck
on a single question.
Section 2: Coding + SQL (12 Marks)
This section had two pattern-based coding questions, where we had to write either Python code or
pseudocode to find the sum of the series.
The series were:

1. 3, 8, 15, 24, 35, ... (1 mark)

2. 2, 9, 28, 65, 126, ... (3 marks)

The test also included four SQL questions (2 marks each). They were all based on common analytical
queries and mainly tested your understanding of aggregation, ranking, and grouping.
The questions were:

1. Find the best, worst, and average sales for each salesperson.

2. Find the second-highest sale made by each salesperson.

3. Rank the regions based on their average sales.

4. Count the number of salespeople who made no sales in each quarter.

Overall, I felt this round was quite manageable if you have a decent grasp of aptitude and SQL. My advice
would be to practice SQL beyond just basic queries, be comfortable with GROUP BY, aggregate functions,
CASE WHEN, subqueries/CTEs, and window functions like RANKO and DENSE_RANKO. For the coding
part, don't overthink it, being able to recognize number patterns is more than enough.
--- PAGE 3 ---

3. HR Round [This was an extra interview taken on spot only for about 3-4 candidates not all]

This round was a little unexpected. While everyone else was waiting for or attending their technical
interviews, I was suddenly called for the HR round first. It caught me by surprise, but the interview itself
was very relaxed and lasted around 5-7 minutes.
The HR started with some basic questions to understand my motivation for applying. Some of the questions
I was asked were:

• Tell me about yourself.

• Why did you apply for the Business Analyst role?

• What do you know about the role?

• What does InCred do?

My advice would be to spend 15-20 minutes researching the company before the interview. Know what
InCred does, its major products/services, and why you're interested in working there. Along with that, be
clear about why you're interested in becoming a Business Analyst, what responsibilities the role involves,
and how your background aligns with it. Since the round is conversational, answer honestly and confidently
instead of trying to give rehearsed responses.

4. Technical Interview 29 Students Appeared]

The technical round started with a brief introduction, where I was asked to introduce myself and walk
through my background. Since the interviewer had my resume in front of her, the discussion quickly shifted
to my projects and the technologies I had used.
The first few questions were based on my project. Some of the questions I was asked were:

• Explain the difference between Random Forest and XGBoost.

• When would you prefer Random Forest over XGBoost and vice versa?

• Which model takes longer to train and why?

• Do you know what SHAP (SHapley Additive Explanations) is?

• If not SHAP, what other techniques can be used to determine feature importance?

The interviewer was more interested in understanding my thought process than hearing textbook definitions.
The interview then shifted to business case studies.
Case Study 1
I was given the following scenario:
A D-Mart store has a ground floor that sells groceries and daily essentials and a first
floor that sells apparel and clothing. Currently, 80% of the sales come from the ground
floor and only 20% from the first floor. How would you increase the sales split to 70:30?
The interviewer gave me a few minutes to think before answering.
--- PAGE 4 ---
For questions like these, don't jump to the first solution that comes to your mind. Try to think from multiple
perspectives. I structured my answer around factors such as:

• Demographic factors (age groups, families, students, etc.)

• Geographic factors (store location, nearby residential/commercial areas)

• Behavioural factors (shopping patterns, purchase history)

• Psychographic factors (lifestyle, preferences, fashion trends)

• Store layout and customer journey

• Promotions, discounts, loyalty programs, and bundling offers

The interviewer wasn't expecting one perfect answer. Instead, she wanted to see how broadly and logically I
could think about the problem.
Case Study 2
The second case was from the lending domain.
Suppose a person earns 225,000 per month, and you have access to all the non-personal
SMS messages received on their phone. How would you decide whether this person
should be granted a loan?
The first thing I did was ask a few clarifying questions instead of making assumptions. For example:

• Is the person a salaried employee or self-employed?

• Is the employment permanent or contractual?

• Which city or location does the person belong to?

• Are there any existing loans or EMIs?

The interviewer appreciated asking relevant questions before proposing a solution.
I then discussed how the SMS data could be used to extract useful signals, such as:

• Credit card payment behaviour

• Utility bill payments

• Spending patterns across different categories

• Transaction frequency

You could also suggest that Machine Learning or NLP could be used to categorize SMS messages and build
spending and repayment profiles to assist in the credit decision.
Overall, these case studies were testing how creatively I could think, how structured my approach was, and
whether I considered multiple perspectives before arriving at a solution.
Towards the end of the interview, I was asked if I had any questions for the interviewer. I genuinely think
this is one of the most underrated parts of any interview. It's your opportunity to show that you're not just
looking for a job, but that you're genuinely interested in this role and this company.
--- PAGE 5 ---
I asked two questions:

1. "If I were selected for this role, what skills or technologies would I primarily be working with?

Since I have around five months before joining, I'd like to use that time to prepare so that I can
contribute from Day 1ạ
I feel this question reflected my willingness to learn and showed that I was already thinking about
how I could add value once I joined.

2. "You've been with InCred for quite some time. How have you seen yourself evolve over the

years?"
This led to a really interesting conversation. The interviewer was very warm and shared her own
journey from graduating with a B.Tech from VJTI to growing within the company over the years and
eventually becoming a Vice President.
The interview ended on a very positive and warm note. My biggest takeaway is to never waste the
opportunity to ask questions. Instead of asking something you could easily find on Google, ask questions
that reflect curiosity, enthusiasm, and a genuine interest in the role. A good conversation at the end can leave
a lasting impression just as much as your answers throughout the interview.
My Advice
If you're preparing for a Business Analyst interview, don't focus only on technical concepts. Practice solving
open-ended business problems. Whenever you're given a case:

• Spend a minute structuring your thoughts.

• Ask clarifying questions instead of making assumptions.

• Break the problem into different dimensions.

• Explain your reasoning clearly.

• Don't stop after one solution, explore multiple possibilities.

A structured thought process is often valued more than arriving at the "perfect" answer.

5. Case Study Round [11 Students Appeared]

The final round was the Case Study Round and, just like the technical interview, it began with a brief
introduction. One of the interviewers found my major project interesting, so we spent a few minutes
discussing it in detail. He asked several follow-up questions to understand my approach, the challenges I
faced, and the decisions I made while building it.
After that, I was given the following business case:
Assume you are the CEO of Air India. The company is currently running at a loss. How
would you turn it into a profitable business?
I was given a few minutes to think about the problem. Before I started answering, the interviewer clarified
that he wanted me to structure my response by focusing on:

• How would you reduce costs?

• How would you increase revenue?

• Consider both short-term and long-term strategies.

--- PAGE 6 ---
I found this clarification very helpful because it gave me a framework to organize my thoughts.
Some of the points I discussed were:

• Analyze the relationship between routes, demand, and travel timings to optimize flight scheduling

and maximize seat occupancy.

• Reduce the number of low-occupancy flights and focus on routes with consistently high demand.

• Partner with reliable third-party vendors for services such as fuel procurement, catering, and ground

operations wherever it is cost-effective.

• Optimize fleet utilization by rotating aircraft based on maintenance schedules and route requirements

instead of keeping aircraft idle.

• Hire and train young technicians, reducing hiring costs while creating a strong long-term workforce

through career development opportunities.

• Introduce or strengthen customer loyalty programs and premium lounge access to improve customer

retention and encourage repeat travel.
They were more interested in seeing whether I could balance both cost optimization and revenue generation.
Towards the end of the interview, I again made sure to ask a question:
"When selected candidates are assigned to teams, is the allocation based purely on
business requirements, or are the candidates' interests and preferences also taken into
considerationẠạ
The interviewer explained how team allocation generally works within the organization, after which they
informed me that the results would be announced soon.
My Advice
For case study rounds, don't rush to answer immediately. Spend a minute understanding the objective and, if
needed, ask clarifying questions. Then structure your response into clear buckets (for example, cost
reduction vs. revenue growth, short-term vs. long-term). Interviewers are usually evaluating your
problem-solving approach, business acumen, and structured thinking. Even if you can't think of the "best"
answer, presenting multiple logical perspectives will leave a much stronger impression.
5 students were offered the job, including me :)
--- PAGE 7 ---
Don't get attached to opportunities that aren't yours yet. Prepare sincerely, give every company your best,
learn from every rejection, and move on. Every bit of effort compounds, even if you can't see it immediately.
One day, those efforts will come together in ways you never expected.
There's a verse from the Bhagavad Gita that I kept coming back to during placements:
"You have a right to perform your duty, but never to the fruits of your actions. Do not let the results of your
actions be your motive, nor let your attachment be to inaction."
This verse reminded me to focus on what I could control - my preparation, my consistency, and my attitude
and let go of everything else.
So keep showing up. Keep preparing. Trust your timing. Trust the process.
Good things have a way of finding those who don't give up.
All the best! You've got this.

journey.howSecured:
The placement process began with a Pre-Placement Talk (PPT), where the company introduced InCred
Finance, its business, the role being offered, and the kind of work expected from candidates. I would
strongly recommend paying close attention during this session, as it gives a clear idea of what the company
values and the type of problems they solve. Make note of any interesting points or initiatives that stand out,
as these can be useful during the interviews.
After the PPT, I went through InCred's website to understand their products, services, and business model in
more detail. It is helpful to know what the company does, how it operates, and how technology and analytics
are used within the organisation. If possible, also explore any blogs, articles, or technical resources related to
the company, as they provide additional context and can help you answer company-specific questions
confidently

1. Resume Shortlisting [ No of candidates -> ~250]

The next stage was the resume shortlisting process, which took place on 21st July. I personally did not make
any changes to my resume specifically for this role, as it already reflected my interests in Al and Machine
Learning. However, looking back, I believe there are a few things that can significantly strengthen a resume
for this role.
I would recommend having at least one strong project based on classical machine learning, such as
classification or regression models. Along with that, having projects in deep learning and Generative Al
application creates a well-rounded profile. In my case, my projects covered classical machine learning,
deep learning, and Generative Al, which demonstrated exposure to different areas of Al.
Another important aspect is having at least one meaningful internship experience. It does not necessarily
have to be in the exact same domain, but it should clearly demonstrate problem-solving skills and practical
industry experience.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Before submitting your resume, I also suggest checking it on Resume Worded and aiming for an ATS score
of 80 or above. While this is not a guarantee of selection, it helps ensure that the resume follows good
formatting and includes relevant keywords.
Finally, the most important point is that every project listed on your resume should be something you can
explain in depth. Be prepared to discuss your approach, the technologies used, the challenges you faced, and
the reasoning behind your decisions, as interviewers may ask detailed questions about any project you
mention.
Shortlisted Resume:
= [AnuraagBagal_data.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1CRfgQ71mKfqX2-fW-wbfHCiMmA9qpdHH/view?usp=sharing)
2.
Pen-Paper Test [No of candidates -> 116] {75 mins}
Section 1: Aptitude (8 Questions, +3/-1)
Topics Included:

• Coordinate Geometry (Line & Curve Equations)

• Speed, Time & Distance

• Time & Work

• Number Systems

• General IndiaBIX-style aptitude questions

Difficulty: Easy to Moderate
My Attempt: Attempted 6 out of 8 questions to maintain good accuracy because of the negative marking.
Preparation Advice:

• Practice aptitude questions from IndiaBIX regularly.

• Accuracy is more important than attempting every question.

• Coordinate Geometry, Speed-Time-Distance, Work-Time and Number Systems were the major topics

asked

• If you finish the IndiaBIX questions, generate similar aptitude questions using ChatGPT or practice

from GeeksforGeeks.
--- PAGE 3 ---
Section 2: Technical (12 Marks, No Negative Marking)
Python Pseudo-code (4 Marks)
The Python section mainly tested logical reasoning through pseudocode and number pattern recognition.
Questions:
Predict the sum of a series (1 Mark)
Example:
3, 6, 15, 24, ...
Pattern:
n' + 2n
Predict the sum of the sequence (3 Marks)
Example:
2, 9, 28, 65, 126,...
Pattern:
n3 + 1
Preparation Advice:

• Be comfortable reading Python pseudocode.

• Revise loops, conditions and basic functions.

• Practice common quadratic and cubic number patterns.

SQL (8 Marks)
The SQL section consisted of multiple related tables followed by four SQL queries.
Tables: Salesperson, Regions, Quadrants
Questions Asked:

• Find Avg/Max/Min sales for each salesperson.

• Find the second-highest sale in every region.

• Rank regions based on average sales.

• Find salespersons who did not make a sale in their assigned region/quadrant.

--- PAGE 4 ---
Preparation Advice:

• Complete LeetCode SQL 50 thoroughly.

• Focus on JOINs, GROUP BY, HAVING, Window Functions, Aggregate Functions and Subqueries.

• If you find yourself weak in any SQL topic, generate similar tables and SQL questions using

ChatGPT and practice until you become comfortable with that concept.
Overall Preparation Advice

• SQL is the most important part of the written test, so prepare it thoroughly.

• Practice IndiaBIX aptitude questions to improve both speed and accuracy.

• For Python, focus on understanding pseudocode and number patterns rather than advanced

programming.

• Don't get stuck on one question. Move ahead and return later if time permits.

• From my experience, the test appeared to have a section-wise cutoff, so try to perform consistently in

both sections instead of relying on just one.

3. Interview Round 1 [No of candidates -> 29] {40 mins}

The first interview was a mix of technical and business-oriented questions. Based on previous interview
experiences, I was expecting the discussion to be largely technical, so I had primarily prepared my resume,
projects, and machine learning concepts. However, the interview turned out to be quite different from what I
had anticipated.
The interview began with my introduction. During my introduction, I mentioned my hackathon project,
which naturally led the interviewer to ask about it in detail. She asked several questions related to the
project, including:

• Why I chose the particular machine learning model.

• The features that were engineered.

• The evaluation metrics used.

• The meaning of AUC-ROC and F1-score.

• Why LightGBM was selected and how it was implemented.

This technical discussion lasted for less than 10 minutes. After that, the interviewer kept my resume aside
and shifted entirely towards business case studies and guesstimates.
The first case study involved a D-Mart store, where the ground floor generated 80% of the revenue while
the first floor generated 20%. I was asked how I would increase the first floor's contribution to 30%. I
--- PAGE 5 ---
started by structuring the problem and proposing one possible solution. The interviewer then asked me to
come up with another completely different approach. Since I had not practised many case studies
beforehand, I struggled to think of an alternative framework and was unable to expand beyond my initial
idea.
The second case study was about deciding where to open a new Starbucks outlet in Mumbai. My initial
approach was customer-centric, where I segmented the population based on purchasing power, footfall, and
the target demographic. The interviewer again asked me for another approach. After thinking for some time,
I requested a hint, following which she suggested considering geography. I then divided Mumbai into
different regions and discussed factors such as commercial areas, workplaces, accessibility, and customer
concentration while deciding the ideal location.
The next question was a guesstimate: Estimate the number of toasters sold in Mumbai every month.
I approached it using a structured estimation framework by making reasonable assumptions and calculating
the final estimate. The interviewer then asked me to solve the same problem using another approach, which I
attempted by changing the segmentation and assumptions.
Towards the end of the interview, I was given a short quantitative problem involving revenue percentages
based on the earlier D-Mart case. Although I understood the problem and was close to the solution, I could
not arrive at the correct final answer within the given time.
The interview concluded with the interviewer asking if I had any questions. I asked about the internship, the
technologies used by the team, and her role within the company. This led to a brief discussion about the
work culture and the nature of projects at InCred.
Preparation Tips
Although this round began with technical questions, the majority of the interview focused on case studies,
guesstimates, and structured business thinking. I would recommend preparing both technical concepts
and business problem-solving instead of focusing only on your resume.
Some topics that I found useful are:

• Basics of Machine Learning concepts related to your projects.

• Evaluation metrics such as Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC.

• Be able to justify your model selection and explain your feature engineering process.

• Practise business case studies (market entry, revenue growth, profitability, location strategy, etc.).

• Practise guesstimates using multiple approaches, as interviewers may specifically ask for alternative

solutions.
Things to Remember

• Do not panic if the interviewer suddenly changes the direction of the interview.

• Think aloud while solving case studies so the interviewer can understand your reasoning.

• It is perfectly acceptable to ask for a hint if you are genuinely stuck.

• Confidence and a calm approach matter just as much as arriving at the perfect answer.

• Even if you feel the interview did not go perfectly, continue giving your best in the subsequent

rounds. I personally felt this round did not go very well, but I was still shortlisted for the next stage
--- PAGE 6 ---

4. Interview Round 2 [No of candidates > 11]

The final interview consisted of a panel of three members. Two of them were from the technical/business
team, while the third panelist mainly observed the interview and did not ask any questions.
The interview began with a brief introduction about myself. I spoke about my academic background, what
motivated me towards the FinTech domain, my participation in hackathons, and my internship experiences.
Based on my introduction, I was asked to rate myself in Python and SQL, for which I rated myself 8/10 in
both.
One of the interviewers jokingly asked whether I relied on ChatGPT while programming in Python. This
gave me the opportunity to explain one of my projects where I had implemented a Transformer model from
scratch using Python, NumPy, and PyTorch. We briefly discussed the implementation, after which the
interview moved away from technical questions. Compared to the first round, the technical discussion was
very brief.
The majority of the interview revolved around a single business case study.
Business Case:
I was asked to assume the role of the Head of Collections for a lending company.
The interviewer explained the following scenario:

• Around 90% of customers repay their loans on time.

• Out of the remaining 10%, around 5% are eventually recovered through the field agent team.

• The remaining 5% become unrecovered loans.

I was asked how I would improve this collection process.
Before answering, I first clarified what information and resources were available to me. I asked whether I
had access to customer information, field agents, and tele-calling teams. Initially, I approached the problem
from a business perspective by discussing customer features, credit scores, transaction history, underwriting,
and how analytics or machine learning could help identify customers who were likely to default.
The interviewer immediately pointed out that my solution was more suitable for the Head of Business,
whereas I was expected to think like the Head of Collections, where the loans had already been disbursed.
Instead of defending my answer, I acknowledged the feedback, took a minute to rethink the problem, and
completely changed my approach.
This time, I focused on improving the existing collection process itself. I discussed:

• Evaluating whether the tele-calling team was successfully reaching customers.

• Ensuring reminders and notifications were being delivered effectively.

--- PAGE 7 ---

• Identifying communication gaps between the company and borrowers.

• Using the field agent team not only for collections but also for educating customers about repayment

schedules, reminders, and app usage.

• Collecting insights from these interactions and passing them on to the business team so that future

lending strategies could be improved
The interviewer appreciated this revised approach and continued asking follow-up questions based on
different scenarios. One such question involved customers who deliberately refused to repay despite having
the capacity to do so. I discussed possible actions such as reducing future loan eligibility, increasing scrutiny
for repeat borrowers, limiting credit exposure, and initiating legal proceedings wherever appropriate.
The discussion continued for nearly 20 minutes, with the interviewers frequently asking me to justify every
statement I made. Rather than looking for one correct answer, they were more interested in understanding
my thought process and the reasoning behind my decisions.
Towards the end of the interview, I was given the opportunity to ask questions. I enquired about the
technologies used during the internship, the type of machine learning models used within the company, and
whether interns would get opportunities to work closely with those models.
Overall, I felt this interview went significantly better than my first round. Although I come from a technical
background and had limited exposure to business case studies, I realised that clear communication,
structured thinking, and the ability to adapt after receiving feedback were equally important. Remaining
calm and articulating my reasoning clearly helped me throughout the discussion.
Preparation Advice:

• Prepare business case studies even if the role appears to be technical.

• Listen carefully to the interviewer's feedback and be willing to modify your approach.

• Think aloud while solving case studies so that the interviewer understands your reasoning.

• Communication skills play a major role in business-oriented interviews.

• If you receive feedback that your approach is incorrect, don't panic. Pause, rethink the problem, and

continue with a more suitable solution.
After the interview, we waited for around 2-3 hours before the final shortlist was announced.
A total of 5 candidates were selected for the role, and I was fortunate to be one of them.
--- PAGE 8 ---
Final Thoughts:
Going into the interviews, I expected them to be mostly technical. Instead, both rounds focused much more
on business case studies and practical problem-solving. One possible reason (though this is only my
assumption) is that my resume may have already demonstrated the technical skills they were looking for, so
they wanted to evaluate my communication and problem-solving abilities instead. However, many of my
peers had completely different interview experiences, so don't expect a fixed pattern, be prepared for both
technical and non-technical questions.
The biggest lesson I learnt was to stay calm. Even when I got stuck, I took my time, asked questions, and
explained my thought process clearly instead of panicking. Communication matters just as much as
technical knowledge.
For preparation, build a strong foundation in SQL, be comfortable with at least one programming language
(python), practice basic DSA, and start aptitude preparation a few weeks before placements.
Lastly, don't judge your interview performance too quickly. I walked out of my first interview convinced I
wouldn't be shortlisted, yet I made it to the next round. Placements are unpredictable, so stay confident, keep
preparing, and give every interview your best.

journey.howSecured:
Everyone had applied for the role via Superset, and out of everyone that applied, 27 people were
shortlisted. Our best guess at the time was that they had selected candidates based on our pointers, since
everyone that was shortlisted had a high pointer. Mine was 9.27.
For the 27 shortlisted candidates, we were told that we would have Group Discussions (GDs) and then
interviews.
Group Discussion (GD) [27 people appeared, 7 shortlisted for next round]
We were divided into 3 groups for the GD, and my group had 8 people. Each group was given different
topics:

- T1: "Will Al replace software engineers in 10 years?"

- T2 (My topic): "Does data privacy seem far-fetched in today's era?"

- T3: "Should the government regulate AI?"

The time given for the GD was 2 minutes to prepare, 8 minutes to speak, and 2 minutes to conclude. I was
the first one to speak, meaning I started the discussion. Later, I was able to make one more point. There
were 2 people in my group who did not get an opportunity to speak a single point. So, try to be careful
here-given how short the time is, make sure to make at least 2 points.
After the GD, 7 people were shortlisted for the interviews.
Technical Round - 1[7 people appeared, 3 people moved for next round]
I was the 2nd person to be interviewed. They started by scanning my resume and asked which project I
would like to discuss in detail. I said I would like to discuss my UPI Analytics project because it closely
aligns with the role (which involves analytics) and it has a finance element to it as well.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Now, I did not just discuss the project verbally; instead, I showed them the live hosted project via my site.

- My site: https://prasadgade.dev/

- Project 1 showed: https://upi-analytics.streamlit.app/

Initially, the project did not open on their laptop due to a firewall blocking it, but the second interviewer
pulled up his phone and saw the project. I got lucky here that he took the effort to open it on his phone.
Then, we discussed the project for about 5 minutes.
Later, the conversation switched to Python coding. Since this was an analytics role and the company uses
Python, knowing Pandas and NumPy was a must. I will be honest: I am very well aware of how NumPy
and Pandas work, but I did not know all the exact syntax. Here were the questions and how they went:

- Write a Pandas query to find department-wise mean salary: I was able to write this one.

- What is the difference between concat and merge in a dataframe? I was able to explain the function, but

I got the syntax wrong, and I was informed by the panel right there that I got it incorrect.

- What is a lambda function and write one example: I was able to do this.

- What is list append vs. list extend? I was a bit hesitant initially but was able to answer.

- Aggregate vs. Transform in Pandas: I got this correct.

- Add one column named 'average salary' to each row (similar to a window function and partition in

SQL): I did not know how to do it in Python, so I asked them if I could write it in SQL. They said no, it's
alright.
I was also asked one DSA question:

- How to find if a Linked List has a cycle: I knew this question from the Neetcode 150 sheet, so I

immediately told them the Fast and Slow pointer approach. Understanding that I knew the approach, they
asked me to write the pseudocode, which I was able to do. Then they asked if there were any other
approaches I could think of. I said yes, using a Hash Set to keep track of nodes and then returning cycle if
we have seen the node previously.
They then asked if I had any questions for them. During the intro, one of the interviewers had mentioned
that he was just 2 batches senior to us from DY Patil college. So, I asked him how the transition has been
at Nomura from a student to an employee. I don't know if I got brownie points for the question or not, but
that ended Tech Round 1.
As we were waiting outside, me and 3 other students were told that we were selected for the next rounds
(Tech Round 2 and HR). These rounds happened in parallel, meaning while I was giving Tech Round 2,
another candidate was giving their HR round.
--- PAGE 3 ---
Technical Round - 2 3 people appeared
This round started with him asking for my introduction. Then we started talking about my first internship
(which I did during my diploma). It was a data analytics internship where I learned Power BI, so I
discussed that.
Later, he asked about an experience on my resume: Independent AI & Software Developer for a
Confidential Client (NDA-Protected). Since this is NDA protected, I told him clearly that I would not be
able to discuss the details about the client or what the product is, but I could talk about the engineering
methodologies, tools, and frameworks I used. I then went on to explain all the technicalities behind it.
Then came a series of behavioral/situational questions:

- Why Nomura / Why this role? I talked about how Nomura is one of the leading

institutes in finance, and since this is an analytics role, my entire profile aligns with it (my projects, my
internship, etc.).

- What do you know about the role and where did you study it from? I shared the info about the role and

said I studied it online and from LLMs. He asked if I talked to someone in person for guidance about the
role, to which I honestly said no.

- "Assume a senior of yours gives you work which you have 0 knowledge about and you have to submit

in 2-3 hours. What will you do?" I said initially I would talk to the senior if they are available to clear my
doubts; otherwise, I would do research on my own using the internet and LLMS. I also gave an example
of a past experience where I was in the exact same situation and had to figure things out on my own.

- Do you like what you work on? What drives you? What will get you to get up on a Monday and start

working? I answered about my interest in data analytics, ML, and the joy I get when I automate tasks with
machines.
Then he moved to my exposure in finance:

- I mentioned I am doing a management minor where I had some exposure to finance.

- He asked me a financial term. I don't even remember what it was, but I honestly said, "Sir, I am not

aware of it."

- What are your goals wrt your career? A pretty standard question.

- What are the factors which can lead to a change in oil prices in the short term and long term? I answered

geopolitics and government financial policies.
Then he went back to behavioral:
--- PAGE 4 ---

- Describe yourself in 3 words: I said Integrity, Empathy, and Hardworking.

- How can you say that you have empathy? Here, I was able to showcase my portfolio

(https://prasadgade.dev). I explained the whole philosophy of why I made my site and how it is structured
for different users (technical users as well as non-tech users like my parents and friends). This showed
how I put myself in others' shoes.
The Risk: After this, he asked, "Do you have any questions for me?" At this point, having fumbled the
two finance questions, I decided to take a huge risk and asked him: "Will there be any reason that you will
not hire me today?ạ"i
(Note: This question could have backfired very badly!! I took the chance, but do this at your own risk).
To this, he said, "Yeah, there could be several reasons for not selecting you. We might get a better
candidate, or another candidate might have a better passion for finance than youại
This actually worked out to my luck, because I used his answer to extend the conversation back into my
finance project (https://upi-analytics.streamlit.app/). I explained how this project proved my interest and
passion for finance. I shared a few insights from my analytics,
like:

1. Did you know that despite being the financial capital of India, Mumbai is not 1st in terms of UPI

payments, rather Pune is? (He was genuinely surprised and intrigued by this).

2. The average amount of transactions reduces during the festive season. (You would think the opposite

should happen, right? But the data says otherwise).
I was able to thoroughly explain both insights, and he seemed very happy. Remember, my interview was
technically over, but because I asked that bold question at the end, I was able to extend the conversation.
He then casually asked about my family background, where I am originally from, how the change from
Nashik to Mumbai has been, what my day looks like when I'm free, and my hobbies.
HR Round [3 people appeared - finally 1 selected]

- Where are you from?

- Tell me something famous about Nashik.

- What do you love more, Nashik or Mumbai, and why?

- What are your hobbies?

--- PAGE 5 ---

- Favorite IPL team? (I said CSK).

- Why CSK? Shouldn't MSD retire? My Answer: Obviously, this was a light-hearted question, but I was

able to turn this into an HR-style answer. I said I admire MSD due to his leadership qualities and his
down-to-earth attitude. I quoted a line MSD once said: "I do not want people to remember me as a good
cricketer, rather I want them to remember me as a good personẠạ

- Name one emerging player from the IPL you think would do wonders for TeamIndia.

- Talk about my experience as an Independent Al & Software Developer. (We had a similar conversation

about this experience as in the previous round).

- Tricky Question: "Because of Al, companies are removing freshers despite that, you were able to get

this role as an Independent AI Developer. What is your take on this?"
After this, we were sitting in the top office lobby. One thing to note here is that only 3 people were given
a chance for the HR and Tech 2 rounds. They did not even consider the rest of the people who had their
Round 1 interview, maybe because they had already found their candidates. I got lucky because I was the
2nd to be interviewed overall.
Then the TPC came outside and told me I was selected!
Now surprisingly Nomura only selected one person as opposed to previous years. So yeah happy and
humble to be selected.
My Placement Journey (Rejections before Success)
My journey actually started in my 3rd year when BNY came for summer interns. I was shortlisted for the
OA, gave Interview 1 and Interview 2. But in the end, I was kept on a waiting list, which left me
incredibly disheartened.
When our actual placement season started in July 2026:

- First was JPMC. The roles were non-tech, so I did not apply (even though the CTC was very good).

- Applied for IDFC First Bank > Could not clear the OA.

- Applied for PhonePe > Could not clear the OA.

- Applied for WorkIndia -> Resume was not shortlisted.

- Applied for AUXO AI -> Could not clear the OA.

- Applied for UBS -> Was not able to land an interview.

I faced all these rejections. The UBS process and Nomura process were on consecutive days. After getting
rejected by UBS, I was feeling very disappointed. The next day I had the Nomura process. I talked to a
few friends and my mom and dad to calm my nerves, went for Nomura, and got selected!
--- PAGE 6 ---
Let me tell you, the placement process does involve luck. So do not worry if you don't get placed early.
You just have to crack one company, not every company. I always kept telling myself one thing: "The
question is not IF I will get placed. The question is WHEN I will get placed." Do not doubt yourself. It is
just a matter of time before you get things right.
Crucial Advice & Resources:

- Practice DSA seriously. I will honestly admit I was very late in doing DSA, and even now I wouldn't say

I have the best DSA skills, but do enough that you can clear the OA of average companies. I practiced
DSA via Striver's A-Z sheet and Neetcode (did the 150 list first, then 250).

- Neetcode: https://neetcode.io/

- Striver: https://takeuforward.org/dsa/strivers-a2z-sheet-learn-dsa-a-to-z

- Practice SQL: Many students ignore SQL, but it is equally important. I practiced from LeetCode SQL

50: https://leetcode.com/studyplan/top-sql-50/

- Aptitude: Practice from https://www.indiabix.com/ and the FeelFreeToLearn YouTube channel:

https://www.youtube.com/@FeelFreetoLearn

- Use LLMs to your advantage: Make LLMs your friends and ask them anything and everything you want

to learn. I feel using LLMs to learn any topic is much better than watching YouTube videos because you
can clear your doubts in Real-time.

- Roadmaps: If you want to learn a particular skill, follow: https://roadmap.sh/

ALL THE BEST FOR YOUR PLACEMENTS!! DO YOUR BEST, TRUST YOURSELF, AND HAVE
FAITH.

- LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/prasad-gade05/

- Phone: +91 8446240041

Important Dates

• Round 1 (Executive Summary): 4th - 11th June

• Round 2 (In-Person Presentation): 22nd June

• Round 3 (Hackathon): 3rd - 4th July

ROUND 1- Executive Summary

This is the preliminary round. You are given the problem statement and then expected to prepare a summary
document that explains what you understood about the problem and a brief explanation of your proposed
solution. The summary had to include sections such as:

• About Us

• Brief Understanding of the Problem Statement

• Proposed Solution

• Dependencies and Tech Stack

Our problem statement was about improving financial access for underprivileged people. Since everyone has
access to LLMs today, most teams end up proposing very similar solutions - websites, apps, chatbots. We
stood out by building on WhatsApp instead, since it's an app already used by millions across India and needs
no separate download or onboarding. That single decision became our biggest differentiator through every
round. Keep the summary crisp and well-structured. We also included a rough architecture diagram and a UI
mockup of the WhatsApp conversation flow, which I think helped the panel visualize the solution instead of
just reading about it.
Try and include architecture diagrams, UI mockups or any other visual references as they won't spend much
time on each document so you need to leave an impression in their minds and better present/convey your
solution.
--- PAGE 2 ---

ROUND 2: Presentation Pitch

26 teams were selected from our college for this round. We were required to prepare a presentation and pitch
it to the Nomura panel at our college. The format consisted of a 10-minute presentation followed by a
5-minute Q&A session. (The timings are quite strict so adhere to the time limit)
I would say this is actually the most important round out of all(even the final hackathon included) as this
round will set the entire tone for the final hackathon.
Keep the ppt around 10 slides and try to use as minimal text as possible. Judges won't spend time reading
your slides. Keep descriptive images in the slides if possible for eg we kept user journeys of various
intended users that showed not only the different users the solution was meant for but also highlighted the
different features that were there instead of making a text heavy slide for features.
Make sure to keep highlighting your key Point Of Difference, you should have no more than 1-2 POD that
would stick in the minds of not only the judges that are there on the panel of presentation but also the
buddies and mentors that would be present on the day of the hackathon. For us we were the "WhatsApp
Team" of the hack and every buddy present on the hack knew about our idea, they might not have
remembered our team name but knew what we were doing and came and interacted with us on the final day.
Lastly, don't try to pressure yourself to give a perfect pitch as things are bound to go wrong, be flexible,
know your idea thoroughly and don't wing the answer to a question with anything that you can't back.

ROUND 3: Final Hackathon

7 teams were shortlisted from our college and around 31 teams participated in the hackathon overall
This was probably the most memorable and exciting round.
The hackathon was held on 3rd and 4th July. We were asked to visit the Nomura office on 2nd July for tech
setup. Pick-up and Drop-off for all three days are provided by Nomura.
You'd be working on a remote desktop setup by nomura and would be asked to install all the requirements
on the setup day. But for us due to some errors we were allowed to install dependencies even during the
coding sprints. For this I'd recommend implementing 80-90% of your idea in the time you'd have before the
hackathon days. This would give you a better idea as to how to structure your workflow, what dependencies
are needed and most importantly what all errors you might face. Try and not use socket programing if
possible and if doing try and do it with free tier ngrok as that was the only thing that was working.
Each team will be assigned a buddy and a mentor, the buddy might be exclusive or common between teams
and the mentor had 4-5 teams under him. The buddy will be with you at all times and help you with anything
you need from refreshments to technical error, they won't help you solve code errors though. You will see
the mentor at only 3 instances, 1st would be at your 1st evaluation which would be around dinner time(make
sure to check the event planner that would be there to see exact times or ask the buddy). Here most teams
might be ahead of you which was the case with us too and we were panicking a bit, but make sure to explain
your idea properly to the mentor, the mentor may or may not be technically inclined so make sure to see to
that and answer accordingly and again don't make promises that you can't keep. Then the 2nd time would be
after the coding sprints are over again an evaluation would be done before the final presentations, and if you
are able to achieve everything that you told your mentor it would leave a great impression.
--- PAGE 3 ---
After the 2nd evaluation final presentation would start. The no. of panelists varies; it can be 5-8. There were
8 people in our panel,3 buddies, our mentor, 3 judges and even the CIO of Nomura Services India. If there are
more people in your panel don't panic, this actually means more people are interested in your idea, be calm,
present properly and answer the questions. If asked about a feature that you haven't implemented, address it
dont try to fake it, give an explanation as to how you could incorporate it in the project in the future. The
judges are not only accessing what you have built but also what your idea could become and how much of it
can be done by you.
In the end, be confident in your idea, don't try to show more than what you can actually implement and
enjoy the event as much as you can. Our team was arguably the most relaxed team there and we finished our
prototype 6-7 hrs before the coding time actually ended and still managed to win the hackathon, so don't
think that you need to make something complex and code for 24 hrs to win, your idea matters and the way
you plan and execute it matters.

journey.prep:
• Resume (This is where placements actually begin)

Before worrying about OAs or interviews, ask yourself one question:
"Will my resume even get shortlisted?"

• Maintain an ATS score of 70+.

• Keep your CGPA above 8.0. If possible, 8.5+ is the safest zone and makes you eligible for almost

every company.

• Tailor your resume according to the Job Description (JD) instead of sending the same resume

everywhere.

• Keep different versions of your resume (SDE, ML, etc.) ready beforehand

• Every point on your resume should be something you can explain confidently for 10-15 minutes if

needed.

• Numbers always make your resume stronger. Quantify your work wherever possible.

• Keep your resume clean, one-page, and ATS friendly.

Personally, maintaining a good CGPA and tailoring my resume helped me get shortlisted for companies like
JPMC, AUXO AI, WorkIndia, as these were all the companies that sent out the applications by then.
Though I was not allowed to sit for JPMC.

• DSA & Competitive Programming

This is probably the single most important part of placement preparation. I never stopped doing DSA, even
while working on internships, hackathons, or personal projects.

• Be consistent rather than solving hundreds of questions in one week.

• Solve LeetCode Daily and GFG POTD whenever possible.

• Follow a structured sheet like Striver A2Z.

• Give as many LeetCode Weekly/Biweekly, CodeChef Starters, and Codeforces contests as

possible.
One regret I have is that I wasn't as consistent with Competitive Programming as I was with LeetCode and
GFG. Looking back, I definitely feel doing more contests would've improved my problem-solving speed.
Remember, Interviews test your thinking process. OAs test your speed. Practice both.

• Core Subjects

Never underestimate Computer Science fundamentals. Most interviewers are more interested in how well
you understand the basics than how many frameworks you've used.
Resources I Used :

• DSA: Striver A2Z Sheet (You can also go for CSES problem set)

• OOP (Java): Kunal Kushwaha

• DBMS: Love Babbar (One Shot)

• Operating Systems: College Notes + Online PDFS

--- PAGE 10 ---

• Computer Networks: College Notes + Online PDFs

• SQL: LeetCode SQL50

For SQL, completing SQL50 is more than enough for most companies. But you can definitely find some
other resources as well online.

• Development & System Design

Projects help you get shortlisted. Fundamentals help you clear interviews. Both are equally important.

• Build projects where you actually understand every design decision. Don't build basic projects, build

something that shows your understanding of the concepts and also that you can think at scale.

• Don't just integrate an API know why you chose it over alternatives.

• Learn System Design concepts like APIs, databases, authentication, caching, scalability, queues, and

deployment.

• Al can generate code today, but companies still need engineers who can design systems, justify

trade-offs, and solve real business problems.
One thing that really helped me during KakushIN was that I had already worked on similar projects and
spent time understanding System Design instead of only focusing on implementation.
Finally..., Placements are unpredictable. Sometimes you clear every round and still don't get selected.
Sometimes you don't even expect an opportunity, and it completely changes your journey. I got rejected in
the final rounds of summer internships I really wanted. I couldn't even sit for a few companies because my
hackathon dates overlapped with their placement process. I didn't win the hackathon either.
Yet somehow, that's where I received my first placement offer.
That's why I truly believe this: Hard work gives you the ability. Preparation gives you confidence. Luck
gives you the opportunity. None of them work well alone.
Keep learning.
Keep building.
Keep applying.
Your breakthrough might come from the place you least expect.

• Kakushin 10.0 Resources: • [Kakushin_10.0_Exceptions_Anurag](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1xrwWo5M7dpVgJd4o2OUDlKy2DvZXziHl?usp=sharing)

• LinkedIn: Anurag Singh

Background :
Before you start reading my experience, here's one thing I genuinely believe after going through this
journey: don't measure your preparation by your rejections. I used to think success was simply the sum
of hard work, skill, and luck. But after these last few years, I see it differently-it's multiplicative. You can
work incredibly hard and become technically strong, but if luck doesn't knock at least once, you'll keep
wondering when your turn will come. At the same time, luck alone won't help if you haven't prepared for the
opportunity. You need both.
--- PAGE 11 ---
I solved DSA problems, practiced CP, built projects, completed internships, explored System Design,
strengthened my CS fundamentals, participated in hackathons, and maintained a good 9+ CGPA. I was
preparing for the usual placement process-OAs, technical interviews, and HR rounds. But things didn't
always go my way. I couldn't make it through JPMC Code for Good, and after reaching the final round of
the Barclays Summer Internship, I was rejected there as well. Every rejection made me question myself,
but I refused to let one bad result define years of preparation.
When Nomura KakushIN 10.0 was announced, getting placed through a hackathon wasn't even on my
checklist. My team registered with a simple mindset: "Let's give it everything we've got and see where it
takes us." I never imagined that while preparing for traditional placements, my very first offer would come
through a hackathon. That was the biggest blessing-I got placed before the placement season had even
started. The flip side was that the hackathon overlapped with companies like IDFC and JPMC, and after
getting selected, I couldn't sit for any other companies. We also didn't win the hackathon, which honestly
hurt because we had poured everything into it. The next morning was the PhonePe OA; after an almost
sleepless 24 hours, I wasn't in the right state to prepare or perform. Looking back, I wouldn't change a thing.
If this journey taught me anything, it's this: prepare as if luck doesn't exist, but stay humble enough to
know that when your moment arrives, luck is simply rewarding the effort you've already put in.
All the very best! I hope to see you writing your own interview experience here next year.

Overview of Nomura Kakushin 10.0 :
KakushIN 10.0 is Nomura's flagship innovation competition organized by the Information Technology
Division (ITD). Unlike traditional campus placements, KakushIN evaluates participants on innovation,
technical expertise, teamwork, and problem-solving through real-world business challenges.
Competition Overview :

• Team Size: 2 members

• Participants: 1000+ teams (National Hackathon)

• Grand Finalists: 31 teams

• Venue: Nomura Office, Powai

• Final Round: 24-hour on-site hackathon

Selection Process :

1. Executive Summary Submission

• Submit an innovative solution for the given problem statement.

2. Executive Summary Presentation

• Present the proposed solution before Nomura leaders and domain experts.

• Evaluation based on innovation, technical feasibility, scalability, and business impact.

3. Grand Finale

• Top 31 teams were invited to Nomura's Powai office.

• Build a working prototype within 24 hours.

--- PAGE 2 ---

• Final presentation and live demonstration before the judging panel.

Hackathon Logistics

• All finalists were called to the Nomura office one day before the hackathon for onboarding and

environment setup.

• Development was carried out on Nomura-provisioned AWS EC2 instances, accessed from our own

laptops.

• Participants were provided limited access to Agentic Al tools to assist with development.

• Mentors and judges regularly interacted with teams, reviewed progress, and provided guidance

throughout the event.

• Meals and refreshments were provided throughout the three-day event.

• Pickup and drop transportation was arranged by Nomura for all three days (setup day, hackathon day,

and wrap-up day), ensuring participants could focus entirely on the competition.
My Experience
It was a unique opportunity to experience how engineers solve problems in an enterprise environment,
collaborate under pressure, and build production-oriented solutions using industry-grade infrastructure.

1. Executive Summary Submission: [ Open to Everyone - Actual count was not disclosed ]

The first round required teams to submit an Executive Summary based on the given Problem Statement.
The objective was to propose an innovative, scalable, and technically feasible solution while clearly
explaining its business impact. Since our problem statement revolved around Agentic Al, we ensured that
the document focused not only on the final solution but also on how the agents interacted, communicated,
and made decisions through a well-defined workflow.
Key Components Included :

• Understanding of the Problem Statement

• Proposed Solution & USP

• Agentic AI Workflow

• High-Level Architecture Diagram

• Core Features & Business Impact

• Technology Stack & Deployment Plan

• Dependencies, Package Versions & Environment Details

Tips :

• Understand the Problem Statement first. Every feature should directly solve a problem mentioned

in the PS.

• Have a clear USP. Don't build generic features; give judges a reason to remember your solution.

• Document your architecture and Agentic AI workflow from Day 1-it becomes extremely useful

in later rounds.

• Lock your dependency versions early and verify compatibility. Fixing version conflicts during the

hackathon wastes valuable time.

• Understand every line of your solution. The judges can quickly identify whether something was

genuinely designed by your team or simply copied.
--- PAGE 3 ---

• Think from a business perspective first. Ask yourself,ạiIf I were the client, would this feature

genuinely solve the problem?" A technically brilliant feature that doesn't solve the business objective
adds little value.
Appendix Suggestion: Since the Executive Summary has a page limit, move detailed
architecture diagrams, complete Agentic Al workflow, API flow, database schema, dependency
list, version matrix, and implementation details to the Appendix. This keeps the main document
concise while providing supporting technical details if required.
I think the last tip is probably the biggest differentiator. Many teams spend time adding more features,
while very few spend time making sure everything works together without dependency issues. Having
a stable environment, fixed package versions, and a clear architecture saved us a significant amount of time
during the Grand Finale.

2. Executive Summary Presentation [26 teams were selected for this round]

After the Executive Summary evaluation, 26 teams from SPIT were shortlisted for the offline presentation
round. Nomura conducted the presentations on our campus, where HR representatives, Senior VPs, and
technical leaders visited SPIT to evaluate the shortlisted teams. There were 4 parallel panels, each
assessing teams independently as per the presentation guidelines. Our slot was scheduled after the lunch
break. Initially, the waiting made us anxious, but as time passed, we became more relaxed and used the
extra time to mentally rehearse our presentation one last time.
Presentation Structure

• 15 minutes - Presentation

• 5 minutes - Q&A

What We Focused On

• Clear understanding of the Problem Statement.

• High-level architecture and Agentic Al workflow.

• Business impact backed by research papers, news articles, and real-world statistics.

• UI mockups and implementation roadmap.

• Clear division of work between both team members.

• Practical implementation plan for the hackathon.

My Tips

• Follow the presentation guidelines strictly. Don't skip any section mentioned by Nomura.

• Manage your time well. Several teams couldn't finish within the allotted 15 minutes. We completed

our presentation almost exactly on time while covering everything we had planned.

• Keep the audience engaged. A presentation shouldn't feel like someone reading slides. We kept it

conversational, added light humour wherever appropriate, and made sure the panel remained
interested throughout.

• Have a USP. Give the judges something they'll remember after seeing 20+ presentations.

• Support your claims. Back important ideas with research papers, news articles, market data, or

statistics instead of making generic statements.
--- PAGE 4 ---

• Know your solution inside out. If you've mentioned a technology, architecture, or AI workflow, be

prepared to justify every design decision.
Q&A
Most of our allotted Q&A time was surprisingly spent discussing and appreciating different aspects of our
solution. Towards the end, the panel asked practical implementation questions such as:

• If you're shortlisted for the hackathon, how much of this solution can you realistically build in 24

hours?

• What happens if Al services are unavailable during the hackathon?

Fortunately, we had already discussed these scenarios while designing our architecture. Instead of
overpromising, we honestly explained what could be completed within the given timeline and how our
system would continue functioning with fallback mechanisms leading to graceful degradation if certain AI
components were unavailable. Since both of us had previously worked on similar Al-based projects,
answering these questions felt natural.
Overall, we walked out of the room feeling satisfied. We believed we had communicated our ideas well and
answered every question confidently. The results were announced 4-5 days later, and while waiting, I was
busy shifting to a new house, so I didn't have much time to overthink the outcome. Finally, during the IDFC
FIRST Bank PPT on 25th June, the TPC informed us that we had been shortlisted for the Grand Finale.
Orientation & Environment Setup: [7 Teams ]
The finalists were called to the Nomura Powai office one day before the hackathon. Think of it as a
Pre-Placement Talk, but much more hands-on. The entire day was dedicated to understanding the problem,
setting up our development environment, and making sure everyone was ready before the actual 24-hour
hackathon began.
What Happened?

• HR welcomed all the finalist teams and explained the schedule, rules, code of conduct, and

expectations inside the Nomura premises.

• The CSR team explained the business side of the problem statement and how our solution could

create a real impact for the NGO we were building it for. This helped us think beyond just writing
code.

• The Tech Team conducted a short masterclass on the tools we would be using during the hackathon,

including:

• Claude Code

• Antigravity and Al Studio

Don't treat this session casually. Ask every doubt you have. We asked a lot of questions,
understood the limitations of each tool, and even started discussing our execution strategy
immediately after learning that Claude Code had limited tokens.
Meet Your Tech Buddy:
Every team was assigned a Tech Buddy who stayed with us throughout the hackathon.
--- PAGE 5 ---
My advice? Make full use of them.
They know the environment better than anyone else and are there to help not judge. Whether it's
debugging, infrastructure issues, or understanding the provided tools, don't hesitate to ask. Also, take this
opportunity to network with them. Everyone we interacted with was incredibly friendly and supportive.
Environment Setup
Before leaving for the day, everyone had to prepare their development environment.
This included:

• Logging into the Nomura-provided AWS EC2 instance through Remote Desktop (using our own

laptops).

• Installing Python requirements.

• Installing npm/node packages.

• Uploading datasets (if required).

• Verifying that the project could run successfully.

Linux users: Boot into Windows before coming. The setup process is much smoother since the
provided environment is designed around Remote Desktop.
One Mistake That Cost Many Teams Time
If there's one thing I'd tell every future participant, it's this: Lock your versions before the hackathon.
In our Executive Summary, we had already documented all package versions and dependencies. That
preparation saved us.
Unfortunately, during setup, the EC2 machines ended up installing the latest package versions instead of
the versions we actually required. Our project depended on Python 3.12, but the environment wasn't
configured accordingly, and because of the restricted permissions, we couldn't simply install another version
ourselves. Even GitHub access was blocked, and the systems were heavily monitored, so bringing pre-built
code or downloading random packages wasn't an option.
Luckily, we had already tested everything locally using the exact same requirements file. So although the
setup couldn't be completed that evening, we knew that once the environment was fixed, we'd be up and
running in just a few minutes the next morning. Several teams lost a significant amount of time because of
compatibility issues.
Moral of the story: Before you submit your requirements file, sit with your Tech Buddy and verify every
dependency, every package version, every model version, and every environment requirement. It'll
save you hours during the hackathon.
Wrapping Up
Nomura had taken care of almost everything for us:

• Pickup & drop facility

• Lunch

--- PAGE 6 ---

• Evening high tea & refreshments

• Development infrastructure

• Tech support throughout the event

All you really needed to bring was your laptop and your preparation.
After heading home, my teammate and I quickly discussed our execution plan for the next day so we knew
exactly where to start once the hackathon began.
One last tip: Go home, finalise your strategy, and get a good night's sleep. Trust me, the next 24 hours are
going to be intense. I didn't sleep enough, and I definitely felt it the next day.

3. Grand Finale [ 7 teams from SPIT were selected for this round]

We had to report to the Nomura Powai office early in the morning. After checking in, our Tech Buddies
escorted us to our assigned rooms, and the 24-hour coding sprint officially began.
The First Few Hours
Before writing a single line of code, fix your setup first.
Since we had already planned everything during the orientation day, we spent the first few hours ensuring
our environment was working correctly. In fact, we deliberately avoided using the provided Al agents
initially, which ended up saving a good number of Claude Code tokens for later when we actually needed
them.
A couple of teams in our room spent almost half the day fixing dependency and compatibility issues, while
we were able to start development much earlier.
One lesson: Never ignore package versions. A small compatibility issue can easily cost you a
few hours in a 24-hour hackathon.
Evaluation Round 1 :
During the hackathon, every team was assigned an Evaluator who periodically reviewed the project. Think
of these evaluations as technical interviews, except instead of talking about your resume, you're defending
the product you've been building.
Our evaluator was extremely friendly, but he wanted us to justify every major decision.
Some of the topics we discussed included:

• Why we chose our overall architecture.

• How our Agentic Al workflow functioned.

• Why did we trained our adaptive learning model the way we did

• How our personalised dataset was generated and utilised.

• API choices (Claude vs Gemini) and why we used each where appropriate.

• Why we avoided a cloud-hosted RAG database and switched to a local vector-based approach.

• Scalability considerations.

• Business impact of every major feature.

--- PAGE 7 ---
Fortunately, this is where my preparation over the last three years really helped. All those personal projects,
internships, system design sessions, ML projects and understanding the math behind them and computer
science fundamentals finally came together.
One thing I realised is that if you genuinely understand your project, the evaluator doesn't have to keep
asking questions-you naturally end up answering them while explaining your thought process.
The only major feedback we received was that one of our UI components wasn't updating efficiently.
I suggested using a Cron Job to periodically refresh the data, cache the responses, and display cached
values between updates instead of querying repeatedly. The evaluator appreciated the approach and later
suggested another feature where NGOs could generate revenue using the platform.
One important piece of advice: Don't overpromise. If someone asks what you'll complete by tomorrow
morning, be realistic. Evaluators remember your commitments and compare them against your final
implementation during the next review.
Through the Night...
As the night progressed, the project slowly stopped looking like an MVP and actually started feeling like a
real product. One of the most memorable parts of the hackathon wasn't coding. It was the people.
Throughout the night, Tech Buddies, engineers, mentors, senior developers, and even members of the
KakushIN organizing committee kept visiting different rooms to see everyone's progress. Around 3 AM,
many of them came over to our desk after hearing about our project from others. Even the core managing
committee members of Kakushin 10.0 asked us if we can explain our project as they heard it from someone
that it's something unique. They appreciated our idea and even shared presentation tips for the final judging
round. One thing I'd strongly recommend is: Talk to everyone who visits your desk. Don't treat them as
judges. Treat them as mentors. Many of the questions asked during the final presentation were things we had
already discussed informally with Nomura engineers during the night. Those conversations genuinely helped
us improve both our product and our pitch. By morning, we had built everything we had planned. We
somehow managed to squeeze in barely 1-2 hours of sleep before the next evaluation.
Evaluation Round 2
The second evaluation was much smoother. We had incorporated the feedback received earlier,
demonstrated the completed MVP, explained the improvements, and showcased the final workflow. The
evaluator seemed satisfied with the progress and wished us luck for the final presentation.
Final Presentation
Once coding ended, every team prepared for the final presentation. The judging panels consisted of very
senior leaders from Nomura, and to our surprise, our presentation was attended by the Technology Head
of Nomura India. This round was less about coding and more about business. Because of all the discussions
we had throughout the hackathon-with evaluators, Tech Buddies and mentors we were already prepared
for most of the business questions. The discussion revolved around:

• Business impact.

• Scalability.

--- PAGE 8 ---

• User adoption.

• Future roadmap.

• Technical decisions.

• Practical implementation.

One thing I realised here is: You're not just building software. You're solving a business problem
through technology. That mindset completely changes how you present your project.
Results
After the presentations, we finally got some time to relax, have lunch, and wait for the results. Since our
presentation slot was towards the end, we even managed to polish our slides one last time. When the winners
were announced... our team wasn't among them. I'll be honest. That moment hurt. We had spent the last
7-10 days thinking about nothing except this hackathon. We genuinely believed we had a chance of
winning. I went home disappointed. The very next day was the PhonePe Online Assessment, but after
almost ten days away from regular DSA practice and barely any sleep, I couldn't prepare properly. I
remember sitting there wondering how I was going to restart my placement preparation from scratch. For a
couple of days, it felt like all that effort had gone unnoticed.
And then, 3-4 days later... I received a call from the TPC. I had been selected for the Nomura ITD
Internship. I still remember sitting there in complete disbelief. Out of the 14 students from SPIT who
reached the Grand Finale, 7 students were selected in total four from the winning teams and three
individual selections from three different teams. I was fortunate to be one of those three. If this
experience taught me anything, it's that luck really is a factor. You can control your preparation, your
attitude and your effort-but sometimes the final outcome isn't entirely in your hands.
A huge thank you to Aryan Tikam. This journey wouldn't have been the same without him. He was an
incredible teammate smart, dependable, and someone I could always rely on.
Final Tips

• Fix your environment before coding

• Lock dependency versions and test them beforehand.

• Use Al tools wisely don't burn all your tokens in the first few hours.

• Make full use of your Tech Buddy.

• Think about security and governance too. Some teams were asked about topics like JWT

architecture, Prompt Injection, and mitigation strategies.

• Never overcommit during evaluations.

• Understand every technology, model, API, and architectural decision in your project.

• And finally... enjoy the experience. Very few people get to spend 24 hours building alongside some

of the best engineers in the industry. Even if you don't win, you'll come back with lessons that stay
with you far longer than any trophy

• Participate in Hiring hackathons you never know what lies in the future.

7 people received the offer (Internship + Performance based PPO)
--- PAGE 9 ---

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
• Resume (This is where placements actually begin)

Before worrying about OAs or interviews, ask yourself one question:
"Will my resume even get shortlisted?"

• Maintain an ATS score of 70+.

• Keep your CGPA above 8.0. If possible, 8.5+ is the safest zone and makes you eligible for almost

every company.

• Tailor your resume according to the Job Description (JD) instead of sending the same resume

everywhere.

• Keep different versions of your resume (SDE, ML, etc.) ready beforehand

• Every point on your resume should be something you can explain confidently for 10-15 minutes if

needed.

• Numbers always make your resume stronger. Quantify your work wherever possible.

• Keep your resume clean, one-page, and ATS friendly.

Personally, maintaining a good CGPA and tailoring my resume helped me get shortlisted for companies like
JPMC, AUXO AI, WorkIndia, as these were all the companies that sent out the applications by then.
Though I was not allowed to sit for JPMC.

• DSA & Competitive Programming

This is probably the single most important part of placement preparation. I never stopped doing DSA, even
while working on internships, hackathons, or personal projects.

• Be consistent rather than solving hundreds of questions in one week.

• Solve LeetCode Daily and GFG POTD whenever possible.

• Follow a structured sheet like Striver A2Z.

• Give as many LeetCode Weekly/Biweekly, CodeChef Starters, and Codeforces contests as

possible.
One regret I have is that I wasn't as consistent with Competitive Programming as I was with LeetCode and
GFG. Looking back, I definitely feel doing more contests would've improved my problem-solving speed.
Remember, Interviews test your thinking process. OAs test your speed. Practice both.

• Core Subjects

Never underestimate Computer Science fundamentals. Most interviewers are more interested in how well
you understand the basics than how many frameworks you've used.
Resources I Used :

• DSA: Striver A2Z Sheet (You can also go for CSES problem set)

• OOP (Java): Kunal Kushwaha

• DBMS: Love Babbar (One Shot)

• Operating Systems: College Notes + Online PDFS

--- PAGE 10 ---

• Computer Networks: College Notes + Online PDFs

• SQL: LeetCode SQL50

For SQL, completing SQL50 is more than enough for most companies. But you can definitely find some
other resources as well online.

• Development & System Design

Projects help you get shortlisted. Fundamentals help you clear interviews. Both are equally important.

• Build projects where you actually understand every design decision. Don't build basic projects, build

something that shows your understanding of the concepts and also that you can think at scale.

• Don't just integrate an API know why you chose it over alternatives.

• Learn System Design concepts like APIs, databases, authentication, caching, scalability, queues, and

deployment.

• Al can generate code today, but companies still need engineers who can design systems, justify

trade-offs, and solve real business problems.
One thing that really helped me during KakushIN was that I had already worked on similar projects and
spent time understanding System Design instead of only focusing on implementation.
Finally..., Placements are unpredictable. Sometimes you clear every round and still don't get selected.
Sometimes you don't even expect an opportunity, and it completely changes your journey. I got rejected in
the final rounds of summer internships I really wanted. I couldn't even sit for a f
