Important Dates

• Round 1 (Executive Summary): 4th - 11th June

• Round 2 (In-Person Presentation): 22nd June

• Round 3 (Hackathon): 3rd - 4th July

ROUND 1- Executive Summary

Getting Shortlisted in Round 1 and Round 2 is extremely difficult.
In this round, we were given a problem statement and asked to submit a two-page executive
summary. The summary had to include sections such as:

• About Us

• Brief Understanding of the Problem Statement

• Proposed Solution

• Dependencies and Tech Stack

Everyone has access to LLMs, so most teams end up researching similar ideas and proposing similar
solutions. This makes it difficult to stand out. I would recommend thinking outside the box and coming up
with an idea that genuinely catches their attention. For example, our problem statement was about improving
financial access for underprivileged people. While most teams focused on building websites or mobile
applications, we decided to leverage WhatsApp, an app already used by millions across India. This became
our biggest USP
Your summary should contain well-defined and concise points. Including diagrams or UI mockups is an
added advantage, as they demonstrate clarity of thought and a better understanding of your solution.

ROUND 2: Presentation Pitch

--- PAGE 2 ---
26 teams were selected from our college for this round. We were required to prepare a presentation and pitch
it to the Nomura panel at our college. The format consisted of a 10-minute presentation followed by a
5-minute Q&A session. (The timings are quite strict so adhere to the time limit)
This was honestly the most nerve-racking round because we finished our presentation the night before the
pitch.
Make your PPT descriptive with more images than text. One of the biggest reasons we finished our PPT so
late was because it was initially too text-heavy, and we later had to redesign several slides by replacing text
with visuals.
The one thing I would recommend is adding User Journeys to your PPT so as to show the judges how the
user would actually go through while using your solution.
My teammate and I started with a skit to catch the attention which directly correlated with our USP.
Be sure to know your solution inside out as the questions can be asked for any feature or any point. We were
asked about data security and the working of our features.
Memorizing your presentation script usually never works as I forgot mine halfway through the presentation,
but since I knew the solution I was able to explain and answer the judges' questions.
Our panel had 3 judges. Highlight key features (USPS) and keep the judges engaged, as they'll hear many
similar solutions.
Be sure to use the feedback of the judges in your final hackathon.

ROUND 3: Final Hackathon

7 teams were shortlisted from our college and around 30 teams participated in the hackathon overall
This was probably the most memorable and exciting round.
The hackathon was held on 3rd and 4th July. We were asked to visit the Nomura office on 2nd July for tech
setup. Pick-up and Drop-off for all three days are provided by Nomura!
You would most probably be working on your own laptops which would be connected to their AWS instance
so that no one can access pre-written codes and have to start afresh.
We were provided with Claude Code for development. We were also allowed to use APIS, provided they
were free and did not require paid API keys. Access to all other LLMs was blocked.
Each team is assigned a mentor who plays a very crucial role in the hackathon as they would help you solve
difficulties while evaluating your performance.
The hackathon was an incredible experience. Everyone at Nomura was extremely supportive and
welcoming. Every aspect of the event was thoughtfully planned, from food and refreshments to resting areas
and recreational activities. It was probably the most well-organized hackathon I have ever seen. A late-night
pizza party, along with plenty of snacks and energy drinks, kept everyone going, although we were too
anxious to eat much
There were no difficulties faced during the hackathon process other than the installation of our specified
python version which was later resolved.
I would recommend being well-versed in both the financial and technical aspects of your solution. Since the
evaluation panels are randomly assigned, you may face judges with either a technical or a financial
background, so you should be prepared to answer questions from both perspectives
--- PAGE 3 ---

1. Online Assessment (60 minutes)

2. Interview Round 1 (Tech Interview)

3. Interview Round 2 (Resume + Behavioural Interview)

1. OA (Probably more than 100 students appeared)

Honestly, I had decided I'll simply mark B for all aptitude questions and try to solve DSA thoroughly. I did
so, but in the DSA questions, I choked a lot. And I passed partial test cases in both ( 1-2 were left in first,
and only 2-3 passed in 2nd). However, I was able to solve them both after the test :p. I did not even expect
that I'll be shortlisted, so I went home and slept for 2.5 hours, and woke up to me being shortlisted (LOL).
Yeah so it was pretty much luck based for me, however, there were a handful of people who were able to
solve both the questions.
Aptitude had probability, combinatorics, ratio and proportion, profit/loss statements. Really really high
weightage of probability and ratio and proportion.
The first question in the DSA part was something like this :
Given an array, you can modify one number in the array such that the overall GCD of the array is as great as
possible.
Sol: Maintain a prefix and suffix GCD, and then at every index, take take ged(prefix[i-1],suffix[i+1]), and select
the maximum among them.
This was the most similar question I could find : Queries for GCD of all numbers of an array except
elements in a given range - GeeksforGeeks
The second question was :
CSES - Ferris Wheel
--- PAGE 2 ---
For OA, try solving 1400-1500s on codeforces, I think that's pretty much all you need. And please solve
aptitude questions, a lot. Aptitude alone could've shortlisted people.
Try maintaining a CGPA > 8 or 8.5, as it will make you eligible for any campus placements very very
comfortably.

2. Round 1 (Tech) [Around 40-50]

I was called in late (after all the other final shortlisted candidates were done with their round 2, I was about
to give my round 1 •°). The interviewer had two panelists, a male senior SWE, and a female app dev.
Both of them immediately recognized one of my projects, because the teammate that I had worked with
had already presented that during this round 1. So they kind of skipped over it. Then they asked me to
introduce myself. Keep it like a brief of your resume, something like this :
Hello, I'm Aaryan Mantri. I'm a third-year Computer Engineering student at Sardar Patel Institute of
Technology, expecting to graduate in May 2027. I'm maintaining a X CGPA (say only if it's high > 8.8) and
I'm deeply passionate about full-stack development and building efficient systems.
[work experience, if any, doesn't really matter as they don't expect much for a summer internship, but it does
help in interviews as you have something to talk about.]
On the project side, I'm particularly proud of [Project]', (explain project, why you made it, what effects it
had, your motivation behind it, and something unique that you did in that project, because look, they've seen
hundreds and thousands of projects, why does your project stand out?].
[Explain some achievements]
Finally, I've taken on several leadership roles. [Explain PORS (1-3 lines per POR)]. These roles have really
helped me develop my communication and leadership skills alongside my technical abilities.
I'm eager to bring this combination of hands-on development experience and leadership to a challenging
new role
Then since my resume was tilted towards a bit of system design, they asked me a question, "If I had to send
an excel with thousands of rows, how do I do iti And I wasn't even aware of such a situation, so I casually
said we can send it in batches/distribute it in a cache. And then we moved towards some DSA.

1. In an array of size N - 1, containing 1-n numbers, one of them is missing, find that number - > classic

XOR trick, but in my case I gave them two approaches, using the XOR trick, and sum of n natural
numbers formula.

2. Given a goal string and an input string, find if we can obtain the goal string by rotating the input

string.
Eg : Goal string = "HELLO"', input string = "LLOHE", output = true.
My approach: assign indexes to the goal string, like H = 1, E=2, ... O = 5, then plot it back to the
input string, so LLOHE becomes 3 4 5 1 2. Then there will only exist an utmost one or such index
where arr[i] > arr[i+1], in this case, only 5 > 1, elsewhere arr[i]<arr[i+1]. But it had a really easy
--- PAGE 3 ---
solution, that is to just concatenate the string and search for substring. They coined my solution as
"Sometimes we tend to over engineer questions" in a joking manner.
After that we moved on to Java, where I was asked some Java questions about constructors, abstract classes
(I failed both of them) and a pass by value vs pass by reference. I was also asked about virtual tables in C++,
which I wasn't aware of.
Then they asked me some puzzle questions
Frog in the Well, Math Puzzles
Tricky Logical Interview Problem | Genius Puzzles
They concluded by asking me if I had any questions for them. NEVER SAY NO HERE. Ask questions that
show your curiosity about the firm/Software Engineering in general.
Some questions :
I asked about

1. Why legacy codebases are not re written into clean and modular code, but are reused again and again

(they said that it's going to be financially expensive)

2. What does a daily scrum look like at Russell (I don't remember their answer)

2. Why is Russell Investments' logo blue in color i ("You'll have to ask that to the digital marketing

team)

3. [Techno HR [ 10-15 people appeared for this round]

Unlike many others, my 2nd round was very comfortable. The interviewer directly started with a DSA
question.
Given a singly LL, re-arrange the LL such that all even nodes come after the odd nodes. Additionally,
odd nodes should be sorted and even nodes must maintain their original order.
Eg: 187342
Sol :137842
Approach: I asked them if there were any additional constraints that I have to follow, to which he
answered that you can't use arrays, you have to use LL. To which I asked if I can use extra LL to store
some nodes, to which he agreed. ALWAYS ASK CLARIFYING QUESTIONS, IT WILL WORK IN
YOUR FAVOUR. Think out loud. I jotted down some steps, and kept asking him for discussions.
Always make the interviewer feel like you're discussing it with him, that's the entire key to cracking
interviews.
I explained my approach to him, which included splitting and storing odd and even valued linked lists
(1 7 3 and 8 4 2). Sort the LL using any sorting algorithm (merge sort + floyd's hare and tortoise
algorithm in my case), and then merge them back. So my question was a leetcode medium DSA
(modification of sort LL and separate LL). It was fairly quick. I explained the pseudo code to him and he
was satisfied with it.
Next, he asked me about lambda functions. I used an example of a DSA question and how I use lambda
--- PAGE 4 ---
functions in competitive programming, and how it has helped me.
He was done asking me questions, and then asked me if I had any questions, I asked him the same
questions I asked in round 1. Additionally, I also asked him if I can get to learn from different teams and
domains like Finance, Legal, Operations, as I may interact with them at Russell, which was a question he
really liked. NEVER ASK AN INTERVIEWER IF HE HAD EVER MESSED UP IN CODE 9.
I had my personal reasons to ask that, but if you want that role, please don't :p. Always ask questions
that make it seem like you're really interested and looking forward to joining the company, while
upholding learning ethics.
6 students were selected for the tech role, and 1 for the research role. I got in for the tech role.

more individual-level such as "What are your expectations from your career?"
", "What kind of work

1. Maintain a CGPA of 8.0+ - This is the eligibility cutoff for the initial shortlisting round for most

opportunities, with some having 8.5+

2. Know your basics well - Have good knowledge of OOP, Operating Systems, PnC, Probability,

SQL and the syntax of your preferred language (or the language the company focuses on) as the OA
and Interviews mostly focus on them. And try to look up interview puzzles online, i wish i had done
that, puzzles are really common in interviews. One more that comes to mind is 12 marbles riddle,
Ted-Ed has a series on logic puzzles, i think it might be helpful to do that.

3. Do DSA consistently - You don't need to go deep into competitive programming, but build a strong

foundation so that you can solve LeetCode Medium questions on your own.

a simple return due to time limits). I wasted too much time on the 20 MCQs before attempting
coding, so my advice is to attempt coding first since it carries more marks.

4. Match your resume to the job - Align your projects and skills with the role you're applying for.

Include moderately relevant or slightly unrelated projects if they're impressive or if you can
relate the skills learned to potential interview questions.
--- PAGE 4 ---

5. Be ready to justify your choices - You should be able to explain your projects and answer questions

about the technical skills mentioned in your resume.

6. Write project titles like short summaries - Keep them clear and descriptive, since that's often

what interviewers notice first when scanning your resume.

1.
Online Assessment [ 100+ candidates appeared for this round]
The online assessment consisted of a 1-hour MCQ and programming test conducted on the
HackerEarth platform. It comprised a total of 22 questions: 20 MCQS focused on mathematics and
logical reasoning, and 2 programming problems. Each MCQ carried 4 marks, while each
programming question carried 20 marks.
Eligibility to appear for the assessment required a minimum CGPA of 8.0.
The mathematics and logical section featured questions based on permutations and
combinations, probability, and ratios with a few questions on filling the blank line of code or
predicting output of a given program, with several problems involving colored balls and
wine-water mixing ratios. Not entirely sure but a few people, including me thought a few of the
options were wrong.
The programming section included two problems of different difficulty levels:

• The first was a LeetCode medium-easy (Codeforces 1100) level question involving sorting,

greedy algorithms, and two-pointer techniques.

• The second was a LeetCode medium-hard (Codeforces 1400) level problem focused on

number theory, prefix and suffix GCDs, and implementation.
Overall, the test was considered challenging, and only a few candidates managed to solve both
programming questions successfully.
Brushing up on PNC, probability and ratios will help you a lot, along with DSA, like doing the
NeetCode 250 or Leetcode 150
--- PAGE 2 ---
2.
Interview Round 1 [ 40+ candidates appeared for this round]
This round was conducted within 2 hours after the OA (approx 20 minutes after the OA results came
out). Since this was my second time giving interviews on campus, I didn't feel very nervous here.
The interviewers were very welcoming and helpful, they even gave gentle nudges when I got stuck,
which kept me calm throughout.
They began by asking why I chose this role over a purely technical one; I explained that my skills
and interests aligned more with this domain. They then asked about my finance knowledge, I
admitted it was limited (mostly from movies), but when they asked about terms like "investment"
and "IPO" I explained my understanding of IPOs.
The technical portion focused heavily on Python and core computer-science concepts. I was asked
Python syntax and semantics questions (what certain constructs can and can't do), time complexity
for operations, and methods for built-in data structures. They quizzed me on differences between list,
dictionary, set, and tuple (e.g., whether lists can hold mixed types), how to access keys and values in
a dict, and common list/dict operations like appending and joining,searching using operators and
methods. There were also NumPy/Pandas questions (what they're used for, the two primary pandas
structures, how to add a column, and how to access/perform on a cell) and SQL questions (types of
joins, the difference between WHERE and HAVING, and query examples involving WHERE,
HAVING, and aggregations).
Finally, they gave two puzzles. The first was the classic bird-and-two-trains problem: two trains
approaching at 50 km/h, 100 km apart, with a bird flying back and forth at 100 km/h until the trains
meet and the second was the probability of at least one head when tossing three coins. I attempted
the bird problem by summing incremental distances, but wasn't able to solve it (the intended solution
uses total time and s=vts-vts=vt), and I explained my thought process for both problems. The
interviewer emphasized explaining my reasoning as I worked, which I think mattered as much as
arriving at the correct answer. The interview lasted about 20-25 minutes.

3. Interview Round 2 [15+ candidates appeared for this round]

This round was conducted at varying times. For me, it took place around 3-4 hours after my first
interview, while some other candidates had it much sooner. Like others, mine was a one-on-one
discussion with the Director, and it felt more like a conversation than a formal interview. I was
interviewing for the Investment Research Intern role.
The Director began by asking a simple pandas coding question, to find the difference in closing
prices of stocks from the previous day. I couldn't recall the exact syntax, so I wrote a basic version
and explained my thought process, including how I'd handle edge cases like the first element.
He then asked me why I chose this role, to which I replied that I'm interested in building new
things, as reflected in my resume and that I enjoy experimenting with new ideas and
technologies like MCP, LLMS, and integrations into projects (I phrased this as such because
their CEO mentioned about LLM during the orientation round).
--- PAGE 3 ---
Next, he asked if I had any relevant projects in this field, and I described my project on portfolio
management using LLMS, ML, and NLP. He followed up by asking about my finance knowledge
, I admitted I didn't have much, and he didn't probe further.
At one point, he mentioned that my portfolio seemed to focus mainly on machine learning, and
asked what I would do if the role didn't involve ML. I explained that I've also worked in backend,
frontend, and data science, so I could contribute in those areas too. He didn't seem entirely
convinced but moved on politely.
Toward the end, he asked if I had any questions for him. I asked about the specific nature of the
work involved in this role. He explained that it focuses on developing and testing new investment
strategies using algorithms on historical data, but not necessarily using machine learning. I
connected this to data science and said that it still felt similar in spirit; exploring hypotheses, trying
multiple models or algorithms, and analyzing which performs best and why.
Finally, I asked a few broader questions about how the company collaborates with external
managers for areas without dedicated divisions, how profits and risks are managed, and what
happens if a manager underperforms. He responded very clearly, avoiding heavy financial jargon,
and came across as humble, approachable, and genuinely engaging.
In the end, I was offered the Investment Research Intern role at Russell Investments. Among the 7
shortlisted candidates, the remaining 6 were offered the Tech Intern role. (Note: candidates had to
choose their preferred role before the OA, and I had opted for Research, while the others had chosen
Tech.)

Remember that preparation is not a one-day effort. Start early, practice consistently, and surround yourself

journey.howSecured:
1. Online Assessment (60 minutes)

2. Interview Round 1 (Tech Interview)

3. Interview Round 2 (Tech Interview)

All Three Rounds were conducted on the same day.

1. OA [100+ candidates appeared for this round ]

Duration: 60 minutes (Hackerearth)
Format: 20 MCQs (4 marks each) + 2 Coding Questions (20 marks each)
Tip: Before attempting MCQS, quickly read both coding questions. This helps you understand how much
time you'll need for DSA. If the coding questions are tough and time-consuming, solve them first and then
attempt MCQs.
Plan your strategy before starting the test -- decide whether you want to focus on solving the DSA questions
or aim to get maximum MCQs correct. Both paths can help you clear the OA, but with limited time, it's
almost impossible to do everything perfectly. So be clear about your approach from the beginning and stick
to it.
MCQ Section
Most questions were from Probability and Permutation & Combination, while a few were based on time and
space complexity of algorithms. I focused first on the time complexity questions as they were straightforward
and could fetch accurate marks. For probability and combinatorics, since they were lengthy and
calculation-heavy, I guessed a few remaining questions.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Coding / DSA Section
Tip: When in doubt, always start with a brute force solution.
Question 1 - Sorting + Two Pointers (Greedy Approach)
It was similar to this problem https://cses.fi/problemset/task/1090 where you can sort the array and try to
greedily pair largest value with smallest value within k and then accordingly move the pointers
Question 2 - Maximize GCD by Modifying Exactly One Element
You have an array of integers. You are allowed to change exactly one element to any value. Your goal is to
maximize the GCD of the entire array after this modification.
My initial approach was a straightforward brute force idea: for every index in the array, I assumed that
element would be replaced, and then calculated the GCD of all the remaining elements. I repeated this for all
indices and kept track of the maximum GCD obtained. This method was logically correct and helped me
pass 6-7 test cases, but it was inefficient because for every element I was recomputing the GCD of the entire
array, which resulted in a time complexity of around O(n' log n).

2. Interview Round 1[60+ candidates appeared for this round]

Tip: Make a strong first impression, be honest if you don't know something, ask for constraints and
clarifications when solving problems, and explain your answers in a simple, clear way without using
unnecessary technical jargon. Also, always ask at least one question at the end - it shows interest and
maturity.
A day before the interview, I had only revised OOPs concepts from an Apna College YouTube video and
then went to sleep. I wasn't very stressed about the interview because my intention was just to experience it,
understand where I currently stand, and prepare better for future interviews. I genuinely didn't expect to get
shortlisted and was still debating whether or not I even wanted this internship. But things turned out
differently - when the shortlisted names from the OA were announced, my name was on the list. I quickly
ran to get my resume photocopied and within minutes, I was sitting inside the interview room.
The interview started in a very unexpected way. They didn't ask for my introduction, didn't ask about my
resume or projects. Instead, they casually asked, "How did your OA go?" and immediately followed it with
a DSA question. Both interviewers were technically strong and straight to the point, which initially surprised
me, but I decided to go with the flow.
The first problem they asked was to rotate an array https://leetcode.com/problems/rotate-array/ .
I explained multiple approaches - one was using an extra array and placing elements in their new
positions, and the other was a more efficient approach using Python slicing
def rotate (arr,k):
--- PAGE 3 ---
k = k % len(arr)
return arr[-k:] + arr[:-k].
I could see from their expressions that they were satisfied with my thought process.
After that, they moved on to OOPs concepts like abstraction, polymorphism, and types of polymorphism.
Since I had revised these the night before, I could answer well. I had stopped revising at runtime
polymorphism, so for a moment I couldn't explain it. I told them honestly that I couldn't recall it clearly, and
then after they gave a small hint, it clicked and I was able to answer.
Next, they asked questions from SQL - mainly the difference between WHERE and HAVING, and which
one is executed first. I answered that WHERE is applied before grouping and filters rows, while HAVING is
applied after GROUP BY on aggregated results. I also mentioned that WHERE executes first. They then
asked me about Normalization. I explained 1NF first, and when they asked about 2NF, I took a moment,
recalled it, and then explained till 3NF. Thankfully, they didn't go into 4NF.
After that, they moved to core algorithms. They asked me to explain divide and conquer, so I explained it
using merge sort. Then they asked me to explain binary search, its time complexity (O(log n)), and what
condition must be satisfied to apply it. At first, I missed it, but then I smiled when I realized the simple
answer -- the array must be sorted.
Towards the end, they asked if I had any questions for them. Even though I hadn't prepared any, I didn't
want to say no. So I asked, "What kind of work do you do daily, and what kind of problems do you deal
withiạiThey shared their experiences openly, and the conversation ended on a positive note. I knew from
their smile, I was going for round 2.
PS: Always keep smiling even if you don't have any answers ‚the interviewer will guide you

3. Interview Round 2 [ 20+ candidates appeared for this round]

Tip: Talk to other candidates to understand what kind of questions are being asked, but most importantly,
don't back down in the interview room. Stay confident, trust your reasoning, and keep explaining your
thought process clearly - that's what truly leaves an impression.
The second round was conducted on a rolling basis, meaning interviews were happening at different times
for different candidates. I was supposed to have mine after the lunch break, but since I didn't go anywhere
and was sitting outside, they unexpectedly called me in early. Interestingly, another person who was called
along with me had to wait for 2-3 hours before getting his turn, so I considered myself lucky to be
interviewed sooner.
Once again, there were no questions about my resume, projects, or background. They began the
conversation casually, asking how my first round went, and then jumped straight into technical questions.
The interviewer asked about my favorite data structure, to which I confidently replied, "Heaps." He
immediately followed up with, "What about Graphs?" I was honest and said, "Earlier, I used to skip the
graph problems on LeetCode POTD, but later I studied the topic thoroughly and solved over a hundred
graph problems since it's one of the most important topics in DSA." He nodded, satisfied with the response,
and moved on to the main question.
--- PAGE 4 ---
I was given a singly linked list:
1→2→3→4→5→6→7→8
and the expected output was:
7→2→5→4→3→6→1→8
The constraint was to solve it in On) time and O(1) space.
Most Similar Question : https://leetcode.com/problems/reorder-list/
At first glance, I was completely blank, but I didn't panic. I began by observing the pattern and asked a
clarifying question: "If there were an odd number of nodes, how would the pattern change?" This helped me
think aloud and show my reasoning process. I started identifying possible patterns - like reversing the odd
nodes while keeping the even nodes as they were - and simultaneously considered how to perform the
operation in-place, since using an array or another linked list wasn't allowed.
Initially, I thought of the slow and fast pointer approach, but soon realized it might not fully help here. Then
I tried dry-running the given example by moving towards the second-last node, while maintaining two
pointers - head and next - at the start, so I could manipulate pointers directly in place. The interviewer
interjected and asked if I could do it using two pointers. I paused, thought through it, and modified my
approach accordingly. Then he pushed further -- "Can you do it using just one pointer?" I smiled and said
no, explaining that one pointer was needed at the start and one at the end for proper swapping. That seemed
to satisfy them.
After a few minutes of discussion, the other interviewer, who had been mostly silent till now, looked slightly
bored and said, 'Okay, just code it.' That caught me off guard for a moment, but I composed myself and
started coding while explaining my logic step by step. I coded quickly and somewhat hastily, narrating my
thought process as I went. Thankfully, they didn't test it on additional cases, which he had initially
mentioned. Later, I found out from seniors who had cracked the same company that they had the same
interviewers and even the same question - their main goal was not to test perfection but to assess
confidence and problem-solving under pressure.
Despite the challenging question, I never let my confidence drop. Towards the end, they asked if I had any
questions for them. I asked, "What's the biggest difference you've observed between the kind of work you
do that impacts real people and what we, as students, learn in classiạiThe second interviewer, who had been
quiet most of the time, smiled and said, "That's a nice question," and answered fondly.
By that point, I was exhausted but relieved that it was over. I was surprised that the entire round consisted of
only one question - no resume, no project discussions, nothing else. Later, I learned that different panels
had different formats, but I happened to get the most technical one both times. One of the interviewers later
mentioned, "We know from your resume that you've achieved a lot - we just wanted to test your
problem-solving skills and understanding of core concepts." That line stayed with me.
PS: Don't think much about implementation problems, just do what is asked by you.

4. Interview Round 3

--- PAGE 5 ---
After completing the previous rounds, we waited until around 5:00 PM, expecting one more interview
round. However, the coordinators later announced that the shortlisted candidates for the next stage would be
declared in the evening, and the final interactions, if any, would take place the following day. Honestly, I felt
a wave of relief - I thought my interviews were over, and I had already made peace with the idea that I
wouldn't be shortlisted.
Looking at other panels where the interviews were more conversational and focused on resumes and
projects, I felt sure that my highly technical interviews might not have worked in my favor. I was simply
glad that I had given my best and wouldn't have to go through an HR round the next day.
But later that evening, the results were announced - and to my complete surprise, the names they read out
weren't for another round, but for the final internship selection. Hearing my name on that list genuinely
shocked me. It was an unexpected and wholesome moment.

journey.prep:
• Know your resume inside out. Anything you mention can become an interview question, so be

prepared to explain every project, skill, and achievement. Never Lie in your resume it's okay it has
less content rather than false content. Content length doesn't matter your hold on that content matters
how much that is that's far more important/

• Focus on DSA consistently. It's better to solve problems regularly than to cram a week before

interviews. I would. For internships DSA is not as much important until you apply for Trilogy and
companies like these. But should have knowledge for standard data structures and algorithms
beforehand. You can practice platforms like leetcode and codeforces as well as atcoder.

• Master the fundamentals. OOPs, DBMS, OS, and Computer Networks are asked more often than

many people expect. Start making short notes on these as before interviews those would be really
handy to brush up important concepts. GFG and InterviewBit are also great platforms to practice and
learn these

• Have 2-3 solid projects. Quality matters much more than the number of projects. Be able to explain

the motivation, design choices, and your contributions.

• Talk through your approach while coding. Let the interviewer know what you're thinking instead

of silently writing code. THINK OUT LOUD always for anything not only DSA questions.

• Write clean and explainable code. Interviewers care about your thought process as much as the

final solution.

• Stay calm if you get stuck. Interviewers often care more about how you recover and reason through

a problem than whether you get the pertect answer.

• Be honest. If you don't know something, admit it and explain how you would go about learning or

solving it. Interviewers always focus on how honestly you are answering and explaining the things to
him/her.

• Don't compare yourself with others. Placement season can be stressful, but consistency and

patience matter much more than short bursts of preparation.

• Never Give Up. You will achieve everything in life and even better than this so one opportunity

never decides your faith. Just trust yourself and God and the process Everything sooner or
later will fall in right place

interview aptitude will not matter that much then
Stay calm and focused during the OA because there will be sometime that so many people are giving OA
will i be able to go to next round just focus on OA you think there is too much competition but there is not

2. [Round 1: Technical Interview [ 40+ candidates]

I wasn't very confident about my aptitude test and honestly thought I wouldn't qualify. I wasn't included in
the first list of shortlisted candidates, which made me even more doubtful. However, I was pleasantly
surprised when my name appeared in the second shortlist.
When I entered the interview room, I was extremely nervous. There were two interviewers, and they
immediately made me feel comfortable by offering me water and asking me to relax.
The interview began with a DSA question on isomorphic strings. I was given two strings, for example, s1 =
"abc' and s2 = "efg', and asked whether one string could be converted into the other through character
--- PAGE 3 ---
replacement. I started by explaining the brute-force approach and then moved on to an optimal solution
using maps (or vectors) to track character mappings.
Since I had worked on some projects in React Native, the second interviewer asked me questions related to
it. These included differences between React Native and React.js, components specific to React Native, and
concepts like the threading model. I was also asked about the difference between the bridging model and the
new architecture.
Next, I was asked some basic system design questions related to my projects. The focus was on how I would
scale my application to handle a million users and how I would make my codebase modular. From my
experience, internship interviews usually don't go very deep into system design, but it's important to be
familiar with basic concepts like horizontal vs vertical scaling, sharding, and modular design.
After that, I was asked a few OOP-based questions. As I answered them, the interviewers kept modifying the
questions to test my understanding more deeply, which made this part of the interview quite engaging and
slightly lengthy.
Towards the end, I was asked if I had any questions. I would strongly recommend always asking questions
about the company, team culture, or the role because it shows your interest and curiosity. I asked a question
regarding their devops pipeline how they work, which technologies are used.
Overall, despite starting off nervous, the interview turned out to be a great learning experience.

3. [Techno HR] [ 10-15 candidate ]

Then they asked me which language do i prefer so i answer C++ then they are some core oops questions

Then I was asked to implement a binary search tree they didn't mention as it as a binary tree but they

So i understood the question. Always keep asking questions until you don't have a complete

--- PAGE 4 ---

journey.howSecured:
Resume Shortlisting (CE/CSE only) -> Online Assessment -> Technical Interview -> HR Interview

1. Online Assessment [120 candidates]

The test was held on SHL Platform at college itself.  Navigation was not allowed you can't go back that's
important to note. It was a 90 mins test divided into 4 sections,

1. Logical Reasoning 12-13mins 14Qs

2. Quantitative Aptitude 15mins 12Qs

3. DSA 45mins 2Qs

4. English Comprehension 15mins 12Qs

The questions were quite typical I got 2-3 blood relations questions, age related, direction related (if you
start from south-west move 180 degree clockwise then move 270 degree anticlockwise which direction will
your back finally face), coding-decoding, vectors (5km north then 2 km west then 3km south then 8km 5km
west what is the shortest distance from starting position ), LCM-HCF, Permutation, Divisibility( 4522 is
NOT divisible by __), Percentage, patterns, Speed-distance and Simple interest
For English part basic sentence formation checks, Synonyms, 3-4Qs on a passage.
DSA part was different for all I got extremely easy ones,

1. Check how many characters land in same position after reversing the string kinda like

palindrome. I passed all the testcases.

2. You are given an integer k,  sort the  first k  array ele ments in ascending and rest others in

descending that's it!! Again, all cases passed.
I made sure I finish the section within 5-10mins as many times when most of us get easy questions, the time
in which you complete becomes important hence do not waste time su bmit quickly and move ahead.  I think
most of them got doable questions.

2. Technical Interview [34 candidates]

Interview Prep Story
We received shortlisting at around 7.30pm and interviews were next  day at 9am but I didn't panic because I
somewhere knew that this hopefully will be last and final technical interview so I started my prep at around
9pm then slept for 3-4hrs again woke up at 3am and started with OOPs. Did around 45mins conversation with
Claude, revised everything then went for projects . I had made docs for all my projects and internship work
any possible technical or business -related cross question I was somewhat ready for it. Then did a little
DBMS/SQL revision and done… lets start with what reallyy happened…
Actual Interview
There were 4 panels I was the 3rd or 4th one, from my prep you might have seen that I didn't do DSA as such
but but but some of the panels were asking dp based question like Coin Change. I was panicking and just
prayed that I get some other panel and luck was in my favour that day. I think that I got the chillest panel.
I went in greeted them with big smile , they were quite swee t both from Senior DevOps team ig south africa
division. My interview was entirely RESUME BASED , I introduced myself first thought they would ask
about my internship work but they asked about the committee work which I didn't do so just cooked some
random story and they were impressed. We talked about this for 10-15mins I just don't know why they were
so much interested in that, it was just 2 lines in my resume.
Then we moved to my project the first project which SEO Rank tracking, I explained why it is important for
small scale businesses so he had multiple follow -up questions on this how will you market this t o a brand?
How can you guarantee them about improvement in their rankings? Almost all these questions were business
related nothing technical as such. I told him how SEO analysis would help the brands find their Target Market,
customer segmentation and so on. Just kept on talking and they liked it
One of my project had JWT since I had already made docs on such important topic I was aware on all possible
things he could ask but he just wanted surface level knowledge.
Since he was f rom DevOps side he asked that why my resume doesn't have a devops project while most of
the candidates had such projects so I told him honestly that we did make a project during our DevOps lab but
I  didn't put any efforts into it hence now I want to learn and then only if I have good confidence then only I
will mention it in my resume.  He appreciated the honesty and we moved on to last part of interview
He asked me to explain all types of Joins and w rite a query using joins so I made up my own ta bles and
explained all kinds of joins. After this he asked if I had any questions, so I asked since he was from South
Africa division did he ever visit there and can we get a chance too, then I asked how transunion is making a
platform somewhat similar to AWS or Google Cloud since this was mentioned during PPT I asked about this.
Then about a few services that transunion offers, we had discussion on that.
With this interview ended around 35-40mins. I was genuinely lucky that I got such good panel because
as I said in other panel candidates were asked to write oops code or coin change code . Try to have a
smile and be confident because you really can't predict in which direction the interview might go. I had
prepared for something else and was asked random things.. so just go with the flow.

3. HR Interview [11 candidates]

This round took place after lunch break at around 3pm, there were two panelists. I was asked with "Who
is Dishant?" so I gave my introduction as third person. Then was asked about Mini Project since that was
in a group, I was asked typical question, how did you get idea to do this? How to work as a team? Later
on, was asked about my family background, school and whether I was ok to relocate or not.
I asked her about the CSR activities that are done and that was the end.
Around 10-15mins of conversation.

At 4.45-5pm results were announced, 10 of us were selected and felicitated!!

MISTAKES YOU MUST AVOID:

1. Lying or Overstating in your resume

Please do not lie about the technical stuff as after just 1-2 follow-up questions, interviewers can easily
understand if you have deep understanding what you have written or not, if you are not 100% sure just
don't write. Each and every technology you write you must be able to back that up.

2. Don't get intimidated by the competition around you

When I saw there are so many non-tech hungry people around me , I didn't apply for JPMC thinking
that I just don't stand a chance against them but later on many people who were kinda tech heavy also
got selected. This is same thing happened in ISS's OA when I saw there are almost 300 people giving
OA I already made up my mind and didn't do well in that OA too.

3. Don't take rejections too hard

This year UBS didn't take normal OA they followed a different process and only 45 people had been
selected I thought that this opportunity was on a silver-platter hence I must get selected and I reached
till interviews but luck didn't take my side, I messed the interview very bad couldn't answer simple
OOPs questions and got rejected. That just hit me so bad that for day or two I couldn't do anything
and was just depressed and wasted lot of time.

4. You have to do more than just DSA

For few months of placement prep I was just focusing on DS A but I didn't pay much atte ntion on
OOPs, SQL, Aptitude prep and Java fundamentals . You must know java in -depth although I did my
dsa in python most of the companies expect java and sql to be the must know things.

Be ready since this year companies had a completely random shortlisting for OA most of them
wanted little to some work-ex like UBS and WorkIndia so try to do some int ernship. Also keep
your CGPA above 8 , even though can 't do anything about your 10 th ,12th score that is a lso
considered by companies and always tailor your resume according to the company's JD.

I have seen that even though you might have crossed the cgpa cutoff still your resume won't be
shortlisted so check the ATS Score to o. Since our batch was the first with increased intake no t
everyone gets shor tlisted so have a well rounded profile - cgpa, internships, projects, extra -
curricular you must have all these things.

1. Resume Shortlisting (121 candidates shortlisted)

least 70 on https://resumeworded.com/

2. TransUnion PPT

asked "What were your two biggest takeaways from the PPT?" So make sure you understand what
TransUnion does, what they emphasized during the presentation, and what interests you about the
company.

3. Online Assessment (121 candidates appeared)

This was conducted after the PPT on the day itself and consisted of English, Logical Aptitude,
Quantitative Aptitude and 2 Coding Questions. Each of these sections were timed so speed is critical.
English was based on Grammar, Vocabulary, Reading comprehension, Understanding the main idea
of a passage
Logical Aptitude included Number series, Odd one out, Pattern-based questions, Basic logical
reasoning. I practised aptitude using ChatGPT by asking it to give me the important formulas and
then quiz me with difficult questions. If you have time, do practise from IndiaBix as well; they have
good-level questions.
Quantitative Aptitude included Ratios and proportions, Simple interest, Time and work, speed and
distance, Percentages, Basic arithmetic as far as I remember.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Coding : (2 Q's in 45 min) I got two very easy coding questions, both based on arrays/strings. One
question involved removing vowels from a string. The other was a basic array-based problem.
However, the coding questions are shuffled between candidates, so your experience can be very
different. Some students may get two easy questions, while others may get a more difficult one. So
don't prepare assuming that the coding round will be easy.

4. Shortlisting (34 candidates shortlisted)

The OA results came out at around 8 PM, and the interviews were scheduled for the next morning.
This meant there was very little time between getting shortlisted and the interview. I ended up
studying almost the entire night and got around 3.5 hours of sleep.
If you get shortlisted late at night and have an interview the next morning, you should ideally only
need to revise, not learn everything from scratch.
The night before, focus on: Resume → Projects → Core CS → SQL → DSA → Company
Also, practise speaking your answers out loud as if you're answering the interviewer. This really
helped me with my communication, especially because I tend to get anxious. It helps you structure
your thoughts and stay calm during the actual interview.

5. Technical Interview (34 candidates appeared)

The interview experience can vary a lot depending on the panel. In my case, the interview focused
heavily on projects. I was asked if I could demonstrate my projects live, show my GitHub
repositories, and explain my code and database schema.
At one point, they asked me to open specific files from my code, so know your project directory
structure and where things are. Be ready to open VS Code and demonstrate your project. So for
the projects on your resume:

* Know your project structure and code at a basic level.

*
Understand your database/schema.

* He prepared to explain chalenges and how you solved them.

Know why you chose your technologies/ why not other tech stacks
You don't need to know every line of code, but you should genuinely understand what you have
built. Other candidates were asked more technical questions, including DSA, SQL and Core CS. So
prepare for all three areas.
And if you don't know the answer to something, don't panic or try to make up an answer. Just be
honest and say that you're not sure about it right now, but you'd look into it after the interview. It's
completely okay to not know everything, they don't expect you to.
--- PAGE 3 ---

6. HR Interview (11 candidates shortlisted)

The HR round was more conversational. I was asked:

* Whether I was comfortable with relocation

* How do vou handle Team conflicts / working with people

For the team conflict question, I answered with a story. You can use an incident from your own life
that shows how you handled a disagreement and reached a solution.
Using the STAR framework can make your answer much more memorable and impactful. Generic
answers like "I communicate with my teammates and resolve conflicts" don't really tell the
interviewer anything about you, whereas a real story gives them something to remember. This also
works well for other HR questions like "Tell me about a challenge," "Tell me about a time you failed,"
"Tell me about a time you showed leadership," etc.
The main thing they seemed to evaluate was how you communicate, how confidently you
present yourself, and whether you genuinely want to learn and work with the company. So
don't try to sound overly rehearsed. Be authentic and confident.
Finally 10 candidates were shortlisted for TransUnion!
Useful Resources & Prep Tips
Projects: I used AntiGravity as my mock interviewer. Give it each project and ask it to explain the
codebase, architecture, database, tech choices, challenges, and ask follow-up questions.
SQL: https://eetcode.com/studyplan/top-sql-5Q/ is useful, but you can start by asking ChatGPT to
create sample tables and practise basics like SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY and HAVING and then move
to SQL50
DSA: Practice LeetCode or Striver's A2Z Sheet. Also practise taking input and producing output for
complete Java programs, not just LeetCode functions.
Puzzles: https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/aptitude/puzzles/ has good puzzles. I always kept a
puzzle tab open and solved one whenever I needed a break from studying.
OOPS : https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/java/java-interview-questions/
--- PAGE 4 ---
My Advice :)
One thing that really helped me find my weak points was practising interviews with my friends.
It's very different from studying a question and actually having to answer it when someone is sitting
in front of you. Practice introducing yourself & don't make it too generic. Try to say something about
yourself that isn't already on your resume instead of just describing your projects. When you're
asked to explain your projects, practise a 1-2 minute explanation for each one: what it is, why you
made it, what features you're proud of, what you contributed, etc.
Also practise answering HR questions and thinking aloud while solving technical questions. These
things become much easier when you've actually said them out loud before.
And honestly, placement is going to happen on one random day when you least expect it.
Until then, you might constantly have that feeling of uncertainty "When am I going to get placed?
What if I don't?" I had the same feeling, and I genuinely did not expect to get placed on the day I got
placed at TransUnion. It just happened.
So don't spend too much time worrying about the future. Keep preparing and keep going.
And if you don't get selected somewhere even if you make it all the way to the interview round and
then get rejected, allow yourself a few days to feel bad about it. It hurts, and that's completely okay.
Then get back up and start preparing for the next company.
Give every opportunity your 100%, but don't let one rejection define you.
The right opportunity will find you. Keep putting in the work, trust the process, and don't
give up. You might be closer than you think!!
If anything, feel free to reach out to me at : Linkedin- Rachel Fernandes

1. Resume Shortlisting

Resume shortlisting was done based on CGPA. Approximately the first 115 applicants were shortlisted for
the Online Assessment (OA).
--- PAGE 2 ---

2. Online Assessment [110-115 students]

The assessment consisted of four sections:

1. Logical Reasoning:

This section consisted of questions based on patterns, blood relations, coding-decoding, seating
arrangements, etc. The questions were not very difficult, but speed and accuracy were important. There were
15 questions to be solved in 15 minutes. I would recommend aiming for a high score in this section.

2. Aptitude:

There were 12 questions to be solved in 15 minutes. Questions were based on topics such as speed-distance,
ratios, profit and loss, probability, etc. I would recommend practising aptitude questions from IndiaBix, as
similar types of questions are commonly asked in OAs. Speed and accuracy are again very important here.

3. Coding:

The coding section had 45 minutes and consisted of 2 questions.
One important thing I noticed was that the difficulty of the coding questions varied significantly from person
to person. Some students received two relatively easy questions, while others received a combination of an
easy and a medium/hard question. Therefore, the difficulty of the questions you get can have a significant
impact on your performance.
For me, the first question was relatively easy, and I was able to pass all the test cases. The second question
was harder, and I was able to pass only 5/12 test cases. (At this point, I thought I probably wouldn't make it
to the interviews, but never say never! :)
The questions were based on arrays, strings, hashmaps, binary search, greedy algorithms and DP.

4. Verbal Reasoning:

This was the easiest section for me. It had 12 questions with 15 minutes to solve them. The questions
included reading comprehension, grammatical errors and similar verbal reasoning concepts.

3. Technical Interview [34 candidates ]

I was the first candidate on my panel and my interview started at approximately 10:00 am.
Here again the questions and difficulty level vary across panels. All the panels had 2 panelists.
Firstly, they asked me to introduce myself (keep this script ready). I highlighted one backend heavy project,
my app dev internship and talked about the research paper I had published. I think the direction of the
interview and the questions that follow are influenced by your introduction. So prepare your intro
accordingly.
After the intro, they picked the first project and told me to explain the schema and asked in brief about how I
had implemented some of the functionalities. They asked me why I had used MongoDB and not SQL
database (Design choices are often questioned in interviews, so keep such answers ready). Then they asked
me when we should use SQL related databases and when to use NoSQL with one example each.
--- PAGE 3 ---
After this they asked me to write 3 SQL queries. The first two I got correct, then he twisted the third
question a little. I explained to him my approach but I was not able to write the whole query correctly. (Just
tell whatever you know instead of being silent).
He then asked me a DSA question similar to the Coin Change DP problem on LeetCode, but here he wanted
to know how many coins of each denomination were used. I was not able to come up with the DP solution
for this, so I asked if I could explain the greedy approach instead. He told me to write the code on paper and
then he gave me a sample input and told me to dry run the code on that input.
(Be ready to write codes on paper, I was asked to write code on paper in one other interview too).
He was satisfied with that approach and explanation.
Then he asked me about JWT tokens, how they are generated, how they are renewed, their significance etc.
After this he told me to talk about my research paper, what was unique, how did I implement that etc.
I was asked about the difference between ML and DL.
He then asked me to explain 4 pillars of oops with examples for each.
Lastly he asked me about my Barclays minors and 10th and 12th percentages.
He asked me if I had any questions for them to which I asked what technologies do I need to equip myself
with if I were to work at TransUnion. The technical interview thereby concluded on this note.

I was called for the HR interview 20-30 minutes after my technical interview. There were 2 panelists here

She concluded the interview by asking about my family background and whether I had any questions for

journey.prep:
1) The months leading up to the placement (January to June End) is extremely crucial for learning new

skills and sharpening your problem solving skills. However, the moment companies start coming in
the start of July, it becomes very important for you to stop learning new things and just revise the
things you have learnt in these past weeks/months. This is crucial as this will prevent you from being
overwhelmed and make you more confident for the OAs and Interviews.

2) Although, it is appreciable to be ambitious. I would not recommend skipping applying to companies

due to less CTC/Salary. Having location preference is fine but if the role the company offers aligns
with your interests, DO NOT skip it. At least try to get an OA or Interview Experience out of it.
Lastly, instead of sharing resources that you already know of. I would like to share the analysis of my
shortcomings in the previous companies that could help you get placed earlier and with better packages.

1) JP - Didn't Apply

2) IDFC - Applied but couldn't get myself registered due to some technical error

3) PhonePe - Couldn't make it to the interview. Solved 1 problem completely and 1 partially.

The OA in total had 4 questions having 50,70,110 and 120 points respectively. My total score was
89(70+19).
Moral: Rome was not built in a Day. I tried to do my very best by learning concepts and practicing
questions that I had never seen just one day before the OA. This is not how one can reach the
interview where people reach by months of grinding. I would advise to read Interview experiences of
PhonePe or get in touch with the seniors who are placed to get genuine roadmaps.
WorkIndia and AuxoAl - Applied but resume didn't get shortlisted

5) UBS and Nomura - Applied but resume didn't get shortlisted + CGPA was a factor, it was observed

that only the people who had approx 8.8+ could reach the offline rounds for both (I might be
wrong).
Either way, these 4 companies made me realise my mistake and led me to change the resume
completely for my upcoming companies. Please do not repeat this mistake, keep your CGPA the
best you can and get your resume proof read by seniors/mentors and also have an ATS score above
70.

6) ISS - Could not clear OA. Made me realise that grinding DSA is not enough. Core subjects have to

be respected and revised on a daily basis. The OA was conducted on Google Form and it was all
MCQs with a +1 for correct answer and -0.25 for wrong answer.

7) Dolat Capital - Could not clear OA. This was one particularly disheartening as the OA questions

were pretty straightforward and this was my 3rd failure after PhonePe and ISS. It had 3 coding
questions and 6 MCQs.

8) Infosys - I absolutely have no words for this. It was the first time where I could not even pass a

single test case in any question. The questions asked over here are completely different and
traditional DSA practice might/might not help. It is not as difficult as compared to the ones asked in
CP contests but the questions were lengthy and required prior practice. If you are seriously targeting
this company then make sure to dedicate and modify your preparation a little bit.

9) Incred - Resume didn't get shortlisted. Wasn't really keen on the business analyst role anyways.

--- PAGE 6 ---

10) IDfy - The first company for which I could clear the OA and reach Interview. The OA had 1 SQL

query and 4 Coding Questions to be done in 90 minutes. After solving the SQL in 10 minutes, I
proceeded to apply a brute force solution to ¼ questions where I was able to pass 8, 10 and 7 test
cases respectively out of 15. For the 4th question, I couldn't think of even a brute force approach
and hence I hard coded the given test cases to get some points. Luckily enough, even for the hidden
test cases the output was visible even if the input wasn't. This helped me pass 5/15 test cases in that
question too. This OA made me realise that even if I don't have the best solution in that heat of the
moment with a little presence of mind and smartness I can clear OAs.
As far as the Interview experience is concerned, the first round was pretty straightforward asking questions
in and around my projects. Even the core subjects' questions revolved around CCN (TCP vs IP and DNS)
which I was very comfortable with. Lastly the DSA that was asked was binary search on sorted array and
then binary search on rotated sorted array. This round helped me build confidence for my future placement
processes.
The second and the final round of this process was again a Tech round and not a HR one. This one was
particularly humbling as this was where the interviewer picked a ML project from my resume where he was
sure that I had not created a Database and asked me to design my schema in front of him on the spot.
Although I had prepared my projects inside out, I was not ready for a question that challenged me to think
and discuss on the spot. I created and modified tables, relationships and constraints as per the interviewers'
needs and still after each modification he didn't look happy. After a point I was just panicked, frustrated and
all given up. This interview experience made me promise myself that even after I get placed, I would never
stop learning and always make designs on my own without being dependent on AI.
I strongly advise you all to study system design extensively along with DSA/CP and even if there is less
time available I would recommend you to develop your thinking so you can at least be able to make
schemas.

11) Wissen - Disappointing performance. Although I was able to solve the SQL query and MCQ

correctly. For the DSA questions I was only able to pass the given test cases in one question and
given+2 extra in another one. This one broke my confidence as the question didn't feel very tough
upon upsolving.
journey.howSecured:
The placement process began with a shortlist of 121 students. Although the criteria were undisclosed, it
seemed that a CGPA above 8.0 was required.
A CGPA above 8.0 would suffice the cutoff of most companies but I would still recommend you to push to
8.5+ if possible. My CGPA was 8.19 as of the end of 6th Semester.
The PrePlacement Talk was held on 6th August at roughly 12:30PM. Sitting for each PrePlacement Talk is
almost a compulsion and I would highly recommend you to take notes of the company's products, the
company's values and the people who are presenting the talk along with their roles in the company.

1. [Online Assessment] [ 121 Candidates ]

The Online Assessment was divided into 4 sections namely Logical Reasoning, Quantitative Aptitude,
Coding and Verbal Ability ( the section names might be a bit different).
Logical Reasoning: This section consisted of 15 questions to be done in 15 minutes from topics like
coding-decoding (example: AQPR -> BRQS then what is SQOK), directions (example: if you face the
south-east direction then rotate 90degree clockwise and then 180 degree anti clockwise. what direction
would you be facing) and a few blood relations questions.
Quantitative Aptitude: This section consisted of 12 questions to be done in 15 minutes and topics included,
Ratio and proportion, profit/loss and percentage increase/decrease. This section was quite simple and
intuitive.
Coding Section: This section consisted of 2 questions to be done in 45 minutes.
The questions were random for all candidates and even though the majority of them had both easy questions
it becomes crucial to not miss out on any topic as you could unfortunately be one of those candidates who
receive one easy and one medium/tough question.
--- PAGE 2 ---
My questions were

1) The input array was called the product IDs and we were required to return the quantity of products

sold which was defined as the sum of digits of product ID
Input array = [54 13 511 982 20]
Output array = [9 4 7 19 2]
I iterated through the input array, calculating the sum of the digits using a while(n>O) loop and the
pushing back the sum into the answer vector.

2) Sort the digits till kth position in descending order and the rest in ascending order

Input:
K=3
Array: 13 6 8 2 3 5 4
Output : 63123458
Here I made two temporary vectors, one till the kth number and another one from the k+ 1st number till the
end. Sorted the first temporary vector in descending order and the second vector in ascending order. At last I
pushed back values from both the vectors into the answer vector.
Upon thinking about the question after reaching home, I realised that those 3 extra vectors were kind of
unnecessary and I could have done something like
sort(arr.rend() - k, arr.rend();
sort(arr.begin() + k, arr.endO);
Both these questions were Leetcode style (the main function and parameters were already defined, and you
just had to return the answer vector from your defined function to the main function).
I was able to pass all test cases in both the questions.
Verbal Ability: This section consisted of questions such as 'what part of the sentence is grammatically
incorrect' and paragraph based questions to test your comprehension skills.
--- PAGE 3 ---
2.
[Tech Interview] [ 34 Candidates were selected for Interviews]
The Interviews were scheduled a day after the PPT and OA day(7th August). The shortlist arrived on the 6th
August at 7:45 PM leaving less time for preparation. I prioritized revising my projects section on the
resume as I knew it had been my weak point all along. Even after prioritizing the majority of time
towards projects, I took an hour to brush upon my core subjects and DSA. It is very important for you
to cover all things and be balanced even in your last minute preparation.
I was 21st on the 34 person shortlist they had arranged the list CGPA wise) and my turn to interview came
at 1:00PM. Luckily enough, as soon as I was about to enter, all the panelists called for a lunch break
and it was announced that the interviews would resume at 2:00PM. This gave me time to have some
food and get energized before my turn.
Upon returning from lunch break, I was the first person to get interviewed. I greeted the panelists with a firm
handshake and then they asked me to introduce myself. My introduction was pretty dull as I only
mentioned my name, branch and college (I strongly discourage you to do this and I would suggest you
to be ready with a strong and confident introduction).
The interview started with basic questions on Java OOPS where they asked me about the 4 Pillars.
Upon describing each pillar to them, they asked me to write the code for Polymorphism and Encapsulation
on paper. For the polymorphism part, I wrote code for both method overloading and method overriding.
As far as the encapsulation part is concerned, I created a private variable in my class and wrote public getter
and setter methods for the same.
Then the panelists asked me what is the use of Stack in Java. I panickingly replied that during recursion an
internal stack is used. Now that I think about it, the answer they expected might have been that Stack
Memory is used to store Primitives and Object References. As I had spilled out the word recursion, the
interviewer then asked me to explain it and write down an example using recursion. I chose the simplest
example, factorial and explained to them the thought process as I wrote the base case and the recursive
equation.
The interviewer then asked me if I remember the question I received in my OA and my solution to it. To
which I replied yes and explained the logic. He then asked me to write down the code on paper.
(Important thing to note is that even though you don't remember the question it's fine as they have it on
their laptops. I was lucky enough to receive easy questions and solve them completely but it is better to
be honest with the Interviewer in case you were able to pass only a handful of test cases by brute torce or
some hardcoding as he MIGHT have your solution on his laptop too).
The conversation then shifted to DBMS where I was asked to explain Cardinality (1-1, 1-N, M-N) using
examples of my choice. I can't exactly recall what example I had chosen but it was a simple one using
Students, Teachers, Courses etc. Then the topic shifted to Normalization where again I was allowed to
take example tables of my choice and apply normalization on it. Luckily the interviewer stopped me
after I was done applying 2NF as I was anyways not very comfortable with the higher normal forms.
Then I was asked a SQL query where I had to find the total number of employees. They told me to assume
the tables, columns and constraints as per my need and just provide them with the final query.
--- PAGE 4 ---
I wrote something like :
SELECT d.department name, COUNT(e.employee_id) AS total
_employees
FROM Employee e
JOIN Department d ON e. department_id = d.department id
GROUP BY d.department_id, d.department name;
After writing this query , I was asked about types of joins and the differences. At last the SQL section of the
interview ended with them asking me what Stored Procedures were and the advantages of using them.
At the very end of the Interview one of the interviewers asked me how good I was at solving puzzles to
which I replied that I am not the best but I do enjoy solving them with my friends on a regular basis.
To which he asked me a very simple question:
There are 3 temples and 2 ponds. At the very beginning I had x flowers. I visit each temple sequentially and
at each temple I place y flowers. After the first and second temple visit I also take a dip in the pond
where my remaining flowers get doubled. After repeating this process when I placeiy flowers' in the
third temple, I have nothing left. What is the value of x and y.
I explained systematically how my count of flowers are affected by each temple visit and pond dip.
i) After the first temple visit my remaining flowers: x-y
il) After first pond dip : 2(x-y) = 2x-2y
iii) After second temple visit : 2x-2y -y = 2x-3y
iv) After second pond dip : 2(2x-3y) = 4x-6y
v) After third temple : 4x-6y -y = 4x-7y
vi) 4x-7y=0. Therefore, x = 7 and y = 4.
Then the interviewer just asked me to substitute these values into the problem and dry run through it.
Lastly before leaving the Interview I asked the interviewer their names and their Roles at the company.

3. ¡HR Interviewl [ 11 Candidates appeared for this Round]

The interviewers greeted me by introducing themselves and then asked for my introduction. This time along
with my name and department, I shared about my hobbies and interests. Then they proceeded to ask me
one small question on my project (it was not technical at all, so no need to worry). After that one of the
