customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
1) The months leading up to the placement (January to June End) is extremely crucial for learning new

skills and sharpening your problem solving skills. However, the moment companies start coming in
the start of July, it becomes very important for you to stop learning new things and just revise the
things you have learnt in these past weeks/months. This is crucial as this will prevent you from being
overwhelmed and make you more confident for the OAs and Interviews.

2) Although, it is appreciable to be ambitious. I would not recommend skipping applying to companies

due to less CTC/Salary. Having location preference is fine but if the role the company offers aligns
with your interests, DO NOT skip it. At least try to get an OA or Interview Experience out of it.
Lastly, instead of sharing resources that you already know of. I would like to share the analysis of my
shortcomings in the previous companies that could help you get placed earlier and with better packages.

1) JP - Didn't Apply

2) IDFC - Applied but couldn't get myself registered due to some technical error

3) PhonePe - Couldn't make it to the interview. Solved 1 problem completely and 1 partially.

The OA in total had 4 questions having 50,70,110 and 120 points respectively. My total score was
89(70+19).
Moral: Rome was not built in a Day. I tried to do my very best by learning concepts and practicing
questions that I had never seen just one day before the OA. This is not how one can reach the
interview where people reach by months of grinding. I would advise to read Interview experiences of
PhonePe or get in touch with the seniors who are placed to get genuine roadmaps.
WorkIndia and AuxoAl - Applied but resume didn't get shortlisted

5) UBS and Nomura - Applied but resume didn't get shortlisted + CGPA was a factor, it was observed

that only the people who had approx 8.8+ could reach the offline rounds for both (I might be
wrong).
Either way, these 4 companies made me realise my mistake and led me to change the resume
completely for my upcoming companies. Please do not repeat this mistake, keep your CGPA the
best you can and get your resume proof read by seniors/mentors and also have an ATS score above
70.

6) ISS - Could not clear OA. Made me realise that grinding DSA is not enough. Core subjects have to

be respected and revised on a daily basis. The OA was conducted on Google Form and it was all
MCQs with a +1 for correct answer and -0.25 for wrong answer.

7) Dolat Capital - Could not clear OA. This was one particularly disheartening as the OA questions

were pretty straightforward and this was my 3rd failure after PhonePe and ISS. It had 3 coding
questions and 6 MCQs.

8) Infosys - I absolutely have no words for this. It was the first time where I could not even pass a

single test case in any question. The questions asked over here are completely different and
traditional DSA practice might/might not help. It is not as difficult as compared to the ones asked in
CP contests but the questions were lengthy and required prior practice. If you are seriously targeting
this company then make sure to dedicate and modify your preparation a little bit.

9) Incred - Resume didn't get shortlisted. Wasn't really keen on the business analyst role anyways.

--- PAGE 6 ---

10) IDfy - The first company for which I could clear the OA and reach Interview. The OA had 1 SQL

query and 4 Coding Questions to be done in 90 minutes. After solving the SQL in 10 minutes, I
proceeded to appl

journey.howSecured:
Rounds:

1. Resume Shortlisting

2. Online Assessment

3. Technical Interview

4. HR Interview

1. Resume Shortlisting

The process began with resume shortlisting. It was mostly done on the basis of CGPA. I would
advise to maintain a CGPA of at least 8.0 or 8.5 to get shortlisted in most companies. Also tailor
your resume according to JD. Around 121 students were shortlisted after this round.

2. Online Assessment [121 students ]

There were four sections in this round: Logical reasoning, Quantitative aptitude, Coding, Verbal
ability. Each section was timed.
--- PAGE 2 ---

1. Logical reasoning: 15 questions were to be solved in 15 mins. Fairly straightforward

questions like direction, age, decoding names, etc. were asked.

2. Quantitative Aptitude: Ratio-proportion based, mixtures, work and time type of

questions were asked. 15 mins were allotted to this section. You get approximately 1min
to solve each question, calculators were not allowed in this section and most other OAs
that I had appeared. Therefore, practice solving aptitude questions under time constraints.

3. Coding Section: 45 mins were given to this section. I had 2 easy questions so I could

complete it within 15 mins and pass all the test cases.

1. Remove vowels from a given string.

2. Given an array of numbers. Initially amount-0 add the number from array to amount if

that number is divisible by x.
Some of the applicants had also got questions where they had to use HashMaps, Priority
Queue and other data structures. DSA was asked in almost all the companies so do not
skip it!!

4. Verbal Ability: In this section simple english vocabulary questions like synonyms,

antonyms, grammar based questions like what is correct sentence for the given
sentence,etc. There were also paragraph based questions.
Solving standard IndiaBix questions was enough for logical, quantitative and verbal section. I
had also referred to career ride youtube channel for preparing aptitude.

3. Technical Interview [ 35 students ]

The shortlist for interviews arrived on 6th August in the evening. We had interviews the next day
at around 10 AM. There were 2 interviewers in each panel. My interview lasted for around
20-30mins. The interviewer asked me to introduce myself. The introduction is important as it
can decide what the interviewer will ask. Highlight your strengths in introduction. The
interviewer asked me if I was comfortable with JAVA. Java was my primary language so I
said yes. They asked me about OOP. I explained OOP highlighting examples in short. Then I
was asked about 4 pillars of OOP: Encapsulation, Abstraction, Polymorphism, Inheritance.
Then I was asked to implement each of these four in code. I was also asked to implement
runtime polymorphism. Difference between compile time polymorphism and runtime
polymorphism and how compile time polymorphism internally works. Then they moved to
SQL. They asked me to write a query for finding 2nd highest marks in the students table.
This was a pretty easy question. I answered with 2 approaches. Then they asked me what
normalization is, what are relations in tables (1to 1, 1 to many, etc.). I was asked to draw
tables and establish many to many relation in it. So I created a students table, course and
enrolls table. Then they looked at my resume and asked me about different databases I had
--- PAGE 3 ---
used. (I had used Pinecone, MongoDB, PostgreSQL and Redis in my resume). I was asked
why and how I used them in my projects and what is the difference between them. I was also
asked to write MongoDB schema I had used in my project and sample queries in MongoDB.
I could draw the schema (in BSON format) but I had completely forgotten about the query
syntax. I told them I could not recollect the syntax. Then they asked if I would be willing to
relocate as they had no office in Mumbai. I said yes. Then they asked if I had any questions
for them. I asked them what was the biggest challenge they encountered in a project at
Transunion. They said it was handling massive data. This was the end of the interview.
Useful Tip:

1. Don't miss these topics at any cost as they will be asked in almost all companies: OOPs,

SQL, Aptitude, DSA.

2. Know every line of your resume. You should have a justification for why you used a

given tool in your project.

3. It's ok to not know something in an interview. If you don't know something, accept it.

4. Your selection also depends on what interview panel you get, so luck is involved. Give

your best in every interview!

5. No tool is better than ChatGPT when it comes to revising for an interview. You can

prepare for your projects, HR questions, MCQS using ChatGPT.

4. HR Interview [11 students]

I was called for the HR round at around 1:30 PM. There were 3 interviewers in my panel. The
interview began with a warm greeting. The HR asked me to introduce myself. She went through
my resume and particularly liked the name I had given to my project: "PyscheLens. She asked
me why I gave this name and why it is important to give meaningful names to projects. I was
also asked to explain this project. I answered it in the form of a story and the interviewer was
very impressed. Then she asked me about the group projects on my resume and how we divided
the work among ourselves. Then the interviewer asked me about my family, if I had any plans
for higher studies. Then she asked me if I was willing to relocate. Finally they asked me if I had
any questions. I asked them what growth at TranUnion looks like and what I should prepare if I
get selected. The interview lasted for about 15 mins. 10 students were selected after this round
and I was one of them.

1. Use the STAR method to answer situation based questions.

2. Try to explain your projects to HR in the form of a story.

3. Do ask questions at the end. It shows that you are curious about the company.

--- PAGE 4 ---
Lastly, I would say that the placement journey is not easy. There will be days when you prepare
your heart out and still receive a rejection. After a few rejections, you may start questioning
yourself, your preparation, your abilities, and even whether you will get placed at all. I know this
feeling because I have been there too. But remember, those difficult moments are also the
moments when you are being tested. They are teaching you patience, resilience, and the ability to
keep going even when you don't have any guarantee that things will work out. So, do not give
up. Believe in the preparation you have put in. Believe in the skills you have built. And most
importantly, believe that one rejection cannot decide your future. I got my TransUnion offer at a
time when I expected it the least. I had already experienced enough rejection to feel exhausted,
and I wasn't even expecting this opportunity to work out. But sometimes, life surprises you when
you have almost stopped expecting it to. So keep applying. Keep preparing. Keep learning from
every interview. Keep grinding, even on the days when you don't feel like it. You never know
which opportunity will finally be the one that changes everything. And when things don't happen
according to your plan, trust the process. What God has planned for you is good, often better
than what you could have planned for yourself. Sometimes the door you desperately want to
open doesn't, because there is another door waiting for you that you couldn't see yet. So don't let
rejection make you believe that you are not capable. Your journey is different, your timing is
different, and that's okay.
Keep faith. Keep working. Keep showing up. Your opportunity will come.
If you ever need any guidance regarding placements, interviews, resumes, or preparation, please
feel free to reach out to me at
Contact: 7709341361
LinkedIn: Valencia Dmonte

1. [Online Assessment] [Eligible Students Appeared : 80]

The online assessment was conducted on Coderbyte sharp at 8:30 AM. It was divided into four distinct
sections, testing programming, machine learning, databases, and fundamental concepts.
Section 1: Python Programming
Implementation of basic Bubble Sort strictly from scratch without using . sort () or built-in functions.
Section 2: Machine Learning Notebook
A single code file containing 4 blank snippets where you had to write the implementation logic. This
covered end-to-end data tasks including Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA), missing value handling and
preprocessing, aggregation, and basic model setup using pandas and scikit-learn.
Section 3: SQL
A straightforward database query focusing on joining two tables and filtering aggregated data.
Section 4: Technical MCQs
Multiple-choice questions testing core machine learning intuition, standard Python syntax, and CS
fundamentals.
Points to Remember:
Manage your time well across coding and MCQS. Keep basic pandas transformations and array
manipulation logic right at your fingertips so you don't waste time looking up trivial syntax. Around 24
students were shortlisted for the next stage.

2. [Group Discussion Round] [24 Candidates Shortlisted]

The shortlisted students were divided into 3 groups of 8 students each. The discussion lasted for around 40
minutes per group.
The panel was very warm, polite, and receptive. This was not an aggressive debate round; they were
genuinely observing how structured your thoughts were, how clearly you communicated, and whether you
--- PAGE 2 ---
could build meaningfully upon points made by your peers. Active listening, avoiding talking over others,
and summarizing logically went a long way here. 8 candidates were shortlisted for the interview rounds.

3. [Technical Interview Round] [8 Candidates Shortlisted]

Duration was around 45 to 50 minutes. I was the very first candidate scheduled for the interview slot.
The interview started with a self-introduction where I walked them through my academic background, prior
internships, and core technical stack before steering toward my primary domain: Al and Deep Learning.
Project Deep Dive:
The panel spent nearly 20 solid minutes grilling me on my AI and deep learning projects. They went deep
into architectural choices and theoretical foundations. They questioned me thoroughly on convolutional
layers in CNNS, feature mapping, Vision Transformers (VIT), and attention mechanisms. For Generative
Adversarial Networks (GANs), they asked what exact architecture variant I used, why I chose it, and how
the generator-discriminator loss balance was maintained. They also demanded exact mathematical formulas
for evaluation metrics and pressed me on the precise performance numbers and benchmark scores my model
achieved
Live Coding:I was given an algorithmic coding problem to implement Insertion Sort from scratch. Once
implemented, they added a follow-up variation asking to retrieve the second largest element from the
structure. Scenario-Based ML: They presented practical, real-world machine learning problem statements
requiring structured logical reasoning, data handling strategies, and architectural decisions under real
constraints.
Points to Remember:
Own every single line on your resume. If you mention high-level architectures like Transformers or GANS,
be prepared to explain the underlying math, loss functions, hyperparameter choices, and exact benchmark
figures. Also, talk through your code out loud while implementing live algorithmic problems.

4. [HR Round] [Shortlisted Candidates]

The HR round lasted about 20 to 30 minutes. It was very calm, friendly, and conversational. Questions were
centered around: My personal background and journey into tech, my long-term career vision and aspirations,
my core strengths and genuine weaknesses, backed by real academic and project experiences, situational
questions on handling workplace pressure, team dynamics, and adaptability. Be genuine, grounded, and clear
about your motivations. Frame your weaknesses alongside the concrete actions you are taking to improve
them.
The final results were announced on the same evening. 2 students were selected for the role, and I was
fortunate to be one of them.
--- PAGE 3 ---

journey.prep:
My placement journey involved applying to around 46 companies on Superset and appearing for 40+ online
assessments. What helped me most was learning from every OA and interview. I used to maintain a record
of the questions asked in previous interviews, identify my weak areas, and work on them before the next
opportunity.
--- PAGE 5 ---
Revise DSA, know your resume and projects thoroughly, and practise under time limits. I could have done
better in prompt engineering and time management, so always practise writing precise prompts and submit
at least a minute before the deadline.
Most importantly, believe in yourself. Rejections are part of the process. Don't compare your progress with
others; keep learning from every OA and interview, work on your weak areas, and keep applying. You may
face many rejections, but consistency and improvement really matter.
journey.howSecured:
A. At Home:
a. Communication Test (28th Sept 2026, retest on 1st Oct 2026)
b. Final Assessment Test (28th Sept 2026)
B. At College:
a. Online test (8th Oct 2026)
b. Interview (8th Oct 2026)
1.
Communication Test [Everyone gave the test]
The communication test was conducted from home on 28 September 2026, with a retest on 1 October
because few candidates couldn't access the previous one. It had 29 questions divided into five sections.

1. Reading Comprehension: Passage-based MCQs testing understanding, inference, and reasoning. One

passage discussed Universal Basic Income (UBI) trials in Finland and Kenya.
Example questions:

• What is the main purpose of the passage?

• What did the Finnish trial reveal about employment and well-being?

• Why can't these trials establish whether UBI would work at a national scale?

2. Listening Comprehension: Audio-based questions testing understanding of details, speaker intentions, and

emotions.
Example: How does a business owner feel about no longer knowing every customer personally? (the ans
was in the audio, just listen properly)

3. Spoken Communication: Timed video responses on personal experiences and workplace situations.

Example questions:

• Describe someone who influenced your career positively.

• Would you prefer giving difficult feedback face-to-face or in writing?

--- PAGE 2 ---
For the career question, I spoke about my NCC senior who trained me for AIVSC 2025 and helped me
develop discipline and perform under pressure. I connected this guidance to my achievement of becoming
Best Pilot of AIVSC 2025.

4. Business Communication Writing: Workplace messages and longer opinion-based writing tasks.

Example questions:

• Write a message explaining that your car is unavailable for a shared lift and request someone to

cover your turn.

• Inform your team about a change from approach A to approach B.

• Should cities charge drivers to enter busy areas during peak hours?

• Should regular meetings be limited to 30 minutes?

5. Grammar and Sentence Correction: MCQs on subject-verb agreement, relative pronouns, sentence

structure, and parallel construction.
Examples included choosing between has been and other verb forms, correcting sentences involving
"neither...nor," and selecting grammatically correct phrases.
Preparation Tips

• Practise passage-based questions and answer strictly from the given text.

• For speaking, use a simple structure: answer, reason, example, and conclusion.

• For writing, follow the word limit and keep the tone natural and professional.

• Revise basic grammar rules and read each sentence carefully before selecting an option.

2. Final Assessment Test [Everyone gave the test]

This round was conducted from home on 28 September 2026. It mainly tested hand-eye coordination, quick
thinking, attention, and memory retention through interactive games.
One task involved observing several balls on a screen, including one ball of a different colour. A
matching-figure question followed, requiring a True/False response. This pattern repeated three or four
times, after which I had to select the coloured balls in the sequence in which they had appeared.
Preparation and tips:

• Practise visual memory, pattern recognition, and quick decision-making games.

• Pay attention to the sequence of objects and colours, not just their individual appearance.

• Stay focused throughout the task, as information from earlier screens may be needed later.

• Accuracy is important, but you must also respond within the available time.

--- PAGE 3 ---

3. Online Assessment [77 shortlisted candidates]

The online assessment was conducted at college on 8 October 2026. It had four rounds, with different time
limits and problem-solving requirements. At the beginning, we had to select a technology/language option,
such as React or Node.js, which was relevant to the later Al debugging and function-development questions.

Round 1: Basic DSA - 30 minutes

This was a basic data structures and algorithms coding question. I found it relatively easy and completed it
in around 15 minutes, with all test cases passing.
Tip: Focus on correctness first, consider edge cases, and use the remaining time to verify the solution.

Round 2: Prompt Engineering - 15 minutes

We were given a problem and had to write a complete prompt for an Al system to generate the required
solution. The generated code was not visible, and we could not directly inspect which test cases were failing.
The question text also could not be copied, although the test cases were copyable.
Initially, I wrote two prompts explaining the expected answer in my own words, but no test cases passed. I
then added the implementation approach, explaining that a dictionary should be used to store values and
retrieve them as required. This improved the result, and 5 out of 6 test cases passed before time ran out.
Tip: A prompt should describe not only the expected output but also the implementation logic, constraints,
edge cases, and expected behaviour.

Round 3: AI Debugging - 35 minutes

A complete website (frontend + backend) with a faulty feature was provided, along with an Al assistant. The
assistant gave hints about dependencies and possible issues rather than directly supplying the answer. Direct
questions asking it to solve the evaluation problem were restricted.
This I was not able to complete.
Tip: Understand the existing code flow, inspect the relevant components and dependencies, reproduce the
issue, and use Al hints to guide debugging rather than depending on it to generate the entire fix.

Round 4: AI Function Development - 30 minutes

This round provided frontend and backend code and required adding the functionality described in the
problem statement. I was able to implement the main functionality, but the implementation was only partial
by the end of the round.
Tip: Read the complete requirements first, identify the essential functionality, and prioritise a working
end-to-end implementation before spending time on additional details.
Important:
I submitted the first question with sufficient time remaining, and it displayed a green tick. For the second
and third questions, I attempted submission in the final 10 seconds, but errors appeared and the green tick
--- PAGE 4 ---
was not displayed. I was unsure whether the code had been submitted automatically, so I checked with HR,
who said they would verify it with the technical team.
My strongest advice is to submit every question at least one minute before the deadline. Wait for the
submission confirmation or green tick rather than assuming the code has been saved. Reserve the final
minutes for submission and verification.

4. Interview [6 shortlisted candidates]

The final round was a technical-cum-HR interview based mainly on my resume, projects, internship,
technical skills, and workplace scenarios.
Questions asked

• Tell me about yourself. I introduced myself and summarised my technical background and

experience.

• Give a brief overview of your projects. I explained the projects listed on my resume.

• What are you doing in your AI/ML internship at NeoSkillz? What difficulties did you face? I

discussed my internship project and the challenges involved in building it.

• What is the difference between REST APIs and FastAPI? Which is more secure?

• A team has a very close deadline. Three members are capable but overloaded, while the fourth

member is struggling. What would you do?
I explained that I would prioritise the critical work first, then help the struggling teammate. Rather than
making one person responsible for all the extra support, each team member could help in turns so that
nobody's own work was neglected. I would also share useful resources, references, and Al tools to help the
teammate complete their tasks.

• Why should we hire you? I gave my prepared answer, highlighting my technical skills, learning

ability, and project experience.

• What do you know about Capgemini? I answered based on my understanding of the company.

Finally 4 candidates were selected for the final offer, results were announced on 16th Oct. (Actually there
were 5 names but 1 of us got another company before this result).

1. English Assessment round (from home)

2. Cognitive Assessment round (from home)

3. Technical Assessment (on campus)

4. Technical Interview (on campus)

1.
English Assessment [ 170+ students gave the test ]
This round was purely based on grammar, writing skills, listening skills, speaking skills, and
decision-making. The assessment consisted of multiple sections, each testing a different skill.
The first 10 questions were behavioural and situational judgment questions. These were not necessarily
related to workplace behaviour but focused more on general decision-making in different situations. For
example, one question described a situation where two countries were at war and asked what you would do.
The options included taking one side, negotiating between the countries, or appealing for peace. I do not
remember the exact wording or all the options.
The next section was listening comprehension. We were given a short audio clip of approximately 20
seconds, which we had to listen to carefully and answer four questions based on the audio.
The following section was reading comprehension, where a paragraph was provided, followed by five
questions based on the information in it.
The next section was the speaking assessment through video questions. We were given two questions and
had to record our answers. Everyone received different questions. I was asked, "How does a typical day
differ between working from home (WFH) and working from the office (WFO)? Does this affect team
collaboration and communication?" and "Tell me about a technology you use every day, what you use it for,
and why." Some of my friends received questions such as "Tell me something about your friend."
The next section tested grammar and sentence correction. Each question contained a sentence with an
underlined portion, and we had to choose the option that best replaced the underlined part while maintaining
grammatical correctness. There were 10 questions in this section.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Lastly, there were four email-writing questions. Each question described a particular situation and
specified the points that had to be included in the email, along with the tone to be used. For example, one
question asked us to write a polite email to our landlord about a leak in the rented house while highlighting
the urgency of the issue. Another asked us to write an email to a client informing them that the project
deadline was being extended or delayed. I do not remember the other two questions exactly.
This was a easy round

2. Cognitive Assessment (All those who gave english assessment)

This round was conducted on the same day, approximately two hours after the English assessment. It
consisted of five sections and was quite tiring. The assessment included puzzles, some behavioural
questions, and tasks where we had to remember the sequence of dots while being interrupted by other
questions. I do not clearly remember all five sections.
The last section was particularly time-consuming and consisted of 100 questions. Each question described a
situation, and we had to respond using a slider with options ranging from Strongly Disagree, Disagree,
Neutral, Agree, and Strongly Agree.
The assessment also had technical issues, as only five questions appeared on each page and the questions
loaded very slowly. In some cases, it took approximately 10 minutes for the questions on a page to load
Despite these delays and the lengthy assessment, I was eventually able to complete the round.
The English assessment retest was also conducted for everyone who needed it because some candidates
had experienced problems during the initial assessment. However, the cognitive assessment retest was
conducted only for candidates who had faced issues during their original test, rather than for everyone.

3. Technical Assessment (77 students shortlisted for this round)

This round was conducted on campus, with representatives from the company present at the venue. We
were instructed to arrive by 7:45 AM, as the assessment was scheduled to begin at 9:00 AM sharp. Before
starting the test, our Aadhaar cards were verified to unlock access to the assessment. The company
representatives then gave us a brief introduction to the company and explained the assessment process.
On the first page of the assessment, we had to select one of five frameworks: React, Django, Flask,
Node.js, or Spring Boot. I selected Spring Boot because I was more confident in it than the other options.
My advice would be to choose the framework you know best rather than selecting one simply because
it seems easier. I saw some candidates choose React because it was a frontend framework and seemed easy
to them, even though they were not thoroughly familiar with it.
The assessment consisted of four sections, each with a fixed time limit.
The first section was DSA (25 minutes). However, I would not describe the questions as typical DSA
problems. They were relatively easy if you were confident with programming language syntax, array
--- PAGE 3 ---
manipulation, and accessing data structures. My question was related to product management. I was given
an array of products, each containing an ID, name, and price, along with a queries array in the form [type,
value]. There were three types of queries: the first required finding products with prices greater than the
given value, the second required finding products with prices lower than the given value, and the third
required finding products whose IDs were smaller than the given value. For each query, we had to print the
names of all products satisfying the specified condition. Everyone received different questions in this
section.
The second section was Prompt Engineering (15 minutes). We were given a situation in which we had to
retrieve logs for the endpoint with the highest number of errors, following a specific output format. Our task
was to write a prompt that would make the Al generate the desired output. The test cases would pass if the
prompt correctly captured the requirements and produced the expected result. This question was common to
everyone, although some of my friends were unable to pass all the test cases.
The third section was Debugging (30 minutes). We were given a buggy application based on the framework
we had selected at the beginning of the assessment. An Al assistant was available to help us, but it did not
directly provide the complete solution. My suggestion would be to ask the Al assistant general questions
about the codebase and the flow of execution rather than immediately asking it to fix the bug. I started
by asking which files handled the relevant logic, including the controller, entity, and repository. Once I
understood the structure, I began debugging the application. I was able to pass only two test cases. The
number of test cases varied depending on the selected framework.
The final section was Feature Development (40 minutes), which I found to be the toughest part of the
assessment. We were given a feature to implement in the application, and the implementation was evaluated
using test cases. In my case, there were six test cases, but I was able to pass only one by the end of the
allotted time.

4. Technical interview (only 6 students were shortlisted for interviews)

There were three interview panels, and the interviewers arrived later in the day rather than being present
during the morning assessment. I was the second candidate to be interviewed in my panel.
When I entered the room, the interviewer initiated a handshake, introduced himself by name, and I
introduced myself as well. He did not ask me for a formal self-introduction and instead took a quick look at
my resume before starting the interview.
He first asked me whether I wanted to become a Data Engineer or a Cloud Engineer. I replied that I was
comfortable with both roles and that my skills, projects, and experience aligned with both. He then asked me
what I understood by the role of a Data Engineer and what a Data Engineer actually does. Following that, he
asked me to rate my proficiency in Python.
Next, he asked me to design a complete data engineering pipeline. I began by explaining the data source,
how the data would be collected, and where it would be stored. The interviewer challenged my approach
several times with follow-up questions. For example, he asked how I would handle millions of rows of data.
I suggested processing the data in chunks and using object storage such as AWS S3. He then asked me
questions about AWS S3, which I was able to answer because I had used it in one of my projects. However, I
could not complete the entire pipeline before he moved on to the next question.
--- PAGE 4 ---
He then asked whether I knew MySQL and PostgreSQL, as both were mentioned on my resume. After that,
he asked me about the difference between OLAP and OLTP. I was not familiar with these terms and
admitted that I did not know the answer. I genuinely thought I had lost the interview at this point.
He then asked me to design a database schema for DMart. I created an ER diagram and explained the
entities and their relationships. He asked how the tables were related in terms of primary keys and foreign
keys. He also asked me about fact tables and dimension tables, but I was unfamiliar with those specific
terminologies at the time.
The interviewer then moved on to object-oriented programming (OOP) and asked why we needed it,
followed by a question about the four pillars of OOP. After that, he asked why Git, GitHub, and GitLab were
mentioned on my resume and why we needed them. I explained their purpose and how they were used.
He then presented a practical scenario: could I merge my code directly if I did not have the necessary
permissions? I replied that I would raise a pull request, and a maintainer or supervisor would review it. If
everything was correct and the CI pipeline had passed all the tests, the authorized person could merge the
code. He followed up by asking whether we could merge the code directly if doing so would make it live. I
explained the concept of blue-green deployment in response, and he seemed satisfied with my answer.
After that, he asked me about one of my projects but did not go into much technical detail. He was mainly
interested in a general overview.
The next topic was SDLC and its stakeholders. He asked who the stakeholders in the software
development life cycle were, and I mentioned clients, the business team, the project manager, and the
development team.
He then gave me a situational question. He asked me to imagine that I had become good friends with a client
and that the client was now asking me to implement an additional feature. I fumbled a little while answering
this question. I initially said that I would conduct a proper risk analysis of the proposed feature and identify
the modules that would be affected. The interviewer then asked whether I would implement the feature for
free. I replied that I would inform the client that the additional feature would incur extra costs and could
push the project deadline forward. He then asked whether I needed to inform the project manager as well. I
agreed that the project manager would need to be kept in the loop throughout the process. I felt that I had not
handled this question as confidently as I could have.
Towards the end of the interview, the interviewer asked me whether there was anything he should have
asked me but had not. I took this opportunity to bring up my final-year major project, which he had not
asked about earlier, and gave him an explanation of the project.
The interview ended with another handshake, and I left the room. We had expected an HR interview to
follow, but no further interview took place. Instead, we were asked to leave for the day.
The results were announced approximately one week later, and fortunately, I was selected for the final
offer! In total, 5 candidates were selected. However, one of the selected candidates had already accepted an
offer from another company and therefore could not accept this offer.
--- PAGE 5 ---

journey.howSecured:
The placement process was quite different from that of other companies visiting our campus. Since
Capgemini was visiting our campus for the first time, we had no idea what to expect. Moreover, we noticed
that the company had changed the test format this year, so practising previous years' questions was not very
useful, TBH.
PROCESS:

1) English Communication Test (28th Sept 2026, retest on 1st Oct 2026) (both from home)

2) Assessment Test (28th Sept 2026) (from home)

3) Brief Presentation ( 8th Oct 2026)( from college)

4) Online Assessment (8th Oct 2026) (from college)

5) Interview (8th Oct 2026) (from college)

1. [English Communication Test] [Everyone who applied were eligible ]

This test was conducted twice and in both times there was slight change in the format of the test and yeah
the change was not that good. The test that happened on 28th Sept there were technical issues faced by many
in our colleges so due to which a retest was conducted. The test duration was just 1 hour so managing time
was the key, since there were a lot of things to be covered in the given time but the test difficulty was from
easy to medium but it was lengthy.
The test format was:
1 Reading Comprehension: A reading comprehension passage was provided, similar to the ones we
encounter in board exams, followed by five MCQS. However, the passage was quite long and contained
--- PAGE 2 ---
some filler and fancy words. Make sure that even if you don't understand these words, you can at least
understand the overall context of the sentence.
My passage was about a research study involving time-zone-based clocks, and five MCQs were asked based
on it.
2 Email Writing: There were 2 email that we had to write, one was formal and the other was informal (it
wasn't mentioned but since you all have given boards you will understand automatically)
I had written email in the these format:
Subject:
Para 1 : Intro
Para2: Conveying what is asked
Para 3 : Conclusion
Regards/Thanking you
Name
This was the format I used. Make sure you manage your time wisely, as a word limit was specified for each
email, and your response had to stay within that limit. Also, make sure you write naturally and don't use any
external tools, as the test instructions included a disclaimer stating that submissions would be checked for
plagiarism.
3 Listening Comprehension: Around 2 or 3 questions were there where an audio would be played and based
on that audio you have to answer the mcq question, pretty straightforward and easy section
4 MCQ: Eight standard grammar-based MCQs were asked. Most required us to identify the grammatically
correct sentence or choose the correct tense or verb.
This section was easy, but make sure you understand that sounding correct and being grammatically correct
are two different things. Don't make the same mistake I did! I realised my error when I rechecked my
selected answer.
5 Essay Writing: This section was not present in the original test. However, during the retest, two MCQs
were removed and this section was added. We had to write two essays: one of around 100-200 words and
another of around 300-400 words.
Note: The disclaimer about plagiarism was also included here
You must attempt the test smartly because mcq's are quick to wrap up, so I finished mcq and then I
attempted email as both were of 10 marks each and afterwards I attempted essay because each essay was of
just 1 marks only lol.
--- PAGE 3 ---

2. [Aptitude Assessment] [ Everyone who filled the form]

This is not the regular aptitude which you give in the other company's OA, this was completely different
one, it had around 6 to 7 sections and each section had its own time limit. It was conducted on the AON
platform.
It was not tough but it was based on pure memory retention and it's last section was just normal hr
questions.
Few Questions that I can recollect are:

• One section showed multiple balls in different frames. In each frame, a particular ball would

light up, and at the end, we had to identify the order in which the balls had lit up.

• One entire section was like a game involving multiple blocks, a ball, and a hole. We had to

move the ball into the hole using the minimum number of moves by rearranging the blocks.

• There were some other memory-retention games and true-or-false questions, such as

identifying whether a pattern was symmetrical.
The last section was untimed and consisted of HR-related questions. Each question presented two opposing
options, and we had to choose which side we preferred. We could select either extreme or a slightly
moderate option on either side. However, we couldn't remain neutral by choosing the middle; we had to
answer every question.
Many students encountered errors during this test, and I was one of them. For some reason, the particular
error I faced did not seem to affect anyone else. I had already completed three sections, so I was afraid to
refresh the page. However, the error persisted for almost 1.5 hours, so I eventually logged out and logged
back in.
To my surprise, I was able to complete the remaining sections. There was a specific time window during
which we were allowed to log in. Surprisingly, I was able to log in even after closing the application
following the 1.5-hour error, while some other students were unable to do so. I would consider myself lucky
in this situation.
A retest was conducted for the specific group of students who had been unable to complete the test.

3. [Online Assessment] [ 77 were shortlist ]

Before this round, at 8 a.m., we attended a brief presentation about the company, followed by a briefing
about the test. The interview was scheduled to take place on the same day.
The online assessment was conducted on HackerEarth through Superset. It consisted of four rounds, each
with different time limits and problem-solving requirements.
At the beginning, we had to select a technology or language option, such as React, Node.js, Django, or
Spring Boot. This selection determined the framework used in the subsequent Al debugging and
function-development questions.
--- PAGE 4 ---

Round 1: Basic DSA - 30 minutes

I received a HashMap question that was simple but somewhat tedious. I had to use three HashMaps to solve
it. Initially, I was unable to pass all the test cases, but eventually, I managed to clear them all.
When you are unable to pass some test cases, you might become anxious. During such moments, it is
important to stay calm so that you can identify the bug and fix it.
The question involved domain names and request IDs. Another table contained queries being sent to those
domain names through router IDs. We had to count the number of requests received by each domain through
the respective router IDs. I cannot recall the exact question, but it involved counting requests, updating the
counts, and returning a list of lists.
Other candidates also received questions related to hashing, so no DP or graph questions were asked.

Round 2: Prompt Engineering - 15 minutes

We were given a problem statement and had to write a prompt that would be passed to an Al assistant. The
Al would then generate a solution, and we had to ensure that it passed the test cases. This section was
essentially designed to test whether we could write an effective prompt within a short time, especially since
the expected output had to follow a specific format. I was able to pass all the test cases.

Round 3: AI Debugging - 35 minutes

We were given a buggy application based on the framework we had selected at the beginning of the
assessment. An Al assistant was available to help us, but it did not directly provide the complete solution.
My suggestion would be to ask the Al assistant general questions about the codebase and the flow of
execution rather than immediately asking it to fix the bug.
I started by asking which files handled the relevant logic, including the controller, entity, and repository.
However, since it had been a long time since I had independently debugged a development project, I was
unable to pass even a single test case.
Eventually, even the Al assistant started providing generic explanations instead of answers specific to the
given codebase.

Round 4: AI Function Development - 30 minutes

The same repository that we had been given for debugging was used for the feature-development round. We
had to implement a new feature, and after several attempts, I managed to pass one test case.
An Al assistant was provided for this round as well, and it worked similarly to the one provided during the
debugging round.
--- PAGE 5 ---
4 [Interview] [ Only 6 were shortlist ]
There was only one interview round, which was entirely technical; there was no separate HR interview.
There were three panels, and each panel interviewed two candidates.
I was the last person to be interviewed by my panel. I was not particularly nervous because I had attended a
few interviews before and had also participated in mock interviews. When I realised that I was about to be
called in, I took a sip of water to clear my throat and took a deep breath. I knocked on the door and asked,
'May I come in, sir?
He welcomed me with a smile and asked me to take a seat. He asked for my resume and invited me to
introduce myself. He then examined my resume very closely. I had completed a two-month remote
internship, and he commented that two months was too short and that I should have worked for a longer
period. Before I could explain the circumstances, he started reviewing the projects listed on my resume. He
asked about their tech stacks and functionality while I explained them.
Meanwhile, I was wondering whether the comment about my internship had created a bad impression.
However, I focused on making the most of the remaining interview time. He then explained the interview
structure: I had to draw the architectures of all three projects on paper, explain them, and then discuss my
internship.
Make sure you know your projects inside out. If you cannot answer questions about your own projects, it
creates a very bad impression, so avoid making this mistake. Along with preparing your introduction, make
sure you understand how you would scale your projects.
I took my time explaining each component and covered everything I could about the projects, including the
motivation behind building them. Make sure you keep explaining things even when the interviewer asks you
to draw or write something. For example, while drawing the architecture, I explained what happened after
each request and how the different components interacted. After I had finished explaining my second project,
he stopped me and said that was enough for the day. He then told me that the interview was over.
At that point, I was confused about why he had stopped me even though he had said that I would be
explaining all my projects and discussing my internship. I wondered whether I had not performed well
enough. However, he then asked whether I had any questions for him.
I ended up asking him four questions about his role, his experience at Capgemini, and whether freshers were
given live projects. Before asking my final question, I said, "Sir, this is the last question I wanted to ask
you." He laughed and said that I could ask as many questions as I wanted.
I was still not entirely satisfied with my interview performance. However, before leaving the room, I
thanked him for giving me the opportunity. We shook hands, and he said, "If everything goes well, I'll see
you once your semester is done." This was like a huge relief for me.
The result was declared eight days after the interview, and I had finally secured a placement! A total of four
students received offers. Initially, five students had been selected, but one of them accepted an offer from
another company.
--- PAGE 6 ---
Useful Tip and My Placement Story:
FIRST THING LET ME TELL YOU VERY HONESTLY, THE PLACEMENT PROCESS IS NOT
VAGUE, BUT EXTREMELY VAGUE, AND LUCK PLAYS A MAJOR ROLE.
Sometimes, you won't even understand why things are happening the way they are. Then, suddenly, the next
day, you might find yourself placed.
Do not compare anyone's journey with yours because your path is completely different. Sometimes when
you look around you will see people getting placed and you are still fighting yourself everyday to secure a
placement but trust me that too shall pass dont worry. I had two or three friend groups, and in all of them, I
was the only one left to get placed. The rest of my friends had secured placements during the initial months
of the placement season.
Placements started in early June, with the first company visiting our campus. I wanted to get placed before
college reopened, but unfortunately, I couldn't. Once college started, I wanted to get placed before the
mid-semester exams, but that didn't happen either. Then, I hoped to get placed before Ganesh Chaturthi, but
I was still unsuccessful. Eventually, I stopped having expectations and started believing that whatever
happened would ultimately be good for me. Finally, I got placed during Navratri, which I consider very
auspicious.
I interviewed with Dolat Capital, where candidates with strong C++ skills were required. I had studied C++
for just one day before the interview, yet I cleared almost two interview rounds before being rejected in the
second technical round because I lacked experience with C++. My primary language is Java. After that, I
was rejected in the final round at Edra Labs. Then came Capgemini, where I finally secured a placement.
I started learning DSA after completing my second year. Although I started late, I was fairly confident in my
DSA skills because I remained consistent. Many people will suggest that you try competitive programming. I
tried it too, but I wasn't motivated enough to continue, so I stuck to LeetCode, which I honestly believe is
sufficient for placements.
Since I started DSA late, I missed opportunities in my second year when companies hired students for
internships that could lead to PPOs . Therefore, I would advise you to start DSA in your second year itself.
By then, you will already have a foundation in coding from your first year. However, even if you start late,
as I did, don't worry. Just stay consistent. Despite starting late, I was able to solve more questions than many
other candidates.
For the Dev part I would say that try taking parts in hackathon because the projects you build there are some
real life problems and companies love candidates who understand real world problems and are eager to solve
them and also in hackathon you build the project in one day which might take up a whole month if you build
by your own. And on top of that you even have the experience of working in the team so its win win.
Resources which I had used for preparing for the placements:
DSA- Strivers sheet (I think they had changed their website so have ig removed some questions and made
their overall website worst imo so use this if you dont like Hynts) (Not mine btw)
There is also this channel codeStoryWithMik this is also an excellent resource to solve daily questions or
some leetcode questions. Sometimes his explanation is even better than Striver, his graph and dp playlist is
also excellent. If you have time you can check it out but if you don't, striver is enough.
--- PAGE 7 ---
Dev- Lean the initial html and css from code with harry and then from JS I switched to Sheriyans Coding
school which had excellent stuff till full stack web development. For other tech stacks I have no idea but
since many banks visit our campus I had created normal CRUD in spring Boot by learning from CoderArmy
CS fundamentals: Since you had all these subjects in you previous sems you would be having the idea so
you can watch the one shots from youtube so that you can brush up the concepts or else you can revise from
gfg too and then just solve the mcq from again gfg.
OOPs: Kunal kushwaha is the best guy out there to learn oops, every thing is explained in very detailed way
Aptitude: Practise it from IndiaBix it is more than enough
SQL: Leetcode 50 is what you should do, I would say practise Leetcode 50 at least twice or thrice before the
placements so you would be good but since I got bored revisiting the same questions so I solve questions
from here dataL emur I was able to revise every concept which is sufficient for the interviews
System Design: Earlier it was just phonePe that used to ask about it but recently I have noticed that many
companies have been asking about it. So it's better to be prepared for it. Dont worry its not at all difficult just
understand which components and used and what are their tradeoff and then understand how you will use
these components to scale your own projects, because mostly they will ask you scale your own project or
sometime they would ask you to pick any app and then design it scalable architecture so be sure to be ready
with an app(pick youtube as its easy to understand watch neetcode's video about it) and your projects
architecture.
The GOAT debate of Language: You can do DSA with any language which you like but personally I opted
for Java because many companies visiting our campus prefer Java so it's better if your first Language is Java
itself.
Final Tips:
Before going to the interview do a bit of research about the company as during the ppt they may open the
floor for Q and A, or they might even ask facts about the company so it's better to create the early
impression because these are the same people who you will meet for the interview.
I was unable to clear the OAs of several companies, which was very disheartening. Trust me, I know how it
feels. However, don't let small rejections undermine your confidence in your skills. Even if you feel
vulnerable, take a break of two or three hours if needed, and then get back in the game.
Mock interviews will help you a lot, so try to participate in as many as possible. During the placement
process, you may be assigned mentors who are already working in the industry. They are there to guide you,
and if you ask them, they may even conduct mock interviews for you. I participated in almost three mock
interviews.
Before any company visits make sure you have understanding about the company's process and also solve
the previous year company wise DSA with this site: PYQ
I would like to conclude by saying that I was in Category A in the placement readiness test, yet it took me
almost four months to get placed. Meanwhile, many students from Categories B and C secured placements
earlier than I did.
--- PAGE 8 ---
So, don't worry; it's all part of the process. The more patient and persistent you are, the easier it becomes to
navigate the placement process. Rejection is also a part of the journey. Accept it, but don't let it discourage
you. Take some time to reflect on what went wrong and make sure you don't repeat the same mistakes. At
some point, revising and reading the same material can become monotonous and boring. However, you have
to keep going, so stay consistent and keep pushing yourself.
Lastly, I would say that you should surround yourself with good friends. When I got placed, I could see the
relief and joy in their eyes too. They have been incredibly supportive and helpful throughout the process. If
you are going through a difficult phase, be open with your parents. They have experienced difficult times
themselves and can give you advice that no one else probably can.
Trust your preparation, have faith in God, and believe that you will eventually get what you deserve.
I WISH YOU ALL THE VERY BEST, AND REMEMBER, THE SKY IS NOT THE LIMIT !!!!!
(Yes, I'm writing "the sky is not the limit" again so that you don't think it's a typing error. ©)

journey.prep:
I want to preface this section by saying, please do take care of your mental health. Placements are a hectic
time to be a college student. I was fortunate enough to have had options regardless of my placement status
but even if you don't, take a step back and remember you are only around 20-21. We still have a lot of time
ahead of us. I myself got very close to securing a position in companies like Nomura (Twice), JPMC, ISS
Stoxx and more. I almost always ended up reaching the last round and losing out at the very end. Regardless,
it is important to remember to not give up hope and keep pushing through despite the results. Sometimes it is
not you, it's just your luck that needs a turnaround. So, keep your chin up and keep going no matter what life
throws at you. I know it may seem a little disingenuous coming from someone like me who got placed but
trust me and give yourself a chance, it will be worth it.
On a more technical note, here are some of the resources that I used and found to be helpful:

1. MIT YouTube Channel ( CS Fundamentals, Al, Mathematics and so much more )

2. Stanford YouTube Channel ( CS Fundamentals, Al, Mathematics and so much more )

3. Jim Kurose YouTube Channel ( Computer Networking )

4. 3Blue1Brown YouTube Channel (Al and Mathematics)

5. NeetCode 150 / SQL 50 (DSA and SQL)

6. IIT Madras BS Degree for Data Science and Applications ( Though the degree is paid, most of the

resources are available for free online)

7. StatQuest YouTube Channel (Al and Data Science)

8. GeekForGeeks, TutorialsPoint, etc. ( CS Fundamentals )

No word here was written with the help of Al, for better or for worse. As such, I get the rare privilege to
personally thank you for reading all the way to the end and wholeheartedly wish you a sincere best of luck
for all your future endeavours.
journey.howSecured:
1. Screening Round on HackerEarth (14/08/2026)

2. Machine Coding Round (18/08/2026)

3. Technical Round 1(18/08/2026)

4. Technical Round 2 (18/08/2026)

5. Interview with the Head of Engineering (19/08/2026)

1. Screening Round on HackerEarth [ Around 40 student were shortlisted for this round]

It has been more than a month since this process was conducted so apologies in advance for any hazy details
but I'll try my best to keep it as accurate as possible. The CGPA criteria was 8.5+ while applying which was
the first major hurdle to cross ( My CGPA at the time of application was 9.28). I would assume they also
shortlisted candidates on the basis of one's resume's ATS score so make sure your resume is polished as
well. I recommend Resume Worded for calculating your resume's ATS score. From what I have seen,
anything above 60 is good but I'd recommend getting it above 70 ( The one I submitted scored 78).
As for the screening round, there were 3 coding questions:

1) A sort of non-DSA question about reverse proxies in which you are given a list of requests and are

asked to route the requests to their respective services and finally output which machine handled
which request.

2) A simple DSA question on Dynamic Programming

3) A simple DSA question using Two Pointers

Note: I don't consider myself to be that good at DSA, so when I say they were simple questions, I actually
do mean they were pretty doable. The first question was very non-typical and no one I know was able to
fully solve it (including me), so just try to pass as many test cases as possible.
--- PAGE 2 ---

2. Machine Coding Round | 11 candidates appeared for this round] (2 Hours )

In this round, we were asked to code a server using the framework of our choice over the duration of 2
hours. I chose Flask for its simplicity and the ease of multithreading. We were invited to a Zoom meeting for
which we were supposed to be ready for at 9am ( The actual timings were from 10:30am to 1:30am). The
entire process was conducted from home. The meeting actually began a little after 10:30 during which we
were briefed about the process and eventually were assigned our individual Zoom breakout rooms. We were
alone in our respective Zoom breakout room along with one mentor/evaluator from Edra Labs (Don't worry,
they are nice and helpful people) who provided us with the problem statement when the clock started
running. A single mentor was responsible for multiple rooms as such he was not in the room throughout the
entire coding round but you could call upon him for queries/help by using the 'Raise Hand' feature in Zoom.
Once you were done with your code, we had to roughly explain it to our assigned mentor/evaluator and
submit it as a zip on a GForm provided at the end. After this, we were allowed to leave the meeting and were
told to wait for any calls from Edra Labs.

3. Technical Round 1 (Note: From here onwards, the people from Edra Labs directly called the

participants eligible for the next round. As such, the exact number of participants for each round is
not known. It is extremely important to pay attention to your phone as they may call you at any
time after your rounds. If you are like me and keep your device on silent or DnD indefinitely,
you should toggle both off for the duration of this process.) (30 Minutes )
I got a call at around 1:37pm informing me that I have been shortlisted for this round (Note that I was done
pretty early with my machine coding round at around 12:30pm ). Another zoom meeting was scheduled for
me for this round (3:00pm - 3:30pm ) during the call itself post my approval. My interview started with the
interviewer giving his introduction and what he does over at Edra Labs. Then he asked me to introduce
myself and go through my resume. I talked about myself and the various projects I have done. We went on
to talk about the various functional and non-functional requirements of several of my projects along the lines
of - What does this do?, Why did you make it?, How many requests could it handle at once?, How would
you go on to scale it?, Why did you choose the tech stack that you did? - and so on. Several of my projects
were Al-related and happened to contain topics the interviewer was familiar with. As such, we went on a
very conversational tangent about various topics until time ran out. It was pretty enjoyable and the
interviewer felt very easy to talk to. The interview ended with him asking if I had any questions for him, to
which I only asked about the projects they work on at Edra Labs. I suppose the key takeaway here would be
to not lie on your resume. Actually do and be familiar with the projects you are mentioning on your resume
and talk about them passionately.

4. Technical Round 2(30 Minutes )

I got a call about being shortlisted for this round at around 4:17pm. I do not exactly remember when my
interview was but it was around 5pm. This interview was a bit more technical asking questions about
Computer Networks, OS, etc. (What happens when you search something?, How does a page load?, etc.).
After that, it went more of the same as the first round as we once again ended up conversing and talking
about my projects, open-source contributions, Linux and AI. Once again, it was very fun talking to the
--- PAGE 3 ---
interviewer and I felt comfortable talking with him throughout the interview. At the end, he mentioned it
was fun talking with me and used the last 5 or so minutes to ask the final question he was meant to ask
before we ended up on a tangent. It was less of a DSA question and more of a logical puzzle - Assuming a
language that can only store 2 digit integers, how would you perform addition? I was able to mostly answer
it but missed a trick about just performing 99 - x to check for overflows instead of raising an exception or a
flag and checking that. He nevertheless seemed satisfied with my solution as well and was rather excited to
talk about the solution on a whiteboard. Once again, I was asked if I had any questions, to which I asked
about the technologies used over at Edra Labs.

5. Interview with the Head of Engineering [ 4 candidates appeared for this round] (Note: This was

the final round for us. There was no HR round.) (30 Minutes )
I was informed about being shortlisted for this round on the same day but the final round was scheduled for
the next day ( 19th August 2026) at 2:00pm - 2:30pm. The issue was that I was also shortlisted for
BlackRock's process which was also happening on the same day. As luck would have it, I ended up getting
shortlisted for the final round of BlackRock as well and it got scheduled at around the same time as my Edra
Labs. Huge props to the folks over at the CCD, they managed to postpone my BlackRock interview to be at
around 4pm rather than 2pm. Allowing me to give both the interviews without sacrificing my prospects to be
in one of the companies. They were also kind enough to provide me with a cabin to give my Edra Labs
Interview in as the BlackRock process was offline. The final interview took place on schedule at 2pm. This
one was the scariest of them all as the interviewer was a senior and pretty stern. He asked me to explain the
code I wrote for the machine coding round line by line and asked detailed questions about why I did what I
did. He asked me to send parallel requests to one of my endpoints and log the times in the console. I had
forgotten how to send parallel curl requests (It's the -Z option) and asked him whether I could look up the
syntax which he allowed. I was trying to avoid the Al overview which he noticed and said I could refer to it
if I wanted. I finally managed to send the requests as he wanted (He took the opportunity to ask me a little
about bash, like why couldn't I just use && to send the parallel requests among a few other questions.
Luckily I was familiar with bash scripting and was able to answer them.). However, the logs printed suggest
the requests were off by 0.000x or so seconds. I was genuinely flummoxed. I hadn't even noticed the
difference at first and claimed that they were parallel for which he corrected me. I accepted that I hadn't
noticed it and apologized after which he went on to ask me why my code wasn't logging the same time for
each request despite being multithreaded. I genuinely had no clue and told him as such, but I also told them I
had theories as to why it may be so and presented them to him with the disclaimer that they might be
incorrect. The answer to me seemed to be natural variation and how you can't really time requests to be truly
parallel but that didn't seem like a satisfying answer, hence I also presented a few other theories. He had a
poker face throughout the interview and I honestly thought I had flunked it by this point. He ended the
interview, asking me to look into why that happened and asked if I had any questions for him. I just asked
about his role at Edra Labs. By the end of it, I had given up hopes but I also had the final BlackRock
interview to give which went extremely well.
I got a call from the CCD at 8:44pm, notifying me that I was the only candidate selected for the role. I
genuinely couldn't believe it. I completely thought I had messed up too much in the final round but ended up
landing the offer. I suppose, you should never lose out on hope. It isn't over until it is over.
--- PAGE 4 ---

Prep-placement talk GD and Interview all took place on 30/09/2026

1. Resume Shortlisting [~200 students had applied]

Since the role at Colgate-Palmolive was IT-focused, I tailored my resume to highlight projects and skills
relevant to the job description. I included my Al based and full stack apps to demonstrate my experience
with software development, databases, backend systems, APIs, and Al integration. I also highlighted my
technical skills in Python, SQL, and web technologies, along with my ability to learn new tools and solve
real-world problems.
I recommend keeping your resume to one page, ensuring it is ATS-friendly, and tailoring it to the company's
JD rather than using a generic resume. You can use tools like ResumeWorded to assess your resume and
identify areas for improvement. Mind it that this is for cross-checking your resume, don't waste time
tailoring it to perfection.
Academic performance, including 12th-grade marks and CGPA, can also influence shortlisting, depending
on the company's eligibility criteria. Meeting the required cutoffs can be an advantage, but selection also
depends on your projects, technical skills, resume relevance, and the overall applicant pool. Sometimes,
shortlisting can be unpredictable, so keep improving your resume and applying consistently.
--- PAGE 2 ---

2. Online Assessment [ 30 students ]

The OA was from home at 4-5 pm, MCQ format and of 30 questions.
The OA covered DSA (binary trees, sorting algorithms, and Minimum Spanning Tree using Prim's
algorithm), Operating Systems (disk scheduling, CPU scheduling using SJF, and inode structures), and
DBMS (functional dependencies, Armstrong's axioms, and normalization forms such as 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, and
BCNF). It also included Computer Networks, focusing on the OSI model and the Presentation Layer, along
with C++ programming concepts such as destructors, global and local variables, object creation, and output
tracing.

3. Group Discussion [ 30 students ]

3 groups of 10 people
My topic was 'Are exams right way to assess someone's intelligence'
The discussion lasted about 20 min where last 3 min where given to conclude your points
Always try to initiate the discussion or be in the first 3 people to start the discussion to catch the
panelists attention.
2 mins time is given beforehand to jot down the points before the discussion.
Write brief bullet points and pros and cons and do not pick a side as it is a discussion and not a
debate.

4. Technical + Hr Interview [15 students ]

I was the first one to give the interview so I had no idea what type of questions were asked by the panelists.
There were two panelists
The interview started with a brief introduction and a walkthrough of my resume. Towards the end of my
introduction i stated that would you like me to elaborate on one of my projects technicalities, setting the tone
of the interview in my favour.
They asked surface level questions on each of my projects and then deep-dived into one of my projects.
I was asked if the database was static or dynamic if static what changes would you make, if i want to migrate
the data, how would I do it safely without causing a downtime issue.
I was asked how would you design a website where many students are filling a form and high traffic
shouldn't affect the web app.
Then i was asked if i click on a login button what happens in the backend behind the scenes in depth.
After a while I was comfortable with the panelists and was confident with my answers. Then they asked
behavioral questions like if a team mate is calling sick with a deadline for your project how would you
handle the situation.
And if a project cannot be completed before the deadline what measures would you take.
They also asked me about why you chose this branch and why not CSE/CE.
--- PAGE 3 ---
The key to a good interview is to remain composed before you answer. I know it's better said than done, but
as I had given 2 interviews and a group discussion before this company I was aware of the body language,
tone and familiarity with the interview room. Never use negative words like not, no, I am not aware etc.
Always use positive alternatives like I am yet to explore this area, I am yet to have hands-on experience in
this technicality etc.
Do not get excited if you know the answer to a question, take a pause, assess your thoughts and start from
the basics and stretch it with all the technicalities you are aware of and relate it with your resume. As you
can see I have implemented this in my XYZ project. It makes an impression that you have practical
experience of the question asked
In the end I asked them a questions:
In the pre placement talk it was mentioned that there is In job posting and interns get to experience a
variety of roles.
What would you expect a 6 month intern to be like? As in do you expect him to master a specific
stack or get as much experience and explore a variety of stacks.
We were under the impression that an HR round was going to take place but the results were announced at
3:00 pm 8 out of 15 people were offered the internship.
