journey.prep:
The biggest thing that helped me through the process was being able to reason through problems even
when I didn't immediately see the full solution. The interviewers weren't just checking if the final answer
was perfect -- they were watching how I approached the problem, whether I could explain my thought
process, and whether I could break things down logically.

1. DSA

Focus on common patterns rather than memorizing individual questions. In particular, revise:

• Arrays and strings

• Hashing

• Binary search

• Trees

• Sorting

• Dynamic programming

• Two pointers

• Intervals

• Basic greedy problems

It also helps to practice writing code without an IDE occasionally -- several of my interview questions
had to be written on paper.

2. SQL and DBMS

Revise:

• Joins

• GROUP BY and aggregate functions

• Subqueries

• CASE statements

• Primary and foreign keys

• Normalization

• ER diagrams

• One-to-many and many-to-many relationships

• Converting ER diagrams into relational tables

The SQL questions weren't necessarily very hard, but knowing the fundamentals cold matters a lot.

3. Resume

Know everything on your resume -- don't list a technology or project you can't explain. For each project,
prepare a short walkthrough covering: Problem → Your solution → Technologies → Your contribution →
Challenges → Result. Be ready for follow-ups too -- if you mention something like Flask, MySQL, JWT, or
Redis, expect to be asked why you used it and how it works.

4. Practice explaining your thought process

Don't work on a problem silently for too long -- explain what you're thinking as you go. For example: "I
think I can use binary search here because the condition changes from good to defective only once."
This shows the interviewer you understand the underlying logic, even before you've finished writing the
code.

5. Don't panic if you make a mistake

I wasn't able to write one SQL query fully correctly in the technical interview, but I still explained my
reasoning and moved forward. If you get stuck, don't give up -- explain what you know, clarify your
assumptions, and work toward the answer.
Things I could have done better

• Prepared more thoroughly for harder DP problems -- I only passed about half the test cases on

the DP question in the online test.

• Understood many-to-many relationships better, including how to model and query them in a

relational database.

• Reasoned through the cycle-time aspect of the traffic-signal problem faster in the final round.

For future candidates, I'd suggest not preparing only the easiest DSA questions -- the assessment and
interviews can combine multiple concepts at once.
Final Advice
The overall process was fairly problem-solving oriented. I'd recommend preparing DSA and SQL
seriously, but don't neglect your resume, projects, and communication. Most importantly, don't try to
bluff when you don't know something -- explain your approach honestly and show you're willing to
reason through the problem. Demonstrating logical thinking mattered even when my final answer
wasn't perfect. On interview day: stay calm, listen to the full question before starting, clarify
requirements if needed, and explain your approach as you solve.
Good luck to everyone appearing for Wissen! All the best.
journey.howSecured:
The Wissen placement process consisted of an online coding assessment followed by two interview
rounds. Around 270 students appeared for the initial assessment, roughly 40 were shortlisted for the
technical interview, and the final selection came after the subsequent interview rounds. In total, 9
students were offered the role -- 7 with Internship + Full-Time Employment, and 2 with Internship only.

1. Online Coding Assessment (HackerEarth) [~270 candidates]

The first round was an online coding assessment on HackerEarth, lasting about 2 hours, with two DSA
questions and one SQL question worth a total of around 195 marks. I scored 105 marks, and about 40
students were shortlisted for the next round -- based on the scores I saw, the effective cutoff seemed
to be around 100 marks, though it wasn't officially announced.
DSA - Tree Question
This problem asked for the longest "harmonious" path in a tree, where every node's value had to satisfy
a condition relative to the average value of its ancestors and a given K. I solved it using an iterative DFS
with a stack holding the current node, the sum of its ancestors, the ancestor count, and the current path
length. At each node, I computed the ancestor average, checked the condition, and continued into its
children -- updating the maximum path length whenever I hit a leaf. I solved this one completely.
DSA - Dynamic Programming Question
This was the tougher of the two -- selecting sites/towers based on position and profit while respecting a
minimum distance constraint, with a bonus for sites picked at a particular distance. I sorted the sites by
position and built a DP array tracking the best achievable profit up to each site, using binary search to
find the last valid site that wouldn't violate the distance constraint. I got roughly half the test cases to
pass -- this was the hardest question for me in the assessment.
SQL Question
This involved calculating the completion rate of different training courses -- joining the training course
and training result tables, grouping by course, counting total participants, counting how many scored
above 50, and computing the percentage. Results had to be sorted by completion rate descending, then
course name ascending. I solved this one fully.
Preparation Tips for This Round
Practice DSA under time pressure, especially trees, DP, binary search, and greedy/optimization
problems. Don't skip SQL -- the question wasn't especially hard, but it needed a solid grip on joins,
aggregation, conditional counting, and sorting. Also, solving two questions completely was enough to
clear this round, so it's often better to nail the easier questions than burn the whole test on one hard
problem.

2. Technical Interview [~40 candidates]

The second round was an offline technical interview, about an hour long with one interviewer, focused
on problem-solving, DSA, and SQL/database concepts. Some answers had to be written out on paper.
DSA / Problem-Solving Questions
One question involved processing email addresses -- separating name and domain, organizing the data
using a hash set, and splitting a domain's list once it crossed a certain size. I had to write this out on
paper, so explaining my logic clearly while writing mattered a lot.
Another question was based on binary search, built around a machine producing good and defective
products. In one version the sequence looked like GGGGGGDDDDDDD, and I had to efficiently find the
index of the first defective product. In a trickier version, like GGGGGDDDDDDDGGG, I had to find both
the first and last defective product. The point of the question was really about recognizing when binary
search applies instead of defaulting to a linear scan.
SQL / Database Question
I was asked to design an ER diagram for a database and convert it into a relational design, with a focus
on handling a many-to-many relationship -- I explained how this needs an intermediate/junction table
holding keys from both related entities. I was then asked to write a SQL query based on the design, and
while I didn't get it fully correct, I was able to explain my reasoning clearly. The interviewer seemed
more interested in my approach and logical thinking than a perfect answer, and I moved on to the next
round.
Preparation Tips for This Round
Focus on being comfortable with fundamentals rather than memorizing solutions, since DSA questions
often show up wrapped in real-world scenarios. Revise OOP concepts; DBMS and SQL, especially ER
diagrams, relational mapping, and many-to-many relationships; common DSA patterns like binary search
and hashing; and your resume and projects. Above all, think out loud -- even an imperfect final answer
shows the interviewer how you reason through a problem.

3. Director Round - Final Interview

The third round was an online Director Round, about an hour long with one interviewer. It opened with
some basic questions about me and my resume/projects -- the questions I personally got were fairly
basic, but candidates should be ready to go deeper, since the level of questioning can vary a lot from
person to person.
Problem-Solving Question - Traffic Signal
This one involved an intersection with a traffic signal, where I had to distribute available green-light time
across roads given constraints like minimum and maximum green-light time, total cycle time, and the
gap before a signal turns green again after turning red. It was more about problem-solving and logical
thinking than something memorizable -- I worked through it, though I got a bit stuck reasoning about
the cycle-time aspect.
Coding Question - Minimum Meeting Rooms
Given the start and end times of several meetings, I had to find the minimum number of rooms needed
so no two overlapping meetings shared a room -- written out on paper. The key idea was to find the
maximum number of meetings happening simultaneously, which gives the minimum rooms required.
Resume and Project Discussion
The interviewer asked about me and discussed my projects, though the questions I received stayed
mostly at a basic level. Even so, I'd strongly recommend knowing your projects thoroughly -- why you
picked them, your role, the tech used, database design, key features, challenges and how you solved
them, why you chose a particular technology, and how the project could be improved. A conversation
that starts basic can get deeper fast depending on your answers.
My Performance
I was able to answer everything asked of me, though I spent a bit of extra time on the cycle-time part of
the traffic-signal problem. When I asked for feedback afterward, it was mostly positive.

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
The biggest thing that helped me through the process was being able to reason through problems even
when I didn't immediately see the full solution. The interviewers weren't just checking if the final answer
was perfect -- they were watching how I approached the problem, whether I could explain my thought
process, and whether I could break things down logically.

1. DSA

Focus on common patterns rather than memorizing individual questions. In particular, revise:

• Arrays and strings

• Hashing

• Binary search

• Trees

• Sorting

• Dynamic programming

• Two pointers

• Intervals

• Basic greedy problems

It also helps to practice writing code without an IDE occasionally -- several of my interview questions
had to be written on paper.

2. SQL and DBMS

Revise:

• Joins

• GROUP BY and aggregate functions

• Subqueries

• CASE statements

• Primary and foreign keys

• Normalization

• ER diagrams

• One-to-many and many-to-many relationships

• Converting ER diagrams into relational tables

The SQL questions weren't necessarily very hard, but knowing the fundamentals cold matters a lot.

3. Resume

Know everything on your resume -- don't list a technology or project you can't explain. For each project,
prepare a short walkthrough covering: Problem → Your solution → Technologies → Your contribution →
Challenges → Result. Be ready for follow-ups too -- if you mention something like Flask, MySQL, JWT, or
Redis, expect to be asked why you used it and how it works.

4. Practice explaining your thought process

Don't work on a problem silently for too long -- explain what you're thinking as you go. For example: "I
think I can use binary search here because the condition changes from good to defective only once."
This shows the interviewer you understand the underlying logic, even before you've finished writing the
code.

5. Don't panic if you make a mistake

I wasn't able to write one SQL query fully correctly in the technical interview, but I still explained my
reasoning and moved forward. If you get stuck, don't give up -- explain what you know, clarify your
assumptions, and work toward the answer.
Things I could have done better

• Prepared more thoroughly for harder DP problems -- I only passed about half the test cases on

the DP question in the online test.

• Understood many-to-many relationships better, including how to model and query them in a

relational database.

• Reasoned through the cycle-time aspect of the traffic-signal problem faster in the final round.

For future candidates, I'd suggest not preparing only the easiest DSA questions -- the assessment and
interviews can combine multiple concepts at once.
Final Advice
The overall process was fairly problem-solving oriented. I'd recommend preparing DSA and SQL
seriously, but don't neglect your resume, projects, and communication. Most importantly, don't try to
bluff when you don't know something -- explain your approach honestly and show you're willing to
reason through the problem. Demonstrating logical thinking mattered even when my final answer
wasn't perfect. On interview day: stay calm, listen to the full question before starting, clarify
requirements if needed, and explain your approach as you solve.
Good luck to everyone appearing for Wissen! All the best.

The Wissen Technologies placement process consisted of an Online Assessment (OA) followed by two
rounds of interviews. The OA was conducted on 31 July 2026, both interview rounds were conducted on 1st
Aug 2026, and the final result was announced on 3 August 2026.
The overall process was:

1. Online Assessment (OA) - 31/07/2026

2. Technical Interview - 1/08/2026

3. Director Round - 1/08/2026

1. Online Assessment (OA) | No of candidates who appeared for this round]

The Online Assessment was conducted on 31 July 2026. All eligible candidates were allowed to sit for
the OA. The assessment consisted of:

• 2 DSA coding questions

• 1 SQL question

• 5 MCQs

DSA Questions
The first DSA question was based on Dynamic Programming (DP). The second DSA question was based on
a Binary Tree. Both questions required understanding the underlying concept rather than simply
implementing a standard algorithm. Therefore, it is important to be comfortable with the fundamentals of
DSA and be able to identify which data structure or algorithm is appropriate for a given problem.
SQL Question
There was one SQL question based on:
--- PAGE 2 ---

• CTE (Common Table Expressions)

• GROUP BY

The question required understanding how to structure a query using a CTE and then perform aggregation
using GROUP BY.
There were 5 MCQS. The questions included:

• Finding the output of a given piece of code

• Aptitude-based questions

• Programming/technical concepts

Preparation Suggestions
For coding preparation, practicing medium-level problems on LeetCode, or similar platforms is useful.
Along with solving problems, focus on understanding the approach and complexity rather than memorizing
solutions.
For SQL, practice do solve sql 50

2. Technical Interview (40 candidates appeared)

The first interview round was a Technical Interview and was conducted on 1 Aug 2026. The interviewer
focused primarily on Data Structures, Database Design, SQL and choosing appropriate data structures for a
given problem. The interview consisted of three major sections.
Question 1 - DSA Array List / Bucket Formation
The interviewer first gave a problem involving a list of numbers:
[1000, 2000, 500, 2500, 3000]
The requirement was to create buckets such that the sum of the elements in each bucket is not more than
5000.
The resulting buckets were:
[[1000, 2000, 500], [2500], [3000]]
The interviewer then asked a follow-up question. If a bucket contains 3 or more elements and all the
elements are divisible by both 5 and 10, then that bucket should be split into individual elements.
For example:
[1000, 2000, 500]
contains three elements and all of them are divisible by 5 and 10, so it should be split into:
[11000], [2000], [500], [2500], [30001]
Question 2 - Database Schema Design
The interviewer then gave a database-design scenario involving:

• Actors

• Films

• Multiple sequels for each film

• Actors appearing in multiple films

--- PAGE 3 ---

• IMDb ratings for films/sequels

The task was to design an appropriate relational database schema.
I designed separate tables for:

• Actor

• Film

• Cast/Actor-Film Mapping

• Sequel

The mapping table handled the many-to-many relationship between actors and films, while the
sequel-related table maintained the relationship between a film and its sequels. The interviewer then asked
me to write SQL queries based on the schema I had designed. He also asked several follow-up questions
about my database design, including why I had created the tables in that particular way and how the
relationships between the entities were being maintained.
Question 3 - Choosing the Appropriate Data Structure
The interviewer then gave a scenario involving logs with timestamps. The question was essentially about
how to efficiently access logs corresponding to a particular timestamp. The appropriate data structure
discussed was a B-Tree, because it provides efficient searching and indexing, with operations typically
taking O(log n) time. The discussion also involved the idea of organizing/indexing the log data so that a
specific timestamp could be accessed efficiently rather than scanning all the logs.
Preparation Suggestions
For this round, I would strongly recommend revising:

• Arrays and ArrayLists

• HashMap and HashSet

• Trees

• B-Trees / database indexing

• Time and space complexity

• SQL

• DBMS

3. Director Round (16 candidates appeared for this round)

The second and final interview was a Director Round. This round lasted significantly longer and was more
like a technical discussion combined with resume discussion rather than a traditional question-and-answer
interview. The interviewer first asked me to walk through my resume. He asked about my work experience at
Adhyayan Classes, where I had taught students and also worked on developing a portfolio website for the
classes. I explained that I had developed and hosted the website and mentioned the technology/deployment
setup, including Vercel, Render, GoDaddy domain. The interviewer was particularly interested in the fact that
I had worked with the GoDaddy domain and deployment process, which led to further discussion about the
project. The interviewer then moved to my project section and asked about my project PeerMint. One of the
major discussions was around JWT authentication.
He asked about:

• What JWT is

--- PAGE 4 ---

• How JWT works

• Different ways of storing JWTs

• Advantages and disadvantages of different storage methods

• Security concerns

• CSRF

• XSS

• How different attacks can affect authentication systems

The questions were not limited to definitions. The interviewer focused on understanding whether I knew
why a particular approach should be used and what its security implications were. The interviewer then
asked about REST APIs and whether I knew about any alternatives. I discussed REST and also mentioned
GraphQL. The interviewer also asked me to explain DNS resolution. This required explaining what happens
when a user enters a domain name and how the domain gets resolved to the corresponding IP address. The
interviewer then moved to my third project and asked me to explain RAG (Retrieval-Augmented
Generation). I explained the complete pipeline starting from the basics, including What RAG is, Document
processing, Chunking, Embeddings, Vector representations, Vector search, Retrieval, Passing retrieved
context to the LLM, Generation of the final response, pgvector and its role in storing/searching vector
embeddings. The interviewer asked questions throughout the explanation, so it was important to understand
every component rather than simply knowing the definition of RAG.
The interviewer then asked me about my favorite programming language. I answered Java. He then asked
me to design and write a Cab Booking System in Java on paper. I was expected to write the solution with
proper Classes, Objects, Data structures, Methods, Java syntax, Appropriate data structures.
The interviewer continuously monitored my approach and asked follow-up questions while I was writing the
solution. For example, when I initially considered a particular approach, he asked whether a HashMap could
be used to achieve faster access. This tested whether I could evaluate and improve my design while solving
the problem. The interviewer then asked me to write a function that would return the cars near a user's
current location in sorted order, along with the time required for each car to reach the user.
I represented the input conceptually as:
getCars(Car[ll] cars, int[]I] grid)
The Car[][] matrix represented the locations of cars.

• If a car was present at a particular cell, the cell contained a Car object.

• If no car was present, the cell contained null.

The int[]I] grid contained the time required to reach each corresponding cell.
For example, if:
grid[1][]] = 12
then reaching cell (1,1) would require 12 minutes.
The task was to determine the cars relevant to the user's current location (x,y) and return them along with the
corresponding time required to reach the user.
I used a structure conceptually represented as:
HashMap<Car, Integer>
where the Car represented the vehicle and the integer represented the estimated time required to reach the
user's location. The interviewer also asked follow-up questions about the approach and the data structures
--- PAGE 5 ---
being used. I wrote the solution on approximately three pages of paper, including the class structure,
methods, data structures and algorithm. The interviewer continuously interrupted with questions and
suggestions, so the round tested not only coding ability but also the ability to think, adapt and improve a
solution while being questioned. This round was considerably different from the first technical interview. It
was more of a discussion and problem-solving round.
Final Result:
The final result was announced on Monday, 3 August 2026. I was selected for the SDE Internship +
Placement opportunity at Wissen Technologies. Finally 9 candidates were offered the job

The Wissen placement process consisted of an online coding assessment followed by two
rounds of interviews. Approximately 270 students appeared for the initial assessment, out of
which around 40 were shortlisted for the technical interview. Following the subsequent interview
rounds, 9 students were ultimately selected - 7 received Internship + Full-Time Employment
offers, while 2 received Internship-only offers.
Online Assessment: (~270 candidates) There were 8 questions in total → 5 MCQS covering
general aptitude, OS, and OOPs concepts, 2 DSA questions, and 1 SQL question.

• A) Ancestory: Find the max length path from root to leaf such that for every node in the

path, abs(avg of values of ancestors of node - value of curr node) ≤ k. Input given as n,
value, leftchild], rightchild[], k.

• B) Sandbar: Given a position array xI and prize array PI], once you take the prize at a

position you can't take another within distance d -i ≤ d based on positions, not indices).
If you take a pair exactly at j-i = d+1 after claiming i, you get a bonus b. Find the max
prize obtainable.
I managed to solve correctly all 5 MCQs and one of the DSA questions (Ancestory).
Interview Round 1 (40 candidates) (1 hr 30 min):
This round was honestly quite manageable by anyone with a bit of DSA experience could clear
it without much trouble. We started with a walk-through of my resume along with a few standard
questions, which took about 10 minutes. From there, the interviewer moved into DSA and asked
which language I was most comfortable with - I said C++. The format was old-school: explain
my approach first, then code it out on paper with strict syntax, taking care of input and output.
The first problem involved an array of G's and B's (like G,G,G,B,B,B,B) where I had to find the
first and last B, both when the array was sorted and when it wasn't. Next was a sorted array of
random numbers where I had to print all numbers between 120 and 150 using binary search.
After that came a question involving a vector of social media posts, where I had to count the
number of hashtags in each post and return the posts) with the highest count (accounting for
--- PAGE 2 ---
ties), and then figure out which hashtag was used most across all the posts - an
unordered_map handled this nicely.
The one genuinely tricky question in this round was a system design-style problem: designing
the "top k searches" feature you often see on e-commerce sites, like when you tap the search
bar and see your 3 most recent searches. The expected answer was a doubly linked list
combined with a hashmap, and I was able to explain and code this correctly.
Following that, the interviewer shifted to SQL and asked me to draw an ER diagram for a
scenario: an actor works in many movies/shows, a movie/show can have multiple actors, and a
film can have several sequels - with each sequel having a different IMDB number despite
belonging to the same film. I had to mark primary and foreign keys and define the relationships.
My diagram held up well, and as a follow-up, the interviewer asked me to write a SQL query to
find movies with only one actor, my soln was a simple GROUP BY on actor-film entity with a
COUNT = 1 condition.
Toward the end, I got the chance to ask my own questions, so I asked about the internship's
training process and the overall work culture, and they were happy to answer in detail.
Interview Round 2 (45 min):
This round was conducted by the company's Executive Director, whereas the previous round
had been taken by a junior developer.
This round had just one DSA question, a traffic light scheduling problem. The premise: a
traffic signal only exists if it connects two or more roads. You're given an array representing
average vehicle traffic at each road (e.g., [100, 20, 110, 0]) along with a total cycle time t (say,
120 seconds). Within this cycle, each signal must turn green exactly once, in the order of the
roads, with each green phase lasting a minimum of 10 seconds and a maximum of 60 seconds.
The goal is to distribute the signal timings to minimize overall vehicle wait time, and the cycle
then repeats. The output should be an array representing the schedule. This is essentially the
same as a LeetCode discussion question on traffic signal management. I got this one right, it
mostly came down to applying ratio and proportion logic while handling edge cases around the
10s/60s bounds.
Next came an OOP design question that had me confused. I was asked to design the class
structure for how an air conditioner works, covering components like the temperature sensor,
condenser, and fan, and how these objects would interact with each other. If you're preparing for
this company, it's worth practicing this style of "given an application, design the classes"
question.
The conversation then moved toward Al, since I mentioned I'd completed a GenAl course with
Vizura and had built a small language model (SLM) on my own. This opened up a broader
discussion, the interviewer asked what RAG is, the difference between an LLM and an agent,
what an Al harness and guardrails are, and how agents retain context across a conversation. I
--- PAGE 3 ---
leaned on real-lite examples while explaining these, which the interviewer seemed to
appreciate.
When it was my turn to ask questions, I asked about growth opportunities for freshers at Wissen
and how they use Al internally, and got a thorough answer about the agents they've built and
how they're integrated. My advice here would be to genuinely show curiosity about the role and
the process during these conversations, it tends to come through positively.
Ultimately, I was offered an Internship + FTE.
